Players trade freely.
cons: A teammate may have no card to give.
One player's mistake can cost the whole table.

pairs.tendency: All players work towards one goal, and each question moves a card closer to where it is needed.
pros: The table has one aim.
Questions are open.
cons: Players with few cards get few asks.
One loud player can take over the asking.

pairs.tendency: Each player has a secret goal, so a question for a card can be read in two ways.
pros: Asking can hide a plan.
Players guess each other's goals from questions.
cons: A plain question can give you away.
A player who never asks stands out.

pairs.tendency: The game ends when the story does, and each card you ask for adds a scene to the tale.
pros: The cards carry the story.
Players share what happens next.
cons: A story can drag if the asks run on.
A tale may end before every player has had a turn.

pairs.tendency: Nobody wins or loses, so people ask for cards to see what happens, then look at the table at the end.
pros: Players ask out of curiosity.
The talk afterwards can be long.
cons: A game with no target can feel slack.
Players may stop asking when nothing is at stake.

pairs.tendency: Each player decides what doing well means, and their questions follow their own goal.
pros: Players ask for different things.
Nobody needs to beat another.
cons: Goals can clash with each other.
A player with no goal may not know what to ask.

pairs.tendency: Nobody wins, and the game goes on until one player is left with the card nobody wants, so you ask to pass it on.
pros: The last card matters.
Everyone else is simply safe.
cons: The loser is known only at the end.
Players avoid asking the one holding the unwanted card.

pairs.tendency: The aim is to keep playing, so each question is a way to give someone else something to do.
pros: Asking helps the game continue.
Players share the questions round.
cons: No end may come.
A game that never finishes can wear a table out.

pairs.tendency: The game is made so that nobody can win, and each question and answer shows what you expect from a game.
pros: Questions show what players expect a game to do.
Players talk about what they expected.
cons: Some players leave early.
Nobody knows when to stop asking.

pairs.tendency: You play alone against the cards, and the questions you ask are to the deck, which answers by turning a card.
pros: The pack answers the asks.
The table is cleared by degrees.
cons: A stuck layout ends the game.
There is no other player to learn from.

pairs.tendency: You play several short games in a row, and what you learned about a player's hand in one game helps in the next.
pros: Players carry their knowledge forward.
Short games make a long evening.
cons: A player who loses once can stop asking.
Tired players ask the same question every game.

pairs.tendency: Every point you pick up counts against you, so you ask others for cards of little value and hope they hand over the cheap ones.
pros: Low cards become the prize.
A rival can pass you a costly card.
cons: Asking for the wrong card adds points.
Players may refuse to answer.

pairs.tendency: You have to land exactly on the target, so you ask for the one card that makes the number come out right.
pros: Questions are about a number.
A near miss is easy to see.
cons: Going over costs you the win.
Players wait for a single card.

pairs.tendency: The aim is turned upside down, so players ask for cards they want to give away and avoid the ones they want to keep.
pros: Questions go the wrong way round.
Players keep an eye on their own hands.
cons: New players mix up what to ask for.
A winner is found only at the end.

pairs.tendency: Everyone plays at the same time on their own, so asking another player is the only time you affect them.
pros: The game is quiet until someone asks.
Each ask matters more.
cons: Players may forget to ask.
A player who builds alone never has to reply.

pairs.tendency: Players attack and steal on purpose, so a question for a card is a strike aimed at one rival.
pros: A target is clear.
A hit is felt at once.
cons: A player who is asked often feels singled out.
Rivals remember who asked them.

pairs.tendency: Players change the board and feel each other through it, so an ask is how one player reaches another directly.
pros: Asks break up the quiet.
Board and cards both matter.
cons: An ask comes as a surprise to a quiet table.
Players may not feel they are in the same game.

pairs.tendency: Everyone is on one team against the game, and each ask is a request for help.
pros: Asking is friendly.
Hands are shared in plain view.
cons: A loud player can run the table.
The game can win by itself if players are not careful.

pairs.tendency: Players mostly work together, but each has a private reason to win a bit more, so a question can have two meanings.
pros: Players help and tease each other.
A small secret changes each ask.
cons: A hidden aim can sink a team plan.
Trust is hard to read.

pairs.tendency: Two teams play against each other, and a teammate may ask for a card you hold, which you hand over freely.
pros: Teammates share cards without fuss.
Rival teams watch questions between partners.
cons: A clumsy question tells the other side your plan.
A team with one quiet player is easy to read.

pairs.tendency: Most players are on one team, but one is secretly against them, so a question may be a trap.
pros: Asks can hide a lie.
Players watch each other closely.
cons: A traitor can get cards by asking nicely.
Suspicion can stop all asking.

pairs.tendency: Players are far apart and send their questions by post or message, so an ask can wait days for an answer.
pros: The game can last a long time.
Each question is thought through.
cons: Waiting can last weeks.
A player who stops writing ends the game.

pairs.tendency: One player is not at the table, but a ghost can answer a question with a card on their behalf.
pros: A missing player still takes part.
A ghost gives hints.
cons: The table argues what the ghost would say.
The absent hand cannot ask back.

pairs.tendency: One player runs the world and answers when others ask for a card, deciding what is handed over.
pros: A single voice settles disputes.
Asking can open up the story.
cons: The game master carries a lot of the work.
A player may disagree with a ruling.

pairs.tendency: The game is played in a street or a market, and anyone passing may ask for a card or be asked.
pros: Strangers can join in.
Questions are called out loud.
cons: Crowds make it hard to hear.
People drift in and out and lose the thread.

pairs.tendency: One player faces all the others, and the others take turns asking each other for cards to plan against the lone player.
pros: The group can plan together.
The lone player gets more if they win.
cons: The lone player hears every ask.
The group can get in each other's way.

pairs.tendency: You play alone against the pack, so every ask is a draw from the deck and a yes is a lucky pull.
pros: Anyone can play at any time.
Results can be compared with a friend later.
cons: Nobody can answer back.
The game has no one to bluff.

pairs.tendency: Dice and draws decide most of what happens, so a question only changes who gets the lucky card.
pros: Anyone can win.
Games finish quickly.
cons: Asking has little power.
Players with careful plans can feel ignored.

pairs.tendency: Dice and draws decide a lot, but a question can mend a low draw by asking for the card you missed.
pros: A low draw does not end the game.
Asking is a repair.
cons: A repair only works if the other player has the card.
Players can ask for the same card again and again.

pairs.tendency: Your choices count most, and a bit of luck decides which cards others hold when you ask.
pros: Choices of who and what to ask pay off.
A little luck keeps each game new.
cons: A lucky draw can undo careful asking.
Players can plan too far ahead.

pairs.tendency: There is no luck, so asking is about memory and guessing from earlier questions.
pros: The smartest player tends to win.
Players learn from each question.
cons: New players can feel lost.
Games between mismatched players end early.

pairs.tendency: The cards are read as a message, so a question for a card is a way of asking the deck a question.
pros: A card is a sign to think about.
Players talk about what a card could mean.
cons: Readings can differ.
Nobody can add up the result.

pairs.tendency: You succeed by sensing when others will act, so you ask when you feel a player is about to give up a card.
pros: Players act together.
Friends often get it right.
cons: Strangers find it hard.
A wrong guess breaks the mood.

pairs.tendency: A roll is looked up on a table that says what happens, and a question for a card can be answered by that table.
pros: Dice add to the story.
The table surprises players.
cons: A roll can send the story off course.
Looking things up takes time.

pairs.tendency: Every card is visible, so asking for one is a way to move it, since nobody needs to learn what you hold.
pros: Nobody is surprised by a hand.
Players can plan far ahead.
cons: A question tells nothing new.
There is nothing to guess when you ask.

pairs.tendency: Each player holds cards nobody else can see, and every question is a guess about what is in someone's hand.
pros: Asks carry guesses and hints.
Players bluff by asking.
cons: A question gives away your hand.
A player with few cards is easy to read.

pairs.tendency: Some players have a secret role, and the cards they ask for may match it or hide it.
pros: Asks hide a role.
Players try to spot who is who.
cons: A strange question gives a spy away.
Players stop trusting what they hear.

pairs.tendency: You use clues to work out hidden facts, and each answer to your question is one more clue.
pros: Yes and no both tell you something.
The facts narrow as the game goes on.
cons: A question can waste a turn if it tells you nothing.
Notes pile up.

pairs.tendency: You lie about what you hold, and you can ask for a card you do not need to mislead the table.
pros: A false ask hides your real aim.
Players guess who is lying.
cons: A bluff that is caught costs you trust.
A wrong guess hurts a rival who was honest.

pairs.tendency: One player knows a secret rule, and others find it by asking and being told no.
pros: Each no teaches something.
Newcomers learn by trying.
cons: Players can feel they are being tested.
A question that breaks the rule loses a turn.

pairs.tendency: One player sees the answer and may only hint, so a question for a card gets a picture instead of a word.
pros: Hints stand in for speech.
Guessers think about the pictures.
cons: A hint can point the wrong way.
The one who knows has to wait while the others guess.

pairs.tendency: The map starts hidden and is turned over as players explore, and a card you ask for can show a new area.
pros: Exploring and asking go together.
The map surprises players.
cons: Nobody knows what lies ahead.
A card may reveal an area no one can reach.

pairs.tendency: One hand is spread face up while the others are secret, so a question for a card may be answered from the open hand.
pros: One hand is shared knowledge.
Players can check what they ask.
cons: Everyone sees what the open hand holds.
The open hand loses its secrets quickly.

pairs.tendency: Some points are kept secret, so you ask for cards to move your score without anyone knowing who is ahead.
pros: Nobody can add up the table for sure.
Questions work as a way to guess scores.
cons: A player can only guess who is winning.
A hidden lead is a surprise at the end.

pairs.tendency: One player acts at a time round the table, so everyone else listens to the questions and the answers.
pros: Players learn from each turn.
Each question is heard by all.
cons: Waiting is long with many players.
The last to ask gets what is left.

pairs.tendency: Everyone chooses in secret at once, so players write down who they ask and the answers come out together.
pros: Nobody waits for a turn.
Questions come out at the same time.
cons: A clash of two asks can stop both.
It is hard to see who asked what.

pairs.tendency: Anyone can ask at any moment, so the quickest voice gets the card.
pros: The table is loud and busy.
Reactions are fast.
cons: Slower players get left out.
Two asks can arrive at once.

pairs.tendency: Each turn has a clock, so you have a few seconds to pick a player and name a card.
pros: Turns stay short.
Players decide fast.
cons: A rushed ask can name the wrong card.
Time runs out on players who think slowly.

pairs.tendency: The game runs over real days, so you ask one question each morning and wait for the answer.
pros: The game fits into a week.
Each ask can be planned.
cons: Waiting is a big part of the game.
A forgotten turn can stall the table.

pairs.tendency: The game slows players down, so there is a pause before each ask and a breath before each answer.
pros: Questions are more careful.
A calm table is easy to join.
cons: A pause can feel long.
Quick players grow restless.

pairs.tendency: The game speeds up, so early asks are slow and late asks come in a rush.
pros: The end comes quickly.
Players feel the speed rise.
cons: Late asks can be sloppy.
A slow start can be forgotten.

pairs.tendency: A lucky throw gives you another go, so you can ask a second player straight away.
pros: A lucky player gets many asks.
Chains of turns can happen.
cons: Others wait through a long run.
A run of extra turns can empty a rival's hand.

pairs.tendency: The game comes in stages, so you pick cards in the first stage by asking, then play with them in the second.
pros: The first stage sets up the second.
Asking has a long-term reason.
cons: A hand picked early can turn out useless.
Rules change at the switch and trip up newcomers.

pairs.tendency: The board works like a real system, such as a market, and asking for a card stands in for a trade.
pros: Asks look like real trades.
Players see how a market moves.
cons: The model can be hard to follow.
A trade can have effects nobody planned.

pairs.tendency: Each player acts as a real group, such as farmers or a village council, and each ask is made from that group's need.
pros: Asks come from a role.
Players see the problem from another side.
cons: A player may ask for what their role needs, even when they want something else.
A role with few cards gets few answers.

pairs.tendency: Everyone draws from one limited store, and a question can ask a player to give up some of theirs for the group.
pros: One store feeds the whole table.
Players see when the store is running low.
cons: A greedy ask can empty it.
Players get cautious about asking.

pairs.tendency: What you do now shows up a few rounds later, so a card you ask for today may only matter in round five.
pros: Early asks have a late result.
Players plan ahead.
cons: The link between ask and result is hard to see.
A card may come too late to help.

pairs.tendency: Players agree a new rule for everyone, then play on to see how it changes the asking.
pros: A rule can be tested safely.
The table sees the result.
cons: A new rule can confuse the table.
Players may not agree on the result.

pairs.tendency: After the game, everyone talks through which questions they asked and what they learned.
pros: Players look back at their asks.
The talk can link the game to real life.
cons: It adds time at the end.
Quiet players may say little.

pairs.tendency: What you do changes the game for ever, so a card you ask for may be torn up or marked.
pros: Each ask leaves a mark.
The next game starts where this one ended.
cons: Nothing can be undone.
Players hold back from asking for a rare card.

pairs.tendency: The rules make a point about the world, and the cards you ask for show what the game values.
pros: The rules say something.
Players can talk about what the game claims.
cons: The point can be missed.
Players may disagree with it.

pairs.tendency: What happens in the game carries into real life, so an ask for a card can cost a real favour.
pros: The game feels real.
Friends see how they treat each other.
cons: A hard ask can strain a friendship.
A lost card can leave a real debt.

pairs.tendency: Points stand for something that matters, like kindness, and players ask for cards that raise the number.
pros: The score shows what the game values.
Players talk about what the numbers mean.
cons: Players chase points over the thing itself.
A number can replace the idea.

pairs.tendency: Players practise a way of living that does not exist yet, and they ask each other for cards to make it work.
pros: Asking works as a way to share.
Players feel how a future might be.
cons: The future is hard to picture at first.
Players may not take it seriously.

pairs.tendency: Each throw of the dice moves a pawn along the track, and the other players bet against the bank on where it will stop. The bank pays at set odds when a guess is right.
pros: Every throw has bets riding on it.
Everyone watches the dice, whoever's pawn is moving.
cons: The bank's turn takes longer than the rest.
Bets can pile up faster than the pawns move.

pairs.tendency: Cards are picked one at a time from a shared row, and the bank offers odds on which card goes next. Once the pick is made, the bank pays the winning guesses.
pros: Picks become something to bet on.
Players read what the others want.
cons: The bank has to track many guesses at once.
A pick made only to win a bet can leave a hand with gaps.

pairs.tendency: The bank sells an item to whoever offers the most, and side bets on the winning offer are paid at fixed odds. Two kinds of money change hands in the same round.
pros: Offers carry a second risk.
A player can win money without winning the item.
cons: Two sets of money to keep track of.
Rounds run long.

pairs.tendency: One player keeps taking risks for points while the others bet against the bank on when they will stop. When that player goes bust, the bank collects every bet on stopping.
pros: Everyone watches one player's nerve.
The bank can be paid at any moment.
cons: Most bets are lost to the same bust.
The risk-taker plays with an audience.

pairs.tendency: Players hold spots on a map, and the others bet against the bank on who will hold the most spots at the end. The bank pays out when the map is counted.
pros: Bets give a reason to watch a map you have no pieces on.
Players can back a rival's rise.
cons: Bets placed early can hold up the board for a long time.
Players with pieces on the map can nudge the result.

pairs.tendency: Workers take jobs on the board, and bets against the bank are placed on which job will be taken first. Jobs that many people want are the ones most bets name.
pros: Job choices are watched closely.
Bets show which job players think matters.
cons: Each placement is slowed by the betting round.
Bets on one job can draw players away from it.

pairs.tendency: Players lay colours and shapes into patterns, and others bet against the bank on which pattern finishes first. The bank pays at set odds as each row fills.
pros: Half-built patterns draw attention.
Odds change as a pattern grows.
cons: The bank stops to work out odds each turn.
A nearly finished pattern attracts all the bets.

pairs.tendency: Each player holds a hand and picks when to play each card. Others bet against the bank on which card comes down next.
pros: Cards held back become secrets worth guessing.
Players study each other's habits.
cons: The bank deals with every guess.
A hand played to fool the bettors can cost the player a turn.

pairs.tendency: Each round of cards makes a trick, and anyone may bet with the bank on who wins it. The trick is played, then the winning bets are paid at fixed odds.
pros: Every trick has a small bet inside it.
Players have a reason to watch cards they do not hold.
cons: The bank is kept busy through a whole hand.
A player who leads often can be bet on again and again.

pairs.tendency: Players make deals with each other while the bank offers fixed odds on the outcome. A deal that changes the odds has to be struck before the bank throws.
pros: Deals have a price in the bank's odds.
Players learn who is sure of themselves.
cons: Talk can go on while the bank waits.
A promise made to win a bet may be broken later.

pairs.tendency: Players gather sets of matching things, and others bet against the bank on whose set will fill first. Each missing piece changes how the bank sees the odds.
pros: A set on the table is also a bet.
Players watch each other's piles.
cons: Counting who is close takes time.
A player one piece short collects the glances.

pairs.tendency: Tiles join up into a shared map, and bets go to the bank on what the next tile will build. A road or a field gets named before the tile is turned.
pros: Every tile draw has a guess attached.
The map becomes something to read ahead.
cons: Turns slow down while bets are made.
A bank that can see much of the pile can read the odds too easily.

pairs.tendency: One player says a line and the next answers it, while the bank offers odds on how long the chain will last. When the chain breaks, the bank pays.
pros: A chain is watched for its loosest link.
Players listen to each other closely.
cons: The bank listens to every answer.
A quick answer can end the chain on purpose.

pairs.tendency: Nobody may talk, so the bank's bets are placed by pushing coins forward and the throw is made without a word. Winners are paid in the same silence.
pros: Bets have to be read from the coins.
Players follow each other's hands.
cons: Odds cannot be explained out loud.
A mistaken bet is hard to put right.

pairs.tendency: On a turn a player may change a rule, and that includes the odds the bank pays. Bets placed earlier may be paid under a rule that no longer stands.
pros: The odds themselves can be played with.
The bank can be challenged.
cons: Players argue over what an old bet is worth.
The bank's role can be changed away.

pairs.tendency: Each player speaks as a character at a gambling table, and the bank is one more part to play. Bets are placed as the character would place them.
pros: Betting becomes a way to show who a character is.
The bank can have a voice of its own.
cons: Staying in character slows the throw.
A character who always bets the same way can be easy to guess.

pairs.tendency: The bank flicks, stacks or throws something, and the others bet on whether it will land. A shaky hand changes what the odds ought to be.
pros: The bank's hand is watched.
Bets can go on a steady finger.
cons: Nerves can change the throw.
The bank cannot pass the task to anyone else.

pairs.tendency: The map is drawn as play goes on, and the bank takes bets on what will be drawn next. A new road or river is paid for as soon as it appears.
pros: The map has something to guess about.
Whoever draws holds a secret for a moment.
cons: Drawing pauses the betting.
The drawer can steer the bets by what they draw.

pairs.tendency: Players put money on a throw while the bank throws and pays at fixed odds. The money and the odds sit on the table together.
pros: The rules are quick to teach.
The bank adds a rotating role to the plain bet.
cons: Much of the game depends on luck.
The bank keeps track of each player's stake.

pairs.tendency: Hidden hands are held while chips go in the pot, and the bank sits outside the pot with separate bets on who will win it. A bank bet can be placed before any hand is shown.
pros: A bet can be made without holding a hand.
A player can read the table to place a bet.
cons: The bank is far from the game being played.
Players with high hands cannot always say so.

pairs.tendency: Each player picks a side before play, and the bank prices each side's chance of winning. Odds follow what each side is made of.
pros: Choosing a side is also a signal.
Odds give a quick idea of each side's size.
cons: Players with a plain side may be left out of the bets.
Pricing sides takes time.

pairs.tendency: Before play, a player says what they will do, and the bank takes bets on whether they will manage it. A claim of three tricks has odds attached.
pros: Every claim can be backed or doubted.
A bold call draws bets.
cons: Each call needs its own price.
A player who loses a contract can lose a bet too.

pairs.tendency: A captured piece changes sides, and bets with the bank name who will hold the most pieces after each turn. A lead can swing in a single move, so the odds swing too.
pros: Odds change after each capture.
Players keep watching a board that keeps moving.
cons: The odds are worked out again and again.
A late capture can wipe out many bets.

pairs.tendency: A player in jail waits for a teammate, and the bank takes bets on whether the rescue will work. The jailbreak is the moment the bank pays out.
pros: Rescues turn into a gamble.
The jailed player has something to watch.
cons: The bank needs a clear rule for when a rescue counts.
Waiting in jail can last through many bets.

pairs.tendency: Pieces close in around one another, and the bank takes bets on which piece will be taken next. A piece with one gap left is the one most bets name.
pros: A tight board can be read for odds.
A single gap draws all eyes.
cons: The bank judges which piece is closest.
A move that opens a gap can change every bet.

pairs.tendency: A player who is behind gets a way to jump ahead, and the bank adjusts the odds to match. Backing a trailing player can pay more.
pros: Bets on the person behind pay well.
A lead is not settled until late.
cons: Odds move often.
A player can lose on purpose to collect a catch-up.

pairs.tendency: The dice or cards decide everything, and the bank pays winners at fixed odds. There is nothing to choose except how much to bet.
pros: The rules take almost no time to learn.
Players can stay relaxed.
cons: Turns do not ask for much thought.
Nothing a player does changes the outcome.

pairs.tendency: One player is It and chases the rest, while the bank offers odds on who is caught next. When a tag happens, the bank pays out on the new It.
pros: A chase becomes something to watch.
The runners can lay bets on each other.
cons: The bank follows a game that keeps moving.
A runner can be caught more often when many bets name them.

pairs.tendency: On a turn a player picks who is hit, helped or traded with, and the bank takes bets on who will be chosen. Players can pick a name just to spoil a bet.
pros: Choosing becomes a public act.
Odds show who players expect to be targeted.
cons: A bet can change a choice.
Picks can be made to annoy a bettor.

pairs.tendency: Two sides try to link up across the board, and players bet with the bank on who completes a chain first. A gap in a chain changes the odds at once.
pros: A chain can be read at a glance.
The board shows which side is nearer.
cons: Bets slow a game that is meant to be quiet.
A single cut can undo a long chain and many bets.

pairs.tendency: Every choice beats one other choice and loses to a third, and the bank sets even odds on each. No choice wins every time, so no bet is safe.
pros: Odds are easy to set.
Players watch for each other's habits.
cons: Bets even out over many rounds.
A player on a hunch can beat a careful one.

pairs.tendency: A player shows a pair or a run they hold to score points, and the bank offers odds on which combinations get declared. A declaration reveals a little of the hand.
pros: Showing a pair gives away a clue.
Bets reward careful watching.
cons: A hand shown can be a hand beaten.
The bank keeps a record of declared cards.

pairs.tendency: Each player has a power nobody else has, and the bank's odds depend on whose power is used. A player with a rare power is priced differently from one with a plain power.
pros: Odds can be set for each player.
Players study each other's powers.
cons: Each person carries a different price to remember.
A power used only to win a bet can feel out of place.

pairs.tendency: A player may offer to double what the game is worth, and the bank can double its odds too. The other player either accepts or gives up the points already at stake.
pros: Large wins and large losses sit close.
A double is a message about the hand.
cons: Money piles up quickly.
A player can be forced to quit by a double.

pairs.tendency: A player who can capture has to, and the bank takes bets on which capture will be forced. Players can set up a position so the forced move is easy to guess.
pros: Moves can be read in advance.
A forced move gives the bank a sure bet to price.
cons: The odds can be near certain.
A bet on a forced move offers little reward.

pairs.tendency: A character gets more power as play goes on, and the bank sets odds on who will be able to beat a later challenge. A character who has grown is priced differently from one who has not.
pros: Odds follow how far each character has grown.
Early choices feed later bets.
cons: The bank keeps a record of every character.
A character who has grown can pull most of the bets.

pairs.tendency: Each player repeats the list so far and adds one item, and bets go to the bank on who will break the chain. Every turn the list gets longer and the odds change.
pros: Bets can be placed on a memory.
The group joins in with a long list.
cons: Betting adds to the number of things to remember.
A long list can end the game early.

pairs.tendency: A more skilled player starts with less, and the bank sets odds to match the head start. A bet on the player with the handicap pays less or more depending on the gap.
pros: The bank has a reason to price both players.
The handicap makes bets less obvious.
cons: Judging the gap falls to the bank.
A handicap set wrongly will show up in the bets.

pairs.tendency: One player hides while the others hunt, and the bank takes bets on how long the hunt will last. When the hider is found, the bank pays on the time.
pros: A hunt turns into a countdown.
The hider can listen for the bets.
cons: The game ends once the hider is found.
The hider can be tempted to give clues.

pairs.tendency: A piece hops over another into the space behind it, and the bank offers odds on the next jump. A line of pieces with empty spaces behind is where bets are placed.
pros: Jumps are easy to see coming.
A gap in a line shows a likely move.
cons: Long chains of jumps are hard to price.
One jump can set off several more.

pairs.tendency: A player keeps some dice and rolls the rest, and the bank takes bets on the final hand. After each reroll the odds shift.
pros: Every reroll changes the odds.
Players choose which dice to keep and bet on the result.
cons: Rerolls give the bank many jobs.
A hand close to done pulls in the bets.

pairs.tendency: A piece that lands on another sends it back to the start, and the bank takes bets on where each piece will land. A safe space is where the bank pays the least.
pros: Landing spots are worth reading.
Safe spaces make the bank's job simpler.
cons: One landing can undo a long run.
Bets on a piece close to home may never pay.

pairs.tendency: Three in a row lets a player remove an enemy piece, and bets with the bank name who forms the next row. A board with two pieces in line is where the bets gather.
pros: Near-rows draw bets.
A row is a clear thing to bet on.
cons: Rows are made and broken often.
Bets on one row can be spoiled by a single move.

pairs.tendency: Letters are built into words, and the bank takes bets on which word will be played next. A dictionary settles any argument over whether a word is real.
pros: Words can be guessed at.
Players use what they know of language.
cons: Players argue over spellings.
The bank cannot price a letter it has not seen.

pairs.tendency: A tile can be added only if its number matches the end of the line, and the bank offers odds on the next number called. When no match exists the player misses a turn.
pros: The ends of the line show what is likely.
A missed turn can be bet on.
cons: The bank needs to know which tiles are out.
A player who holds the missing number holds the secret.

pairs.tendency: Finished sets are laid face up, and the bank takes bets on who will meld next. Other players can add cards to a set already down.
pros: A meld shows what a player holds.
Others can build on it.
cons: Bets on melding depend on cards no one sees.
A set open on the table can be added to by anyone.

pairs.tendency: Each piece has a power that works once, and the bank offers odds on when it will be used. Once the marker is taken away, the bank pays on that bet.
pros: Waiting for a power to be used builds suspense for bettors.
Players can bluff by holding a power back.
cons: Bets on timing are hard to price.
A power used early can disappoint everyone who bet on it.

pairs.tendency: A player offers a move and the other player may refuse it, while the bank takes bets on which way the answer will go. A turn down is paid out like any other result.
pros: Moves become offers.
The refusal is also a bet.
cons: Turns take longer.
A player who always refuses is easy to bet against.

pairs.tendency: A message passes along the table, and the bank takes bets on how much it will change. When it arrives, the bank pays on the result.
pros: The message is something to bet on.
Players listen closely.
cons: The bank cannot check the message on the way.
The last player may be told what bets were made.

pairs.tendency: Players choose cards and hand them to another player before play, and side bets with the bank guess what will be passed. A high hand and a low hand are only known once cards are received.
pros: The pass is a secret worth betting on.
Players guess at each other's choices.
cons: Nothing pays until the cards have changed hands.
A pass made to confuse the bettors may cost the player a hand.

pairs.tendency: One player sets up and the other chooses a side, and the bank takes bets on which side will be picked. The setup is judged before the bets close.
pros: The setter is watched closely.
Odds show how even the split looks.
cons: Bets can only be placed after the setup.
The chooser can pick the side most bets named.

pairs.tendency: A piece that reaches the far end turns into a more powerful piece, and the bank offers odds on which piece gets there. A pawn near the end draws more bets than one at the back.
pros: A piece near the end is closely watched.
Promotion gives the bank a clear moment to pay.
cons: Pieces in the back go unnoticed.
A block in front of the pawn can undo many bets.

pairs.tendency: Teams run a race in legs, and the bank takes bets on which team will win each leg. A handover is the moment the odds change.
pros: Each leg is its own bet.
The crowd can follow a team.
cons: One race means several payouts.
A dropped baton can undo many bets.

pairs.tendency: Stones in a safe shape cannot be taken, and players bet with the bank on who builds one first. A stone close to a safe shape is where the bets go.
pros: A shape is easy to point at.
Players have a goal to watch.
cons: The bank judges how near a shape is.
The other player can break a shape before it is whole.

pairs.tendency: Winning tricks is only the way to reach named prize cards, and the bank takes bets on who will take each prize. A single card can win more than one prize.
pros: Prizes can be bet on one by one.
A trick has more than one thing riding on it.
cons: The bank has several bets for each trick.
A card that wins two prizes can pay out twice.

pairs.tendency: Cards in the middle are open to all, and the bank offers odds on which hand makes the most of them. Each new card changes what the bank thinks.
pros: Open cards give everyone something to read.
Bets can follow the table cards.
cons: Each reveal changes the bets.
A card that helps nobody leaves the bank with an easy round.

pairs.tendency: Everyone puts a counter into the middle, and the bank takes bets on who will win it. If nobody wins, the pot grows and so do the bets.
pros: A growing pot draws bigger bets.
Each round is worth more than the last.
cons: The bank can owe a lot at once.
A pot that never gets won can wear a table out.

pairs.tendency: Seeds are scooped from one pit and dropped round the others, and bets go to the bank on where the last seed lands. A player who counts well can see the answer before the bank does.
pros: Counting seeds becomes a skill worth backing.
Players watch each other's pits.
cons: A bet can be settled by counting.
A mistake in counting spoils the round.

pairs.tendency: An extra hand lies face down in the middle, and the bank takes bets on who will take it. A player who buys the spare hand may pay with their bet.
pros: The spare hand is a prize.
Choosing to take it says something about the player's own hand.
cons: Nobody has seen the hand the bank is pricing.
Players who skip it may lose out.

pairs.tendency: Some spaces keep a piece safe and others send it back, and the bank sets odds by the square a piece is about to reach. A piece two squares from a trap is priced differently.
pros: Squares carry their own odds.
Players can read the track.
cons: Every special square is one more thing for the bank to remember.
A trap can cancel a long run of bets.

pairs.tendency: Every card, unit or item has a price, and the bank offers odds on what players will buy. The cost of a card is the clue the bank uses to guess the buy.
pros: Prices give a clue to the bank.
Players weigh what to spend.
cons: Money moves in two places at once.
A player short of money can be left out of the bets.

pairs.tendency: A fixed amount is shared between several places, and the bank takes bets on where the most will go. The split is shown only when all players reveal.
pros: A split is a secret worth guessing.
Players can read each other's habits.
cons: Bets wait for the reveal.
A player who bluffs the split can fool the bank.

pairs.tendency: Everyone moves until the music stops, and bets with the bank name who will be caught. The signal comes without warning and the bank pays on the slowest player.
pros: The signal is the moment of the bet.
The whole group is watched.
cons: The bank cannot see every player at once.
Players can slow down on purpose to change the result.

pairs.tendency: Players put cards back and draw new ones, and the bank offers odds on how many cards are swapped. A big swap hints at a low hand.
pros: The number of swaps tells a story.
Bets can follow the swap.
cons: The bank counts every swap.
A player may swap just to hide a high hand.

pairs.tendency: Thrown cards go in one pile, and a player may take it all if they can use the top card. The bank takes bets on who will pick it up.
pros: A big pile pulls bets.
Taking the pile is a clear moment to pay on.
cons: The bank is left guessing who has the right card.
A player holding a useful card can wait for a larger pile.

pairs.tendency: One suit beats the others, and the bank takes bets on who holds the most trumps. A low trump can win against a high card of another suit.
pros: The trump suit gives the bank a way to set odds.
Players count trumps as they fall.
cons: Bets can be wrong because of one low trump.
Hands without trumps are priced low.

pairs.tendency: A player plays both sides on two boards, and the bank offers odds on which board ends first. Moves made on one board change the bets on the other.
pros: Two boards give two lots of bets.
A player attacks and defends at once.
cons: The bank needs to keep track of both boards.
A bet can be lost on a board that nobody was watching.

pairs.tendency: A wild card can stand for any other card, and bets with the bank name who holds one. A set that looks one short may only be waiting for a wild card.
pros: A hidden wild card makes the odds harder to read.
Players guess what a rival is holding.
cons: Odds change with every wild card drawn.
One wild card can finish many sets at once.

pairs.tendency: A line that leaves one edge comes back on the other, and the bank takes bets on where a piece will reappear. A piece near the edge can show up on the far side.
pros: The board loses its edges.
Players have to rethink where pieces are.
cons: Edge bets are harder to price.
Newcomers lose track of a piece that has gone round.

pairs.tendency: One player has a secret and the others ask yes or no questions, and the bank takes bets on how many questions it will take. Each answer shrinks the list, so the odds shift.
pros: Every question narrows the field.
Players compare their guesses.
cons: The bank follows each answer.
A sharp question can shorten the game and end bets early.

pairs.tendency: The first to the end wins, and the bank prices each runner's chance of getting there first. The runner at the front draws the shortest odds.
pros: Everyone can see who is in front.
Bets shift each time the lead changes.
cons: The bank pays out on a single result.
A runner far behind may not draw any bets at all.

pairs.tendency: Points are counted at the end, and players bet with the bank on who will have the most. The score is the bank's guide to the odds.
pros: Scores give a clear base for odds.
Players can back the leader or a rival.
cons: Bets have to wait for the final count.
A late jump in points can undo early bets.

pairs.tendency: Players are knocked out one by one, and the bank takes bets on who will be next to leave. The last one standing wins the largest bet.
pros: Each exit is a payout.
Players who are out can still bet.
cons: A knocked-out player has nothing to do but bet.
The bank can owe many small bets at the end.

pairs.tendency: All players win or lose together, so the bank takes bets on whether the group will last. Players bet against their own team or for it.
pros: A shared fate can be bet on.
Players can show their faith in the team.
cons: Betting against the team can feel odd.
A player could bet on a loss and help it happen.

pairs.tendency: All players work for one goal, and the bank offers odds on the goal being reached. If it is, the bank pays those who backed the team.
pros: The goal has a price.
Doubters and believers can sit side by side.
cons: The bank pays on one result only.
Bets against the goal pull against the team.

pairs.tendency: Each player has a secret goal, and the bank takes bets on which goal a player has. A bet that names the goal gives away a guess.
pros: Guesses about goals are bets in themselves.
Players watch each other's moves for clues.
cons: A bet may tip off the player being guessed at.
The goal-holder can play to mislead the bettors.

pairs.tendency: The game goes on until the story ends, and players bet with the bank on how it ends. A happy ending and a tragic one carry different odds.
pros: Players guess at the end of the story.
Odds follow the mood of the story.
cons: The bank cannot know the ending until it comes.
A player can steer the story toward a bet.

pairs.tendency: Nobody wins, so the bank has nothing to pay, and the bets turn into guesses about what will happen. The table talks about what was made after.
pros: Bets become a way to talk about what might happen.
Nothing is lost at the end.
cons: The bank has no result to settle on.
Bets with no payout may be dropped.

pairs.tendency: Each player decides what doing well means, and the bank takes bets on whether they will reach it. One player may aim to save a single piece and another every piece.
pros: Goals are priced one by one.
Players state their aims out loud.
cons: The bank sets different odds for each player.
A player can pick an easy goal to win a bet.

pairs.tendency: The game goes on until one player loses, and the bank offers odds on who it will be. Everyone else is simply safe.
pros: The loser is the focus of the bets.
Players can bet against themselves for safety.
cons: Only one bet pays at the end.
The player named by most bets may be teased.

pairs.tendency: The aim is to keep playing, so the bank is paid with turns, not a final result. Bets are settled round by round, and the game can run for years.
pros: The bank has a lasting role.
Bets are settled often.
cons: There is no last count.
The bank may be stuck holding the same role.

pairs.tendency: Nobody can win, so a bet against the bank can only be on how the game refuses a result. The bank pays out on whatever the game does instead.
pros: Bets are about how the game behaves.
Players learn what the game does.
cons: The bank cannot set odds in the usual way.
Bets may never be settled.

pairs.tendency: One player plays alone against the cards, and others bet against the bank on whether they will clear the table. The game says lost if the player gets stuck.
pros: The onlookers have a stake in a solo game.
The player is watched closely.
cons: The lone player may feel pressure from the bets.
The bank waits on a long solo run.

pairs.tendency: Several short games are played, and the bank takes bets on each one and on the final tally. After two wins from three, the bank can close the bets.
pros: Bets can be placed again after each game.
A comeback changes the odds.
cons: The bank has a lot of bets to settle.
Bets on a game already decided can be wasted.

pairs.tendency: The player with the fewest points wins, and bets with the bank name who will pick up the least. Players avoid points while the bettors back the ones doing so.
pros: A low score is easy to name as a bet.
Players try to stay clear.
cons: The bank turns its usual idea of a leader upside down.
Players may take points on purpose to confuse bets.

pairs.tendency: A player has to land exactly on the target, and the bank takes bets on who will hit it. Going past it costs the win.
pros: The final step is something to bet on.
Close players are watched.
cons: Near misses need pricing too.
A player can be stuck waiting for the exact number.

pairs.tendency: The aim is turned upside down, so the player who gives everything away wins and the bank pays out on that. Bets on the one in the lead are really bets on the one losing.
pros: The usual odds are reversed.
Players need to think the other way round.
cons: The bank can slip into the old way of pricing.
New players may bet on the wrong side.

pairs.tendency: Everyone plays their own game side by side, and the bank offers odds on whose game finishes first. Each player has their own odds.
pros: Bets are the only link between the players.
Each player is priced one by one.
cons: Players hardly affect each other except through bets.
The bank has more to watch than there is to see.

pairs.tendency: Players attack each other on purpose, and the bank takes bets on who will win each clash. A target can find that others are betting on its loss.
pros: Each fight has its own bet.
Players can see who is likely to be hit.
cons: A player under attack also carries the bets.
A grudge can grow from a bet.

pairs.tendency: Players change the board and never attack each other, and the bank offers odds on what the board will look like. Players feel one another's moves through the board.
pros: The board is what the bets are about.
Bets stay calm because nobody is attacked.
cons: A bet on the board may miss a quiet change.
The bank cannot see who is to blame.

pairs.tendency: Players are on one team against the game, and the bank takes bets on whether the team will win. The bank is the only outsider.
pros: The bank plays against the whole team.
The group can lay a bet on itself.
cons: The odds depend on a single result.
A team that is sure of itself leaves the bank little to price.

pairs.tendency: Players mostly work together, with a small private reason to win more, and the bank offers odds on who gains most. A cooperating player may also be a quiet rival.
pros: Bets can name the rival.
The group watches for those who bend the team plan.
cons: Trust gets tested by the bets.
A player may sink the team to win a bet.

pairs.tendency: Two teams play each other, and the bank takes bets on which team will win. Teammates can bet together or against each other.
pros: Teams have a reason to cheer.
Bets split the table in two.
cons: A team member who bets on the other side causes trouble.
Odds depend on the size of each team.

pairs.tendency: Most players are on one team and one is secretly against them, and players bet with the bank on who the traitor is. A wrong guess costs the bettor.
pros: Suspicion has a price.
Players watch each other for slips.
cons: The traitor knows who is accused.
A bet can give the traitor cover.

pairs.tendency: Players are far apart and send their turns by letter, and the bank sends back results by post. Bets take as long as the game to pay.
pros: A game can last weeks.
Waiting for a result is part of the play.
cons: Money moves slowly.
A lost letter can leave a bet unsettled.

pairs.tendency: One player is not at the table, and the bank takes bets on what that absent player would do. The absent player's moves come from a ghost or an old record.
pros: An empty chair can be bet on.
Players guess at someone who is not there.
cons: The bank cannot ask the absent player.
The ghost can win bets without being in the room.

pairs.tendency: One player runs the world for the others, and the bank can be that player or a separate one. Bets can be on what the game master will describe next.
pros: The game master's choices become guessing games.
The bank can add dice rolls to a story.
cons: The game master has two jobs at once.
Bets can pull the story off course.

pairs.tendency: The game is played in a street or market, and passers-by can join the bets. The bank may be a shopkeeper or a child.
pros: Anyone can add a bet.
Onlookers become players.
cons: A crowd is a lot for the bank to handle.
A new face may not know the odds.

pairs.tendency: One player takes on all the others, and the bank offers odds on who will win. The lone player is paid more if they win, so the odds already lean to the many.
pros: A single player has high odds.
The group stands together.
cons: The bank sets odds that favour one side.
The lone player can be tempted to bet on losing.

pairs.tendency: A player plays alone against the pack, and the bank takes bets from friends watching. Nobody else acts, so luck and the player's choices decide the result.
pros: Friends can place a bet on a solo game.
The player is cheered on.
cons: Only one result to pay on.
The player may feel watched.

pairs.tendency: The dice and draws decide most things, and the bank pays at fixed odds. Skill barely matters, so bets are close to pure luck.
pros: Odds can be exact.
A new player is on equal terms.
cons: Bets cannot be improved by thinking.
A losing streak is just a streak.

pairs.tendency: Dice rule the game but players have rerolls, cards or choices to soften a low throw, and the bank sets odds with these in mind. A player with a spare reroll is priced differently.
pros: Odds reflect what a player holds.
Players can fight back against a low roll.
cons: The bank has more to weigh.
A spent reroll changes the bet.

pairs.tendency: Choices matter most, with a small touch of luck, and the bank sets odds on who plays most skilfully. A skilled player draws shorter odds.
pros: Odds can follow skill.
A lucky throw still matters.
cons: Skill is for the bank to judge.
A player can hide their skill to collect higher odds.

pairs.tendency: There are no dice, so the bank can only take bets on who is the cleverer player. The result is read from the moves.
pros: Odds follow what the players have shown.
Bets are about the players alone.
cons: A new player has no record to price.
The bank cannot set fixed odds with confidence.

pairs.tendency: Dice are read as a message, and the bank takes bets on what the sign will say. A throw is read for meaning and never added up.
pros: The sign gives players something to think about.
The reading is shared.
cons: The bank cannot pay out on a meaning.
Players may argue about what the sign says.

pairs.tendency: Players succeed by sensing when the others will act, and the bank offers odds on who will move together. A group that is in step gets the shortest odds.
pros: Friends who know each other draw short odds.
Players watch for small signs.
cons: Odds are hard to write down.
A new player is out of step.

pairs.tendency: A roll is looked up on a table that says what happens next, and the bank takes bets on which entry will come up. Each line on the table has its own odds.
pros: The table doubles as an odds chart.
The story gets a touch of luck.
cons: Pricing means reading the whole table.
A rare entry may never come up.

pairs.tendency: Everything is visible, so the bank has nothing to hide, and the odds come from what all can see. Bets are about skill.
pros: The bank and players see the same board.
Odds are open.
cons: Nobody has a secret to bet on.
Clever players can work out each bet.

pairs.tendency: Each player holds cards nobody else can see, and the bank takes bets on whose hand ranks highest. The bank itself may not see them either.
pros: Hidden cards make bets worth making.
Players bluff the bettors.
cons: The bank prices what it cannot see.
A bet can reveal a hand.

pairs.tendency: Some players have a secret role, and the bank offers odds on who is who. A bet on a role shows a guess.
pros: Guessing a role is a bet.
Players watch for slips.
cons: A bet can warn the person it names.
The bank keeps a list of who bet on whom.

pairs.tendency: Clues point to hidden facts, and the bank takes bets on the answer. Each clue changes the odds.
pros: Clues become price changes.
Players reason aloud.
cons: Early bets pay most and late bets pay least.
A clue that points the wrong way can mislead the bettors.

pairs.tendency: A player lies about what they hold, and players bet with the bank on whether the lie works. A raised bet may be a bluff or a true claim.
pros: Bets can be a way to bluff.
Players read faces and voices.
cons: The bank cannot tell who is lying.
A bluff can win more than the real hand.

pairs.tendency: One player knows a secret rule and the rest find it by breaking it, and the bank takes bets on who will find it first. Each mistake is told no.
pros: Learning is something to bet on.
Newcomers can be priced longer.
cons: The bank has to know the rule.
A player who guesses right early ends the bets.

pairs.tendency: One player knows the answer but can only give hints, and the bank offers odds on the guessers getting it. The hint-giver watches the bets come in.
pros: Hints become price changes.
The group works together on the guess.
cons: The hint-giver may feel the bets.
The bank cannot judge a hint that is unclear.

pairs.tendency: The map starts hidden and is turned over as players explore, and the bank takes bets on what lies ahead. A tile turned over decides every bet on it.
pros: Each tile is a small reveal.
Players explore and bet together.
cons: Bets wait on the turn of a tile.
The first to explore may pay for others.

pairs.tendency: One hand is laid face up for all to see, and bets with the bank are placed on how it will be played. The open cards give bettors something to study.
pros: An open hand can be read.
Bets can be more exact.
cons: The bank has less to hide.
A player may be bet against as soon as the hand is open.

pairs.tendency: Some points are kept secret, and the bank takes bets on who is ahead. Nobody can add up the scores for sure.
pros: Bets are made on a guess.
Players watch each other's behaviour.
cons: The bank holds information others do not.
The bank may be asked to reveal a score.

pairs.tendency: One player acts at a time, and the bank takes bets between turns. The bank throws once per player.
pros: Rules are easy to follow.
Everyone has time to think.
cons: Others wait through each turn.
A big table makes the bank's turn rare.

pairs.tendency: Everyone chooses in secret and reveals together, and the bank takes bets on the reveal. The bank pays all winners at once.
pros: No one waits.
The reveal is a shared moment.
cons: The bank has many bets to pay at one time.
A late bet is hard to place.

pairs.tendency: There are no turns, so anyone may act at any moment, and the bank takes bets whenever they come. The fastest hand gets there first.
pros: The table is always busy.
Quick players are favoured.
cons: The bank cannot keep up.
Slow players may never get a bet in.

pairs.tendency: Each turn runs against a clock, and the bank offers odds on whether the move comes in time. When the time runs out the move is lost.
pros: The clock becomes part of the bet.
Players hurry.
cons: The bank has a clock to watch.
A rushed move can lose a bet.

pairs.tendency: The game runs on real days, and the bank takes bets each morning. A player makes one move a day and the bank pays out when the days are done.
pros: Bets can be left to settle over time.
Waiting is part of the game.
cons: Bets placed days ago have to be remembered.
A bet can be forgotten.

pairs.tendency: The game slows players on purpose, and the bank takes bets in the pauses. A breath before each move gives time to think about the odds.
pros: There is time to weigh a bet.
The pace calms the table.
cons: Bets are slow to settle.
Players may lose track of what was bet.

pairs.tendency: The game speeds up as it goes, and the bank has less time to take bets. At the end everything comes in a rush.
pros: Bets get quicker.
The finish comes as a rush for everyone.
cons: The bank falls behind.
Late bets can be missed.

pairs.tendency: A lucky throw gives another go at once, and the bank takes bets on how many turns a player will get. A player on a run draws the bets.
pros: A run is something to watch.
Luck can pile up for one player.
cons: One player can keep collecting from the bank.
Other players wait a long time.

pairs.tendency: The game comes in stages with different rules, and the bank takes bets at each stage. What happens in the first stage sets up the second.
pros: Bets can change with the stage.
An early lead can be priced for later.
cons: Each stage's rules are new to the bank too.
A new stage can undo old bets.

pairs.tendency: The board works like a real system, and the bank takes bets on how it will move. A move has the effect it would have in real life.
pros: Bets teach how the system works.
Players learn from the odds.
cons: The bank needs to understand the system.
A simple model may give the wrong odds.

pairs.tendency: Each player plays a real group with its own needs, and the bank offers odds on which group gains. A farmer and a shopkeeper bet differently.
pros: Bets show what each group wants.
Players see the problem from another side.
cons: Each group gets its own price.
A group with little money cannot place large bets.

pairs.tendency: Everyone draws from one limited store, and the bank takes bets on when it will run out. If players take too much, nothing is left for any of them.
pros: The end of a store can be bet on.
Players see how fast it falls.
cons: Betting on the end can make it come sooner.
A player who bets on a shortage has a reason to take more.

pairs.tendency: A move shows its effect only a few rounds later, and the bank holds bets until then. A choice made now is paid for much later.
pros: Bets teach patience.
Players see how choices add up.
cons: The bank holds bets for a long time.
A bet can be forgotten before it is paid.

pairs.tendency: Players agree a new rule and play on, and the bank offers odds on what it changes. The rule is tested before it is kept.
pros: A rule becomes something to guess at.
Players learn by trying.
cons: The odds move with the rule.
A rule tried once may not show its full effect.

pairs.tendency: After the game, everyone talks it through, and the bank shows what bets were won and lost. The table asks why the odds were what they were.
pros: Bets give the talk something to hold on to.
Players learn how they judged chances.
cons: A long talk can follow a short game.
Players who lost may not want to speak.

pairs.tendency: What players do changes the game permanently, and the bank cannot undo a payout either. Torn cards and stickers stay in the next game.
pros: Bets carry on into the next game.
The game keeps a record.
cons: A big loss cannot be taken back.
New players start with an old history.

pairs.tendency: The rules make a point about the world, and the bank's odds are part of that point. A game that pays for building roads tells players what it values.
pros: Odds say what the game thinks matters.
Players can talk about what the bank rewards.
cons: The bank is part of the argument.
A bank that pays one thing may push players to ignore another.

pairs.tendency: What happens in the game carries into real life, so the bank's bets are real money or a real promise. A friendship is on the table with the coins.
pros: Bets mean something.
Players take care.
cons: A lost bet can follow players home.
The bank holds more than the game.

pairs.tendency: Something that matters is turned into points, and the bank pays in those points. Players chase the points over the value they stand for.
pros: Bets show what players chase.
The game shows how a number can replace what it was meant to measure.
cons: The bank pays in the wrong thing.
Players may lose sight of the original value.

pairs.tendency: Players practise a way of living that does not exist yet, and the bank takes bets on how it will go. A village that shares everything is tried out.
pros: Bets can test an idea.
Players feel how the future might be.
cons: The bank has to guess at things nobody has seen.
The odds may be only guesses.

pairs.tendency: A coin goes down before every roll, and the same roll that moves your piece also decides who picks up the coins.
pros: Every roll counts twice.
Players watch each throw closely.
cons: One roll can move you forward and empty your pile.
Rounds slow down when everyone bets each turn.

pairs.tendency: A throw decides who picks first from the shared row, and everyone puts a coin on the result before it lands.
pros: Going first in the draft costs coins.
Players guess how much the front of the row is worth.
cons: A lost bet can come right after a lost pick.
Throwing for order adds a pause to every round.

pairs.tendency: Bidders offer coins for a prize, then a final throw decides whether the winning bid pays off.
pros: Bids turn into bets on luck.
Players learn what others think a prize is worth.
cons: The top bidder can lose everything on one throw.
Bidding and then throwing doubles the waiting.

pairs.tendency: One player keeps throwing for points while everyone else bets on the roll where they will stop.
pros: Onlookers have a stake in someone else's turn.
Stopping early is a choice that others read.
cons: Players without a turn wait with coins down.
A bust on the table feeds every other bet.

pairs.tendency: Two players with pieces in one region put stakes down and throw, and the winner of the throw keeps the region.
pros: A fight over a region can end in one throw.
Players pick which regions to risk.
cons: A region held for many rounds can vanish on a roll.
Long plans for a hold are hard to make.

pairs.tendency: When two workers want the same job, each side puts a stake down and a throw settles who gets it.
pros: Clashes over one spot are settled in seconds.
Players choose where to risk a stake.
cons: A blocked worker can also lose a bet.
Throws cut into the planning.

pairs.tendency: Before the dice pick the next tile, players bet on which colour will come up, since that tile may finish somebody's pattern.
pros: A plan can be backed with coins.
Players guess what the others need.
cons: A lucky throw can finish a pattern for the wrong player.
Betting adds steps between tiles.

pairs.tendency: Cards in hand can raise or lower what a bet pays, so a player thinks about when to play a card before the throw.
pros: Held cards give a reason to wait.
Players weigh each card against a stake.
cons: A card saved for a bet may never be used.
Hands and bets are two things to keep track of.

pairs.tendency: Before a trick is played, players put stakes on a coin toss that picks who leads.
pros: Players put coins down for the lead.
Every hand starts with something at risk.
cons: The toss can give the lead to a hand that cannot use it.
Each trick takes longer with a toss in front of it.

pairs.tendency: Players talk over what to wager and trade shares in each other's bets. Some agree to split the winnings before the dice land.
pros: Deals about stakes come up all the time.
Players can back each other's bets.
cons: A promise to split can be broken after the throw.
Talk before every throw slows the game.

pairs.tendency: Players put cards from their sets on the table as stakes, so one roll can finish a set or take a piece out of one.
pros: A set can be finished in a single roll.
Players decide which cards to put up.
cons: A set that is nearly done can be lost on a throw.
Some players keep their most valued items off the table.

pairs.tendency: A throw decides who may place the next tile on the shared map, and players bet on it beforehand.
pros: Coins ride on who places first.
The map changes under everyone's stakes.
cons: One throw can cost a player both the bet and the placing.
Players wait while each throw is settled.

pairs.tendency: One player calls and the next answers, and the chain ends with a throw that settles bets on how long it ran.
pros: Players guess where the chain will break.
The chain gets a shared thing to bet on.
cons: A bet on the chain can pull attention away from the answers.
The throw cuts into the rhythm of calling.

pairs.tendency: With nobody talking, a coin pushed forward before the dice are thrown is the only sign of a bet.
pros: Stakes show who feels sure.
The coins are all there is to read.
cons: A misread coin cannot be explained.
Raising or backing out needs a clear signal.

pairs.tendency: A player can change a rule on their turn, even how much a throw pays, so the stakes change shape between throws.
pros: Odds can be rewritten during play.
Payouts become something to talk about.
cons: A payout can be changed after the bets are down.
Players need to keep track of the rules as they stand.

pairs.tendency: A gambler, a merchant and a guard each put stakes on a throw in their own voice, and the roll becomes a scene.
pros: Bets carry a character.
A throw gives the story a turning point.
cons: Stakes can pull a story off its path.
Scenes stop while the throw is settled.

pairs.tendency: Players bet before someone flicks a counter at a target, so the flicker feels the weight of every stake.
pros: Skill and betting share one moment.
Watchers have a stake in a steady hand.
cons: A shaky hand can empty the table.
Players betting on others have nothing to do but wait.

pairs.tendency: Players draw the map as they go, and bets are placed on what the next throw will add to it, such as a river or a wall.
pros: The map grows out of the stakes.
Players guess what the world needs next.
cons: Drawing takes longer than throwing.
Bets on drawings are hard to judge.

pairs.tendency: A pot grows while hidden hands compete, and a throw on the side settles a second bet on the table.
pros: Two kinds of bet run at once.
A player can hedge one bet against the other.
cons: The pot and the throw can get mixed up.
Two sets of stakes take time to settle.

pairs.tendency: Players choose their sides first, then put stakes on a throw to see whose choice pays out.
pros: A chosen side becomes a bet.
Players show how sure they are of their pick.
cons: A side chosen in a hurry can lose its stakes at once.
Choosing and then betting makes for a slow start.

pairs.tendency: Before play, one player says what they will do, and the others bet on whether a throw lets them keep the promise.
pros: A call is backed with coins.
Others have a stake in the caller's luck.
cons: A throw can undo a careful call.
Calls cannot be changed once the bets are down.

pairs.tendency: A captured piece joins the captor, and players bet on a throw that decides if the capture holds.
pros: A capture can swing back in a roll.
A stake on a throw can win a piece back.
cons: A lead can change hands twice in one turn.
Players need to track whose piece is whose.

pairs.tendency: A caught player waits in jail while a throw decides whether a rescuer reaches them, and the table bets on the outcome.
pros: The wait in jail has a stake attached.
Rescues draw bets from the whole table.
cons: A jailed player has little say in the bet.
Waiting players watch bets they cannot join.

pairs.tendency: A throw gives the next stone a region of the board, and players bet on whether it will close a ring or break one.
pros: A single throw can end a siege.
Players guess where the next stone will go.
cons: A lucky throw can spoil a long plan.
Chance breaks up the quiet planning of surrounding.

pairs.tendency: A player who is behind gets a free stake or a second throw, so the bets round the table tilt towards them.
pros: Players who trail keep a stake in the game.
The leader is watched by everyone.
cons: A leader can be caught by one throw.
Players may hold back to collect the help.

pairs.tendency: When chance alone decides, the only choice left is how much to put down before the throw.
pros: The stake is the whole decision.
A round takes seconds.
cons: Nothing else shapes the result.
A long run of throws can start to look the same.

pairs.tendency: Before each chase, the runners put stakes on whether It will catch them, and the watchers back It.
pros: Runners can bet on themselves.
Watchers get a part in the chase.
cons: A bet can change how hard a runner runs.
Tag slows down while players place bets.

pairs.tendency: You name who is hit, then the others bet on a throw that says whether the hit lands.
pros: Naming a target starts the betting.
Targets can bet on themselves.
cons: A player named twice can lose twice.
Three or more players can gang up through their bets.

pairs.tendency: Two players build chains across the board, and a throw gives out the next stone while bets ride on each gap.
pros: Every stone is worth a bet.
Players watch every gap in a chain.
cons: A throw can hand the next stone to the player who is cutting.
One throw can break a chain built over many turns.

pairs.tendency: Each choice beats one and loses to another, so a bet on which choice comes up is never safe.
pros: No bet wins every time.
Players study each other's habits.
cons: A player who repeats a pattern gets caught.
A long run of one choice can drain a pile.

pairs.tendency: A player shows a pair or a run to score, and a throw decides how much the declared combination pays.
pros: The dice set what a declared hand pays.
Players can bet on what others hold.
cons: Showing a combination tells the table what is in a hand.
A throw can cancel a declared score.

pairs.tendency: One player's power lets them throw twice, another's lets them see the coin first, and each bets in their own way.
pros: Odds differ round the table.
Each player has their own way to bet.
cons: Players need to learn every power before they bet.
One power can make a player's bets hard to match.

pairs.tendency: Part-way through, a player offers to double what the throw is worth, and the other player accepts or gives up the stake.
pros: Stakes grow in steps.
Players read each other's nerve.
cons: A double can end a game early.
A quick double leaves little time to think.

pairs.tendency: A throw puts a piece in reach, and the forced capture that follows is something others have already bet on.
pros: Bets can predict forced moves.
A throw can set up a trap.
cons: A forced move can be hard to see coming.
A player with only one move has nothing to bet on.

pairs.tendency: A character gains power as play goes on, so early bets are small and later throws carry larger stakes.
pros: Stakes grow with the character.
Players can look back at their early bets.
cons: Early throws matter less.
A late throw can undo a long climb.

pairs.tendency: Players bet on who will lose the list, and a coin decides who adds the next item.
pros: Memory gets a stake.
Players listen closely to each other.
cons: A slip can cost both coins and the list.
Long lists make for long waits.

pairs.tendency: A more experienced player starts with less, and the stakes are set to match, so a small bet from one side meets a larger bet from the other.
pros: Odds can be set to match skill.
Both sides have a real chance.
cons: Setting the odds can take longer than playing.
Players can disagree about the right handicap.

pairs.tendency: One player hides something, the others bet on where it is, and a throw gives out an extra clue.
pros: Every guess costs coins.
Seekers read each other's bets for signs.
cons: A bet can give away where a seeker is looking.
A hider who watches the bets can tell who is close.

pairs.tendency: Before a hop, players bet on a throw that says whether the piece lands, so a long hop becomes a risk.
pros: Each hop has coins on it.
Players weigh long hops against short ones.
cons: A missed throw can undo a plan of hops.
Chains of hops take a long time to settle.

pairs.tendency: Bets are laid before the first roll, but the player can keep dice and roll again, so a stake can swing after it is placed.
pros: Players watch each reroll.
Keeping dice gives some control.
cons: The first roll tells little about the last.
Rerolls add waiting.

pairs.tendency: When one piece lands on another and sends it back, any stakes riding on the second piece go back with it.
pros: Landings matter to anyone with coins down.
Safe spaces matter more.
cons: One landing can lose a whole stake.
Players park pieces on safe spaces and wait.

pairs.tendency: Each row of three can be backed with a stake on the throw that places the next piece.
pros: Rows are worth a risk.
Players guess whether a row will be broken.
cons: A throw can break a row you built.
Players watch the rows more than the bets.

pairs.tendency: Letters are drawn or thrown, and players bet on how long a word they can make from them.
pros: Players say how sure they are.
A dictionary settles bets.
cons: A long word can end a bet in a dispute.
Words are slow to build.

pairs.tendency: A tile can only go next to a matching number, and players bet on a throw that gives the number they need.
pros: Players guess which ends will stay open.
Missing a turn now costs coins.
cons: A throw can hide the tile you need.
Missed turns pile up.

pairs.tendency: Finished sets go face up, and players bet on whether a throw lets them add to a laid set.
pros: Open sets are easy to read.
Players can add to the sets of others.
cons: Laying a set shows what is in hand.
A bet on an old set can stay open for a long time.

pairs.tendency: Each piece has a power that works once, so a player may use it to change a throw after placing a bet.
pros: A power can rescue a bet.
Players guess who has used theirs.
cons: A power used too early is gone.
Players with spent powers have nothing in reserve.

pairs.tendency: You offer a throw, and the other player can accept it or name a different stake.
pros: Both sides agree the bet.
Players find out what the other side will not accept.
cons: Offers can go back and forth for a long time.
A refusal can end the round.

pairs.tendency: A message travels by whisper, and the last player bets on what it said at the start, with a coin toss for who guessed closer.
pros: Players bet on how a message changes.
The end of the chain gets a stake.
cons: Nobody can check the message until the end.
A joke whisper can ruin the bets.

pairs.tendency: Players pass cards and then bet on a throw, with the cards they received setting how bold they dare to be.
pros: Received cards tell players how much to risk.
Passing hands a clue to the next player.
cons: A bet may rest on cards chosen by someone else.
Passing before betting adds a step.

pairs.tendency: One player sets the odds and the other picks a side, so the setter has a reason to make the bet even.
pros: Odds are set to be even.
The chooser takes the side they like.
cons: Setting odds takes thought.
A careless setter hands the chooser a clear pick.

pairs.tendency: A piece that reaches the far end turns into a more powerful piece, and players bet on a throw to say whether it gets there.
pros: Players bet on a piece's long route.
Reaching the far end carries a reward.
cons: A piece can be lost one step from promotion.
A player with nothing to promote has little to bet on.

pairs.tendency: Teams run a race in legs, and bets are laid on the throw that decides how far each leg goes.
pros: Each leg gets its own bet.
Teams watch every handoff.
cons: One long wait can undo a team.
Betting between legs slows the race.

pairs.tendency: A shape that cannot be captured is the goal, and a bet rides on whether a throw lets a player finish it before they are surrounded.
pros: A shape gives a bet a clear target.
A finished shape cannot be lost.
cons: A throw can break a half-built shape.
Bets pile up on shapes that never get finished.

pairs.tendency: Winning tricks is the road to the prizes, and a throw before the hand sets which named card is worth a bet.
pros: Prize cards get a stake.
Players chase named cards.
cons: A prize can be lost to a single card.
A player chasing a prize can miss the rest of the hand.

pairs.tendency: Cards in the middle are open to everyone, so a throw before the reveal sets how much players put in.
pros: Everyone sees the same cards.
Bets reflect shared knowledge.
cons: Shared cards leave little to hide.
A throw can turn a sure-looking bet into a loss.

pairs.tendency: Everyone puts a counter in the middle, and a throw picks who takes it, and if nobody wins the pot grows.
pros: The pot grows every round.
Players wait for a big one.
cons: A long run of draws can grow the pot out of reach.
A big pot raises the stakes of the next throw.

pairs.tendency: Seeds are dropped one by one round a ring of pits, and a bet is placed on where the last seed will land.
pros: Players count ahead.
A last-seed bet can be checked at once.
cons: Counting seeds slows each turn.
A wrong count costs a stake.

pairs.tendency: A spare hand lies face down in the middle, and players bet on a throw to say who may take it.
pros: Players pay for a chance at the hidden hand.
Players guess what it holds.
cons: The winner of the bet still does not know what they got.
Putting cards back takes another round.

pairs.tendency: Some squares keep a piece safe and others send it back, so the stakes on a throw change with the square it stands on.
pros: Each square has its own risk.
Players choose which squares to aim for.
cons: A single square can undo a stake.
Players learn the squares before they bet.

pairs.tendency: Every bet has a price in coins, so a big stake is bought like a card.
pros: A stake can be bought.
Players choose what to spend on.
cons: Coins spent on bets are gone.
A big price keeps out players with little.

pairs.tendency: A fixed amount is shared between several places, and each place is a separate bet on a throw.
pros: Players spread their risk.
Players show which places matter to them.
cons: A lot in one place leaves little in another.
Several throws take a long time.

pairs.tendency: Everyone moves until the signal, and a bet is placed on who will be slowest to freeze.
pros: Players watch each other.
Bets sit on the moment the music stops.
cons: Players may stall to win a bet.
A signal leaves little time to place a stake.

pairs.tendency: Players put cards back and take new ones, and a throw decides whether the new cards count for their bet.
pros: A new card can change a bet.
Players choose when to swap.
cons: Swapping tells others what a player lacks.
A bet already placed cannot be changed.

pairs.tendency: The discard pile is a stake for a throw, and any player may pick up the whole pile if they can use the top card.
pros: A pile can grow into a prize.
Players decide when to pick up.
cons: A big pile is hard to use.
Waiting for a pile slows the table.

pairs.tendency: Players back a suit before the dice name the trump, so one suit suddenly beats all the others for the hand.
pros: Players back a suit.
