A named suit changes the value of every card.
cons: A suit named after the bets can empty a hand.
Early bets are made without knowing the trump.

pairs.tendency: Two boards run side by side with a stake on each, so one throw can win on one board and lose on the other.
pros: Two bets can balance each other.
Players watch both boards.
cons: Two boards leave less time for each throw.
Two sets of stakes are hard to follow.

pairs.tendency: A wild card can stand in for any card, so it can complete a hand a player has bet on.
pros: A wild card makes a bet worth backing.
Players hold wild cards back.
cons: Other players cannot tell what a bet rests on.
A wild card can win a bet on its own.

pairs.tendency: A piece that runs off one edge comes back on the other, and bets on a throw can follow it round.
pros: No edge makes a piece safe.
Pieces keep moving.
cons: A piece can run into its own pursuer.
Bets on a piece that keeps circling are slow to settle.

pairs.tendency: One player knows a secret and answers yes or no, and the others put stakes on the next answer before a coin is tossed.
pros: Each question has a price.
Players learn from every answer.
cons: Guessing the last answer can use up the pile.
Only two answers leave little to bet on.

pairs.tendency: The first to the end wins, and bets let players put coins on who gets there.
pros: Players back the runner they trust.
A race has a clear end.
cons: A lead can vanish on a throw.
Bets laid early are made on little.

pairs.tendency: Points are added up at the end, and each throw changes the totals, so the bets move with them.
pros: A running score shows who is ahead.
Players know what each throw is worth.
cons: A big bet at the end can swing everything.
Players need to add up often.

pairs.tendency: Players drop out one by one and the last one left takes the stakes.
pros: Every drop-out grows the pile.
Players can tell when others are close to out.
cons: Dropped players wait with nothing at stake.
A throw can knock a leader out.

pairs.tendency: All players win or lose together, so the stakes belong to the group and a throw decides whether the group keeps them.
pros: Players decide together how much to risk.
Everyone shares a loss.
cons: One bold bet can end the game for all.
Players may disagree about how much to put down.

pairs.tendency: Everyone works toward one goal, and the group puts stakes on throws that move it closer.
pros: Players aim at one target.
Each throw is watched by all.
cons: Players with different views of risk may clash.
One throw can set back the whole group.

pairs.tendency: Each player has a secret goal, and the size of a stake can give it away.
pros: Bets can hide a goal.
Players read each other's wagers.
cons: A big stake can show what a player wants.
Players spend time guessing.

pairs.tendency: The game ends when the story does, and a bet on a throw can decide a turn in the plot.
pros: Throws can write the next scene.
Players bet on how the story ends.
cons: A bet can pull a story towards a quick end.
Throws pause the telling.

pairs.tendency: Nobody wins, so the stakes only record what happened, and players look back at which bets were taken.
pros: Players can talk about each bet afterwards.
Stakes show what players cared about.
cons: Bets that pay nothing lose their point.
Players may drift without a goal.

pairs.tendency: Each player names their own aim and sets stakes to suit, so one player bets small to stay in while another puts everything down.
pros: Stakes show each player's aim.
Players can follow different aims.
cons: Results are hard to compare.
A cautious aim and a bold aim sit awkwardly at one table.

pairs.tendency: Nobody wins, and the game goes on until one player loses, so the stakes go to whoever is left safe.
pros: Players watch who is nearest to losing.
Safe players can bet freely.
cons: The player in trouble has few ways to recover.
A long game can turn on one throw.

pairs.tendency: The aim is to keep playing, so stakes are small and move round, and a throw passes coins on while the game carries on.
pros: Coins move round the table.
Players can keep betting for years.
cons: Nobody ever wins the pile outright.
A game that does not end is hard to measure.

pairs.tendency: The game cannot be won, so a bet on a throw pays out in a way that never adds up to winning.
pros: Each bet shows that the game will not be won.
Players meet an odd result.
cons: Players may stop betting once they notice.
A payout with no goal can seem pointless.

pairs.tendency: You play alone against the cards, and the throw becomes a bet against yourself or against a friend watching.
pros: A friend can back or doubt your play.
A solo game gets a small audience.
cons: A lost bet adds to a lost game.
Players follow the layout and the throw at once.

pairs.tendency: A run of short games each starts with a bet on a throw, and the games add up to a running total.
pros: Players can recover in the next game.
Bets build into a running total.
cons: Losing the first throw can set the tone.
A lead of two games ends play early.

pairs.tendency: The fewest points win, so a bet on a throw is a bet that you will pick up little.
pros: Players back low scores.
A big throw becomes something to avoid.
cons: Players bet low and wait.
A big roll can ruin a low score.

pairs.tendency: A player needs the exact number to finish, so bets are placed on whether a throw gives it.
pros: Each throw near the end draws bets.
Players count the spaces left.
cons: Going past the number can lose the stake.
Players can wait a long time for the exact throw.

pairs.tendency: The aim is to give everything away, so a bet on a throw is one more way to lose coins.
pros: Losing a bet is a step towards the aim.
Players watch others hold back.
cons: Winning a throw can be unwelcome.
It is hard to tell who is trying.

pairs.tendency: Everyone bets on their own throws at the same time, and each pile is nobody else's business.
pros: Everyone plays at once.
Players do not wait for each other.
cons: There is little to watch except your own throw.
Players only meet when they compare piles.

pairs.tendency: Players target each other, and a bet on a throw says who gets hit.
pros: Coins ride on every hit.
Rivals have a clear stake against each other.
cons: A hit can take stakes from the target.
Grudges can build over repeated throws.

pairs.tendency: Players act on the board, and a throw decides how the changes affect each bet.
pros: Players feel each other's work through stakes.
A blocked space changes the odds.
cons: A bet can be lost without anyone aiming at you.
The board is slow to read.

pairs.tendency: Everyone is on one team, so bets on a throw go into a shared pile.
pros: Players back each other's throws.
A shared pile means a shared hope.
cons: A lost throw is lost by everyone.
One bold player can pull the team along.

pairs.tendency: Players mostly work together but each has a private reason to win, so a bet on a throw carries a private hope.
pros: A group bet can hide a private bet.
Players guess whose throw is for whom.
cons: A friend's bet can turn out to be a rival's.
Trust gets spent each time a throw is called.

pairs.tendency: Two teams put stakes against each other, and each team picks who throws.
pros: Teams choose their thrower.
Teammates share a pile.
cons: A thrower carries the whole team's stake.
Teams spend time deciding.

pairs.tendency: One player secretly works against the rest, and an odd bet can give them away.
pros: Odd bets show up.
Players watch each stake for a sign.
cons: An honest bet can look like a traitor's.
Players may stop betting to stay out of suspicion.

pairs.tendency: Bets are posted in letters, and a coin is tossed at a time everyone agreed.
pros: Waiting for a result is part of the game.
A bet can be thought over for days.
cons: A letter can arrive after the throw.
Players need to trust each other's tosses.

pairs.tendency: One player is away, so someone else holds their stake and makes the throw on their behalf.
pros: An absent player still has a stake.
Others speak for them.
cons: A throw made for someone else may land against them.
Nobody can ask the absent player about their stake.

pairs.tendency: One player runs the world and sets the odds, and the others bet on the throws the game master calls for.
pros: The game master sets the stakes.
Players bet on a story.
cons: The game master carries every rule.
Players wait while odds are set.

pairs.tendency: In a street or a market, a passer-by can add a coin to a throw and join the bet.
pros: Anyone can join a bet.
Coins from strangers raise the stakes.
cons: Nobody knows who will turn up.
Strangers may leave with winnings.

pairs.tendency: A lone player takes on the group and is paid more on a win, while the group shares each stake.
pros: The lone player gets larger odds.
Losses are spread across the group.
cons: A lone player faces many bets at once.
The group talks over every bet.

pairs.tendency: A single player throws against the pack and bets against their own record.
pros: A bet can track a streak.
Players can compare with a friend afterwards.
cons: Nobody else is there to collect the stakes.
A bet against yourself has no winner at the table.

pairs.tendency: Dice decide most of what happens, so bets follow luck, with few choices beyond the size of the stake.
pros: Stakes follow luck.
Anyone can win a round.
cons: Skill barely changes the result.
Streaks of luck can run for a long time.

pairs.tendency: A reroll or a rescue card lets a player place a bet and then protect it.
pros: A stake can be protected.
Players weigh whether to buy a reroll.
cons: Protection costs coins.
Players can spend more than they win.

pairs.tendency: Choices mostly decide the game, with a small throw to add chance, so bets go on the throw while the choices set the odds.
pros: Choices change the odds.
A throw keeps the result open.
cons: A skilled player can set odds that others miss.
A small throw can still end a long plan.

pairs.tendency: In a game of pure planning, a throw to settle a bet is the only chance in sight.
pros: One chance event stands out.
Players study the throw closely.
cons: A throw can undo careful planning.
The throw may seem out of place to some players.

pairs.tendency: The dice are read as a message, and a bet is placed on how the sign will be read.
pros: Players bet on a meaning.
Each throw gives players something to talk over.
cons: A reading can go either way.
Nobody can check a reading.

pairs.tendency: Players try to act at the same moment, and a bet is placed on whether that moment comes before a throw.
pros: Players watch each other closely.
A stake sits on a shared moment.
cons: A bet can break the quiet that attunement needs.
Players may act early to win.

pairs.tendency: A table says what each number means, so a bet on a throw is also a bet on which event comes up.
pros: Bets can follow a story.
A roll writes the next scene.
cons: A bet may pay out for an event nobody wanted.
Every throw sends someone to look up the table.

pairs.tendency: Everything is visible, so the throw is the only unknown, and every bet is about that.
pros: Players can work out the odds.
Bets are made in the open.
cons: Nothing else is left to surprise anyone.
Players can agree on the odds and stop betting.

pairs.tendency: Players hold cards no one else can see, and they bet on a throw while guessing what the others hold.
pros: Players read bets for clues.
A hidden card changes the stake.
cons: A bet can give away a card.
Players guess more than they check.

pairs.tendency: A secret role shapes how a player bets, so a spy might stake little and a villain stake a lot.
pros: Roles show in stakes.
Players use bets to question each other.
cons: A bet may be read as a sign when it is only luck.
Players accuse others on thin evidence.

pairs.tendency: Each clue is paid for with a stake before a throw, and players use clues to find hidden facts.
pros: Clues have a cost.
Players choose which clue to buy.
cons: A clue can come with a lost stake.
Players can run out of coins before they find the answer.

pairs.tendency: A player lies about a hand or a throw, and the others bet on whether to believe it.
pros: Stakes make a lie cost something.
Players study faces.
cons: A bluff that works can empty a pile.
Players slow down to read each other.

pairs.tendency: One player knows a secret rule, and a newcomer loses stakes when they break it by accident.
pros: Rules are found by losing coins.
Newcomers watch the old hands.
cons: A newcomer can lose stakes before knowing the rule.
Players may stop betting until they learn it.

pairs.tendency: The player who knows the answer can only give hints, and the others bet on a throw to say which hint they will trust.
pros: Trusting a hint costs a stake.
Players weigh hints against stakes.
cons: A hint can be read in many ways.
Bets slow down the guessing.

pairs.tendency: The map is hidden until players explore, and each step is a bet on what lies beyond.
pros: Exploring is a risk.
Players pool what they find.
cons: A step can lead to a lost stake.
Players hesitate to reveal.

pairs.tendency: One hand lies face up for all, so everyone can bet on what it will do when a throw is made.
pros: An open hand can be read.
Players can compare it with their own.
cons: An open hand gives plans away.
Whoever holds the open hand has no secrets.

pairs.tendency: Some money is kept secret, so no one knows who is ahead before the throw.
pros: Players guess who is ahead.
A bet can show the size of a pile.
cons: Nobody can add up the table.
A big bet can give away a secret.

pairs.tendency: One player acts at a time, and the others place stakes on that player's throw.
pros: Everyone watches each throw.
Turns give the game a rhythm.
cons: Waiting players have little to do.
Long waits with many players.

pairs.tendency: Everyone picks a stake in secret and reveals together, and one throw settles them all.
pros: No one waits for a turn.
Stakes are revealed side by side.
cons: Players cannot adjust after seeing the others.
Settling every bet takes a moment.

pairs.tendency: Anyone may act at any moment, so stakes go down and throws are made as fast as hands allow.
pros: The quickest player sets the pace.
Players act on instinct.
cons: Arguments start over who threw first.
Slow players fall behind.

pairs.tendency: A clock runs on each turn, so a player has to place a stake and throw before time is up.
pros: Choices are made quickly.
The clock adds pressure.
cons: A late stake can be lost.
A rushed bet can be a careless one.

pairs.tendency: The game runs over days, with one bet and one throw each morning.
pros: A bet can be thought over.
Players check in every day.
cons: A day passes before a result.
Players may forget a throw.

pairs.tendency: The game slows players down, with a pause before each stake and a breath before each throw.
pros: Players have time to think.
Throws carry weight.
cons: A round takes a long time.
Waiting can wear on players.

pairs.tendency: The game speeds up as it goes, so stakes get larger and throws come faster.
pros: Stakes rise with the pace.
The end comes in a rush.
cons: Late bets are made in a hurry.
Early rounds seem slow by comparison.

pairs.tendency: A lucky throw gives another go, so a player can win a bet and throw again at once.
pros: One win can lead to more.
Streaks become possible.
cons: A lucky player can take every stake.
Others wait through a long run.

pairs.tendency: The game has stages, such as picking cards and then playing them, and bets can be placed at the end of each stage.
pros: Each stage has its own bet.
Choices in stage one change the stakes in stage two.
cons: Bets in stage one are made with little knowledge.
Stages add time between throws.

pairs.tendency: The board works like a real system, so a throw stands for an event such as rainfall and the bet is on its effect.
pros: A throw has a real-world meaning.
Players learn about risk.
cons: A throw cannot show every real detail.
Bets may be mistaken for forecasts.

pairs.tendency: Each player plays a group such as farmers or a council, and each group bets on the throw in its own interest.
pros: Each group risks something different.
Players see why others bet as they do.
cons: A bet for one group can hurt another.
Players need time to learn their roles.

pairs.tendency: Everyone draws from one limited supply, such as water, and bets are placed on how much a throw takes from it.
pros: Players watch the supply.
A bet becomes a claim on the supply.
cons: A big bet can drain it for everyone.
Players may bet early to get a share.

pairs.tendency: The result of a bet shows only a few rounds later, so a player lives with a stake before it pays.
pros: Players wait for results.
A stake can be rethought along the way.
cons: The link between a throw and its result can be forgotten.
Waiting leaves stakes tied up.

pairs.tendency: Players agree a new rule and then bet on a throw to see what it changes.
pros: A rule is tested with real stakes.
Players see how a rule changes the odds.
cons: A rule tested once tells little.
Players may argue after a lost bet.

pairs.tendency: After the game, players go back over each bet and ask why they staked what they did.
pros: Bets give them things to talk about.
Players see their own habits.
cons: Talking takes as long as playing.
Players may remember bets differently.

pairs.tendency: A lost bet tears up a card or marks the board for ever, so stakes leave a trace on the next game.
pros: Stakes leave marks.
The next game starts from here.
cons: A lost bet cannot be undone.
Players may avoid betting to keep things whole.

pairs.tendency: The rules say something about the world, and a bet on a throw shows what the game rewards.
pros: Payouts make the point.
Players notice what gets paid.
cons: A payout can say more than was meant.
Players may stop betting to avoid the message.

pairs.tendency: Real money or a promise rides on a throw, so a bet carries into daily life.
pros: A throw matters beyond the table.
Players speak carefully before betting.
cons: A lost bet can affect a friendship.
Players may drop out to avoid it.

pairs.tendency: A number stands for something like health, and players bet points on a throw to gain more of it.
pros: Bets show what a number is worth.
Players see a value turn into a stake.
cons: Players may chase the number only.
The thing the number stands for gets forgotten.

pairs.tendency: Players practise a way of living, such as sharing everything, and bet on throws that test it.
pros: A new way gets tried with stakes.
Players see how it might feel.
cons: A throw can make the future look easy or hard.
Real life has more than one throw.

pairs.tendency: Pieces walk round a path on the roll of a dice, and some spaces are betting stops where everyone looks at their hidden cards and decides whether to stay in.
pros: The betting happens at fixed places on the path.
The hidden cards matter even while the dice run the trip.
cons: Every betting stop pauses the walk.
A short roll can miss the stops where chips change hands.

pairs.tendency: Each round opens with a pick from a passed hand of cards, and then chips go in on whatever was kept. The cards you passed on tell the next player a little about what you wanted.
pros: Each bet rests on cards a player chose.
The hand is partly built by your own choices.
cons: Passed cards let others guess your hand.
The picking round delays the first bet.

pairs.tendency: One stack of chips pays for prizes at the auction and also backs the hidden hand in the pot, so every offer is a hint about the cards. A big offer on a prize can mean a winning hand, or a bluff.
pros: One stack of chips does two jobs.
Offers hint at what the hand holds.
cons: Chips spent on a prize cannot go in the pot.
A player short on chips has to pick one job.

pairs.tendency: Take another card or another throw, then decide whether to put in more chips. The pot grows with every step, and one step too far loses everything already in it.
pros: The pot grows with each step.
The table watches for the moment someone stops.
cons: A bust costs every chip already in.
Stopping early leaves the pot to whoever carries on.

pairs.tendency: Regions on a map are fought over, and chips go in on hidden cards that might win a contested region. A player may raise hard in one region and give up the others.
pros: Bets show which region matters to a player.
Hidden cards add surprise to a map fight.
cons: Chips spent in one region are missing from another.
A bluff in one region can leave a different one open.

pairs.tendency: One job space on the board is the betting table, and a worker standing there stops everyone else from raising that round. The other spaces earn the chips the table needs.
pros: The betting table is a space players compete for.
Jobs done elsewhere feed the chip stack.
cons: Only one player bets at a time.
Workers waiting for the table sit idle.

pairs.tendency: Rows and shapes of tiles grow on each side of the table, and the hidden hand holds the tiles that could finish them. Chips go in faster as a pattern gets close.
pros: Bets climb as a pattern nears its end.
Chip piles hint at which tiles are held.
cons: A broken pattern loses the chips behind it.
Tiles held back sit idle until they are played.

pairs.tendency: A player keeps two high cards back for a later round and goes on betting on them. The pot grows while the hand shrinks.
pros: Saved cards give a reason to wait.
Each card played shows part of the hand.
cons: Playing a card early gives away a plan.
A used-up hand cannot back another raise.

pairs.tendency: Players bet on how many tricks the hand will win, and every trick played shows a little more of what was held.
pros: Early tricks prove or break a bet.
A raise before play is a guess about the others.
cons: One lost trick can end a raise on the spot.
By the last trick, everyone knows the hand.

pairs.tendency: Talk comes before each bet. One player offers a deal to fold, another says their hand is huge, and nobody can check either claim.
pros: Talk gives a second way to read people.
Deals can split a pot between friends.
cons: Side deals can break one big pot into small ones.
Long talks slow every round.

pairs.tendency: Matching cards pile up in secret, and players bet on whether the set will be finished. A set missing one card is the point where bets climb.
pros: The size of a bet hints at how close a set is.
Each card taken raises the next bet.
cons: A set one card short can cost every chip put in on it.
Others can block a set by taking the card it needs.

pairs.tendency: A shared map grows tile by tile, and players bet on a hidden tile they hope to place next. Everyone sees the map but only the holder sees the tile.
pros: The map shows which tiles are left.
Bets follow the shape of the map.
cons: Chips on a tile that no longer fits are wasted.
A player has to follow the map and the chips at once.

pairs.tendency: One player calls out a word and the next answers it, with a chip going in at every answer. A reply can raise the stakes.
pros: Calls and replies set a beat for the bets.
Each answer shows how sure a player is.
cons: A reply has to follow the call, which limits the raises.
A long chain makes the pot slow to settle.

pairs.tendency: With no talking at all, a raise is the only way to say anything. A player who wants to say something pushes chips forward.
pros: Chips become the only signal.
Faces and timing are watched closely.
cons: Nobody can ask what a raise meant.
A wrong guess about a raise goes uncorrected.

pairs.tendency: On a turn a player can change a rule, such as what beats what, instead of making a bet. A hand with chips behind it can lose its value in one move.
pros: Bets stay open to surprise.
A rule change can turn a losing hand into a winner.
cons: A change can wipe out chips already in.
Players keep stopping to re-check the rules.

pairs.tendency: Each player acts as a character who bets the way that character would, such as a nervous clerk or a proud landlord.
pros: Betting style tells a story.
Bluffs come with a voice and a face.
cons: Staying in character can push a player into a raise a plain player would skip.
Acting takes time at every bet.

pairs.tendency: Bets are placed before each flick or stack, and the cards in hand give another reason to carry on or stop. A shaky hand at the tower can show in the bet.
pros: Steady hands and cards both count.
Nerves show at the table.
cons: A shaking hand can give away a bluff.
Two kinds of skill at once can confuse new players.

pairs.tendency: The map is drawn as the game goes, and players bet on hidden cards that say which part of it will count.
pros: Every new area changes what a hand is worth.
Cards give a bet a place to point at.
cons: An early bet can point at land that is never drawn.
Drawing stops the betting for a while.

pairs.tendency: Before play each person picks a deck or an army, and the first bet is on how that pick will do against the hidden choices of the others.
pros: The choice of side is a first bet.
Players learn each other's habits from the picks.
cons: A pick can meet an opponent it cannot beat.
Picking takes a long time before any chip moves.

pairs.tendency: A player says aloud what they will do, then puts chips behind the promise. Missing the target costs the chips, and the opponents know exactly what to stop.
pros: The call and the bet say the same thing twice.
A bold call draws bold bets.
cons: A failed contract costs chips and points.
A called target is hard to keep hidden.

pairs.tendency: Taking a piece turns it to the captor's side, and the chips riding on it change sides too. A pot that looked safe can swing in a single capture.
pros: A lead can change in one move.
Bets follow the fights on the board.
cons: Pieces and chips can be lost together.
Late raises can meet sudden reversals.

pairs.tendency: A caught player sits in jail with their chips still in the pot. A teammate who frees them brings them back into the betting.
pros: A rescue brings a player back to the bet.
Teams can share one pile of chips.
cons: A jailed player cannot raise.
Long waits leave a player out of whole hands.

pairs.tendency: Stones close in around an enemy group, and players bet on hidden cards that might break the ring. A surrounded player may raise to pretend they hold a way out.
pros: The board and the cards both hint at plans.
A bluff can slow a closing ring.
cons: When the ring closes, the chips bet on escape are lost.
The board and the chips both have to be read.

pairs.tendency: Trailing players are given an extra card or more chips, so the back of the table can go after a big pot.
pros: Trailing players stay in the hands.
A leader's raise can be met.
cons: Help can make a bluff harder to read.
A lead may last only a few hands.

pairs.tendency: A card is turned and the result says who takes the pot, so the only thing left to choose is how many chips to put in beforehand. The hidden cards have nothing to protect.
pros: Bets scale a result that luck decides.
Rounds go quickly.
cons: Choices about raising do not change who wins.
There is nothing in the other players to read.

pairs.tendency: Whoever is It chases the rest, and a pot of chips goes to whoever is not It when the round ends. Cards in hand grant a dash or a safe spot.
pros: Running puts action between the bets.
Cards decide the safe moments.
cons: Being It at the end can cost the pot.
Players need space to run.

pairs.tendency: On a turn a player raises and names who has to answer it. The one named can stay in or drop out.
pros: Naming a target makes a raise personal.
Others watch who is picked and why.
cons: A target may be picked again and again.
In bigger groups the pick can fall to a few players.

pairs.tendency: Stones are linked from one side of the board to the other, and cards in hand offer ways to extend or cut a chain. Bets rise as a chain gets near the far side.
pros: A nearly finished chain draws raises.
Cards offer ways to cut a chain.
cons: Cutting a chain wipes out its owner's bets.
Board and hand both need watching.

pairs.tendency: Every choice has one it beats and one that beats it, so a bet on one choice can be met by its counter.
pros: Every bet can be answered.
No hand wins every time.
cons: Reading the cycle takes several rounds.
Meeting the same counter again and again can empty a stack.

pairs.tendency: A player shows a pair for points and keeps the rest of the hand hidden while chips keep going in.
pros: A shown pair gives out part of the hand.
Points arrive before the pot is won.
cons: Showing a pair tells others what is held.
The cards left hidden may be worth less than hoped.

pairs.tendency: Each player has a power others cannot copy, such as seeing one card or paying less to stay in. The same raise costs different amounts at different seats.
pros: Every player bets from a different footing.
Others try to guess a power from a bet.
cons: The same raise can cost two players different amounts.
New players have several powers to learn.

pairs.tendency: Either side can double the pot part-way through, and the other has to match it or give up what is in. It adds a second kind of raise to the usual ones.
pros: A double sends a loud signal.
Chips can multiply fast.
cons: Giving up after a double loses a bigger share.
Two raising rules at once can confuse.

pairs.tendency: If a capture is open, it has to be taken. An opponent can leave a piece out as bait and raise on a hidden hand while the other player cannot refuse.
pros: Bait moves can be paired with bets.
The board and the chips both give clues.
cons: A forced capture can leave a hand with few options.
A raise can trap a player who has no choice.

pairs.tendency: Characters get stronger over the game, and the cards behind the bets grow with them. A hand that looked small at the start may win a late pot.
pros: Early bets can aim at a later hand.
Waiting adds to what a hand can do.
cons: Folding early gives up the growth.
Players further along can raise at will.

pairs.tendency: Each player says the list so far and adds one item, with chips going in on every turn. Forgetting a word costs chips.
pros: Memory becomes part of the bet.
Cards are the secret part and the list is the spoken part.
cons: A forgotten item loses chips.
Long lists slow the table.

pairs.tendency: A player with a clear lead starts with fewer chips or fewer cards in hand, so both sides have a chance to raise.
pros: The gap shows in the first bets.
Both players have reason to stay in.
cons: A short stack folds sooner.
The size of the handicap has to be agreed before the first chip goes in.

pairs.tendency: Someone hides an object while the rest hunt, and each hunter bets on whether a clue card in hand will lead to it.
pros: Search and betting work together.
Clues change in value as the hunt goes on.
cons: Chips on a wrong guess are lost.
Waiting for the hider slows the table.

pairs.tendency: A piece hops over another to land behind it, and the hidden hand backs a bet that it will hop again. A chain of hops can end a round.
pros: Double hops raise the stakes.
Bets track moves on the board.
cons: One jump can swing a pile of chips.
Eyes move between the pieces and the chips.

pairs.tendency: Dice are kept or rolled again, and chips go in after each roll. Cards in hand can change a result.
pros: Every roll gives a new reason to raise.
Cards offer a way to alter the dice.
cons: Chips pile in before the last roll.
Rolling and betting several times drags.

pairs.tendency: Landing on a piece sends it back to the start, and its owner can raise on hidden cards to win chips back.
pros: A sent-back piece leaves a pot to recover.
Safe spaces are places to rest and bet.
cons: One landing can undo several turns.
A pile of chips can sit behind a piece far from the finish.

pairs.tendency: Three in a row lets a player take an enemy piece, and cards in hand add a reason to raise as a row gets close.
pros: Row building shows in the chip piles.
Taking a piece also takes away the other player's footing.
cons: Once a row is blocked, nobody raises on it.
Hand and board compete for attention.

pairs.tendency: Letters on the table form words, and a hidden hand of letters backs a bet on which word can be finished.
pros: Bets track word length.
A dictionary ends arguments about who won.
cons: Letters held back cannot be used on the table.
Players who know more words have an edge.

pairs.tendency: Tiles are added to the end of a line only if the number matches, and a player with none misses the turn. Chips go in before each tile.
pros: Open ends tell others what you need.
Chips are staked on tiles you may not have.
cons: A missed turn leaves a bet standing with no reply.
Tiles run out toward the end of a line.

pairs.tendency: A player lays a finished set face up, where anyone can add cards to it. A meld shows part of a hand while chips stay in the pot.
pros: Laid sets cut the number of hidden cards.
Others can add to your set.
cons: A meld gives away what you hold.
Chips can be locked in before a meld is made.

pairs.tendency: A power that works once can wait for a big pot and then change a hand. The marker for it sits face up, so everyone knows it is still there.
pros: Timing a power becomes a bet.
Others hesitate while the marker sits.
cons: Using it early loses it for the big pot.
Others may fold early to stay clear of a power.

pairs.tendency: A raise is offered as a move, and the other player can turn it down or pick between two raises on offer.
pros: Offers give the other player a choice.
Offers show what a player would accept.
cons: A turned-down raise can cost the offerer chips.
Two-way offers double the thinking per turn.

pairs.tendency: A raise is whispered along a line of players, so the amount that arrives may not be the one that was sent.
pros: Bets pass through a chain.
Guessing the original amount is a puzzle.
cons: A garbled raise can cost the wrong person.
Nobody can check until the end.

pairs.tendency: Before betting, each player hands some cards to a neighbour and takes what they give. A hand you built up can be changed by someone else.
pros: Passed cards are a signal.
Your hand depends on your neighbours.
cons: You cannot see what you get until you have chosen.
Passing and betting make two stages.

pairs.tendency: One player sets up the stakes and the other picks a side. A setup that favours one hand can be turned down by the picker.
pros: Setters aim for an even start.
The picker weighs the hidden hand against the setup.
cons: A lopsided setup sends the picker to the other side.
Setters may keep early raises small.

pairs.tendency: Reaching the far end makes a piece stronger, and players bet on whether a piece will get there.
pros: Pushing forward pays in power.
Bets ride on a piece's route.
cons: Pieces left behind may lose chips.
Opponents can aim at blocking one piece.

pairs.tendency: Team legs run one after another, and the team pot grows with each hand-over. The hidden cards say whether the next runner is worth backing.
pros: The pot passes on with the baton.
Teammates see each other's stakes.
cons: A late leg can lose the lot.
A slow runner holds up the chips.

pairs.tendency: A shape that cannot be taken gives a goal to build toward, and cards in hand help to build it. Bets come when the shape is near.
pros: A safe shape gives bets a target.
Opponents try to surround the shape.
cons: A broken shape loses chips.
Players may fold when a shape is blocked.

pairs.tendency: Winning tricks matters only for named prizes, so the betting is on who will hold the highest trump or the Jack.
pros: Bets aim at particular cards.
Few cards decide the pot.
cons: One card can win several prizes at once.
Losing a prize card early ends many bets.

pairs.tendency: Cards face up in the middle belong to all, and a bet is on how your hidden pair joins with them.
pros: Open cards give everyone shared facts.
Each new card changes the bets.
cons: Another player may hold a pair that fits the middle cards more closely.
Late cards can undo early raises.

pairs.tendency: Each player adds a counter to the middle, and the betting chips join them. If nobody wins, the whole pile stays and grows.
pros: The pot grows each drawn round.
Everyone has a reason to stay in.
cons: Raises get bigger as the pot grows.
One win collects the lot.

pairs.tendency: A player scoops the seeds from one pit and drops them one at a time into the pits that follow. Players bet on the pit where the last seed lands, and a hidden card says which pit to scoop.
pros: Seed counts can be worked out ahead.
Cards add secret information.
cons: A wrong count loses chips.
Counting seeds and chips together is a lot to do.

pairs.tendency: Face down in the middle is a spare hand, and a player can swap for it or leave it.
pros: Taking the spare hand is a bet.
Others guess why a swap was made.
cons: A swap can wipe out chips put in on the old hand.
Nobody knows the spare until a swap is made.

pairs.tendency: On the track a safe space protects a piece, and other spaces send it back or cost a turn. A square can also be the place where a bet is made.
pros: Squares give the bets a place.
Safe squares offer a rest.
cons: A sending-back square costs chips.
A missed turn leaves chips idle.

pairs.tendency: Cards are bought with the same chips that keep a player in the betting.
pros: Buying and betting draw on one stack.
A hand costs something to build.
cons: Spending on cards leaves less for raises.
An expensive hand is costly to give up.

pairs.tendency: A player divides a set number of chips between several places, each with its own hidden hand.
pros: Spread chips decide where to fight.
A bluff in one place leaves the others open.
cons: Putting a lot in one place leaves another thin.
Hidden hands multiply the places to watch.

pairs.tendency: Play goes on until the music stops, and then all bets are called together.
pros: Sudden stops force quick bets.
Hesitation shows.
cons: Quick bets leave little time to read others.
Slow players are caught out.

pairs.tendency: Before the bet, a player may throw back cards and draw new ones, then bet on the changed hand.
pros: Swapping tells others what was needed.
A new hand is a new bet.
cons: Cards thrown back give away a plan.
Swapping adds a step to each round.

pairs.tendency: A pile of thrown cards can be picked up whole, and a bet goes on whether the pile helps.
pros: Pile contents are known to all.
Taking a big pile changes a hand in one go.
cons: A big pile can bury a hand.
Others hold their bets back until the pile is taken.

pairs.tendency: One suit beats the rest, and the betting turns on whether a player holds trumps.
pros: The trump suit decides which hands count.
Low trumps can win.
cons: Raises ride on one long suit.
A hand without trumps loses chips.

pairs.tendency: Chips are staked on two boards played side by side, and the hidden hand counts on only one of them.
pros: Chips can be spread between boards.
Players attack and defend at once.
cons: The hand backs only one board.
Keeping track of both takes effort.

pairs.tendency: With a wild card in it, a hand could be many things.
pros: Wilds make every hand uncertain.
Raises can hide a wild.
cons: A wild can finish a hand on the last turn.
Players cannot count on any hand.

pairs.tendency: The edges of the board join, so a line running off one side returns on the other. A raise made on a line that looks blocked may still be safe.
pros: Lines can come from unexpected sides.
Bluffs have extra routes.
cons: New players miss threats from behind.
The board takes longer to read.

pairs.tendency: The hidden hand is the secret, and the others ask yes or no questions about it, betting on what it is.
pros: Questions shrink the list of hands.
Bets follow the answers.
cons: A wrong guess costs chips.
Answers reveal the hand.

pairs.tendency: Everyone runs to the end and chips pile in on cards that help a runner get there first.
pros: Speed makes every bet urgent.
Leaders can be raised against.
cons: A stalled runner loses chips.
Betting breaks the pace.

pairs.tendency: Points come from several sources, and the pot is one of them.
pros: Winning hands add points.
Folding saves chips but adds none.
cons: A small pot and a big pot count differently.
Fold-heavy play scores slowly.

pairs.tendency: Running out of chips puts a player out of the game, until one is left.
pros: Chips are lives.
Folding keeps a player in.
cons: A big loss can end a player.
Out players wait.

pairs.tendency: The team beats the game together, so chips go into a common pot to survive.
pros: Players vote with chips.
Hands can be talked about.
cons: One player's fold can cost the team.
Talk about hidden cards is limited.

pairs.tendency: The team has a target to reach, and each player bets on their cards in support of it.
pros: Raises tell teammates how close a hand is.
Teammates can pool chips.
cons: Showing a hand helps the team but breaks the secret.
One doubtful player slows the team.

pairs.tendency: Besides the hidden hand, every player holds a secret goal, so a raise can be about either.
pros: Two hidden things per player.
Raises are harder to read.
cons: A raise may serve a goal and not a hand.
Misreading is frequent.

pairs.tendency: Play stops when the story is finished, and players bet on which ending a hand will bring about.
pros: Bets steer the plot.
Hands become story pieces.
cons: The ending can arrive before the chips are settled.
Players can disagree about which ending counts.

pairs.tendency: With no winner, the chips mean whatever the players decide they mean. Betting on a hidden hand shows how much that hand matters to you.
pros: Raising becomes a form of talk.
Chips can be given freely.
cons: A pot nobody wins needs an agreed place to go.
Some players stop raising when nothing is at stake.

pairs.tendency: One player is happy to stay in every hand, another wants the biggest pot, and each decides for themselves what a win looks like.
pros: Players bet for different reasons.
The same raise can mean two things.
cons: A fold can be a win for someone.
Results are hard to compare.

pairs.tendency: The game stops when one player loses, and nobody wins. Chips show who is closest to being that loser.
pros: Bets show who is most at risk.
Safe players can stop betting.
cons: Players near the loss may raise often.
A safe player has no reason to put chips in.

pairs.tendency: The pot is never taken in full, so chips keep moving round the table and hands are played for the next round.
pros: Betting keeps chips in motion.
Hands are played toward the next round.
cons: There is no clear end to the chips.
A player who runs out has to be given more.

pairs.tendency: Chips go into a pot that nobody can take, so each raise leads nowhere on purpose.
pros: Raises are made for their own sake.
Players see their own habits.
cons: A pot may lead nowhere.
Some players refuse to bet at all.

pairs.tendency: A lone player takes on a layout of cards and puts chips in the pot for each try.
pros: Bets measure how sure you are.
No bluff is needed.
cons: A stuck layout loses the chips.
There is no opponent to read.

pairs.tendency: Several short games run in a row, with chips carried over from one to the next.
pros: Chips carry from game to game.
A lost hand has a later chance.
cons: One heavy loss can end the series early.
More rounds mean more waiting.

pairs.tendency: Points count against you and so do chips left in the pot, so a hand full of high cards is a risk.
pros: Folding avoids points.
Low cards can be a plan.
cons: Raising with low cards gives them away.
The pot and the points pull in different directions.

pairs.tendency: A hand wins only when it adds up to an exact total, so players bet on getting close. Going past loses the hand.
pros: Bets follow the running total.
Players weigh each risk.
cons: Overshooting costs the hand.
The last few points are hard to land.

pairs.tendency: The aim is upside down, so the hand that gives away the most wins the pot.
pros: A raise can mean the hand is trying to lose.
Old habits get in the way.
cons: Others cannot tell a fold from a plan.
A bluff looks odd.

pairs.tendency: Everyone plays their own hand at the same time and compares only at the end. Chips go in against the table, but nobody touches another player's cards.
pros: Players focus on their own hand.
Little arguing.
cons: Little to watch between turns.
Bets get no direct reply.

pairs.tendency: Players attack each other on purpose, and a raise is one more way to hit.
pros: A raise forces an answer.
Grudges show.
cons: A target can be ganged up on.
Players may fold out of fear.

pairs.tendency: Players change the board instead of hitting each other, and chips go in on how much a change will hurt a rival's hand.
pros: A board change is felt later.
Bets are quiet.
cons: Players may not know why they lost chips.
Causes are hard to trace.

pairs.tendency: Players share one target against the game, and chips come from a single team stack.
pros: One stack for all.
Hands can help each other.
cons: Showing hands helps but breaks the secret.
One player's raise spends everyone's chips.

pairs.tendency: The group plays as a team, but each player has a private reason to come out ahead, and the pot is where those reasons show.
pros: Cooperation and betting mix.
Players guess who is holding back.
cons: A greedy raise can hurt the team.
Trust slips.

pairs.tendency: Two teams pool their chips, and teammates can send signals to each other through their raises.
pros: Teammates read each other's bets.
Team stacks last longer.
cons: One player's fold can leave a partner alone.
Hidden signals between teammates may be argued about.

pairs.tendency: A hidden traitor works against the team and uses raises for cover. A traitor can raise to drain the team's chips.
pros: Suspicion falls on raises.
Honest players get blamed.
cons: Bets cost trust.
A traitor's fold looks like caution.

pairs.tendency: Over weeks, bets go out and come back by letter, and each hand stays in a sealed envelope until the pot is called.
pros: Waiting is part of the bet.
Bluffing happens in writing.
cons: Weeks pass before a pot is settled.
Letters can go missing.

pairs.tendency: A ghost or a faraway relative counts as a player without being there, with a hand face down and a marker standing in for them.
pros: The absent hand still counts.
Others guess what it holds.
cons: Nobody can ask the absent player anything.
The pot may be taken by an unseen hand.

pairs.tendency: The game master runs the world and holds the bank, deciding whether a bet pays.
pros: The game master sets the prices.
Characters bet on their own cards.
cons: The game master has to track every pot.
Players depend on one person for payouts.

pairs.tendency: Passers-by join in on the street, the chips are seeds or bottle caps, and hands are hidden in pockets.
pros: Anyone can join.
Stakes are small.
cons: People come and go mid-hand.
Settling pots in a crowd is loud.

pairs.tendency: A lone player faces everyone else and takes a larger payout on a win, and the hidden hand is theirs alone.
pros: The lone player's bet is large.
The others can share information.
cons: One player alone bears all the raises.
The others may over-plan together.

pairs.tendency: Chips are your own, and the hand is hidden only from yourself until it is played.
pros: Nobody to bluff.
The result can be compared later.
cons: Nothing to read.
Chips lost go nowhere.

pairs.tendency: Most of the result comes from dice and draws, and chips go on how lucky a hand looks.
pros: Bets are guesses.
Easy for a new player.
cons: Skill at reading rarely matters.
Winning streaks come from luck.

pairs.tendency: Luck is softened by re-rolls and swaps, and chips can pay for them. A hard roll can be rolled again for a price.
pros: Chips buy second chances.
Choices about when to pay.
cons: Buying too many rerolls empties the stack.
Players may wait too long to pay.

pairs.tendency: The result rests mainly on choices, and the cards add a little luck.
pros: Reading others earns chips.
Luck still shows in the last cards.
cons: A lucky draw can undo a plan.
A careful player can lose to a lucky one.

pairs.tendency: There are no dice, so the hand is the only secret.
pros: Bets read as pure judgement.
Patterns of play get seen.
cons: No luck to blame.
A beginner can be out-read quickly.

pairs.tendency: Players treat the cards as a message and bet on what it might mean.
pros: Bets become readings.
Talk turns to meaning.
cons: Players disagree about a reading.
A pot can be won by argument.

pairs.tendency: Players try to sense when others will act, and a raise lands at the same moment as the others.
pros: Group timing replaces calling.
Hands matter less.
cons: A mismatch loses chips.
Hard to teach.

pairs.tendency: A roll on a table says what happens next, and chips go in on the result of the roll.
pros: The story gets bet on.
Table results are public.
cons: A table result can make a hand beside the point.
Rolling slows play.

pairs.tendency: Hands are laid face up, so a raise can only be about a plan.
pros: Raises become plans.
Bluffing disappears.
cons: Nothing hidden to protect.
Folding is obvious.

pairs.tendency: Both are about cards nobody else sees, so the hidden hand is the base of the bet and every raise hints at it.
pros: The same secret serves both.
Faces get read.
cons: Raising gives things away.
A bluff and an honest raise can look the same.

pairs.tendency: Secret roles are added to hidden hands, so a raise might come from the role or from the cards.
pros: Raises mean two things.
Roles can be guessed from bets.
cons: A raise by a role-holder can mislead.
Reading takes longer.

pairs.tendency: Clues are used to work out what others hold, and chips go in on a conclusion.
pros: Betting tests a deduction.
A wrong deduction costs chips.
cons: Folding closes a clue source.
Working things out takes time.

pairs.tendency: The main move is a raise on cards that cannot win, and a big bet can draw folds.
pros: A bluff is a bet with nothing behind it.
Large bets draw folds.
cons: A called bluff loses the chips.
Players grow suspicious.

pairs.tendency: A secret rule is known to one player, and the others find it by breaking it, losing chips each time.
pros: Losses teach.
The secret rule becomes a bluff.
cons: New players lose chips while learning.
The rule keeper has an edge.

pairs.tendency: One player sees the answer and cannot say it, so their chips go in as a hint.
pros: A raise can be a hint.
Others guess what it means.
cons: A misread hint costs chips.
The quiet player carries the load.

pairs.tendency: The map is turned over bit by bit, and bets are placed before each reveal.
pros: Each reveal changes the bets.
Explorers pay in chips.
cons: Early bets are blind.
Revealing slows play.

pairs.tendency: With one hand face up on the table, players bet knowing what it holds.
pros: One known hand hints at the others.
The open hand makes bets easier to size.
cons: Others work out what remains.
Bets involving the open hand come too easily.

pairs.tendency: Scores and chips are partly hidden, so nobody can say who leads.
pros: Nobody knows who leads.
Bets are careful.
cons: The final reveal can surprise.
Players cannot tell when to catch up.

pairs.tendency: Each player in turn matches, raises or folds, so everyone sees the bet before deciding.
pros: Later players see more.
Order matters.
cons: The last player has the final say.
Everyone else waits.

pairs.tendency: All players drop chips into the pot at the same moment, then reveal.
pros: No one is swayed by an earlier bet.
Fast.
cons: No chance to respond to a raise.
Fewer bluffs.

pairs.tendency: There are no turns, so anyone can bet whenever they like, and fast players push the betting along.
pros: Fast raises.
Pressure.
cons: Slow readers lose out.
Disputes about who went first.

pairs.tendency: Each turn has a clock, and if time runs out the hand is folded.
pros: The clock forces a decision.
A pause before a bet is easy to spot.
cons: A fold made by the clock.
Quick bets leave little reading.

pairs.tendency: One bet is made each morning for weeks.
pros: A bluff can run for weeks.
Each bet waits a day for the next.
cons: Players drop out.
A hand is held a long time.

pairs.tendency: Players breathe slowly before each bet.
pros: Time to read faces.
Calm.
cons: The game drags.
Impatience shows.

pairs.tendency: Betting rounds get shorter and the raises have to rise faster each time.
pros: Raises grow.
Short stacks go first.
cons: Little time.
The end comes in a rush.

pairs.tendency: A hit or a throw gives another go, so a player can raise twice in a row.
pros: A double raise.
Momentum builds.
cons: Others wait.
The pot swings.

pairs.tendency: The first stage is picking and betting, and the second stage is playing the cards.
pros: Betting in the first stage sets up the second.
Stakes can change between stages.
cons: A pot placed too early cannot be undone.
Two sets of rules.

pairs.tendency: The board models something real, such as a village market, and chips stand for money in it.
pros: Bets mean real things.
Players link the game to the world.
cons: The model can make a bet feel less like a game.
Detail slows play.

pairs.tendency: Players take the part of groups, such as farmers or a shopkeeper, and each bets in its own way.
pros: Roles shape raising.
Bets show needs.
cons: Some roles hold more chips.
A fold depends on the role.

pairs.tendency: The chips are one limited store that everyone draws from.
pros: Raising drains it for all.
Low chips are seen by all.
cons: Players raise less.
One big raise can empty it.

pairs.tendency: A few rounds pass before a bet takes effect.
pros: Chips placed now pay later.
Players plan ahead.
cons: Cause is hard to link.
Lost chips arrive late.

pairs.tendency: A new rule is agreed, and the next hands are bet under it.
pros: The rule changes the bets.
Easy to test.
cons: A rule may break a hand's value.
Agreeing takes time.

pairs.tendency: Once play ends, everyone talks through the hands and the hidden cards are laid out.
pros: Hidden hands are finally seen.
Players learn each other's bluffs.
cons: Hands shown after the pot is gone cannot change it.
Talk after the game runs long.

pairs.tendency: Chips or cards are torn up or marked, so a lost pot stays lost into the next game.
pros: Losses stay.
Bets count for later.
cons: Players hesitate.
Nothing can be undone.

pairs.tendency: The rules make a point, such as that raising wins.
pros: Rules say who gets rewarded.
Players discuss the point.
cons: The rule can be debated.
Talking it through takes time.

pairs.tendency: The pot holds real money or a promise.
pros: Bets matter outside the game.
Players watch more closely.
cons: Friendships get tested.
Some will not play.

pairs.tendency: Points stand for something that matters, such as kindness, and chips stand for points.
pros: Raising chases the number.
The chip count can replace the thing it measures.
cons: Players forget what it stood for.
A pile of chips looks like success.

pairs.tendency: Players try out a way of living, with chips standing for shared food or time.
pros: Bets are tried on a future.
Players feel the arrangement.
cons: Hidden hands clash with sharing.
Raising against neighbours feels odd.

pairs.tendency: Each player picks a racer before the first throw, and the racers cross the same path with different perks on certain spaces.
pros: The dice keep a race open between unlike sides.
Players can compare their picks before anyone rolls.
cons: A lucky roll can undo a careful pick.
The side matters little when throws set the pace.

pairs.tendency: Players take cards one at a time from a passed hand to make their army, so the side each person ends up with depends on what the others left.
pros: The side is shaped by what the neighbours pass on.
Players learn what the others are collecting.
cons: Late picks come from a thin choice.
Two sides can end up very far apart in power.

pairs.tendency: Players bid money for the characters they will play, so paying a lot for one leaves little for the rest of the side.
pros: Every side shows what its owner was willing to pay.
A bid tells the table what you want.
cons: A low bidder can end with a thin side.
The auction can take longer than the game.

pairs.tendency: A player keeps pulling extra cards into their deck one at a time, and a pull past the limit spoils the deck they have built.
pros: Each pull is a small gamble on the side.
Players watch how far the others dare to go.
cons: A greedy build can fall apart before play starts.
A careful build may still lose to a lucky one.

pairs.tendency: Two armies of different make-up spread across one map, so one side holds the hills while the other holds the river towns.
pros: Unlike armies make each area worth something different.
A side can aim at the areas it holds easily.
cons: An army built for one area can be left behind in another.
Players can spend a long time on the map before the sides meet.

pairs.tendency: Each side comes with its own set of workers, and a spot one side takes is a spot the other side cannot use that turn.
pros: Sides send their workers to different jobs.
A special worker gives its owner a plan to follow.
cons: A spot taken early shuts the other side out of it.
A side with few workers has few choices each turn.

pairs.tendency: One player picks pieces that suit long lines and the other picks pieces that suit mosaics, and each builds in view of the other.
pros: Each side has its own shape to aim for.
Players can see what the other is building.
cons: Two sides may need the same tile.
A side built around one pattern has little to fall back on.

pairs.tendency: The deck a player builds at the start decides what a hand can hold, and then each turn is a choice of which card to play and which to keep.
pros: Each hand draws on cards the player picked earlier.
Keeping a card back is a plan the others can see.
cons: A deck full of high cards can leave a hand stuck.
Players can spend a long time sorting their hands.

pairs.tendency: Each player brings a deck built before play, and the cards from those decks meet in tricks, so a side with a few high cards wins some tricks and loses others.
pros: The deck you built decides which tricks you aim for.
Players can see which cards the others brought.
cons: A deck full of low cards wins few tricks.
A short deck runs out of choices early.

pairs.tendency: Before play the table talks about who takes which side, and during play players trade help between sides that need different things.
pros: Sides that differ give players something to swap.
Deals can pull in players who would stay out.
cons: Talk can run long before anyone moves.
A quiet player can be left with the leftover side.

pairs.tendency: One side needs three of a colour and another needs four of a type, so each player collects towards a different list.
pros: Each side has its own list to collect.
Players can see what the others still need.
cons: Two sides may chase the same card.
A side with a long list takes longer to finish.

pairs.tendency: Each side has its own tiles, and all the tiles go into one shared map, so the finished map shows where the sides have been.
pros: The map records which sides played where.
Different tiles give each side a way to shape the map.
cons: A side with tiles that do not fit may sit out the early turns.
The shared map can grow in a direction one side did not plan.

pairs.tendency: Each side has its own opening line or move, and the other side answers it, so a chain grows out of two different voices.
pros: The two voices make the chain sound different.
Players learn each other's habits quickly.
cons: An answer that does not fit can break the chain.
Players have to know the other side to answer it.

pairs.tendency: Players agree their sides in advance and then say nothing, so each move is the only way to show the other player what the side can do.
pros: Every move carries news about the side.
Players watch each other very closely.
cons: A side that is hard to read can be taken for another one.
A misread move goes uncorrected.

pairs.tendency: Players pick unlike sides and then change the rules on their turns to suit them, so the game drifts towards whoever rewrites it first.
pros: A rule change can repair a side in the middle of play.
Players help shape how the sides meet.
cons: A rule change can undo what a player chose at the start.
Arguing about a new rule can use up the turn.

pairs.tendency: Each player makes a character with a different history and powers and speaks as that character, so the sides meet as people.
pros: Characters give players things to say and do.
Players can act out the differences between sides.
cons: A player with a quiet character may get less to do.
Making a character before play adds time.

pairs.tendency: Each player picks a tool with its own shape and weight, such as a heavy striker or a thin stick, and the shape changes how the throw or the stack comes out.
pros: The side changes how the hands work.
Players can pick a side that suits their own hands.
cons: A shape that suits one hand can be hard for another.
Hand size can decide which side is easy to play.

pairs.tendency: While each side is built, the map is drawn as play goes on, so each side puts down the places it cares about and the other side meets it there.
pros: Each side leaves its mark on the map.
The map shows what the players chose to draw.
cons: A side can draw itself into a corner.
The first drawer decides much of the layout.

pairs.tendency: Players build a side and then say before play what they will win, so the call has to fit the side they made.
pros: A call shows what the player thinks their side can do.
A side built for a big call pays more when it makes it.
cons: A failed call hands points to the other side.
A side built early may not fit the call that is needed later.

pairs.tendency: A captured piece switches to the captor's army, so a piece made for one side is used in a new way by its new owner.
pros: A captured piece brings its own traits to the new side.
A player can change what their army looks like in one move.
cons: A lead made of many captures can vanish in one recapture.
Players have to remember which pieces began on which side.

pairs.tendency: Each team picks its own mix of runners and guards, then catches the other team's runners and holds them in a jail until a teammate frees them.
pros: Teams can pick runners for rescuing or guards for catching.
A team with quick rescuers keeps its players in the game.
cons: A team built only for catching has no one to free its own.
A full jail can leave a team with nobody to send.

pairs.tendency: Armies of different sizes take enemy pieces by closing in on both sides, so a big army spreads thin while a small army stays tight.
pros: A group of pieces stays safe by sticking together.
Different armies need different ways of closing in.
cons: A piece on its own can be taken in one move.
A large army can be hard to keep together.

pairs.tendency: Players begin with unlike sides, and the one who falls behind gets a boost, so the sides stay close for longer.
pros: The boost keeps a trailing side in the game.
A side built to start slowly can use the boost on purpose.
cons: A lead can be cut down on the next turn.
Players can build a slow side just to collect the boost.

pairs.tendency: Players pick their sides, but dice or cards decide every result, so the pick changes nothing about who gains.
pros: The pick gives players something to talk about before the throw.
Games end quickly.
cons: The side picked has no effect on the outcome.
A player who built with care gains nothing for the work.

pairs.tendency: One player is It and chases the rest, and the runners come in different kinds, such as a quick sprinter or a dodger who turns sharply.
pros: Each kind of runner has its own way to escape.
Chasers choose which runner to follow.
cons: A quick runner can still be caught by a lucky touch.
The slowest kind of runner is tagged most often.

pairs.tendency: When a turn lets you pick who is hit or helped, a side that looks easy to beat often becomes the target.
pros: Each side can be picked as a target or as an ally.
The choice of target shows what a player is afraid of.
cons: With three players, the side that is ahead gets hit by both.
An odd side can be ignored because nobody knows it.

pairs.tendency: Each side picks the stones it will use and tries to link one edge of the board to the other, while the other side tries to cut the chain.
pros: Each side shows its own way of linking.
Cutting a chain gives the other side a way to react.
cons: A side picked for speed can be cut by one stone.
Both sides can end up blocking each other for a long stretch.

pairs.tendency: Each side is built to beat one kind and lose to a third, so a player picks by guessing what the other player will bring.
pros: The pick turns into a guess about the other player.
Every side has one thing it beats.
cons: A wrong guess can lose the game before it starts.
A player who sees the other pick first has the edge.

pairs.tendency: A deck built around pairs and runs announces points as it is played, so a side with many pairs scores often.
pros: A deck of pairs scores as play goes on.
The announcement tells others what you hold.
cons: A deck of single cards seldom has anything to declare.
A declared pair shows the other side which cards to hold back.

pairs.tendency: Every player begins with a power of their own and builds the rest of the side to match it, so no two players play quite the same game.
pros: Each power gives a side a clear way to play.
Players can try a side with a power they like.
cons: A power can be useless against one other power.
A player who does not know the other powers can be caught out.

pairs.tendency: Part-way through, a player whose side is ahead offers to double what the game is worth, and the other player gives up or plays on.
pros: A raise tells the other player how a side is doing.
The offer gives a player a way out of a game going the wrong way.
cons: Giving up costs the points at stake.
A raise can be a bluff from a side that is behind.

pairs.tendency: Since any capture on offer has to be taken, a side can bait the other with a piece it is happy to lose.
pros: Sides can set traps with pieces given up on purpose.
A piece on the edge can steer the other player's move.
cons: A forced capture can hand over a move the player did not want.
A side with few pieces to spare is easy to steer.

pairs.tendency: Each player starts with a small side and builds it up through what they do, so two sides that began alike can end far apart.
pros: Early choices show up in the side that grows.
Players watch their own side change.
cons: A side that grows slowly can be caught early.
A lead from early growth is hard to catch.

pairs.tendency: Every side adds one new item to a list that the whole table recites, so the list shows which side added what.
pros: The list gives every player a part in a shared record.
Items from different sides can be told apart.
cons: Long lists are hard to remember.
A player who forgets an item loses a turn.

pairs.tendency: The more practised player starts with fewer pieces and the newer player picks a side with more, so the two sides begin unequal on purpose.
pros: What each player starts with can make the sides close.
A newer player has more to work with.
cons: The more practised player may find the start slow.
Players can disagree about how much to give up.

pairs.tendency: One player picks a hiding side and the others pick a finding side, and the hider chooses a spot that suits their side.
pros: Each side has its own skills at hiding or finding.
Players can swap roles in the next round.
cons: A hiding spot that suits one side can be useless for another.
A long search leaves the hider waiting.

pairs.tendency: Armies of different pieces hop over each other into the empty space behind, so a crowded army gives the other side more to jump.
pros: A hop gives a piece a long move.
Empty spaces behind a line invite hops.
cons: A tight line can be jumped from the back.
Pieces left alone are easy to hop over.

pairs.tendency: Each side begins with its own set of dice, keeps the ones it likes after each throw and rolls the rest again.
pros: The dice a side starts with decide what it aims for.
Rerolling gives a way to fix a throw.
cons: Throws that never reach the target give nothing for the pick.
Players wait while others roll again and again.

pairs.tendency: When a piece lands on another, the other goes back to the start, so a fast side keeps sending a slow side home.
pros: A fast side puts distance between its pieces and trouble.
Safe spaces give a slow side a place to rest.
cons: A piece far along can lose all its progress in one landing.
The side sent back most often can drop out of the race.

pairs.tendency: Players build sides with different pieces and try for a row of three, which lets them take a piece from the other player.
pros: A row helps a side that likes to build lines.
Taking a piece breaks the other player's row.
cons: A side with few pieces finds a row hard to make.
Both players spend turns watching each other's rows.

pairs.tendency: Each side comes with its own letters, so one side can make long words and the other short ones.
pros: A side's letters decide the words it can make.
Both sides use the same dictionary.
cons: A side with rare letters can get stuck.
Arguments about spelling can slow play.

pairs.tendency: A side of tiles with a wide spread of numbers can join the line often, while a side with few numbers keeps missing turns.
pros: Many different numbers mean more ends to play on.
Players can read the ends to guess what the other side holds.
cons: Few numbers mean many passes.
Tiles of one number can run out.

pairs.tendency: Each player lays finished sets face up, and other sides can add matching cards, so a set on the table helps whoever holds a match.
pros: Cards from one hand can go onto another player's set.
Players see which sets the others are building.
cons: Laying out a set early shows the other side your plan.
A side that melds late holds cards that count against it.

pairs.tendency: Each piece in a side has a power that works once, so the player decides which piece uses it and when.
pros: The one-use power makes players watch the timing.
A side can hold a power back as a threat.
cons: A power used too early is gone.
Players can lose track of which powers the other side has left.

pairs.tendency: When one player offers a move, the other side can turn it down or pick between two offers, so every turn has two people in it.
pros: Offering a move shows what you think the other will accept.
The other player has a part in every turn.
cons: A move can be turned down again and again.
Waiting for a reply slows the turn.

pairs.tendency: A message passes along a line of sides and changes as each player hears it, so the end of the line hears something that carries every side's mark.
pros: The message shows what each side added to it.
Players hear how it sounds after others have passed it on.
cons: A message can reach the end with a different meaning.
Nobody can check it before it arrives.

pairs.tendency: Each player builds a deck and then hands some of it to another player before play, so every side includes cards chosen by someone else.
pros: Passed cards mix the sides together.
A player gets cards they did not pick.
cons: Cards given away leave a hole in the deck the player built.
A deck can lose its main plan.

pairs.tendency: One player sets up a side and the other chooses which one to take, so the setter tries to make both match.
pros: The setter has a reason to build evenly.
Each side can be picked on how it looks.
cons: A set-up that leans one way gets chosen at once.
The setter has to give up their favourite side.

pairs.tendency: A piece that reaches the far end turns into a more powerful piece, so a side is built around getting one piece through.
pros: A piece that walks to the far end gives a goal to aim for.
Sides plan to guard a runner.
cons: A piece held back never changes.
Players may spend several turns on one piece.

pairs.tendency: Each team builds its runners and hands a flag over at each leg, so every leg can suit a different runner.
pros: A team can match each runner to a leg.
The team sees which of its players fits each leg.
cons: A slow runner holds up the whole team.
A dropped handover can lose a lead.

pairs.tendency: Each side tries to make a shape that nothing can capture, while the other side tries to break the stones before the shape is done.
pros: The shape gives each side a place to aim for.
Sides can choose where to build first.
cons: A shape that is not finished can be broken.
Waiting to build gives the other side time.

pairs.tendency: Players build decks that aim for the named prize cards, so one deck is built around the highest card and another around a single Jack.
pros: The named cards tell each deck what to aim for.
A single card can win more than one prize.
cons: A deck without the named cards scores very little.
Players can see what the other side is chasing.

pairs.tendency: Each player builds a side from their own cards and then mixes them with cards turned up in the middle for everyone.
pros: The middle cards give each side a chance to change.
Players can all see what is available.
cons: A shared card helps both sides.
A side that relied on its own cards may find the middle of no use.

pairs.tendency: Each player puts a counter into the middle and plays their own side to win it, so the pot grows when nobody wins.
pros: A growing pot gives every side a reason to keep playing.
The pot records the rounds that had no winner.
cons: A large pot makes losing a round hurt more.
A player can leave a round with nothing.

pairs.tendency: Each side has a row of pits, and sowing seeds from one pit round the board can end a move in the other side's row.
pros: The pits on each side give a different pattern of moves.
A long sowing can change the whole board.
cons: A seed dropped in the wrong pit helps the other side.
Players have to count carefully.

pairs.tendency: An extra hand is dealt face down in the middle, and one player takes it, swaps cards into their own and puts some back before play begins.
pros: The spare hand gives one side a second chance at its build.
Buying or swapping makes players think about what they need.
cons: The player who takes the hand gives up cards.
The other sides do not see the swap until later.

pairs.tendency: A side built for fast travel can still lose its place if it lands on a square that sends it back or costs a turn.
pros: A safe square gives a side a place to stop.
A square with a penalty gives the other side a trap.
cons: A piece can lose a turn at the wrong square.
Learning what each square does takes a few games.

pairs.tendency: Each player builds a side of costly cards and spends from a budget to use them, so a side that bought big pieces has less to spend on the next turn.
pros: A price on each piece makes each choice count.
Players compare what they bought.
cons: A costly piece uses up a whole turn of spending.
A side that spent everything early has nothing left.

pairs.tendency: Each player divides one army between several places, so the sides differ in where they are heavy and where they have few units.
pros: Sharing out forces shows what a side values.
Players can guess where the other side has few units.
cons: A force put in one place leaves another empty.
A side can lose a place it left bare.

pairs.tendency: Players choose their sides and move until a signal comes, and whoever is slowest to freeze is caught.
pros: A signal ends all planning at once.
Sides made for quick stops have an edge.
cons: A side that is slow to react is out first.
The signal can come at an odd time and surprise the sides.

pairs.tendency: A player builds a deck and then swaps cards for new ones, so the deck at the start is not always the one that gets played.
pros: Swaps let a player repair a side.
Players learn what the other side wants by what it swaps.
cons: Swapping uses up turns.
The other player may have to agree to a swap.

pairs.tendency: Players build decks and throw cards onto one pile, then take the whole pile when they can use the top card, so a side can end up with a hand it did not build.
pros: A pile gives a side cards it never planned for.
Players watch the top card closely.
cons: A big pile can weigh down a hand.
A player who takes the pile once may need to do it again.

pairs.tendency: A deck with many cards of one suit wins tricks when that suit is named trump, so a deck matched to the trump has the edge.
pros: The trump suit gives one side an advantage.
Players can build a deck to fit.
cons: A deck with the wrong suit loses tricks.
The trump may be named after the deck is built.

pairs.tendency: A player takes opposite sides on two boards at once, so a side attacks on one board while defending on the other.
pros: The sides swap roles from board to board.
Players learn both ends of the same plan.
cons: The two boards ask for attention at the same time.
A move that helps on one board can open a gap on the other.

pairs.tendency: A side holding several wild cards can finish sets that a deck without them cannot.
pros: A wild card fills the gap in a set.
Players can plan around holding one.
cons: A wild card used early is gone.
A side without wild cards depends on luck.

pairs.tendency: Sides move over a board whose edges join, so a piece that runs off one side returns on the other.
pros: No edge gives a side a safe wall.
A line can come back from behind.
cons: A piece near the edge can be attacked from both sides.
Players need time to learn the loop.

pairs.tendency: One player holds a secret about their side and the others ask yes-or-no questions to find it.
pros: Each answer rules out part of the side.
Players learn how the side is built by asking.
cons: Questions can go round in circles.
A side with a simple build is found in a few questions.

pairs.tendency: The sides are built to cross the board as fast as they can, and the first to reach the end wins.
pros: A race shows the speed of each side at once.
Players can choose speed or defence.
cons: A fast side can win from the start.
A slow side never gets a turn at the end.

pairs.tendency: Each player builds a side to earn points from different sources, and the highest total at the end wins.
pros: Several sides can score in different ways.
The score shows how each build did.
cons: A side may collect points that others cannot reach.
Close totals can end in a long recount.

pairs.tendency: Each side is built to knock the others out, and the last one with any pieces wins.
pros: A side built for defence can outlast the others.
Players choose who to knock out first.
cons: Early knockouts leave players with nothing to do.
A side hit first has little time to use its build.

pairs.tendency: Players bring different characters to one shared team, and the game itself tries to beat them all.
pros: Each character fills a gap in the team.
Players can plan what the team needs.
cons: A team with two characters of one kind is short of other skills.
One player's loss can lose the game for everyone.

pairs.tendency: Players build different sides but work for the same goal, so each side has a part to play.
pros: Each side adds something different to the goal.
Players can see how the team fits together.
cons: A missing kind of side can stall the goal.
A loud player can set the plan for the others.

pairs.tendency: Each player picks a side and holds a secret goal, so the side they show can differ from the one they are aiming at.
