pros: A secret goal changes what a side is for.
Players watch each other to guess the goal.
cons: A goal that clashes with the side is hard to reach.
Watching for secrets can slow the game.

pairs.tendency: Each player makes a character and plays on until the story ends, so each side adds a part to the tale.
pros: Each side brings its own turn to the story.
The ending is shaped by the sides in play.
cons: A side that is left out of the story has little to do.
Some players push the story where they want it to go.

pairs.tendency: Players make sides, nobody wins, and the game ends so everyone can look at what the sides made.
pros: The sides can be compared after play.
Players can try odd builds freely.
cons: Without a goal, choices carry little weight.
Play can wander and stop at no clear point.

pairs.tendency: Each player builds a side and picks what counts as a result for it, so two sides are judged by two different measures.
pros: The goal fits the side the player chose.
Players can make a goal that suits their build.
cons: Players comparing results may find no common measure.
A goal set low is easy to meet.

pairs.tendency: Play goes on until one side loses, so everyone else is safe and each side tries to avoid being the one.
pros: Every side has the same aim of staying safe.
A player can aim only at staying safe.
cons: A side that falls behind early is at risk for the whole game.
The game goes on until the loser is clear.

pairs.tendency: Sides are built to keep the game running, so a campaign can last for years.
pros: Each side adds to the history.
Players return to see how their side changed.
cons: Without an end, the game can drift.
New players have a long past to learn.

pairs.tendency: Players build sides for a game that no one can win, so what the sides do shows how the game behaves.
pros: The sides become a way to look at the game.
Players ask what a side is for.
cons: Players who expect a winner may stop.
Effort on the side gets no reward.

pairs.tendency: One player builds a side and plays alone against a layout of cards, trying to clear the table.
pros: A built side faces the same layout each time it is tried.
A player can try another side with the same cards.
cons: The game says lost when the side gets stuck.
Nobody else can help.

pairs.tendency: Players build a new side for each short game, and the player who wins the most games takes the match.
pros: A lost game allows a new side in the next.
Players try different builds in one sitting.
cons: A side built for one game can go to waste.
Play can stop early when nobody can catch up.

pairs.tendency: Each player builds a side that picks up points counting against them, and the fewest wins.
pros: A side can work to dodge points.
Players watch what the others take.
cons: A side that avoids points may do very little.
A single big card can undo a careful hand.

pairs.tendency: Each side tries to land exactly on the target number, so a side that gets close fast has to stop and wait for the right throw.
pros: Players plan moves backwards from the target.
A small number can free a stuck side.
cons: A side that passes the number loses the hand.
Players can wait many turns for the right number.

pairs.tendency: Players pick sides that give everything away, so the winner is the one with the least left.
pros: A side built for giving can lead.
Players move the opposite way to a normal race.
cons: Sides that pile up pieces get stuck.
Players can mistake the aim for the usual one.

pairs.tendency: Each player builds a side and plays at the same time without touching the other, so the sides can be compared at the end.
pros: Each side runs on its own.
Players can watch other builds without being hit.
cons: Players have no way to change the other's play.
The sides never meet.

pairs.tendency: In a straight fight, a side built for attack meets a side built for defence.
pros: A side can be tested at once.
Players choose their target.
cons: A side built for defence can be battered.
A player ganged up on has few ways out.

pairs.tendency: Players change the board instead of hitting each other, so a side feels the other through a wall or a blocked space.
pros: Sides affect each other through the board.
Players can plan for a place before anyone arrives.
cons: A wall built against one side can block its builder too.
Cause and effect are hard to trace.

pairs.tendency: Players pick different roles on one team against the game, and win or lose together.
pros: Each role adds something to the team.
Players can plan the team before play.
cons: Two players with the same role leave a gap.
One mistake can lose the game for the whole team.

pairs.tendency: Players build sides that work together but each has a private reason to win more, so help is offered and held back.
pros: A side may help another for its own gain.
Players learn who can be trusted.
cons: A helping hand may come with a price.
A private goal can break the team's plan.

pairs.tendency: Two teams each build a side, and teammates choose pieces that cover each other.
pros: A team can share a plan.
Teammates cover what a side lacks.
cons: A team with the same pieces repeats itself.
One slow teammate holds the team back.

pairs.tendency: Most players build a team side while one secretly plays against it, so a side that looks like a team has a member working for the other side.
pros: A traitor changes how the team picks its sides.
Players watch each other's builds for signs.
cons: An odd build may be blamed on the wrong player.
Doubts can stop the team from acting.

pairs.tendency: Once the sides are chosen, moves go by letter, so the game can last weeks.
pros: Time between moves lets a player rethink the side.
Waiting becomes part of play.
cons: A letter can be lost or late.
A long game can fade out.

pairs.tendency: A side belongs to a player who is not at the table, so someone else moves it or it follows the rules by itself.
pros: An absent side can be a puzzle for the others.
The game carries the memory of someone who is away.
cons: A side with no one to explain it is hard to read.
The absent player cannot answer for a move.

pairs.tendency: One player runs the world while the others build sides and play characters in it.
pros: The runner can shape the world for each side.
Players get an answer to any question they raise.
cons: The runner has no side of their own to play.
A runner who favours one side can tip the game.

pairs.tendency: Sides are built on the spot in a street or park, so people passing can pick one and join in.
pros: Anyone can join a side.
Players learn from watching.
cons: Crowds can change the number of sides.
A rule made on the spot may not be what passers-by expect.

pairs.tendency: One player builds a side to face all the others, who build a team together.
pros: A lone side can be built with many tricks.
The team can divide its jobs.
cons: The lone side has no one to ask.
The team may argue about its plan.

pairs.tendency: One player builds a side and plays alone against a pack, so the same build can be tried again.
pros: The same side can be tested several times.
Results can be compared with a friend later.
cons: Nobody else is there to react.
A build that fails does not say why.

pairs.tendency: Players pick sides but dice decide most results, so a side matters only at the edges.
pros: The side adds a little to a dice game.
Players have something to choose before the roll.
cons: A side picked with care can lose to one throw.
The build changes little.

pairs.tendency: Players build sides with ways to soften low throws, such as rerolls.
pros: A side can plan for its low throws.
Players keep some control over luck.
cons: A side with many rerolls has less room for other things.
The soft spots can run out.

pairs.tendency: The build decides most of the result, and a roll now and then adds a surprise.
pros: Skill in the build shows up in results.
Players can learn from the same side.
cons: A rare roll can still undo a plan.
A lucky draw can hide an untested build.

pairs.tendency: In a game with no dice the result comes from the build and the play, so each side shows what its owner knew.
pros: A side's build shows in the result.
Players can study the other's build.
cons: An early mistake in the build cannot be blamed on luck.
A new player meets a side they cannot read.

pairs.tendency: Each player picks a side, then throws dice that are read as a message, so each side hears something from the throw.
pros: The throw gives each side something to think about.
Players talk about what a throw means.
cons: A throw can be read in more than one way.
The message may have no effect on the build.

pairs.tendency: Players pick sides and play in step with one another, sensing when the other will act.
pros: A side built on timing needs no dice.
Players learn each other's rhythm.
cons: Two sides out of step can fall apart.
Players cannot say how they know.

pairs.tendency: Players build sides and let a table of dice results say who is met on the road, so the dice add to each side's story.
pros: Each side gets its own story.
A table gives the dice a voice.
cons: A table can send a side in an odd direction.
A roll can overrule what a player planned.

pairs.tendency: Every card and every move is in the open, so each side is known before play.
pros: Players can plan against what they see.
There are no secrets to find.
cons: The first move can be answered at once.
A side can be copied.

pairs.tendency: Each player builds a side and holds cards no one else sees, so the sides are guessed from what is played.
pros: Players can bluff about their side.
Hidden cards keep the other side guessing.
cons: A hand can be misread.
Hidden cards can run out before they are used.

pairs.tendency: Players pick sides and some hold a secret role, so a side may look the same from outside while its members play different games.
pros: A secret role changes what a side does.
Players watch for signs.
cons: A player wrongly accused loses trust.
Players may stop trusting any build.

pairs.tendency: Each player uses clues to work out what the other side holds.
pros: Each clue narrows the other side's build.
Players learn by asking and watching.
cons: A false clue can lead the guess astray.
A long chain of clues takes time to follow.

pairs.tendency: A player can lie about what their side holds, so a side that looks big may be small.
pros: A bluff gives a side a second use.
Players have to read each other.
cons: A bluff that is caught costs the side.
A bluff can be called at the wrong moment.

pairs.tendency: One player holds the rules and the others build sides while finding them out by being told no.
pros: A new player learns by trying.
The rules become part of the build.
cons: A side built on a wrong guess is wasted.
Being told no again and again can wear a player down.

pairs.tendency: One player knows the answer and can only hint, while the others build their sides and guess.
pros: The hints can match each side's build.
Players pick up on small signs.
cons: A hint can mean different things to different sides.
The one who knows cannot fix a wrong guess.

pairs.tendency: The map is hidden, so a side finds out what suits it only by going there.
pros: Exploring tests the build.
Players can find places that suit their side.
cons: A side may walk into a place it cannot handle.
Players know little before they move.

pairs.tendency: One hand is face up for all, and a player may play it along with their own, so one side shows part of what it holds.
pros: The open hand lets others read part of the side.
A player can plan around the open cards.
cons: The open hand gives away the side's build.
The player who plays two hands has more to track.

pairs.tendency: Part of each score is kept secret, so nobody knows who is ahead.
pros: A secret score keeps each side guessing.
Players have to watch each other.
cons: A side can believe it is ahead when it is not.
The game can end with a surprise.

pairs.tendency: Players pick sides and then go one at a time, so a player has time to look over the other's build.
pros: A turn lets a player read the other side.
Players can plan their reply.
cons: Waiting while others move can be long.
A side built to be quick loses its speed.

pairs.tendency: Everyone chooses at the same moment, so each side is shown together with the others.
pros: A reveal puts every side in the open together.
Nobody waits for a turn.
cons: A choice cannot be changed after the reveal.
A side that needs to see the others first loses its plan.

pairs.tendency: Anyone can act at any moment, so the quickest hands decide which side gets there first.
pros: A side with fast pieces has an edge.
Players act when they see a chance.
cons: Slow thinkers can be left behind.
The game can turn into a scramble.

pairs.tendency: A clock runs on every turn, so a complicated side takes more time than a simple one.
pros: The timer makes players choose fast.
A simple build is quick to play.
cons: A move lost to the timer is gone.
A side with many parts runs short of time.

pairs.tendency: Each side makes one move a day, so the game runs on real days.
pros: A side can be changed between days.
Waiting becomes part of the plan.
cons: A player who forgets a day misses a move.
The game can last weeks.

pairs.tendency: A pause comes before each move, so a build can be thought over in the quiet.
pros: A pause gives time to read the other side.
Players notice small details.
cons: A slow game can lose players' attention.
Waiting is hard for some.

pairs.tendency: Players pick sides and play as the pace rises, so a side that starts slowly meets a faster game.
pros: The speed shows which sides keep up.
Players learn to decide quickly.
cons: A side slow to start is hurried.
The end comes in a rush.

pairs.tendency: Some throws give another go at once, so a side with many chances to hit can move several times before the other side moves.
pros: A bonus move can swing a game.
Players hope for a lucky streak.
cons: One player can move many times while the others wait.
A side built for one move at a time gains little.

pairs.tendency: Players build their side in the first stage and play it in the second, so the early choices set up the later ones.
pros: The first stage shapes the second.
Players can plan the whole game.
cons: A build done in stage one cannot be undone in stage two.
Stage one can take as long as stage two.

pairs.tendency: The sides sit inside a model of a real system, such as a village's water, so each side stands for a real group.
pros: The model shows how sides affect one another.
Players learn how a real system works.
cons: A side that does not match the real group gives a false picture.
A simple model leaves out details.

pairs.tendency: Players build sides as groups such as farmers or a council, and each side wants different things.
pros: Each side sees the problem from its own place.
Players can talk about what each group needs.
cons: A side given little to do can feel left out.
Roles can turn into stereotypes.

pairs.tendency: Players build different sides but draw from one limited supply, so a side that takes a lot leaves less for the rest.
pros: The supply links all the sides.
Players can see when taking too much hurts everyone.
cons: A side built to use the most runs the supply down.
One side's take can end the game for all.

pairs.tendency: A side's effects arrive a few rounds late, so a choice made in the build comes back later in play.
pros: A choice at the start bears results later.
Players can plan ahead.
cons: A mistake in the build shows up too late to fix.
Cause and effect are hard to link.

pairs.tendency: With the sides built, the table agrees a new rule and plays on to see what changes.
pros: The new rule tests each build.
Players see which sides it helps.
cons: A rule can favour one build.
A rule that changes a lot can start arguments.

pairs.tendency: After the game, players talk through what each side did and why.
pros: Talking shows what each build was for.
Players hear why others chose as they did.
cons: The talk can take as long as the game.
A player can feel put on the spot.

pairs.tendency: What the sides do changes the game for ever, so the next game starts where this one ended.
pros: The sides carry on into the next game.
Players see a history.
cons: A mistake stays.
A destroyed piece does not return.

pairs.tendency: Players build sides in a game whose rules argue a point, so the sides serve the point.
pros: The sides show what the game says.
Players can talk about what the rules reward.
cons: A player may disagree with the point.
The sides may seem to push one view.

pairs.tendency: Real money or a promise is on the line, so a careless build costs something in real life.
pros: Real stakes make players take care.
Friends see how each other handles risk.
cons: A loss reaches past the game.
Some players stay out.

pairs.tendency: Players build sides that earn points for something that matters, such as health, so the points start to stand for it.
pros: Points make a hard thing easy to count.
Players see what a number leaves out.
cons: Chasing points can push out the thing they stood for.
A side built for points may skip the value.

pairs.tendency: Players build sides for a way of living that does not exist yet, such as a village that shares everything, and play it.
pros: Players get a feel for the new way.
A side can show what a new life needs.
cons: A way that works in play may fail outside.
Players may disagree about what the future looks like.

pairs.tendency: Before a lap, a player says "I will reach the red square in three throws" and then rolls. The dice either back the call or wreck it.
pros: Each throw now has a target.
Everyone watches the dice closely.
cons: One low roll can ruin a call.
Luck decides most of the result.

pairs.tendency: Before the first pick, a player names the cards they will end up with, such as three red ones. Each pick from the shared row then helps the call or gives it away.
pros: Every pick has a reason behind it.
Rivals can guess what to take from the caller.
cons: Others may take the cards the call needs.
Changing the call late loses the picks already made.

pairs.tendency: The winner of the auction is the one who names the contract, and then has to do what they bid. A high bid is a promise with a price on it.
pros: A bid shows how sure the caller is.
Rivals learn what a contract is worth to the caller.
cons: Bidding high makes the contract hard to meet.
Quiet players can be priced out early.

pairs.tendency: Say a player calls twelve points for the round, then keeps pulling to reach it. Stopping early drops the call, and going on risks the points already held.
pros: The player knows in advance where to stop.
The table sees who is nervous.
cons: A bust loses the call and the points.
A missed call can tempt a player to keep pulling.

pairs.tendency: At the start of the round, one player says they will hold four regions by the end. Everyone hears it and moves pieces into those regions to break it.
pros: The call tells rivals where to look.
The caller has a clear plan.
cons: Rivals can aim at the called regions.
A failed call leaves pieces spread thin.

pairs.tendency: The caller names three jobs they will take this round, then sends workers to them. One rival who takes a named spot first spoils the whole call.
pros: Each spot counts for more.
Spots get taken early.
cons: A single rival can wreck a call.
Turn order matters a lot.

pairs.tendency: "I will finish a straight line of blue tiles," says a player before laying any. Every tile after that is checked against the call.
pros: The call turns a loose pattern into a target.
The call is easy to check at the end.
cons: Rivals can block the line.
A called pattern leaves little room to change plans.

pairs.tendency: With a hand of cards in front of them, a player says what they will make of it, such as five points. Then comes the choice of what to play and what to hold back.
pros: The call gives the hand a purpose.
Players think hard about which cards to keep.
cons: A thin hand makes a call risky.
Holding cards back can leave no spare plays.

pairs.tendency: Before the first card is led, a player says they will win three tricks. Partners and rivals change how they play once they have heard it.
pros: The call changes how others play their cards.
Whether the aim is met is plain to all.
cons: Rivals know who to stop.
A call can fail by a single trick.

pairs.tendency: The caller offers a card or a favour to anyone who helps the contract along. Talk carries on while the hand is played.
pros: Talk can make a call more likely.
Promises are made in the open.
cons: Deals can fall apart in the middle of a hand.
Talking eats up time.

pairs.tendency: Three sets by the end of the game: that is the call, and the collecting from then on has that number in mind. Rivals learn which cards to hold on to.
pros: Collecting has a number to reach.
Rivals can see which sets are wanted.
cons: A rival who sits on one card can spoil a set.
Collecting may stop once the call is done.

pairs.tendency: A player says how long a road will grow, then lays tiles to stretch it. Rivals lay their tiles to cut it short.
pros: The road has a length to reach.
The shared map shows how near the call is.
cons: A rival can end a road early.
A call can leave the map lopsided.

pairs.tendency: The first caller names a rule for the chain, such as "every answer ends on a rhyme". Each reply has to fit it, and the first one that does not fails the contract.
pros: The contract gives the chain a rule.
Everyone listens closely to the last line.
cons: One slip ends the chain.
It is hard to think fast and listen at once.

pairs.tendency: With talking banned, the caller has to show the contract with a sign, such as a raised hand or a card laid down early. The others guess what it means.
pros: The call has to be shown with a sign.
Players learn to read each other's signs.
cons: A sign can be misread.
A mistaken sign sinks the whole contract.

pairs.tendency: A rival changes a rule just after the contract is called, so the call is harder to meet. The caller may change another rule in reply.
pros: Rule changes can rescue or ruin a call.
Players think about what each rule does to the call.
cons: Nobody can plan far ahead.
Arguments start over what a changed rule means.

pairs.tendency: "I will bring back the stolen lamp by dawn," says a character, and the player then acts to keep that vow. The vow is the contract.
pros: A vow gives the character a goal.
Players speak in the voice of the character.
cons: A broken vow changes the story.
A player may feel stuck with a vow they spoke aloud.

pairs.tendency: Before the tower goes up, a player calls how many blocks they will place without a fall. The hands then have to do what the mouth said.
pros: Everyone watches the hands.
The call is plain to see.
cons: Nerves can shake the hands.
A fall ends the call at once.

pairs.tendency: Before the pens come out, a player promises their village will reach the river. Others draw too, and some draw things that block the way.
pros: The drawing has a direction from the start.
The map shows who kept their promise.
cons: Others can draw in the way.
A map full of calls can look crowded.

pairs.tendency: The call is five enemy pieces turned before the end. Each capture adds a piece to the caller's side and counts toward the number.
pros: Each capture counts twice.
The caller's side grows with every capture.
cons: The caller's new pieces become targets.
Reaching the number may take many turns.

pairs.tendency: One team calls that nobody on it will be left in jail at the end. A single catch breaks the call unless a teammate gets there in time.
pros: The call asks the team to guard each other.
Rescue runs become the main event.
cons: One caught player can sink the call.
A player in jail is out of the action.

pairs.tendency: The caller names a number of captures, then builds walls of stones around enemy pieces. The other side sees each wall growing and breaks out.
pros: The call shows rivals where the walls are going.
Players read the board for gaps.
cons: Calling early lets a surrounded piece escape.
Setting up the walls is slow.

pairs.tendency: A player who is behind calls a big contract on purpose, because the catch-up rule would carry them forward if it works. A player in front calls a small one.
pros: A call lets players choose how much risk to take.
A player who trails still has a way back.
cons: Leaders may call small and play safe.
A trailing player who calls too much falls further behind.

pairs.tendency: In a game decided by dice, a call is only a guess about what the dice will do. No choice can change the result.
pros: The call turns a throw into a guess with a stake.
Every player gets the same chance.
cons: A call cannot be earned by play.
There is little to do while waiting.

pairs.tendency: Before the round, whoever is It says they will tag three players in one minute. The runners hear the number and decide where to scatter.
pros: It has a number to chase.
Runners know what It is after.
cons: It may tire before the minute is up.
Players near the edge get tagged early.

pairs.tendency: The contract depends on hitting one named rival, so the caller goes after that person. The rival knows what is coming.
pros: The call picks out who will be the target.
The target can prepare.
cons: Others may gang up on the caller.
A rival can feel singled out.

pairs.tendency: "Left edge to right edge in eight turns," calls one player. The other places stones across the path to cut it.
pros: The call turns a chain into a race.
Both sides watch the same line.
cons: One cut stone breaks a long chain.
A fast call leaves gaps in the chain.

pairs.tendency: Because each choice loses to another, a call that "my pick will beat yours" is a guess about what the other player will choose.
pros: Guessing now carries a stake.
Players try to read each other's habits.
cons: Repeated picks give habits away.
One wrong guess loses the call.

pairs.tendency: The caller names a score, then shows pairs from the hand to reach it. Every shown pair tells the others a little about what is left.
pros: Each shown pair counts toward the call.
Shown pairs help rivals plan.
cons: A call can be missed by a card or two.
Showing cards gives away part of the hand.

pairs.tendency: Each player's contract is shaped by their own power. A player who can bend one rule can call things that others could not meet.
pros: Calls differ from player to player.
Players learn each other's powers.
cons: Calls are hard to compare.
A power may make a call too easy for one player.

pairs.tendency: Once a contract is called, either player may offer to double what it is worth. The other accepts the larger stake or gives up the points.
pros: A doubling makes a call count for more.
The caller shows how sure they are.
cons: A doubled failure costs double.
A quick give-up can end the game early.

pairs.tendency: Knowing the rival has to take any capture, the caller sets a trap and calls the loss of two pieces on purpose. The rival has no choice.
pros: A forced move makes a call easier to plan.
The trap can be seen by those who look.
cons: A rival can break the plan by changing the board first.
The caller may lose a piece for nothing.

pairs.tendency: A character names the trial they will face next, such as a cave guardian, and says they will win it before reaching the next level. The call is checked when the trial ends.
pros: The character goes into the next fight with an aim.
Players watch their characters change.
cons: A character who is not ready may lose the trial.
A failed call can leave the character behind.

pairs.tendency: The caller says how long a list they can keep up. Each player adds one item in turn, and the call is tested when the list reaches that length.
pros: Everyone knows how long the list has to get.
Everyone practises memory.
cons: A single slip ends the list.
Long lists take a long time to say.

pairs.tendency: A newer player starts with a head start and calls a modest contract, while an experienced player starts with less and calls a bigger one. The head start decides whose call is easier.
pros: Calls can be sized to each player.
Both players have a call they can reach.
cons: Setting the head start takes talk.
A very large call can still be out of reach.

pairs.tendency: The hider calls how long they will stay hidden, such as five minutes, and then goes off. The seekers hear the number before they start.
pros: The call gives the hunt a time limit.
Seekers know when to give up.
cons: A hider can be found at once.
A long wait leaves seekers restless.

pairs.tendency: Three hops in one turn: that is the call, so the player sets up a line of pieces to hop over. The call can be checked at once.
pros: The player has to plan several moves ahead.
A chain of hops draws a crowd.
cons: Rivals can break the line before it is used.
A missed hop wastes the set-up.

pairs.tendency: A player calls a result before the first roll, such as three sixes. They keep the matching dice and roll the rest until the call is met or the throws run out.
pros: Keeping dice gives some control over a call.
Everyone sees which dice are kept.
cons: Rerolls run out.
A near miss still counts as a miss.

pairs.tendency: The caller says none of their pieces will be sent back this round, and moves with care. A rival who lands on one of those pieces breaks the call.
pros: The call makes safe spaces matter.
Players watch where rivals can land.
cons: One landing sinks the call.
Moves become cautious.

pairs.tendency: The call is three mills before the end. Each mill takes an enemy piece, so the call and the captures push the same way.
pros: One row does two jobs.
Rivals see the rows forming.
cons: Rivals can break a mill before it closes.
A call for many mills can leave few pieces on the board.

pairs.tendency: Seven letters, one word: the caller names it and then collects letters to spell it. Others draw from the same pool.
pros: The caller has one word to aim for.
Players watch each other's letters.
cons: A rival can take the missing letter.
A long word can be out of reach.

pairs.tendency: The caller says they will go out first and plays tiles onto the open ends one by one. A missed turn sets the call back.
pros: Each tile played has a job.
The open ends show what is needed.
cons: A missing number forces a skipped turn.
Rivals can close an end that the caller needs.

pairs.tendency: A player calls two melds before the hand ends and lays sets face up as they finish them. Each laid set shows the others how close the call is.
pros: Each meld is a step toward the call.
Rivals see the progress.
cons: Rivals can add to a meld that was laid.
Laid sets show what is left in the hand.

pairs.tendency: The caller keeps one power in reserve to rescue the contract if things slip. Using it takes the marker off the board for keeps.
pros: A reserved power backs up the call.
Players think about when to spend it.
cons: A power spent early is gone.
A call that needs the power leaves nothing for the next one.

pairs.tendency: The caller offers a contract, and the other player may turn it down or pick between two versions. In the end both of them have shaped the call.
pros: The call is agreed by both sides.
Each offer shows what the caller thinks they can do.
cons: Offers can be turned down again and again.
The start is slow.

pairs.tendency: The first player whispers the contract to the next, and it travels round the table. By the time it comes back, the call may have changed.
pros: The call changes as it travels.
Players enjoy the changes.
cons: Nobody knows the true call until the end.
The last player may act on the wrong call.

pairs.tendency: After the pass, each player calls a contract based on the cards they got. The cards a player hands over also hint at their own plan.
pros: Calls follow from the cards received.
Passing hints at plans.
cons: A call is made with cards chosen blind.
A pass can hand a rival what they need.

pairs.tendency: One player writes the terms of the contract and the other picks a side. So the one who sets the terms tries to make the call even for both.
pros: The setter has to think about both sides.
The pick keeps both sides close.
cons: Setting terms takes thought.
A careless set-up is picked apart at once.

pairs.tendency: Two pieces to the far end: that is the call. Each piece that arrives turns into a bigger one.
pros: Pieces have somewhere to head.
A promoted piece can change the board.
cons: Rivals can block the far end.
Pushing forward leaves the back thin.

pairs.tendency: A team calls its finishing time before the race. Each runner hands over to the next, and the clock decides the call.
pros: A team call needs every runner.
Hand-overs show where time is lost.
cons: One slow leg spoils the call.
A runner can feel the weight of the whole team.

pairs.tendency: The caller says a safe shape will stand on the board within ten moves. The other player tries to surround the stones before the shape closes.
pros: The caller has one shape to finish.
A finished shape cannot be taken.
cons: Rivals can break the shape early.
Building the shape can leave other areas open.

pairs.tendency: The contract names the prize cards a player will win, such as the top trump. Tricks that win no prize add nothing to the call.
pros: The call picks out the prizes.
Players can tell what is worth fighting for.
cons: One rival can beat a call for a single card.
Tricks without prizes feel empty.

pairs.tendency: A player calls the hand they will make from the middle cards and their own. Everyone sees the same middle, so others can aim for the same hand.
pros: The call is tested against shared cards.
Everyone can see the middle.
cons: A rival can finish the same hand first.
A call made early may not fit the middle.

pairs.tendency: The caller says they will take the pot that everyone paid into. If the call fails, the pot stays and grows.
pros: A failed call raises the next prize.
The pot gives every call a reward.
cons: A lucky call can take it all.
A big pot draws many callers at once.

pairs.tendency: The caller names the pit where the last seed will land, then scoops and sows to check. Anyone who counts can see it coming.
pros: The call is a count made in advance.
Counting seeds is part of the call.
cons: A miscount loses the capture.
Checking the count by eye is slow.

pairs.tendency: A player calls a contract and may swap their hand for the spare one first. They gamble on cards that nobody has seen.
pros: The spare hand gives a chance to rescue a call.
Players guess what the spare holds.
cons: The swap may leave the caller with cards that do not fit.
A swap tells the table the first hand did not suit the call.

pairs.tendency: The caller says they will land on one named square, perhaps a safe one, and plans the throws around it. Other squares send a piece back or lose a turn.
pros: Squares on the route start to matter.
Players know which squares to avoid.
cons: A special square can undo the call.
Calls near trap squares are risky.

pairs.tendency: Every card has a price, and a contract has to be paid for too. The caller names the contract and then spends to meet it.
pros: A call can be planned around a budget.
Players count what they have.
cons: Paying for the call leaves less for other things.
Rivals see how much has been spent.

pairs.tendency: The caller says they will hold two places, then shares their forces between them. A rival goes for the place with fewer pieces.
pros: The call fixes where the forces go.
The split shows the plan.
cons: A thinly held place can be taken.
Putting many pieces in one place leaves the other open.

pairs.tendency: Before the music starts, a player calls where they will be when it stops. They move with that spot in mind.
pros: Moving round has an aim.
Everyone watches for the signal.
cons: A late stop spoils the call.
Crowds push for the same spot.

pairs.tendency: After calling, the player swaps cards to suit the contract. Each swap shows the others what the hand is missing.
pros: Swaps move the hand toward the call.
The others learn what is missing.
cons: Swaps can run out.
A hand fitted to the call can be hard to use for anything else.

pairs.tendency: The caller picks up the whole pile to build toward the contract. The pile gives cards and also shows what the rivals threw away.
pros: Picking up the pile can speed up a call.
The pile shows what rivals gave up.
cons: A big pile takes time to sort.
A pile can bury the cards that are needed.

pairs.tendency: Once trumps are named, a player calls how many tricks they will win with them. A low trump can beat a high card of another suit.
pros: Trumps make a call easier to meet.
The called suit is known to all.
cons: Rivals may hold trumps too.
One trump played by a rival can sink a call.

pairs.tendency: On the first board the caller names a contract, while on the second board they play the other side. A move on one board changes what is possible on the other.
pros: The call has to hold across two boards.
Players watch both boards at once.
cons: Attention can run short.
A win on one board can be lost on the other.

pairs.tendency: The caller holds a wild card to fill the gap in a contract and keeps it hidden until the last moment.
pros: A wild card makes a call safer to try.
Players guess who holds one.
cons: A wild card used early is wasted.
Rivals can count wilds and expect the gap to be filled.

pairs.tendency: A line across the edge of the board, from right back round to left, is the call. Rivals who forget the edge is joined miss the threat.
pros: The call uses the joined edge.
The board has no real corners.
cons: New players miss the wrap.
Lines can be cut from both sides.

pairs.tendency: The one who knows the secret calls how many questions the others will need, such as ten. Every answer is yes or no.
pros: The call sets a limit on questions.
Each answer narrows the list.
cons: Questions can run out before the secret is found.
Vague questions use up the count.

pairs.tendency: A player calls the turn on which they will cross the line, then races to meet it. Rivals hear the number and try to beat it.
pros: The caller has a turn to beat.
The race is easy to follow.
cons: A lucky run can beat a leader's call.
A slow start puts the call out of reach.

pairs.tendency: Thirty points is the call, and a call that is met scores in full. Rivals hear the number and set their own.
pros: The call is a score target.
Everyone sees the target.
cons: Missing it can cost the lead.
Players may chase the number and forget the game.

pairs.tendency: The caller says they will outlast two rivals. Each knock-out brings the call nearer.
pros: Knock-outs are counted toward a number.
Rivals see who is next.
cons: A player who is out early cannot help.
Waiting for others to finish is slow.

pairs.tendency: The whole group calls one contract together, such as holding out for ten rounds. If the game wins, they all fail.
pros: The call is shared.
Players talk over their plans.
cons: One careless move sinks everyone.
A single loud voice can steer the call.

pairs.tendency: The group names a goal and each player says which part they will do. The goal belongs to all of them.
pros: The call splits the goal into parts.
Each player knows their own job.
cons: A player who skips a part sinks the goal.
Talk about who does what can take long.

pairs.tendency: Every player has a secret goal, and a public call changes how they play it. A bold call can cover for a true aim.
pros: A called contract can hide a secret goal.
Players try to read each other.
cons: Calls can mislead.
Players can guess aims wrongly.

pairs.tendency: "The hero reaches home," says one player, and that is how the story will end. The game plays on to see whether the call holds.
pros: The call is a promise about the ending.
The ending is checked against the call.
cons: A story can twist away from the call.
A set ending narrows the story.

pairs.tendency: In a game where nobody wins, a call gives the group something to look back on. After play they talk about whether it was met.
pros: The call becomes a point for talk.
Nobody loses points.
cons: A call has no prize.
Players may lose interest in meeting it.

pairs.tendency: Before play, each player says out loud what a win means for them. Others then know what the call is for that player.
pros: A private aim is said out loud.
Players can judge themselves.
cons: Calls cannot be compared across players.
A modest call is easy to meet.

pairs.tendency: The call is simply to stay out of the loser's seat. Every failed call makes it more likely that someone else is the one left.
pros: The call is about staying safe.
Players watch who is at risk.
cons: One failed call can mark the loser.
Players call small to stay out of trouble.

pairs.tendency: The contract is ten more rounds of play. Meeting it means that nobody ends the game.
pros: Lasting is the whole aim.
Players help each other.
cons: A rival can end the game early.
The game can drag on.

pairs.tendency: The contract on offer is one the game cannot reward. Meeting it brings no prize, and the game says so.
pros: The call shows a goal the game will not reward.
Players ask why they call at all.
cons: A call has no end.
Players may leave.

pairs.tendency: Alone against the dealt cards, the player calls how many they will clear before getting stuck. Nobody else can touch the layout.
pros: The player sets a target against the layout.
Nobody else can interfere.
cons: A stuck layout ends the call.
A big call is hard to meet.

pairs.tendency: Two wins out of three is the call, and once that count is reached the match can stop. A lost game can pull the call out of reach.
pros: The win count is set before play.
The match can end early.
cons: One lost game can put the call out of reach.
A player with few wins left may give up.

pairs.tendency: A player calls to finish under ten points, then plays to dodge points. A call that is met takes the round.
pros: There is a ceiling to stay under.
Players avoid picking up points.
cons: One big pick-up breaks the call.
Players may avoid taking action.

pairs.tendency: The caller names the exact roll they need to finish, such as a three. Going over loses the win.
pros: One number is the target.
Players wait for the right number.
cons: A roll that is too high wastes a turn.
The wait can be long.

pairs.tendency: Here the call is to lose the most pieces, and meeting it wins. Everyone gives things away on purpose.
pros: The call turns losing into a plan.
Players hand out pieces.
cons: Rivals try to refuse gifts.
The rules can confuse new players.

pairs.tendency: Each player calls their own contract and builds alone. Nobody can stop another player's call.
pros: Each call stands alone.
Players can work calmly.
cons: There is little to watch in others.
Players compare only at the end.

pairs.tendency: Rivals attack to break the called contract while the caller defends it. Every hit lands on the call.
pros: Attacks aim at the call.
The caller knows who to watch.
cons: One hit can break a call.
Revenge can follow.

pairs.tendency: Rivals break the contract by changing the board, with no attack on the caller. The caller sees the effect without seeing a culprit.
pros: The board carries the effect of the call.
Nobody is attacked directly.
cons: The cause is hard to spot.
Players may blame the board.

pairs.tendency: The team names one contract against the game itself. All of them win or all lose by it.
pros: The team shares a call.
Talk is open.
cons: One mistake costs everyone.
The loudest voice can set the call.

pairs.tendency: The group calls a shared contract, but each player keeps a small private reason to finish ahead.
pros: The call keeps most players working together.
Players can still pull ahead.
cons: Private aims can pull players off the call.
It is hard to tell which players are helping.

pairs.tendency: Each team calls a contract, and teammates play to meet it. The other team plays to break it.
pros: Teams share a call.
Teammates plan together.
cons: A team can blame one player.
Teams have to agree on a call first.

pairs.tendency: One player joins the group's contract call while working against it in secret. The rest try to guess who is steering the call off course.
pros: The call gives the traitor cover.
Players watch each other's moves.
cons: A real call can look like a lie.
Trust breaks down.

pairs.tendency: The contract is written in a letter and posted. The reply takes days to arrive.
pros: The call can sit for a long time.
Both players have time to think.
cons: A call can be forgotten.
Letters can be lost.

pairs.tendency: An earlier call from the absent player is read out at the table. The others play to meet or break it with nobody there to explain it.
pros: A call from the absent player sets the aim.
The call is fixed.
cons: Nobody can explain it.
The call may be read wrongly.

pairs.tendency: "Bring back the bell before dark," says the game master, and that is the group's contract. The players act in their characters to meet it.
pros: The game master sets the stakes.
The call gives scenes a purpose.
cons: Players may feel pushed.
The game master has to keep track of every call.

pairs.tendency: The contract is called out in the street, and people walking past may join. Those who pass can help or break the call.
pros: Onlookers can join.
The call is public.
cons: Interruptions are common.
A call can be lost in the noise.

pairs.tendency: The lone player calls a contract against the whole table, and the others work together to break it. If the lone player wins, they are paid more.
pros: One call faces many.
The group can plan to stop it.
cons: The lone player has no one to talk to.
A big payout draws risky calls.

pairs.tendency: Against the pack, a single player calls a contract and plays through. Afterwards a friend can compare results.
pros: The call is private.
Nobody interferes.
cons: Only luck and the player's choices decide.
Nobody is there to see the call met.

pairs.tendency: In a game decided by dice, the call is a bet on luck. The player puts a stake behind a throw that nobody controls.
pros: The call adds a stake to the dice.
Everyone has about the same chance.
cons: Skill cannot help.
Long runs of low throws can sink a player.

pairs.tendency: The caller has rerolls to rescue a call. The call asks how much of the luck can be softened.
pros: Rerolls give some control.
Players think about when to reroll.
cons: Rerolls run out.
A reroll can come up lower.

pairs.tendency: Mostly skill decides the contract, but a small bit of luck can tip a call either way. The caller plans for what they can control.
pros: The call rests mainly on planning.
A little luck keeps the result open.
cons: A lucky draw can rescue a thin plan.
A late bit of luck can undo a careful call.

pairs.tendency: With no dice, a call is a statement about what the caller can work out. If it fails, the caller made a mistake.
pros: The call measures planning.
Nothing hides behind luck.
cons: A caller who misjudges loses.
New players are at a disadvantage.

pairs.tendency: The throw is read as a message, and the contract is called in answer to what it says. The caller treats the sign as advice.
pros: The call follows the sign.
Players talk about what a throw means.
cons: Readings can differ.
A sign can be bent to fit a call.

pairs.tendency: The contract is that the group will act at the same moment without a signal. Success comes from sensing when the others will move.
pros: The call depends on the group's feel for each other.
Players pay close attention.
cons: A call cannot be forced.
One distracted player breaks it.

pairs.tendency: A player calls a scene's outcome, such as "we cross the river safely", and then the dice are rolled on the table to see what really happens.
pros: The dice test the call.
The story is shaped by both.
cons: A roll can turn a scene upside down.
Players may feel the dice overrule them.

pairs.tendency: Everyone sees every card and move, so a call is made with nothing hidden. Rivals can work out at once what they need to do to break it.
pros: The call is open to all.
Planning is simple to check.
cons: Rivals can see how to stop the call.
There is no bluff in a call.

pairs.tendency: A call is made on a hand nobody else can see. The others guess from the call what the cards might be.
pros: A call hints at the hidden hand.
Players read each other's calls.
cons: A call gives away part of the hand.
A bluffed call can fool a table.

pairs.tendency: Some players have secret roles, and the contract each calls depends on their role. A call can reveal or hide who they are.
pros: Calls can hint at roles.
Players watch for slips.
cons: A call can give away a role.
Everyone second-guesses every call.

pairs.tendency: The contract is to name the culprit, the room and the tool. The caller uses clues to narrow it down, and a wrong call loses.
pros: Clues make the call possible.
Players share what they have found.
cons: A wrong guess ends the call.
Others can copy a call that worked.

pairs.tendency: A player calls a contract they cannot meet and hopes the table believes it. Rivals decide whether to challenge it.
pros: A call can be a bluff.
Players study each other's faces.
cons: A challenged bluff costs the caller.
Doubting every call slows play.

pairs.tendency: A newcomer calls a contract without knowing the secret rule. The other players say no each time the call breaks it.
pros: The call is shaped by what the newcomer learns.
The rule shows itself in the refusals.
cons: Newcomers fail many calls.
Players who know the rule can steer the others.

pairs.tendency: The one who knows the answer calls how many hints they need, then gives hints by pictures only. The others guess.
pros: Hints are capped in advance.
The hint-giver has a clear task.
cons: Hints can be read in the wrong way.
The hint-giver cannot explain.

pairs.tendency: A player calls a route across the map before it is turned over. Each tile revealed either supports the call or blocks it.
pros: The call is a bet on what lies ahead.
The map unfolds as the call plays out.
cons: A blocked path ends the call.
Calls made too far ahead are guesses.

pairs.tendency: One hand is face up, so the caller can see part of what the table holds. A call is made knowing that.
pros: The open hand helps the caller plan.
Everyone can see the open hand.
cons: The open hand takes away some surprise.
The others can plan against the open cards.

pairs.tendency: Nobody can add up the scores for certain, so a called contract is a guess about who is ahead. A big call hints that the caller is behind.
pros: The call shows how a player reads the score.
Players guess at the standings.
cons: A call can give away a low score.
Nobody is sure who is winning.

pairs.tendency: Players call in turn, going round the table. Each call is heard before the next player makes theirs.
pros: Each call can use what was said before.
Calls are heard one by one.
cons: Players near the end know the most.
Waiting with many players is slow.

pairs.tendency: Everyone writes a call in secret and shows it at the same moment. Nobody can adjust a call after hearing another.
pros: Calls are made without hints.
Nobody waits for another's call.
cons: Two calls can clash.
A call cannot be taken back.

pairs.tendency: Players call the moment they are ready, and the quickest caller gets the contract. The slower ones are left with what remains.
pros: The quickest caller claims the contract.
The pace is fast.
cons: Calls are rushed.
Slower players are left out.

pairs.tendency: The caller has twenty seconds to name a contract, and when time runs out a call is made for them.
pros: A clock sets the length of each call.
The pace stays steady.
cons: Players have little time to weigh the hand.
A call made for a player may not fit the hand.

pairs.tendency: A contract is called on Monday and checked on Friday, with moves made each morning between. The call has to last all week.
pros: The call stretches across days.
Players have time to think.
cons: A call can be forgotten midweek.
The wait for the result is long.

pairs.tendency: A slow pause comes before the call, and the caller takes a breath to decide. The slowness lets a call be said carefully.
pros: Nobody is hurried into a call.
Players have time to think.
cons: Slow calls take long to say.
The pace can wear on the table.

pairs.tendency: As the game speeds up, calls have to be made faster. A late call has less time to be met.
pros: Fast play makes each call urgent.
The end comes in a rush.
cons: Late calls often fail.
Players may call without thinking.

pairs.tendency: The caller lands a throw that gives another go, which could finish the contract at once. A lucky player can meet a call before anyone replies.
pros: An extra turn can speed up a call.
Players watch for a lucky throw.
cons: One player can run ahead.
Rivals sit and wait.

pairs.tendency: The first stage is for picking cards and the second for playing them. The call is made between the two, once the cards are known.
pros: The call comes after the choices are made.
The first stage sets up the second.
cons: A pick made early cannot be mended.
The call may not suit the second stage.

pairs.tendency: A group calls how much water the village wells will hold after the dry season, then plays to see what the model says. The call is checked against the system.
pros: The call is a test of what the model does.
Players learn how the parts connect.
cons: The model may surprise the group.
A model that is too simple can mislead.

pairs.tendency: Each role calls the contract that suits their group, such as a farmer's call for water and a shopkeeper's call for customers. The calls clash.
pros: Each role has its own call.
Players see the problem from several sides.
cons: Calls pull in different directions.
Roles with small calls are overlooked.

pairs.tendency: Each player calls how much they will take from the common supply. If the calls add up to more than there is, the supply runs out for everyone.
pros: The calls show the strain on the supply.
Players can see the total before they take.
cons: Calls can be made too high.
One greedy call can empty the supply.

pairs.tendency: The call is made now, but its result shows only some rounds later. Players have to wait to learn whether the call was sound.
pros: A call tests a plan over time.
Players think about the future.
cons: The result arrives late.
A mistake is hard to trace back.

pairs.tendency: The group agrees a new rule and calls what will change because of it. Play then shows whether the call was right.
pros: The call is a prediction about the rule.
Players test the rule together.
cons: The result may not match the call.
The rule may need more rounds to show its effect.

pairs.tendency: After the game, the group looks back at what each call promised and why it did or did not hold. The calls give the talk something to hold on to.
pros: The calls give the debrief a record.
Players explain their reasons.
cons: Memories of a call can differ.
Long talks can wear on the group.

pairs.tendency: A contract, once called and met, changes the game for keeps. A torn card or a sticker stays on the board for the next game.
pros: A met call leaves a mark.
The next game starts from the mark.
cons: A call cannot be undone.
A rushed call stays.

pairs.tendency: The kind of contract the rules allow makes a point about the world. A game that rewards only roads asks players to call only road contracts.
pros: The calls carry the game's argument.
Players see what the game values.
cons: Some contracts cannot be called.
The point may be missed.

pairs.tendency: The contract is a real promise, such as "I will wash up tonight". Meeting it or failing it carries on after the game ends.
pros: The call matters beyond the table.
Players take the call seriously.
cons: A failed call can sour a friendship.
Some players may refuse to call.

pairs.tendency: A contract is called in points, and the points stand for something that matters, such as kindness. Players start chasing the number.
pros: The call makes a value countable.
Players see how a number can replace a value.
cons: Kindness can turn into a points race.
Players may drop the value once the call is met.

pairs.tendency: The group calls a contract for a village that shares everything, then plays to feel how it works. The call is a promise they try out.
pros: The group tries out a future in play.
Players get a feel for sharing.
cons: The trial may not carry over to real life.
Some players may resist the promise.

pairs.tendency: A throw of the dice carries your piece along the path, and landing on a rival piece turns it to your side. One lucky roll can win a piece that stood far ahead of you.
pros: Every throw can swing a piece.
Easy for new players to follow.
cons: A conversion can arrive with no choice made.
A player who just lost a piece can lose another straight away.

pairs.tendency: Cards are picked from a hand passed round the table, and some of them let you turn a rival piece. Taking a card can also take away the conversion your neighbour wanted.
pros: Each pick can block a neighbour's next capture.
Players learn what the others are saving.
cons: Many players mean long waits for a pick.
The last picker may find no capturing card left.

pairs.tendency: Players bid for the right to capture, and the winner of the auction turns a rival piece to their side. Paying for the chance makes every converted piece cost something.
pros: Each conversion has a price everyone can see.
Players weigh a piece against what it costs.
cons: The player with most money can convert again and again.
A big bid can leave the winner with nothing to spend.

pairs.tendency: You keep converting pieces for more points, knowing one failed try loses the ones you just turned. Each capture makes the next try look easy.
pros: Stopping or going on is a choice every turn.
Small gains grow into big ones.
cons: One failed try can undo many turns.
Other players wait while one player keeps going.

pairs.tendency: A region goes to whoever has most pieces in it, and a conversion adds to your count while it takes from your rival's in one move. Border regions change hands often.
pros: A conversion changes two counts at once.
Players watch the regions they might lose.
cons: Regions can swap owners many times.
A big region can fall to one move.

pairs.tendency: Workers sit on job spots, and a converted worker now blocks its old owner from the spot it used to use. Taking a spot and taking a worker both matter.
pros: One capture can shut a job and help you.
Players watch where rival workers stand.
cons: A player with few workers can run out of jobs.
Losing a worker can spoil the whole turn's plan.

pairs.tendency: A rival is halfway through a row of matching pieces, and you turn the piece in the middle to your side. Their pattern breaks, and yours may be finished by the same piece.
pros: One move breaks a pattern and helps another.
Players guard their own half-built rows.
cons: Long building can be lost at once.
The row nearest to finishing draws every attack.

pairs.tendency: You hold cards that let you convert, and you pick whether to play one now or keep it for later. A card kept back shows the others that you passed on a chance.
pros: Saving a conversion card makes a threat.
Players read each other's waiting.
cons: A held card does nothing while it waits.
A hand full of conversion cards can run dry in one round.

pairs.tendency: The player who wins a trick takes one of the played cards into their own pile, so a card another player used now works for the winner. A won trick brings cards and points too.
pros: Winners gain cards from the table.
Players track which cards have changed hands.
cons: The card you play can end up helping a rival.
Tracking every moved card is hard.

pairs.tendency: Players talk about whose piece will be taken next, and a promise not to convert somebody can be bought with a trade. Deals last only as long as the players keep them.
pros: Threats become things to trade.
The table talks as much as it plays.
cons: A broken promise ends a deal.
Quiet players can be left out of the offers.

pairs.tendency: A converted piece or card counts toward your sets, so one capture can finish your set and break your rival's. Everyone watches the sets that are one piece short.
pros: A single move helps one set and hurts another.
Players notice nearly finished sets.
cons: The nearly complete set draws attacks.
A set can vanish in one turn.

pairs.tendency: You place a tile next to a rival's tile and it flips to your side, changing the roads and fields the shared map shows. The picture on the table keeps changing colour.
pros: The shared map changes with each capture.
Players see who holds what at a glance.
cons: Old plans for a road can be spoiled.
A flipped tile can cut a long road in two.

pairs.tendency: Each move is answered by the next player's move, and an answer can win back a piece you just turned. Play goes back and forth, with pieces changing sides each time.
pros: Each answer builds on the last move.
The game stays close between two players.
cons: A back and forth can run on a long time.
With several players, whose answer is due gets lost.

pairs.tendency: Nobody talks, so a conversion arrives without warning and the loser can only look at the board. Players guess each other's plans from where the pieces sit.
pros: Moves are read from the pieces alone.
Surprise captures land with no chatter.
cons: A captured player cannot protest or ask.
Misreading a quiet table costs pieces.

pairs.tendency: On your turn you may rewrite what capturing does, so a taken piece leaves the game instead of changing sides. Once a rule changes, everyone's plan for conversions changes with it.
pros: The meaning of a capture can change mid game.
Players think about the rules before the pieces.
cons: A plan built on the old rule is lost.
Arguments can start about what a capture now does.

pairs.tendency: Your character is caught and now speaks and acts for the other side. The player voices someone who was a friend a turn ago, and the story takes a turn with them.
pros: A change of side becomes a scene to act out.
The story has a clear turning point.
cons: A player may not enjoy playing against old friends.
Scenes of switching can slow the game.

pairs.tendency: A flicked disc knocks a rival piece off its mark and the piece is turned to your colour. Steady hands decide who gains, and a shaky throw gives the piece back.
pros: The whole table watches every flick.
Skill with the hands decides the swap.
cons: A bump to the table can change the result.
Tired hands lose pieces late in the game.

pairs.tendency: A region drawn in your pen colour can be taken by a rival, who then redraws its border in theirs. The sheet of paper becomes a record of who held what and when.
pros: The map shows the history of every swap.
Players can read the story from the paper.
cons: The sheet gets crowded with redrawn lines.
Marks cannot be rubbed out, so old borders stay.

pairs.tendency: A caught piece might change sides or wait in a jail until a teammate frees it. A table using both has to agree which one applies, and a rescue may even win back a piece that was turned.
pros: A rescue can undo a conversion.
Teammates have a reason to stay close.
cons: The two rules can confuse a new table.
A jail with converted pieces slows everything down.

pairs.tendency: A piece with a ring of rival pieces around it is taken and joins the ring's owner. The ring is a trap, and a closed ring also adds a piece to the trapper's side.
pros: Encircling gains a piece and removes one.
Players watch the empty spaces beside their pieces.
cons: A big army can be turned by a small ring.
Players who stay apart can be rounded up one by one.

pairs.tendency: A player far behind gets a bonus move, and a single conversion can erase the lead. The score swings so often that a lead is hard to hold.
pros: The scores stay close.
Players behind keep trying.
cons: A long game can feel as though nothing is settled.
A player ahead may lose several pieces at once.

pairs.tendency: A turned card or a throw says which piece changes sides, and the players only watch. Nothing is chosen, so the conversions follow the dice.
pros: The game is short.
Anyone can win, whatever their age.
cons: Players have nothing to plan.
Conversions can pile up on one player.

pairs.tendency: The one who is It touches a runner, and that runner joins the chasers. The chasing side grows each round while the runners get fewer.
pros: The game speeds up as runners are caught.
Everyone ends up on the same side.
cons: The last runner is chased by a crowd.
Early catches leave players with less to do.

pairs.tendency: You pick whose piece to turn, and the pick makes one player smaller and you larger. With three or more players, the pick also tells the table who you see as a threat.
pros: Each pick says something to the others.
Players can get back at those who hit them.
cons: Picking the leader may start a pile-on.
A player who is picked often can feel singled out.

pairs.tendency: Your stones have to make one chain across the board, and a conversion in the middle of a rival's chain cuts it and may join it to yours. One turned stone can end a long plan.
pros: A single stone can cut a chain.
Players look at the whole board each turn.
cons: A chain nearly done can be lost at once.
Both players watch the same link.

pairs.tendency: Each kind of piece converts one other kind and is converted by a third. The mix of pieces you bring decides which of your rival's pieces you can turn.
pros: No kind of piece wins every time.
Guessing the rival's mix becomes part of play.
cons: A wrong guess hands the rival a piece.
New players need time to learn who beats whom.

pairs.tendency: You show a pair or a run to score while the cards stay in your hand, and a converted card can break a combination a rival was holding. Showing a pair also tells the others what to take.
pros: Scoring happens during play.
Players learn what the others hold.
cons: A shown pair invites attacks on its cards.
Losing one card can ruin a whole combination.

pairs.tendency: One player's power makes their pieces hard to convert, and another's lets them convert two at a time. Each person plays a slightly different game against the same board.
pros: Each player has their own way to win.
Replaying the game feels different.
cons: The table has to learn every power.
Players may feel a rival's power was made for them.

pairs.tendency: After a conversion puts you ahead, you offer to double the game's value. The other player accepts and risks a swing back, or gives up and loses the points already at stake.
pros: A lead can be turned into a bigger prize.
The player behind has to judge their chances.
cons: One swing can then cost a lot.
A refused double ends the game early.

pairs.tendency: If you can capture, you have to, and your capture turns the piece. A rival can offer a piece as bait to pull your capturing piece into a spot where it is taken back.
pros: A rival can steer your move.
Players plan sacrifices several moves ahead.
cons: A forced capture can pull your pieces out of place.
New players often fall for a simple bait.

pairs.tendency: Every converted piece adds to your side's power and takes from your rival's. Later challenges are met with more power than you started with.
pros: Gains add up turn by turn.
Early captures matter later.
cons: A player who falls behind early rarely catches up.
The second half can be one-sided.

pairs.tendency: Each turn a player says the list of converted pieces so far and adds the newest. Remembering who now works for whom becomes part of the game.
pros: Memory is part of play.
The list gives a record of every swap.
cons: Long lists are hard to say without slips.
A forgotten item can start a dispute.

pairs.tendency: A player with more skill starts with fewer pieces, and a newer player gets a real chance because each conversion closes the gap quickly. The two players start unequal and move closer.
pros: A gap can close fast.
Players of different ages can play together.
cons: The newer player can win pieces quickly and lose them again.
The gap needs to be set before play starts.

pairs.tendency: A seeker finds a hider, and the hider joins the seekers. The hunting side grows and the hiding side shrinks until one hider is left.
pros: Hiders turn into helpers.
The last hider is under pressure.
cons: Caught players have to wait with nothing hidden.
Early finds shrink the number of hiders quickly.

pairs.tendency: Your piece hops over a rival's piece and lands behind it, and the piece you hopped over changes sides instead of leaving. A line of rival pieces can become your line in a few hops.
pros: One hop gains a piece.
Chains of hops can change a whole row.
cons: Pieces left next to an empty space are easy to take.
A turned piece can be hopped back at once.

pairs.tendency: You roll your dice, set some aside and roll the rest, and the dice you hold decide whether a conversion works. Keeping high dice makes a capture more likely.
pros: Players decide which dice to hold.
Each roll can raise or lower the odds.
cons: A last roll can ruin the plan.
Waiting for others to finish their rolls takes time.

pairs.tendency: Landing on a rival's piece might send it home or turn it to your side. When both rules are there, the table has to say which happens, and safe spaces protect from both.
pros: Landing on a piece has a result.
Safe spaces give players places to rest.
cons: New players lose track of which rule applies.
A piece sent home loses the progress it made.

pairs.tendency: A row of three lets you take a rival piece, and with conversion the taken piece joins your side, perhaps right into your next row. Building a row can feed the next one.
pros: One row can lead to another.
Players watch each other's pairs.
cons: A rival can break a row by turning one piece.
A player who falls behind loses pieces and the means to build.

pairs.tendency: Pieces are letters, and a word you make turns a rival's letter tile to your colour. The same letter can score for different players at different times.
pros: A letter can change owners many times.
Players look for words that use rival letters.
cons: Hunting for words slows the turns.
A dictionary may be needed to settle disputes.

pairs.tendency: A tile fits an open end of the line if its number matches, and the tile it touches may turn to your side. A line gets longer and changes hands as it grows.
pros: Each tile can change the line.
Players watch the open ends.
cons: A player with no matching tile misses a turn.
A turned tile can close an end a rival needed.

pairs.tendency: You lay a finished set on the table, and a capture lets a rival take over a card from it. A set laid down for safety can lose a card the next turn.
pros: A laid set is open to attack.
Players can add to sets on the table.
cons: A meld can lose cards one at a time.
Cards taken from a set can leave it incomplete.

pairs.tendency: Each piece has a power that works once, and using it to convert a rival piece takes its marker away. Waiting for the right moment is part of the game.
pros: A power comes with a decision about timing.
Everyone knows who still holds a power.
cons: A power used too early is gone.
A power kept too long may never be used.

pairs.tendency: You offer a conversion and the other player can turn it down or pick between two you offer. So each move is decided by two players.
pros: Both players shape each capture.
Offers show what you are willing to give up.
cons: A refused offer wastes a turn.
Players can stall by refusing everything.

pairs.tendency: A message goes along the line, and a player who has been converted passes on a changed message for their new side. Nobody can check it until it reaches the end.
pros: The message can shift along the way.
Players enjoy guessing who changed it.
cons: The final message may be nothing like the first.
Players cannot tell who is on which side.

pairs.tendency: Before play you hand some cards to another player, and those cards may help them convert your pieces. You pass away cards you could use against yourself.
pros: Passing reveals what you fear.
Every hand starts with a mix of players' choices.
cons: A card you pass can come back against you.
You do not see what you receive until you have chosen.

pairs.tendency: One player sets up the board and the other picks a side. The setter has to think about how the first conversion will fall, since either side may be taken.
pros: The setter has a reason to be even-handed.
The start becomes a puzzle in itself.
cons: A setter who misjudges hands over the easier side.
Setting up takes time before play begins.

pairs.tendency: A piece that reaches the far end becomes a more powerful piece, and if a promoted piece is converted the rival gets the promotion. Pushing a piece to the end can hand a rival the stronger piece.
pros: Pieces have something to aim for.
Late captures can matter a lot.
cons: A promoted piece is a prize for a rival.
Players may hold a piece back so as not to risk it.

pairs.tendency: Your team races in legs, and a runner caught in a leg changes to the other team's runner. The teams swap members during the race.
pros: The race changes as runners switch teams.
Every leg matters to both teams.
cons: A team can end up very small.
Teams have to keep track of who runs for whom.

pairs.tendency: Some shapes cannot be captured, so they cannot be converted, and players build them to keep a base. The rival tries to surround the shape before it is complete.
pros: A safe base gives a place to start from.
Players have a clear shape to aim at.
cons: Building a safe shape takes many turns.
A shape half done can be turned in one move.

pairs.tendency: The prizes are named cards, and converting one of them moves its points to you. A single card can win more than one prize.
pros: Everyone knows what the prizes are.
A turned card can move the score a lot.
cons: Players guard the prize cards.
The prize cards can draw all the attacks.

pairs.tendency: Cards in the middle are open to everyone, and a card turned to your side stops being shared. Players watch which cards leave the middle.
pros: The shared cards shrink as the game goes on.
Everyone sees what is left.
cons: A taken card can end a rival's plan.
Shared cards can run out early.

pairs.tendency: Everyone puts a counter in the middle, and the player who converts the last rival piece takes the pot. If nobody does, the pot grows for the next round.
pros: The prize grows when nobody wins.
Players have an extra reason to attack.
cons: A big pot can lead to rash moves.
The player who turns the last piece takes everything.

pairs.tendency: You scoop seeds from a pit and drop them one by one, and where the last seed lands decides which pit you take. The taken seeds go into your store and your rival's pit is empty.
pros: A single sowing can change the count.
Players count ahead before scooping.
cons: The pits shift so fast that plans go out of date.
Counting seeds takes time.

pairs.tendency: A spare hand lies face down in the middle, and the player who takes it may find cards that convert pieces. Taking it also means leaving the rest for a rival.
pros: One player gets a surprise hand.
Players have a first choice to make.
cons: The spare hand can be a gift to one player.
Rivals may feel the deal was uneven.

pairs.tendency: Some squares keep a piece safe from conversion, and others send a converted piece back to its old owner. Players aim for the squares and stay away from others.
pros: Squares give pieces a place to rest.
The board has places that matter.
cons: A piece on the wrong square can be lost.
Players cluster around the same few squares.

pairs.tendency: Turning a rival piece costs a price, and a converted piece may be cheaper than buying a new one. Players weigh what a capture costs against what it brings.
pros: Every capture has a cost to count.
Players choose how to spend.
cons: A player with less to spend cannot convert.
Counting costs slows the turn.

pairs.tendency: You share a fixed amount of strength between several places, and a conversion in one place makes your force there larger and the rival's smaller. Both players are sharing out their strength at the same time.
pros: A win in one place shifts the balance.
Players guess how a rival will share.
cons: A thin place can be lost easily.
One lost place can pull strength from another.

pairs.tendency: The music stops, and the slowest player is caught and joins the other side. The game shifts to a hunt as the players left get fewer.
pros: Players listen for the signal.
Anyone can be caught by being slow.
cons: Players caught early have little left to do.
The last few players are watched by everybody.

pairs.tendency: You put cards back and take new ones to build a hand that can convert, and another player may need to agree to the swap. A swap can hand a rival the card they wanted.
pros: A hand can be tuned before play.
Players watch what others swap.
cons: A swap can help a rival.
Waiting for agreement slows the table.

pairs.tendency: Thrown cards go into one pile, and taking it gives you cards that may convert pieces. The pile you pick up may hold cards a rival wanted.
pros: The pile can hold useful cards.
Players track what was thrown.
cons: A big pile is heavy to carry.
Picking up the pile can hand your hand to rivals.

pairs.tendency: A card in the named suit beats the others, and a captured trump becomes yours to use. A low trump can turn a high card from another suit.
pros: Trumps are worth holding on to.
Players know which cards matter most.
cons: Trumps in a rival's hand are a threat.
The trump suit shapes every conversion.

pairs.tendency: You play two boards at once, attacking on one and defending on the other, and a conversion on one board changes what you can do on the other. Your attention is split.
pros: Both boards depend on each other.
Players think about two places at once.
cons: A mistake on one board can spread to the other.
Turns take much longer.

pairs.tendency: A wild card stands for any piece you pick, so it can turn a rival piece of the kind you need. A wild card in a rival's hand can end a plan.
pros: A wild card fills any gap.
Players hold one for a key moment.
cons: A wild card can be captured and used against you.
Every player wants the wild cards.

pairs.tendency: The edges of the board are joined, so a piece that walks off the right side comes in on the left and can be surrounded from behind. No piece is ever on the edge.
pros: Pieces are always in the open.
Attacks can come from any side.
cons: The board is hard to read at first.
Safe corners do not exist.

pairs.tendency: One player knows which pieces have changed sides, and the others ask yes or no questions to find out. Each answer shrinks the list of who is on which team.
pros: Each answer cuts the list.
Players learn to ask careful questions.
cons: Questions about the wrong piece waste a turn.
The player who answers has nothing to do.

pairs.tendency: A runner caught on the way joins the rival's runner, so the racers swap sides during the race. First to the end wins, but a lead can be turned in a move.
pros: The race can swing late.
Every runner is in danger until the end.
cons: A long lead may mean nothing.
A converted runner may take the lead for the rival.

pairs.tendency: Pieces turned to your side count toward your score, and the same piece scores for different players as it changes hands. The score at the end is the last owner's.
pros: Every conversion changes the scores.
Players count what they might gain.
