cons: A late conversion can change the winner.
Keeping the score takes time.

pairs.tendency: A captured player is not knocked out but joins the capturer, so the field shrinks into one team. The last player alive is facing everyone else.
pros: Nobody sits out.
The field shrinks quickly.
cons: The last player is outnumbered.
The end can feel certain from the middle.

pairs.tendency: The game itself captures your pieces and converts them, and you all try to survive together. Every piece lost to the game is a piece that works against you.
pros: The table has one problem to solve.
Players help each other guard pieces.
cons: A lost piece can turn into a threat.
One player's mistake can hurt everyone.

pairs.tendency: The group works toward a goal, and a converted piece now works against it. The players have to guard each other's pieces and win some back.
pros: Players guard each other.
A win belongs to everyone.
cons: A converted piece can pull the goal further away.
One slow player can leave the team short.

pairs.tendency: Each player has a secret goal, and a conversion may help a rival's goal without anyone knowing. You turn a piece for your own reasons and the others have to guess why.
pros: Captures give hints about goals.
Players read each other's moves for clues.
cons: A converted piece can give your goal away.
You may help a rival without meaning to.

pairs.tendency: A captured character joins the other side of the tale, and the story turns with them. The ending depends on who ends up on which side.
pros: Captures become turns in the story.
The story is shaped by the table.
cons: Key characters can switch sides early.
The story may lose its first plot.

pairs.tendency: Nobody wins, and conversions change how the board looks. At the end you look at the colours and talk about what happened.
pros: The board becomes a picture of the game.
Players can talk about the swaps afterwards.
cons: Captures have no prize to aim for.
Some players may lose interest without a goal.

pairs.tendency: One player is happy to turn a few pieces, and another wants every rival piece on their side. Each player decides what success means, so a conversion means different things to each.
pros: Each player plays for a different aim.
A small gain may satisfy one player.
cons: Players may not agree on who came out ahead.
A player with a high aim may never meet it.

pairs.tendency: The game goes on until one player has lost everything, and a player who is converted keeps playing for a rival. The loser is the last one with nothing left.
pros: Nobody is out early.
Players try to avoid being last.
cons: The loser is known only at the end.
A converted player may help whoever took them.

pairs.tendency: The aim is to keep playing, and conversions keep any side from being wiped out. Pieces change sides again and again, so the game has no clear end.
pros: No side ever disappears.
The game can run for many turns.
cons: There is no moment to stop.
A long game can lose its direction.

pairs.tendency: The game is made so nobody can win, and conversions never settle anything because a turned piece can always be turned back. So the game does not end on its own.
pros: A piece can always change sides.
Players see what a game without a winner feels like.
cons: Players may feel nothing they do counts.
The game can feel endless.

pairs.tendency: You play alone against the cards, and a card in the layout can be turned to your side to clear it. If you get stuck, the game says you lost.
pros: Each card turned is a step forward.
The layout shrinks as you play.
cons: A stuck layout ends the game.
One wrong turn can block the rest.

pairs.tendency: The games are short and the player who wins the most takes the match, so a late conversion can decide one game. Players who lose a game start the next knowing the other player's habits.
pros: Each game ends with a clear result.
Players adjust between games.
cons: One swing can end a game and a match.
A long match can wear players out.

pairs.tendency: Pieces converted to you count against you, so capturing becomes a gift to give. Players avoid taking pieces and try to push them on to others.
pros: Players work to avoid captures.
The aim is turned upside down.
cons: Players may refuse to take pieces.
The game can stall if nobody wants to capture.

pairs.tendency: Converted pieces add to your total, and going past the target number costs you the win. A capture that pushes you too high is a loss.
pros: Every capture is counted against the target.
Players choose when to stop taking pieces.
cons: A last capture can spoil a close finish.
Players may hold back from capturing.

pairs.tendency: The aim is reversed, so you want to be captured, and a converted piece is now a step toward your aim. Players try to give pieces away while others try to hand them back.
pros: Giving away is the aim.
Players think in a different way.
cons: New players mix up the aim.
Rivals may refuse to take what you offer.

pairs.tendency: Everyone builds their own thing, so there is nobody close enough to convert unless a piece is allowed to cross to a neighbour's side. Without that, the conversion rule rarely comes up.
pros: Each player works at their own pace.
Nobody waits for others.
cons: Captures have nobody to reach.
The rule may never be used.

pairs.tendency: Players attack each other on purpose, and every attack takes from a rival and gives to you. So each hit moves the count by two.
pros: Each attack gains and loses at once.
Players target each other.
cons: The player in front draws every attack.
A player hit many times may give up.

pairs.tendency: Players change the board and the rival feels it, and a piece surrounded by walls or blocked spots is converted without a direct hit. The board does the capturing.
pros: Captures come from the board's shape.
Players think about spaces and walls.
cons: A piece can be turned without a warning.
Players may not know who caused a loss.

pairs.tendency: Everyone is on one team against the game, so conversion only goes one way, from the team to the game's side. The team tries to win pieces back.
pros: The team has one task.
Players help to rescue pieces.
cons: A converted piece may need a rescue plan.
One player's loss is shared by all.

pairs.tendency: Players mostly work together, but one may convert a teammate's piece for a private reason. The team has to decide whether that was an accident.
pros: Teams stay mostly together.
A private aim gives a reason to bend.
cons: Trust can break with a single capture.
Teammates may start to watch each other.

pairs.tendency: Two teams play against each other, and a converted piece moves from one team to the other. Teammates have a reason to cover one another.
pros: Teammates guard each other.
The teams change size as play goes on.
cons: A small team can lose heart.
A big team may leave some players idle.

pairs.tendency: A traitor is a player who secretly works against the team, which is like a piece that has been converted without anyone seeing. The team has to work out who changed sides.
pros: Hidden switches create suspicion.
Players watch each other closely.
cons: Accusing the wrong person costs the team.
A hidden traitor can be missed for many turns.

pairs.tendency: Players are far apart and send moves by letter, so a conversion takes days to reach the other player. The waiting is part of the game, and a reply may turn the piece back.
pros: Each move is thought through.
The wait gives time to plan.
cons: A game can last weeks.
A lost letter can stop the game.

pairs.tendency: The absent player is a ghost who cannot answer when their pieces are taken, so the living convert them without a reply. The absent side may turn into the biggest army.
pros: The ghost's pieces can be won.
Players decide what the absent side stands for.
cons: The absent side cannot defend itself.
The game can feel one-sided.

pairs.tendency: The game master decides whether a conversion works and describes what it means in the story. A captured character might switch sides with a speech or a quiet walk away.
pros: The game master gives each capture a scene.
The story keeps going.
cons: The game master holds a lot of power.
A tired game master can slow the game.

pairs.tendency: The game is played in a street or a park, and a passer-by who is tagged joins your side. The players grow in number as people stop to watch.
pros: Anyone can join by being caught.
The game gathers a crowd.
cons: The sides can become very large.
New players may not know the rules.

pairs.tendency: One player takes on all the others, and a member of the group who is converted moves to the lone side. The lone player is paid more if they win.
pros: The lone player grows when they win.
The group has to stay together.
cons: The group can shrink fast.
The lone player's first captures may decide it.

pairs.tendency: You play alone against the pack, and when you turn a piece the pack loses one and you gain one. Nobody else acts, so luck and your own choices decide how it goes.
pros: You can play at your own pace.
The result can be compared with a friend's.
cons: There is nobody to talk to.
A run of lost pieces is yours alone.

pairs.tendency: The dice decide most things, so conversions follow luck and a lead can go in one throw. Players watch the dice more than the board.
pros: Anyone can win.
The game is quick to learn.
cons: Choices rarely matter.
The same player can be turned again and again.

pairs.tendency: Dice start a conversion, but you may re-roll or play a card to soften an unlucky throw. Pieces change sides less by luck than by how you use your help.
pros: Players have ways to answer an unlucky throw.
Luck stays in play.
cons: Using up your help leaves you open.
Players may spend turns working on rolls.

pairs.tendency: Your choices decide most conversions, with a little luck added by a card or a throw. The careful planner usually wins, but not every time.
pros: Planning is rewarded.
A surprise can still happen.
cons: A lucky draw can undo a plan.
Players may blame the dice.

pairs.tendency: There are no dice, so every conversion is planned and every loss is seen coming. The player who thinks furthest ahead usually turns the most pieces.
pros: Each move can be worked out.
Players learn from their losses.
cons: A new player can lose to an expert.
Long thinking slows the game.

pairs.tendency: A throw is read as a message, and the reading says whose side a captured piece joins. The players talk over what the sign means.
pros: The dice start a conversation.
Players give the throw a meaning.
cons: Different readings can start disputes.
The result may not match what players hoped.

pairs.tendency: Players sense when others are about to act, and a conversion works when two players move at the same instant. Friends who know each other's habits do most of the converting.
pros: Players watch each other closely.
A group that knows each other plays smoothly together.
cons: Strangers find it hard.
Moves cannot be planned alone.

pairs.tendency: A roll is looked up on a table, and the table says who you meet or what is taken. A capture becomes a turn in a tale the dice write.
pros: The dice write part of the story.
Each capture comes with an event.
cons: The table is read each time.
Rolls can lead the story away from a plan.

pairs.tendency: Everything is on view, so every conversion can be seen coming and planned against. Players can count the pieces and see who is ahead.
pros: Nothing is hidden.
Players can plan far ahead.
cons: A mistake is clear to all.
Players may spend a long time thinking.

pairs.tendency: Cards in a hand are secret, so you do not know which rival can convert. A rival may be holding a card that turns your key piece.
pros: Hidden cards make a threat.
Bluffing is possible.
cons: Players may lose pieces by surprise.
Guessing a hand is hard.

pairs.tendency: Some players have a secret role, and a converted piece may change its role and its side. Nobody knows who is on which team.
pros: Roles can be mixed up.
Players watch for clues.
cons: A converted player may not know their new role.
The table may lose track of teams.

pairs.tendency: Clues show which pieces have changed sides, and players work out who holds what. Each conversion leaves a clue for the others to follow.
pros: Each capture leaves a trail.
Players work it out together.
cons: A missed clue can lead to a wrong guess.
Players need to keep notes.

pairs.tendency: You pretend you can convert a piece when you cannot, and a rival has to guess. A bluff can keep a rival away from a piece they could take.
pros: A bluff can protect a piece.
Players learn to read faces.
cons: A caught bluff costs a turn.
A real threat may be ignored as a bluff.

pairs.tendency: One player knows the conversion rule and the others find it out by breaking it. The first captures teach the newcomers what the rule is.
pros: Players learn by playing.
The rule becomes a secret to find.
cons: Newcomers lose pieces while learning.
The player who knows the rule has the advantage.

pairs.tendency: A player who knows which pieces have changed sides may only give hints with pictures or gestures. The others guess who is now on which team.
pros: Hints replace answers.
The table works together on a guess.
cons: A hint can be misread.
The player with the secret cannot speak.

pairs.tendency: The map starts hidden, and a conversion may turn up a tile that was not seen before. Players explore and capture at the same time.
pros: Exploring can bring a surprise.
Captures show new places.
cons: A move into the unknown can lose a piece.
The map is not known when plans are made.

pairs.tendency: One hand lies face up, and a player may use it to convert pieces and their own. Everyone sees the cards that could turn a piece.
pros: The open hand can be read by all.
Players can plan around it.
cons: The player using it has two hands to track.
The open cards cannot be kept secret.

pairs.tendency: Some points are kept secret, so nobody can tell how far a conversion has moved the score. Players guess who is ahead from the pieces on the board.
pros: Captures leave the score unclear.
Players guess from what they see.
cons: A player may attack the wrong rival.
A hidden score can bring a surprise ending.

pairs.tendency: One player acts at a time, so a conversion is followed by a pause while the others watch. The player who has lost a piece plans an answer for their own turn.
pros: Each capture is seen by all.
Players have time to plan a reply.
cons: Waiting can be long with many players.
A pause lets the capturer's lead sink in.

pairs.tendency: Everyone picks a move in secret and all reveal together, so two players may go for the same piece. The piece goes to one of them, or to neither.
pros: Players guess each other at the same moment.
Nobody waits.
cons: Two moves can clash over one piece.
The result of a clash can be unclear.

pairs.tendency: Anyone can act at any moment, so pieces change sides again and again as players race to be first. The quickest hands turn the most pieces.
pros: The game never pauses.
Quick players take most pieces.
cons: Slower players are left out.
It is hard to keep track of the board.

pairs.tendency: Each turn has a clock, and a conversion made in the last second leaves no time for a reply. A move not made in time is lost or made for you.
pros: Time forces a decision.
The game moves quickly.
cons: A rushed move can lose a piece.
Careful players may run short of time.

pairs.tendency: The game runs for days or weeks, and a conversion on Monday may be turned back by Tuesday. Waiting is part of playing.
pros: There is time to plan.
Pieces can change sides many times.
cons: A long game can lose players.
A missed day can cost a piece.

pairs.tendency: The game slows players down on purpose, so each conversion comes after a pause and a breath. The slowness is part of the play.
pros: Each capture feels weighty.
Players think before they act.
cons: A game can take a long time.
Players may lose attention while waiting.

pairs.tendency: The game speeds up, so conversions come more often as timers shrink. The end arrives in a rush, with pieces changing sides faster than anyone can count.
pros: The pace grows each round.
The end comes in a rush.
cons: Mistakes grow with the speed.
New players may fall behind.

pairs.tendency: You convert a piece and go again straight away, so a lucky player can turn many pieces before anyone else moves. A run of conversions can end a game in a single turn.
pros: One capture can lead to more.
A run can change the score at once.
cons: Other players wait through a long turn.
A player who is ahead can pull away quickly.

pairs.tendency: In the first stage you pick your cards, and in the second you use them to convert pieces. What you chose in the first stage sets up what you can capture in the second.
pros: Choices carry over to the next stage.
Players plan in two steps.
cons: A mistake in stage one shows up later.
The second stage can feel set from the start.

pairs.tendency: The board works like a real system, such as a field that changes owner, and a conversion has the effect it would have in real life. Players see what happens to a whole area when one piece changes sides.
pros: Captures show how a system shifts.
Players can compare the game with real events.
cons: A simple rule leaves out many real details.
A model can look settled when it is not.

pairs.tendency: Each player plays a group with its own needs, and a converted piece means that group has switched allegiance. Players see how a group might be persuaded or forced.
pros: Players see the problem from another side.
Each switch has a reason.
cons: A group that is converted may lose its voice.
Players may not agree on why a group switched.

pairs.tendency: Everyone draws from one limited store, and a conversion moves some of the store from one player to another. If the store runs out, it is gone for everyone.
pros: Captures change who draws from the store.
Players see the effect of taking too much.
cons: A big capture can empty the store.
Everyone loses when the store is gone.

pairs.tendency: A conversion shows its full effect a few rounds later, the way a choice this year shows up years on. Players may not see which capture caused a loss.
pros: Choices have lasting results.
Players learn to wait for outcomes.
cons: It is hard to link cause and effect.
A turned piece can hurt its new owner later.

pairs.tendency: Players agree a new rule for conversions, then play on to see what it changes. A rule can be tried safely before it is used for real.
pros: Rules can be tested at the table.
Players see what each rule does.
cons: A rule that seems fine can break the game.
Agreeing a rule takes time.

pairs.tendency: After the game, everyone talks about why pieces changed sides and how it compares with the real problem. Each capture becomes a question for the group.
pros: Captures give the group things to discuss.
Players explain their reasons.
cons: Players may remember the order differently.
A long talk can follow a short game.

pairs.tendency: A converted piece is marked for ever, with a sticker or a tear, and the next game starts where this one ended. Nothing can be turned back.
pros: Each capture leaves a mark.
The game has a history.
cons: A mistake stays on the board.
A game with many marks is hard to start fresh.

pairs.tendency: If capturing always converts, the game says something about how people change sides. Players feel the claim by playing it.
pros: The rules say something about the world.
Players can argue with the claim.
cons: Not every player agrees with the point.
The point may be missed if players only chase the win.

pairs.tendency: A converted piece carries a real cost, such as a promise or a favour owed. The line around the game is thin, and a capture can stay with the players afterwards.
pros: A capture can matter beyond the table.
Players take each move seriously.
cons: A lost piece can sour a friendship.
Players may avoid capturing.

pairs.tendency: Points stand for something that matters, and a conversion moves those points from one player to another. Players start to chase the points instead of what they stand for.
pros: Captures show what the points are worth.
Players may talk about what the points mean.
cons: The thing the points stand for can be forgotten.
Chasing points can lead to odd choices.

pairs.tendency: Players try a way of living where people change sides freely, and conversions show how that would feel. A capture becomes a way to try an idea out.
pros: Players try out an idea.
A switch shows how a new way of living might work.
cons: Players may find it hard to see the game as a practice.
The rule may not match how real people behave.

pairs.tendency: Dice move everyone along the path, and the jail sits on that path. A teammate has to throw the right number to land on it, so freeing a friend depends on one roll.
pros: A rescue gives a reason to travel to one set space.
Teammates call out the number they need.
cons: A jailed player can wait many turns.
A throw that goes past the jail wastes the turn.

pairs.tendency: Cards go round the table and each player keeps one. A jailed player's seat is awkward, because someone has to pick for them or the row goes by.
pros: A pick can be saved for a friend in jail.
Teammates talk about which card to leave in the row.
cons: Passing slows down while a seat is stuck.
The jailed player's hand may fall behind.

pairs.tendency: Teammates bid coins for the right to move first, and a rescue run can be bought with a high bid. The jailed player watches the auction with no say in it.
pros: Coins put a price on freeing a friend.
Teams argue about what a rescue is worth.
cons: The team with more coins frees its people sooner.
A jailed player cannot bid.

pairs.tendency: A runner keeps going for one more step towards the jail while a guard waits nearby. If the runner is caught, the jail gets a second prisoner.
pros: Every rescue is a gamble.
The waiting players watch each step closely.
cons: A greedy run can leave two players in jail.
Jailed players have nothing to do while others take chances.

pairs.tendency: Teams hold parts of a map, and the jail is one of those parts. Whoever holds the ground around it decides which rescuers get in.
pros: Holding the area around the jail blocks rescues.
Pieces spread out across the map.
cons: A team that owns the jail's corner can keep prisoners for a long time.
Rescuers have to push through a crowd.

pairs.tendency: Workers go onto job spots, and one spot is the jail door. If a worker sits there, nobody else can free anyone that turn.
pros: One taken spot stops a rescue for a round.
Players plan which spot to grab first.
cons: A prisoner waits another round behind a blocked door.
Players grumble when their spot is taken.

pairs.tendency: A player lays tiles into a line, and a caught teammate leaves a gap in the pattern. Freeing them fills it again.
pros: A rescue puts a piece back into the pattern.
Players notice gaps that need filling.
cons: A pattern with a gap in it stalls.
Time spent on rescues is time not spent laying tiles.

pairs.tendency: A card in hand can act as a key. A player keeps one back until a friend is caught, then plays it at the right moment.
pros: A kept card has a clear job.
Players read each other's hands for a key.
cons: A card saved for a rescue may never be played.
Holding it leaves the hand smaller.

pairs.tendency: Winning a trick can open the jail door, so a trick has a prize beyond its cards. The partner stuck inside is waiting on who takes the next lead.
pros: Partners play to win tricks for each other.
A trick matters beyond its points.
cons: A hand of low cards leaves a partner in jail for rounds.
Players hold back cards to protect a friend.

pairs.tendency: The jailed player can call for help, and rivals can offer a swap: let mine go and I will leave yours. The jail becomes a place for deals.
pros: Prisoners can be traded by agreement.
Talk decides who walks out first.
cons: A deal can be broken once the door is open.
Jailed players spend turns arguing.

pairs.tendency: Players gather matching groups, and a caught player cannot add to their set. A rescue means the set can grow again.
pros: A freed player goes back to collecting.
Teams plan around who is free to add cards.
cons: A jailed player's set stops where it is.
Rivals can finish their sets while a friend waits.

pairs.tendency: The shared map grows as tiles go down, and the jail tile can end up anywhere. Rescuers lay tiles to build a road to it, and guards lay tiles to cut that road.
pros: Players can build a path to the jail.
The map shows where each prisoner is held.
cons: One tile can cut a path in two.
The jail may end up far from everyone.

pairs.tendency: A player calls a rescue and the next player has to answer with a move that fits it. The chase goes back and forth this way, one move answering another.
pros: Every call gets an answer.
A rescue is built up one reply at a time.
cons: A reply that does not fit breaks the chain.
A jailed player is left out of the back-and-forth.

pairs.tendency: Teammates cannot say who is in jail or who is going to help. They show it by where they stand and when they move.
pros: Rescues rely on reading a friend's move.
Teams invent signs of their own.
cons: A jailed player cannot call out.
Two players may run for the same jail while another friend is missed.

pairs.tendency: A player can change the rule so that the jail opens after two turns, or so that nobody can be caught near the door. The jail is one of the first things to be changed.
pros: A trapped team can change its own situation.
The jail itself can be altered.
cons: A new rule can undo a rescue plan.
Teams argue over what the new rule means.

pairs.tendency: Each player speaks as a character, so the jailed friend has a name and a reason to wait, and the rescuer says why they would risk the walk.
pros: A rescue becomes a scene.
Players speak for the people in jail.
cons: A jailed player has little to do for long stretches.
Play slows down while each rescue is acted out.

pairs.tendency: To open the jail, a rescuer has to flick, stack or balance something. A shaky hand leaves the friend inside.
pros: A rescue depends on a steady hand.
Everyone watches the attempt.
cons: A wobble at the wrong moment ruins it.
Players with unsteady hands rarely free anyone.

pairs.tendency: The map is drawn as play goes, so the jail is a place somebody puts down on paper, and the road to it gets drawn too.
pros: The jail can go where the group chooses.
Players draw routes to a friend.
cons: A jail drawn far away makes rescues long.
The paper fills up with routes.

pairs.tendency: Pieces surrounded on the board go to the jail instead of off the board, so a surrounded stone can come back. A friend whose stones reach the jail brings it home.
pros: A surrounded piece is not lost for ever.
Players think twice before closing a wide net.
cons: Surrounding takes many moves and a rescue can undo it.
Prisoners can pile up.

pairs.tendency: A team with many people in jail gets a lift, such as a free release or an extra move. A team that is behind has a way back.
pros: A team with many prisoners keeps a chance.
The lead can shrink.
cons: A lead built from captures can vanish.
Players may let a friend be caught to get the lift.

pairs.tendency: Dice or cards pick who is caught and who is freed. Nobody chooses where to run, so a rescue is only a lucky result.
pros: A rescue needs no plan.
Rounds go fast.
cons: A jailed player cannot do anything about it.
Teammates have nothing to work out together.

pairs.tendency: The chaser touches runners and the touched go to jail. A friend slips past to free them, and the chaser has to guard the door and chase at once.
pros: A touch sends a runner to jail.
Runners dash to free a friend.
cons: The chaser cannot watch everyone.
Caught players stand and wait.

pairs.tendency: On a turn, a catcher picks which player to go after, and may pick the rescuer instead of the prisoner.
pros: Catchers go after the players who try to help.
A target is chosen by name.
cons: A rescuer who is popular with the other side is caught again and again.
With three or more players, one person may be picked every round.

pairs.tendency: A player wants one unbroken chain across the board, and a captured stone breaks it. A rescue can mend the chain at once.
pros: A rescue can join a chain again.
The other side aims for the stones in the middle.
cons: One capture cuts a chain in two.
Players guard their key stones.

pairs.tendency: Each choice beats one other and loses to a third, so a catch depends on picking what beats the runner's choice. A rescue works the same way against the guard.
pros: Guard and rescuer each guess the other's pick.
No fixed plan works every time.
cons: A wrong guess loses a rescue.
The same pick cannot be repeated for long.

pairs.tendency: Players show a pair held in the hand to score, and a jailed player cannot declare. A rescue gets them back to declaring.
pros: A freed player scores again.
Declared pairs tell rivals what is in a hand.
cons: A jailed player misses chances to score.
Declaring early gives away which friend to guard.

pairs.tendency: Each player has a power of their own, so one player may run fast while another opens locks or hides. The team picks who goes to the jail.
pros: A team can send the right person for the job.
One power may open the jail at once.
cons: Losing the rescuer leaves the rest stuck.
Rivals aim at the player with the key power.

pairs.tendency: A player offers to double what the game is worth, and the other side takes it or gives up. A jail full of prisoners changes how likely each side is to accept.
pros: The number of prisoners changes the offer.
A rescue can swing the game.
cons: A double offered just before a rescue lands costs the offerer the points.
Players may give up so as not to see their side jailed.

pairs.tendency: If a capture can be made, it has to be made. A bait piece can pull a guard away from the jail door, and the guard has no choice but to go.
pros: A bait piece draws a guard off the door.
Rescuers can plan around a forced move.
cons: A forced capture can send a piece to jail by mistake.
Players lose choice on their own turn.

pairs.tendency: A character earns more power as play goes, so a freed prisoner may come out more skilled than a new one. A long stay in jail can cost a character their gains.
pros: Rescuers gain skill as the game goes on.
A freed friend is worth more than before.
cons: A jail can set back a character who was growing.
Early captures count for more than late ones.

pairs.tendency: The list is spoken round the table and each player adds one item. A jailed player misses their turn to add, and the others have to keep the whole list in their heads.
pros: Players keep the list going for a friend.
A freed player has to catch up on what was said.
cons: A skipped turn makes the list harder to hold.
Jail adds a gap that is easy to trip on.

pairs.tendency: One team starts short, with fewer rescuers or an extra guard at the jail door. The stronger side gives something up on purpose.
pros: Both sides have a chance.
The jail can be tuned to the group.
cons: A handicap can be argued over.
The short team may still be caught early.

pairs.tendency: One player hides and the others hunt. A hider who is found goes to the jail, and a hider who reaches it unseen frees the rest.
pros: Hiding has a goal.
A free hider can reset the whole hunt.
cons: A found hider waits in a fixed spot.
Seekers cannot leave the jail unwatched.

pairs.tendency: A piece hops over another into the empty space behind it, so a rescuer can hop over a guard and land in the jail. A hop over a guard can also send that guard to jail.
pros: A jump can reach the jail in one move.
Players watch lines of pieces for a path.
cons: A line of guards can block every hop.
A jumped piece can be lost.

pairs.tendency: A player rolls all the dice, keeps the ones that show the number the jail door needs, and rolls the rest again.
pros: Players keep what they need for the door.
A reroll gives another try at a rescue.
cons: Several rolls may pass without the right number.
Others wait while one player rolls again and again.

pairs.tendency: Landing on another piece sends it back to the start. Landing on the jail space frees a friend and also threatens whoever stands there.
pros: Landing on the jail space does two jobs.
Players watch where opponents can land.
cons: A freed piece can be sent back soon after.
The same piece may be sent back and jailed in one round.

pairs.tendency: Three in a row earns a capture, and the taken piece goes to jail instead of off the board. A freed piece comes back and may help break the row.
pros: A row sends a piece to jail without ending it.
A rescue gives a broken row a second chance.
cons: Players building rows leave the jail unguarded.
A mill made often fills the jail.

pairs.tendency: Each player holds letters, and the jail opens when a rescuer spells a word from their hand. A dictionary settles any dispute.
pros: A rescue comes from spelling a word.
Players check each other's words.
cons: A hand with few letters rarely makes a word long enough.
Dictionary checks slow the game.

pairs.tendency: Tiles join the line only where the numbers match. A jailed friend may wait on one tile with the right number.
pros: A jailed player waits for a certain tile.
Players hold on to tiles they need.
cons: No match means a missed turn, and the jail waits longer.
The team may not hold the number at all.

pairs.tendency: Players lay finished sets face up, and others can add to them. A caught player's set stays on the table, and a friend can add cards to it while they wait.
pros: A set on the table can be kept going by a friend.
Melds show what each side holds.
cons: Rivals can add to the set too.
A jailed player cannot add their own cards.

pairs.tendency: Every player gets one power to use a single time. A jail key can be one: use it to free a friend and the marker is gone.
pros: A one-time release is always ready.
Teams argue over when to use it.
cons: Used early, it leaves no way to free later prisoners.
Once spent, the marker is gone for ever.

pairs.tendency: A rescuer offers a move and the other player may turn it down or choose between two. A refused rescue costs a turn.
pros: A rescue offer might be accepted.
Offering two moves hides which one you want.
cons: A refused rescue wastes the turn.
Each turn takes longer with two people deciding.

pairs.tendency: A whisper travels down a line of teammates, and a rescue plan can change on the way. Nobody can check it until it arrives.
pros: A plan travels without the guards hearing.
The sender hopes it arrives as sent.
cons: A changed message sends the wrong rescuer.
Jailed players cannot check what was said.

pairs.tendency: Cards handed to a teammate before play may be the very ones you need after that teammate is caught. They sit in the jail with them.
pros: A teammate holds cards you passed.
Passing early shapes a later rescue.
cons: A passed card is stuck until the rescue.
You cannot take it back at once.

pairs.tendency: One player sets up the jail and the guards, and the other chooses which side to play. The setter has to guess which side will be picked.
pros: The jail and guards are placed with both sides in mind.
The setup becomes a puzzle.
cons: A jail set close to one team gets that team picked.
The setup takes a long time.

pairs.tendency: At the far end a piece is promoted to a stronger one. A promoted rescuer may be able to reach the jail from far away.
pros: Reaching the end changes a rescuer's power.
A far-off piece becomes worth sending.
cons: A runner pushing for the end leaves friends in jail.
Guards hold back to watch the end.

pairs.tendency: Teams run in legs and hand a flag to the next runner. A jailed runner holds the flag, so a leg stops until someone frees them.
pros: A rescue can restart a stuck leg.
Teammates wait for the flag.
cons: One jailed runner halts the whole team.
Handing over near the jail is risky.

pairs.tendency: Some stone shapes cannot be captured, so they never go to jail. The stones outside the shape are the ones caught and rescued.
pros: Safe shapes keep some pieces out of jail.
A rescue matters most for the pieces outside.
cons: Building the shape takes moves that could go to a rescue.
Pieces left outside are the ones caught.

pairs.tendency: Certain named cards are the prizes, and a jailed player cannot help win them. A partner wins them alone until the rescue.
pros: Partners cover for each other.
A prize card is tied to who is free.
cons: A caught partner can lose a card to rivals.
A late rescue can come after the prize is gone.

pairs.tendency: Cards face up in the middle belong to everyone. A jailed player can still see them and plan what to do once free.
pros: Jailed players keep playing in their heads.
Everyone sees the same cards.
cons: A jailed player cannot use the middle cards.
A rescuer knows what the guard can see.

pairs.tendency: The pot grows when nobody wins, and a release can be paid for from it. A prisoner may cost chips to free.
pros: A pot can pay for a release.
A growing pot makes a rescue more tempting.
cons: Chips spent on rescues leave less for the winner.
A big pot makes the guards watch harder.

pairs.tendency: Seeds go into pits, and captured seeds are kept in a jail pit. A rescue sows them back round the board.
pros: Captured seeds sit in one pit and can come back.
The jail pit is easy to see.
cons: Sowing a rescue also drops seeds into the other side's pits.
Counting seeds takes time.

pairs.tendency: An extra hand is dealt face down to the middle. A team with a prisoner may take it to have cards while they wait for the rescue.
pros: The spare hand gives a team that is behind a way to catch up.
Teams decide whether to keep or swap it.
cons: Taking it uses up coins.
Rivals see which team took it.

pairs.tendency: Some squares have rules of their own, and the jail is one of them. Others keep a piece safe or send it back.
pros: Safe squares let rescuers rest.
The jail is one special square among several.
cons: A send-back square can undo a rescue.
A missed turn on a square delays a friend's freedom.

pairs.tendency: Every unit has a price, and freeing a friend costs coins just as playing a card does.
pros: A rescue has a price tag.
Players weigh a rescue against buying something else.
cons: A team short of coins leaves its friends in jail.
Money spent on rescue means fewer units.

pairs.tendency: A fixed number of pieces is shared out between places, so sending some to the jail leaves fewer elsewhere. The other side is sharing out theirs.
pros: Guards and rescuers come from one fixed supply.
The other player is splitting too.
cons: A big rescue leaves other places thin.
Guessing where the other side sends its people is hard.

pairs.tendency: Everyone keeps moving until the signal, then freezes. A rescuer has to judge how close to the jail to be when it comes.
pros: The signal sets the moment for a catch.
Players creep towards the jail before it.
cons: A frozen rescuer is caught in the open.
The slowest player is caught, which fills the jail.

pairs.tendency: A player puts cards back and takes new ones, hunting for the card that opens the jail.
pros: Swapping can find the rescue card.
Players dig for the card they need.
cons: A swap uses a turn.
Others see what was put back.

pairs.tendency: A team may pick up the whole discard pile to hunt through it for the card that opens the jail.
pros: A big pile may hold a key.
Players watch what goes onto the pile.
cons: Taking the pile loads the hand with cards.
A key card left in the pile can be taken by rivals.

pairs.tendency: One suit beats the rest, so a trump card can free a friend by beating whatever the guard plays. Spending it on a rescue means it is gone for the tricks.
pros: A trump card beats the guard's card.
Players keep trumps back for rescues.
cons: A trump spent on a rescue is gone for tricks.
Rivals count the trumps left.

pairs.tendency: A player is a rescuer on one board and a guard on the other, so they work for and against a rescue at once.
pros: One player plays both sides of a rescue.
A rescue on one board may weigh against a capture on the other.
cons: Attention splits between two boards.
A piece freed on one board can be caught on the other.

pairs.tendency: A wild card can be played as any card, including the one card a jail needs.
pros: A wild card can open a jail that asks for a certain card.
Players keep wilds back for the right moment.
cons: Once played, the wild is gone.
Rivals watch who holds the wilds.

pairs.tendency: On this board the right edge meets the left, so a rescuer who runs off one side comes back on the other. A jail in a corner can be reached from two sides.
pros: A jail has many ways in.
Guards cannot rely on an edge.
cons: Guards have to watch all sides.
Runners vanish off one side and appear on the other, which confuses the chaser.

pairs.tendency: The secret is where the prisoners are held, and the rescuers ask yes or no questions to find the jail.
pros: Each answer shrinks the list of jails.
Rescuers learn by asking.
cons: Many questions may pass before a rescue starts.
The one who knows can only say yes or no.

pairs.tendency: Rescue takes time in a race, so a team has to decide whether to go back for a friend or run on. A caught leader loses the lead at once.
pros: A rescue has a cost in time.
Leaders can be dragged back.
cons: A team that stops to rescue falls behind.
A caught leader loses their place.

pairs.tendency: The highest score wins, and time in jail scores nothing. Freeing a friend puts their points back into the count.
pros: A rescue brings a player's points back.
Teams add up what freed friends earn.
cons: A jailed player earns nothing.
A late rescue is worth little.

pairs.tendency: Jail stops being out. A jailed player can come back, so the last player standing is the one nobody can rescue.
pros: Knocked-out players can return.
The game lasts longer.
cons: The last one standing is hard to name.
A player in jail may sit out a long time.

pairs.tendency: Everyone wins or loses together, and the game does the catching, so the players free each other against it.
pros: Every rescue counts for the whole table.
Everyone cares who is in jail.
cons: One jailed player can sink the group.
Players rush to help the same friend.

pairs.tendency: The team works towards one goal, and only free players can add to it.
pros: A freed player adds to the goal.
The group measures progress by who is free.
cons: Jailed players cannot help with the goal.
A rescue delays the team's goal.

pairs.tendency: Every player hides a goal of their own. A rescue can show a goal, or a player may leave a friend in jail because their own goal needs it.
pros: A rescue may show a player's goal.
A player may skip a rescue to hide their aim.
cons: Teammates ask why a friend was left.
A player might pretend to be caught.

pairs.tendency: A capture and a rescue make a chapter of the story. The story ends when it ends, not when the jail is empty.
pros: A rescue can be a turn in the story.
Players decide how the chapter ends.
cons: A long stay in jail can drag the story.
Once the rescue is told, the next chapter has to start.

pairs.tendency: There is no winner, so capture and rescue are just things to do. Players look at who ended up in jail and who got out.
pros: Players can rescue for its own sake.
The jail is a place to look at.
cons: With no prize, players may not bother to rescue.
Nothing marks a rescue as finished.

pairs.tendency: Players set their own aims. One wants to free every friend and another wants never to be caught.
pros: Goals differ in the jail.
Players explain their aims to each other.
cons: A team has trouble agreeing on who to rescue first.
Rescuers and prisoners may want different things.

pairs.tendency: Nobody wins. The player left in jail when the game ends is the one who loses, and a rescue makes someone else safe.
pros: A rescue passes the risk to someone else.
Players try to avoid ending up in jail.
cons: A jailed player might be left there.
Rescuers decide who stays, which can be pointed.

pairs.tendency: The aim is to keep play going, and a rescue keeps everyone in. A jail that holds too many stops the play.
pros: A rescue keeps players in the game.
Guards may let prisoners go.
cons: A jail cannot hold players for ever.
The game has no clear end.

pairs.tendency: Every rescue is followed by another capture, so the loop never ends. The game shows what it is like to be freed again and again.
pros: Capture and rescue repeat without end.
The loop itself is the point.
cons: No one wins by rescuing.
Players may stop caring who is in jail.

pairs.tendency: A lone player has cards stuck in a jail pile, and a rescue is a move that frees them. A locked layout is a loss.
pros: A lone player has a goal of freeing cards.
The layout holds the jail.
cons: A stuck layout ends the game.
No teammate is there to help.

pairs.tendency: Several short games are played in a row. A team caught early in one game can try a different rescue plan in the next.
pros: A lost game does not end the match.
Teams try other rescue plans between games.
cons: A rescue plan that worked is known to rivals.
Each game resets the jail.

pairs.tendency: Points count against you, so each turn in jail adds to a player's total. A rescue stops the count.
pros: A rescue stops a prisoner gaining points.
Players want to be freed early.
cons: Time in jail adds up.
A rescuer who is caught adds to their own count.

pairs.tendency: A rescuer has to land on the jail with the exact count. A step too far loses the turn.
pros: An exact count is needed to reach the jail.
Players count their steps with care.
cons: Overshooting the jail loses a turn.
A jailed player may wait for one exact number.

pairs.tendency: The aim is turned round, so a player may want to stay in jail. A rescuer who frees a friend can hand them a loss.
pros: Players try to get caught.
A rescuer may free a friend who wanted to stay.
cons: A rescue can hurt the friend it frees.
Others cannot tell if a capture was on purpose.

pairs.tendency: Everyone plays at the same time, each with their own jail. Nobody can reach another player's jail to free them.
pros: Each player's jail is theirs alone.
Players compare how they are getting on.
cons: A rescue needs a teammate who is not there.
Nobody can free anyone but themselves.

pairs.tendency: A capture is aimed at one player, and the rescue is the answer. Taking someone to jail and freeing them again becomes a back-and-forth between two people.
pros: A capture is aimed at one player.
A rescue can feel like revenge.
cons: A feud may start.
Players sent to jail may stay angry.

pairs.tendency: Nobody attacks directly. They build walls round the jail instead, and those walls are still there when a rescuer arrives.
pros: Blocks on the road to the jail work quietly.
A rescue meets changes made long before.
cons: Walls built early can seal a jail.
Players feel it as being blocked, not attacked.

pairs.tendency: The whole table is on one team against the game, so every rescue is shared work.
pros: Everyone shares the rescue work.
The game's guards are the one enemy.
cons: A team that loses its rescuers loses the game.
Waiting in jail is hard to watch.

pairs.tendency: The table works as one side for most of the game, but each player has a small private reason to win more than the rest. A rescue can be slow if a private goal is in the way.
pros: Rescue is mostly shared.
A private goal can delay a rescue.
cons: Players doubt each other's rescuers.
A jailed player cannot be sure of help.

pairs.tendency: Two teams guard their own jails and send rescuers into the other's. Capture and rescue sits most easily here.
pros: Teams guard the jail and send rescuers.
Teammates know who to help.
cons: A big team crowds the jail.
A team down to one runner has little chance.

pairs.tendency: One player is secretly against the rest. The traitor may skip a rescue or let a guard catch the helper, and nobody knows why it failed.
pros: A rescue may not be what it looks like.
Players suspect those who skip rescues.
cons: A traitor can leave a friend in jail.
A rescuer who fails gets blamed.

pairs.tendency: Moves travel by post between players who live far apart. A jail can hold someone for weeks, and a rescue plan takes a letter to arrive.
pros: Plans are written down.
A rescue takes patience.
cons: A friend can wait for weeks.
A plan can be old before it arrives.

pairs.tendency: One player is not at the table, and that player is the one held in the jail. They can send a hint about the way in.
pros: The jailed one need not be present.
A hint from the absent player can guide a rescue.
cons: An absent player cannot be asked.
Rescuers work from guesses.

pairs.tendency: One player runs the world, the jail and the guards. Rescuers say what they plan and the game master says what happens.
pros: A rescue is planned out loud.
The game master can make the jail feel real.
cons: The game master has a lot to track.
The same person guards and judges.

pairs.tendency: In a street or park game, anyone passing may join. A passer-by can free a friend, or be caught.
pros: A passer-by can free a prisoner.
Players come and go.
cons: The jail fills with strangers.
The group changes in the middle of a game.

pairs.tendency: One player catches everyone else, and the others free each other.
pros: A lone guard tries to hold many prisoners.
The rest take turns rescuing.
cons: The lone player cannot watch every door.
If everyone is caught, nobody is left to rescue.

pairs.tendency: A lone player faces the pack, so no teammate can free them. The only rescue is one the pack allows.
pros: A lone player's rescue depends on luck.
Results can be compared with a friend afterwards.
cons: A caught piece may stay caught.
No teammate is there to help.

pairs.tendency: Dice decide most of what happens, so a rescue happens when the throw allows it.
pros: Rescue is a matter of throws.
Players keep hoping for a number.
cons: Skill gives little help.
A jailed player waits for a lucky throw.

pairs.tendency: A reroll can save a rescue that a first throw ruined, but the rerolls are limited.
pros: A reroll can save a failed rescue.
Players can set aside unlucky throws.
cons: Rerolls run out.
Spending one on a rescue leaves none for the next.

pairs.tendency: A rescue is planned by choice, and one die adds a surprise at the end.
pros: Planned rescues can still be upset by a throw.
Choices count for most.
cons: A careful plan can still fail on one die.
Players blame the dice.

pairs.tendency: There are no dice, so both sides can work out each other's moves, and a rescue goes to whoever plans further.
pros: Both sides can work out each move.
Rescues are won by planning.
cons: A mistake leaves a friend in jail with no luck to blame.
Long thinking between moves.

pairs.tendency: The group reads a throw as a sign and talks about whether it says the jail opens or says wait.
pros: A throw acts as a sign for the rescue.
Players talk over what it means.
cons: Players may read it differently.
A throw that says wait holds a friend in jail.

pairs.tendency: The rescuer and the friend in jail have to move at the same moment, without a word.
pros: Rescuer and prisoner act together.
Teams develop a sense of timing.
cons: A rescue out of step fails.
It is hard to explain to new players.

pairs.tendency: A table says what the dice mean, such as the guard falling asleep. So a rescue picks up events nobody planned.
pros: The dice may open the jail in a way that adds to the story.
Rescues come with details.
cons: Table entries may not suit the rescue.
The dice may hold a friend in jail for a long time.

pairs.tendency: Everything is visible, so every guard, rescuer and prisoner can be seen. A rescue cannot hide.
pros: Every move toward the jail is visible.
Players can see traps.
cons: A rescue cannot be a surprise.
Guards see each rescuer coming.

pairs.tendency: A rescuer may hold a key card that no one else can see. The guard has to guess whether it is real.
pros: A hidden key can surprise.
Players bluff about holding the key.
cons: A rescuer without the card is stuck.
Guards cannot tell a real rescue from a bluff.

pairs.tendency: Roles are dealt in secret, so the player coming to free you may belong to the other side. A prisoner cannot tell a friend from a trap.
pros: A rescuer may secretly be on the other side.
Prisoners are unsure who is a friend.
cons: A rescue can be a trap.
Players doubt their rescuers.

pairs.tendency: Clues point to which jail holds which friend. Rescuers compare notes before they run.
pros: Clues lead to the right jail.
Players compare notes.
cons: Rescuers may chase the wrong clue.
Time passes while the friend waits.

pairs.tendency: A player pretends to run for the jail to pull the guards away, or hides that the jail is empty.
pros: A fake rescue draws guards away.
Guards guess which approach is real.
cons: A bluff that fails gets the bluffer caught.
Suspicion grows round the table.

pairs.tendency: One player knows the secret rule, perhaps how the jail opens. Newcomers find it by being turned away at the door.
pros: Players learn what frees a friend by trying.
Players who know keep the secret.
cons: Prisoners wait while rescuers guess.
New players feel stuck.

pairs.tendency: The jailed player knows which door opens, but can only hint. The rescuers read the hints and try.
pros: A jailed player can hint at the way in.
Teammates read the hints.
cons: Hints can be misread.
The one who knows cannot speak openly.

pairs.tendency: Nobody sees the map at the start, so the rescuers do not know where the jail is until they find it.
pros: Finding the jail is part of the rescue.
Scouts look for it.
cons: A scout may find it only to be caught.
The jail may be far from where the rescuers start.

pairs.tendency: When a player is jailed, their hand is laid face up and a teammate plays it for them until the rescue.
pros: A jailed player's hand can still be played.
Rivals see the open hand.
cons: Nothing in that hand stays secret.
The teammate has two hands to manage.

pairs.tendency: Part of the score is hidden, so no one knows what a jailed player has. A rescue changes the secret score without showing it.
pros: A rescue can change a secret score.
Players guess who is ahead.
cons: Nobody can tell how much a rescue is worth.
Rivals guess from who is caught.

pairs.tendency: One side moves at a time, and a guard who sees the rescuer coming has a turn to prepare.
pros: Each side sees the rescuer's move before replying.
Guards can set a trap for the turn.
cons: Long waits between turns.
Prisoners wait many turns.

pairs.tendency: Moves are chosen in secret and shown together, so guards and rescuers commit to a place at the same moment.
pros: Guards and rescuers pick together.
The reveal shows who went where.
cons: A wrong guess means a catch.
A rescuer cannot react to what the guard does.

pairs.tendency: There are no turns, so a rescuer dashes to the jail when the guards look away.
pros: Speed decides rescues.
Nobody waits for a turn.
cons: Quick players dominate.
Slow players stay in jail.

pairs.tendency: A timer runs on every turn, and a rescuer has to move before the sand runs out.
pros: A clock presses the rescuer.
Guards also have little time.
cons: A move lost to the clock leaves the friend waiting.
Hurried moves lead to catches.

pairs.tendency: The game runs on real days, so a friend can sit in jail for a whole weekend. A rescue is planned over days.
pros: Jail lasts as long as real days.
Plans are made over days.
cons: A friend may wait many days.
Players may leave before the rescue.

pairs.tendency: A pause comes before every move, so a rescue becomes a slow walk to the jail with the guards watching.
pros: Each step of a rescue is slow.
Guards and rescuers watch each other.
cons: A rescue takes a long time.
Prisoners wait longer.

pairs.tendency: Play gets faster as it goes, so rescues come in a rush near the end.
pros: Rescue gets faster.
Guards have to react quickly.
cons: Late captures are hard to undo.
Early moves matter less.

pairs.tendency: A rescue can be followed by a second move, such as running away with the friend.
pros: A rescuer can free and run in one turn.
Lucky players move many times.
cons: A player with extra turns can empty the jail.
Others sit and watch.

pairs.tendency: The first stage is for picking cards and the second has captures. What a team picks in stage one decides who can rescue in stage two.
pros: Stage one prepares the rescuers.
Jail rules apply only in the later stage.
cons: Choices in stage one limit a rescue in stage two.
Players change tactics at the stage.

pairs.tendency: The jail stands for a place where people are held until someone pays or speaks for them, so the board starts to show how that works.
pros: A rescue can show how release works.
Players see a real system in the game.
cons: Rules have to match the real system closely, so the game grows heavy.
Players may disagree with how the model works.

pairs.tendency: Players take the parts of the guards, the prisoners and the prisoners' families, each with its own needs.
pros: Each group has its own reason to free or hold.
Players see the jail from different sides.
cons: Roles may want opposite things.
A prisoner's group has little to do.

pairs.tendency: Rescuers all draw from one supply to pay for a rescue. Too many rescues empty it for everyone.
pros: Rescues draw from a shared supply.
Players argue about who uses it.
cons: Too many rescues empty the supply.
Teams may delay a rescue to save it.

pairs.tendency: A capture shows its effect a few rounds later, and a rescue plan may take rounds to pay off.
pros: A rescue planned now frees someone later.
Players plan ahead.
cons: A capture's effects are seen late.
It is hard to tell which move caused which result.

pairs.tendency: Players agree a new jail rule, such as two rescuers needed at the door, and play on under it to see what it changes.
pros: Players can test jail rules.
They see what each rule does.
cons: A tested rule can change a team's plan.
Players argue before settling.

pairs.tendency: Once play ends, the players talk over who was left in jail and why, and what would have changed it.
pros: Talk covers who got rescued and who did not.
Players explain their choices.
cons: Someone may feel left in jail.
The talk takes time.

pairs.tendency: A freed prisoner carries a mark that stays on the board, and a capture can never be undone. The next game starts from here.
pros: A rescue marks the board.
The next game starts where this one ended.
cons: A rescue cannot be undone.
A prisoner's mark stays on.

pairs.tendency: If rescue is hard to do, the rules say something about getting out. The game makes its point through the jail.
pros: The rescue rules carry a point.
Players talk about what the jail stands for.
cons: The rules might be read in different ways.
The point may be missed.

pairs.tendency: A promise to come back for a friend is a real promise, and a friend left in jail may feel it after the game.
pros: A rescue becomes a real promise.
Players take the jail seriously.
cons: A friend left in jail may stay upset.
Real stakes can strain friendships.

pairs.tendency: The game gives a point for each rescue, and players start chasing the score.
pros: A point for each rescue turns care into a score.
Players chase rescues.
cons: Some rescues are made only for the points.
The score can replace the care.

pairs.tendency: Players practise a way of living where anyone caught is always freed. They see what it would take to keep nobody in jail.
pros: Players try a future with no one left in jail.
They learn what that would ask of them.
cons: The pretend rule feels strange at first.
Keeping the rule up takes effort.

pairs.tendency: Dice move your pieces along a path, and a piece falls when two of the other side's pieces land on either side of it. A throw can walk you into a gap or let you close one.
pros: Every throw may set up a capture.
Players watch where each die could send a piece.
cons: A piece can be lost to a throw nobody planned.
Luck decides who gets to close the gap.

pairs.tendency: Players pick cards from a shared row, and some cards say where a piece may go. One pick can give you the card that closes a ring and take it away from the next player.
pros: A pick can hand you a trapping move.
Players watch which card the next player needs.
cons: The last pick may leave only cards that help nobody.
Slow with many players.

pairs.tendency: Players offer money for the right to place the next piece, so the spot that closes a ring goes to the highest offer. Money spent on one capture is gone for the next.
pros: Players decide what one trap is worth.
The price of a move shows how much someone wants it.
cons: Spending a lot can leave you unable to answer the next threat.
A player with more money can close more rings.

pairs.tendency: Each extra piece you place around an enemy piece could win it, but each one also leaves a gap in your own side. Stopping early keeps what you hold.
pros: A greedy turn can win several pieces.
Players choose when to stop.
cons: One more try can lose the pieces already gained.
Careful players wait while others gamble.

pairs.tendency: A part of the map belongs to whoever has the most pieces in it, and ringing an enemy piece there removes it and gives you the spot. The fights happen at the edges of each area.
pros: Taking a piece also takes its place on the map.
Players guard the edges of their areas.
cons: Spread-out pieces are easy to ring.
A lost corner can lead to a lost area.

pairs.tendency: Workers sit on job spaces, and a worker standing alone can be taken by pieces placed beside it. A taken worker leaves its job open for the rest of the turn.
pros: Every job space is also a place to fight.
Players think about who stands next to whom.
cons: Losing a worker closes a job.
Some spaces are risky to use.

pairs.tendency: Lines and mosaics are made from the same pieces that can ring an enemy piece, so a gap in a pattern is a gap in your guard. Building and trapping pull on the same pieces.
pros: One piece can serve a pattern and a trap.
Players read each other's lines for gaps.
cons: A broken pattern can cost several pieces in a row.
Every piece has two jobs and can only do one at a time.

pairs.tendency: Cards in your hand tell you where pieces may go, so holding the right card for the right moment lets you close a ring. Saving it means you play something else for now.
pros: A saved card makes a trap possible later.
Players choose when to spring it.
cons: Holding a card leaves less to play today.
With no fitting card, the enemy piece walks free.

pairs.tendency: Each trick is won by the highest card, and the winner leads next and gets the next placement. Winning a trick can mean winning the right to close a ring.
pros: Winning a trick gives a placement.
Players count cards to guess who will lead.
cons: A lost trick hands the other side the first move on the board.
There are cards and a board to keep track of at once.

pairs.tendency: Two players talk and agree to ring a third player's piece together. A promise to hold back can be broken the moment the gap appears.
pros: Players can team up to close a ring.
A deal can save a piece.
cons: Promises get broken at the last square.
Long talks slow every turn.

pairs.tendency: A captured piece that belonged to a set breaks that set, so a ring can wreck what someone spent many turns gathering. Players choose between guarding their set pieces and going after the other player's.
pros: Taking one piece can break a whole set.
Players guess which pieces matter most to the others.
cons: Set pieces left in the open get ringed.
Guarding takes moves away from collecting.

pairs.tendency: A tile laid next to a piece can close the last open side of a ring, so the map takes shape while the captures happen. A single tile is enough to trap a piece.
pros: The shape of the map decides where rings can form.
Each tile can open or close a gap.
cons: A tile can seal a piece in with no warning.
Plans change with every new tile.

pairs.tendency: One player moves and the next answers with a move of their own, so a ring is built one reply at a time, each piece answering the one before. The answers get easier to guess as the chain grows.
pros: Each move invites a reply.
Rings grow in clear steps.
cons: A reply can be forced by the move before it.
Players can predict the next answer.

pairs.tendency: Nobody speaks, so a player closes a ring and the other side learns of it only from the board. Partners guess each other's plans from where the pieces go.
pros: Every placement is a message.
Players learn to read the board closely.
cons: Teammates cannot warn each other of a trap.
A misread signal loses a piece.

pairs.tendency: Instead of a move, you can change a rule, such as how many sides have to be covered before a piece is taken. A change can free a trapped piece or make an ordinary piece easy to take.
pros: A rule change can free a ringed piece.
Players test what a new rule does to captures.
cons: A plan made for the old rule can fall apart.
Players argue over what the rule now says.

pairs.tendency: Each player speaks as a character, and a capture gets told as a story: a guard is cornered, a messenger is cut off. The board shows the result of what the characters chose.
pros: Captures come with a reason.
Players act in character as they place pieces.
cons: Staying in character can lead to a move that loses a piece.
Telling the story slows play.

pairs.tendency: Pieces are flicked, stacked or thrown into place, so the hand decides whether a piece lands beside the one you want to ring. A shaky hand can leave a gap or knock a ring apart.
pros: Every placement is a test of the hand.
Players watch each other's aim.
cons: A shaking hand can lose a capture.
Knocked pieces need an agreed place to go back.

pairs.tendency: The map is drawn as people play, so the lines they draw decide which pieces run out of room. A drawn wall or river can close one side of a ring.
pros: Drawing a wall can start a trap.
Players shape where the fights happen.
cons: A map drawn in a hurry may hide a gap.
Players can argue about what a line means.

pairs.tendency: A player who falls behind gets help, such as an extra piece, so a ring that took many turns can be broken by a late arrival. The lead is never fully closed.
pros: A trailing player still has a way back.
Rings are harder to keep sealed.
cons: A ring built with care can be undone.
Players ahead sometimes avoid taking more.

pairs.tendency: Ringing a piece needs choices, and here the dice or cards decide everything. With both, a piece is taken only if the draw happens to put pieces around it, and nobody picks the spot.
pros: Each draw is quick.
Players of any age can join.
cons: Planning a ring has no effect.
Captures come from the draw alone.

pairs.tendency: It chases the others, and a runner hemmed in by other players cannot get away. A runner can be caught by a touch or by being boxed in.
pros: There are two ways to catch a runner.
Runners learn to stay near open space.
cons: A hemmed-in runner is caught at once.
Chasing wears out the player who is It.

pairs.tendency: On your turn you pick which player to squeeze, and a ring on one player's piece takes a turn away from another. With three players, two can gang up on the third.
pros: Players pick whom to squeeze.
Alliances can form around one victim.
cons: One player may be ringed by everyone.
Choosing a target can make an enemy.

pairs.tendency: Both blocks use the same pieces: a stone that joins your chain is also a stone that can be surrounded. A ring around one stone cuts your chain in two.
pros: Each stone helps a chain and a guard.
A ring can win by cutting.
cons: A chain with one captured link is split.
Players juggle two goals with one stone.

pairs.tendency: Pieces come in kinds that beat each other in a cycle, so a ring only works when the pieces around are of the kind that beats the one inside. No kind is safe from all the others.
pros: Players guess which kind the other will place.
No kind of piece wins every time.
cons: A wrong guess loses the piece.
A ring plan falls apart if the other player switches kinds.

pairs.tendency: Showing a pair or a run scores points while the cards stay in your hand, and the cards tell the other side what you could place next. The board fight goes on while the points come in.
pros: Points come in while pieces are being placed.
A declared hand shows what a player may do next.
cons: Showing a pair gives away a move.
Players follow a hand and a board together.

pairs.tendency: Each player has a power the others lack, so one side's pieces may need three pieces around them to be taken while another's need two. Players learn the powers by trying them.
pros: Each side has its own way to trap.
Powers come to light during play.
cons: A protecting power makes a ring less worth building.
Explaining every power takes time.

pairs.tendency: With a ring half closed, you offer to double what the game is worth. The other player accepts and risks a bigger loss, or gives up and loses the points at stake.
pros: An offer to double shows a trap is near.
The other player has to read the board fast.
cons: A double on a ring that breaks costs twice as much.
Giving up early loses points without a fight.

pairs.tendency: If a ring can be closed, you have to close it, even when closing it opens a hole behind you. A player can offer a piece as bait to pull the other side out of place.
pros: Players can bait a forced ring.
Moves are easy to predict.
cons: A forced capture can pull a piece off a safe spot.
Some turns leave no choice at all.

pairs.tendency: A piece that has been through many fights gains power, so a seasoned piece needs more pieces around it before it is taken. New pieces are easy to ring.
pros: Old pieces are harder to ring.
Players protect a piece that has grown.
cons: Early pieces are easy to take.
Taking a seasoned piece uses many others.

pairs.tendency: Each player says the whole list so far and adds one item, then places a piece. A slip in the list can cost a turn while the other side closes a ring.
pros: Remembering adds pressure to each turn.
Players watch each other for slips.
cons: A long list leaves little time to watch the board.
One slip may cost a piece.

pairs.tendency: The more experienced player starts with fewer pieces, so there are fewer to build a ring with and fewer to lose. The newer player has a chance to ring a lone piece early.
pros: The newer player can ring a lone piece.
Both sides start unequal on purpose.
cons: With few pieces, each one lost counts for more.
Players have to agree on the handicap first.

pairs.tendency: One piece hides, and the hunters close in, placing pieces on every side of where they think it is. A hider who is found is already ringed.
pros: Hunters guess, then close in.
The hider can move in secret.
cons: A hider may never be found.
A found hider has little room to run.

pairs.tendency: A piece hops over another and lands behind it, so there are two ways to take: hop or surround. A hop can also carry a piece out of a ring that was nearly shut.
pros: A hop can jump out of a ring.
Players mix hops with rings.
cons: A hop can open the gap a ring needed.
Two taking rules are harder to remember.

pairs.tendency: Dice say how many pieces you may place this turn, so keeping high dice means a long run of placements around one target. Rerolling the rest can raise that run or lose it.
pros: Players choose which dice to keep.
A high roll can place several pieces around one target.
cons: Rerolling can throw away a high die.
Rolling takes time before any piece moves.

pairs.tendency: A piece landed on goes back to the start, while a ringed piece is taken for the rest of the game. A safe space can guard against landing and still leave the piece open to a ring.
pros: There are two ways to lose a piece.
Safe spaces give some shelter.
cons: Players guard against two threats at once.
The two losses last for different lengths of time.

pairs.tendency: Three in a row takes a piece, and four pieces around one take it too. The same pieces that make a row can surround, so one placement can threaten both.
pros: Rows and rings both take pieces.
One placement can make two threats.
cons: Defence has to cover rows and rings.
A broken row opens a gap for a ring.

pairs.tendency: The pieces are letters, and a letter with enemy letters on every side is taken, which breaks any word it was part of. A dictionary settles word disputes but not ring disputes.
pros: Taking a letter breaks a word.
Players hunt for words and rings at once.
cons: A missing letter ruins a word.
Arguments over words slow the game.

pairs.tendency: A line of tiles grows from its two open ends, and pieces placed at both ends cut it off from growing. A player with no matching tile misses a turn while the ring closes.
pros: Open ends are clear targets.
Players choose which end to block.
cons: A closed end can leave a player with tiles they cannot play.
Missed turns let the other side close more.

pairs.tendency: Players lay sets of cards face up, and a played set marks the pieces it covers as guarded. Cards added to the set extend the guard to more pieces.
pros: A meld shows what is guarded.
Other players can add to a meld.
cons: Cards laid down reveal your plans.
Guarded pieces tie up cards.

pairs.tendency: Each piece has a power that works once, such as slipping out of a ring. Once the marker is gone the piece is as easy to ring as any other.
pros: A single power can free a trapped piece.
Players pick when to use it.
cons: A used piece is easy to ring again.
Holding the power too long can lose the piece anyway.

pairs.tendency: You offer a move and the other player may turn it down or pick from two you offer. If your offer puts a piece next to theirs, they can see the ring coming.
pros: Offers show a player's plan.
The other player can steer away from a trap.
cons: An offer next to their piece warns the victim.
Offering two moves takes two moves that are safe for you.

pairs.tendency: A message about where to close a ring travels from player to player by whisper. It may change on the way, and the last player acts on what arrives.
pros: Teams can plan a ring in secret.
A changed message can send pieces to the wrong place.
cons: Nobody can check the message.
A mistaken ring leaves a gap.

pairs.tendency: Before play, each player hands over cards without seeing what they get back. The cards you pass decide which placements the other player can make against you.
pros: Choosing what to pass gives a hint.
Given cards can help a ring against you.
cons: You cannot see what you will get.
The card you pass may be the one that traps you.

pairs.tendency: One player sets up the starting board and the other picks a side. If the setup leaves a piece almost ringed, the other player takes that side, so the setter has to make it even.
pros: The setter tries to make both sides equal.
The chooser reads the board before picking.
cons: A setup with a near ring is easy to read.
Setting up takes thought before play begins.

pairs.tendency: A piece that reaches the far end becomes a more powerful piece, and a runner on its way there can be ringed before it arrives. Pieces left at home hold the starting end.
pros: Players push pieces forward for the change.
A promoted piece needs more pieces to ring.
cons: A lone runner can be ringed on the way.
Pieces sent forward leave gaps behind.

pairs.tendency: A team plays in legs, and each runner hands on to the next. A piece taken in one leg is missing when the next runner starts.
pros: Team members depend on each other.
One leg can set up the next runner.
cons: One lost piece slows the whole team.
Players wait for their own leg.

pairs.tendency: A safe shape cannot be surrounded, so building it is a way out of a ring. The other player races to ring your stones before the shape is done.
pros: A safe shape gives a goal to build towards.
The other player tries to stop the shape in time.
cons: Building a shape takes several moves while the ring closes.
Stones outside the shape stay open.

pairs.tendency: Prizes are named cards, and a piece can carry one, so ringing that piece takes the prize with it. The piece that holds a prize draws every enemy piece towards it.
pros: Everyone knows which pieces matter.
A prize on a piece makes it a target.
cons: Prizes on one piece mean one risk.
A ringed prize piece can change the score at once.

pairs.tendency: Face-up cards in the middle can be used by anyone, and a card that lets a piece go next to another is open to both sides. A card taken by one player is gone for the other.
pros: Both players see the same options.
Players guess which card the other will take.
cons: A face-up card can help the enemy ring you.
Taking a card denies it to the other side.

pairs.tendency: The counters in the middle go to whoever wins, and each ring that closes can win them. If nobody wins, the pot grows and the next ring is worth more.
pros: A ring can win the pot.
A growing pot raises the value of each capture.
cons: Players squeeze harder as the pot grows.
A long game without a capture lets the pot swell.

pairs.tendency: Seeds are dropped one at a time into the pits that follow, and a last seed that fills a pit between two of yours can take what sits beside it. Counting the seeds shows where the last one will land.
pros: Players plan runs of seeds that squeeze a pit.
Counting shows where a run ends.
cons: A run can feed the pits you meant to take.
Counting slows each turn.

pairs.tendency: An extra hand sits face down in the middle, and one player may take it, swap it or buy it. It might hold the cards that close a ring, and the buyer pays for the chance.
pros: A spare hand can offer a new route to a trap.
Players weigh taking an unknown hand.
cons: Taking the spare hand costs a move.
The spare hand may hold nothing that helps.

pairs.tendency: A safe square guards the piece on it, so a ring around it cannot be closed. A square that makes you miss a turn gives the other side time to shut the gap.
pros: Safe squares give an escape.
Some squares can hold a piece in place for a ring.
cons: A missed turn gives the enemy time to close in.
Players steer clear of certain squares.

pairs.tendency: Every piece has a price, and a ring takes several pieces, so taking one enemy piece can cost a lot. A cheap piece can still fill the last gap.
pros: Players weigh the price of a ring.
Low-cost pieces still count in a ring.
cons: Surrounding a costly piece uses up much of what you have.
Spending on one trap leaves little for defence.

pairs.tendency: You share a fixed number of pieces between several places, and a place left thin can be ringed. Both sides share out at once and cannot see where the other put theirs.
pros: Players guess where the other put their forces.
A thinly held place invites a ring.
cons: Putting many pieces in one place leaves another with too few.
Both sides commit before anything is shown.

pairs.tendency: Everyone moves until the signal, then freezes, and whoever has pieces on all sides of an enemy piece takes it. Players hurry pieces into place while the music plays.
pros: The signal sets the moment of capture.
Players move into position while play runs.
cons: A late move leaves a gap open.
The signal ends the set-up with no warning.
