pairs.tendency: You put cards back and draw new ones, looking for the card that lets you place the last piece around an enemy. A swap uses a turn, and another player may have to agree to it.
pros: A player can search for the card that closes a ring.
A swap gives a second chance.
cons: Swapping uses a turn while the enemy closes in.
The player who has to agree can refuse the swap.

pairs.tendency: On your turn you can pick up the discard pile if the top card can be used straight away, such as a card that places a piece around an enemy. The pile brings many cards at once.
pros: A big pile gives many cards at once.
Players watch what is thrown away.
cons: The pile adds cards you cannot use.
A thrown card can help the next player trap you.

pairs.tendency: One suit is named trump, so a low trump can win a trick over a high card, and the winner gets to close a ring. Players save trumps for the moment the ring is one piece short.
pros: A low card can still win.
Players count how many trumps are left.
cons: Saving trumps means losing other tricks.
A trick lost near the end can leave a ring open.

pairs.tendency: You are one side on one board and the other side on the second, so while you ring a piece on the first, one of your own can be ringed on the second.
pros: You attack and defend at the same time.
Every move is two decisions.
cons: Eyes on one board miss the other.
A gain on one board can be a loss on the other.

pairs.tendency: A wild card can stand for the one card you need to place the last piece around an enemy. The other side may guess you hold one when a ring looks almost done.
pros: One card can close a ring.
Players hold wild cards back for the right moment.
cons: A near ring tells the other side you may hold a wild card.
Wild cards spent early are gone when the ring needs them.

pairs.tendency: The edges join, so a piece in a corner has neighbours across the join, and a ring has to use pieces from the far edge too. No piece can hide against a wall.
pros: Every piece can be reached from all sides.
Rings can close across the join.
cons: Corners give no shelter.
Players overlook the far edge.

pairs.tendency: One player secretly picks a piece to guard, and the others ask yes or no questions to find it before they ring it. Each answer shrinks the places it could be.
pros: Questions narrow down where to place.
Answers show the hunters where to look.
cons: Asking uses up turns.
A wrong guess wastes a ring.

pairs.tendency: Runners head for the end, and a runner boxed in cannot move on. Stopping to ring an enemy loses ground in the race.
pros: Runners become targets.
Players choose between racing and blocking.
cons: Blocking slows your own runner.
A runner boxed in can drop from first to last.

pairs.tendency: Each captured piece adds to the score, so every ring is worth points. Players weigh which piece is worth the pieces it takes to ring it.
pros: Every capture counts.
Players compare what each ring would score.
cons: Chasing a capture can lose points elsewhere.
The tally needs checking.

pairs.tendency: A player whose pieces are all ringed is out, and the last one with pieces left wins. Early exits mean some players sit and watch.
pros: A ring can end a player's game.
Remaining players watch for the next target.
cons: Players who go out early wait.
Groups often gang up on whoever has the fewest pieces.

pairs.tendency: The game places enemy pieces to ring the players' pieces, and the players cover each other's open sides. One piece ringed can open a gap for the next.
pros: Players guard each other's flanks.
Talk helps plan who covers what.
cons: Losses can spread from piece to piece.
A gap left by one player costs everyone.

pairs.tendency: Players work together to ring one target piece and place pieces around it from different sides. Success is shared, so one player's gap hurts the whole group.
pros: Players place pieces around the same target.
Everyone wins or nobody does.
cons: Agreeing on the next piece takes time.
Players can block each other's placements by mistake.

pairs.tendency: A player may ring a piece for a secret reason, and nobody can tell why it was taken. Others guess the goal from the pieces that are ringed.
pros: A capture hides its reason.
Players guess goals from rings.
cons: A capture can give the goal away.
Plans can clash without anyone knowing.

pairs.tendency: Captures get told as scenes, and a ring that closes marks the end of a chapter. The game ends when the story does, whatever the board shows.
pros: Captures become scenes.
Pieces mark the steps of a story.
cons: A capture may not fit where the story is going.
The story can stall when no ring is possible.

pairs.tendency: Nobody wins, so pieces are placed and taken with no prize at the end. Players look at what the rings made and talk about it.
pros: Players watch the patterns that appear.
Captures become something to talk about.
cons: With no goal, there is no reason to close a ring.
Play can drift with no direction.

pairs.tendency: One player may want to keep a single piece alive and another may want to ring as many as possible. Each ring helps one goal and may hurt another.
pros: Players aim for different rings.
Success is personal.
cons: Players cannot tell who is ahead.
A ring that helps one player can ruin another's goal.

pairs.tendency: Nobody wins, and the game goes on until one player loses, perhaps the first to have a last piece ringed. Everyone else is safe.
pros: Everyone avoids being the one ringed.
Players guard their last piece.
cons: Players who are safe may stop paying attention.
The end can be a long wait.

pairs.tendency: The aim is to keep playing, and every ring takes a piece out of the game. Taking too many ends play, so players hold back from closing every ring.
pros: Players think about how many pieces to take.
Captured pieces can come back in.
cons: Ringing everything ends play.
Open rings may be left alone on purpose.

pairs.tendency: Ringing a piece wins nothing, since the game cannot be won. Taking a piece loses its usual meaning, and players may ask why they chased it.
pros: A capture is made with no prize.
Players question the urge to take pieces.
cons: Players expect a result that never comes.
Play can stop part-way.

pairs.tendency: You play alone against a layout of cards, and cards are removed by surrounding them with your own. A stuck layout ends the game with a loss.
pros: You play at your own speed.
Rings clear cards from the table.
cons: A stuck layout ends the game.
Nobody else is there to watch the move.

pairs.tendency: Several short games are played in a row, and a ring game is quick, so one round can end in a few moves. A trap found early gets copied in the next round.
pros: A lost game can be answered next round.
Players try different traps.
cons: An opening trap gets copied once it is seen.
Repeated rounds can feel like the same game.

pairs.tendency: Taking a piece gives you its points, and the fewest points wins. So ringing an enemy piece hurts the one who rings it.
pros: Players avoid ringing.
A player can bait the other into capturing.
cons: Every capture adds points to the capturer.
Players wait for others to make the capture.

pairs.tendency: A piece near the end needs an exact count, and a ring around its last squares can block it from landing. Going past the number loses the win.
pros: Rings can block the last squares.
Players wait for the exact throw.
cons: A ringed piece cannot use the count it needs.
A throw that goes past loses the win.

pairs.tendency: Players want to lose all their pieces, so a ring is a gift to the one inside. A player may refuse to ring someone who is trying to be taken.
pros: Players try to get ringed.
A capture helps its target.
cons: Players refuse to ring someone who wants it.
The rule about who rings whom can confuse.

pairs.tendency: Each player works on their own board, so no player's pieces can be ringed by another. Rings only touch the game's own pieces.
pros: Each player works at their own pace.
Players compare results afterwards.
cons: Nobody can stop another player with a ring.
There is little to watch on other boards.

pairs.tendency: Players go after each other on purpose, and a ring is an attack aimed at someone. Everyone sees who is closing in on whom.
pros: Everyone knows who is attacking.
A ring is a clear hit.
cons: A player can be ringed by two at once.
Players hold grudges after a capture.

pairs.tendency: Walls and spots count as sides of a ring, so building a wall changes who can be ringed. Players feel the threat through the board before any piece is taken.
pros: A wall counts as one side of a ring.
Threats show up in the shape of the board.
cons: A wall built by one player can help another's ring.
The effects of a move show up late.

pairs.tendency: The team plays against the game and rings the game's pieces together. A missed gap lets a piece go free for everyone.
pros: The team plans rings together.
Players share the load.
cons: One missed gap lets the game's piece loose.
A mistake costs everyone.

pairs.tendency: Players ring the game's pieces together, but each has a private reason to be the one who closes the last side. They watch who places the final piece.
pros: The team rings pieces and each player keeps a private aim.
Players watch who closes the last side.
cons: Who gets the capture gets argued over.
A private aim can leave a gap in the ring.

pairs.tendency: Partners cover each other's open sides while the two teams try to ring each other's pieces. A lost partner leaves the other one open.
pros: Partners cover open sides.
Teams ring pieces together.
cons: One capture can weaken both partners.
Teams argue about plans.

pairs.tendency: One player secretly works against the team and leaves a side of the ring open. A gap that was meant to be shut points towards whoever left it.
pros: A missing side in a ring points to someone.
Players watch who places pieces.
cons: Honest players get doubted.
A traitor can open a side without being seen.

pairs.tendency: Moves go by post, so a ring takes weeks to close. Each move is thought over, and the other player may close the gap before your letter arrives.
pros: Each move gets careful thought.
Players have time to see a ring coming.
cons: A trap set long ago can be forgotten.
A lost letter stops the game.

pairs.tendency: One player is not at the table, so their pieces stay where they are and can be ringed without a reply. Nobody can speak for them.
pros: The absent player's pieces never move.
Others can plan a ring at leisure.
cons: Nobody defends the absent pieces.
The ring takes pieces from someone who is not there.

pairs.tendency: The game master runs the world and decides when a piece counts as ringed. The game master can set up a trap or allow an odd case.
pros: A trap can be part of the world.
Odd cases get a ruling.
cons: The game master has to track every piece.
Players depend on the game master's rulings.

pairs.tendency: The game is played on the street with chalk, and anyone passing can join a ring. Stones or bottle caps stand in for pieces.
pros: A passer-by can join in.
Pieces can be anything lying around.
cons: Passing feet can wreck the board.
Players come and go in the middle of a ring.

pairs.tendency: The many ring the one player's pieces, and the lone player has to watch every side at once. The lone player earns more when they win.
pros: Many players can ring a single piece.
The lone player is paid more for winning.
cons: The lone player is outnumbered at the edges.
The group has to agree where to close.

pairs.tendency: You play alone against the pack and ring its pieces one by one. Nobody else acts, so your choices and the shuffle decide it.
pros: There is no waiting for others.
You can retry at once.
cons: Nobody is there to surprise.
Results can only be compared afterwards.

pairs.tendency: Dice decide most things, so a ring closes when the dice put pieces in the right places, with little room to plan. Anyone can end up ringing anyone.
pros: Anyone can win a ring.
There is little to plan.
cons: Skill counts for little.
A careful plan can be undone by one roll.

pairs.tendency: An unlucky roll can be softened by a re-roll, so a throw that opens a gap can be thrown again before the other side closes it. Players decide when to spend a re-roll.
pros: A re-roll can close a ring.
Timing the re-roll is a choice.
cons: Re-rolls run out.
Spent re-rolls leave a gap open later.

pairs.tendency: Rings are planned by choice, but a die decides some placements. A ring one piece short may wait on a lucky number.
pros: Planning decides most of the ring.
A small chance of luck shifts a plan.
cons: A ring can wait on one number.
A die can still upset a planned ring.

pairs.tendency: With no dice, a ring is planned many moves ahead, and the other player can see it coming. The one who sees further closes the gap first.
pros: Every ring comes from a plan.
Players read the board far ahead.
cons: A missed gap cannot be blamed on luck.
Games between players of unequal skill end quickly.

pairs.tendency: A throw is read as a message, such as which side to guard. The throw tells where to place a piece, and the player decides what it means.
pros: A throw gives a reason to place a piece.
Players talk about what a sign means.
cons: Different readings of one throw can split a team.
A sign can point to a gap that does not matter.

pairs.tendency: Two players sense when the other is about to move and place pieces at the same moment to close a ring without talking. A partner out of step leaves a gap.
pros: Partners can close a ring without a word.
Players learn each other's habits.
cons: A partner moving at the wrong moment opens a hole.
Strangers find it hard to close a ring together.

pairs.tendency: A roll is looked up on a table, and a result may say a guard is cut off. The dice write part of the story and the pieces on the board decide how it ends.
pros: The dice name the reason for a capture.
The table gives each ring a story.
cons: A roll can place a piece that does not fit the plan.
Looking things up slows play.

pairs.tendency: Everything is visible, so every ring is seen coming. The question is whether the other player can leave in time.
pros: Every threat can be read.
Players can plan far ahead.
cons: A ring cannot be hidden.
Players slow down to check every side.

pairs.tendency: Hidden cards say which ring can be closed, so no one knows who holds the card for the last side. Players bluff about what they hold.
pros: A hidden card can close a ring.
Players try to guess which card is held.
cons: A hidden card makes a gap look safe.
A bluff about a ring can cost a turn.

pairs.tendency: Roles are secret, so a player rings a piece without knowing whose side it belongs to. Some captures hit a friend.
pros: A capture can hit a friend.
Players look at who rings whom.
cons: Rings cause doubt about who is on which side.
A mistaken capture is hard to undo.

pairs.tendency: Clues point to where a hidden piece is, and the hunters build a ring on the clues. A wrong clue sends the ring to the wrong place.
pros: Clues tell hunters where to place.
A ring can confirm a guess.
cons: A ring on a wrong guess wastes pieces.
Clues arrive slowly.

pairs.tendency: You threaten a ring you cannot close, hoping the other player moves away. The other player has to decide whether you hold the pieces.
pros: A threat can move a piece.
Players watch each other's pieces for a bluff.
cons: A bluff called leaves you with a gap.
Moving from a bluff can walk into a real ring.

pairs.tendency: One player knows a secret rule, perhaps how many sides close a ring. Others find it only by being told no, so the first rings are guesses.
pros: The secret rule shapes the first rings.
Newcomers learn by trying.
cons: Early pieces are lost to a rule nobody knew.
Being told no again and again slows the start.

pairs.tendency: One player sees where the ring is meant to close but may only give hints, such as pictures. The others have to guess which square the hint points to.
pros: The hints become clues about the ring.
The helper watches the others guess.
cons: A hint can be read as the wrong side.
The helper sees a gap stay open and cannot say so.

pairs.tendency: The map starts hidden, so a piece may be ringed by a wall nobody knew was there. Areas are turned over only when a player explores them.
pros: Exploring can reveal a wall to use.
Players find sides of a ring as they go.
cons: A hidden wall can trap a piece.
Nobody knows where it is safe to step.

pairs.tendency: One hand lies face up, so everyone can see which placements it can make. Rings against that hand's pieces can be planned openly.
pros: The open hand shows its next moves.
Others plan rings against it.
cons: The open hand has no secrets to guard.
A ring against it can be seen from the first move.

pairs.tendency: Captures add to scores that stay secret, so nobody knows how much a ring is worth. Players guess who is ahead from who they see closing in.
pros: A ring may add secret points.
Players guess the worth of each capture.
cons: Nobody knows who is ahead.
A player may ring the wrong rival.

pairs.tendency: One player moves at a time, so everyone sees a gap and has a turn to close it. Plans for a ring are made while others take their turns.
pros: A ring is seen forming well before it closes.
Each move can be answered.
cons: Waiting for a turn takes long with many players.
A ring half closed gives the victim a turn to leave.

pairs.tendency: Everyone chooses in secret and reveals together, so two players may place into the same gap on the same turn. A piece you meant to ring may have moved.
pros: Every ring is a guess about the others.
Nobody waits for a turn.
cons: Two pieces may land in one gap.
A ring planned on last turn's board may miss.

pairs.tendency: Anyone may act at any moment, so the quickest hand closes the ring. A piece cannot be defended once someone has started to surround it.
pros: The quickest player closes the ring.
Players watch every side of the board.
cons: Slow players lose pieces.
Players grab at the same gap.

pairs.tendency: Each turn has a clock, so a ring planned slowly runs out of time. A move that is lost to the clock leaves a gap open.
pros: The clock pushes players to act.
Quick moves can close a ring.
cons: Running out of time can cost a capture.
There is no time to think through a long plan.

pairs.tendency: One move is made each morning, so a ring closes over days and the victim has all that time to see it. Waiting is part of the play.
pros: Players have time to think about each move.
A ring can be seen days before it closes.
cons: A missed day leaves a gap.
A long wait between moves can lose the thread.

pairs.tendency: The game slows players down on purpose, with a breath before each move. Each piece is placed slowly around the enemy, and the victim watches.
pros: Each placement is deliberate.
Players watch each ring grow.
cons: A slow ring is easy to escape.
The wait before each move stretches the game.

pairs.tendency: The game speeds up as it goes, so rings that were slow at the start close in a rush near the end. Timers shrink while pieces are still being placed.
pros: Rings close quickly near the end.
Players learn to act faster each round.
cons: Late moves are made in a hurry.
Mistakes pile up toward the end.

pairs.tendency: A capture gives you another go at once, so one ring can lead to another. A lucky player can chain several captures before anyone replies.
pros: A capture can lead to another.
Players look for rings that link up.
cons: A chain of captures can end a game in one turn.
The other side waits through a long turn.

pairs.tendency: In the first stage pieces are placed and nothing can be taken, and in the second stage rings begin. How the pieces were placed in stage one decides who can be ringed.
pros: Stage one sets up the rings of stage two.
Players plan ahead for the second stage.
cons: A careless placement in stage one shows up later.
Players cannot take back their first placements.

pairs.tendency: The board works like a real system, such as a village cut off from its water sources, so a ring has the effect it would have in life. Cutting off a source shows who loses water.
pros: A ring shows who is cut off from what.
Players see the effect of cutting a supply.
cons: A ring can cut off a place that other players needed.
The picture needs explaining before it makes sense.

pairs.tendency: Each player plays a group with its own needs, and a ring around one group's piece cuts it off from the others. Players see the problem from where their group stands.
pros: A ring shows how a group gets cut off.
Players understand a group by playing it.
cons: A group with few pieces can be ringed quickly.
Players may defend their group and forget the others.

pairs.tendency: Everyone draws from one limited thing, and a ring around the supply keeps others from reaching it. If players take too much, it runs out for everyone.
pros: A ring can protect or cut off the supply.
Players see who needs the resource.
cons: A ring around the resource can empty it for the rest.
Over-taking leaves nothing for anyone.

pairs.tendency: What you do now shows its effect a few rounds later, so a piece placed today closes a ring only after several turns. The victim does not see the cost at once.
pros: A piece placed early pays off later.
Players think ahead about where a ring will form.
cons: A slow ring is easy to forget.
Results arrive turns after the move.

pairs.tendency: Players agree a new rule, such as how many sides close a ring, then play to see what it changes. Two sides is a quick game and four is a slow one.
pros: Players see what a rule does to captures.
A rule can be tested safely.
cons: Changing the count changes every plan.
Players may disagree about the result.

pairs.tendency: After the game, players talk about which rings worked and why. They compare the board with the real problem the game was about.
pros: Players look back at each ring.
The talk turns captures into lessons.
cons: Remembering old moves is hard.
The talk can run longer than the game.

pairs.tendency: A captured piece is torn up and never comes back, and the next game starts from the board as it ended. Each ring leaves a mark that stays.
pros: Captures carry over to the next game.
Players think hard before closing a ring.
cons: A ring cannot be undone.
The next game starts with fewer pieces.

pairs.tendency: If the only way to take a piece is to hem it in on every side, the game says something about land and power. Players see what the rule rewards by what they end up doing.
pros: Rings show what the rules reward.
Players talk about what the game seems to say.
cons: The point may be missed by some players.
Players can disagree about what the rules mean.

pairs.tendency: A ring takes something real from a real person, such as a promise, money or a favour. Players hesitate before closing the last side.
pros: Players weigh each ring more carefully.
Friends see how each other plays.
cons: A capture can spill into real life.
Players may avoid the game.

pairs.tendency: A ring takes points, and the points stand for something that matters, such as kindness. Players start to ring for the points and forget what they stand for.
pros: A ring shows what the points stand in for.
Players see how points steer them.
cons: Chasing points can push out the reason for them.
The number gets more attention than the thing.

pairs.tendency: Players practise a way of living, such as a village that shares everything, and a ring shows who is cut off from the shared supply. They see how it might feel before trying it.
pros: A ring shows who the new way leaves out.
Players try a future safely.
cons: Not every part of a future fits on a board.
Players may take the practice as a prediction.

pairs.tendency: A player far behind lands on a shortcut square or throws a second time, and one turn can bring them level with the pack.
pros: The back of the pack stays in the race.
Every throw is watched by everyone.
cons: A long lead can vanish in one turn.
The leader has little to plan around.

pairs.tendency: The player in last place picks first from the shared row, so the card the leader wanted is gone before their turn.
pros: The trailing player sees the whole row.
Each pick shapes what the leader can take.
cons: The leader can feel held back for scoring.
The order of picks needs to be tracked every round.

pairs.tendency: Players behind on points start each round with extra coins, so they can outbid the leader for the next prize.
pros: Money flows towards the back.
Every auction stays open to all.
cons: The leader may be priced out of the items they need.
A player can lose a little on purpose to collect the coins.

pairs.tendency: Someone far behind keeps pushing because a bust costs them little, while the leader stops early to guard a lead.
pros: The player at the back takes bigger risks.
The leader's turns get shorter and more careful.
cons: A late bust can still end a comeback.
Players at the front may stop sooner than the game expects.

pairs.tendency: The player holding the fewest regions gets extra pieces each round, so a map that one player seems to own is split up again within a few turns.
pros: Small holdings can grow quickly.
Borders keep moving.
cons: Owning a region does not mean keeping it.
Players spend turns defending instead of expanding.

pairs.tendency: Whoever trails places their workers first next round, and takes the spot that everyone else was waiting for.
pros: The player behind gets the pick of the jobs.
Spots change hands from round to round.
cons: The leader may wait for the leftovers.
A key spot can be taken by the same player several rounds running.

pairs.tendency: A player behind gets a free tile to finish a half-built row, so a pattern can close while the leader is still collecting.
pros: Gaps in a pattern can be filled by the game.
Players check each other's rows often.
cons: Careful planning can be undone by a free tile.
The leader's pattern may stay open for many turns.

pairs.tendency: The player in last place draws extra cards, so they hold a bigger hand than the leader who plays from a small one.
pros: The player behind has more choices each turn.
Hand size shows who is ahead.
cons: Holding more cards takes longer to decide.
The leader has fewer options when it matters.

pairs.tendency: Players who have won few tricks lead the next hand, or swap a low card for a new one before play starts.
pros: A trailing player can set the pace of a hand.
Low cards can be traded away.
cons: The leader plays second more often.
Winning tricks early earns the leader less than it seems.

pairs.tendency: Everyone knows who is behind, so deals lean towards that player, who can trade a bonus for favours.
pros: The player behind has something to offer.
Talk at the table changes with the score.
cons: The leader finds few partners.
Players argue about who counts as behind.

pairs.tendency: The player with the fewest sets takes a free card from the pile, so a set of two can become a set of three in one go.
pros: Small collections grow quickly.
Players watch which sets are almost full.
cons: The leader has to guard sets that are nearly done.
A big set can be matched by a free card.

pairs.tendency: A player behind lays two tiles in one turn, and can close a road or a city before the leader gets there.
pros: The player behind makes bigger moves.
The shared map changes in jumps.
cons: A shape the leader planned can be closed early.
Turns become uneven in length.

pairs.tendency: The player who is behind gets the last word in the chain, so the next line in the exchange is theirs.
pros: Trailing players steer where the chain goes.
The exchange keeps passing between players.
cons: Others wait while one player answers twice.
The chain can lose its rhythm.

pairs.tendency: Nobody talks, so the help shows on the table: the trailing player puts down an extra card in view and nobody can comment on it.
pros: Help is visible to all.
The group reads the table for clues.
cons: Players cannot say why they are puzzled.
Silent players may misread who is behind.

pairs.tendency: A player uses their turn to add a bonus for last place, and the leader answers by rewriting it on theirs.
pros: Rules about the score can be argued over by moves.
Help can be added or removed.
cons: Rule changes can undo the help.
Players spend turns on rules instead of moves.

pairs.tendency: The character who is losing gets a lucky break in the story, such as an ally who turns up at the door.
pros: The story leans towards the character behind.
Players see the help as part of the tale.
cons: Characters ahead may seem to lose their luck.
Players can feel the story is being steered.

pairs.tendency: A player who is behind throws from a closer line or aims at a bigger target, while the leader keeps the usual distance.
pros: The player behind gets an easier next try.
Hands still decide every throw.
cons: The leader plays at a distance that stays harder.
Players argue about where the line goes.

pairs.tendency: The player behind draws first on the shared sheet and puts a road or a river where it suits them, cutting the leader's land off.
pros: The player behind shapes the map.
Everyone's drawing ends up linked.
cons: The leader's land can be split up.
The sheet fills up with the trailing player's marks.

pairs.tendency: The throw already decides everything, and the help adds a rule that pays extra to the trailing player on certain numbers.
pros: The help is another number that comes up.
Players are never sure who will gain.
cons: There is nothing to choose, so the help is only a wait.
The game stays short but the order keeps changing.

pairs.tendency: The slowest runners get a head start or a safe spot, and It has to count to five before moving.
pros: Slow players last longer.
Fast players are kept busy.
cons: Tagging a runner who has a head start takes more effort.
Quick runners may slow down on purpose.

pairs.tendency: With help for the trailing player, everyone picks the leader to hit, since that is the quickest way to level the game.
pros: The leader draws every attack.
The player behind is spared.
cons: Holding a lead gets harder.
Hits on the leader can start grudges.

pairs.tendency: A player behind adds a free stone that can fill a gap in their chain, so a cut line can be joined again.
pros: A broken chain can be mended.
Both sides keep working at cutting the other's line.
cons: A blocked chain can reopen.
The cutting player's work is undone by the free stone.

pairs.tendency: When the leader's choice is revealed, the trailing player gets to choose again, so they can pick the answer that beats it.
pros: The player behind answers with what they know.
No choice is safe for the leader.
cons: The leader may lose after a win.
Players guess what others will pick.

pairs.tendency: A player behind scores double for a declared pair, such as a king and queen of one suit.
pros: Declared pairs gain more.
Others learn what a player holds.
cons: Declaring early tells the leader about your hand.
Players are tempted to hold back cards to declare later.

pairs.tendency: A player who trails unlocks a second power, so their side of the game has a rule no one else has.
pros: The player behind plays with extra rules.
Each player plays their own version.
cons: Powers can pile up on one player.
Players need to remember several rule sets.

pairs.tendency: The player behind offers a double, and the leader has to accept it or give up the points on the table.
pros: A trailing player can raise the price.
The leader faces a choice.
cons: A double can end the game early.
The leader may give up points to avoid a risk.

pairs.tendency: The leader has to capture when they can, and a trailing player sets bait so the capture drags the leader's piece into a trap.
pros: A forced move can be used against the leader.
The player behind decides where pieces end up.
cons: A bait costs the player a piece.
Planning a trap takes several moves.

pairs.tendency: A character gains power faster when behind, so later challenges meet characters of nearly the same size.
pros: The gap in power stays small.
Every player takes on late challenges.
cons: Early moves count for less.
The leader has less reason to play carefully.

pairs.tendency: The player who is behind adds two items in one turn, or reads the list from a card while others recite from memory.
pros: The player behind has help with remembering.
Everyone listens to the list as it grows.
cons: The list grows faster on that turn.
Others may feel the card slows the game.

pairs.tendency: A handicap sets the gap before the first turn, and the help keeps adjusting it as the score changes.
pros: The game stays close at the start and in the middle.
An uneven start does not settle the result.
cons: Two sets of rules to keep in mind.
The leader may feel their lead is taxed twice.

pairs.tendency: The seeker who has found the fewest gets a hint, and the hider who was found first gets longer to hide next time.
pros: Slow seekers get a clue.
Hiding times change with each round.
cons: Hints can end a long search quickly.
Hiders may take longer settling.

pairs.tendency: A player with few pieces left may jump twice in one move, so a single turn can clear several of the leader's pieces.
pros: One move can change the board.
The player behind takes bigger steps.
cons: The leader can lose a lot at once.
Pieces cannot be left in a line.

pairs.tendency: The player behind gets one more reroll than the others, so they can keep trying for a set the leader already holds.
pros: More rolls for the player behind.
Every extra roll is watched.
cons: The leader's set can be matched by a late roll.
Waiting for the extra roll slows the table.

pairs.tendency: Safe squares cover the trailing player's pieces, while the leader's piece sent back to the start loses the most ground.
pros: The player behind is safe on more squares.
A send-back swings the score by a lot.
cons: The leader's piece is a bigger target.
A lead can disappear in one landing.

pairs.tendency: A player down to a few pieces may move any piece to any empty point, so a row of three can appear from nowhere and take a piece.
pros: A small army can still make a row.
Empty points matter to both sides.
cons: The leader has to watch every empty point.
Rows can be broken before they close.

pairs.tendency: The player behind draws extra letters and scores more for long words, so a short list of tiles can still make a big word.
pros: The player behind has more letters to work with.
Long words earn extra.
cons: Rack changes slow the turn.
Players check the dictionary more often.

pairs.tendency: A trailing player draws from the pile until a tile fits, so they never miss a turn while the leader waits for a match.
pros: The player behind does not lose turns.
Tiles in the pile are used up quickly.
cons: The leader may miss turns more often.
The pile runs low early.

pairs.tendency: A player behind may add cards to other people's melds for points, so a set the leader laid down feeds the trailing player's score.
pros: Melds on the table help more than one player.
Players watch each other's sets.
cons: The leader's work earns points for others.
Laying down a set early gives help away.

pairs.tendency: A player who trails gets a fresh marker for a spent power, so they can use it a second time.
pros: One power can be used twice.
Choosing when to use it matters more.
cons: Others learn which powers are left.
The leader may save a power for fear of the second.

pairs.tendency: The player behind gets the last say on the leader's offered move, and may turn it down or take the other choice.
pros: The trailing player can steer the leader's move.
Offers are made carefully.
cons: The leader's turns depend on another player.
A turned-down offer wastes the turn.

pairs.tendency: The team whose message has been garbled most gets to ask for one repeat, so a whisper can be checked once before it moves on.
pros: The message can be fixed once.
Everyone listens harder.
cons: A repeat slows the line.
The team ahead may not hear the repeat.

pairs.tendency: The leader passes their highest cards to the player behind before play begins, and the trailing player passes low ones.
pros: Hands are set up before play.
Choosing what to pass matters.
cons: The leader starts with a smaller hand.
Cards cannot be viewed until chosen.

pairs.tendency: The pie rule evens out the first move, and the help keeps evening it out as the score changes.
pros: The game is close from the start.
The start and the finish are both watched.
cons: Players may set up a start for the help to follow.
The first player may spend longer on the set-up.

pairs.tendency: A trailing player's pieces promote one row earlier, so a piece that is halfway can turn into a bigger piece.
pros: The player behind reaches the far end sooner.
Pieces that were left behind matter.
cons: A leader's piece can get caught in the way.
The leader has to defend the far rows.

pairs.tendency: The team that is behind runs a shorter next leg, so the baton arrives at the finish before the leader's.
pros: A gap between teams can close in one leg.
Every leg is watched.
cons: A fast team may run a longer leg.
The order of runners is argued over.

pairs.tendency: A trailing player gets a free stone that completes a safe shape, so a group the other player was surrounding is suddenly out of reach.
pros: A group in danger can become safe.
The goal is clear to see.
cons: The surrounding player loses their work.
Players look for the missing stone from the start.

pairs.tendency: The player behind gets the first claim on one of the named prize cards, so the highest trump may go to them before a trick is played.
pros: The prizes are not decided by tricks alone.
Players keep an eye on which prizes are left.
cons: The leader can lose a prize without a fight.
Prize cards need to be tracked every hand.

pairs.tendency: The trailing player chooses which shared card is turned up next, and the whole table can use it.
pros: The shared row follows the player behind.
Everyone works from the same cards.
cons: The leader gets help from the trailing player's choice.
The shared cards give the same chance to all.

pairs.tendency: The trailing player takes a bigger share of the pot, so a pot that has grown over many rounds can lift them level.
pros: The pot is worth more to the player behind.
The pot keeps growing when nobody wins.
cons: The leader gets a smaller share.
With a big pot, each round carries more.

pairs.tendency: A player with fewer seeds in their pits gets an extra sowing move, so a short row of pits can reach the full ones.
pros: A small pit can reach far.
Players count seeds before each turn.
cons: The player ahead guards the pits on the far side.
An extra move takes the pit count out of reach.

pairs.tendency: The player behind picks from the spare hand first, so the extra cards go to the one at the back.
pros: The trailing player has first choice.
The spare hand changes hands often.
cons: The leader may take a hand with low cards.
Looking through the spare cards takes time.

pairs.tendency: One square sends the leader back while another moves the trailing player ahead, so the track can turn a lead into a gap.
pros: Squares change who is ahead.
The track is learned over several games.
cons: Players can aim for the squares.
A safe square may be avoided.

pairs.tendency: Players behind pay less for each card or unit, so they can buy what the leader pays full price for.
pros: Prices fall for the player behind.
The same money buys more.
cons: Items run out sooner.
The leader pays more for the same thing.

pairs.tendency: The trailing player gets extra forces to share out, so they can cover another place the leader has left open.
pros: One more place can be covered.
Both sides share out their forces.
cons: Forces grow thin in every place.
The leader has to guess where the extra goes.

pairs.tendency: The player who has been caught most often gets a head start when the signal comes, and the next seat is theirs.
pros: Slow players get a chance to win.
The signal is watched by all.
cons: The same players catch up more often.
Players may fall behind on purpose.

pairs.tendency: A trailing player may swap three cards while the leader swaps two, so their hand can be remade before it is played.
pros: More cards can be swapped.
Hands change quickly.
cons: The leader works with a hand that is harder to change.
Another player may have to agree to the swap.

pairs.tendency: A trailing player picks up the discard pile without having to use the top card, while the leader needs a match.
pros: The pile is open to the player behind.
The pile grows when nobody takes it.
cons: A big pile is hard to hold.
The leader sees the pile go.

pairs.tendency: Players behind choose the trump suit for the next hand, so low cards in that suit beat the leader's high ones.
pros: The trailing player names the suit.
Trump changes from hand to hand.
cons: The leader's high cards may lose.
Players plan their hands before the suit is named.

pairs.tendency: A player can be ahead on one board and behind on the other, so help is handed out on each board separately.
pros: Help is aimed at one board.
A player can be both attacking and defending.
cons: Two boards mean two scores to track.
Help on one board can hurt the other.

pairs.tendency: Trailing players are dealt extra wild cards, so a set that was one card short is finished from the first hand.
pros: Missing cards can be filled.
The player behind reaches sets sooner.
cons: The leader sees their sets matched.
Wild cards run out early.

pairs.tendency: A piece far behind can come in from the other side after wrapping, and arrive close to the leader's line.
pros: A piece at the back can come out in front.
Distance on the board is shorter than it looks.
cons: Pieces can be caught from behind.
The leader has to watch both edges.

pairs.tendency: The guesser with the fewest points gets two extra questions, so the list of things it could be shrinks faster.
pros: The player behind learns more.
Each answer cuts the list.
cons: The secret keeper has to answer more often.
Extra questions slow the game.

pairs.tendency: The help shortens the trailing player's path in a race, while the leader's finish line stays as far as before.
pros: The gap in a race can close.
The result stays open until the end.
cons: Early moves lose some of their weight.
The leader loses speed.

pairs.tendency: Players behind earn bonus points on scoring turns, so the final scores end up close.
pros: Scores stay near each other.
The last turns still matter.
cons: Early points count for less.
The leader's lead shrinks by rule.

pairs.tendency: A player near knock-out gets a shield or a second life, so the last two or three players are often closer in strength than they began.
pros: Players near the end stay in the game.
Knock-outs come later.
cons: The game runs longer.
The last player has had more help.

pairs.tendency: The help goes to whoever has the least health, so the group lifts its most hurt member before moving on.
pros: The whole group stays alive longer.
Players decide who gets help.
cons: The helped player takes up the group's turns.
The group has to track every player's health.

pairs.tendency: One shared score leaves nobody behind another, so the help has to be aimed at a person's own position, such as the size of their hand.
pros: Help follows each player's own cards.
The group keeps one goal.
cons: There is no clear leader to catch.
Players may argue over who needs the help.

pairs.tendency: Players cannot tell who is behind because goals are secret, and a bonus given to one player tells the rest a little about their goal.
pros: A bonus can give a goal away.
Players watch who gets help.
cons: Secret goals get harder to keep.
Trailing players may refuse the help to hide their goal.

pairs.tendency: The story turns in the trailing character's favour, with a lucky meeting or an open door, while the ending stays open for all.
pros: The story moves towards the player behind.
Every character gets a part in the ending.
cons: The story can feel steered.
An ending may arrive before the help does.

pairs.tendency: With no score, nobody is behind in numbers, so the group has to agree who needs help, such as the quietest player.
pros: The group chooses who gets help.
Nobody is ranked.
cons: There is no number to measure help by.
The help rests on opinion.

pairs.tendency: Each player says what behind means for them, and the help is given against that word, so one player's gap may be another's finish.
pros: Help follows each player's own aim.
Goals are said out loud.
cons: Players can disagree about the gap.
The leader is hard to name.

pairs.tendency: The player closest to losing gets help, so several players end up in danger together and the loser is named late.
pros: Several players stay at risk.
The loser is not clear until the end.
cons: Players near the end wait longer.
The game can run on past the point it seemed over.

pairs.tendency: Help for those behind keeps players near each other, so the game has no clear leader and no reason to end.
pros: The game goes on longer.
Players stay near each other.
cons: Nobody is clearly ahead.
The ending is hard to find.

pairs.tendency: The game has nothing to win, so the help closes gaps between scores that mean nothing, and players may laugh at it.
pros: The help shows what the game is refusing.
Players notice the gap between scores and aims.
cons: The help has no goal to serve.
The point of the help can be lost.

pairs.tendency: Playing alone, the help comes as an extra undo or a free card when you are stuck, so a blocked table can open again.
pros: A stuck game can be freed.
Each undo is counted.
cons: The layout is easier to beat.
The help may come too late.

pairs.tendency: The loser of the last game starts the next one or gets a head start, so several games in a row stay open.
pros: A lost game can be made up.
The series stays open until later.
cons: A winning streak is harder to build.
The finish may come late.

pairs.tendency: The player with the most points gets a chance to dump them, so a big pile of points can be cut down in one round.
pros: Large totals can fall quickly.
Players hold their points close.
cons: The leader hides nothing.
Players watch each other's piles.

pairs.tendency: A player who is behind may finish on any number within two of the target, while the others need the exact one.
pros: The trailing player has more ways to finish.
The target is easier to reach.
cons: The leader may overshoot waiting for the exact number.
The finish rule differs between players.

pairs.tendency: The player holding the most cards gets to give some away for free, so the one furthest from winning can empty their hand in a turn.
pros: Giving away is quicker for the player behind.
The last cards are watched.
cons: The leader keeps a hand that is hard to empty.
Players may hold cards back on purpose.

pairs.tendency: Players cannot hinder the leader, so the help comes from the bank as a bonus handed to whoever is behind.
pros: Help comes from the game alone.
Each player keeps building their own.
cons: There is no way to slow the leader.
Players only see the gap grow or close.

pairs.tendency: The leader becomes the target, and attacks on them cost less than attacks on anyone else.
pros: Attacks have a clear aim.
The leader is always watched.
cons: The leader takes the most hits.
Players may hold back an attack to keep from being the leader.

pairs.tendency: The trailing player gets squares that block the leader, so the leader feels the help as walls and gaps on the board.
pros: The board carries the help.
Players never attack directly.
cons: The leader finds a route closed.
Walls can slow everyone down.

pairs.tendency: Help goes to the character with the fewest cards, so the team lifts the one at the back before the game can win.
pros: The team looks after its lowest member.
Everyone shares one result.
cons: Help takes a turn away from another.
Players may argue who needs help.

pairs.tendency: The help goes to the player whose private score is low, and the others may hesitate, since helping costs them a little.
pros: Players balance a shared goal against a private score.
Players weigh each offer.
cons: Others may refuse to help.
The group can split over who gets the help.

pairs.tendency: The team behind gets an extra move or card, and the partners work out together how to use it.
pros: Teammates plan the help together.
The gap between teams can close.
cons: The leading team may feel held back.
Talking about the help can take time.

pairs.tendency: A player who claims to be behind may be the traitor, so the group argues over who gets the help.
pros: The help is a test of who is trusted.
Players watch each other's claims.
cons: The traitor can get help meant for others.
The group may help the wrong person.

pairs.tendency: A player behind sends two moves in one letter, so a game that lasts weeks can close a gap in a single post.
pros: Fewer letters are needed to catch up.
The wait between moves is used.
cons: The other player waits longer.
A letter with two moves is easy to misread.

pairs.tendency: The game keeps a score for the absent player, and the help flows to them through dummy moves when they fall behind.
pros: The absent player stays in the game.
The table plays for someone who is away.
cons: Players make moves for a person who is not there.
The absent player cannot say if the help is wanted.

pairs.tendency: The game master nudges the story towards the player behind, with a helpful stranger or a found item.
pros: The game master decides how much help.
Help arrives inside the story.
cons: Players may see through it.
The game master has to watch every player's position.

pairs.tendency: A passer-by who joins late starts with a bonus, so a new player can stand beside those who began earlier.
pros: Latecomers can join in.
The game stays open to anyone.
cons: Players who began earlier see their lead cut.
The bonus has to be explained to each new player.

pairs.tendency: The side that is behind gets the help, so the lone player or the group takes the extra move, depending on the score.
pros: Help goes to either side.
The lone player's pay stays high.
cons: The group may feel helped less.
Players argue about which side is behind.

pairs.tendency: Playing alone against the pack, the help comes as extra draws, so a run of low cards can be broken by a free one.
pros: A losing run can be cut short.
You can compare your result with a friend.
cons: The pack is easier to beat.
There is no one else to measure the help against.

pairs.tendency: Dice already decide most of what happens, and the help lets the player behind throw again when they fall too far.
pros: A second throw helps the back.
Luck still decides the order.
cons: Skill has even less to do.
A lead means little until the last throw.

pairs.tendency: Re-rolls soften a low throw and the help softens a low score, and both can be in play at once.
pros: Luck and score are both eased.
Players have several ways out.
cons: There are more rules to remember.
A low throw and a low score are fixed by different tools.

pairs.tendency: A little luck is added to the skill, and the help keeps the less practised player from dropping out.
pros: A beginner stays close to an expert.
Skill still counts.
cons: A clever move does not always pay.
The expert may feel their skill counts for less.

pairs.tendency: A beginner can stay close to a player who has played for years, since the help hands them points that skill would not.
pros: A new player has a chance.
The game still rests on thought.
cons: The skilled player's lead is cut by the game.
The result may not match the play.

pairs.tendency: The player behind may read the throw twice and pick the reading, so the sign can be taken a different way.
pros: A throw has more than one reading.
Players talk about what a throw means.
cons: The sign loses some of its weight.
Readings may be argued over.

pairs.tendency: The group slows down to let the player who is behind catch the rhythm, and the next act waits for them.
pros: The player behind can find the pace.
Everyone listens closely.
cons: The others have to wait.
The rhythm of the group may break.

pairs.tendency: The player behind rolls on a table with more lucky events, so the dice write kinder parts of the story for them.
pros: The story bends for the player behind.
Dice still write the tale.
cons: Each player needs a table of their own.
Players can read the help in the story.

pairs.tendency: Everything is visible, so the leader sees the help coming and can plan around it.
pros: Help is open to all.
Players can work out the next turn.
cons: The leader knows their lead will be cut.
Nothing is left to surprise.

pairs.tendency: The player behind draws extra cards that nobody else sees, so the others cannot tell how close they are.
pros: A hidden hand grows.
Others have to guess.
cons: The help is easy to hide.
Players cannot tell if the help changed anything.

pairs.tendency: A bonus to the player who is behind shows who is not winning, which narrows down who holds which secret role.
pros: The help gives a clue.
Roles are guessed from who gets help.
cons: A hidden player can pose as one who is behind.
The help can point at the wrong person.

pairs.tendency: The player behind gets a clue for free, so a trailing player can close a gap in the mystery with one reveal.
pros: A free clue narrows the list.
Players compare what they know.
cons: The leader's search is overtaken.
A clue can show more than the leader wanted.

pairs.tendency: A player who is behind may bluff about how far, so others do not know whether the help is deserved.
pros: Players watch each other's claims.
A bluff can bring the help early.
cons: Players may not trust the score.
A caught bluff costs the help.

pairs.tendency: Newcomers are forgiven their first broken rules, so a player who has just learned the secret rule loses less by breaking it.
pros: New players break rules with less cost.
The secret rule is learned by trying.
cons: The player who knows the rule has less to enjoy.
The first mistakes tell little.

pairs.tendency: The hinter gives an extra hint if the guessers are behind, so the picture or sign tells them a little more.
pros: The guessers get another clue.
The hinter picks what to show.
cons: More hints make guesses easier.
The hinter has to keep track of the score.

pairs.tendency: The player behind turns up one more area than usual, so a hidden part of the map is shown to them first.
pros: The player behind sees more.
The map opens in a new order.
cons: The leader goes into hidden land.
Others see which areas were turned.

pairs.tendency: The player behind plays the open hand more often, so the hand laid face up is theirs to use.
pros: The open hand is theirs.
Everyone sees the cards.
cons: The player behind plays two hands.
Others know what the open hand holds.

pairs.tendency: Scores are kept secret, so nobody can tell who is behind, and the help is paid out from a hidden count.
pros: Players guess who is ahead.
The help rests on a number only one can see.
cons: Help can go to the wrong player.
Players cannot check where the help went.

pairs.tendency: The player in last place goes first in the next round, so the order of turns follows the score.
pros: The trailing player acts early.
The order changes each round.
cons: The leader waits longer.
Players need to remember who goes first.

pairs.tendency: Everyone chooses at the same moment, and the player behind gets a second pick that is revealed with the rest.
pros: Help arrives at the reveal.
Nobody waits.
cons: The others cannot tell who has the extra pick.
The reveal takes longer.

pairs.tendency: The fastest players wait a short while before they can act again, so a slower player gets to the cards first.
pros: Slower players reach the cards.
Anyone can act at any moment.
cons: Quick players spend time waiting.
The wait has to be watched.

pairs.tendency: The player behind gets more time on the clock, so a long think costs them nothing while the leader hurries.
pros: The trailing player can think longer.
The clock shows who is behind.
cons: The leader plays with less time.
Players watch each other's clocks.

pairs.tendency: A trailing player makes two moves in one day, so a game that runs over weeks can close a gap on a Monday.
pros: The gap can close while waiting.
Waiting is part of the play.
cons: The leader sees a lead shrink overnight.
Players have to check the log each morning.

pairs.tendency: The slow pace gives the player behind time to plan their jump, and the pause before each move works for them.
pros: The player behind can plan.
The pause is used by all.
cons: A long pause lets the leader plan too.
The wait for the help is long.

pairs.tendency: The game speeds up, so help that arrives late may come too late, and help that arrives early is lost in the early rounds.
pros: The help has to land at the right time.
Players watch the speed.
cons: A late bonus may come after the end.
The rush leaves little room for the help to work.

pairs.tendency: Extra turns go more often to the trailing player, so one lucky hit can bring several moves in a row.
pros: Trailing players move several times.
A hit gives a reward.
cons: A run of turns can swing the game.
The leader may sit out a long stretch.

pairs.tendency: Results from the first stage turn into starting bonuses for the second, so the player behind arrives with an edge.
pros: The first stage affects the second.
Players know what they bring.
cons: Winning early earns less.
Two stages mean two sets of help.

pairs.tendency: In a village water game, the group sends extra water to the village that has least, which shows how aid moves in real life.
pros: The model shows how help flows.
Players see who has less.
cons: Water sent to one village leaves another short.
The model gets harder to read.

pairs.tendency: The group with the least gets support, as a council might give, and the others see what that costs them.
pros: Each group sees the help from where it stands.
The roles show who is left out.
cons: The helping group gives something up.
Players argue for their own group.

pairs.tendency: Helping the players behind means drawing from the shared resource, so it empties sooner for everyone.
pros: Help is paid from the common pool.
Everyone can see the pool fall.
cons: The pool may run out early.
The leader and the helped share the loss.

pairs.tendency: The help lands a few rounds later, so a trailing player waits while the leader's lead may have grown by then.
pros: Help comes after a wait.
Players plan for the next few rounds.
cons: The gap may grow before it closes.
The help may arrive after it is needed.

pairs.tendency: Players agree catch-up help as a new rule and play on to see who gets it and what it changes.
pros: The rule is tested in play.
The group sees its effect.
cons: The rule may change the game's feel.
A rule that does not work has to be dropped.

pairs.tendency: After the game, players talk about who the help went to and whether it changed the ending.
pros: The help can be talked over.
Players share what they saw.
cons: Talking it over can outlast the play.
Players may disagree about what the help did.

pairs.tendency: A bonus tears a card up or puts a sticker on the board, so the help stays for the next game.
pros: The help is kept.
The next game starts from where this one ended.
cons: A change cannot be taken back.
The same player may get help again.

pairs.tendency: A game that gives help to those behind says that a player who is losing deserves another chance, and players read the rule as a claim.
pros: The rule says something about the world.
Players talk about it.
cons: Others may disagree with the claim.
The game can be read as taking a side.

pairs.tendency: Real money is on the table, so help for the player behind looks like a gift, and arguments start over whether it is allowed.
pros: The stakes stay open.
Friends talk about what is allowed.
cons: The help can strain a friendship.
Money can change hands over the help.

pairs.tendency: Points stand for kindness, so help for the one behind lets them earn more, and players start chasing the help.
pros: Players see what points reward.
The help shows what the points have taken the place of.
cons: Players chase the number.
Kindness can become a way to score.

pairs.tendency: In a village that shares everything, help for the one with least is what sharing looks like, and players feel it from inside.
pros: Players try sharing in practice.
The help makes the future visible.
cons: The leader gives something up.
Players may find it hard to accept the help.

pairs.tendency: Everyone throws and walks the path, and the throw is the only thing that happens on a turn. The order on the board is set by the dice and nothing else.
pros: Turns take a few seconds.
Anyone can lead, whatever their age.
cons: Nothing a player does changes where they land.
Players drift off while others throw.

pairs.tendency: A row of cards sits in the middle, but the card each player takes is drawn blindly, so passing the row round does not give anyone a pick. The cards still travel from hand to hand.
pros: Everyone sees the same row.
Cards keep moving round the table.
cons: The choosing step has nothing in it.
Players who like picking have no pick to make.

pairs.tendency: Players name a price, then a throw names the buyer whatever was offered. After a few rounds the offers stop meaning anything, since the highest bid wins no more often than the lowest.
pros: Players still talk about prices.
Offers can turn into a joke at the table.
cons: Money spent buys no extra chance.
Players stop bothering to bid.

pairs.tendency: A card is turned for each player and it says keep going or stop. The player never gets to say "one more", because the card says it for them.
pros: Turns are over in seconds.
Everyone watches each card turn.
cons: The risky choice is taken away.
A run of lucky cards is only watched.

pairs.tendency: A throw decides which pieces land in which region, so the map fills up with whatever the dice allow. The player who holds the most spots got there by luck.
pros: The map changes with every throw.
A region can change hands in one turn.
cons: Holding a spot says nothing about planning.
Nobody can defend what they own.

pairs.tendency: A die sends each worker to a job, and two workers can be sent to the same one. The first to arrive blocks the rest.
pros: The board fills up quickly.
The jobs on offer are easy to read.
cons: Placing a worker takes no thought.
A player can be shut out of every job by one roll.

pairs.tendency: Tiles come out of a bag and are placed as drawn. A neat line of one colour turns up only when the draws hand over the right tiles.
pros: The pattern grows in front of everyone.
A lucky draw can finish a row at once.
cons: Planning a pattern has little to work on.
A run of wrong colours leaves a gap for many turns.

pairs.tendency: The hand is dealt, but a die picks which card is played, so holding one back for later cannot happen. The hand is only a list of what will be played.
pros: Players see their whole hand from the start.
Every deal reads differently.
cons: Saving a card means nothing.
Holding a hand turns into waiting.

pairs.tendency: Each player turns the top card of their pile with no choice, and the highest card takes the trick. The deal alone says who wins.
pros: A trick is over in seconds.
The winner is named at once.
cons: No card is kept back for the right moment.
Winning the lead gives the winner nothing to decide.

pairs.tendency: Players talk and trade, but every deal is about things that luck hands out. A promise is made over a throw that has not happened yet.
pros: Players talk a lot.
Deals can be made about the next roll.
cons: A promise can fall apart on the next throw.
Talking cannot change the result.

pairs.tendency: Cards come in by draw, and a set is finished when the right ones turn up. A player cannot go and look for the missing piece.
pros: Sets grow slowly in front of each player.
Everyone can see who is close.
cons: The last piece can take many turns to arrive.
There is no way to speed it up.

pairs.tendency: Tiles are drawn from a bag and placed where they fit, with no say in which tile comes out. The map is made of whatever the bag gives.
pros: Every game gives a new map.
Each player adds a piece to the same picture.
cons: Roads can end in dead ends no one planned.
Nobody can steer the map.

pairs.tendency: One player calls a word or a move, and the reply is read off a card or a die instead of being thought up by the next player. The chain goes on, though no player is answering anyone.
pros: The chain takes silly turns.
Replies come fast.
cons: The reply no longer comes from a second player.
Players only read out what turns up.

pairs.tendency: Nobody speaks, and nobody has anything to show either, since the cards come out by luck. Players sit quietly and watch each other turn cards.
pros: The table stays calm.
Players watch each other's faces.
cons: Silence adds little when nobody has a choice.
Players may begin to fidget.

pairs.tendency: A player can change a rule on their turn, while the dice still settle every result. Rule changes only change how a throw is read, so a high roll may be turned into a low one.
pros: Players can reshape how the dice are read.
A rule change has a clear effect on luck.
cons: A rule change is the only decision anyone makes.
Rules can pile up until the dice mean little.

pairs.tendency: A character is played in voice and manner, while a die says what happens to them. The player can say what the character wants, and the throw settles it.
pros: Players act out the scenes.
Stories take sudden turns.
cons: One roll can sweep aside a character's plan.
Players may feel they are along for the ride.

pairs.tendency: Players flick or stack pieces, then a die says who scored, so a steady hand makes no difference. The flick still happens, but the score comes from the die.
pros: Players move and handle real things.
The table gets lively.
cons: Steady hands earn nothing.
A die can undo a clean flick.

pairs.tendency: Players draw the map, and chance says what appears on it: a card calls for a river, a throw says where it goes. The map holds places nobody would have picked.
pros: Maps look odd and different each time.
Players join up strange pieces.
cons: Planning the drawing is no use.
Two players can draw things that clash.

pairs.tendency: Players run and tag, but a coin or a throw picks who is It each round, whatever happened in the chase. Running away does not change who gets tagged.
pros: It changes hands at once.
Escaping earns nothing.
cons: Running away has no use.
Players may slow down when they notice the chase changes nothing.

pairs.tendency: A player picks who is hit, helped or traded with, and a die says what happens to that person. The choice sets who it lands on, never how hard.
pros: Players can pick a side.
Grudges can grow even with dice.
cons: The choice cannot make a hit any stronger.
A hit may be heavy or nothing at all, by a roll.

pairs.tendency: Stones go down by draw, and a chain across the board forms only when the draws line up. The dice also decide when a chain is cut.
pros: Chains grow in odd directions.
One draw can join two groups.
cons: A player cannot plan a route.
The other side cannot cut a chain on purpose.

pairs.tendency: Each choice beats one other and loses to a third, yet chance picks the choice, so no player picks. The cycle turns into a chart of who wins, read off the roll.
pros: The chart keeps every choice in use.
Results come quickly.
cons: Nobody can guess the opponent.
The cycle is built for guessing, and here there is nothing to guess.

pairs.tendency: Holding a pair or a run lets a player declare it for points, but the hand came from the deal. Declaring is only reading out what luck gave, and some hands have nothing to declare.
pros: Declaring is quick.
Everyone hears what the others hold.
cons: Hands come with no building up.
A hand with no pair scores nothing that round.

pairs.tendency: Each seat has its own power, and a throw decides when it works. A power fires when a number comes up, not when the player picks the moment.
pros: Each seat plays differently.
Powers give a seat its own look.
cons: A power can sit unused for the whole game.
A power may fire at a useless time.

pairs.tendency: A player offers to double the game's worth, and the other accepts or gives up, with no way to read the position. The only guide is a guess about the next throw.
pros: Each offer is a clear moment.
Stakes can climb quickly.
cons: The offer is made blind.
One throw can wipe out a big pile of stakes.

pairs.tendency: A capture has to be taken when one is on the board, and chance decides whether one is on offer. Pieces are taken when the dice allow, and the taker has no say.
pros: Captures happen often.
Both players can see what is forced.
cons: Nobody can set a trap.
A player cannot avoid a capture.

pairs.tendency: A character gains power with each success, and success comes from the dice. The player who throws high early ends up with more power, and later challenges are easier for them.
pros: Characters change as the game goes on.
Early luck carries forward.
cons: A low start can never be made up.
Players watch the same few leaders grow.

pairs.tendency: Each player repeats the list and adds one item, and a card or die picks the item. The list becomes a string of odd, unrelated things to remember.
pros: Memory gets a real test.
The list gets silly.
cons: Players cannot choose easy items.
Late turns are long recitals.

pairs.tendency: A player known to win often starts with fewer stones, but when dice decide everything there is no skill gap to close. The handicap only takes away from someone who had no edge.
pros: Players start with different amounts.
The handicap is easy to see.
cons: The reduced player loses ground for no reason.
Nobody can explain the result.

pairs.tendency: The hiding place is picked by a draw, and finding is settled by a throw. Searching turns into waiting for a number.
pros: Hiding places surprise everyone.
The search can end on one throw.
cons: Looking carefully gives no help.
A hider cannot pick a clever spot.

pairs.tendency: A piece hops over another into the empty space behind it, but dice choose which piece hops and when. A row of pieces can fall for no reason anyone planned.
pros: Hops can come in chains.
The board empties quickly.
cons: A player cannot set up a hop.
One throw can clear a row.

pairs.tendency: Dice are rolled and rolled again, but setting some aside is a choice, so the two blocks clash. If a player may keep dice, chance no longer decides everything.
pros: Players watch every throw.
Rerolls keep the dice moving.
cons: Setting dice aside brings back choices.
The rules need a line to say which block wins.

pairs.tendency: A piece lands on a space where another stands and sends it home. The dice pick the landing, so a piece is sent back by luck and nobody aimed for it.
pros: A leader can lose everything in one throw.
Players groan or cheer together.
cons: A sent-back piece starts again from nothing.
Safe spaces are the only protection.

pairs.tendency: Three in a row lets a player take a piece, but rows form only when draws drop pieces side by side. Most mills come by accident and cannot be blocked.
pros: A row can appear without warning.
Taking a piece is a clear moment.
cons: Players cannot stop the other side's rows.
Players build rows without aiming.

pairs.tendency: Letters come by draw and cannot be swapped, so words come out of whatever turned up. A hand of odd letters gives odd words.
pros: Strange words turn up.
A dictionary settles arguments.
cons: A hand of rare letters gives little to build.
A player's skill with words counts for nothing.

pairs.tendency: Tiles are turned from a pile and set down where they fit, or not at all. A line grows only as far as the draws allow.
pros: The line grows without planning.
Matches are easy to check.
cons: Many turns end in a miss.
Players wait for a tile that fits.

pairs.tendency: A finished set is laid face up, and others can add to it. Sets form by draw, so a meld appears when the right cards arrive.
pros: Melds are open to all.
Others can add to a set.
cons: Nobody can aim for a set.
Sets arrive at odd moments.

pairs.tendency: Every piece has a power that works once, and a throw says when it fires. The marker comes off when it does, so luck uses up the power and nobody picks the moment.
pros: Each power is a small surprise.
Markers show what is spent.
cons: Nobody chooses when to use it.
A power can go off when it helps nobody.

pairs.tendency: A move is offered and the other player may turn it down. When a die gives the move, a refusal only swaps one throw for another.
pros: The other player has a part in each turn.
A refusal can be argued over.
cons: A refusal changes nothing that matters.
Turns run long with back-and-forth.

pairs.tendency: A message goes from player to player, and a die decides how it changes on the way. The die garbles it, and nobody mishears anything.
pros: Messages end up funny.
Everyone waits to hear the end.
cons: Nobody can be blamed for a change.
The change says nothing about who listened.

pairs.tendency: Cards are handed on before play, and what comes back is a draw. The player chooses what to give but not what to get, so passing fixes nothing.
pros: Players think about what to give.
Hands change before play.
cons: The choice of what to give hardly affects what comes back.
Hands read the same whatever is passed.

pairs.tendency: One player sets up and the other picks a side, but there is nothing to even out when the dice rule both sides alike. The first player arranges a start, the second picks, and the throws decide anyway.
pros: Picking a side is quick.
Setting up takes little time.
cons: The pie rule has no work to do.
Both sides play the same dice.

pairs.tendency: A piece that reaches the far end turns into a more powerful piece. When dice give the moves, reaching the end is a matter of throws.
pros: Reaching the end marks a moment.
Promotions change the board.
cons: Pushing forward is a gamble with no say.
A lucky piece can be promoted in a few throws.

pairs.tendency: Teams run in legs and hand over a flag, and a die gives the speed of each leg. The runner's practice makes no difference.
pros: Teams cheer for their runner.
A close race goes down to the last leg.
cons: Practice does not help the runner.
Teams cannot choose their order.

pairs.tendency: Some shapes cannot be captured, but with stones put down by a draw a safe shape turns up only by chance. Players cannot work towards one.
pros: A safe shape is a clear sign.
The other player can see it too.
cons: A safe shape cannot be planned.
Surrounding stones is done blindly.

pairs.tendency: The prizes are named cards, such as the highest trump, and whoever is dealt the card wins the prize. Tricks lead nowhere, since the deal already says who gets what.
pros: Prizes are known from the start.
Players watch for the named cards.
cons: The prize goes to whoever is dealt it.
Winning a trick gives the winner nothing extra.

pairs.tendency: Some cards sit face up in the middle for everyone, and hands come from the deal. The same middle cards serve the whole table, and a player can only wait for the next one.
pros: Everyone sees the same middle cards.
Luck is shared out openly.
cons: Hands depend on the deal.
Waiting is the only thing left to do.

pairs.tendency: Everyone puts a counter in the middle, and a throw names the winner. If nobody wins, the pot grows into the next round.
pros: The pot grows each round.
A big pot draws every eye.
cons: A win depends on one throw.
Players lose their counters without a say.

pairs.tendency: Seeds are scooped from a pit and dropped round the board, but a die picks the pit. Sowing becomes a counting job, with seeds travelling to places nobody chose.
pros: Seeds travel round the board.
Counting seeds shows what is coming.
cons: The choice of pit is made by the die.
Pits empty without anyone planning.

pairs.tendency: An extra hand lies face down in the middle, and one player takes, swaps or buys it. Its cards came from the deal, so taking it is a blind gamble.
pros: The spare hand gives the table something to talk about.
Players eye it as it is passed.
cons: A swap is a guess.
The spare may hold less than the hand it replaced.

pairs.tendency: Some spaces keep a piece safe, send it back or skip a turn. The throw lands a piece on a square, and the square does the rest, so the squares are the only part anyone can point at.
pros: The board has a few spots to remember.
One square can swing the game.
cons: A player cannot avoid a square.
The die and the squares decide everything between them.

pairs.tendency: Every card has a price, but cards come by chance, so a player spends on whatever was drawn.
pros: Costs are clear on each card.
Players count what they hold.
cons: Choosing what to buy has little scope.
Costly cards can sit unused.

pairs.tendency: A fixed number of pieces is shared across several places, and a die does the sharing. The other side's split also comes from a die.
pros: Forces end up in odd places.
Both splits come as a surprise.
cons: Putting a lot in one place is not a choice.
A split can leave one place empty.

pairs.tendency: The music stops and everyone freezes or grabs a seat, but a draw names who is out. Quick hands win nothing, because the caught player was chosen already.
pros: The signal still makes a stir.
Everyone reacts at once.
cons: Reaction speed counts for nothing.
The caught player is named by luck.

pairs.tendency: Cards are put back and new ones taken from the pile, so each swap is another draw. A hand changes, and nobody knows whether it improved.
pros: Hands change often.
A swap gives a fresh start.
cons: A swap can bring back the same cards.
Swapping becomes a way to wait.

pairs.tendency: The top card of the discard pile shows by luck, and picking up the whole pile depends on whether it can be used. A pickup is a matter of luck.
pros: The pile can swell.
A pickup changes the table at once.
cons: A player may get a heavy pile for nothing.
A player may be left holding a pile they did not want.

pairs.tendency: One suit beats the others, and the deal says who holds it. A low trump can still win a trick against a high card, so the hand with the most trumps takes most of the tricks.
pros: A trump makes the winner easy to see.
Reading the suit takes no thought.
cons: Whoever holds the trumps takes most tricks.
A hand without trumps can do little.

pairs.tendency: Two boards run at once, and a player attacks on one and defends on the other, but dice move both. A player throws for both sides at once.
pros: Two games run side by side.
Wins and losses split across the boards.
cons: Attack and defence come from the throw.
The second board doubles the waiting.

pairs.tendency: A wild card can stand for any card, but it turns up only when the draw brings it. Whoever draws one ends a long wait at once.
pros: Drawing one brings a cheer.
A set can finish all at once.
cons: A wild card adds no choice.
A player without one has to wait.

pairs.tendency: The board edges join, and throws carry pieces round and round with no edge to stop a run. A line that leaves on the right comes back on the left.
pros: Pieces can go round and round.
No corner traps a piece.
cons: A game can go on without a clear end.
Lines can arrive from behind.
