pairs.tendency: One player knows a secret and the others ask questions, but a coin gives the answers. The secret is no longer in play, and the list of things it could be never gets shorter.
pros: Questions are quick.
Answers are short.
cons: Answers carry no information.
The guessing never gets anywhere.

pairs.tendency: The first to the end wins, and throws set the speed. The winner is whoever throws high most often.
pros: Races are easy to follow.
Every turn moves the race.
cons: A leader can be passed by one throw.
The finish is a matter of waiting.

pairs.tendency: The highest score wins, and points come from throws or draws. The score is a running total of luck.
pros: Totals are simple to add up.
Everyone can see who leads.
cons: The total says nothing about choices.
The last round can flip everything.

pairs.tendency: Players are knocked out one by one, and chance picks who goes. Early exits are only draws, and those who leave wait out the rest.
pros: Each knock-out is clear.
The field thins in a way anyone can follow.
cons: Going out early is nobody's mistake.
Knocked-out players wait a long time.

pairs.tendency: The whole table wins or loses together against the game, and the dice are the game. Survival depends on the throws of everyone at once.
pros: Players cheer together.
Everyone shares the same result.
cons: Nobody can help the dice.
A losing run cannot be turned around.

pairs.tendency: All players aim at one goal, and each throw moves everyone nearer or not. Everyone can see the goal, and nobody can plan how to get there.
pros: Each throw helps the whole table.
Everyone pulls the same way.
cons: Plans have nothing to work on.
Nobody can say who got the table there.

pairs.tendency: Each player has a secret goal, but whether it is reached comes down to luck. A player can only watch for it, so there is little to hide.
pros: Secret goals stay secret.
Players guess at each other's goals.
cons: A secret goal cannot be worked towards.
Bluffing about a goal has no effect.

pairs.tendency: The story is played through, and the dice choose the ending. Players watch the story arrive at an ending nobody picked.
pros: Stories end in odd ways.
Players tell the story together.
cons: The ending may not follow from earlier events.
Nobody can steer towards the ending they want.

pairs.tendency: The game ends with no winner, and players look at what happened. With chance alone, what happened is a record of throws, so the talk afterwards is about luck.
pros: Nobody carries away a loss.
Players talk about the throws.
cons: There is little to look at afterwards.
Players may ask what the game was for.

pairs.tendency: Each player names what counts as a result for them, and luck brings what it brings. A goal can be met or missed with no effort, and a player may change it after seeing the throw.
pros: A player can aim at small things.
Goals differ across the table.
cons: A goal can be met with no effort.
Goals can be moved to fit the throw.

pairs.tendency: Nobody wins and one player loses, and chance picks who. The loser is whoever draws the last card, so the loss comes with no mistake to point to.
pros: Everyone else is safe at once.
The loser is clear.
cons: The loser did nothing wrong.
Players dread the final draw.

pairs.tendency: The aim is to keep playing, and with chance alone the game can run for ever, because nothing builds up.
pros: Play can continue as long as people stay.
Nobody is pushed to end it.
cons: Nothing marks progress.
Players may drift away.

pairs.tendency: The game is made so that nobody can win, and chance would only hand out a win anyway. Players throw, and nothing is awarded.
pros: Everyone can see that the throws lead nowhere.
The point is easy to grasp.
cons: Nothing is gained from any throw.
Players may stop after a few turns.

pairs.tendency: A solo player tries to clear a layout of cards, and the shuffle decides whether it can be cleared. Winning shows only that the cards fell right.
pros: A solo game is quick to play.
Setup is easy.
cons: The shuffle sets the result.
A win says nothing about the player.

pairs.tendency: Several short games are played, and each is a throw, so the series is a count of throws. A lucky player can end it at two wins to none.
pros: Games are short.
A series can stop early.
cons: A winning streak is only luck.
The series can be over after two throws.

pairs.tendency: Every point counts against you, and points are handed out by draw. The winner is the one who was dealt the least.
pros: Players hope for low draws.
Totals are easy to compare.
cons: Nobody can avoid points.
The winner is simply the one dealt little.

pairs.tendency: A piece has to land exactly on the last space, and with a die it needs one exact number. Many throws miss, and a piece can sit one step from the end for many turns.
pros: Players wait on one number.
A finish can arrive from nowhere.
cons: Players get stuck one step from home.
Overshooting wastes throws.

pairs.tendency: The aim is turned upside down and players try to give everything away. Chance picks what is given away, so there is no way to try to lose.
pros: Wins and losses swap places.
Players cheer for odd results.
cons: Trying to lose does nothing.
Players cannot tell the aim from the usual one.

pairs.tendency: Everyone plays at once without touching each other's game, each with their own dice. The table is a row of separate games.
pros: Everyone plays at the same speed.
Nobody waits for others.
cons: Players hardly talk to each other.
The winner shows only at the end.

pairs.tendency: Players attack each other on purpose, but a die decides whether the attack lands. An attack is a request to the die.
pros: Players target each other.
Hits draw loud reactions.
cons: A planned attack can fail by a roll.
Grudges build on luck.

pairs.tendency: The board changes by throw, so no player built the wall that blocks another. Walls and gaps appear without anyone choosing them.
pros: The board tells a story.
Changes are open to all.
cons: Nobody can be blamed for a wall.
Players cannot block each other on purpose.

pairs.tendency: The whole table is on one team against the game, and the game throws too. The team has no moves to coordinate.
pros: The team shares every result.
Nobody is left out.
cons: There is nothing to discuss.
Players watch the same throws.

pairs.tendency: Players share a table goal with a small private reward on top, but luck hands out the private reward. Nobody can pull ahead of the team on purpose.
pros: Players share a goal.
A private reward adds a small twist.
cons: The private reward is won by luck.
Playing for yourself makes no difference.

pairs.tendency: Two teams play, and teammates have nothing to plan, so they throw in turn and add up. The result belongs to a side, and no member did anything to earn it.
pros: Teams cheer together.
Scores belong to a side.
cons: Teammates have no plan to share.
A team's loss cannot be traced to anyone.

pairs.tendency: One player secretly plays against the team, but a traitor has no moves to give them away or to do any harm. So the guessing has nothing to go on.
pros: Players suspect each other.
Accusations fly.
cons: A traitor has no moves that show.
Nobody can be caught out.

pairs.tendency: Players far apart play by post, and each letter carries a throw while the reply carries another. Weeks pass for a handful of numbers.
pros: A letter is something to look forward to.
The post makes waiting part of play.
cons: A game takes months for a few results.
A far-off player has to be trusted to throw honestly.

pairs.tendency: One seat belongs to a player who is not there, and dice make their moves for them.
pros: The missing player still takes turns.
The empty seat is easy to run.
cons: The absent player has no say.
Players may forget whose turn it is.

pairs.tendency: One player runs the world, but with chance alone they only read tables and say what the dice say.
pros: The game master narrates the throws.
Players listen to the results.
cons: Running the world is only reading results.
The game master has no say over the story.

pairs.tendency: The game is played in a street or a market, and a passer-by can join in a second, because there is nothing to learn. A newcomer stands on equal terms with a regular.
pros: Newcomers join in a moment.
A crowd can gather.
cons: Skill has no edge to show.
Regulars who come back every day have no edge over a newcomer.

pairs.tendency: One player takes on all the others, and the sides are set by seat. The lone player's bigger payout is a prize for luck.
pros: The lone player is easy to spot.
The rest agree on one target.
cons: Neither side can plan against the other.
The bigger payout goes to luck.

pairs.tendency: A solo player throws and watches, and no one else acts. The result can be compared with a friend's afterwards.
pros: Easy to set up.
It can be played at any hour.
cons: A solo game with no choice is a wait.
There is nobody to talk to during play.

pairs.tendency: Both blocks say the same thing, one saying most and the other saying all. Where both sit on the canvas, all wins and the small choices that remained are gone.
pros: The rules stay short.
Both blocks point the same way.
cons: The little skill that was left is gone.
The blocks overlap, so one adds little.

pairs.tendency: Re-rolls and cards soften luck, while chance alone says nothing can be done. They pull against each other: with both there, every re-roll is a chance to act, so luck no longer decides alone.
pros: Re-rolls give players something to do.
A low throw can be answered.
cons: The two blocks contradict each other.
Players argue over whether re-rolls are allowed.

pairs.tendency: Players try to plan, then the dice undo the plan. The blocks disagree on how much luck is allowed, and the table has to decide which one holds.
pros: Players try to plan.
Some turns allow a choice.
cons: The roll can undo a plan.
The rules disagree on how much luck is allowed.

pairs.tendency: A game of pure thinking sits beside a game with nothing to choose, and the two cancel each other out. The table cannot tell which block rules a given turn.
pros: The game can be read two ways.
Planning shows in some turns.
cons: Skill and chance block each other out.
Players do not know what to practise.

pairs.tendency: The throw is read as a message instead of being counted, though chance alone says the throw also settles who gains. Players read each throw and then see the score go the other way.
pros: A throw gets talked about afterwards.
Players give each throw a reading.
cons: The reading may disagree with the score.
Players can argue over what a throw meant.

pairs.tendency: Players try to sense when the others will act, but a throw has no sign to sense. They look for patterns in how someone reaches for the dice, and there are none.
pros: Players watch each other closely.
The table goes quiet.
cons: Sensing others changes nothing.
Players hunt for patterns that are not there.

pairs.tendency: A roll is looked up on a table that says what happens next, and with chance alone the table is the whole game. The dice write the story.
pros: The story takes odd turns.
Players read out the results.
cons: The story has no plan.
The characters have no say.

pairs.tendency: The board is open to every eye, yet nobody can see the next throw, and the throw decides everything.
pros: The board is open to all.
Nobody can claim a hidden move.
cons: Seeing everything gives no help with the next throw.
The open board hides only the dice.

pairs.tendency: Hands are kept secret, but a card is played in order, so holding it hidden protects nothing. A player looks at their own cards and has nothing to decide.
pros: Hands are kept secret.
Players look at their own cards.
cons: A secret hand has no move to hide.
Bluffing has nothing to work on.

pairs.tendency: Roles are handed out in secret, but nobody has a choice to act on, so a role never shows. Players study each other for signs that cannot appear.
pros: Each player gets a secret.
Players guess at each other.
cons: A role does nothing to the result.
Nobody can give themselves away.

pairs.tendency: Clues come from dice or draws, so the clues add up to nothing. Players keep notes on facts that were never fixed.
pros: Players keep notes.
Clues look like clues.
cons: Clues mean little when they come from chance.
A careful note-taker has no edge.

pairs.tendency: Players hide the dice under a cup and say a number, and others call it a lie or accept it. The claim cannot change who gains, so the lie is for show.
pros: Players say numbers with a straight face.
The cup keeps everyone curious.
cons: A claim changes nothing in the result.
Calling a lie has no reward.

pairs.tendency: One player knows a secret rule and the others find it out by breaking it. With chance alone, the only secret rule is how a throw is read, and it can be guessed only by luck.
pros: Newcomers learn by trying.
The knower keeps a straight face.
cons: A rule about dice can be guessed only by luck.
Players may spend a long time on nothing.

pairs.tendency: One player sees the answer and gives hints about a card turned by luck. The guessers are guessing at a draw.
pros: Hints draw laughs.
Guessers talk it over.
cons: Guessing a drawn card is a plain guess.
The hint-giver's skill adds little.

pairs.tendency: Each map tile is turned face up by luck, and nobody picks where to go. The map grows as it is explored, and a path can lead nowhere.
pros: Each turned tile is a surprise.
The map is different every game.
cons: Choosing where to explore means nothing.
Players can walk into dead ends.

pairs.tendency: One hand lies face up and plays itself, with a player reading the cards out.
pros: The open hand shows what is coming.
Players learn how the cards run.
cons: Playing it takes no thought.
Seeing the hand does not help.

pairs.tendency: Hidden scores are only hidden dice results, so players guess who is ahead and have no way to tell from play.
pros: Nobody knows the score.
The end brings a surprise.
cons: Watching the others tells a player nothing.
Secrets are kept for no purpose.

pairs.tendency: Each turn is a throw and a result, one player after another.
pros: Turns are short.
Everyone waits calmly.
cons: Waiting is most of the game.
A big table spends a long time between throws.

pairs.tendency: With nothing to choose, everyone throws together and compares. Nobody has a secret to keep, so the reveal is only a read-out.
pros: Nobody waits.
The reveal is quick.
cons: Choosing in secret has nothing to hide.
Players may throw at different speeds.

pairs.tendency: Anyone can act at any moment, so players throw dice as fast as they can. Throwing faster changes nothing about the numbers.
pros: Everyone acts at once.
Hands fly.
cons: The race to throw first leads nowhere.
Quick hands and slow hands get the same results.

pairs.tendency: Each turn has a clock, but a move that is only a throw needs no time. The clock runs out only when someone forgets to throw.
pros: A sand timer sits on the table.
Every turn has a limit.
cons: The clock adds hurry where nothing needs thought.
Players run out of time doing nothing.

pairs.tendency: The game runs over days and weeks with one throw each morning. Waiting is part of playing, though the wait is for a number.
pros: A short move each day.
Players check in with a small daily habit.
cons: The game takes weeks for a few throws.
Players can forget to throw.

pairs.tendency: The game slows down on purpose, with a breath before every throw. The wait is long, and the result was fixed by the dice all along.
pros: Each throw gets its own moment.
The table is calm.
cons: All the waiting leads to a plain throw.
Slow turns hold no decisions.

pairs.tendency: The throws come faster each round and the end rushes in. Players have no time to think, though there was never a choice to think about.
pros: Rounds get shorter.
The end comes in a rush.
cons: Speed hides that there is nothing to decide.
The result is clear after a few throws.

pairs.tendency: On some throws a player gets another go, so a lucky player can throw many times before anyone else. A run of luck turns into a run of turns.
pros: A lucky streak can run on.
Others watch from the side.
cons: A leader can pull far ahead.
Others wait a long time between turns.

pairs.tendency: The game comes in stages, and the first stage hands out a random start for the second. Nothing done in stage one was chosen, so the second stage starts from luck.
pros: Each stage looks different.
The second stage starts from the first.
cons: Stage one is only throwing.
Players have nothing to set up.

pairs.tendency: The board models a system, such as a village waiting for a late monsoon, and the throws stand for things outside anyone's control. Players see how much the system depends on luck.
pros: Throws stand for things like the weather.
Players see how much depends on luck.
cons: Players cannot change how the system moves.
The model says nothing about what people could do.

pairs.tendency: Each player stands for a group, such as farmers or a village council, but the throw acts for the group. The group never makes a choice.
pros: Each seat has a name.
Players know who they stand for.
cons: A seat's name changes nothing in play.
A farmer's needs have no way of being shown.

pairs.tendency: Everyone draws from the water under the village, and throws set how much each takes. Running dry is luck, and nobody can hold back.
pros: The shared supply shrinks in plain view.
Everyone sees the level drop.
cons: Holding back is not possible.
The group cannot talk its way out of running dry.

pairs.tendency: A result from three rounds ago is read out now, so the effect arrives late, with no action to link it to. Effects turn up with no cause in sight.
pros: Results arrive after a wait.
Players look back at old throws.
cons: A late result teaches nothing.
Players cannot tell what caused what.

pairs.tendency: Players agree a new rule and play on, but luck swamps what the rule changes.
pros: Players test an idea.
A new rule changes the table talk.
cons: Nobody can tell whether a rule worked.
The same rule gives different results on a second try.

pairs.tendency: The talk afterwards is about what luck did, and every answer points back to the dice.
pros: Players talk it over.
Questions come naturally.
cons: There is little to learn from.
Talk drifts to who was lucky.

pairs.tendency: A throw chooses which card is torn up or which sticker goes on the board. The next game starts from marks that luck made.
pros: The board carries its history.
The next game starts where this one ended.
cons: A torn card cannot be got back.
Marks come from throws no one chose.

pairs.tendency: The rules say that things are decided by luck, whatever people do. That is the point the game makes about the world, and the table can talk about it.
pros: The rules say something plain.
Players can talk about the point.
cons: The point may not be what the designer meant.
Players may feel nothing they do matters.

pairs.tendency: Real money or a real promise rides on a throw, which makes it plain gambling.
pros: Every throw carries weight.
Everyone watches the dice.
cons: A real loss follows a throw nobody chose.
Friends can fall out over luck.

pairs.tendency: The game turns something that matters into points, and the points are handed out at random. The number says nothing about the thing it stands for.
pros: A number is easy to track.
The gap between number and value is plain.
cons: Effort earns no points.
Players chase points that mean nothing.

pairs.tendency: Players practise a new way of living, but the only thing rehearsed is luck. The way of living gets no test, because nobody makes a choice in it.
pros: Players try out a new way.
Setting up is easy.
cons: The rehearsal teaches nothing about choices.
The future looks decided already.

pairs.tendency: It rolls a dice and runs a piece along the path after the others, and a tag happens when It lands on a runner's space. The runners roll too, so everyone is racing on the same track.
pros: Dice decide how close It gets.
A runner can be tagged by one lucky throw.
cons: A long run of low rolls leaves It stuck far behind.
Nobody can plan an escape past the next throw.

pairs.tendency: Between rounds of chasing, players pick cards from a shared row, and the cards give moves or speed for the next run. A runner who picks last may start the chase with a slow card.
pros: Each pick shapes the next chase.
Players watch what others take.
cons: Waiting to pick pauses the running.
The last pick is often a leftover.

pairs.tendency: Before each chase, players offer tokens for a head start, and the highest offer buys it. Whoever pays most runs first, but has fewer tokens for the next round.
pros: A head start has a price.
Players size up each other's tokens.
cons: A big bid can leave you empty next round.
The auction takes longer than the chase.

pairs.tendency: Each runner keeps running to collect points from spots on the field, while It closes in. Running one more spot adds points, and a tag wipes out the pile collected so far.
pros: Every extra step adds points.
Players watch It before deciding to stop.
cons: A tag costs everything in the pile.
The last runner out may end up with nothing.

pairs.tendency: The field is cut into zones, and runners hold a zone by standing in it when the round ends. It tags anyone who sits still, so holders have to keep leaving and coming back.
pros: Zones give the chase a map.
Holding a zone means choosing where to stand.
cons: Runners cannot guard a zone and flee at once.
The zone nearest It empties first.

pairs.tendency: Runners place their workers on job spots, and each spot gives a gain but is open to one player only. It chases the workers, and a tagged worker goes home and misses the next job.
pros: Job spots give runners a reason to stay put.
A taken spot blocks the others.
cons: Staying on a job makes a runner easy to catch.
A tagged worker loses a turn of work.

pairs.tendency: Runners lay tiles to make a pattern while It chases them around the table. A tag can knock a runner's last tile off, so building and dodging fight for the same turn.
pros: Tiles stay on the table while the chase moves.
Runners plan the pattern before the run.
cons: A tag can undo a half-built row.
The pattern is hard to finish with It nearby.

pairs.tendency: Each runner holds cards for dodges, sprints and hiding, and picks which to play as It comes close. A runner who spent the sprint card early meets the next tag with an empty hand.
pros: Cards give each escape a cost.
Players think about when to save a card.
cons: A used card cannot be used again.
A runner with few cards is easy to guess.

pairs.tendency: Players lay a card each, and the winner of the trick becomes It for the next chase. Winning the cards means taking on the chaser's job.
pros: A card win gives the lead role.
Cards pick who chases next.
cons: Winning a trick can put you in the chase.
Players may lose a trick on purpose.

pairs.tendency: Runners talk to each other and trade promises, such as "I'll block It for you if you share your safe spot." It listens in, and a deal made out loud tells It where to go.
pros: Deals can pull runners together.
Talk makes the chase a group matter.
cons: Promises can break in the middle of a run.
It can use what it overhears.

pairs.tendency: Runners dash between spots to pick up matching tokens while It looks for a runner carrying a nearly full set. A tag may take a token away, so the collector with most tokens is the clear target.
pros: The chase points at whoever holds the most.
Runners choose which tokens to chase.
cons: A tag costs a collector their set.
Players with few tokens are left alone.

pairs.tendency: The field is built from tiles that players lay as they go. Runners add paths to escape and It adds walls to cut them off, so the map changes under the chase.
pros: The map grows turn by turn.
A new tile can open an escape or close one.
cons: Runners cannot count on a path staying open.
Tile laying slows the pace of the chase.

pairs.tendency: It calls a word or a move, and the runners have to answer with the matching word or move before It reaches them. A wrong answer makes the runner freeze.
pros: The calls set the beat of the chase.
Runners listen closely to It.
cons: A slow reply gets a runner caught.
Players who mishear a call lose a turn.

pairs.tendency: Nobody speaks during the chase, so runners show where to go with a glance or a tap. It watches faces for a hint, and a runner who looks at a hiding place gives it away.
pros: Silence makes every look matter.
The group learns each other's signs.
cons: Runners cannot warn each other aloud.
A wrong signal can send a friend into It's path.

pairs.tendency: On a turn, a player may swap a rule, such as how far It may reach. After a few changes the chase is played under rules nobody started with.
pros: The chase never stays the same.
Players watch each other's rule edits.
cons: A rule change can make the lead for It vanish.
Players may argue over what a rule means.

pairs.tendency: Each player speaks as a character, such as a thief running from a guard, and It plays the one doing the catching. A tag turns into a scene in which the caught character says what happens next.
pros: The chase comes with a story.
Players decide what their character would do.
cons: Talking in character slows the running.
A caught character can be left out of the scene.

pairs.tendency: The chase is run with the hands, such as flicking a counter across a table away from It's counter. A tag is a counter hit, and a shaky hand makes a runner easy to touch.
pros: A flick can save or lose a runner.
Skill in the hands shows right away.
cons: Tired hands lead to clumsy flicks.
Bumps can knock other pieces about.

pairs.tendency: Players draw the map as they play, and runners add paths and hideouts that It later has to find. The chase can only go where someone has drawn.
pros: Runners shape the field they run on.
The map becomes a record of the chase.
cons: A runner can draw a trap for themselves.
Drawing pauses the chase.

pairs.tendency: When It tags, it chooses who takes the next role, and in some versions each runner may also choose whom to help. The choice of who to chase is made in the open, and the others react.
pros: A pick changes who is under pressure.
Players read the choice as a message.
cons: The same runner can be chosen every round.
Runners may gang up on one player.

pairs.tendency: Runners try to link one chain of stones from one side of the board to the other, while It moves along the board cutting the links by touching them. A broken chain has to be rebuilt from the gap.
pros: Runners make a chain while dodging.
It can cut a link anywhere along the chain.
cons: A long chain is hard to guard.
Rebuilding a cut chain takes many turns.

pairs.tendency: Runners and It pick moves that beat one another, such as a dash that beats a hide, a hide that beats a lunge and a lunge that beats a dash. It tags only when its pick wins against the runner's pick.
pros: Every pick can be answered.
Players try to guess each other's choice.
cons: A runner cannot rely on one move.
A string of wrong guesses ends in a tag.

pairs.tendency: Runners show a pair of cards to score and then keep the pair in hand to use later. A runner who declared a pair is known to hold it, and It aims at the one with the most points.
pros: Pairs give points while the chase goes on.
Declared cards tell others what a runner holds.
cons: A shown pair draws the chaser.
The runner with a pair has to run more often.

pairs.tendency: Each runner has a power of their own, such as a double step or a hiding spot, and It has a power too. The chase differs from player to player because nobody is running the same race.
pros: Each runner has a plan of their own.
Players learn each other's powers.
cons: A power may suit one chase and not another.
New players may need time to learn every power.

pairs.tendency: During a chase, a runner may offer to double the points at stake. The other side can accept and play on or give up the round and pay what is on the table.
pros: A bold runner can raise the stakes mid-run.
The other player has to size up the chase.
cons: A double offer can be a bluff.
A run that was close can end in a sudden surrender.

pairs.tendency: If It can tag, it has to, even when that sends it away from another target. A runner may offer a nearby space on purpose to pull It off course.
pros: A runner can use It's duty.
Players spot the bait.
cons: It may be dragged away from the chase it wanted.
A runner can be tagged by a step they planned.

pairs.tendency: Each tag or escape adds a power to the player's character, such as longer reach or faster feet. Players who win early chases meet later chases with more to use.
pros: Success gives a reason to try again.
Characters look different after a few rounds.
cons: Early wins can build up a lead.
New players start behind.

pairs.tendency: Each runner says the whole list so far and adds one new item before running to the next spot. A runner who forgets an item is out of breath and open to a tag.
pros: Players remember and run at once.
The list is made together.
cons: A long list slows a runner down.
One slip makes the whole table start over.

pairs.tendency: The faster player gives away a head start, such as starting a pace behind or taking It's role for longer. The chase is set up so a slower runner has a real chance to get away.
pros: Different players can race together.
Both players think they have a chance.
cons: The head start can be hard to set.
A runner may feel the gap was made for them.

pairs.tendency: A runner hides while It counts, then It hunts, and a tag is made on a found runner by touching them before they reach home. Hiding and running become two parts of one round.
pros: Hiding gives the chase a start.
The seeker has to look before running.
cons: A hider with a clever spot may never be caught.
A found runner has to make a sudden dash.

pairs.tendency: It hops over a runner's piece to land behind it, and the hop counts as the tag. Runners can leave gaps on purpose so that a hop ends in a place the runner has watched.
pros: A hop is the way to tag.
Players leave gaps with care.
cons: A chain of hops can end a runner at once.
Pieces next to each other are easy to jump.

pairs.tendency: It rolls its dice and keeps the high ones, then rerolls the rest to reach for a runner. The more dice it sets aside, the shorter the reach left to chase with.
pros: Throwing again gives It a second try.
Players watch which dice are kept.
cons: It may run out of rerolls just short of a tag.
A runner's escape depends on a few throws.

pairs.tendency: A tag is made by landing on a runner's space, and the runner goes back to the start. Safe spaces on the track give a runner a spot where It cannot touch them.
pros: Safe spaces give runners somewhere to rest.
Players plan landing spots.
cons: A runner near the finish can be sent all the way back.
Safe spaces may be crowded.

pairs.tendency: A runner who makes a mill of three in a row may remove It's piece from play. It tags runners to break the row before it forms.
pros: Building a row can end a chase.
The chaser has a clear target.
cons: A broken row means starting over.
Runners crowd into the row and are easy to tag.

pairs.tendency: Runners hold letters and run to the table's centre to lay out words, while It chases the one with the most letters. A tag takes a letter away, and a word cannot be finished with a gap.
pros: Letters give runners a goal.
Everyone is thinking about words and about It.
cons: A tag can break a word in half.
A long word needs time that It does not allow.

pairs.tendency: A runner adds a tile to a line only if the tile matches an open end, then runs to the next end. It stands at the open end that many runners need, and a runner with no match loses a turn.
pros: Open ends give the field a shape.
Players track which numbers are left.
cons: A runner may have to skip a turn.
It can wait where the match is needed.

pairs.tendency: Runners lay sets of cards face up on the table and then run to add matching cards to those sets. A tag on the way takes the runner's carried card, which cannot be added until it is won back.
pros: A laid set can be added to by others.
Cards on the table are plain to see.
cons: A tag can strip a runner of the last card needed.
Players wait on the table for a card.

pairs.tendency: Every runner has one special move, such as a long leap, that works once. After it is spent, the runner looks like everybody else, so It watches who is saving a move and who has used one.
pros: Players save the move for when it counts.
Players read when to use a power.
cons: A spent power cannot be used again.
A runner may waste the move on a safe round.

pairs.tendency: A runner offers a move, and It may refuse it or choose between two moves on offer. A runner has to make an offer that It will accept and still lets the runner get away.
pros: Each move has to be offered with care.
Both sides give their view of a move.
cons: The chase slows as offers pass back and forth.
A refused move wastes a turn.

pairs.tendency: A message goes along a line of runners, and It listens for the changed version to learn who is in the chain. A tag stops the message wherever the runner stood.
pros: The message changes on the way.
The group works to keep the message.
cons: A tagged runner breaks the chain.
Nobody can check the message until the end.

pairs.tendency: Before a chase, each player chooses cards to hand to a neighbour without seeing what they get back. A runner may pass the card that would have helped the chaser.
pros: A pass gives and takes at once.
Players learn what a neighbour needs.
cons: A runner may be handed a useless card.
Passing takes place before the chase begins.

pairs.tendency: One player places the runners and It on the board, and the other player then picks which side to play. The setter tries to make the start fair for both sides, since the other may pick the side that looks easier.
pros: The setup has to suit both sides.
Both players think about the start.
cons: A setup that favours one side is spotted.
Setting up takes longer than the first move.

pairs.tendency: A runner who reaches the far edge of the board turns into a faster piece, and It tries to tag the runner before it gets there. Running forward can end the chase or start a new one.
pros: The far edge is a goal worth the run.
Players push forward under pressure.
cons: A promoted runner may be harder to catch.
It may leave the rest of the field unguarded.

pairs.tendency: The team runs in legs, and a tag on a runner means the baton has to be passed back to the start of that leg. It chases the leg currently running, so each hand-over is a moment of risk.
pros: Teams share the running.
Everyone on the team has a turn.
cons: A tag in the final leg can undo the whole run.
Waiting for a hand-over leaves some players standing still.

pairs.tendency: Runners build a shape with their stones that cannot be captured, and a runner inside the shape cannot be tagged. It tries to catch runners before the shape is complete.
pros: A finished shape gives a place of safety.
Players build towards something.
cons: The shape takes several turns to finish.
Runners outside the shape are left open.

pairs.tendency: The prizes are named cards, and runners dash to win the tricks that carry them. It chases the runner holding the key card, since a tag can move the card to someone else.
pros: A card names what is worth running for.
Everyone knows which cards matter.
cons: The runner with the key card is chased.
A single card can swing a round.

pairs.tendency: Cards in the middle are open to every player, and runners run to the centre to use them in a hand. It waits near the middle, because every runner has to pass through.
pros: The middle of the table draws everyone.
Players build hands from shared cards.
cons: The middle is the easiest place to be tagged.
Runners crowd the centre.

pairs.tendency: Everyone puts a counter into the middle, and the runner who is never tagged in the round takes the pot. If It tags everyone, the pot stays and the next round is worth more.
pros: A growing pot makes each round matter more.
The prize is plain to see.
cons: A pot that keeps growing makes It's job heavier.
Players can end a round with nothing.

pairs.tendency: A runner scoops up a pit of seeds and drops them along the pits ahead, and the seeds mark the path of the run. It takes a pit where the last seed lands, so runners count seeds to avoid ending a sowing near It.
pros: Counting seeds shapes the path.
Players plan several pits ahead.
cons: A wrong count puts a runner next to It.
Scooping and dropping takes time.

pairs.tendency: A second hand lies face down in the middle, and one player may swap it in before the chase starts. A runner who takes the spare hand may find a card that It would have wanted.
pros: A spare hand gives a second try.
Players guess what the spare hand holds.
cons: The swap happens before anyone can run.
A spare hand can hold cards that help less than the original.

pairs.tendency: Some squares are safe for runners, some send a runner back and some make a player miss a turn. It uses the sending-back squares to herd the runners, and runners keep the safe squares for the last dash.
pros: The track tells players where to go.
Squares can protect or catch.
cons: A runner who lands on the wrong square is tagged by the board.
Players see the same squares each game.

pairs.tendency: Every move, such as a sprint or a hiding place, has a price, and runners pay from a small purse. It pays for reach, so a chase becomes a matter of who runs out of money first.
pros: A move costs something.
Players think about price before running.
cons: A runner who spends early cannot flee later.
Saving up can mean standing still.

pairs.tendency: A team shares a fixed number of runners across several routes, and It cannot be everywhere. Putting many runners on one route leaves another open.
pros: A team picks where to send its runners.
The chaser cannot guard every route.
cons: A route with few runners is easily cut off.
The other player is splitting too.

pairs.tendency: Everyone moves around until a signal sounds, then freezes, and It can tag only runners who are still moving. A runner who guesses the signal early can stop while others are caught.
pros: The signal sets the pace.
Players listen and run.
cons: A slow stop gets a runner caught.
The signal may be missed in a noisy room.

pairs.tendency: A runner may put cards back for new ones before the chase, hoping for a dodge or a sprint. Swapping also shows It what the runner needs.
pros: A swap gives a second chance at the hand.
Players read each other's swaps.
cons: A swap can turn up a card that helps less.
Swapping uses up the turn.

pairs.tendency: Cards thrown away go into one pile, and a runner may pick up the whole pile if the top card can be used straight away. Whoever picks up the pile is slowed by the weight of cards, and It gets closer.
pros: Picking up the pile gives many cards at once.
Players watch the top card.
cons: A big pile slows the runner.
The pile can fill with cards nobody wants.

pairs.tendency: One suit is named for the round, and a runner who plays a low trump beats a high card in another suit. A trump card may let a small runner beat the chaser's card in a face-off.
pros: A trump gives a low card a chance.
Players track which cards are trumps.
cons: Trump cards decide face-offs.
A round without trumps can feel flat.

pairs.tendency: You are runner on one board and It on the other, so you flee and chase in the same turn. A tag on one board leaves you free to chase on the other.
pros: Both roles come in one turn.
Players think about two boards.
cons: Attention is split between boards.
A slip on one board is felt on the other.

pairs.tendency: A wild card stands for any card, so a runner can play one to dodge, sprint or hide as needed. It also keeps a wild card, and neither side knows when the other will use one.
pros: A wild card fits any need.
Players save the wild card for a tight spot.
cons: A wild card is used up in one play.
A runner without one has fewer ways out.

pairs.tendency: The edges of the board are joined, so a runner who leaves one side comes back on the other. It can chase in either direction, and a runner who thinks the edge is a wall is caught from behind.
pros: The board has no corners to hide in.
Players learn to read the edges.
cons: A runner can be tagged from an unexpected side.
New players keep forgetting the edges join.

pairs.tendency: It asks yes-or-no questions to find out where a hidden runner is standing, and each answer narrows the field. A runner who answers in the wrong order gives away the hiding place.
pros: Questions shorten the list of places.
Runners answer with care.
cons: A badly placed question wastes a turn.
The chase waits while questions go back and forth.

pairs.tendency: The first runner to reach the end wins, and It chases anyone who gets too far ahead. A runner in front is also the nearest to It's reach.
pros: The leader is the main target.
Players decide when to run ahead.
cons: A lead can vanish with one tag.
Runners at the back are rarely chased.

pairs.tendency: Points are given for each round without a tag, and It scores for each runner it catches. The player with the highest score at the end wins, whether runner or chaser.
pros: Every round adds to a total.
Players see the scores climb.
cons: A single tagged round may not cost much.
Someone may keep chasing the same runner for points.

pairs.tendency: Each tag knocks out a runner until only one is left. The last runner wins, and the knocked-out players watch the end of the chase.
pros: The chase has a clear finish.
The last few runners are watched by everyone.
cons: Knocked-out players wait for the rest.
Early rounds leave some players with nothing to do.

pairs.tendency: All runners work together to stay free until time runs out, with It controlled by the game. Runners cover each other and share safe spots, and if It tags one, the whole team loses.
pros: Runners protect one another.
The team shares one goal.
cons: One slip ends the game for all.
A player who slips up can feel the weight of the team.

pairs.tendency: The team has a goal, such as carrying every token to a safe place, and It chases whoever carries one. Runners hand tokens off before It arrives.
pros: The goal draws the team together.
Hand-offs happen in the open.
cons: A tagged carrier drops the token.
A team may crowd around the carrier.

pairs.tendency: Each runner has a secret aim, such as reaching a certain spot, and It does not know who wants what. A runner who heads for a goal gives it away to anyone who watches.
pros: Goals give runners a reason to move.
Players guess each other's aims.
cons: A runner who hides a goal may run in circles.
A chaser can read the goal from the path.

pairs.tendency: The chase is part of a story, and it ends when the story does. A caught runner may stay in the game and be written into the next scene.
pros: The chase leads into a scene.
The story comes from the chase.
cons: The chase may be cut short for the plot.
Players wait for a scene to finish.

pairs.tendency: The chase goes on with no winner and no score, and when players stop they talk about what happened. Nobody loses a tag, because there is no tally.
pros: Runners and It simply play.
The talk afterwards fills the gap.
cons: Without a goal, runners may drift.
The chase can end with no clear moment.

pairs.tendency: Each runner says what a successful round means for them, such as staying free through one round or tagging a friend. It also has a goal, and the same chase may look like a win to one player and a loss to another.
pros: Players decide what the chase is for.
Different goals can sit in one game.
cons: Two players may measure the same chase differently.
A group needs time to agree on goals.

pairs.tendency: There is no winner, and the chase goes on until one player is the loser. Everyone else is safe, so It chases hard to avoid being the last It.
pros: Only one person ends up as the loser.
Players race to leave the chase.
cons: The loser sits out in the last round.
Players who are safe stop caring.

pairs.tendency: The chase is meant to carry on, so runners avoid leaving anyone behind and It lets runners back in after a tag. The game stops only when players choose to stop.
pros: A tag does not end the game.
Players stay in the chase.
cons: The chase has no natural end.
Players may drift away from a game with no finish.

pairs.tendency: The chase is built so It can never finish catching everyone, and the runners can never fully escape. A runner who tries to win finds the board pushing back.
pros: Players notice what the rules will not allow.
Players talk about why they ran.
cons: The game gives no prize for effort.
Players may stop after a few rounds.

pairs.tendency: You play alone against a laid-out table of cards and run a single piece around it while a set of rules plays It. You win by clearing the table before the rules tag you.
pros: The game plays the chaser.
A solo player has no need to wait.
cons: One mistake can leave you stuck.
There is no opponent to learn from.

pairs.tendency: The players run several short chases, and whoever wins the most chases wins the match. Roles swap after each one, so everyone is It in turn.
pros: Short chases make a match.
Every player takes both roles.
cons: A player who loses early may not catch up.
A long match means many chases.

pairs.tendency: Each tag adds a point to the player caught, and the player with the fewest points when time ends wins. Runners try to stay clear and It tries to give points to the right person.
pros: Staying free keeps your score low.
Tags have a cost.
cons: A single tag can end a hope of winning.
Players may avoid being It.

pairs.tendency: A runner has to land exactly on the final space to win, so a throw that goes past leaves them standing near the end. It waits near the finish for anyone who needs a small number.
pros: The last spaces are slow.
Runners wait for the exact throw.
cons: A runner near the end is an easy target.
A high throw can lose the win.

pairs.tendency: The aim is turned round, so the player who gets tagged most often wins, or the runner who lets It catch them first. Players try to be caught and It tries to avoid catching.
pros: The chase runs backwards.
Players have to unlearn old habits.
cons: Players often forget the aim mid-round.
A runner may be too keen to run away by habit.

pairs.tendency: Every runner is chased on their own board, and It moves between boards without touching other players. Players race their own board while others do the same.
pros: Each player has a run of their own.
Everyone plays at the same time.
cons: Players rarely see each other's chases.
The result may feel far from the table.

pairs.tendency: It tags a runner on purpose, and runners may tag back to push It away. Players go after each other face to face, and each tag is a target-and-reply.
pros: Each tag is aimed at a person.
Players answer one another.
cons: Players may hold a grudge after a tag.
A player can be chased every round.

pairs.tendency: Players do not touch each other. They block paths, close doors and change the board, so It finds a route cut off. A runner meets the chase as walls and closed paths.
pros: The board does the chasing.
Players change the field, not each other.
cons: A blocked path can trap a runner.
It is hard to say who caused a tag.

pairs.tendency: The whole team plays against the chase, with the game acting as It. Everyone wins by lasting to the end and loses when the last runner is tagged.
pros: The team shares each escape.
Everyone has a say in a move.
cons: A tagged player may have caused the loss.
One loud player can make the choices.

pairs.tendency: Runners work together to stay out of reach, but each has a small private aim, such as being the last one free. A runner may leave a friend in It's path to reach that aim.
pros: Runners help each other most of the time.
A private aim gives a reason to hold back.
cons: A friend may leave you to be tagged.
Players watch each other's moves for signs.

pairs.tendency: One team is the chasers and the other team the runners, and they swap after a round. Chasers pass signals to cut off a route while runners spread out.
pros: Each side plans together.
The chase becomes a team matter.
cons: A gap in a team is found fast.
Waiting players lose interest.

pairs.tendency: One runner is secretly helping It, and tells It where the others are hiding. The runners try to find out who is the traitor before they are all tagged.
pros: A hidden helper changes every escape.
Runners watch each other's moves.
cons: A runner might blame the wrong friend.
The traitor is often found by a slip.

pairs.tendency: Players send letters with their moves, and the chase takes days. It writes where it looks next and the runner replies with where it ran.
pros: The chase is a series of letters.
Waiting is part of the game.
cons: A tag arrives long after it happened.
Players lose track of the chase between letters.

pairs.tendency: One chaser is not at the table, such as a ghost who only leaves hints or an old record of a past game. The runners run from a presence they cannot see, and the hints say where it was last.
pros: The chaser is never seen.
Players read clues about it.
cons: The ghost never takes part in the talk.
Runners may not know when it is near.

pairs.tendency: One player runs the world and plays It, describing the chase while the others play runners. The game master decides how far a tag reaches.
pros: The chase is told as a story.
The game master can change the pace.
cons: The game master has to track many runners.
Runners have to trust the game master's calls.

pairs.tendency: The chase is played in a street or a park, and passers-by can join as runners or as It. Anyone can be tagged, and the game spreads past those who started it.
pros: Anyone can join the chase.
Spectators become players.
cons: Players may collide with passers-by.
The game has no set end.

pairs.tendency: One player is It against all the others, who work together to avoid being tagged. The lone chaser scores more for each tag.
pros: The chaser has a bigger prize.
The runners plan together.
cons: The lone chaser is tired by the last round.
Runners can trap a lone chaser.

pairs.tendency: You play alone against a pack that acts by rules, with no other player chasing you. The pack moves after each of your turns, and luck and your own choices decide the run.
pros: A solo run needs no one to wait for.
Your result can be compared with a friend later.
cons: There is no one to read or bluff.
The pack's moves start to repeat.

pairs.tendency: Dice or cards decide who gets tagged, and the runners make few choices. A runner may be caught after one low throw, whatever the plan.
pros: A round is over quickly.
New players are not at a disadvantage.
cons: Planning makes little difference.
Players may feel the result was not theirs.

pairs.tendency: Dice decide how far It can reach, but runners hold cards to soften a low throw, such as a dodge or a shield. A runner can still be caught, though not without using something.
pros: Cards cushion low throws.
Players choose when to use them.
cons: A runner out of cards has no cushion.
The cards slow the round down.

pairs.tendency: The chase is mostly decided by choices of path and timing, with one dice throw to add a surprise. A careful runner usually escapes, but a lucky throw can still catch them.
pros: Choices matter most.
A bit of luck keeps rounds uncertain.
cons: A careful plan can still fall to one throw.
Players may argue over a lucky tag.

pairs.tendency: The chase is all paths and timing, with no dice, so the player who plans further ahead catches the other. A player who reads the board two moves ahead keeps ahead of It.
pros: Planning decides the result.
Players learn to read each other.
cons: A new player meets an expert and loses fast.
Long thinking slows the chase.

pairs.tendency: Dice are thrown and read as a message, such as "go the way you did not plan", and the runners take the sign into the chase. It reads the same sign and may use it to guess.
pros: A throw gives something to think about.
Players read meanings together.
cons: A sign may point both ways.
The reading takes longer than the run.

pairs.tendency: Runners and It try to sense when the others will move, like friends who speak at the same moment. A tag happens when It acts at the same time as the runner.
pros: Players watch each other's rhythm.
A pair who match each other move as one.
cons: A runner who loses focus is caught.
Players cannot say why a tag happened.

pairs.tendency: A roll is looked up on a table that says what the chase turns into, such as a runner meeting a stranger on the road. The dice make the chase part of a story.
pros: The dice add events to the chase.
Players tell the story as it happens.
cons: A table entry may stop the chase for a long scene.
A roll may end the chase at an odd moment.

pairs.tendency: Everything is open on the table, so It sees every runner's position and the runners see It's. A tag comes from planning, with no guesses about what is hidden.
pros: Everyone can see the whole chase.
Players plan on what they see.
cons: A runner cannot surprise It.
The shortest path may be easy to spot.

pairs.tendency: Each runner holds cards that no one else can see, such as dodge cards, and plays one as It comes near. It guesses which card is held, and a runner may bluff by hesitating.
pros: Hidden cards keep It guessing.
A pause can fool the chaser.
cons: A runner with few dodge cards has to hide it.
A bluff can fail and cost a tag.

pairs.tendency: Some players have a secret role, such as a runner who is secretly It's friend. The chase is run with players unsure of who may be tagged and who may help.
pros: A secret role changes every move.
Players watch for slips.
cons: A friend can be taken for a foe.
A secret role may be found early.

pairs.tendency: It uses clues, such as footprints on the board, to work out which runner is where. A clue gives a place to look, and a right guess ends in a tag.
pros: Clues point the chase.
A chaser can plan from evidence.
cons: A wrong guess wastes a turn.
Runners may leave false clues.

pairs.tendency: A runner pretends to head one way while planning to go another, and It has to decide whether to believe the move. A runner who fakes a dash and then hides can slip away.
pros: A fake move can fool the chaser.
Players study faces and pauses.
cons: A bluff that fails ends in a tag.
A player who bluffs often is read quickly.

pairs.tendency: One player knows a secret rule, such as a spot where tags do not count, and the others learn it by breaking it. Runners test spots and It learns from where they are safe.
pros: New players learn by trying.
A secret rule gives the first chase an edge.
cons: A runner who breaks a rule is told no.
The group may feel left out of the secret.

pairs.tendency: One player sees where the chase has to go but may only give hints. The runners guess from the hints which way to run, and It watches the hints too.
pros: A hint can steer the whole group.
The group has to read the hints together.
cons: A hint can be misread and send a runner to It.
The player with the answer cannot help more.

pairs.tendency: The field is hidden until a runner steps into it. Tiles are turned over as the chase moves, and a runner may run into a dead end or find a safe spot.
pros: Every step opens something new.
The chase keeps changing.
cons: A runner may enter a dead end.
It may not know where to look.

pairs.tendency: One hand lies face up for everyone to see, and a player may play from it and from their own. The open hand tells It which dodges are left.
pros: One hand is plain to see.
Players can plan around the open cards.
cons: Open cards help the chaser.
The player with the open hand has less to hide.

pairs.tendency: Points are kept secret, so nobody knows who is ahead. It chases whoever it thinks has the most, and runners hide their gains.
pros: Nobody can add up the scores.
Players guess who is ahead.
cons: It may chase the wrong runner.
A guess about a score may be wrong at the end.

pairs.tendency: Runners and It move one at a time round the table. A runner can plan an escape while It waits, and every move is watched by everyone.
pros: Each move is seen in full.
Players can plan their turn.
cons: A tag comes after a long wait.
Waiting for others slows the table.

pairs.tendency: Everyone picks a move in secret and reveals together, so the runners and It move at the same moment. A tag happens when the choices cross.
pros: Nobody waits to move.
Players guess each other's picks.
cons: A tag may seem to come from nowhere.
A runner cannot react to It's move.

pairs.tendency: There are no turns, and anyone moves whenever they can. The quickest runner escapes and the quickest chaser tags, so the chase is a scramble.
pros: Speed decides most things.
Everyone is busy all the time.
cons: Quick players take over the game.
Arguments over who moved first are common.

pairs.tendency: Each move has a clock, such as a sand timer, and a runner who is slow loses the move. It also runs against the clock.
pros: The clock makes each turn short.
Players pick quickly.
cons: A slow runner is caught.
Rushed moves go wrong.

pairs.tendency: The chase runs over days, with one move each morning. A runner thinks of an escape over breakfast, and It plans its next move on the way to school.
pros: Waiting becomes part of the chase.
Players have time to plan.
cons: A tag comes a day after the move.
Players may forget whose turn it is.

pairs.tendency: Everyone has to move slowly, with a pause and a breath before each step. The chase becomes a slow walk in which It reaches out and a runner leans away.
pros: Each move gets time.
Players watch each other closely.
cons: A tag takes a long time to come.
Players may lose patience.

pairs.tendency: The chase speeds up as rounds pass, with a shorter timer and more runners moving. By the end It is racing to tag before the game finishes.
pros: The pace picks up each round.
The last round is a rush.
cons: Early rounds feel slow.
Players may make errors at the end.

pairs.tendency: A tag or a lucky throw gives another go straight away, so a chaser can tag two runners in a row. A runner who gets an extra turn can run twice as far.
pros: A lucky player can move many times.
The game can change in one turn.
cons: Other players sit out for a long time.
A lead can come from luck.

pairs.tendency: The first stage is spent hiding and placing, and the second is the chase itself. What a runner does in the first stage decides where they stand when the chase starts.
pros: The first stage sets up the second.
Players plan from the start.
cons: A mistake in stage one shows up in stage two.
The chase starts late.

pairs.tendency: The board shows a real system, such as a village's fields and wells, and It stands for a pressure like a drought. Runners move water and crops, and a tag means a place dries up.
pros: The chase stands for a real problem.
Players see cause and effect.
cons: A tag stands for a real loss.
The model may be too simple for the real case.

pairs.tendency: Each runner plays a group, such as a farmer or a shopkeeper, and It plays the pressure on that group. A tag means something different to each role.
pros: Each role feels the chase differently.
Players see the problem from another side.
cons: A role may have little to run from.
Roles can be hard to keep apart.

pairs.tendency: Runners and It draw from one limited store, such as water in a village. If It tags too fast the store runs out for everyone.
pros: One store links all the players.
Taking too much affects all.
cons: A tag takes from the store.
The last player to take may find it empty.

pairs.tendency: A tag shows its effect only a few rounds later, such as a runner who slows down two turns after being touched. Players can see the cost of a chase only after the chase is over.
pros: Effects arrive later.
Players think a few rounds ahead.
cons: A cause is hard to link to its effect.
Players may forget which tag caused what.

pairs.tendency: Players agree a new rule, such as It having a shorter reach, and run the chase to see what it changes. After the round, they decide whether to keep it.
pros: A rule can be tested in play.
The group decides together.
cons: A rule may need several rounds to show anything.
Players may disagree on what a rule changed.

pairs.tendency: After the chase, everyone talks through what happened, who ran where and why. Players compare the chase with a real chase, such as a game of tag in a school yard.
pros: Players learn from the talk.
Everyone has a say.
cons: The talk takes longer than the chase.
Players who were tagged early may stay quiet.

pairs.tendency: Every tag leaves a mark on the board, such as a sticker, and the next chase begins where the last ended. The board fills with marks, so later chases run over old ones.
pros: Each chase leaves a record.
Every tag stays on the board.
cons: Nothing can be undone.
A full board is hard to run on.

pairs.tendency: The rules of the chase say something about the world, such as a chase in which runners are always caught for having less. Players feel the point while running, before anyone says it aloud.
pros: The rules carry a message.
No speech is needed to make the point.
cons: A message in the rules may be missed.
Players may disagree with the point.

pairs.tendency: A tag costs something real, such as a promise to wash the dishes or a favour owed. The chase carries on past the game into the afternoon.
pros: A tag matters after the game.
Players take the chase seriously.
cons: A friendship can be tested by a tag.
Players may refuse to join.

pairs.tendency: Points stand for something that matters, such as health or kindness, and runners chase the points and lose sight of the thing itself. It tags the runner who is gaining the most points.
pros: The score takes the place of the value.
Players see what a number can hide.
cons: Runners may stop caring about what the points mean.
The chase turns into points hunting.

pairs.tendency: Players practise a way of living, such as a village that shares everything, and It stands for a problem that arrives. Runners try sharing to stay out of reach and see how it feels.
pros: The chase tests a future way of living.
Players feel what sharing would be like.
cons: The test is only a short game.
Real life may differ from the game.

pairs.tendency: After the dice carry your piece forward, the space you stop on decides which rival is within reach. A big throw can land you beside the player you wanted to hit.
pros: The throw sets who you can pick.
Hits come from where you stop.
cons: A throw can leave nobody in reach.
Plans change after every roll.

pairs.tendency: Each pick from the shared row is also a hit on one player, because you take the card they were waiting for. Everyone sees whose card just vanished.
pros: Taking a card can hit a named rival.
Players can read who is after whom.
cons: Victims remember who took their card.
A pick for spite can leave your own hand thin.

pairs.tendency: You raise a bid only to drag one rival into paying more than they planned. The player who is being squeezed can drop out or bid back.
pros: A raise can be aimed at one buyer.
Bids show who wants what.
cons: A target may pay too much and have nothing left.
Two rivals can bid each other up while a third wins cheap.

pairs.tendency: When a risk pays off, you pick which rival loses points, so each daring turn ends in a named victim. The others watch your pile grow and wait to see who pays.
pros: A big risk can end in a big hit.
Players follow every throw closely.
cons: A failed risk loses your own points and leaves no hit.
One victim can be picked on every round.

pairs.tendency: Each turn you pick whose region to push into, and a rival's map shrinks one piece at a time. With three or more players, the one you attack may not be the one who holds the most.
pros: Attacks go where they are chosen.
Thinly held spots on the map get noticed fast.
cons: The player left alone can grow while two others fight.
A pushed-out player may stay angry for the whole game.

pairs.tendency: Sending a worker to a job also blocks a named rival from it, so where your workers go works as a message to one player.
pros: A placement can double as a block.
Rivals learn what you are after.
cons: The same victim can be shut out each round.
Players spend turns watching one another's workers.

pairs.tendency: While you build your own pattern, you take the tile one rival needs and leave another alone. Your pattern grows while the rival's stops.
pros: Building and blocking happen in one move.
Players watch each other's rows.
cons: A blocking tile may not fit your own pattern.
A rival can be stalled for several turns.

pairs.tendency: A card kept in hand waits for the target it suits, and you play it when the right rival is in range. The rest of the table sees you holding something.
pros: Cards wait for the right moment.
Players read your pauses.
cons: A kept card can sit unused.
The target may be gone by the time the card comes out.

pairs.tendency: Whoever wins a trick can pick who takes the cost, so a lead card is often meant for one seat. Players read each card for who it was played against.
pros: A trick can be won against a chosen player.
Cards say who is being aimed at.
cons: One seat can be hit round after round.
The winner picks a target before seeing the next trick.

pairs.tendency: Players talk about who will be hit next and offer deals to be left alone. Picking a target turns into something you can bargain over.
pros: Targets can be traded for favours.
Talk shows who is worried.
cons: A deal can be broken once a hit lands.
The quietest player may be named first.

pairs.tendency: You grab or steal the card a rival needs to finish a set, so your choice of victim comes from reading their collection.
pros: A steal can end a rival's set.
Players keep track of other people's piles.
cons: Your own set waits while you hit someone.
A rival who is close to a set draws every hit.

pairs.tendency: A tile can be laid to cut off one player's road or field. Where it goes depends on whose plan is closest to done.
pros: A tile can shut a rival out.
The shared map shows who is next.
cons: A blocking tile may help a third player.
A player who thinks over every tile keeps the others waiting.

pairs.tendency: A call can be aimed at one player, who has to answer in front of everyone. The chain bends towards whoever was called.
pros: A call picks who answers.
The group hears each answer.
cons: The called player can feel put on the spot.
A chain that keeps landing on one person leaves the others out.

pairs.tendency: Nobody talks, so a target is chosen by a look, a card or a moment of timing. The others work out who you mean from what you play.
pros: A pick can be made with no words.
Players read signals closely.
cons: A hit can be taken for a mistake.
Two players may aim at different people at once.

pairs.tendency: A new rule can be written to land on one player, and the whole table sees at once who it is aimed at.
pros: A rule can be a hit.
The table sees who the rule is for.
cons: The target may rewrite the rule next turn.
Rules start to name particular people.

pairs.tendency: Your character picks a rival character to help or cross, and the pick comes from who your character is in the story.
pros: Picks follow the character.
Players speak up for their choices.
cons: A character's grudge can drag out for hours.
A target can feel the pick is about them, not the character.

pairs.tendency: A flick, throw or pull is aimed at one player's piece or tower, and the hands decide if it lands. A shaky aim can hit the wrong person.
pros: Aim and target are one choice.
Everyone watches the throw.
cons: A miss may hit a bystander.
Players with steady hands pick on others more.

pairs.tendency: Whoever holds the pen can place a river or a wall beside one player's land. The map ends up showing who was picked.
pros: The map records every pick.
Players can see old grudges on paper.
cons: A hazard drawn near one player stays there.
The mapmaker can pick on the same person again.

pairs.tendency: While you build your own chain, you pick which rival's chain to cut. In a game of three or more, cutting one chain can leave you open to the next.
pros: One cut can stop a whole chain.
Players watch the longest line.
cons: A cut helps the player you did not pick.
A cutter can lose track of their own link.

pairs.tendency: Each choice beats one other and loses to a third, so aiming at a player means guessing which choice they will make.
pros: A pick needs a guess about the other player.
Every move has an answer.
cons: A player who is easy to read can be caught in a loop.
You may get hit by the choice you were hoping to beat.

pairs.tendency: Showing a pair or a run tells the table what you hold, so rivals pick you as a target. A player with a big declaration draws attacks.
pros: A declaration scores points straight away.
Rivals know what you hold.
cons: The scorer becomes the target.
Hiding your hand costs points.

pairs.tendency: Each player has a power only they have, so you pick a target by looking at whose power worries you.
pros: Picks follow the powers.
Each hit feels different.
cons: Players can gang up on the one with the most useful power.
Powers may go untested if nobody is picked.

pairs.tendency: Offering to double is aimed at one player, who either accepts or gives up the points at stake. The offer works as a challenge.
pros: A double can push a rival out.
A refusal ends the game early.
cons: Players watch for the right moment to offer.
A target who gives up loses what is on the table.

pairs.tendency: A forced capture lets you leave a piece open so a certain rival has to take it. Your choice of target is set by what you force them to do.
pros: A pick can force a move.
The victim's reply is easy to guess.
cons: A forced rival may set a trap for you.
Plans can break if the capture goes wrong.

pairs.tendency: A character that grows in power becomes the obvious target, and a player who leads in growth gets picked on.
pros: Growth draws attention.
The leader is easy to find.
cons: A hero who has not grown may be left alone.
Hits slow a rival who was ahead.

pairs.tendency: Each turn you add an item and name who recites next. Picking a target means picking who faces the longest memory test.
pros: Picks follow who forgets.
The list gets longer on each turn.
cons: A target can freeze in front of everyone.
A single slip ends a long run for the victim.

pairs.tendency: The player who starts with less is either the one others aim at or the one they leave alone to keep play close.
pros: Targets are picked for being behind.
Players choose how kind to be.
cons: The handicapped player may feel watched.
The player with the most can be hit by all.

pairs.tendency: You pick which seeker to tip off or mislead, so the hiding becomes a message to one player.
pros: The hider chooses who to help.
Seekers read each other's looks.
cons: A tipped-off seeker finds the target at once.
A false trail can send a seeker far away.

pairs.tendency: A hop can be aimed at one player's piece, and which one you jump decides who loses ground.
pros: A jump can pick off a piece.
Moves show who is next.
cons: A jump can leave you open to a return hop.
The victim may have no piece left near the edge.

pairs.tendency: After you set your dice aside, you choose which player takes the hit from the result. Keeping a high throw can mean a heavy blow for one person.
pros: A set of high dice, once kept, is aimed.
Players lean in for every roll.
cons: You may stop on a low result and miss.
The target waits while you roll again.

pairs.tendency: Landing on a rival sends them back to the start, so you steer your piece to the player you want to knock back.
pros: Moves are chosen to land on someone.
Rivals watch where you can reach.
cons: A piece sent back may return angry.
Safe spaces can save the target.

pairs.tendency: When you make a mill, you pick which of the other pieces to take, and so which player to hit.
pros: A row gives you a pick.
Players guard their next row.
cons: Breaking your own row to move costs you.
The player with few pieces is the one picked.

pairs.tendency: A word can be played to block one player's letters, and the word you choose decides who is hurt.
pros: A word can both score and block.
Players read each other's spaces.
cons: A blocked player may have no way to play.
The dictionary can end a quarrel and slow the game.

pairs.tendency: A tile placed on an open end can leave the next player with nothing to match, so what you lay decides who misses a turn.
pros: A tile can make a rival pass.
The open ends say who is stuck.
cons: A pass may help the player after them.
You cannot block everybody at once.

pairs.tendency: Adding cards to a laid-out set may help or hold back a named player, so you pick whose meld to add to.
pros: A card can help one rival more than another.
Players see every meld on the table.
cons: A helped player can pull ahead.
Giving cards away can run down your own hand.

pairs.tendency: A one-use power lands on a single target, so everyone watches to see who it will be used on and when.
pros: A power is spent on one player.
Players guess when it will come.
cons: Once used, it is gone.
Waiting for it can worry players more than the use itself.

pairs.tendency: You offer a move aimed at one player, and they answer with a yes, a no or a pick from two. The target can push back.
pros: The victim gets a voice.
Offers show what you think they will accept.
cons: A turned-down move wastes a turn.
A target can make you play a move you did not want.

pairs.tendency: You pick who gets the message, and a message sent to a rival can be bent on its way.
pros: The sender picks the first listener.
Messages change in the middle.
cons: Nobody can check the middle players.
A target can end up with a message that was meant for someone else.

pairs.tendency: The cards you pass go to one named player, so you choose who gets a gift and who gets a trap.
pros: A pass is a pick.
The receiver sees what you chose to give.
cons: A hand of low cards passed on may come back at you.
You cannot see what you get until you choose.

pairs.tendency: The first player sets up an even start, and the second picks a side, so the target is chosen at the same moment as the side.
pros: The setup is made to be fair to both sides.
The second player gets the last word.
cons: The first player may hide a trap in the setup.
A side that looks even can hide a weakness.

pairs.tendency: A piece that reaches the far end turns stronger, and you pick which rival feels it first.
pros: A promoted piece goes after a chosen player.
Players race to the far end.
cons: The promoted piece makes a clear target itself.
Pushing forward leaves your own side open.

pairs.tendency: In a relay, you pick which rival leg to get in the way of, and a hit on one runner slows the whole team.
pros: A block on one runner slows a team.
Players watch each handover.
cons: A blocked runner can lose the whole race.
Players on your own team wait while you hit others.

pairs.tendency: A safe shape protects your stones from attack, so rivals pick targets that have not made one yet.
pros: Safe stones drop out of the picking.
Players rush to build a shape.
cons: A player who has built nothing safe becomes the main target.
Stones stay put to keep the shape.

pairs.tendency: When prize cards are named in advance, whoever holds one becomes the person to pick on.
pros: The holder of a prize is easy to find.
Players track the named cards.
cons: A prize holder is hit again and again.
One card can lose a player two prizes.

pairs.tendency: Cards turned face up in the middle serve every player, so a target is picked by who can make most of them.
pros: The middle cards show who is in reach.
Everyone can plan from the same cards.
cons: A hit can take away a card from several people.
One player can make more of the middle than the rest.

pairs.tendency: A pot that grows from round to round makes the player closest to winning it the one others aim at.
pros: The pot draws attention.
A growing pot raises what each hit is worth.
cons: The player in front is hit hard.
Rivals may let the pot grow while they take turns attacking.

pairs.tendency: Where your last seed lands decides which pit you can take, so you pick a target by counting seeds ahead.
pros: A pit is chosen by counting.
Players follow each handful of seeds.
cons: A count can go wrong by one.
A full pit makes a clear target.

pairs.tendency: The player who takes or buys the spare hand has paid for it, so rivals look at them next.
pros: A purchase marks the buyer.
Players read what the swap shows.
cons: The buyer may be hit before any card is played.
A spare hand left alone gives nothing.

pairs.tendency: A square that sends a piece back or skips a turn can be used on a rival if you can nudge them onto it.
pros: A square can be aimed.
Players watch their path ahead.
cons: A trap square can catch you too.
A target may take a longer way round.

pairs.tendency: A costly card or item goes onto one target, and you decide who is worth the price.
pros: Money goes into a single hit.
Players keep track of each other's funds.
cons: A hit can leave you with nothing to spend.
A cheap target can be passed over.

pairs.tendency: You share your forces across several places, and each share is aimed at a different rival. A big share on one leaves another alone.
pros: A split spreads the hits.
Players guess where the big share will go.
cons: A thin share is easy to push over.
The player you ignored can slip ahead.

pairs.tendency: When the signal comes, the player you grab or chase is picked in a second. The slowest is the target.
pros: A pick is made in a moment.
Everyone watches the signal.
cons: There is little time to think.
A slow player is caught most rounds.

pairs.tendency: You swap cards with one chosen player, so picking who to swap with gives something to both of you.
pros: A swap needs a partner.
Players read what each swap gave away.
cons: Both hands change.
A player might refuse to swap.

pairs.tendency: Throwing a card on the pile can bait a certain rival, who may then pick up the whole pile.
pros: A card on top can tempt a rival.
The pile shows what has been played.
cons: A big pile weighs down the one who takes it.
A rival may leave the pile to someone else.

pairs.tendency: A trump can be played to beat one rival's high card, so you pick whose trick to win.
pros: A low trump can beat a high card.
Players count the trumps left.
cons: A trump used early may be missed later.
The player with no trump is easy to beat.

pairs.tendency: You attack on one board and defend on the other, so the rival you target on the first board is the one aiming at you on the second.
pros: One pick is made on two boards.
Players watch both boards at once.
cons: A hit on one board can bring a hit on the other.
A tired player drops one board.

pairs.tendency: A wild card can stand for the one card that hurts a named player, and the table cannot tell until it is played.
pros: A wild card goes where it is needed.
Players hold back wilds for the right target.
cons: A wild played early is gone.
A target may guess who holds the wild cards.
