pairs.tendency: On a joined board no player is far from you, so any rival can be picked. A piece leaving one edge can turn up beside another player.
pros: Any player is within reach.
Edges stop being safe.
cons: A hit may come from behind.
Players have to watch the whole board.

pairs.tendency: You pick which player to put a question to, and that choice shows which one you suspect.
pros: Questions can be aimed.
Each answer narrows the list.
cons: A target may answer to mislead.
Asking one person leaves the others with no clue.

pairs.tendency: You aim at the runner in front, since a hit on the leader changes who crosses the line first.
pros: A hit on the leader changes the race.
Players watch the front.
cons: The player at the back is left alone.
A runner in front draws every attack.

pairs.tendency: Hitting the top scorer is the obvious move, and when everyone does it the leader keeps being pulled back.
pros: The leader loses points.
Players see who is ahead.
cons: Everyone may hit the same person.
The player in second place can go unnoticed.

pairs.tendency: Every hit is aimed at the player nearest the exit, and the others may agree to team up on them.
pros: Hits go to the one who is closest to going out.
Teams of two can form.
cons: The first to fall watches the rest.
A player with no friends goes first.

pairs.tendency: With everyone on one side, a target is a threat or a hurt teammate who needs help. Choosing it means choosing what to deal with first.
pros: Players pick who to rescue.
The group has to agree on the order.
cons: An unanswered threat gets larger.
A teammate who waits may be lost.

pairs.tendency: There are no rivals, so the pick is a teammate to help. The choice sets who carries the load this turn.
pros: Picking a teammate shares the work.
Everyone is working on the same aim.
cons: One player may do most of the carrying.
A teammate left out can feel overlooked.

pairs.tendency: The target you pick can give away your goal, since a hit on one player says something about the secret you hold.
pros: A hit can hide or show a goal.
Players study each other's picks.
cons: A careless pick tells everyone what you want.
A false target can fool one player and lose another.

pairs.tendency: The story shapes who is picked: a hero, a rival, a friend. Whom you hit becomes part of how the story ends.
pros: Targets come from the plot.
Players have a reason for each pick.
cons: A story can shift if the wrong person is chosen.
The ending depends on who was hit.

pairs.tendency: With no winner, picking a target means choosing who to play with or against for its own sake. A hit has no score to gain.
pros: A pick is a way of playing, with nothing to win.
Players say why they chose.
cons: A hit can seem to have no reason.
Nothing tells you if a pick was right.

pairs.tendency: Your own goal decides your target, so two players with different aims may pick the same person for opposite reasons.
pros: Picks follow personal aims.
Players say what result they are after.
cons: The same hit can mean two things.
One player's help is another's block.

pairs.tendency: Everyone hopes to avoid being the loser, so hits are aimed to leave one particular person stuck at the end.
pros: Hits move towards a single loser.
Players keep an eye on who is last.
cons: The one who is picked on may be out of luck all game.
Safe players can stop paying attention.

pairs.tendency: Targets are picked so that nobody drops out, and a hit is light enough to leave the person playing.
pros: Hits are kept gentle.
Players aim to keep everyone in.
cons: A big hit is held back.
Play can drift without a push.

pairs.tendency: A game that cannot be won leaves the choice of target with no prize behind it. Players pick someone and then see what the choice says.
pros: Picks mean nothing for a score.
The choice shows what players care about.
cons: There is no reason to pick except your own.
The game may leave players unsure why they chose.

pairs.tendency: Playing alone leaves no other player to pick, so the target is a card or a pile in the layout.
pros: The pick is a card on the table.
No rival can be harmed.
cons: There is nobody to talk to about a choice.
The choice of target loses its pull.

pairs.tendency: Between short games you choose who to take on next. A rival beaten in the first game may become your target in the second.
pros: Picks carry over from game to game.
Players remember old defeats.
cons: A grudge can build up over three games.
The player who loses early may be left alone.

pairs.tendency: Handing points to someone is the hit, so you pick whose pile gets what you want to be rid of.
pros: Giving is the attack.
Players watch who is low.
cons: The leader gets nothing to pass on.
The victim ends with more than they began.

pairs.tendency: You aim at the player who is close to the exact number and push them past it, or hold them back from landing on it.
pros: A hit can undo a nearly finished run.
Players watch who is one step away.
cons: A near-winner gets picked on turn after turn.
A hit may leave you the same distance from the end.

pairs.tendency: Picking a target means choosing who gets stuck with what everyone is trying to avoid, so a hit works like a gift.
pros: A hit is a gift to the victim.
Players dodge what is passed to them.
cons: The target may be happy with the hit.
The usual order of friend and enemy turns round.

pairs.tendency: Nobody touches anyone else's work, so a target can only be reached by comparing results. You pick a rival whose score you want to match.
pros: A pick is a rival to watch.
Players build side by side.
cons: There is no way to hit anyone.
Players can lose interest in each other.

pairs.tendency: Players attack, steal and sabotage on purpose, and picking the target is the main choice of the turn. The victim knows who did it.
pros: Every attack has a name on it.
Players have clear reasons to be angry.
cons: A victim may hit back at once.
Quarrels can carry on past the game.

pairs.tendency: You hit a player by changing the board near them, so they feel it but may not know it was meant for them.
pros: A hit can look like an accident.
Players read the board for clues.
cons: A target may blame the wrong person.
A change to the board may land on someone else.

pairs.tendency: Nobody is a rival, so picking a target means choosing who gets the help or which problem gets the effort.
pros: Picks are made for the group.
Players talk about the order.
cons: A problem left alone grows.
The player who is helped first may get most of the effort.

pairs.tendency: The group works together, but each player has a small private reason to pick one teammate over another.
pros: A pick can help the group and one person.
Players watch each other's reasons.
cons: A helped teammate may pull ahead alone.
Trust can wear thin after a few picks.

pairs.tendency: The team picks one opponent as its joint target, and a hit on that person is felt by the whole other side.
pros: Teammates aim together.
A team can plan a pick.
cons: Teammates may disagree about who to pick.
The one picked may be left to cope alone.

pairs.tendency: The traitor picks targets in secret, and the others try to spot who is being hit more often than chance would give.
pros: A traitor's picks leave a pattern.
Players study who is being hurt.
cons: A wrong guess blames a friend.
The traitor can hit a friend and still pass as one.

pairs.tendency: A target is named in a letter, and the player waits days to find out who chose them.
pros: Picks arrive late.
The target has time to reply.
cons: Waiting can drag on for weeks.
A letter can go astray.

pairs.tendency: The absent player cannot hit back, so the group may pick them or leave them out. A target who is not there says nothing.
pros: An absent target cannot answer.
The group chooses how to treat them.
cons: Hits on the absent player leave nothing to see.
Picking them every time can feel odd.

pairs.tendency: The game master can aim a danger at a single player, while the players choose targets among the people they meet in the world.
pros: The master picks for the world.
Players pick for their characters.
cons: A player picked by the master may feel singled out.
The master has to watch that everyone gets a turn.

pairs.tendency: In a street game anyone passing can become a target, and a hit may land on someone who joined a minute ago.
pros: Targets can be strangers.
Players change from one minute to the next.
cons: A new player may not know the rules of the hit.
A hit can draw a crowd.

pairs.tendency: The lone player picks among many opponents, while the group picks the same single person. One side has many targets, the other has one.
pros: The group has one aim.
The lone player can split the others.
cons: The one player takes every hit.
The group may argue over who goes first.

pairs.tendency: Alone against the pack, the target is a card or a pile, since there are no other players to hit.
pros: A pick is a card or a pile.
Nobody can answer.
cons: There is no one to help or harm.
Choice of target means little.

pairs.tendency: The dice choose where a hit lands, and your choice of target can be cancelled by one low throw.
pros: A throw can undo a pick.
Players cheer or groan together.
cons: A planned hit can fail for no reason.
Little in a pick can be learned from.

pairs.tendency: You choose a target, throw, and then use a re-roll or a card to steer the hit if it misses.
pros: A pick can be saved after a miss.
Players have choices after the throw.
cons: A re-roll may be used up on one hit.
A target can use a card to dodge.

pairs.tendency: Planning decides who you hit, and a small amount of luck decides whether the hit works.
pros: Plans carry the pick.
Luck adds a surprise to the result.
cons: A careful plan can still miss.
A hit that works by luck can seem undeserved.

pairs.tendency: With no dice, a hit goes where you aim it, and the victim can often see the plan coming.
pros: A hit lands where it is aimed.
Players study the board.
cons: A target can see it coming.
Picks can take a long time to make.

pairs.tendency: A throw is read as a sign, and the sign points to a player. The dice seem to choose the target for you.
pros: A throw names a target.
Players talk about what the sign means.
cons: The reading can be argued over.
A target may feel picked by fate.

pairs.tendency: Targets are picked by feeling, since players sense when someone is about to act. A hit may land on the person who looked up.
pros: A pick follows a sense of the table.
Players watch each other's breath and eyes.
cons: A hit can be a guess.
The wrong feeling can fall on an innocent player.

pairs.tendency: A roll on the table says who you meet, so a hit can come from a story result and not from your own choice.
pros: A roll can name the target.
The story decides part of the pick.
cons: Players give up some say.
A pick can seem to come out of nowhere.

pairs.tendency: Everything is visible, so a target is picked with every fact known and the victim can see it coming.
pros: All picks are made in the open.
Players can work out what each will do.
cons: A hit is rarely a surprise.
Each pick can stall the game while it is worked out.

pairs.tendency: Cards in hand are secret, so you pick a target by guessing what they hold.
pros: A pick rests on a guess.
Players study each other's faces.
cons: A wrong guess wastes a hit.
A target with nothing to hide gets hit by mistake.

pairs.tendency: Hits are aimed at the person you think is the villain, and a wrong pick hurts a friend.
pros: A pick can be a wrong accusation.
Players watch each hit for a clue.
cons: A friend can be hurt.
The villain can sit quietly behind the argument.

pairs.tendency: Each hit or question to one player gives a clue, so choosing the target is also choosing what you learn.
pros: A pick brings a fact.
Players ask with a purpose.
cons: A question to one person leaves another unexamined.
A clue may point the wrong way.

pairs.tendency: Pretending to aim at one player can hide your real target. A bluff makes a rival look like the person you want to hit.
pros: A feint can cover a pick.
Players watch for lies.
cons: A bluff can be called.
You may fool a friend by mistake.

pairs.tendency: The player who knows the secret rule can pick a target by naming whoever breaks it. Newcomers find out why they were picked.
pros: A target is picked for breaking a rule.
Newcomers learn by being named.
cons: A new player can be caught several times over.
The knower has a lot of say.

pairs.tendency: The player who knows the answer chooses which guesser to give a hint to, so the target of the hint is who gets help.
pros: A hint goes to one guesser.
Others read who is being helped.
cons: A guesser who is skipped may fall behind.
A hint meant for one can be taken by another.

pairs.tendency: Turned-over areas show where rivals are, so a target can only be picked once the map shows them.
pros: A pick waits for a reveal.
Players explore before they strike.
cons: A hidden rival cannot be hit.
Exploring can lead into someone else's trap.

pairs.tendency: One face-up hand shows its cards to all, so whoever plays it is easy to aim at.
pros: A visible hand is easy to read.
Players plan against what they can see.
cons: The player of the open hand cannot bluff.
The open hand has no way to dodge a hit.

pairs.tendency: No one can add up the scores, so a target is picked by a guess about who is ahead.
pros: Picks go by guesses about points.
Players watch for slips.
cons: A guess can hit the wrong leader.
Someone behind may be left alone.

pairs.tendency: One player acts at a time, so each pick of a target is seen by all and answered on the next turn.
pros: Every pick has an answer.
Players take time to plan.
cons: The next hit can be a long wait away.
A target can plan a reply.

pairs.tendency: Everyone chooses a target in secret, then all reveal together. Two players may pick each other, or a lot may pick one.
pros: Picks are made at the same moment.
There is little waiting.
cons: A pile-on can happen without a plan.
Nobody can reply to a pick before it lands.

pairs.tendency: Anyone can hit anyone at any moment, so the target is often whoever is quickest to reach.
pros: Hits come at once.
Players keep watch the whole time.
cons: Slow players are hit most.
A pick has little time to be thought through.

pairs.tendency: A clock runs while you choose, so the target is picked fast. When time runs out, the pick may be made for you.
pros: Picks are quick.
The clock puts pressure on the choice.
cons: A rushed pick can land on a friend.
A pick that runs out of time is lost.

pairs.tendency: Over days, one pick is made each morning, and the chosen player has the whole day to think about it.
pros: Picks come slowly.
The target can think about a reply.
cons: A hit stays in mind between moves.
Long waits can cool the game.

pairs.tendency: A long pause before each pick gives you time to look at every rival, and the targets can feel the wait.
pros: The pick comes after a breath.
Players look at each other.
cons: The wait can make a target nervous.
Picking can feel heavy.

pairs.tendency: As the game speeds up, picks come faster and targets change quickly.
pros: Picks come faster and faster.
Hits stack up late in the game.
cons: There is less time to think.
A target may have no time to reply.

pairs.tendency: An extra go lets you hit the same player twice or move on to a second one.
pros: A chain of hits is possible.
One lucky throw can swing the game.
cons: The target gets no turn in between.
Others wait a long time.

pairs.tendency: A pick in the first stage can set up the second, so someone you helped early may face you later.
pros: Early picks carry over.
Players think ahead to the second stage.
cons: A kind early pick may be repaid with a hit.
The first stage may feel long if picks are slow.

pairs.tendency: Hitting one part of the system sends effects through the rest, as it would in life, so the pick of a target shows how things connect.
pros: A hit has side effects.
Players see how parts depend on each other.
cons: A hit meant for one can reach all.
The system can be hard to follow.

pairs.tendency: Each player plays a group, and a target is another group whose needs clash with yours. The pick is made from where your group stands.
pros: Picks come from a group's needs.
Players argue from their role.
cons: A group may be hit for being in the way.
A pick can seem personal when it is not.

pairs.tendency: Taking from the common stock hurts everyone, yet you can pick who bears more of the loss.
pros: A pick can share the cost unevenly.
Players watch who takes what.
cons: A greedy hit can empty the stock.
Everyone can lose when one is picked.

pairs.tendency: A hit made now shows up some rounds later, so the target may not know who chose them.
pros: A hit arrives late.
Players plan ahead.
cons: A target can be hurt by an old pick.
It is hard to link a pick with its result.

pairs.tendency: Players agree a new rule and then watch who it hits. Picking a target by the rule makes the rule itself the thing being tested.
pros: A rule is tested by who it hits.
Players see what the rule does.
cons: A rule that hits one player feels odd.
A tested rule may be dropped after one round.

pairs.tendency: After the game, players talk about why they picked each target, and a choice made quickly in play gets explained.
pros: Picks are looked at again.
Players hear each other's reasons.
cons: A target may find out who chose them.
Old grudges can come out in the talk.

pairs.tendency: A hit that cannot be undone stays on a chosen player, and the next game starts with that mark.
pros: A hit lasts into the next game.
Players think before they pick.
cons: A victim cannot recover.
One early pick can follow a player for a long time.

pairs.tendency: If the rules reward hitting one kind of player, the game says something about who counts as a target.
pros: The rules point at certain players.
Players can read what the game is saying.
cons: A rule can seem to name a person.
Players may argue about whether the point is true.

pairs.tendency: A real friend is the target, so picking them has a cost outside the game. A hit on the table can leave a mark after it.
pros: A pick carries real weight.
Players think about each other's feelings.
cons: A hit can turn into a quarrel.
Players may avoid picking anyone.

pairs.tendency: A hit takes away points that stand for something like kindness, so choosing a target means choosing whose value drops.
pros: A hit removes a kind of worth.
Players see what the points stand for.
cons: A target can feel judged.
Players may start chasing the points instead of the value.

pairs.tendency: Players practise choosing who to help or hit in a way of living that does not exist yet, to see how a pick would feel there.
pros: Picks show how a new world would work.
Players try out choices without real cost.
cons: A pick in the game may not match a pick in life.
The group may disagree about the new rules.

pairs.tendency: The dice tell each piece how far it travels, so a chain across the board grows only where the throw lets a piece land. The other player cuts the chain by sitting in the gap.
pros: Dice add surprise to a linking race.
Both players watch every throw.
cons: A chain can stall when the roll is short.
Plans for a link are hard to keep.

pairs.tendency: Players take turns picking from a shared row of cards, and each card lets them place a stone in one spot on the board. Taking a card also takes away the spot your opponent needed.
pros: Each pick helps one chain and blocks the other.
Players can read each other's plans from what they take.
cons: The last pick is often a leftover.
The row can run dry before a chain is finished.

pairs.tendency: Players offer chips for the right to place the next stone, and the winner picks the spot that joins or cuts a chain. A big offer for one key space leaves little for the next turn.
pros: The price of a space shows how much it matters.
A cut can be bought.
cons: Chips run out and then a chain cannot grow.
An opponent with more chips can place several stones in a row.

pairs.tendency: A player keeps placing stones to stretch a chain towards the far side, but each extra stone risks a throw or draw that wipes the chain out. Some players stop with a short chain; others go for the edge.
pros: Every extra stone makes the chain look nearer to done.
Players cheer or groan at each risk.
cons: A long chain can vanish in one turn.
Stopping early gives the other side time to cut.

pairs.tendency: The board is split into areas, and holding an area also gives a piece of the chain you need. Winning the middle area often decides which side gets linked up.
pros: Holding ground and linking go together.
A big area is easy to see and aim for.
cons: Defending every area leaves gaps in the chain.
The middle becomes crowded early.

pairs.tendency: Each worker sits on a job, and one job lets you lay a stone on the board. When the stone job is taken, the other player has to wait a turn before cutting your chain.
pros: Taking a job can hold up the other side.
Players plan which job to grab first.
cons: Only one stone can be laid per job.
Players wait while the favourite job is taken.

pairs.tendency: One player builds a shape out of tiles while the stones on the board have to join up from side to side. A chain that also makes the right pattern scores twice, but the pattern asks for stones in set places.
pros: A stone can serve two aims at once.
The board shows progress on both.
cons: A pattern can force a stone into a spot that cuts the chain's path.
Two aims make turns slower.

pairs.tendency: Cards in hand tell you where a stone may go, and saving a card for later keeps a gap ready for the moment it counts. Spending the cards early fills the board faster but leaves the hand thin.
pros: Holding a card keeps an option open.
Players weigh now against later.
cons: An empty hand leaves no way to fix a cut.
Keeping cards back can slow the chain.

pairs.tendency: Winning a trick lets you place a stone, so the player who takes the most tricks gets the most stones towards the far side. The trump suit becomes a way to link up while the other player tries to break the line.
pros: Each trick has a clear prize on the board.
The cards in play are easy to follow.
cons: A thin hand can lose a whole round of stones.
Card luck decides who links first.

pairs.tendency: Players talk about where stones will go, such as asking an ally to leave a gap open. A promise to leave a chain alone can be broken on the next turn.
pros: Deals can open a path for a chain.
A broken promise is felt right away.
cons: Talk can go on for a long time.
A deal can help the player who is already ahead.

pairs.tendency: Collecting a full set of matching things earns the right to place a stone, so a player who gathers sets fast builds a chain fast. Players gather things and watch each other's piles.
pros: The set gives each stone a clear price.
A pile shows who is about to place.
cons: Gathering takes turns away from cutting.
A set can be stolen just before it fills.

pairs.tendency: The tiles you lay become the board, so a chain is formed by tiles that line up edge to edge. A tile put down to cut the other player's path may also change your own path.
pros: The board is built and used at once.
A single tile can change both chains.
cons: Every placement opens spots for the other player.
A late tile can block both sides.

pairs.tendency: One player places a stone, and the next has to answer with a stone in reply, so the chain grows as a back and forth between two players. Each answer has to fit the call before it.
pros: The chain has a rhythm of call and reply.
Players read each move as a message.
cons: An answer is forced even when a cut is needed.
The pattern can be copied and so predicted.

pairs.tendency: Stones go down with no talk at all, so the only message is where a stone lands. A player reads a line of stones as a hint, and the other player reads it as a threat.
pros: Every stone says something to the other player.
The board becomes quiet and still.
cons: A mistaken reading can open a cut.
Teammates cannot explain a plan.

pairs.tendency: A player can change a rule on a turn, such as which sides of the board count for linking. A chain that was one move from done can be pushed out of reach by a new rule.
pros: The target for linking can move.
Players invent new ways to cut.
cons: A close chain may be undone by one rule.
Arguments about the new rule can take a while.

pairs.tendency: Each player acts as a character who wants to link two places, such as two villages with a road. Players speak as the character while the stones show where the road runs.
pros: Stones on the board show what the characters build.
Players talk as their characters.
cons: A plan can follow the story and lose sight of the board.
A scene can run longer than the move it explains.

pairs.tendency: A stone only counts if it lands on the spot after a flick or a toss, so a chain depends on steady hands. A miss can knock a nearby stone out of place and break a link.
pros: Each placing is a small show of skill.
A cut can come from a steady hand.
cons: A shaky hand can wreck your own chain.
The table can get knocked.

pairs.tendency: Players draw the map as they go, and a road drawn across the sheet is a link. A line drawn to join two sides can also block a line drawn by the other player.
pros: The map is made of the chain itself.
A drawing records every move.
cons: A messy drawing hides where the gaps are.
Erasing is not allowed, so a mistaken line stays.

pairs.tendency: Each kind of stone beats one kind and loses to another, so a chain made of one kind can be cut by its counter. A player has to guess which kind the other side will use next.
pros: No kind of stone wins on its own.
Players try to guess each other's picks.
cons: A chain of one kind is easy to cut.
Guessing can feel like luck.

pairs.tendency: A player shows a pair or a run from their hand and scores points, while stones on the board are linking up in the background. A run shown on the table tells the other player what is left in the hand.
pros: Showing a combination scores without needing a stone.
The other player learns what you hold.
cons: Points can be won while the chain stands still.
A shown run can warn the other player to cut.

pairs.tendency: Each side has its own power, such as one that jumps a stone over a gap or one that blocks a spot. The two players race to link in different ways, and each learns how the other side bends the rules.
pros: A power can close a gap in one move.
The two sides play out differently.
cons: Learning the other power takes several games.
A power can feel hard to answer.

pairs.tendency: Part-way through, a player whose chain looks close offers to double the game's value. The other player either accepts and keeps cutting or gives up the points already at stake.
pros: A near chain turns into a bet.
Players look closely at each other's chains.
cons: A double can end the game early.
Giving up loses points without a final move.

pairs.tendency: If a stone can be taken, the owner has to take it, even if the taking pulls a piece away from the chain. A player sets a bait so the other side's forced taking opens a gap.
pros: A forced move can be planned for.
Baits give the chain a way past a block.
cons: A forced taking can break your own chain.
A single bait can change a whole line.

pairs.tendency: Wins and clever moves bring new powers to a character who is linking places, such as longer reach or extra stones. Later links are harder to win but a grown character can place more stones in a turn.
pros: Early moves pay off later.
A character gets clearer over time.
cons: A late start leaves little time to catch up.
The player with more powers can rush the chain.

pairs.tendency: Each player says the whole list of stone spots so far and adds one more, and the spots named on the board form the chain. A player who forgets a spot loses a turn.
pros: The chain and the list grow together.
Everyone has to follow each move.
cons: A long list is hard to hold in the head.
Slips can break the flow of a game.

pairs.tendency: The leading player starts with fewer stones or a shorter side to link, so a weaker player can reach the far edge. A handicap that is set too low may leave the leading player cutting every chain.
pros: Two unequal players can still play.
The handicap is stated at the start.
cons: Setting the handicap takes a talk first.
One player may feel watched all game.

pairs.tendency: One player hides a stone or a goal on the board, and the others search for it while building a chain. A found stone could finish the link in one move.
pros: Searching gives a reason to cross the board.
A hidden goal changes where chains go.
cons: A turn spent searching places no stone.
A spot found by luck can end the game.

pairs.tendency: A piece that jumps over another lands behind it, so a jump can cross a gap in a chain in one move. Jumps may also take the stone that was being linked.
pros: A jump can close a gap.
Players look along every line for hops.
cons: A jump can cut a long chain at once.
Planning for jumps slows each turn.

pairs.tendency: Dice set aside after each roll decide how many stones may be laid, so a player keeps the high ones and rolls the rest again. A chain that needs five stones depends on how many dice are kept.
pros: The player picks which dice to keep.
Rerolls give a second chance.
cons: A third roll has to stand.
Dice rolling can slow down a game of placing.

pairs.tendency: A piece landing on another sends it back to the start, so a chain can be broken by landing on its middle stone. Safe spaces on the board let a stone stay put.
pros: A hit can cut a chain in one move.
Safe spaces give a place to rest.
cons: A long chain can be sent home.
Chains that go through open spaces are easy to hit.

pairs.tendency: Making a row of three lets a player take one of the other side's stones, and a stone taken from the middle of a chain breaks it in two. Rows that help the chain also give a chance to cut.
pros: One row can help and hurt at once.
The taking is a clear reward.
cons: A row built for taking can leave a gap in the chain.
Players guard their rows along with their chain.

pairs.tendency: The pieces on the board are letters, and a chain is a line of letters that links two sides and spells a word. A letter placed to cut the other player's word may spell a word of your own.
pros: Letters join the chain to the dictionary.
Players think about spelling as they place.
cons: A word can fail to fit the chain's path.
A dictionary check can stop play.

pairs.tendency: A stone can only be added if its number matches one of the open ends, so the chain grows along a line of matching numbers. A player with no match has to pass while the other keeps going.
pros: The ends show where play can go next.
A match is easy to check.
cons: A passing turn gives the other player time.
Chains can close off at both ends.

pairs.tendency: A player lays a finished set face up and adds matching cards to it later, and the set marks a spot on the board that links to others. Open sets show what the other side can add to.
pros: A laid set stays on the table as a base.
Players can add to each other's sets.
cons: A set on show can help the other player.
Laying cards early gives away the hand.

pairs.tendency: Each stone has a power that works once, such as jumping a gap or sealing a space, and using it removes the marker. A chain can be finished with one power if a player has saved it.
pros: A saved power can finish a chain.
Players try to guess who has one left.
cons: A used power cannot come back.
Waiting too long can lose the moment.

pairs.tendency: On each turn you offer a stone placing, and the other player can turn it down or choose between two. An offer that helps your chain has to look harmless to them.
pros: Each offer shows what a player wants.
Choices come from both sides.
cons: A refusal can block a chain for a turn.
Offers take longer than plain moves.

pairs.tendency: A message about where to place stones moves from player to player, and it may change on the way. A chain built from a changed message may not link up where it was meant to.
pros: The message turns into the plan.
Mistakes make the board look different from the plan.
cons: A single wrong word can send a stone to the wrong place.
Nobody can check until the message arrives.

pairs.tendency: Players hand cards to a neighbour before play begins, and the cards that come back decide where stones can go. A card passed on may help the neighbour's chain later.
pros: Passing shapes what each player can place.
Choosing what to give is a first move.
cons: Cards given away cannot be used.
A neighbour can gain from a card passed in a hurry.

pairs.tendency: One player sets up the first stones and the other picks which side to play. A start that favours the top edge gets chosen at once, so the first player tries to place stones that leave both sides open.
pros: The first stones are placed with care.
Both players think about each side.
cons: A small slip in the setup shows straight away.
The first player works without seeing which side they get.

pairs.tendency: A piece that reaches the far end turns into a more powerful one, which helps a chain reach the edge and then cross more gaps. The far edge is a goal for the chain and for the promotion at once.
pros: The same edge gives two rewards.
Players push forward to the edge.
cons: A promoted piece can cut in many ways.
Staying back to block gives the other side time.

pairs.tendency: Team players pass a stone from one to the next, each placing a leg of the chain. The first team to link every leg across the board wins, and each runner's stone is another link.
pros: Every player adds a part of the chain.
A team can see how far it has come.
cons: A slow runner holds up everyone.
One missed handover breaks the line.

pairs.tendency: A safe shape of stones cannot be taken, so a chain that passes through one has a fixed point. The other player tries to surround the chain before it joins up with the shape.
pros: A safe shape gives the chain a place to rest.
Players aim for the shape first.
cons: A chain away from the shape is open to cutting.
Building the shape can use many turns.

pairs.tendency: The prizes are named cards, and a chain across the board gives a way to win tricks and claim the prizes. A single card could win a prize and also finish a link.
pros: A card can serve two aims.
The prizes are known from the start.
cons: The named cards pull play towards them.
A chain can be dropped for one prize.

pairs.tendency: Cards in the middle can be used by both players, so each can place a stone on the spot a card shows. A card used by one player is not there for the other.
pros: The middle cards are open for all to read.
Both chains can use the same card.
cons: A shared card helps both sides at once.
A card taken in the middle can cut a chain.

pairs.tendency: Each player puts a counter in the middle before play, and the player who links first takes the pot. If no chain is finished, the pot grows for the next round.
pros: A longer game is worth more.
The pot shows what is at stake.
cons: Waiting can keep the pot for later.
A round with no winner leaves players stuck.

pairs.tendency: Seeds are dropped one at a time into pits that follow each other, and a chain of pits you hold links one side to another. Where your last seed lands decides which pits you can take and so which links you break.
pros: A pit counts as a stone in the chain.
A last seed can break a link.
cons: Counting seeds slows play down.
A big sowing can scatter the chain.

pairs.tendency: An extra hand sits face down in the middle, and one player takes it or buys it before play. The cards in it can give a first stone that starts a chain early.
pros: A spare hand gives a different start.
The buyer pays to see what it holds.
cons: A hand taken may not hold what the chain needs.
The first stone can be placed before the other player has acted.

pairs.tendency: Some squares on the board send a stone back, keep it safe or skip a turn, so a chain has to cross them. A player aims for a safe square and keeps the other side on the square that loses a turn.
pros: Squares make some links easier.
The board shows where the traps are.
cons: A chain through a trap square can be broken.
Players plan around squares more than around each other.

pairs.tendency: Each stone has a price, and a chain with cheap stones is slow to cross but cheaper to repair. Spending on a costly stone leaves little for the next link.
pros: Players decide what to buy.
A costly stone can make a bridge.
cons: Money runs out before the far side is reached.
A cheap chain is easy to cut.

pairs.tendency: A player has a fixed number of stones to share between several fronts, so a chain on one front leaves another thin. The other player can cut where the stones are fewest.
pros: Sharing shows what a player thinks matters.
Each front becomes a small game.
cons: A chain can be solid on one side and open on the other.
The other side watches for thin spots.

pairs.tendency: Players keep placing stones until a signal comes, and then everyone freezes. A chain left one stone short at the signal is caught unfinished.
pros: The signal ends the game with no warning.
Everyone moves quickly.
cons: A near chain can be lost to the signal.
Quick moves can place a stone in the wrong spot.

pairs.tendency: Players put back cards and take new ones, hoping for cards that place stones where a chain needs them. Swapping costs a turn that could have cut the other side.
pros: A swap gives a second chance at the hand.
The pile shows what other players threw.
cons: The other chain grows while you swap.
A hand can end up useless for the chain.

pairs.tendency: A player picks up the whole discard pile and can then place stones for the cards in it. A big pile gives a lot of stones, but it also shows the other player what was thrown.
pros: A full pile is worth a turn.
Players watch what goes onto the pile.
cons: A pile taken early can leave a hand full of useless cards.
The pile is a big prize for one player.

pairs.tendency: One suit is named for the hand, and cards in it can place stones that cannot be cut by lower cards. A low trump could win a trick against a high card and so give a stone to a chain.
pros: One suit gives a stone with power.
The trump suit is known by all.
cons: A hand without trumps may lose the stones.
Cutting with trumps can break a long chain.

pairs.tendency: A player takes one side on one board and the other side on a second board. A stone placed to cut on the first board could help the chain on the second.
pros: Each move has two effects.
Players learn to read two boards.
cons: It is easy to lose track of the second board.
A cut on one board may help a rival on the other.

pairs.tendency: A wild card can stand for any stone position, so it can close the last gap in a chain. The other player keeps a wild card back to cut at the key moment.
pros: One card can finish a chain.
Players guess who holds a wild card.
cons: A wild card used early is gone.
A chain waiting for a wild card can stall.

pairs.tendency: The edges of the board are joined, so a chain running off the right comes back on the left. A line that looked cut can reach round the other way.
pros: A chain has more than one path.
The board looks different from a flat one.
cons: Players miss the join at the edges.
Cutting a chain needs stones on both ends.

pairs.tendency: One player knows where the link has to run, and the others ask yes or no questions to find the spots. Each answer shrinks the list of places for the next stone.
pros: A question narrows down the path.
The answers are short and plain.
cons: Many questions are needed to find a long chain.
The player who knows the answer can wait for a slip.

pairs.tendency: Both players race to link their two sides first, and the first to finish wins. A move spent cutting the other chain is a move not spent on your own.
pros: The finish is easy to see.
Both chains grow together.
cons: Cutting costs a turn in a race.
A one-step lead is hard to catch.

pairs.tendency: A chain across the board earns points, and the other points come from other sources, so a chain is one way to score among several. A player may leave a chain unfinished to chase points elsewhere.
pros: A chain gives a clear score.
The scores can be added at the end.
cons: Points elsewhere can pull attention from the board.
A finished chain may not be enough to win.

pairs.tendency: Pieces are knocked out one at a time, and the last player left wins, so a chain gives a place that is hard to knock out. A player who cuts the chain of a rival may knock out the rival's stones with it.
pros: A linked chain can protect its stones.
A knocked out player watches the rest.
cons: An early cut can take a player out.
Waiting for others to be knocked out takes time.

pairs.tendency: All players link a chain together against the game, and the game tries to cut it. If the chain reaches the far side, everyone survives.
pros: The team shares one chain.
Everyone can add to it.
cons: The game's cuts can strike anywhere.
One player's slip is felt by all.

pairs.tendency: All players work to link the same two sides, each laying stones on one chain. They agree on which gaps to fill first.
pros: The goal is plain for all.
Players explain their moves to each other.
cons: One loud player can take over the plan.
Each move needs a short talk first.

pairs.tendency: Each player has a secret goal, and linking a chain may be a goal for one and a cover for another. A stone placed in the open can hide what the player truly wants.
pros: A chain can be a cover.
Players guess at each other's goals.
cons: A cut may help a rival with a hidden goal.
A secret goal can be missed by the player who holds it.

pairs.tendency: The chain across the board is the route of a story, and the game ends when the story does. Each stone adds a scene, and a cut becomes a twist.
pros: The chain follows the plot.
The board becomes a record of the story.
cons: The story can end before the chain does.
Cutting a chain changes the tale for everyone.

pairs.tendency: Stones go down and a chain may form, but nobody wins. Players stop when they like and talk about the lines they made.
pros: A chain is made without a race.
Players look back at the board.
cons: A chain has no clear end.
Nobody has a reason to cut.

pairs.tendency: Each player decides what success means, such as linking one side or building as many chains as possible. Two players on the same board may be working towards two different chains.
pros: Each player judges their own board.
The board can hold two kinds of play.
cons: Players may not know when the game is over.
A cut may not matter to the other player at all.

pairs.tendency: The game goes on until one player loses, and a chain across the board gives a way to stay safe. The players who are linked are out of danger while the one left unlinked falls behind.
pros: A linked chain keeps a player safe.
The last unlinked player is clear to see.
cons: A cut puts a player at risk.
The others can leave one player behind.

pairs.tendency: The aim is to keep play going, so players keep extending the chain and never aim to finish it. A link across the board only opens a new stretch beyond it.
pros: The chain can grow for a long time.
Players share the care of the board.
cons: There is no moment when the game finishes.
The board can get crowded.

pairs.tendency: The board is set so that no chain can be completed, or each link pulls another apart. Players try to link anyway and see what the rules do to them.
pros: The board shows what the rules do not allow.
Players learn by trying.
cons: A chain never reaches the end.
Players can lose patience with the board.

pairs.tendency: A player alone tries to link the sides of a layout of cards, and the game says they lost if they get stuck. Every stone placed closes one door and opens another.
pros: A solo player can try a chain over and over.
The layout is the same each time it is dealt.
cons: There is no one to cut the chain.
A stuck layout ends the game.

pairs.tendency: Players play several short games of linking, and the one who wins the most games wins the match. A chain that fails in one game can be tried again in the next.
pros: A lost game is not the end.
A match can finish early.
cons: A player learns the other side's habits.
Many games take a long time.

pairs.tendency: Each stone left on the board counts as points against its owner, so a chain across the board can be costly to keep. The player with the fewest points wins, and so cutting the other player's chain could add to their score.
pros: Keeping fewer stones is an aim.
A short chain costs less.
cons: A long chain adds to a score.
Players may hold back from placing stones.

pairs.tendency: A chain has to end on an exact count of stones, so one stone over loses the win. A player a stone short can wait while the other player tries to land on the number.
pros: Players count each stone.
The finish needs a careful last move.
cons: A chain that goes too far loses the win.
Players can end up passing while they wait.

pairs.tendency: The aim is turned upside down, so the player who links a chain across the board is the one who loses. Players work to avoid linking while cutting their own lines.
pros: Players think hard before each stone.
The usual plan is turned around.
cons: A chain forms by accident.
New players need a while to see what to avoid.

pairs.tendency: Each player builds a chain on their own board, side by side, and nobody cuts anyone. The first to finish ends the game, and the others can see how far along they are.
pros: Each board is a separate puzzle.
Players can look over at each other's chains.
cons: Nobody can cut the leader.
The game can feel like two games.

pairs.tendency: Players place stones to cut each other's chains on purpose, and a link can be broken by a stone put right in the gap. A chain that lasts through the game has had to defend itself.
pros: Cuts come right away.
Players know who they are playing against.
cons: A blocked player can feel hunted.
A long defence leaves little time for building.

pairs.tendency: Players never attack each other, they only place stones, and a stone put in the gap blocks the other player without a word. Each player feels the board change.
pros: The board does the talking.
A block comes without a direct hit.
cons: Players can feel crowded without knowing why.
A quiet block can be missed until too late.

pairs.tendency: All players work on one chain together, against the game itself. A stone placed by one player helps every other player.
pros: All effort goes into one chain.
Plans are talked through.
cons: A single player can end up steering the chain.
The game's cuts hit everyone.

pairs.tendency: Players link a chain together, but each has a small private reason to be the one who finishes. A player may leave a gap for their own stone and so slow the team.
pros: The team gets the chain done.
Each player has a private aim.
cons: A player may hold back a stone for their own gain.
The team can argue about who places the last stone.

pairs.tendency: Two teams each try to link their sides, and teammates plan together. A team member places a stone to help a partner's line while the other team tries to cut it.
pros: Teammates plan a shared chain.
Each team has a side to guard.
cons: A slip by one partner is felt by the whole team.
Planning aloud lets the other team hear.

pairs.tendency: Most players work on one chain, but one secretly cuts it. The others place stones and watch who leaves a gap that keeps getting wider.
pros: The team watches each stone.
A gap shows who might be the traitor.
cons: A cut can be blamed on the wrong player.
Players start to doubt each other's moves.

pairs.tendency: Players are far apart and send each stone in a letter, so a chain across the board can take weeks to grow. Each reply shows where the other player's chain now runs.
pros: Every move is thought through.
Waiting is part of the game.
cons: A cut arrives long after it was planned.
A missing letter can stop the whole game.

pairs.tendency: One side of the chain is played for a player who is not there, such as a ghost who can only give hints. The present players work out where the absent stones would go.
pros: The empty seat is part of the board.
Players make guesses on its behalf.
cons: The absent side cannot answer a cut.
Players may disagree about what it would have done.

pairs.tendency: One player runs the world and decides what blocks a chain, such as a river or a guard. The others link places on a map while the game master invents the problems in the way.
pros: The world answers each stone.
The game master can adapt the map.
cons: The game master has to be fair to all.
The chain depends on one person's patience.

pairs.tendency: The board is drawn in chalk in a street, and anyone passing can add a stone to a chain. A stranger who joins may link a chain or cut it.
pros: New players can join at any time.
The board sits in the open.
cons: A passer-by may rub out a line.
The chain can change hands many times.

pairs.tendency: One player tries to link the sides alone while the others work together to cut. The lone player is paid more for finishing.
pros: The lone player has a bigger prize.
The group has to agree where to cut.
cons: The group has many stones to place.
The lone player faces many cuts at once.

pairs.tendency: A single player builds a chain from side to side against the pack of cards. Luck and choice decide how the chain grows, and a friend can compare the result afterwards.
pros: The player sets the pace.
The result can be compared.
cons: Nobody cuts the chain.
A chain can end up as luck decides.

pairs.tendency: Dice and draws decide where stones go, so the chain forms by luck. A player can only watch the chain grow or break.
pros: Players share the surprise.
A weaker player can link first.
cons: Choices hardly matter.
A chain gets cut by a throw that nobody planned.

pairs.tendency: A roll decides where a stone lands, but a player may re-roll or move it a step. A chain can survive a low throw if the player has a way to nudge it.
pros: A throw can be softened.
Players have choices to make.
cons: Re-rolls run out.
A nudge uses up a turn.

pairs.tendency: The chain is built by choice, with a small draw of luck deciding some stones. A planned line may meet a random block.
pros: Plans mostly hold.
A small chance keeps games from repeating.
cons: A random block can undo a plan.
A new player can be surprised.

pairs.tendency: No dice and no luck, so only choices decide the chain. The player who reads the board more clearly links first, and each cut is planned.
pros: Every stone is a decision.
Players can learn from each game.
cons: An experienced player wins most games.
A new player has little to hope for.

pairs.tendency: Dice or cards are read as a message, such as which side of the board needs attention. The throw places no stone. It tells the player where to think about linking.
pros: Each throw gives a prompt.
Players discuss what a throw means.
cons: A sign can be read two ways.
The chain depends on how players read it.

pairs.tendency: Players sense when the other is about to cut and place stones at the same moment. A chain grows when two friends reach the same gap together.
pros: Close friends manage it easily.
Stones are placed by feel.
cons: Strangers find it hard to match.
A mistimed stone leaves a gap.

pairs.tendency: A roll is looked up on a table that says what happens, such as a flooded road. A chain of stones is the road, and the dice decide where the story blocks it.
pros: The dice add events to the chain.
The story gives the board a reason.
cons: A table result can cut a chain by itself.
Looking up each result takes a moment.

pairs.tendency: Every stone and every plan is on the board for both players to see. A chain cannot be hidden, so the other player sees each gap you leave.
pros: Each move can be worked out.
Nothing is kept secret.
cons: A chain cannot surprise anyone.
Players spend a long time on each move.

pairs.tendency: Cards in hand are secret, and each one gives a stone position. A player guesses from the board which cards the other holds, and which gap they can fill.
pros: Hidden cards add guessing.
A chain may hide what it needs.
cons: The other player may bluff a block.
A hand can run out of useful cards without warning.

pairs.tendency: Some players have a secret role, so a stone placed to link might be help or a trick. A chain grows slowly while the others watch who adds to it and who cuts.
pros: A role is hidden behind each stone.
Players watch every placing.
cons: A cut may be blamed on an honest player.
Doubt slows the chain.

pairs.tendency: Clues on the board let a player work out where the other player's chain has to run. A player who spots the hidden line can cut it at its narrowest point.
pros: Clues give the board a story.
A cut comes from careful thought.
cons: Wrong guesses waste a stone.
A clue may be read in two ways.

pairs.tendency: A player places a stone as if building a chain towards one side while really aiming for another. The other player has to decide which line to cut.
pros: A false line draws a cut.
Players study each other's habits.
cons: A cut in the wrong place leaves the real line open.
Bluffs are hard to read.

pairs.tendency: One player knows a secret rule about how stones link, and the rest find it by placing stones and being told no. A chain only forms once the others have learned what counts as a link.
pros: New players find the rule by trying.
Each refusal teaches something.
cons: A refused stone costs a turn.
The first chain takes much longer.

pairs.tendency: One player sees where the chain has to run but cannot say it, and only gives hints such as pictures. The others place stones and guess the line.
pros: The hint giver watches the chain form.
Pictures give the game a gentle feel.
cons: A hint can lead to a wrong line.
The one who knows has to wait.

pairs.tendency: The board starts hidden and areas are turned over as stones reach them, so a chain grows into the unknown. A gap can turn out to be a wall.
pros: Each reveal changes the plan.
Players explore as they link.
cons: A chain can lead into a dead end.
Turning over the board takes time.

pairs.tendency: One hand is laid face up, and the chain can be built from the cards in it and from your own. The open hand shows both players which gaps can be filled.
pros: An open hand gives away part of the plan.
Players learn to read a hand.
cons: The player with the open hand has less to hide.
Playing two hands is hard to keep track of.

pairs.tendency: Some points are kept secret, so no one can add up the score for certain. A chain across the board may look decisive but a hidden score can still decide the game.
pros: Players have to guess who is ahead.
A chain may not be the whole story.
cons: A hidden score can undo a chain.
A finished chain may be worth little.

pairs.tendency: One player places a stone, then the other, and each can see the gap that was left. A chain grows one stone at a time while the other player waits to cut.
pros: Each stone is thought over.
Players see the whole board before they act.
cons: A wait can be long with many players.
The first player to move may have a head start.

pairs.tendency: All players choose a stone in secret and reveal together. Two stones may land in the same gap, so a chain and a cut meet on the same spot.
pros: Nobody waits for a turn.
A clash of two stones is a surprise.
cons: A cut cannot be answered until the next round.
Players guess the others' choices.

pairs.tendency: Anyone can place a stone at any moment, and the quickest player takes a gap first. A chain is a rush to fill spaces before the other player cuts them.
pros: The board moves quickly.
Quick players have an advantage.
cons: Slow thinkers fall behind.
Players may reach for the same stone at once.

pairs.tendency: Each turn has a clock, and a stone not placed in time is lost or placed for you. A chain grows in a hurry, and a gap may be closed because the clock ran out.
pros: The clock keeps the game moving.
Players learn to decide fast.
cons: A rushed stone can land in the wrong gap.
Time runs out while a plan is half made.

pairs.tendency: The game runs on real days, with one stone placed each morning. A chain across the board takes weeks, and the other player has a long time to plan a cut.
pros: Players have a day to think over each stone.
The board is checked daily.
cons: A game takes a long time to finish.
Players may forget a move.

pairs.tendency: The game slows down on purpose, with a pause before each stone. A chain is placed one deliberate stone at a time, and the other player has time to see each gap.
pros: Each stone gets full attention.
Players look at the whole board.
cons: Games run long.
Players may lose track of the plan.

pairs.tendency: Timers shrink as play goes on, so the later stones of a chain are placed in a rush. A cut in the late game has less time to be answered.
pros: The pace builds up.
The late game is quick.
cons: Early moves have more time than late ones.
Late slips are hard to fix.

pairs.tendency: A throw or a hit gives another go at once, so a player can place two stones in a row. Two stones may close a gap before the other player can cut it.
pros: A lucky player can leap ahead.
An extra go can surprise the other side.
cons: Two moves in a row can end a chain.
The other player waits while it happens.

pairs.tendency: The first stage is about choosing cards and the second about placing stones. What a player picks in the first stage decides which gaps can be filled in the second.
pros: The first stage shapes the second.
Planning ahead matters.
cons: An early choice cannot be taken back.
The first stage can feel far from the board.

pairs.tendency: The board stands for a real system, such as water pipes between wells, and a chain is a pipe that links the source to a field. A cut is a broken pipe, and the water stops.
pros: The chain has a meaning outside the game.
Players see how a link works in real life.
cons: A model can be simpler than the real thing.
Talk can drift from the move to the system.

pairs.tendency: Each player acts as a group such as farmers or a village council, and each group wants a different link. A chain that helps farmers may cut across the council's land.
pros: Each group has its own aim.
A chain shows whose needs came first.
cons: A link for one group can cut another off.
Roles can stay stuck on one view.

pairs.tendency: All chains draw on one limited supply, such as water under a village. A long chain uses more of it, so the more stones are placed the less is left for the others.
pros: Everyone shares one pool.
A big chain has a visible cost.
cons: The supply can run out for all.
A player who takes more leaves less for others.

pairs.tendency: A stone placed now shows its effect a few rounds later, so a chain looks sound until the delay arrives. A link that seemed safe may fail only after more stones are laid on it.
pros: Early stones have long results.
Players think ahead.
cons: A fault may show up too late to repair.
A cut can be planned in advance.

pairs.tendency: Players agree on a new rule, such as a limit on stones per turn, and play on to see how chains change. A rule that slows the leader may let the other side link up.
pros: A rule can be tested safely.
Players see what the rule changes.
cons: A rule can break the chain's flow.
Trying a rule can take a whole game.

pairs.tendency: After the game, players talk through where chains formed and where they were cut. The board stays as it ended, so each stone can be pointed to.
pros: The board is a record.
Players explain their choices.
cons: Talk can feel long after a game.
Players may not agree about what happened.

pairs.tendency: Each stone changes the board for ever, such as a sticker on a space, and the next game starts from the old board. A chain that crossed the board stays there for the next players.
pros: The board carries a history.
Old chains shape new games.
cons: A cut cannot be undone.
Later games start from fixed spaces.

pairs.tendency: The rules for linking say something about the world, such as a road that counts and a field that does not. A chain across the board shows what the designer thinks matters.
pros: The rules make a point.
A chain shows what the game rewards.
cons: Players may disagree with the point.
A lesson can be lost behind the play.

pairs.tendency: A chain across the board carries a real promise, such as who buys the tea. A cut then feels like a real loss.
pros: The game matters beyond the table.
Players take each stone seriously.
cons: A cut can upset a friendship.
A close game can leave an awkward silence.

pairs.tendency: Points stand for something that matters, such as kindness or health, and a chain earns points for its length. Players chase long chains and may forget what the points were for.
pros: A number stands for a value.
Players see what chasing a number does.
cons: A long chain may not mean more kindness.
Players may care more about the number.

pairs.tendency: Players link places in a village that does not exist yet, such as a shared kitchen to a shared water tank. The chain is a plan, and a cut shows where the plan could fail.
pros: The future is tried on the board.
Players talk about how it would feel.
cons: A plan may look easy on a board.
Real people are harder to place than stones.

pairs.tendency: After each throw, a piece that lands beside another piece starts a showdown. Both players pick a sign in secret, the signs beat each other in a ring, and the loser steps back a few spaces.
pros: The dice decide when showdowns happen.
Each meeting is a small guess.
cons: Many throws pass with no meeting at all.
A lucky roll can force a showdown nobody wanted.

pairs.tendency: Every card in the shared row is one of the ring's signs, so a pick is also a guess about what the next player will want. The hand you pass shows your neighbour which signs you left behind.
pros: Each pick tells others what you hold.
A card is worth more or less depending on who sits next.
cons: Your neighbour reads you easily.
The last picks are mostly forced.

pairs.tendency: Players offer money for a card, and every card beats one sign and loses to another. A high bid shows how much that sign is wanted, so the table can plan a counter before the card is even paid for.
pros: Prices show what players are afraid of.
A cheap card can still win a round.
cons: A big bid gives away your plan.
Money spent early leaves little for later rounds.

pairs.tendency: Each round that you win adds to a streak, and a single loss wipes the whole streak out. After a few rounds your opponent has seen which sign you lean on and aims a counter at it.
pros: Streaks grow quickly.
Players start to watch each other's habits.
cons: One lost round ends a long streak.
Repeating a sign gets punished.

pairs.tendency: The armies on the map come in kinds, and each kind beats one other kind. An attacker has to guess what the defender put in a region before sending troops, and no army is safe everywhere.
pros: No single army wins on every part of the map.
Splitting armies across regions limits a single loss.
cons: Scouting a region takes a whole turn.
A hidden army can undo a long plan.

pairs.tendency: Workers come in kinds, and a worker can bump a worker of the kind it beats off a job space. Taking a space now means thinking about who could knock you out of it.
pros: A taken space can be taken back.
The kind of worker counts as much as the job.
cons: Plans fall apart when a worker is bumped.
Players track which kinds the others still hold.

pairs.tendency: Every colour in the mosaic is cancelled by the colour that counters it, so a neat row needs the right neighbours. A rival can wreck your row by dropping one tile of the wrong kind beside it.
pros: Rows need planning around neighbours.
One tile can reshape a whole pattern.
cons: A neat pattern takes many turns to finish.
Rows get redone more than once.

pairs.tendency: The cards in your hand are signs, and the sign you play only makes sense against what you expect the other player to bring. Holding a card back keeps an answer ready, but the hand can end up with no answer to what shows up.
pros: Waiting keeps your options open.
Past plays tell you what the other player favours.
cons: A hand can hold the wrong signs.
Holding on too long wastes turns.

pairs.tendency: In each trick the cards follow the ring instead of a number order, so a seven can take a nine if it is the right kind. The player who leads picks a kind and the others try to answer it.
pros: No card is always the highest.
Leading is a guess about the whole table.
cons: The order takes a while to learn.
Beginners lose track of which kind beats which.

pairs.tendency: Players talk about which sign they will show, and a promise like "I will play the one that loses to yours" can be made and broken. Deals shape the picks, and the picks show who kept their word.
pros: Deals decide who plays what.
A bluff can be said out loud.
cons: Promises are easy to break.
Talking takes longer than picking.

pairs.tendency: A finished set belongs to one family, and a rival's set from the family that counters it can wipe it out. A player who builds two sets of different families has some cover.
pros: Every set has a known threat.
Two sets spread the risk.
cons: A long build can end in one counter.
Players watch each other's piles closely.

pairs.tendency: Each tile shows a kind of ground, and a tile set next to the kind that counters it cuts the road or covers the field. The shared map grows as a string of answers to the last tile laid.
pros: The map shows who is winning where.
Every tile answers the one before it.
cons: One tile can undo a long road.
Turns slow down while players look for counters.

pairs.tendency: Each call is one of the ring's signs and the reply has to be the sign that beats it. The chain grows like two singers trying to top each other, and each answer opens the next call.
pros: Chains grow quickly.
A reply always comes from the call before it.
cons: Players run out of new answers.
The chain can loop back to where it started.

pairs.tendency: Nobody can talk, so the only way to guess the next sign is to watch what the others played last. A frown or a long pause before a card becomes part of the message.
pros: Habits show on the table.
Quiet rounds go fast.
cons: A friend is easy to misread.
There is no way to explain a mistake.

pairs.tendency: On your turn you can swap which sign beats which. After that the old winners lose, and the player who just built a plan around them has to build another.
pros: A winning habit can be turned against its owner.
The rules become part of the guessing.
cons: Players argue about the new order.
The current order is easy to forget.

pairs.tendency: Each character has a favourite way of acting, and each way beats one other way. Staying in character makes you easy to predict, and a rival who knows your habits can walk into every scene with the answer.
pros: Characters get habits other players learn.
Scenes end with a clear winner.
cons: Staying in character narrows your choices.
A character can get stuck against one rival.

pairs.tendency: The move you try is a flick, a stack or a throw, and each one has a kind it beats. Picking the right counter helps, but your hand still has to carry it out.
pros: Hands and guesses both matter.
A clumsy player can still pick the right counter.
cons: A correct guess can still fail on the flick.
Players hesitate before each try.

pairs.tendency: Players draw regions of different kinds, and a region sits safely only beside a kind it beats. The finished map is a ring of neighbours, each held back by the next.
pros: The map keeps a record of old rivalries.
Neighbours shape every region.
cons: Drawing takes time before play starts.
A large region is hard to defend.

pairs.tendency: A pair or a run you show also belongs to a family, so showing it tells the table which family to play against. You score at once, and the other players learn something about your hand.
pros: Points arrive while the game goes on.
A shown run reveals part of your hand.
cons: Others learn what you hold.
A declared run can be countered on the next turn.

pairs.tendency: Each player's power bends one link in the ring, so a sign that normally loses can win for them. Everyone is working from a slightly different ring, and learning someone else's takes a few rounds.
pros: Each player's game is a little different.
Rivals can study a special link.
cons: There are many matchups to remember.
A power can make one sign hard to answer.

pairs.tendency: After a few rounds you may offer to double what the match is worth. You make the offer when you think you have read the other player's habit, and they have to decide whether you are bluffing.
pros: A correct read is paid in full.
Doubling can also be a bluff.
cons: A wrong read costs twice as much.
Giving up costs the points already at stake.

pairs.tendency: When a piece can capture it has to, and captures follow the ring. A player can leave a piece out as bait, the other has to take it, and the piece that counters the taker answers at once.
pros: Traps are easy to plan.
An offer forces the other player's move.
cons: A forced move can wreck your own plan.
Players check every piece before moving.

pairs.tendency: A character that gains power over time still sits inside the ring, so a grown hero can lose to a small one of the right kind. The climb helps against most things and not against the one that counters you.
pros: Growth has a ceiling.
Small characters keep a chance.
cons: Time spent growing can be wasted.
One counter can end a long climb.

pairs.tendency: Each new item added to the list has to beat the one before it in the ring, so the list becomes a chain of answers. Saying the whole chain back gets harder with every turn.
pros: The chain tells a story as it grows.
Each addition is guided by the last.
cons: Memory gives out as it grows.
The list can loop and repeat itself.

pairs.tendency: The player who starts with fewer pieces or less time can still win a round by guessing right, because every sign in the ring has an answer. A newer player has a chance against a practised one.
pros: Skill counts for a little less.
Both players read each other's habits.
cons: The leader may take fewer risks.
Players argue over the size of the start gap.

pairs.tendency: The hider picks one of several ways to hide and the seeker picks a way to search, and each way of searching finds one kind of hiding place and misses another. Using the same hiding place twice gives it away.
pros: A correct guess is rewarded straight away.
Hiding and seeking answer each other.
cons: Repeating a hiding place gives it away.
Rounds end quickly.

pairs.tendency: Pieces come in kinds, and a piece can only jump the kind it beats. A piece sitting behind the kind that counters its neighbour is safe from one hop and open to another.
pros: Jumps depend on the kind of piece.
Defenders get placed with care.
cons: Many pieces cannot be jumped at all.
Long chains of jumps are rare.

pairs.tendency: The dice show symbols from the ring, you keep some and roll the rest, and you aim at the symbol that beats what your opponent is holding. Seeing their dice first changes what you keep.
pros: Dice and choice both count.
The other player's roll shapes your keeps.
cons: The last roll decides most of the result.
Checking each other's dice drags each turn out.

pairs.tendency: Landing on another player's piece sends it back only if your piece's kind beats theirs. If it does not, your piece is the one that goes home, so a landing is a bet.
pros: Every landing is a gamble.
The kind of a piece counts on every space.
cons: A lucky landing can turn against you.
Players steer away from crowded spaces.

pairs.tendency: A mill lets you take a piece, but only a kind your mill's colour beats. So building a row means choosing which of the other player's pieces you will be allowed to reach.
pros: Taking is tied to the mill you make.
Players plan rows by the kind they want.
cons: Some pieces stay out of reach.
Breaking a row takes several moves.

pairs.tendency: The letters are sorted into themes, and a word from one theme is beaten by a word from the theme that counters it. A word about animals might lose to a word about weather.
pros: Words are chosen by theme.
Players learn words just to counter others.
cons: Players with small vocabularies run dry.
Someone has to check the theme of every word.

pairs.tendency: Each tile carries a symbol from the ring, and you can add a tile to an end only if its symbol beats the one showing. A match is a win over the last tile, not a copy of it.
pros: A match means beating the last tile.
The line grows in a loop of answers.
cons: A tile with the wrong symbol gets stuck in the hand.
Missed turns pile up for some players.

pairs.tendency: A laid set belongs to one family, and others can add to it only if the card fits. A rival can cover your set with a card from the family that counters it.
pros: Laid sets show plans.
Other players can add to open sets.
cons: A large set can be covered in one play.
Players hold cards back to keep answers ready.

pairs.tendency: A one-time power lets a losing sign win once. Everyone knows the power is out there, so each player watches for the round when the other will use it.
pros: Saved powers change how others play.
Everyone watches for the moment of use.
cons: A power used too early is gone.
Players hold back and the game slows.

pairs.tendency: You offer a sign, and the other player may turn it down or choose between two you offer. Offering two tells them you do not plan the third, and a refusal tells you what they expect.
pros: Offers carry a message.
A refusal says something too.
cons: Players read too much into an offer.
Each turn takes longer.

pairs.tendency: The message is a sign passed down a line, and each player may swap it for the sign that beats it. By the time it arrives it can sit far from where it began.
pros: Messages change on the way.
The end result is a surprise.
cons: Nobody can check the middle.
Players blame each other for the change.

pairs.tendency: The cards you pass show your neighbour which signs you do not want, and the cards you get back hint at their plan. You choose before you can see what comes in return.
pros: Passes show plans.
Each player starts with a read of one neighbour.
cons: You pick before seeing what you receive.
A pass can arm a rival.

pairs.tendency: The first player sets up a start where every choice has an answer, and the other picks a side. A setup that favours one sign is easy to spot, so the setter tries to make the ring look balanced.
pros: Setups tend to come out even.
The picker has to read the setup.
cons: Setting up takes thought.
The setter can still be outguessed.

pairs.tendency: A piece that reaches the far end turns into another kind, and you pick the new kind to counter what the other player has nearby. The other side sees the choice and plans around it.
pros: There is a reason to push forward.
The chosen kind changes the board.
cons: A promoted piece can be countered at once.
Players guard the far end.

pairs.tendency: Each leg is run by a runner of one kind, and the order of runners is chosen in secret against the other team's. A runner that meets the kind that counters it loses ground for the whole team.
pros: The order of runners becomes a puzzle.
Teammates have to trust each other's picks.
cons: A mismatched order loses a leg.
Teams argue about the order.

pairs.tendency: A shape is safe against the kinds it beats and open to the kind that counters it. Building towards a safe shape means guessing which kind the other player will bring.
pros: A shape gives a goal to build towards.
Players choose shapes against the likely attackers.
cons: A shape can be useless against one kind.
Building takes many moves.

pairs.tendency: Each named prize card belongs to a kind, and a trick won by a card that counters the prize's kind takes it. A single card can win more than one prize, and a high card can lose to the right low one.
pros: Prizes are tied to kinds.
One card can win more than one prize.
cons: A prize can be lost to the right counter.
Players keep track of the named cards.

pairs.tendency: The cards in the middle each carry a kind, and your own hand is read against them. Everyone sees the same row, so everyone sees the same matchups.
pros: Shared cards give everyone common ground.
Hands are compared to the middle.
cons: A card in the middle helps your rivals too.
Studying the row takes time.

pairs.tendency: The winner of a round takes the pot, and a tie between two equal signs leaves it in the middle to grow. A repeated sign tends to tie, so the pot swells when players stop varying.
pros: Ties make the pot bigger.
Repeating a sign shows up quickly.
cons: The pot can sit for many rounds with no winner.
Players quit when the pot is large.

pairs.tendency: Your last seed lands in a pit marked with a kind, and what you can take depends on whether your kind beats that pit's kind. Counting seeds tells you where you will land, and so what you can take.
pros: Counting seeds matters.
The landing pit decides the take.
cons: A sow is hard to follow to its end.
There is a lot of counting.

pairs.tendency: The spare hand holds the signs that nobody else was dealt. The player who takes it knows which kinds are missing from the other hands and picks a counter to what is still out there.
pros: The spare hand shows what others lack.
Taking it is a read in itself.
cons: Taking it gives away what you think.
Swapping cards back takes time.

pairs.tendency: Each special square is tied to a kind, and landing on it helps you only if your piece's kind beats the square's. Players choose their route by what the squares will do to their piece.
pros: Each square has a counter.
Routes depend on the kind you carry.
cons: Some squares are avoided entirely.
A piece sent back costs time.

pairs.tendency: Each card has a price, but the cheap card can beat the expensive one if it is the right kind. Money does not settle a round, so buying the dear card is only useful if the matchup is right.
pros: Cheap cards can win.
Players weigh price against matchup.
cons: Spending on the wrong kind is lost.
Buying early shows your plan.

pairs.tendency: You share a fixed army out over several places, and in each place your force meets one of the other player's kinds. Putting the right kind in the wrong place loses it.
pros: Where each unit goes decides the result.
Both players are guessing at once.
cons: A wrong split can lose two places.
There is little room to change after placing.

pairs.tendency: When the signal sounds everyone shows a sign at once, and those who lose the ring are caught. Slow players grab the sign they always grab.
pros: A round is over almost at once.
Everyone shows together.
cons: Slow players fall back on habit.
Noise makes it hard to think.

pairs.tendency: You swap cards to get the kind that counters what you expect, and the other players see what you put back. The cards you return show which kinds worry you.
pros: Hands shift towards what is expected.
Swaps show what players fear.
cons: Others read your swaps.
A swap can bring a useless kind.
