pairs.tendency: The pile fills with the kinds players throw away, and picking it up is only useful if you hold something that beats the top card. The bigger the pile, the more it can win or cost you.
pros: The pile shows what has been played.
A large pile is a large reward.
cons: Taking the pile shows rivals your hand.
A heavy hand is harder to play.

pairs.tendency: The ring says each suit beats one other, and the trump suit says one suit beats all. When both rules are there, the trump overrules the ring in its own suit and the ring still governs the others.
pros: One suit stands outside the ring.
The other suits keep their counters.
cons: The trump can make the ring matter less.
Players holding trumps have an easy time.

pairs.tendency: You play both sides on two boards, and a move on one board changes what you expect on the other. An attack on the first board can leave a gap on the second.
pros: Attack and defence happen together.
Each board tells you about the other.
cons: It is hard to track both boards.
Turns take a long time.

pairs.tendency: A wild card can stand for any sign, so it beats whatever is played against it unless the other player also has a wild. Players save wilds for the round where a guess matters most.
pros: One card can answer anything.
Players save wilds for key rounds.
cons: A wild cancels the guessing.
Rivals count how many wilds are left.

pairs.tendency: A piece that leaves one edge comes back at the other, so its counter can arrive from either side. No edge of the board is safe.
pros: There is no safe edge.
Attacks can come from behind.
cons: The board is harder to read.
Corners lose their use.

pairs.tendency: One player holds a secret sign and the others ask yes-or-no questions about it, such as whether it beats the one just played. Each answer shrinks the list, and the answerer learns what the asker is aiming at.
pros: Questions narrow the list of signs.
Answers are short.
cons: Questions tell the answerer your plan.
Rounds go slowly.

pairs.tendency: Each step forward comes from winning a showdown in the ring, and the loser stays put. A leader who repeats a sign can be caught by one lucky counter.
pros: Progress comes from reading the rival.
A leader can be caught in one round.
cons: A draw gives nobody a move.
Many rounds pass before anyone finishes.

pairs.tendency: Wins score points, and the signs may be worth different amounts. The sign that scores most is also the one every rival aims at.
pros: Scores show who read the others.
A high-scoring sign carries a risk.
cons: A repeated sign gets countered.
One big miss can hide inside a total.

pairs.tendency: Each round sends a loser out, and nobody keeps winning with one sign. With many players more than two signs are shown at once, so ties send nobody out and the round repeats.
pros: Everyone has a chance in every round.
Rounds are short.
cons: Early exits mean long waits.
Many players cause many ties.

pairs.tendency: The game sends threats of different kinds, and the team has to answer each with the kind that counters it. Teammates settle among themselves who answers which.
pros: Everyone gets a job.
Team talk matters.
cons: One wrong answer hurts everyone.
One player can end up making the calls.

pairs.tendency: The team's goal can only be reached by beating a chain of obstacles, each of a different kind. Each member covers some kinds, and a kind nobody covers blocks the whole team.
pros: The team plans together against each obstacle.
Each member can cover a kind.
cons: One missing kind blocks everybody.
Players talk a lot about who covers what.

pairs.tendency: A secret goal pushes you towards one sign without telling anyone. Others watch for a pattern in your picks, and playing the sign too neatly gives the goal away.
pros: Goals show up in habits.
Players can bluff with their signs.
cons: Playing too neatly gives you away.
Guesses about others can go wrong.

pairs.tendency: Each scene is a clash between two forces from the ring, and the story goes to the winner of the clash. The next scene starts from who won, so the story turns in a loop.
pros: Stories loop with each win.
Scenes have clear causes.
cons: The ring shapes the story.
Endings can repeat.

pairs.tendency: Players keep showing signs with nobody winning, and at the end they look back at what was played. Patterns in who followed whom show up on the table.
pros: There is time to watch patterns.
Nothing is lost in a round.
cons: Players have little reason to pick with care.
Rounds can drift.

pairs.tendency: One player decides to win using one sign only, another decides never to repeat a sign, and the ring makes some of these goals harder. After the game each player says how close they came.
pros: Goals differ from player to player.
Players learn what the ring allows.
cons: Goals can clash.
Results are hard to compare.

pairs.tendency: Every round finds a loser, and the game ends when one player has lost too often. A player who repeats a sign is the one likely to lose.
pros: Careful players can relax.
One habit can decide the loser.
cons: The last place tends to stay last.
The pressure falls on one player.

pairs.tendency: Because every sign has an answer, the rounds can go on without end, and no sign wins for ever. Players change their signs to keep each other guessing.
pros: Rounds can go on for a long time.
Players change signs to stay in.
cons: There is no natural stopping point.
Players tire.

pairs.tendency: The ring already means no sign wins every time, and the rules add that nobody can win the game. Players see that their guessing leads nowhere and may talk about why.
pros: The point comes across through play.
Players watch the loop go round.
cons: Players look for a goal that is not there.
Rounds end with no result.

pairs.tendency: Alone against the cards, each card in the layout has a kind, and you clear it by playing the kind that beats it. With no opponent to guess, the ring becomes a puzzle of matching.
pros: Each card has a clear match.
A layout can be solved by reading it.
cons: A stuck layout ends the game.
There is nobody to bluff.

pairs.tendency: Over several short games, one sign wins one game, so a player who wants to win the series has to vary. A player who is ahead can stop the series early.
pros: A pattern can build a lead.
The series can stop early.
cons: A streak can be wasted by one loss.
Many short rounds add up.

pairs.tendency: Each win adds points against the winner, so players try to lose the ring on purpose. Both players are aiming for the same result, which makes the rounds slow.
pros: Losing becomes a plan.
Players choose signs they expect to lose to.
cons: Both players aim to lose, so rounds stall.
The score can be hard to follow.

pairs.tendency: Each win moves your marker forward, and you have to land exactly on the target. Near the end a player may want to lose a round on purpose to avoid overshooting.
pros: A win can be turned down.
The choice changes near the end.
cons: A win can overshoot the target.
Players wait for the right number.

pairs.tendency: The aim is turned over, so each player picks the sign they hope will lose. Reasoning goes round in the ring the other way, and each player has to guess how far the other has thought it through.
pros: Everyone reasons backwards.
The ring still holds.
cons: The aim is easy to forget.
Reasoning can loop.

pairs.tendency: Everyone plays their own ring contest against a deck or a table, and nobody touches another player's game. Players compare results at the end.
pros: Everyone plays at the same time.
Each player guesses on their own.
cons: There is little to learn from others.
No one can get in the way of a rival.

pairs.tendency: Two players go head to head with one sign each, and the winner takes something from the loser. A table that sees one player lose often tends to aim at them.
pros: There is a clear winner of each clash.
Targets get picked by habit.
cons: A losing player is picked on.
Players seek revenge round after round.

pairs.tendency: Players place pieces of different kinds on the board and never clash directly. The board then settles which kind beats which, and a rival feels your piece a few turns later.
pros: Rivals feel a piece later.
The board tells the story.
cons: Cause and effect are slow.
It is hard to see who did it.

pairs.tendency: The team plays against a game whose threats follow the ring. Team members share what counters what, and everyone sees the answer being worked out.
pros: Everyone shares the answer.
The team can cover every kind.
cons: One player may decide for all.
Plans cannot be hidden from the game.

pairs.tendency: Most players help the team against a threat, but each has a private reason to get ahead, and the counter that helps the team may cost your own score. Others judge your picks for motive.
pros: Helping and hiding mix.
Players judge each other's motives.
cons: Doubt grows about who is helping.
Team plans can fail.

pairs.tendency: Each team has members who play different kinds, and a team wins by having a counter ready for each of the other team's kinds. A hole in one kind shows up as a lost round.
pros: Teammates cover each other.
Team talk becomes a plan.
cons: Rivals find the gap quickly.
Teams have to talk in secret.

pairs.tendency: The traitor can spoil the team's counter by playing the wrong kind at the wrong moment. A wrong answer can then be a clue, or an honest mistake.
pros: A wrong answer can be a clue.
Players watch every pick.
cons: Honest mistakes look like betrayal.
Doubt slows the game down.

pairs.tendency: Each letter carries one sign and the reply carries the next, with days or weeks between. The long wait gives time to think about what the other will choose.
pros: There is time to think about each reply.
Each letter shows habits.
cons: Rounds are very slow.
A lost letter breaks the chain.

pairs.tendency: The absent player's picks come from a fixed list or an old game, and they always follow the ring in the same order. Others can learn the pattern and play against it.
pros: Their habits can be studied.
There is a pattern to beat.
cons: Bluffing does nothing against a list.
The pattern can be misread.

pairs.tendency: The game master picks a sign for the world each round and the players answer. A master who favours one sign shows it, and one who switches often makes players unsure.
pros: The world has habits.
The master can plan surprises.
cons: One person's choices rule the table.
Players learn the master's habits and play to them.

pairs.tendency: Anyone passing can join a round, so the table fills with strangers whose habits you do not know. A crowd also makes it hard to see who showed which sign.
pros: New players bring new signs.
Rounds are brief.
cons: Strangers' habits are unknown.
A crowd hides the signs.

pairs.tendency: The lone player picks a sign and the others have to agree on a counter. Group members who disagree split their answer, and the lone player slips through.
pros: The group has to agree on one answer.
The lone player holds the surprise.
cons: Group members disagree.
The lone player carries a larger risk.

pairs.tendency: You play against the pack, and the pack follows the ring by chance. Your result depends on the shuffle as much as on your picks, and a friend can compare scores afterwards.
pros: The ring plays out against luck.
Results can be compared later.
cons: There is nobody to read.
Results depend on the shuffle.

pairs.tendency: Dice pick the sign for each player, and the ring then decides the winner. The players have no hand in it, so the ring adds a rule to follow and nothing to choose.
pros: Rounds are quick.
Anyone can win.
cons: There is nothing to choose.
The ring adds little when luck sets the signs.

pairs.tendency: The dice give each player a sign, and one re-roll or swap lets them move it towards what they want. Rivals watch for who spends a re-roll.
pros: An unlucky roll can be repaired a little.
Rivals watch the re-rolls.
cons: A repair costs a turn.
Players hold re-rolls too long.

pairs.tendency: Players pick signs by skill, and now and then a draw changes the sign for them. The ring means skill is mostly a matter of reading the other player.
pros: Most rounds turn on reading the other player.
Surprises are rare.
cons: A draw can undo a careful pick.
New players feel the luck more.

pairs.tendency: There are no dice, only the ring, so the player who reads the other more closely wins more rounds over a long match. A single round is close to a coin toss.
pros: Winning comes down to reading the other player.
Patterns pay off over time.
cons: One round tells you little.
Experienced players run ahead.

pairs.tendency: The throw is read as a message, and each message has a counter message that the asker looks for in the next throw. A throw is placed in the ring and then talked about.
pros: The throw becomes a story.
Readings can be discussed.
cons: Readings vary from person to person.
There is no clear score.

pairs.tendency: Players try to show the same sign, or the one that beats the others, at the same moment. If everyone leans towards the same sign, one player who plays its counter takes the round.
pros: Sensing others pays off.
Rounds go quiet before the reveal.
cons: It is hard to say why a guess worked.
Players copy one another.

pairs.tendency: A table says who you meet on the road, and each meeting is settled by a clash in the ring. The dice write the encounters and the ring settles them.
pros: The dice write the encounters.
Fights have a clear rule.
cons: The same table gets repeated.
The story follows the ring.

pairs.tendency: With everything on the table the ring has no secret: if players pick in turn, the second player picks the counter every time. To keep the contest open, the picks have to be hidden or made together.
pros: Counters are plain to see.
Order of play changes the result.
cons: The second player wins every round.
Players need a way to pick at once.

pairs.tendency: Each player holds cards of different kinds that nobody else can see, so a play is a guess about the other hand. A player who has only one kind in hand can be beaten by a single counter.
pros: Guessing the hand is the game.
Players can bluff with kinds.
cons: A hand of one kind is easy to beat.
Long thinking slows the table.

pairs.tendency: A secret role can be tied to a sign, and players act in ways that show their sign without meaning to. Watching who plays what turns into a hunt for the roles.
pros: Roles hide in sign patterns.
Each pick gets studied for a role.
cons: Players accuse too quickly.
Roles can be guessed from picks.

pairs.tendency: Clues from past rounds tell you which sign the other player tends to show, and each clue narrows the guess. A rival may play the odd sign just to spoil your notes.
pros: Evidence comes from earlier rounds.
Habits get tracked.
cons: Notes pile up.
A rival can spoil the trail on purpose.

pairs.tendency: You say you will play one sign and then play another, and the ring gives your claim a target because a claimed sign invites its counter. A claim that is believed can be used once.
pros: A claim steers the other player.
Bluffs get read.
cons: A trusted bluff is spent after one use.
Liars get checked more often.

pairs.tendency: One player knows which sign beats which, and the others learn the ring by losing. The first losses teach the most, and the rule holder is ahead until the ring is known.
pros: The ring is learned by playing.
Early losses teach quickly.
cons: Newcomers lose early.
The secret holder starts ahead.

pairs.tendency: The player who knows the answer can only hint, and each hint points towards a sign in the ring. Guessers think about which sign the hint was built to counter.
pros: Hints point to a sign.
Guessers think about counters.
cons: Hints can mislead.
Each round takes time.

pairs.tendency: Each area shows a kind when it is turned over, and you enter only with a kind that beats it. Entering with the wrong kind loses you a turn.
pros: Exploring is a guess.
Each reveal changes plans.
cons: Guessing wrong wastes a move.
Hidden areas slow decisions.

pairs.tendency: One hand lies open, so the table knows which kinds it holds and who plays it. The others plan their counters against known cards while their own cards stay secret.
pros: The open hand gives a hint.
Others plan against known cards.
cons: The open hand cannot hide anything.
The player of that hand has few surprises.

pairs.tendency: Wins are scored in secret, so nobody knows how many rounds the others have taken. Players guess from the signs they remember who is ahead.
pros: Memory of play counts.
Everyone guesses who leads.
cons: The scorekeeping has to be trusted.
Players cannot tell when to change their play.

pairs.tendency: One player picks first and shows, and the second sees it and picks the counter. Turn order gives the second player an edge unless the first pick is hidden.
pros: Order creates an edge.
Hiding the first pick removes it.
cons: With an open first pick, the second player always wins.
Waiting takes time.

pairs.tendency: All players reveal together, which is how a ring is usually played. Nobody sees a pick first, and a round takes a moment.
pros: No player can wait and react.
Play moves fast.
cons: Many players cause ties.
It is hard to see who picked what.

pairs.tendency: Anyone can show a sign at any moment, and the first to show forces the others to answer. The fastest player sets the sign and the others race to counter it.
pros: Answers come fast.
Quick hands decide the pace.
cons: Noise builds up.
Slow readers lose.

pairs.tendency: A clock forces a pick, and when time runs out the sign is chosen for you, often by habit. Short clocks leave less room to read the other player.
pros: Picks come fast.
Habits show under the clock.
cons: A pick made by the clock is close to random.
Pressure leads to repeating.

pairs.tendency: One sign goes out a day for weeks, so the ring plays out slowly and a player's pattern shows up over time. A reply can wait for the morning.
pros: There is time to study patterns.
Plans stretch over days.
cons: The game is slow to finish.
Players forget where they were.

pairs.tendency: A pause before each pick makes players think about what the other will show. The slow pace gives time to doubt a pick before it is made.
pros: The pause lets players read each other.
Rounds feel calm.
cons: The game is slow.
There is time to doubt.

pairs.tendency: Rounds get shorter as the game runs, so later picks are made with less time and more by habit. A player who has varied early may repeat late.
pros: The pace builds.
Habits show late in the game.
cons: Late rounds are mostly guesses.
Slower players fall behind.

pairs.tendency: A win earns another go straight away, so a player who reads the other closely can chain several wins. Others wait while the chain runs.
pros: A correct read pays twice.
Chains of wins are possible.
cons: Trailing players wait.
One streak can end the game.

pairs.tendency: In the first stage you choose which kinds to bring, and in the second you play them out in the ring. A wrong choice in the first stage shows up in the second.
pros: Picking is half the game.
The second stage tests the first.
cons: A wrong first stage cannot be undone.
Setup takes a long time.

pairs.tendency: The parts of the board counter each other like predator and prey, one rising as the other falls. Players watch the numbers move in a loop.
pros: The loop shows in play.
Players watch numbers rise and fall.
cons: Someone has to keep the count.
A model can look too neat.

pairs.tendency: Each group has one group whose wishes it can overrule and one group that can overrule it. Nobody holds the final say for long, so deals have to be made.
pros: Each side sees its limits.
Deals are needed.
cons: Some groups feel stuck.
Players dispute who overrules whom.

pairs.tendency: Each sign draws on the shared pool, and taking a lot beats taking a little, but the pool runs out. Restraint is a sign as well, and it only pays if others show it too.
pros: The pool shows who took what.
Holding back counts as a choice.
cons: Greed can end the pool for all.
Restraint is hard to prove.

pairs.tendency: A sign you play now is beaten by a counter that lands two rounds later, so you plan ahead of the table. The cost of a pick shows late.
pros: Planning ahead pays.
Causes show up later.
cons: The cause is easy to forget.
Blame lands on the wrong round.

pairs.tendency: The new rule changes one link in the ring, and the group plays on to see the result. One changed link can reverse who wins most.
pros: Rule changes show their effect quickly.
Changes are easy to test.
cons: One change can break the loop.
The group talks before each test.

pairs.tendency: After the game, the group looks over the order of signs and which counters were used. Habits that were hidden during play become easy to name.
pros: Patterns are plain afterwards.
Habits get named.
cons: Someone needs to keep notes.
Players may defend their picks.

pairs.tendency: Each win removes a sign from the ring for ever, so the loop shrinks as the game goes on. When only two signs are left one beats the other and the ring is gone.
pros: The ring shrinks as play goes on.
Each pick weighs more as signs run out.
cons: The last signs are forced.
Mistakes cannot be reversed.

pairs.tendency: The ring says that no choice wins for ever, and playing it shows that point about power. A player who wins a few rounds feels the next one coming.
pros: Each round repeats the argument.
Players feel the point in turn.
cons: Players may read other points into it.
The point can feel pushed.

pairs.tendency: With real stakes on the table players try to hide their habits, and the ring makes any habit risky. A loss in a round can carry out of the game.
pros: Players take care with each pick.
Habits come under watch.
cons: Losses carry past the game.
Some players avoid playing.

pairs.tendency: Each sign carries a value such as kindness, and points push players towards the sign that scores. The ring then punishes whichever sign scores most.
pros: Players see how points push their choices.
The ring pushes back.
cons: Values shrink to numbers.
It is hard to say what winning shows.

pairs.tendency: Players practise a way of living where no group stays on top, and the ring gives each group a turn to lead. Leadership passes round the table.
pros: Leadership passes round.
Players feel each position.
cons: Real systems are messier.
A model of the future can be copied wrongly.

pairs.tendency: Each throw moves your piece, and some spaces hand you a card. When the new card makes a pair with one in your hand, you call it out and take the points.
pros: The track gives a steady flow of new cards.
Declaring adds a small scoring moment between throws.
cons: Where you land can matter less than which cards you hold.
Players may stop watching the pieces and watch their hands.

pairs.tendency: Cards go round the table and each player keeps one. A king taken now may pair with the queen you took last round, so you announce it and score.
pros: A pick can build towards a pair.
Players read each other's picks to guess what they are building.
cons: Taking a card for your pair denies another player.
A declared pair tells everyone what to hunt for next.

pairs.tendency: Players bid for cards on offer, knowing a winning card may complete a pair they can declare later. A card that finishes a run is worth more to its owner than to anyone else.
pros: Each player has a private reason to bid high.
Bids hint at what a player holds.
cons: A bidder can overpay for one card.
Hands can end up uneven in size.

pairs.tendency: You keep drawing in the hope of completing a run, and every draw could be the one that ends your turn. Points for a declared run are safe only once you say them aloud.
pros: Declaring early locks in some points.
Waiting could lead to a bigger run.
cons: A bust can lose a half-built run.
Players hesitate before every draw.

pairs.tendency: Cards in your hand can be shown as pairs to earn points, while your pieces fight for parts of the map. Showing a pair can pay for a move on the board.
pros: Two ways to score run side by side.
Points from cards can cover a gap on the map.
cons: Attention splits between hand and board.
Declared pairs may point rivals at your plans.

pairs.tendency: Workers take jobs, and one job gives you cards. A declared pair is another job's reward, so you place a worker to collect the card that completes it.
pros: A taken spot can block a rival's pair.
Players plan a turn ahead.
cons: The card spot is crowded.
A blocked player may have no way to finish a run.

pairs.tendency: Tiles on the table make patterns while cards in hand make pairs and runs. The same colour can serve both, so one choice helps two scores.
pros: One piece can feed two kinds of score.
The table and the hand tell different stories.
cons: Two scoring systems take longer to learn.
Counting both can slow a turn.

pairs.tendency: Every card is held for later, and a pair you declare is paid for at once. Declaring tells others what you hold and keeps those cards in your hand, so you still have to decide when to play them.
pros: Each card might serve two jobs.
A declared pair gives early points while the cards stay available.
cons: Opponents know part of your hand.
Playing a card can break a pair you showed.

pairs.tendency: Between tricks, a player who holds a king and queen of one suit calls it and scores. Playing either card later spends the pair, so players think about which card to lead.
pros: Points come from the hand as well as from the tricks.
A pair of the right suit shapes how a hand is played.
cons: Declared cards are known to everyone.
Breaking a pair to win a trick has a price.

pairs.tendency: Players trade cards across the table to build pairs and runs. A card swapped away might finish another player's run, so deals are watched closely.
pros: Trades can complete pairs for both sides.
Players have a reason to talk.
cons: A deal may hand a rival points.
Hidden hands make it hard to know what a card is worth.

pairs.tendency: You gather groups of matching cards, and the pairs and runs you show on the way count too. A set in progress scores early before it is whole.
pros: Points arrive before the set is finished.
There are several ways to use one card.
cons: Half a set is on display for all to see.
A player may chase small scores and miss a big one.

pairs.tendency: Tiles are laid into a shared picture while hands of cards give pairs to declare. A tile you place may match the suit you are about to show.
pros: Two scores can follow from one plan.
The map grows while the hand gets thinner.
cons: Cards and tiles need separate attention.
Placing a tile may hand a rival a pair.

pairs.tendency: One player calls a card and the next answers with another. If the answers form a pair, the player who built it declares and scores.
pros: Pairs can grow from the chain of answers.
Each reply gives the next player a clue.
cons: A declared pair can end a chain.
Players may answer just to stop a pair.

pairs.tendency: Nobody speaks, so a declaration has to be made by laying the pair on the table. Everyone sees the pair and has to guess what it means for the next play.
pros: The table shows what was meant without any talk.
Play is quiet and watchful.
cons: A pair laid down at the wrong moment can be misread.
Players cannot say why they chose a card.

pairs.tendency: On your turn you may change a rule, so a rule might say that a king and a queen are worth more, or that a run of three is worth nothing. The value of a declared pair changes with each turn.
pros: Players can steer what a declaration is worth.
The scoring table is open to play.
cons: A pair can lose its value after it has been shown.
Players argue about what the rules say now.

pairs.tendency: Each player speaks as a character, and a declared pair is a fact in the story, such as a king and queen standing together at court. The cards turn into things the characters do.
pros: Cards give the story its next scene.
A pair makes a clear moment to act out.
cons: Play can stall while the cards are sorted.
Some players drop the character and answer as themselves.

pairs.tendency: A player flicks or stacks to win cards, then declares what the pair is worth. A shaky hand can leave you one card short of a run.
pros: Skill with the hands earns the cards.
Declaring gives a calm pause after a tense flick.
cons: A steady hand may beat a clever mind.
Losing cards to a toppled stack can break a pair.

pairs.tendency: Players draw the map as they go, and each place they add has a card tied to it. A pair of cards from neighbouring places can be declared as a road or a border.
pros: The drawing gives the cards a setting.
Pairs link parts of the map.
cons: The map can fill with places no one visits.
Players may draw places for points and forget the world.

pairs.tendency: Each player has a power of their own, and some powers make a pair worth extra or let one card stand in for another. Two players with the same cards score different amounts.
pros: Declarations differ from player to player.
Players learn each other's powers by watching.
cons: A power can make one player's pair more valuable.
Players need to remember every other power.

pairs.tendency: A player who holds a high pair may offer to double the game. Declaring the pair first shows what you hold and may tempt the other player into accepting.
pros: A shown pair can be used as a threat.
The offer to double is a form of bluff.
cons: A double can be refused after a pair is shown.
The loser pays for both the cards and the doubled stakes.

pairs.tendency: When a capture is open you have to take it, even if it breaks a pair you meant to declare. A rival can set a trap by offering a capture that costs you your run.
pros: Forced moves are easy to predict.
A trap can be set with a single piece.
cons: A declared pair may vanish when a card is spent.
The player who takes control of the capture has the edge.

pairs.tendency: Each declared pair adds a point of power to your character. After a few rounds the same hand does more than it did at the start.
pros: Early declarations pay back later.
The game gets bigger as it goes.
cons: A player who falls behind has a hard climb.
Late hands depend on early ones.

pairs.tendency: Each player says the whole list and adds an item. If the list gets a king and a queen, the player who added the second card can declare the pair and score.
pros: The list tells who is paying attention.
Pairs appear as a side effect of memory.
cons: A mistake in the list stops the game.
The list grows too long for some players.

pairs.tendency: A player with more experience begins with fewer cards in hand, so they have less chance of a pair to declare. A weaker player starts with a head start of points.
pros: Both players have a chance at a declaration.
A gap in skill is narrowed.
cons: The experienced player may play with caution.
The handicap needs to be set again after each game.

pairs.tendency: A card is hidden somewhere and players search for it. Whoever finds it can pair it with a card in hand and declare the pair.
pros: Searching has a reward on the table.
The found card fits a plan.
cons: Players keep their pairs secret until the find.
The hunt can run on while the hands sit unused.

pairs.tendency: Pieces hop over each other, and a hop that lands on a certain space gives a card. A run you hold in hand can be declared when the hop finishes.
pros: Moves on the board feed the hand.
A long chain of jumps can bring several cards.
cons: Players have to watch the board and the hand together.
A jump to win a card can leave a piece open.

pairs.tendency: You roll dice, keep some and throw the rest again. A pair or a run on the dice can be declared at the end of your throws, much like one in cards.
pros: Dice can build a pair across several throws.
Keeping some dice shows what you are after.
cons: The last roll can undo a plan.
A declared run is gone if you fail to roll it.

pairs.tendency: A piece that lands on another sends it back to the start. Cards held in hand keep their pairs, so a player who has been sent back can still declare points.
pros: Points from cards stay safe on the track.
A setback on the board does not cancel a declaration.
cons: A player sent back may hold back and wait.
Rivals aim at the leader's piece.

pairs.tendency: Three pieces in a row take a piece from the other player, and a declared pair scores points from the hand. Making a row and calling a pair can happen in the same turn.
pros: Two ways to gain an edge in one turn.
Players plan rows and pairs together.
cons: The board and the hand each ask for care.
A turn that does both can end a game quickly.

pairs.tendency: Letters make words, and letters in the hand might make a pair, such as two of the same letter. A declared pair scores before the word is built.
pros: A letter can serve the word and the pair.
Pairs reward spare letters.
cons: A player may keep a pair and lose a word.
A dictionary can slow down a declaration.

pairs.tendency: Tiles are laid to match the open ends of a line. A pair of matching tiles held in hand can be declared, though playing them uses them up.
pros: Hands hold more than one use for a tile.
The line shows which tiles are needed.
cons: Missing a turn may keep a pair stuck in hand.
Playing a tile can break a declared pair.

pairs.tendency: A meld is a set laid face up, and a declared pair is shown and left in hand. The two together give a player a way to show some cards and keep others.
pros: Players pick which cards to show.
A laid set can grow by adding cards.
cons: Showing a meld gives away what you are collecting.
Two kinds of showing can blur together.

pairs.tendency: Each player has a power that works once. A player may save it to turn a declared pair into a bigger score, or use it early to block a rival's run.
pros: The timing of a power adds a choice.
A power can change what a declaration is worth.
cons: Spending it early leaves nothing for later.
A player who holds one may play slowly.

pairs.tendency: You offer a play and the other player can turn it down. If you offer to declare a pair, the other player may refuse and make you hold the cards instead.
pros: Both players shape each move.
An offer can reveal a plan.
cons: A refused declaration costs a turn.
Both players need to pay attention on every turn.

pairs.tendency: A message passes by whisper, and the last player says what arrived. If the message names a pair, the player who holds both cards can declare it.
pros: A message can hint at what a hand holds.
The change on the way can mislead.
cons: A garbled message may name a pair no one has.
Nobody can check the message until the end.

pairs.tendency: Before play, each player hands some cards to another. A player may pass away part of a pair, so the cards left in hand decide what can be declared.
pros: The pass sets up the hands.
Players think about what to give away.
cons: A gift can complete a rival's run.
You cannot see the cards you receive until you have passed.

pairs.tendency: One player sets out a start and the other picks a side. When the start includes a declared pair, the first player tries to make the pair worth the same to both sides.
pros: The set-up is made as even as the maker can.
The chooser has a real choice.
cons: Making the set-up even takes time.
A small mistake in the set-up shifts the whole game.

pairs.tendency: A piece that reaches the far end becomes a more powerful piece, and a declared pair can be another way to reach that end. A player may declare early to afford a promotion.
pros: There are two routes to a bigger piece.
Pushing forward carries a reward.
cons: A player may race ahead and leave the back open.
A declared pair can pay for a promotion a turn too soon.

pairs.tendency: A team runs in legs and hands on a token. At each handover a runner can declare a pair held by the team, which adds points or a head start.
pros: Each leg has a small extra prize.
Team members have to share what they hold.
cons: A declaration can slow the handover.
Runners may wait for the right card.

pairs.tendency: Stones make a shape that cannot be captured, while cards make pairs that can be declared. Both are safe once they are made, and both are plans for several turns.
pros: There are two kinds of finished goals.
A safe shape is a calm base.
cons: Each plan asks for a few turns of care.
A player may finish one and forget the other.

pairs.tendency: Some cards are named in advance as prizes, such as the highest trump. A declared pair gives points on top, so the game pays for both the prize cards and the pairs.
pros: The pairs add a second set of points.
Everyone knows which cards carry weight.
cons: A card can be a prize and also half of a pair.
Players may have to pick between the two jobs.

pairs.tendency: Cards in the middle are open to everyone, so a pair may use a card from the middle and one from your hand. Anyone at the table can see what you need.
pros: The middle supplies cards to build pairs.
Each player reads the same open cards.
cons: A shared card may help a rival too.
Declared pairs become easy to guess.

pairs.tendency: Every player puts a counter in the pot, and one wins it. A declared pair can add to the winner's claim on the pot.
pros: The pot gives declarations a prize.
A pot that carries over makes the next round worth more.
cons: A pair is worth less if the pot is small.
Players can pile up a pot nobody collects.

pairs.tendency: You scoop seeds from a pit and drop them one by one. The seeds are counted, so a pit that ends with a pair of matching numbers can be declared for points.
pros: Counting becomes part of the scoring.
A pit with a pair is a goal.
cons: Seeds are moved around a lot.
Keeping track of both counts takes care.

pairs.tendency: An extra hand sits face down in the middle. A player may swap for it, buy it or take it, and any pair in it can be declared once it is in hand.
pros: The spare hand gives a second chance.
It can finish a run.
cons: A swap may give up a pair you already hold.
Nobody knows what is in the spare hand until it is taken.

pairs.tendency: Some spaces have rules of their own. Landing on one might let you declare a pair for double, or send you back and make you hold your cards.
pros: A square can raise the value of a pair.
Players aim at certain spaces.
cons: A square that sends you back can cost a turn.
Dice can undo a plan.

pairs.tendency: Cards cost something to play, and a declared pair is a free score from cards you still hold. A player has to choose between spending a card and keeping the pair.
pros: Holding cards earns points before they are spent.
Spending has a price.
cons: Keeping a pair can block your own plays.
A hand of costly cards may sit unused.

pairs.tendency: A fixed amount is shared among several places. Cards for a pair take up some of it, so each pair declared means less to put elsewhere.
pros: Players weigh pairs against positions.
Sharing out forces becomes a visible choice.
cons: A pair can leave a place short.
Rivals can aim at the weaker place.

pairs.tendency: Everyone moves until the signal, then freezes. Cards are grabbed on the way, and the frozen player with a pair can declare it before the next round.
pros: The signal makes a break for declaring.
Moving fast brings more cards.
cons: The slowest player may go home with no pair.
Declaring in a hurry can be missed.

pairs.tendency: You put cards back and take new ones, and a swap can finish a pair or a run you plan to declare. Another player may need to agree to the swap.
pros: A swap can turn a thin hand into a pair.
The exchange shows what a player lacks.
cons: A swap can throw away half a pair.
Waiting for an agreement slows the game.

pairs.tendency: All the thrown cards go into one pile, and you may pick it all up if you can use the top card. A big pile can hold several pairs, so picking it up may mean several declarations.
pros: A pile can pay out in points.
A big pile is a target.
cons: The player who takes it holds many cards.
A pile that is picked up too soon holds little.

pairs.tendency: One suit is named trump and beats the rest. A king and queen of the trump suit is a pair players may declare for more points than a pair of another suit.
pros: The trump suit makes some pairs worth more.
Everyone knows which suit to hunt for.
cons: A low trump may be more useful than a high card.
Players who lack the trump suit have fewer chances to declare.

pairs.tendency: You play two boards at the same moment, so the same hand has to serve both. A pair declared for one board may leave a gap on the other.
pros: Each board gives a different use for the cards.
Attack on one board can match defence on the other.
cons: Keeping two boards in mind is a lot to track.
A choice on one board can cost you on the other.

pairs.tendency: A wild card can stand for any card you pick, so it can finish a pair or a run you wished to declare. Players hold wild cards back until a declaration needs them.
pros: A wild card turns half a pair into a whole one.
It gives a hand more ways to score.
cons: Holding a wild card can be a waiting game.
Rivals may guess you hold one when you wait.

pairs.tendency: The edges of the board join, so a line that runs off one side returns on the other. A pair on the cards may be matched to two ends of the board that now touch.
pros: Lines never reach an edge.
Pieces on far sides count as neighbours.
cons: New players lose track of where a line ends.
A declared pair can link two places that look far apart.

pairs.tendency: One player has a secret and others ask yes or no questions. A player may declare a pair as a guess, and the answer shows if the pair fits the secret.
pros: Each answer narrows the list.
A pair can be tested as a guess.
cons: Questions can give away what you hold.
A wrong guess costs a turn.

pairs.tendency: The first to reach the end wins, but declared pairs along the way can move you ahead. A player with many pairs may skip steps while another runs flat out.
pros: Declarations give a way to move faster.
The leader is not always the first to start.
cons: A pair is only useful until the race ends.
Players who race may ignore their hands.

pairs.tendency: Declared pairs and runs add to the score, and the highest total wins. The game becomes a count of what each player has shown over the whole game.
pros: Every declaration is on the scoresheet.
A steady flow of small scores can add up.
cons: Players watch each other's totals.
A late big run can overturn the count.

pairs.tendency: Players drop out one by one, and a declared pair can keep one in the game or shield a piece. A player with no pair left has fewer ways to stay in.
pros: Pairs act as a way to survive.
Holding cards late into the game is worth it.
cons: A player who declares early has fewer cards to defend with.
Those knocked out watch from the side.

pairs.tendency: The whole table works against the game, and each player declares pairs to help the group. A shown pair can pay for a defence that keeps everyone in.
pros: A declaration helps every player.
Players can plan who declares what.
cons: One lost pair can put the group at risk.
Players with large hands may take over the talk.

pairs.tendency: Players share one goal, and every declared pair counts towards it. A run shown by one player moves the whole table closer.
pros: Everyone gains from each declaration.
Hands are talked over openly.
cons: One player holding back a pair slows the group.
A player with few cards has little to add.

pairs.tendency: Each player has a secret aim, and a declared pair may give a clue about it. A player may declare an unrelated pair to throw others off.
pros: A declaration can be a bluff.
Pairs fit some goals and not others.
cons: Others may read your goal from your pairs.
A player who hides every pair may fall behind.

pairs.tendency: The story drives the game, and a declared pair is a beat in it, such as two characters meeting. The game ends when the story ends.
pros: Cards give the story a next step.
A pair marks a scene.
cons: A pair may not fit the story at that point.
Players may hold cards back, waiting for a scene that suits them.

pairs.tendency: Nobody wins, so a declared pair scores nothing and is simply shown. Players lay down what they hold and look at what turns up.
pros: Pairs become something to look at.
Players talk about what they made.
cons: Without points, a declaration has no reason to be made.
Some players may lose interest in the cards.

pairs.tendency: Each player decides what doing well means. One may aim for as many declared pairs as possible, another may keep their hand tight and declare none.
pros: Pairs fit many different aims.
A player can judge their own game.
cons: Players cannot compare scores easily.
A goal may be set so low that it is met at once.

pairs.tendency: Nobody wins, and the game goes on until one player loses. A declared pair can pass the danger to someone else or keep you safe for another round.
pros: Pairs work as a shield.
Players watch who is closest to losing.
cons: A pair does nothing once it has been used.
A player short of cards may be left behind.

pairs.tendency: The aim is to keep play going, so a declared pair is a way to give others a reason to continue. A shown run may open up new moves for the table.
pros: A declaration gives the next player a move.
The game has no end that anyone races to.
cons: Scores matter less, so pairs do little for points.
Play can drift with no sense of progress.

pairs.tendency: The game refuses to be won, so a declared pair scores and then does nothing. Players show their pairs and discover that the points lead nowhere.
pros: Declaring shows a score with nothing behind it.
Players question why they declare.
cons: A pair cannot help anyone win.
Some players keep playing to win anyway.

pairs.tendency: You play alone against the cards. A pair or run held in hand may be shown to clear a part of the layout, and getting stuck ends the game.
pros: Pairs help clear the table.
A solo player can plan a run in peace.
cons: A pair used too soon can leave you stuck.
Nobody else is there to share the result.

pairs.tendency: Several short games are played in a row, and the winner is the one with the most wins. Declared pairs are scored in each game, but only the win counts at the end.
pros: A pair in one game can swing that game.
The series can stop when no one can catch up.
cons: Pairs from earlier games count for nothing later.
A player who loses the first two games may give up.

pairs.tendency: Every point counts against you, so declared pairs score against the player who shows them. A player holding a pair has to decide whether declaring is a cost.
pros: Players think about what to hide.
A pair turns into a risk.
cons: A player may break a pair to avoid points.
The game can reward holding back.

pairs.tendency: You have to land exactly on the target. Declared pairs add small amounts, so a player counts how to reach the number without going over.
pros: Pairs are a way to adjust the total.
Counting becomes a skill.
cons: A pair may push you past the target.
Players can get stuck a few points short.

pairs.tendency: The aim is to give everything away, so a declared pair is a score nobody wants. A player holding a king and queen hopes to lose them to someone else.
pros: Pairs turn into a burden.
Players try to pass cards on.
cons: A player may keep a pair hidden.
The game can reward making odd plays.

pairs.tendency: Everyone plays at once without affecting the others, and each player declares pairs on their own hand. Players compare totals at the end.
pros: Each player builds in peace.
Pairs give a clear count of progress.
cons: Nobody can block anyone else.
There is little to do while waiting for others.

pairs.tendency: Players attack and steal from one another, and a declared pair shows who holds cards worth attacking. A pair on view can make you a target.
pros: A pair can be a warning.
Attacks can be aimed at the player with the highest hand.
cons: A shown pair is easy to steal.
Players learn to keep pairs hidden.

pairs.tendency: Players change the board and not each other. A declared pair may let you take a space that blocks a rival without touching their pieces.
pros: Pairs pay for board moves.
Rivals feel the result through the board.
cons: A rival cannot answer a pair directly.
The board may fill with moves that are hard to read.

pairs.tendency: The whole table is on one team, and every declared pair helps. Players can show their hands and plan which pairs to call.
pros: Open talk about hands is allowed.
Pairs are shared wins.
cons: One player may take charge of the decisions.
A pair held back by one player hurts everyone.

pairs.tendency: Players work together but each has a small private aim. A declared pair helps the group and may also help the player who shows it.
pros: A pair can serve two aims.
Players can guess private aims from what is shown.
cons: Helping the group may cost a player their own aim.
Trust can break when a pair is held back.

pairs.tendency: Two teams play against each other, and teammates may declare pairs that score for the team. A pair held by one partner can finish a run for another.
pros: Partners combine cards.
A team can plan which pairs to call.
cons: Talking in front of the other team is limited.
A partner can break a pair by accident.

pairs.tendency: One player is secretly against the group. A declared pair is a clue, since a traitor may show a pair that helps the group less than it seems.
pros: Pairs give suspects something to explain.
A traitor can use pairs to look helpful.
cons: Honest players may be blamed for a thin hand.
Players start to doubt each declaration.

pairs.tendency: Players are far apart and send moves by letter. A declared pair is written down and posted, and the other player takes it on trust until the next letter.
pros: A pair can be sent and checked later.
Waiting adds time to think.
cons: A letter can arrive late and change the order of play.
Neither player can see the other's hand.

pairs.tendency: One player is not at the table, maybe a ghost who gives hints. The ghost's hints can point at a pair that a living player holds and can declare.
pros: The absent player shapes the game from afar.
Hints can lead to a declaration.
cons: The ghost cannot say much.
Players may misread a hint and chase the wrong pair.

pairs.tendency: One player runs the world, and a declared pair is a card the game master reads as an event, such as a king and queen arriving in town.
pros: The game master turns pairs into story.
Players have a say in what happens.
cons: The game master has more to track.
A pair may not match what the master has planned.

pairs.tendency: The game is played in a street or a park, and anyone passing can join. A declared pair is shouted so everyone nearby hears the score.
pros: New players can join mid-game.
Pairs are shown in the open.
cons: Cards can get lost or dropped.
Passers-by may not know what a declaration means.

pairs.tendency: One player faces all the others, who work together. The lone player can declare pairs for extra pay, while the group has to share what it knows.
pros: The lone player is paid for risk.
The group can pool its hands.
cons: One player carries all the pairs alone.
The group can argue about which pair to block.

pairs.tendency: You play alone against the pack, and a declared pair is a small win with nobody to see it. You can compare totals with a friend afterwards.
pros: Pairs make a clear score to beat.
Play can go at your own pace.
cons: No one reacts to a pair.
A result means little without another score.

pairs.tendency: Cards come from the deck and dice, so a pair arrives mostly by luck. Declaring is just the moment when luck shows up in the score.
pros: The deal makes each hand different.
Players need little planning.
cons: A skilled player has little to work with.
A run of low draws leaves a player with nothing to declare.

pairs.tendency: Luck deals the cards, and swaps or re-draws help you build the pair you want. A declared pair is partly luck and partly the effort spent on it.
pros: Players can work on a hand.
A swap can rescue a thin hand.
cons: Rescuing a hand costs a move.
A pair can still miss by one card.

pairs.tendency: Skill decides which pairs to chase and a bit of luck decides which cards arrive. A careful plan can still fail on a late draw.
pros: Planning leads to more declarations.
Luck leaves room for a surprise.
cons: A plan can fall one card short.
An experienced player wins more often than not.

pairs.tendency: No dice and no hidden draw, so pairs are built by choice and not by luck. Players read each other's declared cards and work out what remains.
pros: Every pair is a result of planning.
Players can count what has been shown.
cons: A beginner is at a loss against a practised player.
Early mistakes are hard to fix.

pairs.tendency: Dice or cards are read as a sign, so a declared pair is taken as a message. The players talk about what the pair means for the question they asked.
pros: A pair gives something to discuss.
The reading belongs to the group.
cons: The pair has no score to settle an argument.
Different players read the same pair in different ways.

pairs.tendency: Players sense when the others are about to act. A pair may be declared by two people at the very same moment, and the match shows how well they read each other.
pros: A shared pause can bring a pair.
Players listen closely.
cons: Rushing a declaration spoils the timing.
Some pairs are missed by a moment.

pairs.tendency: A roll is looked up on a table that says what happens next. If the cards in hand make a pair, the player declares it and gets to change the result of the roll.
pros: Dice tell the story and cards shape it.
A pair gives the player a say.
cons: Tables and cards ask for a lot of looking up.
A high roll can lose its meaning when a pair overrides it.

pairs.tendency: Everything is on view, so a declared pair surprises nobody. Players can see a pair coming and plan against it.
pros: Each declaration can be predicted.
Players can work out what a rival needs.
cons: There is no hidden hand to bluff with.
A pair is a small moment, since all the cards were known.

pairs.tendency: Cards are kept secret until a pair is declared, so a declaration shows part of a hand for the first time. The other players learn what is in it and plan from there.
pros: A declared pair tells the table something new.
Hidden cards keep guesses alive.
cons: Showing a pair gives away a plan.
Waiting too long lets a rival declare first.

pairs.tendency: Some players have a secret role. A declared pair may suit one role more than another, so what a player chooses to show hints at who they are.
pros: Pairs leak small clues.
Players can pick what to show.
cons: A declaration may point at the wrong person.
Roles can be given away by a pair.

pairs.tendency: Clues point to hidden facts, and each declared pair adds a clue about what a player holds. Players note which cards appear and work out which are left.
pros: Each declaration is a clue.
Players can cross things off.
cons: A false clue is hard to spot.
Notes can take over the table.

pairs.tendency: You may claim a pair you do not hold, and others decide whether to believe it. A true declaration and a false one sound the same.
pros: A claim can win points or lose face.
Players watch each other's faces.
cons: A caught bluff costs the bluffer.
Honest players may be doubted.

pairs.tendency: One player knows a secret rule, and others learn by breaking it. A declared pair may be refused because of the secret rule, and the refusal teaches the table.
pros: A refusal gives a clue.
New players find the rule by trying pairs.
cons: The first pairs may all be turned down.
Newcomers can feel lost until the rule is found.

pairs.tendency: One player sees the answer and can only give hints. A declared pair may be a hint, such as a king and queen pointing at a royal answer.
pros: A pair can hint at a theme.
Hints are shown with cards.
cons: The hinter cannot explain a pair.
A guesser may read a pair the wrong way.

pairs.tendency: The map starts hidden and areas are turned over as they are explored. A declared pair may let a player explore an area, which can reveal a place that fits another pair.
pros: Pairs open up the map.
New places bring new cards.
cons: An unlucky reveal can show a dead end.
Players explore to get cards and ignore the map.

pairs.tendency: One hand is laid face up and the rest are hidden. A pair in the open hand is plain to all, and a player may declare it as well as pairs from their own hand.
pros: The open hand is a fact everyone shares.
A player has two hands to work from.
cons: Pairs in the open hand are easy to count.
Playing a second hand takes extra thought.

pairs.tendency: Some points are kept secret, so a declared pair adds a score nobody can fully check. Players have to guess who is ahead.
pros: Pairs hide in the total.
Guessing becomes part of the game.
cons: A declaration leaves a doubt about the real score.
The final count can be a surprise.

pairs.tendency: One player acts at a time, and a pair is declared on a turn. Everyone else watches, so each declaration gets the table's full attention.
pros: Each pair is seen by all.
Players have time to plan.
cons: Waiting for a turn can be long.
Declarations on a late turn come after the table has moved on.

pairs.tendency: Everyone picks in secret at the same moment and reveals together. Pairs may be declared on the reveal, so several players can call at once.
pros: Declarations come together.
Nobody waits.
cons: Two players may claim the same card.
Rivals can only see a pair when it is shown.

pairs.tendency: Anyone may act at any moment, so the first to call a pair gets the points. Players watch their hands and each other all the time.
pros: Quick eyes win pairs.
Declarations come fast.
cons: Slower players miss out.
The table can get loud.

pairs.tendency: Each turn has a clock, and a declared pair has to be called before time runs out. A player who sees a pair late loses it.
pros: The clock makes declaring a race.
Players learn to spot pairs quickly.
cons: A pair seen too late is lost.
A rushed declaration can have a mistake in it.

pairs.tendency: The game runs over days or weeks. A pair can be declared on any morning, and the waiting between moves gives time to think about which cards to keep.
pros: Players can plan with care.
A declared pair can be thought over for days.
cons: Long waits slow the game.
A player may forget what was declared.

pairs.tendency: The game slows players down on purpose, with a pause before each move. A declared pair is made after a breath, and the table waits while it is shown.
pros: Pairs are shown with care.
The pause lets players look at their hands.
cons: Fast players may wait a long time.
Declarations can feel stretched out.

pairs.tendency: The game speeds up as it goes, so pairs have to be called quicker each round. Early on there is time to plan a run, and late in the game it is hard to keep up.
pros: Early rounds allow some thought.
Later rounds bring a rush.
cons: Late pairs are easily missed.
Slower players fall further behind.

pairs.tendency: A lucky throw or a hit on a piece gives another go straight away. A player with a pair can declare it and then use the extra turn to play on.
pros: An extra turn can follow a declaration.
A lucky player can do a lot in one turn.
cons: Others wait while one player acts.
One player can build a lead in a single go.

pairs.tendency: The game has stages, and the first stage is for picking cards. Declared pairs can be built in the first stage and scored in the second.
pros: Choices in stage one pay off in stage two.
The game has a clear shape.
cons: A thin first stage is hard to fix.
Players may rush the first stage.

pairs.tendency: The board works like a real system, such as water moving between wells and fields. A declared pair stands for a decision made by two groups acting together.
pros: Pairs can stand for joint action.
Players see how choices connect.
cons: A real decision may not fit the shape of a pair.
The model can become hard to follow.

pairs.tendency: Each player acts as a real group, such as farmers or a village council. A declared pair is two groups agreeing, and each side scores from the deal.
pros: A pair shows an alliance.
Each role has its own view of the pair.
cons: One group may gain more from the pair than the other.
Players may disagree about what a pair is worth.

pairs.tendency: Everyone draws from one limited store, such as groundwater. Declared pairs let a player take from it, so a run of declarations can empty the store for the table.
pros: Pairs give a reason to take.
The store shows what the table has used.
cons: Players who declare a lot drain it faster.
The group may run dry before the game ends.

pairs.tendency: What you do now shows its effect some rounds later. A pair declared today may pay its points only after a few turns.
pros: Players wait for the result.
Early pairs can pay later.
cons: A player may forget a pair that is still to pay.
The delay makes cause and effect hard to see.

pairs.tendency: Players agree a new rule and play on to see its effect. A rule about how pairs are scored can be tried out for a few rounds and then kept or dropped.
pros: Pairs make a test case for a rule.
The effect shows on the scoresheet.
cons: A rule that changes pairs can change the whole game.
Players may not agree on what the test showed.

pairs.tendency: After the game, the table talks over what happened. The declared pairs make a list to look back on, and each player explains why they called when they did.
pros: The talk has a place to start.
Players recall their own choices.
cons: Memory of pairs fades.
Talk may stay on the points.

pairs.tendency: What you do changes the game for ever. A declared pair may use up the cards, tear them or leave a mark, so the next game starts with fewer.
pros: Each pair leaves a trace.
Choices carry on to the next game.
cons: A pair cannot be undone.
Players may avoid declaring to keep their cards.

pairs.tendency: The rules make a point about the world, so a rule that pays for pairs says something about teamwork or partners. Players see the argument by playing it.
pros: Pairs carry the point of the game.
Players can talk about what the scoring says.
cons: The point may be missed in the rush to score.
Players may disagree with what the rules say.

pairs.tendency: What happens in the game carries into life, such as real money or a promise. A declared pair becomes a real gain or a real debt between the players.
pros: A pair has a real result.
Players take each call seriously.
cons: A declaration can start an argument.
A friendship can be tested by a pair.

pairs.tendency: The game turns something that matters, such as kindness, into points. A declared pair of kind acts scores, and players start chasing the pairs.
pros: Pairs make a value into a number.
Players see what a number leaves out.
cons: The pairs can replace the thing they stand for.
Players may collect pairs and forget why.

pairs.tendency: Players practise a way of living that does not yet exist, such as a village that shares everything. A declared pair shows two people sharing, and the table sees how it feels.
pros: Players get a small taste of the future.
Players can try shared choices.
cons: A pair may feel staged.
The practice may not carry over to real life.

pairs.tendency: Everyone throws the dice and moves along the same path, but one piece may skip a square while another may throw again after a low number.
pros: Two pieces on one square play differently.
A throw means something different for each player.
cons: Players spend time reading each other's powers.
The dice still decide most of how far anyone gets.

pairs.tendency: Cards go round the table and each player takes one, but one player may take a second card from the row and another may look at the cards before they are passed.
pros: Every seat picks in its own way.
A pick shows what that player's power can use.
cons: Picks are hard to compare between players.
The row empties at different speeds.

pairs.tendency: At the auction one player may bid once more after the others have stopped, and another pays less than the amount offered.
pros: Bids depend on who is bidding.
Players guess at each other's limits.
cons: A price break lets a player win without the highest offer.
Others may stop bidding against that player.

pairs.tendency: One player keeps a point after going too far and another gets a free extra try, so each presses on to a different place.
pros: Players stop at different points.
A risk costs each player something different.
cons: Nobody can copy another player's stopping point.
Softening a bust can pull one player far ahead.

pairs.tendency: Each player holds regions on the map, but one player's pieces can cross water and another's count double when a region is tied.
pros: Players fight for the same land in different ways.
A region that is easy for one player to hold is open to another.
cons: Attackers check which powers sit behind each region.
One power can decide which region a player takes.

pairs.tendency: A player puts a worker on a job spot, and a power lets them use a spot that is already taken or place a worker for free.
pros: Taken spots may not stay taken.
Each player has their own way to use the board.
cons: Blocking a spot works on some players and not on others.
Players learn the powers before they plan a route.

pairs.tendency: Everyone builds the same kind of pattern, but one player may swap a tile for another colour and another may place a tile out of order.
pros: The same pattern is reached by different routes.
Players can see what the others' powers help them finish.
cons: A power can finish a pattern that others spent many turns on.
Comparing progress between players is harder.

pairs.tendency: Each player holds cards, and one player's power lets them keep an extra card while another's lets them play two at once.
pros: Hands are played in different ways.
Players watch the size of each other's hands.
cons: Cards that are safe for one player to hold are risky for another.
A hand limit applies to some players and not others.

pairs.tendency: When the tricks start, one player's power lets them play a card from the wrong suit while another's lets them take back a card just played.
pros: A trick can end in a way the others did not expect.
Players learn each other's powers by watching the tricks.
cons: Following suit is not the same job for everyone.
A power can win a trick that looked lost.

pairs.tendency: Players trade and make deals, and one player's power lets them take back a deal while another may force one trade each round.
pros: Deals are priced by what each power is worth.
A player can offer help that only they can give.
cons: Players hide or show their powers to change the price.
Trades can end up lopsided.

pairs.tendency: Players collect matching sets, and one player may count a mixed pair as a set while another may pick one card from the pile each round.
pros: Sets take different amounts of work for different players.
Players can guess at a set from the power an opponent has.
cons: A power that fills sets quickly leaves others behind.
Players track several ways to finish at once.

pairs.tendency: Players add tiles to a shared map, and one player may place a tile touching nothing while another may turn a tile already laid.
pros: The map grows in several directions.
Each player shapes the map in a way only they can.
cons: A tile can suit one player's power and block another's.
The map may end up with odd gaps.

pairs.tendency: One player says a line and the next answers it, and a power lets one player answer twice or skip a reply in the chain.
pros: Each answer can break the pattern in its own way.
Players listen closely to how others answer.
cons: A skipped reply breaks the chain.
Players without a power in the chain wait longer.

pairs.tendency: Nobody speaks, so a power shows only when a player uses it, and the others guess what a sudden move means.
pros: Players learn powers by watching.
Every odd move gives a clue.
cons: Nobody can explain a power to a teammate.
A new power can surprise the whole table.

pairs.tendency: A player changes a rule on their turn, and a power may let someone keep a rule from changing or change two at once.
pros: Rules and powers shift at the same time.
A new rule can undo a player's power.
cons: Some players protect their power with a rule.
Arguments start over which rule applies to which power.

pairs.tendency: Each player acts as a character, and the power is part of who that character is, such as a healer or a thief.
pros: A power gives a character a way to act.
Players think about what their character would do.
cons: Powers can pull a scene towards one player.
Others wait for their turn in the story.

pairs.tendency: Players flick, stack or balance, and one player's power gives an extra attempt while another's gives a larger target.
pros: Hands decide the result for everyone.
Players watch each other's tries closely.
cons: A power to try again can hide a slip.
Other players may see a power as a free shot.

pairs.tendency: As the map is drawn, one player may draw a river that blocks the others while another may redraw one place.
pros: Each player leaves a mark on the map that only they can make.
The map shows who held which power.
cons: Redrawing can undo what another player drew.
The paper fills up quickly.

pairs.tendency: A player offers to double the stakes, and a power lets the other refuse without losing points or double back at once.
pros: The offer changes with each player's power.
Players weigh the offer against what the other can do.
cons: A power to refuse safely can end a run of doubling.
A player with fewer powers may give up early.

pairs.tendency: A capture has to be taken, but one player's piece may skip a forced capture while another's can be forced in only one direction.
pros: Forced moves can be dodged by the right power.
Players aim for the moments where a power helps.
cons: A power that avoids a capture can break a trap.
Players set traps only for powers they know about.

pairs.tendency: Players gain power as they play on top of the power each began with, so a small starting power may turn into a large one.
pros: Each character grows along its own path.
Players pick which power to build on.
cons: Early powers leave players on unequal footing later.
Others cannot catch a player who grew early.

pairs.tendency: Each player adds to the list, and a power lets one player skip a word while another may check a word with a hint.
pros: Each player recalls the list with different help.
Players listen to what others add.
cons: Skipping a word can hide a mistake.
Long lists are hard for any player to carry.

pairs.tendency: An experienced player starts with fewer points while a newer player begins with a power of their own, so the two sides open with different sets of help.
pros: A gap between players can close.
Players pick which kind of help they want.
cons: Two kinds of help can pile up on one side.
Players may argue over how much each help is worth.

pairs.tendency: One player hides while another looks, and a power lets a hider leave a false trail or lets a finder see through one wall.
pros: The hunt changes with each power.
Hiders and finders both have a trick.
cons: Seeing through a wall can end the hunt early.
Hiders may stay out of sight for a long time.

pairs.tendency: A piece hops over another, and one side's pieces may hop two at a time while the other side's cannot be hopped at all.
pros: Hops behave differently for each side.
A piece with a power becomes a target.
cons: A move that is safe for one side is risky for the other.
The hops are learnt only in play.

pairs.tendency: Players keep some dice and roll the rest, and one may keep an extra die while another may change a die by one.
pros: Players choose which dice to hold in different ways.
A power can rescue a roll that went wrong.
cons: Others watch a player's held dice for signs of the power.
The last roll still belongs to the dice.

pairs.tendency: A piece that lands on another sends it home, but one player's piece may land safely on any square and another's cannot be sent back.
pros: A landing can be harmless for some players.
Players aim for squares where a power is missing.
cons: A piece with protection can wait on the track.
Players without protection avoid crowded squares.

pairs.tendency: A row of three lets a player take a piece, and a power lets one player count a row of two or take two pieces at once.
pros: Rows form at different speeds.
A taken piece can depend on whose row it was.
cons: Players watch for rows that need only a power to finish.
A player with a short row can empty the other side.

pairs.tendency: Players build words from letters, and one may use a blank letter while another can keep a spare letter for later.
pros: Words come out in each player's own way.
Powers and letters add up to different words.
cons: A dictionary does not settle what a power allows.
Arguments over a power's reach slow the check.

pairs.tendency: A tile goes on an open end of the line, and one player may play a tile that does not match while another may close one end.
pros: Lines can bend in unexpected directions.
A power can save a stuck hand.
cons: The line may close before some players can use it.
Players with no matching tile still miss turns.

pairs.tendency: Players lay sets face up, and one player's power lets them add to another's set or hold a meld back until later.
pros: A laid set can be used by more than one player.
Players read each other's melds for signs of powers.
cons: A set shared by power can lose points for its owner.
Face-up sets show how far each player has got.

pairs.tendency: Each player holds a power that nobody else has, and each power works only once, so the table waits to see who spends theirs first.
pros: Every player holds a single chance of their own.
Waiting for the right moment becomes part of play.
cons: Once a power is spent, that player has only a plain turn left.
A power nobody has used yet makes the table watch its owner.

pairs.tendency: A player offers a move and the other may accept it, turn it down or pick the second one, and both players have powers that change the offer.
pros: Offers take account of the other player's power.
Both players have a say in every move.
cons: Offers slow down while players check powers.
A power to override a refusal can end the talk.

pairs.tendency: A message goes from player to player, and a power lets one of them change a word or send it back to the start.
pros: Players can choose to bend the message.
Each hand it passes through adds something.
cons: The final message can differ from the first by one power or many.
Nobody can check where the change was made.

pairs.tendency: Before play begins, players hand cards to another player, and a power lets one player look at a card before choosing or send a card back.
pros: Powers shape the hand before the first turn.
The card passed along can hint at the power.
cons: Players know part of what they will get from the power's owner.
A player with a look at the cards has an early edge.

pairs.tendency: One player sets up the start and the other picks a side, and each side holds a power of its own, so the setup has to make both powers even.
pros: Whoever sets up has to think about both powers.
The player who picks can see the powers before choosing.
cons: A power added to the start adds one more thing to weigh.
Setting both sides level takes many tries.

pairs.tendency: A piece that reaches the far end turns into another piece, and a power lets one player promote early or pick what it becomes.
pros: The far end is worth reaching for different reasons.
A promoted piece can carry its owner's power forward.
cons: Players guard the far end against a power they know.
A piece with a power draws attention all the way up the board.

pairs.tendency: A team runs a race in legs, and a power lets one runner skip a leg or hand over a second item.
pros: Each runner brings a different advantage to the leg.
Teams plan who runs which leg around the powers.
cons: A power that skips a leg shortens the race for one team only.
Handovers can fumble when powers change the order.

pairs.tendency: A shape of stones cannot be captured, and a power lets one player make a safe shape from fewer stones or break another player's.
pros: Players have a goal built from their own power.
A shape that is safe for one player is open to another.
cons: Shapes take many turns to set up.
Breaking a safe shape can undo many turns of work.

pairs.tendency: Prizes are named cards, and one player may win a prize with a lower card while another can win the same prize twice.
pros: A prize can go to a surprising winner.
Players aim at the prize their power helps.
cons: A power may win a prize before others see it coming.
Prize cards decide the score, so a power can swing it.

pairs.tendency: Cards in the middle are open to all, and one player's power lets them use a middle card twice or swap one for a card in hand.
pros: The same middle card is worth different amounts to each player.
Players read the middle for what the others can use.
cons: A middle card that suits one power may be of no use to the rest.
The cards in the middle give away part of each plan.

pairs.tendency: Everyone adds to the pot, and a power lets one player take part of it early or add less than the rest.
pros: The pot grows faster for some players.
A player can aim at the pot through their own power.
cons: A player who takes part early leaves a smaller pot for the winner.
A growing pot draws attention to whoever holds a power.

pairs.tendency: A player scoops seeds from a pit and drops them one at a time, and a power lets one player sow backwards or keep a seed.
pros: Each player sows in a different way.
Where the last seed lands depends on the power.
cons: Players count the seeds again whenever a power is used.
A power that sows backwards changes every pit nearby.

pairs.tendency: A spare hand lies face down in the middle, and one player may take it first while another may swap it with their own after looking.
pros: The spare hand is worth more to some players than to others.
Powers decide who reaches it.
cons: Whoever takes the spare hand shows what they want.
A power that reaches it first leaves little for the rest.

pairs.tendency: Some squares on the track have a rule of their own, and a power lets one piece ignore a square or use a safe square twice.
pros: A square means something different for each player.
Players pick a path that suits their power.
cons: A square that sends one piece back may help another.
Players check each square against every power.

pairs.tendency: Each card has a price, and one player's power lowers the price while another's gives a free unit every round.
pros: Players buy with different budgets.
Prices change from player to player.
cons: Players compare what they pay with what others pay.
A free unit every round can empty the stock quickly.

pairs.tendency: Players split their units across places, and a power lets one player move a unit after the split or hide how many they put in one place.
pros: A split can change after the others commit.
Players guess where the power will land.
cons: Hiding the split removes the chance to react.
A late move makes the other players' split look wasted.

pairs.tendency: When the signal comes, players freeze or grab a seat, and a power lets one player move after the signal or hear it early.
