pros: Players watch for the first sign of the signal.
Powers change who is caught.
cons: A player who hears early is rarely caught.
The slowest player may be caught more than once.

pairs.tendency: Players put cards back for new ones, and a power lets one player swap twice or look at the new card first.
pros: Hands are changed in different amounts.
A swap can aim at one power.
cons: Players trade cards at different paces.
A look at the new card removes the risk of the swap.

pairs.tendency: A player may take the whole discard pile if they can play the top card, and a power lets one player take only half or play the top card later.
pros: The pile is worth different amounts to each player.
Players watch what goes onto the pile.
cons: A big pile slows a player with no power to use it.
A player who takes the pile gives away their hand.

pairs.tendency: One suit beats the rest, and a power lets one player choose the trump or play a low trump as a high one.
pros: The trump suit helps different players in different ways.
Players guess at the power from the trumps played.
cons: A player who picks the suit has the first word.
Trumps and powers together can end a trick fast.

pairs.tendency: A player plays two boards at once, and a power used on one board changes what happens on the other.
pros: Attack on one board feeds defence on the other.
A power spreads over two boards.
cons: Players keep an eye on two places at once.
A power that works on one board can leave the other open.

pairs.tendency: A wild card stands for any card, and a power lets one player turn any card wild or use a wild card twice.
pros: Sets can fill from a wide choice of cards.
A wild card is worth more to some players.
cons: Wild cards and powers together make hands hard to guess.
A hand can finish in one move.

pairs.tendency: With the board edges joined, one player's power lets a piece wrap round an edge twice in a turn while another's pieces stop at the edge.
pros: Players come at each other from both sides.
A power changes which edges are open.
cons: No place on the board is a safe corner.
A piece with a power can appear where nobody looks.

pairs.tendency: One player holds a secret and the others ask yes-or-no questions, and a power lets one asker ask twice or one answerer pass.
pros: Questions shrink the list at different speeds.
Players shape their questions around their powers.
cons: A power to ask twice shortens the game for one asker.
A passed answer gives no information.

pairs.tendency: The first player to the end wins, and each racer has a power that only they can use, such as a shortcut or a push.
pros: Each racer takes a different route.
Players watch for the power that makes the final dash.
cons: A shortcut makes the front runner harder to follow.
The lead can change in a single move.

pairs.tendency: Whoever has the most points wins, and a power lets one player score extra in one area or take points from another.
pros: Points come from different places for each player.
Players track the scores of those with powers.
cons: A power that scores twice can be missed until the end.
Totals are hard to compare during play.

pairs.tendency: Players drop out one by one, and a power lets one player stay in after a hit or put a dropped player back in.
pros: The last players have different ways to stay.
A power can change when a player drops out.
cons: Players with no protection are often dropped first.
A player who is out waits a long time.

pairs.tendency: Everyone survives or loses together, and each player's power covers a different part of the danger, such as healing or scouting.
pros: Each person has a job nobody else can do.
The team depends on every power.
cons: If one player drops out, a power is gone.
Powers that cover the same job waste a turn.

pairs.tendency: The team aims at one goal, and each player's power adds a different step towards it.
pros: Every player has something to give to the goal.
Players plan around each other's powers.
cons: The goal stalls if a power is held back.
A player may wait for another's power to be ready.

pairs.tendency: Each player has a secret goal and a power of their own, and the power may hint at the goal or point the other way.
pros: Players use powers to hide their goals.
A power can be a clue.
cons: Others guess at goals from the powers used.
A power that suits a goal gives that goal away.

pairs.tendency: The story ends when it ends, and each player's power lets them steer it in a way only they can, such as a twist or a flashback.
pros: The story takes turns that no single player plans.
Each power changes the story in its own way.
cons: A power may pull the story towards one player.
The ending can read as one player's choice.

pairs.tendency: Nobody wins, so each power simply changes what happens, and players try them to see what comes out.
pros: Powers are tried for what they do.
Players look at the result afterwards.
cons: Without a goal there is no sign of which power mattered.
Play can drift if no one picks a power to try.

pairs.tendency: Each player sets a goal of their own, and their power points one way, which may match the goal or pull against it.
pros: Players pick goals that suit their powers.
Goals differ between players.
cons: A player may choose a goal that leaves the power with no use.
The table has no shared measure of how each is doing.

pairs.tendency: Everyone plays until one player loses, and a power lets one player pass a loss to another or avoid it once.
pros: Players use powers to stay out of last place.
A loss can be moved around.
cons: A player with a power to avoid it is safe for a while.
A player without one can be left as the loser.

pairs.tendency: Players want the game to run on, and each power gives something to the next round, such as a new character or a change to the rules.
pros: Each power adds to the game without ending it.
Players watch for the power that keeps things moving.
cons: A power that ends play can be unwelcome.
Powers may pile up over many sessions.

pairs.tendency: Nobody can win, so each power only shows that the game will not reward it.
pros: Powers become something to look at.
Players see what each power does.
cons: The powers lead nowhere.
Players may drop the game when no power helps them win.

pairs.tendency: A single player faces the cards, and a power gives them a way round a stuck layout, such as a skip or an extra look.
pros: A power can open a stuck layout.
Players have a way out of a tight spot.
cons: A power that skips a card can empty the table too soon.
With one player, nobody else has a power to compare.

pairs.tendency: Players play several short games in a row, and each game may bring a different power, or a power may carry over from the last game.
pros: Powers change across the games.
A player who lost can try a new power.
cons: A power that carried over can win a second game as well.
Players compare how a power did in each game.

pairs.tendency: The player with the fewest points wins, and a power lets one player drop points or hand them to another.
pros: Points move between players.
Players use their powers to avoid points.
cons: A power that hands on points makes its owner a target.
A low score can hide the power that earned it.

pairs.tendency: A player has to land on the target exactly, and a power lets one player overshoot once or step back to the right number.
pros: Powers help players hit the number.
Overshooting costs some players and not others.
cons: Players wait for the right number.
A power to correct a miss ends the waiting.

pairs.tendency: The aim is turned upside down, and each power helps a player give away cards or take the last move.
pros: Powers work in reverse.
Players use their own powers to lose in different ways.
cons: A power that gives away cards is easy to read.
Players may hold back a power to avoid winning by accident.

pairs.tendency: Everyone builds on their own at the same time, each with a power that does not touch the others.
pros: Players can see what the powers do side by side.
Each player works at their own pace.
cons: Players compare totals only at the end.
Powers seldom reach another player.

pairs.tendency: Players hit each other on purpose, and each power is a weapon or a shield that only one of them has.
pros: Each attack lands differently.
Players choose a target by its power.
cons: A player with a shield draws attacks away from others.
A weapon in one player's hands can end the fight too soon.

pairs.tendency: Players change the board and feel the changes later, and a power lets one player alter squares or block lines in a way only they can.
pros: Changes made with a power stay on the board.
Powers reach other players without a direct hit.
cons: A board changed by a power may block the player who made the change.
Others can trace a change back to one power.

pairs.tendency: The whole team plays against the game, and each player's power covers a different job.
pros: Everyone has a part.
The team plans around the powers it holds.
cons: A power left unused is a lost turn.
One player can end up directing all the powers.

pairs.tendency: Players work together but each keeps a private reason to win, and a power can serve the team or its owner.
pros: A power can help the team and its owner.
Players watch how others use powers.
cons: A power used for private gain can break the team's plan.
Trust shifts with each use.

pairs.tendency: Two teams play, and the powers on one team can be set against those on the other.
pros: Teams plan around who holds which power.
Players learn what their partners can do.
cons: A team with matching powers repeats itself.
A team with a missing power has a gap.

pairs.tendency: One player secretly plays against the rest and holds a power the others do not know about, such as a disguise.
pros: The traitor hides a power as well as a role.
Players read powers for signs of betrayal.
cons: A power used oddly gives a player away.
Players may suspect the wrong person after a power is used.

pairs.tendency: Players write to each other, and a power may be named in a letter, used in a reply or kept back until later.
pros: Powers can be described in words.
Players have time to plan a move around a power.
cons: A power can be misread in a letter.
A reply can take weeks to arrive.

pairs.tendency: One player is away, and the others play the absent player's power on their behalf, or give it as a hint.
pros: The absent player's power still has an effect.
The others take turns acting for them.
cons: A power used on someone's behalf may be used wrongly.
The absent player cannot answer back.

pairs.tendency: One player runs the world, so each player's power comes from the game master, who also decides when it works.
pros: The game master can fit each power to the story.
Players ask the game master what a power allows.
cons: Powers depend on one person's rulings.
The game master has more to track.

pairs.tendency: The game is played in a street and anyone can join, so a power may be handed to a new player on the spot.
pros: New players can pick up a power in a moment.
Passers-by can see the powers at work.
cons: A player may leave with their power.
Powers have to be easy to explain on the street.

pairs.tendency: One player takes on all the others, and the lone player holds a power no one else has while the others share a smaller one.
pros: The lone player has a special tool.
The group combines its powers.
cons: The lone player carries all the work.
The group may argue over who uses which power.

pairs.tendency: You play alone against the pack, and your power changes one rule of the game for you.
pros: A power gives the one player a plan.
Results can be compared with a friend afterwards.
cons: No other player has a power to react to.
Luck can undo a careful plan.

pairs.tendency: Dice decide most of what happens, and a power gives one player a small say, such as moving a die by one.
pros: A power gives a player something to choose.
Players see a small bit of control.
cons: Dice still decide most turns.
A power may be used too rarely to matter.

pairs.tendency: A low throw can be softened, and each player has a power that does it in a different way, such as a re-roll or a card.
pros: Players recover from low throws in different ways.
Each power is a safety net of its own.
cons: A player with a bigger net takes bigger risks.
Powers that soften luck can slow the game.

pairs.tendency: The game depends on choices with a little luck, and each power gives a player a different skill to work with.
pros: Choices come from the power as well as the board.
A touch of luck keeps the result open.
cons: Players with a power may win more often than skill alone allows.
Players need time to learn the powers.

pairs.tendency: With no dice, each power is a plain fact that both sides can work out in advance.
pros: Players can plan far ahead.
Powers become part of the puzzle.
cons: A power that goes unnoticed can decide the match.
Players who know the powers well win more often.

pairs.tendency: Dice are read as a sign, and each player reads the throw through their own power.
pros: The same throw can mean different things.
Players talk about what a throw tells them.
cons: A power can add a meaning that others do not accept.
Readings can end in an argument.

pairs.tendency: Players try to act at the same moment, and a power lets one player sense the others' timing or act early.
pros: Players watch each other's breathing.
A power sharpens a sense of timing.
cons: A power that reads timing can break the shared moment.
One player's power can pull the group out of step.

pairs.tendency: The dice are looked up on a table, and each player's power lets them re-read a result or add a line.
pros: The table gives each player a different story.
Powers change what a roll says.
cons: A re-read result can clash with another player's story.
Players spend time looking things up.

pairs.tendency: Everything is visible, including every power, so each player sees exactly what the others can do.
pros: Players plan against known powers.
Nothing is hidden.
cons: Players may spend a long time on one move.
A power with a clear answer is met at once.

pairs.tendency: Cards are hidden and powers may be hidden too, so players guess at both a hand and a power.
pros: Players bluff about powers as well as cards.
Each use of a power hints at what is hidden.
cons: Players track two kinds of secret.
A hidden power can catch everyone off guard.

pairs.tendency: Roles are secret and each role has a power, so using a power shows what role a player has.
pros: Powers give identities away.
Players pick when to use a power.
cons: Using a power too soon gives away the role.
A power held back may never be used.

pairs.tendency: Clues point at hidden facts, and the powers of the players are among the clues, since a power points to a role or a place.
pros: Players use powers as evidence.
Clues can come from how a power was used.
cons: A power may point at the wrong answer.
Players can follow false leads.

pairs.tendency: Players lie about what they hold, and a player can claim a power they do not have.
pros: Players can claim powers.
Others guess whether a claim is true.
cons: A bluff about a power can fail when it is checked.
Players who bluff often lose the table's trust.

pairs.tendency: One player knows a secret rule, and each power is another secret that the others find by trying.
pros: Players learn rules and powers by guessing.
The first use of a power is a lesson.
cons: Newcomers do not know which rules are secret.
Players may blame a power for a rule.

pairs.tendency: One player sees the answer and gives hints, and a power lets the hint-giver add a clue or lets a guesser ask once.
pros: Hints can be sharper.
Guessers have a way to ask.
cons: An extra clue can make the guess too easy.
A guess may settle on the wrong power.

pairs.tendency: The map is hidden until explored, and a power lets one player see a square early or turn two squares at once.
pros: Explorers learn the map at different rates.
A reveal shows what lies ahead.
cons: Others follow a player who reveals.
The first to reveal gives hints to the rest.

pairs.tendency: One hand lies face up, and a power lets a player use that open hand in a way only they can.
pros: The open hand can be played with different powers.
Players see what the open hand might do.
cons: A power used on the open hand is visible to all.
Players may play against the open hand more than against each other.

pairs.tendency: Scores are secret, and a power lets one player see another's score or hide their own.
pros: Players guess at who leads.
A power adds a way to find out.
cons: A power that shows a score gives that player a view the rest lack.
Nobody can check a claim about the score.

pairs.tendency: Players take turns round the table, and each turn uses the player's own power.
pros: Each turn looks different from the last.
Each turn shows another player's power at work.
cons: Waiting is long when a power takes time.
A power used on the last turn leaves little time to reply.

pairs.tendency: Everyone chooses at once, and a power lets one player change their choice after the reveal or see the others first.
pros: Choices are tested against powers.
Players guess at the powers behind a choice.
cons: A power to look first removes the surprise.
Players with no power act without knowing.

pairs.tendency: Anyone can act at any moment, and a power may work faster or give a second action.
pros: The quickest player with a power gets there first.
Powers add a reason to act now.
cons: Players with a slow power fall behind.
The table can get loud and confusing.

pairs.tendency: Each turn has a clock, and a power lets one player add seconds or stop the clock.
pros: Players with time powers can think longer.
The clock and the power both shape a move.
cons: A player who adds time slows the rest.
A power that cuts time shortens other players' turns.

pairs.tendency: Moves happen once a day, and a power lets one player move twice in a day or save a move for later.
pros: Waiting becomes part of the plan.
A saved move can be used on the day that suits it.
cons: A power may be used on a day nobody expects.
Days pass between uses.

pairs.tendency: The game slows players down, and a power lets one player pause the others or take a pause of their own.
pros: Each pause is used differently.
Players watch what each power does in the slow moments.
cons: A power that adds a pause can stall the table.
Slow play makes powers easy to forget.

pairs.tendency: The game speeds up, and a power lets one player slow the clock or speed it for the others.
pros: Powers decide who meets the speed.
Players adjust to a faster pace in different ways.
cons: A power that speeds the game raises the pressure on others.
Late rounds leave little time to use a power.

pairs.tendency: A hit or a throw gives another go, and a power lets one player win extra turns more easily or deny them to others.
pros: Turns come in uneven numbers.
A player with a power can chain moves.
cons: Others wait while one player moves again.
One power can move a piece many times in a row.

pairs.tendency: The game has stages, and a power may work in one stage only or change when the stage changes.
pros: Early choices set up a power for later.
Players plan which stage a power fits.
cons: A power that works in only one stage may go unused.
Players learn the powers again for each stage.

pairs.tendency: The board models a real system, and each power stands for a part of it, such as a canal or a market, with its own effect on the rest.
pros: Players see how each part affects the whole.
Powers can be tied to real jobs.
cons: A power that changes the system can break the model.
Players learn the model through the powers.

pairs.tendency: Each player acts as a real group, and the power is what that group can do, such as farmers who can plant or a council that can pass a rule.
pros: Players see a problem from where their group stands.
Powers differ as real groups do.
cons: A group with a small power may be left out.
Players may argue for their own group.

pairs.tendency: Everyone draws from one limited supply, and a power lets one player draw more or protect a share.
pros: Taking more shows in the supply.
A player with a power to protect holds a reserve.
cons: The supply can run out sooner when a power draws more.
Others see the drop and respond.

pairs.tendency: Actions show their effects a few rounds later, and a power lets one player speed an effect up or delay it.
pros: A power changes when the effect lands.
Powers add to the wait.
cons: Effects arrive after the cause is forgotten.
Players blame the wrong turn.

pairs.tendency: Players agree on a new rule and try it, and each power shows how the rule works out for that player.
pros: A rule can be tested through different powers.
Players see who gains from a rule.
cons: A rule that suits one power may harm another.
The test only covers the powers in play.

pairs.tendency: Afterwards players talk about what happened, and each describes how their power shaped their play.
pros: Players hear a view from each seat.
Players talk through what each power did.
cons: A power may be remembered wrongly.
The discussion lengthens the session.

pairs.tendency: What players do stays on the board for the rest of play, and a power can be used up or torn out as part of the change.
pros: A power's effect can carry into the next game.
Players think before they use a power.
cons: A lost power cannot be brought back.
The next game starts where this one left off.

pairs.tendency: The rules make a point, and the powers are part of it, since who gets which power says something about the world.
pros: Powers say something about the people they belong to.
Players ask why each power was given.
cons: Players may disagree over what the powers say.
A power can say more than its designer meant.

pairs.tendency: What happens in the game carries into real life, and a power makes it easier for one player to win real money or a promise.
pros: A power changes what real things are at risk.
Every power at the table gets watched.
cons: A player with a power may be asked to give it up.
Friends may argue over a win.

pairs.tendency: Points stand for something that matters, and a power lets one player earn those points more quickly.
pros: Players see how values turn into points.
A power shows which values count.
cons: Players chase the points over the thing itself.
A power can reward only one kind of value.

pairs.tendency: Players practise a way of living, and each power stands for a role in that life, such as the keeper of the seed store.
pros: Players try a role before it exists.
Each power shows a job someone would do.
cons: Powers may seem unreal when tried at a table.
Some roles may be missing.

pairs.tendency: Halfway round the track, the player in front offers to double the game, and the other has to answer while the dice have not yet fallen.
pros: The dice turn the offer into a real gamble.
The leader can raise the price at any point on the way.
cons: A run of low rolls can follow an accepted offer.
Giving up early hands over the points at once.

pairs.tendency: While the shared row of cards goes round, one player offers to double the game. The other studies the row and the picks made so far to guess who is ahead.
pros: The picks so far give clues for the answer.
Each pick can also hint at how sure a player feels.
cons: An offer can come before the picks make sense.
One late pick can undo the lead behind the offer.

pairs.tendency: After a few auctions, one player offers to double the game, and the other counts the money they still hold. A thin purse makes saying yes hard.
pros: Money left over becomes part of the answer.
The offer works like one more bid.
cons: A player short of coins can seldom accept.
Doubling can end an auction run early.

pairs.tendency: Each round already risks what you banked, and the offer to double makes a bust cost twice as much. Both raise the price of a loss at once.
pros: Players watch every throw or draw.
Stopping early starts to look sensible.
cons: One bust can wipe out a doubled stake.
A player with a lead may stop taking risks.

pairs.tendency: Both players hold patches of the map when one offers to double. The other counts the spots each side holds and whether a few moves could flip them.
pros: The map shows who is ahead.
An offer makes the other side count their spots.
cons: A single move can flip an area after the offer.
Losing an area now loses twice the points.

pairs.tendency: Job spaces fill up, and a player who took the jobs the other needed offers to double. The one locked out sees what refusing would cost.
pros: Taken spaces show the standing.
The blocked player sees what the offer means.
cons: A player locked out of jobs has a hard answer to give.
Doubling late leaves few rounds to catch up.

pairs.tendency: Two players build rows and mosaics side by side. One offers to double when their pattern is nearly done, and the other counts how many tiles they still need.
pros: Progress on a pattern is easy to read.
The other side can count the tiles needed.
cons: A pattern can be blocked after the offer.
One missing tile costs double.

pairs.tendency: A player with a full hand offers to double, and the other cannot see a single card. They guess from how long the player has held back plays.
pros: Held cards make the offer a guess.
Cards kept back can be a bluff or a threat.
cons: A wrong read of the hand is paid for twice.
Careful players may wait too long to offer.

pairs.tendency: After a few tricks, the player leading offers to double. The other counts which high cards are gone and what is left in their own hand.
pros: Played cards give clues.
Tricks won so far show the standing.
cons: A late offer leaves few tricks to play.
One last trick can swing the whole stake.

pairs.tendency: Players talk about the offer as well as the game. One may say "I'll hold off doubling if you give me this", and the other weighs it.
pros: Talk can include the stakes.
Doubling can be traded for something else.
cons: Promises about doubling can be broken.
Bargaining slows the game down.

pairs.tendency: One player holds two of the three sets they need and offers to double. The other looks at the table to see which set pieces are still around.
pros: Sets still out show the odds.
The offer tells the other side what to block.
cons: If the last piece never comes, the loss is doubled.
Players may hide their sets until late.

pairs.tendency: Tiles go down to make a shared map, and one player offers to double when a road or city looks nearly closed in their favour. The other checks which tiles could still change it.
pros: Open edges show what is still undecided.
A nearly closed shape shows why the offer came.
cons: One tile drawn late can wreck a plan.
A shared map gives both players the same facts, so offers get weighed carefully.

pairs.tendency: Two players trade lines or moves in a chain. One breaks off to offer doubling, and the other answers it the way they answer everything else, with a reply.
pros: The offer becomes part of the chain.
Replies can carry a hint.
cons: Saying yes or no breaks the rhythm.
A chain that stops can be hard to restart.

pairs.tendency: Nobody may speak, so the offer to double crosses the table as a gesture, such as sliding a marker forward. The other takes it or pushes it back.
pros: The offer is made without a word.
Players watch faces and hands closely.
cons: A gesture can be misread.
Both sides may be unsure whether an offer was made.

pairs.tendency: A player who can change a rule on their turn may change what doubling does, or add a rule that makes the offer cost more.
pros: Rules can be bent around the offer.
Doubling could turn into trebling.
cons: A rule change can undo a safe answer.
Nobody can be sure what an accepted offer will cost.

pairs.tendency: A character in the story offers to double a wager with another character, and the players speak as those characters when they decide.
pros: The wager comes out of the story.
Choices follow what a character would do.
cons: A character's pride can push a player to accept.
Points at stake can sit oddly next to a story.

pairs.tendency: Before a tricky flick or a tall stack, a player offers to double, trusting steady hands. The other watches the fingers for shakes.
pros: Hands decide what the offer is worth.
Players watch each other closely.
cons: A single slip costs double.
Nerves can shake a hand.

pairs.tendency: Half the map is on paper when one player offers to double. The other looks at what has been drawn and guesses what is still to come.
pros: The drawn part of the map gives clues.
The offer is a bet on the unfinished half.
cons: A single line can change who is ahead.
Players may keep the map vague to hide a lead.

pairs.tendency: A player sets up a forced capture that leads to a gain and then offers to double. The other can see the chain coming but cannot step out of it.
pros: Forced moves make the next turns easy to read.
An offer after a trap is clear.
cons: The trapped player has to accept or lose points.
One forced capture can end the game.

pairs.tendency: The player whose character has grown more powerful offers to double. The other guesses whether the gap will keep widening.
pros: Growth shows who is ahead.
A late offer rests on a long record.
cons: The gap tends to widen as play goes on.
A player behind rarely catches up.

pairs.tendency: Each player says the whole list so far and adds one item. One offers to double once the list is long enough to trip the other.
pros: A long list makes the offer a real test of memory.
Players listen closely to every item.
cons: Forgetting one item now loses twice as much.
Long lists drag out each turn.

pairs.tendency: A handicap already tilts the start. When the player who began with more offers to double, the other decides whether the handicap has done its work.
pros: A handicap gives the answer something to rest on.
The offer shows how the leader feels.
cons: A handicap set too low shows up in the stake.
The handicapped player may never accept.

pairs.tendency: The hider offers to double the game while the others are still searching. The searchers think about how long they have already looked.
pros: Time spent hunting shows the standing.
The hider gains time while the others decide.
cons: A close search costs double.
Searchers may give up too soon.

pairs.tendency: A player lines up a double jump and offers to double before making it. The other sees the jump and decides whether they can block it.
pros: The jump is visible to both sides.
The other side sees the threat in full.
cons: A blocked jump leaves the offer costly.
A taken piece swings the stake quickly.

pairs.tendency: After the second roll, a player with a promising set of dice offers to double before the last reroll. The held dice show how far along they are.
pros: Held dice show progress.
The last roll is still open.
cons: A final reroll can change everything.
Doubling before it is a gamble.

pairs.tendency: Pieces get sent back to the start, so a lead can vanish. A player far ahead offers to double, and the other thinks about landing on that piece.
pros: A piece sent back changes the standing in one turn.
Safe spaces make some leads firmer than others.
cons: The leader may lose double after one landing.
Giving up early can feel hasty with a landing still possible.

pairs.tendency: A player with two pieces in a row and a third ready to drop offers to double. The other tries to break the row first.
pros: A nearly made row shows the threat.
A piece taken from the row changes the numbers fast.
cons: Breaking the row uses up the other player's turn.
A late offer may come after the row is already broken.

pairs.tendency: Letters lie on the table and one player offers to double after spelling a long word. The other checks which words are still possible.
pros: A long word shows a lead.
The dictionary settles whether the offer was sound.
cons: A hunted word can be taken first.
Spelling arguments hold up the offer.

pairs.tendency: The line has two open ends, and a player who still holds tiles that fit offers to double. The other counts their own matches.
pros: The open ends show what each hand needs.
Passing a turn gives away what you lack.
cons: A missed turn leaves the lead wide open.
One unlucky draw and the doubled stake is gone.

pairs.tendency: A player lays a finished set face up and offers to double. The other looks at the set and at what they could add to it.
pros: Laid sets show the standing.
Other players can add to sets already on the table.
cons: An added card can shift the score.
The offer comes with a lot of open information.

pairs.tendency: A player with a power still unused offers to double, and the other wonders whether it is saved for this moment.
pros: An unused power hangs over the offer.
A power used at the right time can win a doubled game.
cons: The other side cannot tell which powers remain.
Using a power early wastes it.

pairs.tendency: The player offering a move may offer to double in the same breath, and the other player's say covers both. They can turn down the move, the doubling, or both.
pros: The say covers the stakes as well as the move.
Two decisions arrive in one offer.
cons: Turning down one part can turn down both.
The offer grows complicated to answer.

pairs.tendency: A message travels from player to player, and one offers to double on whether it will arrive the same. Nobody can check until the end.
pros: The result is known only at the end.
The wager rests on what cannot be checked.
cons: If the message changes, whoever bet on it pays twice.
Players may argue over whether it changed.

pairs.tendency: Cards were handed over before play, and the player who kept the cards they wanted offers to double. The other thinks about what they were given.
pros: The pass shapes what each hand holds.
The other side can guess from what was passed.
cons: Cards received may not suit the plan.
A mistaken pass shows up in the stake.

pairs.tendency: One player sets up the board and the other picks a side. When neither side began ahead, an early offer to double is hard to read.
pros: An even start gives neither side an early edge.
The side chosen shapes who offers first.
cons: Neither side knows whom the offer favours.
Few early leads leave little to judge from.

pairs.tendency: A piece one step from the far end gives its owner a reason to offer to double, since it is about to turn into a more powerful piece.
pros: A piece near promotion draws the offer.
The other side can see the promotion coming.
cons: Stopping the piece costs a turn.
A promoted piece makes the stake climb at once.

pairs.tendency: A team on its third leg offers to double, and the other team looks at how far behind they are with legs left to run.
pros: The legs remaining give a way to judge.
Teammates can talk about the answer.
cons: A dropped baton costs double.
Waiting for the team to agree slows the race.

pairs.tendency: A player's stones form a shape that cannot be taken, and they offer to double. The other decides whether the rest of the board can catch up.
pros: A safe shape gives the offer something firm.
The other side can surround the rest instead.
cons: A shape that cannot be taken leaves little to fear.
The offer can come too early, before the shape is done.

pairs.tendency: Winning tricks is only the way to the prizes. A player who holds the named cards offers to double, and the other counts which are still out.
pros: Named prizes tell both sides what to count.
One card can carry more than one prize.
cons: Losing a prize card now hurts twice as much.
Counting the prizes slows each turn.

pairs.tendency: Cards in the middle are open to all, so both players can judge a hand. One offers to double after a card is turned over.
pros: Open cards let both players count the same things.
A new card can shift the offer.
cons: A card turned late can ruin a hand.
The offer is hard to bluff when the middle is open.

pairs.tendency: The pot sits in the middle and grows each round with no winner. Doubling the stakes gives a second way for the prize to grow.
pros: Two things can raise the prize.
A big pot makes giving up costly.
cons: One round can win a huge amount.
A player who gives up leaves what they put in.

pairs.tendency: A player eyeing a pit with the right count of seeds offers to double. The other works out where the last seed would land.
pros: Seed counts let both sides work out the next move.
An offer can follow a long chain of scooping.
cons: If the last seed lands in the wrong pit, the loss is doubled.
Counting every pit takes time.

pairs.tendency: One player took the spare hand and offers to double, and the other thinks about which cards were put back.
pros: The spare hand adds something to guess about.
The swap can hide a lead.
cons: Not knowing the old hand makes an offer risky.
A bought hand may turn out to be worth little.

pairs.tendency: A piece sits one square before a trap, and its owner's rival offers to double. The owner sees how a single step could cost double.
pros: Special squares make the next move easy to see.
Safe squares make a lead feel firm.
cons: A trap square swings the stake.
Missing a turn costs double.

pairs.tendency: Each card has a price in coins. A player who spent little offers to double, and the other counts what they can still buy.
pros: Prices show how much each side has left.
A full purse makes accepting easy.
cons: Spending too much leaves nothing for the offer.
Counting coins slows the answer.

pairs.tendency: Forces are shared out across several places, and one player offers to double after winning the first place. The other looks at how thin they are elsewhere.
pros: The split shows where each side is thin.
One win can change the offer elsewhere.
cons: Spreading too thin now loses twice the points.
A lost place may be hard to win back.

pairs.tendency: When the music stops, the slowest player is caught. An offer to double just before the signal turns a short pause into a bet.
pros: The signal makes the offer sudden.
Players watch for the stop.
cons: Being caught costs double.
The wait before the signal feels long.

pairs.tendency: A player swaps cards to reshape a hand, then offers to double. The other sees how many were swapped and guesses what came in.
pros: The number swapped gives a clue.
Swapping can build or hide a lead.
cons: A swap that misses now hurts twice as much.
Players may swap just to look sure.

pairs.tendency: The pile has grown big, and the player who can pick it up offers to double. The other thinks about what is in it.
pros: A big pile makes the offer loom.
Picking it up changes the hand at once.
cons: A pile of unwanted cards costs double.
Cards in the pile are hard to track.

pairs.tendency: A player holding most of the trumps offers to double, and the other counts how many trumps are left.
pros: The trump suit gives a way to count.
A low trump can still win a trick.
cons: A single trump played late can win double.
Trumps held in secret make the offer a guess.

pairs.tendency: Two boards run at once, and one player is ahead on the first and behind on the second. The offer to double covers both.
pros: Each board gives a different reading.
A lead on one can cover a loss on the other.
cons: A doubled stake counts on both boards.
Players cannot watch both boards at once.

pairs.tendency: A wild card can fill any gap, so a player with one offers to double. The other cannot tell which card it will stand for.
pros: A wild card makes a lead hard to size up.
The offer can rest on a card not yet played.
cons: If the other player holds the wild card, the doubled stake goes their way.
Players watch for who holds the wild.

pairs.tendency: A line runs off one edge and returns on the other, so a threat can arrive from behind. One player offers to double, and the other checks both sides of the board.
pros: The joined edges widen what to check.
A threat can come from either side.
cons: A line from the far side costs double.
Edges are easy to forget.

pairs.tendency: The asker narrows the list with each answer and offers to double once only a few things are left. The one who knows the secret answers.
pros: Each answer shrinks the list.
The offer gets easier to judge as the list shrinks.
cons: A wrong guess costs double.
A long run of questions takes time.

pairs.tendency: Two runners are close to the line when one offers to double. The other measures the gap and the throws or moves left.
pros: The finish line shows the gap.
A race leaves little doubt about what the offer means.
cons: Being overtaken at the last moment loses double.
The leader may offer too late.

pairs.tendency: Scores are close and one player offers to double. The other works out how many points can still be won.
pros: The score gives both sides numbers.
The offer is easy to judge near the end.
cons: A late swing in points now counts twice.
Both sides keep checking the total.

pairs.tendency: Players are knocked out one by one. When two are left, one offers to double, and the other counts who is closer to the end.
pros: The last two make the offer simple.
Players already knocked out can only watch.
cons: Being knocked out early leaves no way back.
A doubled stake can end the game in a single move.

pairs.tendency: Everyone shares the same stake, so an offer to double goes to the whole group. The group answers together or gives up together.
pros: The offer is a group decision.
The whole table shares the answer.
cons: Players may disagree about taking it.
A loss costs everyone.

pairs.tendency: The team reaches for a shared goal, and one member suggests doubling what it is worth. All of them decide together.
pros: The shared goal sets the stake.
Everyone has a say.
cons: Players may not agree on the risk.
A group may take a long while to answer.

pairs.tendency: Secret goals mean nobody knows who is ahead. An offer to double can show a player's aim by who makes it and when.
pros: The offer gives away something about a goal.
Others can use it to guess.
cons: Offering too soon shows a hand.
Declining may hide a secret or may give it away.

pairs.tendency: Players play through a story, and one offers to double what the ending is worth. The other decides whether to risk the ending.
pros: The story gives the offer a place.
The ending carries the stake.
cons: A story can end differently from what the accepting player hoped.
Stakes and plot can pull in different directions.

pairs.tendency: There is nothing to win, so doubling has nothing to double. Players may double the time spent, or what they hope to see.
pros: The offer has to find something else to double.
Players decide what the stake means.
cons: An empty goal leaves the offer unclear.
Players may not take the offer seriously.

pairs.tendency: Each player sets their own aim, so an offer to double raises stakes the other may not care about.
pros: Each goal sets its own stakes.
Players can agree what is being doubled.
cons: A goal that means little makes the offer easy to refuse.
Two goals can clash over what counts.

pairs.tendency: Nobody wins, only one loses. An offer to double raises what that loser pays, and the others stay safe by staying ahead.
pros: Everyone else is safe once one player loses.
The offer points at whoever is last.
cons: The player in last place pays double.
Players ahead have no reason to accept.

pairs.tendency: The aim is to keep playing, and an offer to double puts that at risk, since giving up ends the game for one side.
pros: The offer sets a price on stopping.
Players may accept just to stay in.
cons: Giving up ends the game for one player.
The stake can pull play toward an ending.

pairs.tendency: The game cannot be won, so an offer to double raises the cost of something nobody can collect.
pros: The offer shows what the game is about.
Players may laugh at the doubling.
cons: The doubled stake has no prize to point at.
The offer may turn into a joke at the table.

pairs.tendency: A solo player facing the layout offers to double against the cards themselves, with only the game to say yes or no.
pros: The game's rules answer the offer.
A player can bet on their own skill.
cons: A layout that gets stuck now loses twice over.
Nobody is there to argue about the answer.

pairs.tendency: Players play several short games in a row, and one player offers to double the stake on the next game. The other counts the games each side has won so far.
pros: The games already won show who is ahead.
An offer can come between any two games.
cons: Losing a doubled game can wipe out an early lead.
A player who is behind may accept just to catch up.

pairs.tendency: Every point counts against you, so doubling doubles the harm of each point. The player with the lowest total offers, and the other counts what they hold.
pros: The lowest total makes the offer plain.
Players watch each point they pick up.
cons: A big pick-up costs double.
A trailing player has a reason to refuse.

pairs.tendency: A player one step from the target number offers to double, but the other knows that going over costs the win.
pros: The exact number is easy to read.
Players may wait for the right throw.
cons: Overshooting costs double.
A near finish can drag on.

pairs.tendency: The aim is turned upside down, so the player giving most away offers to double. The other counts what they have left to give.
pros: Giving away shows who is ahead.
The aim runs the other way round from usual.
cons: Anything still held at the end counts twice against you.
New players may mix up who is ahead.

pairs.tendency: Players build their own things side by side, and one offers to double what their own result is worth. The other cannot touch it.
pros: Each side stakes their own work.
The offer is private to one board.
cons: A double on a failing build costs the builder alone.
Players have little to see in each other's work.

pairs.tendency: One player has just taken something from the other and offers to double. The other thinks about hitting back before answering.
pros: Attacks make the offer feel personal.
Revenge can drive an answer.
cons: Answering in anger can lose twice the points.
Players may target the one who offered.

pairs.tendency: Players shape the board and feel each other's moves through it. An offer to double comes after one player has boxed the other in.
pros: The board shows the standing.
The offer follows a change in the board.
cons: A path blocked after accepting means a doubled loss.
Players may take time to read the board.

pairs.tendency: Everyone is on the same team, so an offer to double goes to the whole table and all of them win or lose together.
pros: The answer comes from the whole team.
The team shares the risk.
cons: Nobody escapes a doubled loss.
The team may not agree.

pairs.tendency: Players mostly work together, but one private reason can pull a player toward doubling when the others would not.
pros: The offer shows a private reason.
Others can guess why it came.
cons: A group aim can clash with a private gain.
Trust can wear thin after an offer.

pairs.tendency: One team offers to double, and the other team talks it over before answering.
pros: Teams can share the decision.
Teammates can talk the offer through.
cons: Teams may disagree on the answer.
Talking in front of the other team gives hints away.

pairs.tendency: A player offers to double, and the others wonder whether the offer comes from a traitor who wants the team to lose more.
pros: The offer is a clue about who is secretly on the other side.
The team can watch who pushes for a double.
cons: The traitor can use the offer to cause harm.
Honest players may be doubted for offering.

pairs.tendency: An offer to double goes into a letter and the reply takes days. The game sits at the same score while the offer travels.
pros: The wait gives time to think.
The offer can be written with care.
cons: The game stands still during the wait.
Both sides may forget the exact position.

pairs.tendency: The absent player cannot answer an offer to double, so someone else has to speak for them or the offer waits.
pros: The absent player is still part of the stake.
Others decide on their behalf.
cons: The absent player cannot say yes or no.
The doubled stake may land on someone who was not asked.

pairs.tendency: The game master offers to double what a scene is worth, and the players talk it over among themselves.
pros: The game master can set the stakes.
Players answer as a group or each alone.
cons: The game master may offer too often.
Players may feel pushed.

pairs.tendency: Passers-by watch a street game, and an offer to double is made in front of them. The crowd can see who hesitates.
pros: Onlookers add to the pressure.
The offer is seen by everyone.
cons: A player may accept to look brave in front of others.
A refusal is seen by the whole street.

pairs.tendency: The lone player offers to double against the group, and the others talk it over together before answering.
pros: The lone player is paid more if they win.
The group talks to answer.
cons: Reaching agreement slows the group's answer.
The lone player loses double if the others win.

pairs.tendency: A solo player offers to double against the pack, with nobody to answer but the cards. Luck and choices decide the result.
pros: The player makes the offer to themselves.
A friend can compare results afterwards.
cons: There is no one to refuse the offer.
A loss counts twice.

pairs.tendency: Dice and draws decide most things, so an offer to double is mostly a bet on luck, with little else to weigh.
pros: Luck makes the offer simple to place.
Players need no special skill to answer.
cons: One unlucky run doubles the loss.
The offer says little about who is ahead.

pairs.tendency: Players have ways to soften luck, such as rerolls, so an offer to double depends on whether those are still available.
pros: Spare rerolls make the offer easier to accept.
Players can count what is left.
cons: A used-up reroll leaves the player exposed.
A late offer may be refused for lack of rerolls.

pairs.tendency: Choices matter most, with a little luck. A player who has played carefully offers to double, trusting that luck will not undo it.
pros: Skill gives the offer a firm base.
A bit of luck keeps it uncertain.
cons: One lucky draw can undo a plan.
The more skilled player offers more often.

pairs.tendency: With no dice, the player who sees further ahead offers to double. The other tries to work out the same moves.
pros: The offer comes from thinking ahead.
Both sides can work out the position.
cons: A mistaken plan costs double.
A less practised player may never accept.

pairs.tendency: The throw is read as a message, so an offer to double asks the other to risk what they take the sign to mean.
pros: The sign gives the offer a meaning.
Players talk about what the throw says.
cons: Reading the sign wrongly is paid for twice.
Players may read the same throw differently.

pairs.tendency: Players sense when others are about to act, and one offers to double just as the others feel ready.
pros: The offer can come at a shared moment.
Players read each other's timing.
cons: Acting out of time loses at the doubled stake.
Players out of step may refuse.

pairs.tendency: A roll looks up what happens next in a table, and a player offers to double before the roll. The table can swing the story either way.
pros: The table gives the offer a range of outcomes.
The dice help write the story.
cons: A roll can turn the story against the one who accepted.
Players cannot know what the table will say.

pairs.tendency: Everything is visible, so both players can work out what an offer to double means. The other answers from what they can see.
pros: Both sides see the same facts.
The answer rests on counting.
cons: Nothing is hidden to hide a bluff.
A clear lead makes the offer easy to refuse.

pairs.tendency: Each player holds cards nobody else sees, so the offer to double is a bet on a guess about the other hand.
pros: The offer is a signal about a hidden hand.
Bluffs are possible.
cons: Guessing the hand wrongly doubles the loss.
A cautious player may never offer.

pairs.tendency: Roles are secret, so an offer to double tells the others something about who the player might be.
pros: The offer gives a hint about a role.
Others can watch who makes it.
cons: A role can be given away by the offer.
A false offer may fool the table.

pairs.tendency: Clues point to the hidden facts, and a player who has worked out the answer offers to double before saying it.
pros: The offer comes with a claim about the answer.
The other side can check the clues.
cons: Naming the wrong answer loses twice the points.
A false offer can lead others astray.

pairs.tendency: A player offers to double while holding a thin hand, hoping the other will give up.
pros: A bluff can win the stake without a showdown.
The other side has to read the offer.
cons: A bluff that gets called costs double.
Honest offers get doubted too.

pairs.tendency: One player knows a secret rule. The offer to double asks the others to bet while still working out what the rule is.
pros: The offer raises the price of learning.
Players test the rule while they decide.
cons: Breaking the secret rule now doubles the penalty.
The one who knows the rule can offer with ease.

pairs.tendency: The player who knows the answer cannot say it, so the others offer or decline a double on the hints alone.
pros: The hints give a base for the offer.
Guessers can weigh what they have.
cons: A guess that misses loses twice the points.
The one who knows can only watch.

pairs.tendency: Parts of the map are hidden until explored, so an offer to double is a bet on what lies ahead.
pros: Unexplored ground makes the offer a gamble.
New tiles can change the answer.
cons: A turned tile can swing the stake.
Exploring slows the game.

pairs.tendency: One hand lies face up, so both sides can read part of the position when an offer to double comes.
pros: The open hand gives clues.
The player using it can plan the offer ahead.
cons: The secret hands still leave room to guess.
Playing two hands makes the offer slow to place.

pairs.tendency: Some points are kept hidden, so nobody knows who is ahead when an offer to double arrives.
pros: The offer is a bet on a hidden score.
An offer hints at a lead.
cons: Accepting on a wrong guess about the score doubles the loss.
Players can only guess the totals.

pairs.tendency: One player acts at a time, so the offer arrives on a turn and the other answers on theirs, with the board in front of them.
pros: The offer gets a clear moment.
The other side can think before answering.
cons: A slow answer holds up the game.
The offer arrives only when it is your turn.

pairs.tendency: Everyone chooses in secret at once, so the offer to double can be one of the hidden choices, revealed together.
pros: The offer is chosen without seeing others.
Everyone reveals at the same moment.
cons: Players cannot react to each other's choice.
A surprise offer can catch the table off guard.

pairs.tendency: Anyone may act at any moment, so an offer to double can fly out at once and the quickest answer counts.
pros: The offer can come at any time.
Quick players can use it.
cons: A slow answer loses the choice.
Players may blurt out an answer.

pairs.tendency: A clock runs on each turn, so the answer to an offer to double has to come before time runs out or the move is lost.
pros: The clock puts pressure on the answer.
Players decide fast.
cons: A move made by the clock may cost double.
The offer can arrive near the end of time.

pairs.tendency: The game runs over real days, so an offer to double can sit for a morning or an evening before the other answers.
pros: The wait gives time to think.
Players can make the offer and leave.
cons: The stake hangs over days.
A forgotten answer can lose the game.

pairs.tendency: The game is slow on purpose, so an offer to double comes with a pause before the answer.
pros: The pause slows the decision down.
Players can breathe before deciding.
cons: The wait can feel long.
An impatient player may accept too soon.

pairs.tendency: The game speeds up, so offers to double come faster and the time to answer shrinks as play goes on.
pros: Offers come more often near the end.
Players have less time to think.
cons: A rushed answer costs double.
Players may miss an offer.

pairs.tendency: A lucky player takes extra turns, then offers to double while the other has not moved.
pros: Extra turns can build a lead for the offer.
The other side may have to answer before moving.
cons: A run of moves can make the offer hard to refuse.
A refusal comes after a run the other cannot match.

pairs.tendency: The game has stages, so an offer to double can be made at the end of the first stage and carried into the second.
pros: The first stage sets up the offer.
The stage change is a clear moment.
cons: A mistake in the first stage is paid for twice in the second.
The second stage may play out differently.

pairs.tendency: The board works like a real system, and the offer to double raises what a wrong move does inside it. Players see the effect play out.
pros: The model shows what doubling does.
Players watch cause and effect.
cons: A move in the system can cost double.
Players may take time to see the effect.

pairs.tendency: Each player plays a group with its own needs, so an offer to double lands differently on a farmer than on a shopkeeper.
pros: Each role feels the offer in its own way.
Players speak for their group.
cons: A group with little to lose accepts more easily.
A group with much to lose refuses.

pairs.tendency: Everyone draws from one limited store, and an offer to double raises what taking too much costs.
pros: The shared store shows the risk.
Players watch how much others take.
cons: Overuse costs everyone double.
A greedy player can set off the loss.

pairs.tendency: What you do now shows its effect rounds later, so an offer to double is a bet on an effect not yet seen.
pros: The offer rests on what is coming.
Players have to think ahead.
cons: A late effect can hit double.
Players may not link the effect to its cause.

pairs.tendency: Players agree on a trial rule and play on to see what it changes. An offer to double can be tried as that rule.
pros: The trial shows what doubling does.
Players can test the rule safely.
cons: A rule that does not fit may be dropped.
Players may argue over the result.

pairs.tendency: After the game, players talk about how the offer went and why they answered as they did.
pros: The talk shows how players reasoned.
Players compare the offer to real choices.
cons: Players may remember it differently.
Going over it all adds time after the game.

pairs.tendency: What was done cannot be undone, so an accepted offer to double stays in the game for ever, even into the next one.
pros: The doubled stake carries forward.
Nothing can be undone.
cons: A doubled loss stays.
Players may hesitate to accept.

pairs.tendency: The rules make a point about the world, and the doubling rule says something about risk and who carries it.
pros: The doubling rule makes a point.
Players can talk about what it says.
cons: The point may not be what the designer meant.
Players may disagree on what it says.

pairs.tendency: Real money or a promise rides on the game, so doubling doubles what is at risk in real life.
pros: The offer carries real weight.
Players think hard before accepting.
cons: A real-life loss is twice as large.
A friendship may feel the strain.

pairs.tendency: Points stand for something that matters, so doubling doubles how much of it is risked. Players chase the number.
pros: The offer shows what the points stand for.
Players think about what they are risking.
cons: The number can replace what it measures.
Doubling can turn attention from the value to the score.

pairs.tendency: Players practise a way of living that does not exist yet, and the offer to double tests how far they trust it.
pros: The offer tests trust in the new way.
Players feel how it might go.
cons: A doubled risk can shake a new habit.
Players may not agree on what to risk.

pairs.tendency: A throw says how far you go, and if a piece of the other side sits within reach you have to take it. Some throws walk a piece into a capture its owner did not want.
pros: Dice set up captures nobody planned.
Each throw changes which move is forced.
cons: A single roll can drag a piece into trouble.
Plans fall apart after one throw.

pairs.tendency: Each pick from the shared row can leave the next player with a card that makes a capture the only move. Taking the card others need becomes a way to steer them.
pros: A pick can set up a forced move for someone else.
Players watch what the row hands the next person.
cons: A pick made for one reason can force your own capture later.
The row gets hard to read with many players.

pairs.tendency: Players bid for the right to move first, and the winner can start a capture that the other side then has to answer by capturing back. Paying more buys the chance to start the chain.
pros: A bid buys control over who forces whom.
Players weigh money against a run of captures.
cons: A big bid is wasted if no capture follows.
Winners can run short of money for later turns.

pairs.tendency: Every extra risk can leave a piece where the other side takes it, and the other side has no choice but to take it. Pressing on one step more hands them a move they cannot refuse.
pros: Each risk has a plain cost on the board.
Players can bait a forced capture on purpose.
cons: A greedy step gives away a piece.
Stopping early leaves points unclaimed.

pairs.tendency: Pieces spread over the regions of a map, and one forced capture can pull a piece out of the area it was holding. The other side drops a piece in reach and the hole opens.
pros: Bait pieces can break up a held area.
Players think about which regions to leave open.
cons: A forced capture can empty the area you wanted.
Holding every area at once gets harder.

pairs.tendency: A worker standing on a job can be taken, and taking it frees the spot for someone else. When the capture is forced, a player has to give up a job to take a worker.
pros: Taking a worker frees a job spot.
Jobs near enemy workers carry a risk.
cons: A forced capture can pull a worker off a job you needed.
Players keep workers out of reach.

pairs.tendency: The other side leaves a piece next to your half-made line, and the capture you have to make pulls a piece out of the pattern. A row of tiles becomes something to guard.
pros: Players learn to keep a pattern out of reach.
A pattern can also act as bait.
cons: One forced capture can break a long row.
Long patterns are easy to disrupt.

pairs.tendency: The cards you save for later may include the move that gets you out of a trap. A capture you have to make can use up the very card you were keeping.
pros: Cards in hand can offer a choice between captures.
A saved card gives a way out of a trap.
cons: A forced capture can use up a card early.
Holding cards back leaves pieces in reach.

pairs.tendency: If your card can beat the one on the table, the rule says you have to win the trick. A high card in your hand can pull you into taking a trick you wanted to give away.
pros: Others read your hand from what you had to play.
A low lead can force a high card out.
cons: A high card can drag you into a trick you did not want.
Hands become easy to guess.

pairs.tendency: Two players agree "I will leave your piece alone", and then the rules force a capture anyway. Any deal has to leave out the moves the rules take out of your hands.
pros: Deals have a clear limit.
Talk can aim a player at a forced capture.
cons: A broken promise can come from the rules and not the player.
Arguments start over what was meant.

pairs.tendency: You are one card from a full set, and a piece of yours stands where the other side can capture it. The capture they have to make takes away the thing your set needed.
pros: A nearly full set becomes a target.
Players guard what they have collected.
cons: A forced capture can break a set.
Sets grow slowly when every piece is watched.

pairs.tendency: Laying a tile beside an enemy piece opens a capture the other player has to take. A single tile can pull their piece along a road they never meant to use.
pros: Tiles can be laid as lures.
The map shapes where captures come.
cons: One tile can drag a piece off its road.
The map grows in shapes nobody planned.

pairs.tendency: A player makes a move and the next answers it. When a capture is open the answer is already set, so the call decides the reply.
pros: A call can steer the answer.
The chain of replies is easy to follow.
cons: A forced reply takes the choice out of the response.
The same exchange can repeat.

pairs.tendency: Nobody speaks, so a piece left in reach is a message, and the other player has to answer it with a capture. They read your move without a word being said.
pros: A piece left in reach says something without words.
Players read each other's moves closely.
cons: A forced capture can be mistaken for a plan.
Nobody can explain a mistake.

pairs.tendency: On your turn you rewrite the rule instead of moving. You can end the duty to capture, widen it to more pieces, or make it apply only to you.
pros: A rule change can switch the duty off or widen it.
Players argue for the version that suits them.
cons: Rules shift under a plan already made.
Arguments slow the turn.

pairs.tendency: Your character is gentle, but the rules say that when a capture is open it has to be taken. You explain at the table why the character did it.
pros: The rule gives a character a duty.
Players explain their choices aloud.
cons: A forced capture can clash with the character.
The story stops while the rule is applied.

pairs.tendency: A capture is made by flicking or stacking, and when it is forced you have to try even a shot you would have skipped. A hard shot can miss and leave the piece open.
pros: Forced shots get tried even when they are hard.
Everyone watches each flick.
cons: A missed shot leaves the piece open.
Turns take long when every shot is forced.

pairs.tendency: A road drawn close to an enemy piece opens a capture that the other player has to take. The map shows where each forced move came from.
pros: Drawing becomes a way to lure.
The map records where captures happened.
cons: A drawn road can pull pieces somewhere unplanned.
The sheet fills with lures.

pairs.tendency: Your character gains power by playing, and a forced capture can pull it into a fight before it has grown. Waiting for power is hard when the rule makes you act.
pros: Growth gives an answer to a forced fight.
Players choose when to take a risk.
cons: A forced fight can come too early.
The start of the game is the hardest part.

pairs.tendency: Each player recites the list and adds one item, and the item they add names the piece they took. The list turns into a record of captures in order.
pros: The list records each capture.
Players remember the game as it goes.
cons: The next item is often known before anyone speaks.
Long lists get hard to recall.

pairs.tendency: The player with more pieces starts with fewer, and the weaker side can offer a piece to pull one of their opponent's out of place. The duty gives the smaller side a tool.
pros: The smaller side gets a way to bait.
The handicap shows in who is forced.
cons: A bait can win back what the handicap took.
A big handicap can leave no pieces to use as bait.

pairs.tendency: A hider lets themselves be seen so the seeker has to go after them, and the seeker walks away from the place where another hider sits. One decoy covers for the rest.
pros: A decoy pulls the seeker away.
Hiders work together without talking.
cons: The seeker has to go for the first one found.
A round can end early.

pairs.tendency: A jump is a capture, and when one is open you have to take it. A player offers a piece so the other has to jump into a spot where they get jumped back, and the chain runs on.
pros: Offered pieces set up double jumps.
Players count jumps ahead.
cons: One careless piece lets the other side force a run.
Newcomers see only one move ahead.

pairs.tendency: You keep the dice you like and roll the rest, and the final roll decides whether a capture opens. If it does, you have to take it, even if you kept those dice to avoid it.
pros: Rerolls let you aim at or away from a capture.
Players weigh which dice to keep.
cons: The last roll can force a capture you were avoiding.
Turns include extra waiting.

pairs.tendency: If your move can land on another player's piece you have to, which sends it back to the start. A piece standing alone becomes a trap for anyone passing by.
pros: Safe spaces start to matter.
Players read each throw for landings.
cons: A forced landing can break your own plan.
Sent-back pieces lose a lot of time.

pairs.tendency: Three in a row lets you take a piece, and the other side may be forced to capture and break your row straight away. Rows and captures pass back and forth across the board.
pros: Each side answers a row with a capture.
Players weigh a row against a lost piece.
cons: A new row can be broken at once.
The board empties quickly.

pairs.tendency: Letters are the pieces, and a capture takes a tile out of the word you were building. The rule makes you capture, so you lose the letter at the end whether or not you could spare it.
pros: Players guard the letters they need.
Word plans have to allow for lost tiles.
cons: A forced capture can take the one letter you needed.
Spelling stops while captures are sorted out.

pairs.tendency: A tile matching an open end has to be played if you hold it, so your hand decides your move. Holding the matching tile removes your choice.
pros: The line of tiles is easy to follow.
Players know when a tile is forced.
cons: A player with a matching tile loses the choice.
Hands empty in a set order.

pairs.tendency: A set laid face up shows what you hold. If another player can take a card from it with a capture they have to, so laid sets can be raided at once.
pros: Everyone can see which sets are open to a raid.
Added cards can extend a meld.
cons: A meld can be raided straight away.
Players hold cards back.

pairs.tendency: Each piece has one power, and using it can cancel the duty to capture for that turn. The other side guesses when you will spend it.
pros: A power gives a way out of a forced capture.
Players guess when the other will use theirs.
cons: A spent power leaves the piece open.
Waiting too long loses the piece.

pairs.tendency: You offer two moves and the other player picks one, but if one of them is a capture they have to pick it. An offer can hide a forced capture inside it.
pros: Offers can carry a hidden duty.
The choice is spread between two players.
cons: A refused offer can leave a different capture forced.
Turns run longer.

pairs.tendency: The message tells a player where to go, and by the time it arrives a forced capture has changed the board. The words say one thing and the board says another.
pros: Messages change meaning as the board changes.
Players guess what the message meant.
cons: A forced capture can make the message useless.
Nobody can check it on the way.

pairs.tendency: Before play you hand over cards, and one of them can carry a capture the receiver will have to make. You choose what to give without knowing what you get back.
pros: A passed card can set up a forced capture.
Choosing what to give takes thought.
cons: A card you pass may come back to hurt you.
You cannot look at what you get first.

pairs.tendency: One side sets up the start and the other picks a side, so the person setting up checks who gets the first capture. A start with a forced capture open will be taken or left depending on who it helps.
pros: The setter tries to make a start with an even first capture.
The chooser checks for forced captures first.
cons: A hidden forced chain can tilt the choice.
Setting up takes time.

pairs.tendency: A runner heading for the far end can be pulled sideways by a bait piece before it arrives. A promoted piece may also be forced into a capture on its first move.
pros: A forced capture can stop a runner.
Runners tempt the other side to set a bait.
cons: A new piece may be forced to act at once.
A pulled runner never reaches the end.

pairs.tendency: A runner who has to capture on the way stops to do it, and the next runner waits with the flag. Each stop costs the whole team time.
pros: Teams plan who meets whom.
Teams see where the time went.
cons: A runner can be slowed down on purpose.
Teammates wait on slow legs.

pairs.tendency: Pieces in a safe shape cannot be taken, so the duty only reaches pieces outside it. Pieces not yet in the shape are bait, and a bait can pull one out of the shape.
pros: Finishing a shape ends the threat.
Players race to complete a shape.
cons: Pieces outside the shape are open to forced captures.
A bait can drag a stone out of a half-made shape.

pairs.tendency: The prize cards are named in advance, and when you can take one you have to. A player can lead a prize to drag a card out of another hand.
pros: The prize card pulls players towards it.
Everyone knows what is at stake.
cons: You may be forced to take a prize you did not want.
Others can work out what each player holds.

pairs.tendency: Cards in the middle are face up, and when you can take one you have to. Everyone sees what can be taken, so the middle is full of ready bait.
pros: Everyone can see what is open to take.
Shared cards bring ready bait.
cons: A forced take can break up the hand you were making.
The middle empties fast.

pairs.tendency: The pot grows each round nobody wins, and a bigger pot draws a capture from whoever can reach it. A player has to take a small pot even if they were waiting for a bigger one.
pros: A growing pot makes a bigger target.
Players save a capture for a big pot.
cons: The duty can make a player take a small pot too soon.
Rounds with no winner pile up.

pairs.tendency: The last seed decides what you can take, so choosing a pit is also choosing a capture. When your last seed lands where a capture is open you have to take it, even a small heap.
pros: A pit choice is also a capture choice.
Players count seeds ahead.
cons: A scoop can force you to take a small heap.
Counting slows the turn.

pairs.tendency: The spare hand lies face down in the middle, and a player who takes it may be taking a capture they will then have to make. Swapping becomes a gamble on what the cards force.
pros: The spare hand may hold a forced capture.
Swapping is a gamble.
cons: The hand you take can force your first move.
One player gets to look first.

pairs.tendency: A piece on a safe square cannot be captured, so the duty skips it. A capture that ends on a square that sends you back costs you twice.
pros: Safe squares protect from the duty.
Players use squares as bait.
cons: A forced capture can end on a square that sends you back.
The squares are hard to remember.

pairs.tendency: A capture costs points to make, and when it is forced you pay even if you wanted to save. Prices decide which captures players can afford to leave.
pros: Players can see the cost of each capture.
Spending shows what each player holds.
cons: A forced capture can empty your supply.
Saving for a big buy gets cut short.

pairs.tendency: You have a fixed amount of pieces to share out between places. A small bait in one place can drag a large part of your forces over, and another place is left thin.
pros: A small bait can drag a large force.
Players decide where to be thin.
cons: A forced capture leaves another place thin.
The other side's split is only a guess.

pairs.tendency: When the signal sounds, everyone who can capture has to, all in the same moment. The slowest player is caught, and the rule picks who is slowest.
pros: The signal gives every capture one moment.
Players watch the sound and each other.
cons: Nobody can hold a capture back at the signal.
Many captures at once cause confusion.

pairs.tendency: If the rules let you swap before the capture, you can put back the card that forces it. New cards can bring a fresh duty, so the swap has its own risk.
pros: A swap can clear a forced capture.
Players use the swap to dodge a duty.
cons: New cards may bring another duty.
The pile gets used up.

pairs.tendency: You may take the whole pile if you can use the top card straight away, and when you can you have to. A pile that nobody wants grows big, and then it is forced onto one hand.
pros: The pile grows while players avoid it.
Players read the top card closely.
cons: The duty can push a large pile onto one player.
A big hand is hard to manage.

pairs.tendency: When you can win a trick with a trump you have to, so a low trump gets spent on a trick you would have let go. Players count the trumps that are left.
pros: Trumps decide who is forced.
Players count trumps closely.
cons: A low trump gets spent early.
A trick cannot be given away on purpose.

pairs.tendency: A duty to capture on one board takes your turn away from the other. A bait on the first board can leave a piece open on the second.
pros: Players juggle two duties.
A bait on one board hits the other.
cons: You can be forced on both boards at once.
Players lose track of which board is which.

pairs.tendency: A wild card can stand for the card the duty asks for, so it settles a forced capture. It can also fill a set instead, and then the duty has to be met another way.
pros: A wild card gives a way to meet the duty.
A wild card is a prize for a bait.
cons: Everyone wonders who holds the wild ones.
Using one early leaves the hand short.

pairs.tendency: A piece on one edge can be reached from the other edge, so a forced capture can pull a piece across the join. Corners no longer give shelter.
pros: A piece at the edge is in reach from the other edge.
Corners stop being safe.
cons: A forced capture can send a piece across the join.
Players misjudge the distance.

pairs.tendency: One player has a secret piece. Another asks "is it on that square?", and a yes means the asker has to capture it. A question can carry a duty with it.
pros: Questions can carry a duty.
Answers shrink the list.
cons: A question can force a capture you did not want.
Asking the wrong question loses a piece.

pairs.tendency: A runner in the lead can be stopped by a forced capture on the way. The others set a bait ahead of the leader to hold them back.
pros: A forced capture can stop the leader.
Players set baits ahead of the runner.
cons: A race can be lost on the way by one capture.
The leader has to take the stop.

pairs.tendency: Every capture adds points, so the duty hands you points even when taking them opens up your own pieces. Players give up one piece to win two back.
pros: Points come out of the duty.
Players give a piece to get two back.
cons: A forced take can lose more points than it wins.
Counting the score never stops.

pairs.tendency: Each forced capture takes a piece out of play, and the field gets smaller in steps that others can predict. One forced chain can knock a player out of the game.
pros: Games shorten as captures chain.
Players can see the last few moves coming.
cons: One chain can knock out a player.
Knocked-out players wait a long time.

pairs.tendency: The game's own pieces have to capture whenever they can, so the team knows what the game will do and plans around it. The team lays bait for the game's pieces.
pros: The team can predict the game's moves.
The team uses bait on the game's pieces.
cons: A forced capture by the game can hit the piece the team needed.
A team cannot undo a lost piece.
