pairs.tendency: The list grows past what anyone can remember, and the game is built to show it. Every player fails in the end.
pros: Players find the limit of their memory.
A game that ends in failure for all.
cons: Players leave without a result.
The ending is one they cannot reach.

pairs.tendency: You play alone against a layout of cards and add an item to the list each time you place one. You win by clearing the layout with the list intact.
pros: A solo memory test.
There is nobody to wait for.
cons: Nobody corrects your list.
A single slip ends the attempt.

pairs.tendency: Each short game starts a fresh list, so a player who dropped an item in one game gets another go.
pros: A mistake does not end the whole match.
Players learn how long a list they can hold.
cons: Early items get recited again each time.
The match takes a long time.

pairs.tendency: An error adds a point to your total, and the player with the fewest points wins. A long clean recital keeps your total low.
pros: Clean recitals get noticed.
Players try hard not to slip.
cons: Counting errors needs a referee.
Points pile up on whoever sits at the long end.

pairs.tendency: The list has to reach a set length exactly, and one item too many loses the win.
pros: Players count items as they add them.
Players can block each other's count.
cons: A player may add one item too many.
Counting takes attention away from remembering.

pairs.tendency: The player who recites the whole list correctly loses, so players slip on purpose. To make a believable slip, everyone has to know the true list.
pros: Players have to know the list to fail it.
Wrong answers take some cunning.
cons: A plan is hard to tell from a real slip.
Arguments start over whether a slip was real.

pairs.tendency: Each player keeps a list of their own at the same time, and nobody hears anyone else's. The lists are compared at the end.
pros: Everyone moves at their own speed.
There is little waiting.
cons: Nobody can check your list.
There is little talk between players.

pairs.tendency: A player can interrupt another's recital, add a false item to trip them up, or challenge a slip as it happens.
pros: Players listen hard to each other.
Challenges are out in the open.
cons: Challenges can cause arguments.
Quick speakers pick on slow ones.

pairs.tendency: Players affect each other through the board, and the list records what each one did there. A move on the board puts something on the list for the next player to carry.
pros: Moves on the board change the list.
Nobody is targeted by name.
cons: The link between board and list is hard to see.
Players blame the board for their slips.

pairs.tendency: The whole table recites together against the game, and the game adds items of its own to the list.
pros: Everyone shares the work.
Help passes freely.
cons: One voice can take over.
The game's items catch people out.

pairs.tendency: Players help each other keep the list going, but each one wants to be the person who adds the last item.
pros: Cooperation with a private aim.
Players watch who helps.
cons: Some players hold back help.
It is hard to tell help from a trap.

pairs.tendency: Two teams each keep a list of their own and grow it in turns. The team that holds its list longer wins.
pros: Teammates can prompt each other.
Teams compare their lists.
cons: Teams may whisper wrong items to each other.
Fast speakers take over the team.

pairs.tendency: One player secretly adds wrong items to throw the others off, and the group has to work out who is changing the list.
pros: Players listen for odd items.
Players start to doubt items on the list.
cons: An honest slip looks like sabotage.
Suspicion starts with a plain mistake.

pairs.tendency: Each letter carries the list so far plus one new item. The list can take weeks to grow, and anyone can check it against older letters.
pros: A written copy means memory is not needed.
Players wait days for the next item.
cons: Letters can get lost.
The game takes a very long time.

pairs.tendency: One player is not at the table, but their item sits on the list, left from an earlier game or sent as a hint from a ghost. The group recites it with the rest.
pros: A player who is away still has an item on the list.
The list keeps that player's item.
cons: Nobody can answer questions for the absent player.
Others may recite their item wrongly.

pairs.tendency: The game master gives the first item, describes what is happening, and checks the list as others add to it. They can also rule on whether a recital counts.
pros: One person checks everything.
The story steers which items players pick.
cons: The game master is busy and cannot play.
Players depend on one person's memory.

pairs.tendency: Passers-by can join and add an item, so the list grows with strangers' voices. New players cannot know the earlier items.
pros: Anyone can join.
The list holds items from people passing by.
cons: Newcomers fall behind.
Street noise makes it hard to hear the list.

pairs.tendency: One player recites alone while the group takes turns adding tricky items to the list. The lone player is paid more for success.
pros: The group puts pressure on one reciter.
The reward is clear.
cons: The single player holds the whole list alone.
The group may add very hard items.

pairs.tendency: You draw a card from the pack, name its item and add it to the list. Nobody hears you, so you check the list on paper afterwards.
pros: Nobody has to wait.
You can write the list down.
cons: Nobody catches a slip.
The score rests on your own honesty.

pairs.tendency: The dice or a card choose the next item for you, and you recite the list ending with whatever came up. Remembering is the only part that is yours.
pros: Items come as surprises.
Easy to start.
cons: Players cannot plan their items.
A hard item is only luck.

pairs.tendency: The dice give you the next item, but you may re-roll once or swap it for another. You pick the item that is easiest to place.
pros: Luck is softened.
Players have a choice about the item.
cons: Re-rolls slow the turn.
Players hold back their re-rolls too long.

pairs.tendency: You choose which item to add, and now and then a roll changes your choice. Memory does most of the work.
pros: Choices matter.
A roll adds small changes.
cons: A roll can undo a plan.
Players blame luck for slips.

pairs.tendency: Nothing is random. The list grows only by what players choose to say, so the player who recalls the most wins.
pros: A pure memory test.
There is no luck to hide behind.
cons: The same players tend to win.
New players find it hard to catch up.

pairs.tendency: The throw is read as a sign, and what it points to goes on the list. The list becomes a set of answers to questions the group asked.
pros: A throw carries a meaning.
The list can be read afterwards.
cons: Players read signs differently.
Items cannot be checked as right or wrong.

pairs.tendency: Players try to say the next item together, sensing when each other will speak, and the list is built from those shared moments.
pros: Players listen to breath and rhythm.
Moments of speaking in unison.
cons: Clashes when two people speak at once.
It needs quiet and patience.

pairs.tendency: A roll is looked up on a table, and what the table says becomes the next item. Read in order, the list is the story the dice produced.
pros: Each item is a step in the story.
Every roll brings a surprise.
cons: The table has to be looked up each turn.
Odd items are hard to remember.

pairs.tendency: Every item is written where all can see it, so players read it off the table and do not need to recall it.
pros: Nobody strains to remember.
Everyone sees the same list.
cons: There is little to recall.
Reading takes the place of memory.

pairs.tendency: The items you add come from cards in your hand that nobody else sees, so the list is built from secret supplies.
pros: Players guess what others hold from the items they add.
Bluffing about items is possible.
cons: Running out of cards ends your adding.
Some hands give easy items and others hard ones.

pairs.tendency: Roles are secret, and the items you add can hint at yours. Listeners pick up clues in the list about who is who.
pros: Players read between the items.
Roles shape the choice of words.
cons: Players overthink items.
A truthful player can look suspicious.

pairs.tendency: The list holds clues, and players work out a hidden fact from the pattern of the items.
pros: The list is evidence.
Players compare items.
cons: A wrongly recalled clue leads to a wrong answer.
A long list buries the clue that helps.

pairs.tendency: A player can add an item they never had, or claim to remember what they do not. Others decide whether to challenge.
pros: Players listen for hesitation.
A bluff can pass unnoticed.
cons: A challenge that turns out wrong costs the challenger.
A bluff needs a careful judge.

pairs.tendency: A secret rule decides which items are allowed on the list. Players learn it when an item is refused.
pros: Refused items teach the rule.
The list shows what is allowed.
cons: Players repeat refused items.
Newcomers waste turns.

pairs.tendency: One player knows the full list and may only hint with pictures or sounds while the others try to recite it.
pros: Hints keep the group guessing.
The knower has a clear job.
cons: Hints can mislead.
The knower cannot speak, so slips go uncorrected.

pairs.tendency: Each time an area is turned over, it is named and added to the list. The list holds only what has been found so far.
pros: The list matches the explored part of the map.
Unknown areas stay unknown.
cons: Areas visited early are forgotten.
Going back needs the list.

pairs.tendency: The open hand's cards form a visible list, while the other hands add secret items. Players mix what they see with what they recall.
pros: Part of the list is visible.
The open hand guides guesses.
cons: The open hand shows part of the plan.
Players lean on the open hand and forget the rest.

pairs.tendency: The score for each recital is kept secret, so players guess who has recited the most items.
pros: Guessing about each other's scores.
A reveal at the end.
cons: Players cannot tell whom to challenge.
A secret tally can be wrong.

pairs.tendency: Players add one item each in order around the table, and each one hears all the earlier items before adding their own.
pros: The order is clear.
Each person gets a turn.
cons: Players wait a long time.
The last player has the longest recital.

pairs.tendency: Everyone writes an item at the same moment, then the items are read out together.
pros: Nobody waits.
Reveals bring surprises.
cons: Duplicate items turn up.
Reading all at once makes the order hard to fix.

pairs.tendency: Anyone can call out the next item at any moment, so the list grows in bursts.
pros: Play moves quickly.
Players who act first gain ground.
cons: Two people speak at once.
Slower thinkers get little chance.

pairs.tendency: Each turn has a clock for reciting and adding. If time runs out partway through the list, the turn is lost.
pros: Play stays quick.
Players practise speaking fast.
cons: A turn can stop halfway.
A longer list needs more time but the clock stays the same.

pairs.tendency: One item is added each morning, and the list is kept in writing over days.
pros: The list builds slowly.
The written list can be checked.
cons: Players forget to add their item.
The game goes cold when someone is away.

pairs.tendency: A pause before each recital gives players a breath to think about the list. The list grows slowly.
pros: Calm turns.
Time to recall.
cons: A long game.
It asks for patience.

pairs.tendency: The time allowed for reciting shrinks each round while the list gets longer, so both meet in a rush at the end.
pros: The game ends quickly.
Players practise under pressure.
cons: Slips become more frequent.
The last rounds are a rush of mumbled words.

pairs.tendency: A player who earns another turn adds a second item straight after the first, so one voice may run two items.
pros: A lucky player moves the list on.
More items in one go.
cons: One person recites twice.
Others wait longer.

pairs.tendency: In the first stage the list is built, and in the second it is used. What you added early decides what you need to recall later.
pros: Each stage has a clear shape.
Early items matter later.
cons: The change of stage can confuse players.
Early items are chosen without knowing how they will be used.

pairs.tendency: Items on the list are parts of a system, such as wells or fields, and the list tracks changes to them as play goes on.
pros: Players learn the parts of the system.
Causes are visible.
cons: A real system has more parts than a list can hold.
Parts of the system drop off the list.

pairs.tendency: Each player adds items from the point of view of their group, such as farmers or the village council. The list ends up holding many interests.
pros: Players hear other views.
Items carry needs.
cons: One group's items can crowd out the others.
Players favour their own group.

pairs.tendency: Adding an item draws something from a shared supply, and the list records each draw. The total creeps towards the limit.
pros: Players see the supply shrink.
The draws are recorded.
cons: Over-drawing is easy to do.
Arguments start over who took the most.

pairs.tendency: An item added now has its effect a few rounds later, so players have to remember what they put on the list earlier.
pros: Players link past items to results.
The list explains what happened.
cons: Effects land long after the cause.
Forgotten items produce surprises.

pairs.tendency: The group tries a new rule about the list, such as shortening it, then plays on to see what changes.
pros: The rule gets tested.
Players compare before and after.
cons: A rule can break the list.
Resetting takes time.

pairs.tendency: After the game the list is read out and the group talks about which parts were easy or hard to remember and why.
pros: Players learn about their own memory.
The list is a record to talk over.
cons: Players may disagree about what they remembered.
Some players do not want to talk.

pairs.tendency: Items are written in ink or stuck to the board, and the list from this game starts the next one.
pros: Lists carry over.
Nothing can be undone.
cons: Errors stay.
Early items shape later games.

pairs.tendency: A list that only grows and never shrinks says something about how things pile up. The rules make that point by what they allow.
pros: Players notice what the list favours.
It starts a talk.
cons: The meaning differs from player to player.
Players may not notice the point at all.

pairs.tendency: A real promise or a small bet rides on getting the list right, so a slip costs something outside the game.
pros: Players concentrate.
The result matters beyond the table.
cons: A slip can cause upset.
Friends feel awkward.

pairs.tendency: Each item is worth points for something like kindness or health, and players start choosing items for the points and forget what the items were about.
pros: Players see a number take the place of what it stood for.
Players discuss the choice.
cons: Items lose their meaning.
Chasing points takes over.

pairs.tendency: The items on the list are things a future village does each day, and players add to it to see how a day would feel.
pros: A future is spelled out item by item.
Players test it in words.
cons: Items can drift from what is realistic.
A day is hard to repeat the same way.

pairs.tendency: The player who usually wins starts a few spaces behind the others, or needs a six to leave the start. The dice still scatter everyone along the path, so a head start of five spaces can vanish in two throws.
pros: Newer players begin nearer the finish.
The gap can close by luck and by the rule.
cons: The dice can wipe out the head start quickly.
Nobody can tell if the gap was the right size.

pairs.tendency: Before the first pick, the usual winner gets a shorter row to choose from, or picks last every round. The newer players take the cards that help them most before anyone can block them.
pros: Newer players get first look at the row.
The usual winner reads the row more closely.
cons: Picking last can leave only one card.
The row empties fast for the late picker.

pairs.tendency: The usual winner starts with fewer coins, so in every auction one purse is smaller than the rest. Others can win lots cheaply by bidding just above what that purse can reach.
pros: Newer players can win lots without a big bid.
The coin gap is easy to count.
cons: The short purse may sit out many auctions.
A bid just above the limit can freeze one player out.

pairs.tendency: The usual winner gets a lower stopping limit, such as three throws a turn where the others get five. Each turn the newer players can push on past the point where the usual winner has to stop.
pros: Newer players can take bigger risks for bigger gains.
The usual winner chooses stopping points with care.
cons: The usual winner may stop with little in hand.
A newer player who pushes too far loses the turn all the same.

pairs.tendency: Everyone sets up on the map, but the usual winner begins with fewer pieces. Some areas start empty or already held by others, and the short side has to pick which spots to fight for.
pros: The others hold more of the map early.
The short side has to choose spots with care.
cons: A thin side can be pushed out of a region.
Small gaps in pieces grow as areas change hands.

pairs.tendency: The usual winner has one worker fewer, so one job a round goes undone. Spots on the board fill up sooner for that player, and the others take the jobs they would have wanted.
pros: Newer players reach more jobs each round.
Each placement by the short side carries more weight.
cons: One fewer worker means one fewer job every round.
A taken spot can leave the short side with nothing to do.

pairs.tendency: Newer players build lines of three, while the usual winner has to build lines of four to score. The same tiles lie on the table, but the usual winner needs more of them in a row.
pros: Short lines score for newer players.
Both sides can see the two line lengths.
cons: The usual winner may wait on one missing tile.
Blocking a long line takes only one tile.

pairs.tendency: Starting with three cards while the others hold five, the usual winner sees fewer choices on each turn. Every card played from that small hand leaves it even smaller.
pros: Newer players hold more options.
The small hand pushes quick, clear plays.
cons: The small hand runs out sooner.
A single wasted card shows at once.

pairs.tendency: The usual winner begins each hand a trick down, or has to take one extra trick before any score counts. Others lead with a safe card and let that player chase the missing trick.
pros: The others can play low and wait.
The target for the usual winner is easy to state.
cons: The usual winner may have to win tricks early.
One lost trick can end the chase.

pairs.tendency: The usual winner has less to trade, so deals tilt toward the others. Someone offers a swap that the short side cannot match, and the talk turns to who needs what.
pros: Newer players hold more to bargain with.
Talk soon turns to who has more.
cons: The short side may have little to offer.
Side deals can leave the usual winner out.

pairs.tendency: Newer players need three matching cards to make a set, and the usual winner needs four. Both sides pull from the same pile, and the usual winner starts every set a card further off.
pros: Newer players finish sets sooner.
The same pile feeds both targets.
cons: A four-card set gets blocked by one taken card.
The usual winner is left holding half-sets.

pairs.tendency: The usual winner draws one tile a turn while the others draw two and choose. The shared map grows mostly by other hands, and the roads that reach that player's spots come from them.
pros: Newer players choose between two tiles.
The map still grows from every player.
cons: One tile leaves the usual winner little choice.
A tile that does not fit cannot be swapped out.

pairs.tendency: The usual winner gets three seconds to answer, or has to answer in rhyme, where the others answer in plain words. The chain of calls goes on, and every reply from the usual winner carries the extra rule.
pros: Newer players answer in their own time.
The rhyme rule gives the chain a sound.
cons: The usual winner may stall the chain.
Rhyme can end a line the others want to continue.

pairs.tendency: Newer players may hum one note to signal, while the usual winner stays fully silent and still. All of them place cards in order, and only one side has a cue.
pros: Newer players get one small cue.
The silent player has to read the others closely.
cons: A single hum can break the quiet.
The silent side may place cards too early.

pairs.tendency: The handicap is itself a rule, so a player on their turn can rewrite it. The usual winner is not allowed to propose changes, so only the others can loosen or drop the handicap.
pros: Newer players can reshape the head start.
The handicap can be argued over in the open.
cons: The head start may be changed away at once.
The usual winner can only watch the rule move.

pairs.tendency: The usual winner plays a character with fewer skills on the sheet, and the story hands that character harder scenes. The others play their own characters as written and meet easier ones.
pros: Newer players get easier scenes.
The shorter list of skills gives the usual winner more to act.
cons: Harder scenes can end a character early.
The missing skills come up in every scene.

pairs.tendency: The usual winner uses the other hand, or stands a step further from the target. A newer player flicks, stacks or throws from the usual spot.
pros: Newer players use their normal grip.
The gap is plain to see.
cons: Shaky hands cost a miss.
A step back can turn small misses into many.

pairs.tendency: The usual winner draws with one colour on a small corner of the sheet, while the others have the whole page and every pen. The map grows round the corner and the small drawer works inside it.
pros: Newer players draw anywhere on the sheet.
The small corner gives clear limits.
cons: The corner fills up quickly.
The drawer with one pen can look out of place.

pairs.tendency: The usual winner as hider has to pick a spot close to base or count fewer seconds before the seekers start. Seekers know the hider has less room to hide, so they check the near corners first.
pros: Seekers can search close to base.
The hider uses a small space with care.
cons: A short count leaves little time to move.
A hider who is found at once ends the round early.

pairs.tendency: The usual winner begins with fewer pieces on the board. Every hop the others make now has fewer targets to land beside, and each hop that takes a piece widens the gap.
pros: The others have more pieces to hop with.
Gaps on the board open lanes for jumps.
cons: Each lost piece is a bigger share of a small army.
One double hop can end the game.

pairs.tendency: The usual winner gets two rolls where the others get three. Newer players set aside the dice they like after the first roll and still have one more go.
pros: Newer players get one more try.
The usual winner chooses faster.
cons: Two rolls leave little room to recover.
Dice set aside early may be wrong.

pairs.tendency: The usual winner's pieces get no safe spaces, so every landing by another piece sends them home. Newer players rest on the safe spots and wait for a landing.
pros: Newer players can sit safe and wait.
The usual winner's pieces are worth guarding.
cons: Home is one landing away for the usual winner.
The same pieces can be sent back many times.

pairs.tendency: The usual winner starts with seven pieces where the others hold nine. A mill is harder to make with seven, and a mill by the others takes one of those seven.
pros: Newer players make mills sooner.
The usual winner has to guard each row.
cons: A lost piece is a bigger share of seven.
Few pieces make a mill rare.

pairs.tendency: The usual winner may play only words of five letters or more, and draws one letter fewer. Everyone else plays short words and long ones, and the dictionary rules on the long ones.
pros: Newer players can play any word.
Long words score a lot when they land.
cons: Five-letter words are hard to find in seven letters.
The usual winner is left with unused letters.

pairs.tendency: The usual winner holds three more tiles at the start. More tiles give more chances to match an end, but every tile has to be played before the hand is empty.
pros: Newer players empty their hands sooner.
A large hand holds more ways to match.
cons: More tiles need more turns to clear.
A miss costs a turn with a full hand.

pairs.tendency: The usual winner may lay down only sets of four, while the others lay down sets of three. Newer players put cards on the table early and then add to them.
pros: Newer players meld sets early.
The sets on the table help others to add cards.
cons: The four-card sets take longer to gather.
Cards held for a long set sit in hand unplayed.

pairs.tendency: The usual winner starts with no special power marker, and each newer player holds one. The others choose their moment to spend it and the usual winner has nothing to hold back.
pros: Newer players have a power to save.
Players watch each other's markers.
cons: The usual winner has no surprise to use.
A power spent too early cannot be got back.

pairs.tendency: The usual winner's offers can be turned down, while the newer player's offers have to be taken or traded. So the usual winner learns to offer moves the other would accept.
pros: Newer players can say no.
The usual winner offers moves with care.
cons: A refused move wastes the turn.
The newer player's offer cannot be refused.

pairs.tendency: The usual winner sits at the far end of the line, and the message reaches them after more whispers. The words change on the way and the end player hears the oddest version.
pros: Players nearer the start hear a clearer message.
The far end gets the funniest version.
cons: The message can break by the time it arrives.
Nobody can check what changed on the way.

pairs.tendency: The usual winner passes three cards to the next player, and the others pass only one. The cards come back unseen and the usual winner has given up more of the hand.
pros: Newer players keep most of their hand.
The usual winner chooses what to give away with care.
cons: A big pass hands over a lot at once.
The cards that come back cannot be seen first.

pairs.tendency: One player sets up the game and the other picks the side. A handicap is already built into that setup, so the setup player counts the head start into the cut.
pros: The cut accounts for the head start.
The picker has a real choice of side.
cons: The setup takes longer to judge.
A head start is harder to cut evenly.

pairs.tendency: The usual winner's pieces turn into bigger ones only after reaching the far end twice, and the others promote at the first end. A newer player pushes a pawn forward and gets a new piece quickly.
pros: Newer players promote sooner.
Pushing forward pays off for newer players.
cons: The usual winner needs two trips to the end.
A far-end trip can be blocked.

pairs.tendency: The fastest runner on the team that usually wins runs two legs, or the team starts a few steps behind the line. Teams hand over a flag at each leg and the extra leg is plain at each handover.
pros: Newer teams start nearer the line.
The extra leg is easy to see.
cons: One runner has twice the distance.
A tired runner slows the team.

pairs.tendency: The usual winner needs a larger shape for it to count as safe, while newer players are safe with a small one. Stones arrive on the board and the small shapes lock first.
pros: Newer players build safe shapes sooner.
The larger shape takes more stones.
cons: A big shape is open to being surrounded.
Building a big shape leaves other places thin.

pairs.tendency: The named cards count less for the usual winner's tricks, such as the high trump counting for two points where it is worth four. Tricks still get won, but the prizes in them are smaller.
pros: Newer players score more from each named card.
Players watch the prizes more than the tricks.
cons: The usual winner needs more tricks for the same points.
Losing a named card costs a lot.

pairs.tendency: The usual winner may use only one shared card, and the others may use any two. The middle cards lie face up for all, but they help the usual winner less.
pros: Newer players use more of the middle.
Everyone sees the same open cards.
cons: The usual winner leaves open cards unused.
The same open cards help others more.

pairs.tendency: The usual winner puts two counters in the pot where the others put one. The pot is bigger for whoever wins it, and a draw grows it again.
pros: The pot gets larger every round.
The usual winner pays for the head start up front.
cons: Two counters empty a small purse sooner.
A big pot makes a loss sting more.

pairs.tendency: The usual winner starts with two seeds in each pit and the others start with four. Seeds are dropped round the board, and fewer seeds mean shorter trips and fewer pits reached.
pros: Newer players reach farther round the board.
The seed count shows the head start.
cons: Short trips rarely reach the other side.
Last seeds land close to home.

pairs.tendency: The usual winner may not take the spare hand and picks last when the others swap or buy it. The extra cards go to one of the newer players before the play begins.
pros: Newer players get the extra cards.
The spare hand can change a whole round.
cons: The usual winner starts with the original cards.
Picking last may leave no spare hand to take.

pairs.tendency: The usual winner loses a turn on every special square, while the others lose a turn on only some of them. Each lap past the squares then costs the usual winner a little more.
pros: Newer players pass the squares more easily.
The squares are easy to read.
cons: Losing a turn each time adds up.
Some squares stay safe for the others.

pairs.tendency: The usual winner pays an extra coin for every card or unit, and starts with fewer coins. Newer players buy a unit and pay the normal price.
pros: The others buy more each turn.
Prices are easy to compare.
cons: The usual winner buys fewer things.
The coin gap grows with every buy.

pairs.tendency: The usual winner has seven forces to share out, and the others have ten. Each place gets fewer forces, and the other side can tell which places are thinnest.
pros: Newer players can cover every place.
The usual winner picks places with care.
cons: A thin spread loses several places at once.
A big stack in one place leaves the rest bare.

pairs.tendency: The usual winner starts a step further from the chairs, or has to freeze on the first note. Newer players stay near the seats and wait for the signal.
pros: Newer players reach a seat sooner.
The signal is the same for all.
cons: The usual winner is often the last to sit.
The gap grows if the music stops early.

pairs.tendency: The usual winner may swap one card, and the others may swap three. After the swap each hand is played as it stands, and the newer players have had more chances to tune theirs.
pros: Newer players tune their hands.
One swap makes the choice easy to see.
cons: One swap leaves gaps in the hand.
A hand with three swaps takes longer to sort.

pairs.tendency: The usual winner may take the pile only if the top card matches two ways, while the others need one match. The pile grows, and the newer players pick it up when it is large.
pros: Newer players can take the pile sooner.
The pile builds for whoever can use it.
cons: The usual winner waits for a double match.
A large pile can weigh down the hand that takes it.

pairs.tendency: The usual winner's trump suit counts one rank lower, and the newer players choose which suit is trump. A low trump still wins a trick, but the usual winner's trumps lose to the others' more often.
pros: Newer players name the trump suit.
A low trump still wins tricks.
cons: The usual winner's trumps lose more ties.
Naming the trump suit can give the game away.

pairs.tendency: The usual winner starts the second board a few moves behind the first. The usual winner is attacking on one board and defending on the other, and the late start affects both.
pros: Newer players have the same start on both boards.
Moves on one board change the other.
cons: A late start on the second board is hard to hide.
Watching two boards takes more time.

pairs.tendency: The usual winner gets no wild cards, and each newer player gets two. A set that is missing one piece can be finished by the others, and the usual winner has to wait for the real card.
pros: Newer players finish sets with wild cards.
A wild card can fill any gap.
cons: The usual winner waits for the exact card.
A wild card used early cannot be used again.

pairs.tendency: The usual winner's lines may not wrap round the edge, while the others' lines can. A line that runs off one side comes back in on the other, but only for the newer players.
pros: Newer players can cross the edges.
Lines for the others have no end.
cons: The usual winner stays inside the middle.
The edge works as a wall for one side.

pairs.tendency: The usual winner gets fifteen questions where the others get twenty. Each answer cuts the list of things it could be, and the usual winner has less time to cut it down.
pros: Newer players ask more questions.
Each question has to be chosen with care.
cons: Fifteen questions end sooner.
A wasted question cannot be asked again.

pairs.tendency: The usual winner starts ten spaces back, so the others only need to be quick for a short while. Since the whole game is the race, those ten spaces count at every step.
pros: Newer players start nearer the line.
The gap is easy to see on the track.
cons: A ten-space gap may be too big to close.
The race ends the same way if the gap is wrong.

pairs.tendency: The usual winner starts with minus five points. At the end the totals are added up, and the head start sits in the score from the first turn.
pros: Newer players start with the lead.
The score shows the handicap.
cons: The usual winner chases from behind.
A few missed turns can make the gap too large.

pairs.tendency: The usual winner has two lives where the others have three. Players are knocked out one by one, so the usual winner is the first to be in danger.
pros: Newer players last longer.
The usual winner takes more care in each fight.
cons: One hit costs a larger share of a short life.
Others may aim at the one with fewer lives.

pairs.tendency: The usual winner takes one action a turn where the others take two, so the group carries the extra load together. The game threatens the whole group, which has to cover for one slow player.
pros: Newer players do more of the work.
The team spreads out the jobs.
cons: The usual winner may feel left out.
The team may lose a turn to the short hand.

pairs.tendency: The usual winner may only advise, and the others make the moves that reach the goal. Everyone works toward the same state, and one player holds back on purpose.
pros: Newer players do the moves.
The group talks about each plan.
cons: The usual winner speaks more than they act.
Advice can be ignored.

pairs.tendency: The usual winner has a goal that needs two things, and the others have one. Each goal stays secret, so the others cannot tell which player is working harder.
pros: Newer players pick an easy goal.
Nobody sees the harder goal.
cons: The usual winner has less time for each part.
A double goal gives away the plan when it is half done.

pairs.tendency: The usual winner adds to the story every second turn, and the others add on every turn. Everyone reaches the same ending, and the usual winner has shaped less of the story on the way.
pros: Newer players shape more of the tale.
The story moves along without a score.
cons: The usual winner has fewer chances to steer.
The ending may belong to the others.

pairs.tendency: The usual winner holds something back, but there is no score for it to show up in. Everyone stops at the end and looks at what was made, and the difference comes up only in the talk afterwards.
pros: The head start shows in what each player made.
Nobody has to count it.
cons: A handicap has nothing to level.
The group may skip over it.

pairs.tendency: The usual winner sets a higher goal than the others, such as saving every piece instead of one. All players say their goal at the start and compare at the end.
pros: Newer players set a goal they can reach.
Each player has a clear aim.
cons: A high goal is easy to miss.
The group may argue over who set the harder goal.

pairs.tendency: The usual winner is out after one mistake, and the others are out after two. The game goes on until someone loses, so the usual winner is likely to be the one.
pros: Newer players get a second chance.
Mistakes are counted for all.
cons: The usual winner has less room for a slip.
One slip ends the round for the usual winner.

pairs.tendency: The usual winner makes only the moves that help others carry on. The game does not end, and the head start is spent on keeping it alive.
pros: Newer players keep the play going.
The usual winner learns to help.
cons: The game never shows who is ahead.
The play slows if the usual winner waits.

pairs.tendency: There is no winner to hold back, so the group spends turns asking what the handicap is for. A handicap is meant to even out a contest, and this game has none.
pros: The odd rule starts a talk.
The game shows that a handicap assumes a contest.
cons: The handicap has no target.
The group may stop playing to argue.

pairs.tendency: The usual winner gets one redeal where the player before had three. With one player against the cards, the handicap is measured against an earlier score.
pros: The score from before is the target.
Fewer redeals make each move count.
cons: One redeal leaves little room for error.
A stuck table ends the game sooner.

pairs.tendency: The usual winner has to win three games to take the match, and the others need two. A newer player who wins two straight can stop the match at once.
pros: Newer players need fewer wins.
The match ends once the gap is too big.
cons: Three wins take more games to play.
One loss for the usual winner can be too much to recover.

pairs.tendency: The usual winner starts with ten points added, and the fewest points still win. Every point picked up counts against a player, so the usual winner begins by owing ten.
pros: Newer players start clean.
The head start is a number on the sheet.
cons: The usual winner has to dodge more points.
One heavy round can add to ten at once.

pairs.tendency: The usual winner has to land on the number exactly, while the others can finish if they go past by one. Newer players reach the target and need a little luck to stop.
pros: The others can finish by going over.
The exact target stays the same for all.
cons: The usual winner can overshoot and lose the hand.
A narrow target means long waits.

pairs.tendency: The usual winner begins with more cards to give away. In a game where giving everything away wins, that is a longer way to go, and the others finish sooner.
pros: Newer players have less to give away.
Both sides aim for the same empty hand.
cons: The usual winner needs more turns to get rid of cards.
A slow start can leave the usual winner last.

pairs.tendency: The usual winner begins building with fewer pieces. Each player builds their own thing, so the gap can only be seen by looking across at the other boards.
pros: Newer players have more pieces from the start.
Each player works on their own board.
cons: The gap is not felt until the end.
Nobody can slow anyone else down.

pairs.tendency: The usual winner can attack once a round, and the others can attack the usual winner every time. So the others point their hits at the usual winner more often.
pros: Newer players can hit back more.
Attacks get aimed at one player.
cons: The usual winner takes more hits.
One player may end up as everyone's target.

pairs.tendency: The usual winner moves one piece a turn where the others move two. The others change the board and the usual winner feels it later, because the route has already shifted.
pros: Newer players change the board faster.
The board shows the gap.
cons: The usual winner's route can be blocked.
The usual winner reacts a turn late.

pairs.tendency: The usual winner takes fewer actions and may not give tips. The team beats the game together or loses together, and the newer players have to lean less on that one.
pros: Newer players take the lead.
The team shares its work.
cons: The usual winner may have ideas and no way to say them.
The team may lose a turn waiting on a hint.

pairs.tendency: The usual winner's private reason to win is worth fewer points, so there is less to gain from breaking away. The group works together, and a smaller reward changes who bothers to cheat.
pros: Newer players have more to gain from a private win.
The group works together more.
cons: The usual winner has less reason to try.
A small reward may not be worth a risk.

pairs.tendency: The team with the most skilled players starts with fewer points, or plays one member short. The short side has to share the jobs among fewer hands.
pros: Newer teams start nearer the lead.
Teams talk about who does what.
cons: A short team runs out of hands.
The gap can shift the way the teams plan.

pairs.tendency: The hidden traitor gets fewer actions, and is picked from the side that loses more often. The rest work as a team, so a traitor with less to do hides in the crowd or stands out.
pros: The traitor has less power.
The team has a clearer chance to spot a slip.
cons: The traitor may be found at once.
A traitor with few actions may have no effect.

pairs.tendency: The usual winner waits an extra week before posting each move, so the handicap is measured in days. Letters travel by post and the usual winner sees the others' moves long before they send a reply.
pros: Newer players move first.
The wait fills the days between letters.
cons: A week is a long time to wait for one move.
The usual winner can lose touch with the game.

pairs.tendency: The ghost gives only two hints and the others give four. One player is not at the table, and the hints that reach the guessers are the only help.
pros: Newer players get more hints.
Hints from the absent player count for more.
cons: Two hints leave little to go on.
The guessers wait on a ghost.

pairs.tendency: The game master puts harder scenes in front of the usual winner's character, and softer ones for the rest. The game master runs the world, so the gap is built into what the players meet.
pros: Newer players meet easier scenes.
The game master can adjust the gap during play.
cons: The usual winner may feel singled out.
The game master carries the extra work of balancing.

pairs.tendency: The regulars start behind a chalk line a few steps back, and the people passing by start at the usual line. Anyone walking past can join, and the line tells them how much of a start they get.
pros: Passers-by can join on equal terms.
The chalk line shows the head start.
cons: Regulars may stop coming.
Moving the line can start an argument.

pairs.tendency: The lone player is paid more if they win, and also starts with fewer pieces. So one person begins short against a group that works together.
pros: The group has a lead from the start.
The lone player has a bigger reward to reach for.
cons: The lone player faces many with few.
The group may finish the game too soon.

pairs.tendency: The handicap is set against your own earlier score, such as fewer undos or a shorter clock. There is no one to give a head start to, so the only gap is between today and last time.
pros: The earlier score is the target.
Your own record shows the change.
cons: The short clock may rush each move.
Nobody is there to compare with.

pairs.tendency: The dice decide nearly everything, so a head start of two points is small beside one throw. The usual winner gives up something, and the dice still sort out who gets ahead.
pros: Newer players keep their head start.
The handicap makes the game look more even.
cons: A single throw can erase the head start.
The handicap changes little.

pairs.tendency: The usual winner gets one re-roll where the others get three. The dice still rule the turn, but the newer players have more ways to soften a low throw.
pros: Newer players have more re-rolls.
A re-roll can fix a low throw.
cons: The usual winner has to live with a first roll.
Re-rolls can slow the turn.

pairs.tendency: The usual winner starts with fewer pieces, and a small bit of luck still enters each turn. A lucky draw for the usual winner can close the gap, and choices decide most of the rest.
pros: A lucky card can shift the balance.
Differences in skill show in the choices.
cons: A low draw makes the handicap hurt more.
A small lead can be wiped out by a lucky draw.

pairs.tendency: With no dice, the result follows how the players play, so a handicap can be tuned until the games are close. The usual winner gives up pieces, moves or time and the games get closer.
pros: The result follows the choices.
The size of the handicap can be adjusted after each game.
cons: A wrong guess at the size decides the game.
The same player may win each time with the wrong gap.

pairs.tendency: The usual winner gets fewer questions to ask of the dice, so the throw is read less often. The throw is read as a message with no score attached, and the others ask more questions of it.
pros: Newer players ask more questions.
Each throw is read as a whole.
cons: A throw that is read less carries less meaning.
The gap is hard to measure.

pairs.tendency: The usual winner plays with eyes shut, so they cannot see the others lean in. The others watch each other's faces to sense when to act, and the usual winner has to sense it from sound alone.
pros: Newer players read faces.
The usual winner listens closely.
cons: Shut eyes make timing hard.
The others may act together and leave one behind.

pairs.tendency: The usual winner reads a harder table, so the same roll leads to a harder meeting on the road. The dice write part of the story, and on the usual winner's table the same roll writes a harder part.
pros: Newer players meet kind strangers.
The tables show the gap in the story.
cons: The usual winner meets more trouble.
Two tables take longer to set up.

pairs.tendency: Everything is on show, so every player can see the head start and count what it is worth. Both sides can work out the exact effect of the handicap on each move.
pros: The gap can be counted by anyone.
Both sides plan around it.
cons: The head start cannot be hidden.
Counting the gap can take a while.

pairs.tendency: The usual winner plays with their cards face up, while the others keep theirs hidden. The others can see every card the usual winner holds and plan around it.
pros: Newer players can read the open hand.
The usual winner's plans are on show.
cons: Bluffs are hard to make with an open hand.
Hidden cards stay a surprise to one side.

pairs.tendency: The usual winner's role is told to everyone at the start, and the others' roles stay secret. Everyone can see who the usual winner is, and the rest hide in the crowd.
pros: Newer players keep their roles private.
The usual winner is easy to place.
cons: Nobody has to guess about the usual winner.
The usual winner cannot bluff about who they are.

pairs.tendency: The usual winner has two guesses where the others have three, and gets one clue fewer. Clues point at hidden facts, so with fewer of them the usual winner narrows things down more slowly.
pros: Newer players have more guesses.
Each clue counts for more.
cons: Two guesses end quickly.
A wrong guess is a bigger share of the total.

pairs.tendency: A bluff by the usual winner that is caught costs two chips, and for the others it costs one. Since a caught bluff costs double, the usual winner bluffs less often.
pros: Newer players bluff for less.
Bluffs by the usual winner get watched.
cons: A caught bluff takes more from the usual winner.
The others can call the bluff more easily.

pairs.tendency: The newer players are told one rule before the game starts, and the usual winner is told none. The secret rule is found by breaking it, and the usual winner has more to find out.
pros: Newer players start with a clue.
The usual winner learns by being told no.
cons: Every wrong move shows a rule.
The usual winner may break the rule many times.

pairs.tendency: The usual winner gives the clues with fewer pictures, and the guessers get an extra guess. The clue-giver cannot say the answer, so the guessers have only the hints.
pros: Guessers get more guesses.
Fewer pictures keep each one clear.
cons: Fewer pictures leave less to guess from.
The clue-giver may run out of hints.

pairs.tendency: The usual winner explores one tile at a time, and the others see three tiles from the start. The hidden map is turned over as people explore it, and the others know more of what lies ahead.
pros: Newer players see ahead.
The usual winner finds out as they go.
cons: The usual winner may walk into dead ends.
A tile turned over by one player helps all.

pairs.tendency: The usual winner plays the open hand with no help, and the others may talk it over. One hand lies face up, and the usual winner has to play it without advice.
pros: Newer players can advise.
The open hand is the same for all.
cons: The usual winner plays with little help.
Talking over the open hand slows the play.

pairs.tendency: The size of the head start is kept secret, so nobody knows who is ahead. Some points are hidden, and the handicap adds another hidden number to guess at.
pros: The others keep a lead nobody can see.
Everyone guesses who is ahead.
cons: The head start can go unnoticed.
A guess about the gap can be far off.

pairs.tendency: The usual winner moves after everyone else each round, or skips every third turn. The others get a look at each turn and plan for their own.
pros: Newer players act first.
The usual winner sees what the others did.
cons: Skipped turns add up.
Waiting for a late turn can feel long.

pairs.tendency: The usual winner has less time to choose before the reveal, such as five seconds instead of ten. Everyone picks in secret at the same moment, and the short clock hits one player.
pros: Newer players have longer to think.
All players still reveal together.
cons: The usual winner picks in a hurry.
A rushed pick may be a wrong one.

pairs.tendency: The usual winner waits two seconds after each signal before reaching, while the others grab at once. With no turns, whoever is quickest wins, and the delay gives the others a head start.
pros: The others grab first.
The delay is easy to count.
cons: Two seconds is a long time in a grab.
The usual winner can be left with nothing.

pairs.tendency: The usual winner turns a shorter sand timer, such as ten seconds where the others get twenty. When the sand runs out, the move is lost or made for the player.
pros: Newer players have twice the time.
The clock makes the gap visible.
cons: A short timer can cost a move.
The usual winner may be hurried into a rushed move.

pairs.tendency: The usual winner makes one move every two days, and the others make one a day. The game runs over weeks, so the gap grows with each day that passes.
pros: Newer players move twice as often.
Waiting is part of the play.
cons: The usual winner's moves come few and far between.
The gap is hard to close over days.

pairs.tendency: The usual winner takes a double pause before each move, such as two slow breaths. The slowness is built into the play, and the handicap adds more of it to one player.
pros: Newer players move at the normal pace.
The pause gives time to think.
cons: The usual winner waits longer than the rest.
A long pause can make the game feel stuck.

pairs.tendency: The usual winner begins at the speed the others reach later, such as the fast level from the start. The game speeds up as it goes, so the usual winner begins in a rush.
pros: Newer players start at a gentle pace.
The usual winner meets the full speed early.
cons: The end comes sooner for the fast player.
A fast start leaves less time to learn.

pairs.tendency: The usual winner gets no extra go after a hit, while the others do. Another go comes on some throws, and a lucky newer player can move many times in a row.
pros: Newer players can chain moves.
A hit pays off more for the others.
cons: The usual winner moves once a turn.
A run of extra turns can leave the usual winner far behind.

pairs.tendency: The usual winner carries less from the first stage into the second. What you do in the first stage sets up the second, so a smaller carry-over means a thinner start.
pros: Newer players enter stage two with more.
The second stage shows the first stage's gap.
cons: The usual winner has less to work with later.
A gap from stage one stays through stage two.

pairs.tendency: The usual winner's group in the model starts with less land or water, as real groups often do. The model works like the real system, so the gap spreads through the village.
pros: The model shows an unequal start.
Players see how a small gap spreads.
cons: The short group may run out first.
A model with a gap can feel heavy.

pairs.tendency: One role starts with less, such as a landless farmer next to a council member. Each player plays a real group, so the gap in the roles is a gap in what each group has.
pros: Players see the problem from a smaller start.
The roles differ in what they hold.
cons: The short role has few moves.
Players may argue about who started ahead.

pairs.tendency: The usual winner draws with a smaller cup from the shared water under the village. The others draw with a normal cup, and the pool runs low for all if they take too much.
pros: The others draw more each round.
Everyone sees the pool go down.
cons: The usual winner takes less from the same pool.
A drained pool hurts the small cup first.

pairs.tendency: The handicap shows its effect a few rounds later, not at once. Choices now show up only in later rounds, so nobody knows yet whether the head start was large enough.
pros: The effect of the gap shows up later.
Players plan ahead for the gap.
cons: The gap is hard to judge early on.
A late effect can come as a surprise.

pairs.tendency: The handicap is the new rule the group agrees to try, and then they play on to see what changes. A head start for one side is tested with the whole group watching.
pros: The group sees what the handicap does.
The rule can be dropped after a test.
cons: The test game may be too short to show it.
A rule tried once may not be tried again.

pairs.tendency: After the game, the group talks about whether the head start was felt at the table. They ask what happened and why, and how big the gap seemed to each player.
pros: Everyone says what the gap was like.
The group can change the size next time.
cons: Players may remember the gap differently.
The talk can run long.

pairs.tendency: The usual winner tears up one card for ever, or covers one square with a sticker that stays. The next game starts where this one ended, so the handicap stays on the table.
pros: The handicap carries to the next game.
The change cannot be undone.
cons: The next game starts uneven.
A torn card is gone for every later game.

pairs.tendency: A handicap written into the rules says that some players begin ahead. The players read that message each time they play, whether or not they agree with it.
pros: The rule says something about who starts ahead.
Players can argue with it.
cons: A rule can look like it takes a side.
The argument may be read in different ways.

pairs.tendency: The usual winner stakes more real money, such as ten rupees where the others stake five. What happens in the game carries into life, so the handicap is a cost paid outside it too.
pros: Newer players risk less.
The stake shows what the head start is worth.
cons: The usual winner can lose real money.
A friend may mind paying more.

pairs.tendency: A ten-point handicap stands for something that matters, such as health, and players argue about what ten points handed over really stands for. Players chase points, and the handicap is a number like the rest.
pros: The handicap is a number everyone can see.
Players talk about what the points mean.
cons: A number can hide what it stands for.
Players may chase the number and forget the meaning.

pairs.tendency: A village that shares everything practises giving more to whoever has less, and the handicap is how it is done at the table. Players try out the idea before anyone tries it for real.
pros: Players feel what sharing is like.
The handicap works as a model of giving.
cons: Some players dislike starting with less.
A rehearsed gap may feel different in real life.

pairs.tendency: One player hides a token while the others roll and move along a path, and each space they land on lets them check one spot. The dice decide how many places get searched each turn.
pros: Each throw opens a new place to look.
The path gives the hunt a shape.
cons: A big roll can carry a seeker past the hiding place.
Luck can end the hunt early or drag it out.

pairs.tendency: The hider writes clues on cards and lays them in a row. Seekers pick one at a time, and each pick shows the next seeker what is left.
pros: Every pick tells the others what a seeker thinks matters.
Clues get shared out between seekers.
cons: The last seeker to pick gets the clues nobody wanted.
Slow with many seekers.

pairs.tendency: Seekers bid coins for the right to open a drawer or buy a hint. The highest bid gets to look first.
pros: Players have to decide what a hint is worth.
A seeker with more coins can search more spots.
cons: Coins spent on a wrong spot are gone.
A big bid tells everyone where you think it is.

pairs.tendency: Coins are hidden under cups and seekers keep lifting cups for more. One cup holds a trap that wipes out everything collected so far.
pros: Each lift could pay more.
Seekers watch each other decide when to stop.
cons: One trap cup can erase a long run.
The hunt can end with a seeker holding nothing.

pairs.tendency: The hiding places sit in different regions of a map. Seekers put a piece in every region they search, and the region with the most pieces counts as theirs.
pros: Searching also claims ground.
Seekers have a reason to cover the whole map.
cons: A seeker can hold many regions and still miss the hidden thing.
Pieces pile up in the easy regions.

pairs.tendency: Each seeker sends a worker to search one spot, and a spot with a worker on it is shut to everyone else that round. A seeker can block a place just by standing there.
pros: Seekers can claim a likely spot first.
Blocking a place costs nothing.
cons: Seekers can end up guarding spots that are empty.
The hunt slows when two seekers want the same place.

pairs.tendency: The hidden thing is the tile that finishes a pattern. Seekers fill in their shapes and hunt for the one missing piece.
pros: The pattern shows what to look for.
Seekers have something to do while they search.
cons: A seeker can build around the wrong piece.
Seekers stop searching to finish their shape.

pairs.tendency: Seekers hold cards that stand for searches, hints and tools, and choose when to spend each. A search card played on an empty spot is used up.
pros: Players plan which card to keep for later.
A held card can wait for the right moment.
cons: One wrong play uses up a card.
Players take long to decide with a full hand.

pairs.tendency: Each trick is played for the right to search. Whoever wins it lifts one cushion, so a high card turns into a look under it.
pros: A winning card opens a place to look.
Players read each other's cards and clues.
cons: A seeker who keeps losing tricks never gets to search.
The hiding place may be found by whoever wins the last trick.

pairs.tendency: Seekers trade what they have found. One says "I checked the cupboard, so tell me about the shed", and nobody can check that it is true.
pros: Seekers cover more ground by sharing.
Players learn who they can trust.
cons: A false trade can send a seeker the wrong way.
Talking takes longer than searching.

pairs.tendency: Several things are hidden, and each belongs to a set, such as three keys or three coins. Seekers find them to collect matching sets.
pros: Every find has a use.
Seekers can aim for one set.
cons: A seeker with two keys keeps hunting for the third.
A hunt for one last piece can run on.

pairs.tendency: The map grows as tiles go down, and the hider's mark sits under one of them. Each new tile adds a place to search.
pros: The hunt changes as the map grows.
Seekers decide where to add tiles.
cons: The hiding place may be covered by a new tile.
The map gets wide, so searching takes longer.

pairs.tendency: A seeker calls out a place, the hider calls back a clue, and the next seeker answers with a place of their own. The hunt goes back and forth like two people singing.
pros: Each call gives the next player a clue.
The hunt has a steady rhythm.
cons: A long chain is hard to remember.
One mishearing can ruin the next answer.

pairs.tendency: Nobody speaks, so the hider can only point or leave a mark, and the seekers show where they are heading by moving. All the hints are in what people do.
pros: Players watch every movement.
A small sign can carry a lot.
cons: Seekers can read a sign in the wrong way.
A wrong guess stays hard to fix with no words.

pairs.tendency: On your turn you can rewrite a rule, such as which rooms may be searched, so a seeker near the hiding place can close the door on the others. The hunt changes halfway through.
pros: A seeker can reshape the hunt.
The hider can change the rules too.
cons: Players spend time arguing over each new rule.
A rule change can wipe out someone's progress.

pairs.tendency: The hider plays a ghost or a thief and the seekers play detectives, all speaking in character. The hunt turns into a scene with a character behind each search.
pros: Each search comes with a reason.
Players can invent clues in the voice of their character.
cons: Some players take a while to join in.
The scene can run on after the thing is found.

pairs.tendency: The hider's token sits inside a stack of blocks, and a seeker has to lift pieces out one by one to look. A shaky hand knocks the stack and shows the hiding place to everyone.
pros: Careful hands are part of the search.
A tall stack makes the hunt tense for onlookers.
cons: A clumsy seeker can give the answer away.
A topple can end the game at once.

pairs.tendency: The hider draws the map as the hunt goes on and the seekers add rooms and marks. A hiding place can only be somewhere that is already on the paper.
pros: The map shows where people have been.
Players can see what has been left out.
cons: A messy map is hard to read.
The hider can draw a new room just to hide in.

pairs.tendency: The token is under one of the pieces on the board. A seeker hops a piece, lands in the space past it, and lifts the hopped piece to look underneath.
pros: A hop also gives a look.
Seekers plan a chain of hops.
cons: Lifting a piece can also remove it.
A piece that is already gone cannot be checked again.

pairs.tendency: Each die shows a place to look. Seekers set aside the dice they want, throw the rest again, and stop after a few rolls.
pros: A seeker can aim at certain spots.
Two throws give a second chance.
cons: A re-throw can lose a spot you wanted.
Seekers wait while others throw again and again.

pairs.tendency: Seekers walk towards the hiding place, and landing on another seeker sends that piece back to the start. A seeker close to the end can lose all their walking.
pros: Every landing can undo someone's progress.
Players watch where others stand.
cons: A seeker near the goal can be sent back in one throw.
Players spend turns chasing each other.

pairs.tendency: The hider's token is under one of the other side's pieces. When a player makes a row of three, they remove one of those pieces and look under it.
pros: A row also gives a look.
Players build and break rows at once.
cons: Taking a piece may show nothing.
Blocking rows can matter more than searching.

pairs.tendency: The hidden thing is a word. Seekers guess letters, the word fills in on the table, and the first to say it gets it.
pros: Each guess shows another letter.
Players need to know their words.
cons: A wrong letter helps the others.
A word nobody knows can stop the game.

pairs.tendency: Clue tiles are laid in a line, and each new tile has to match the number at one end. The line of tiles points towards the hiding place.
pros: Each tile pushes the line further.
Seekers see the chain growing.
cons: A seeker with no matching tile misses a turn.
The hunt waits until a matching tile turns up.

pairs.tendency: Seekers lay found clues face up as sets, and other seekers can add matching clues to a set on the table. Every set is open to all.
pros: A set shows what is known.
Seekers can build on each other's finds.
cons: Laying a set shows the others a hint.
A set left on the table can be used by someone else.

pairs.tendency: Each seeker has one special power, such as looking in two spots at once, and can use it a single time. The hider may have one too, such as moving the thing once.
pros: Players pick the moment for their power.
The hider has a surprise too.
cons: A power used too early is gone.
Players wait to use powers and the hunt slows.

pairs.tendency: A seeker names a spot to search, and the hider can allow it or offer two other spots to choose from. The hider has a say in where the hunt goes.
pros: The hider takes part in every turn.
A seeker has to read what the hider will offer.
cons: A turn can end with a place the seeker did not want.
The hider can steer seekers away.

pairs.tendency: The hider's clue is whispered from seeker to seeker, and it can change on the way. The last seeker hears something different from what the first heard.
pros: Players learn how clues change.
The last listener has the hardest clue.
cons: A clue may be garbled by the time it arrives.
Nobody can check the message until the end.

pairs.tendency: Before the hunt, each seeker hands a few clue cards to a neighbour without seeing what comes back. A seeker may give away the clue they most needed.
pros: Clues move around the table.
Players choose what to give away.
cons: A seeker may lose a key clue.
A neighbour may get a clue and not know its use.

pairs.tendency: One player makes the hiding place, then the other picks which side to take, hider or seeker. A hiding place that looks very easy or very hard will be picked over by the other player.
pros: The first player tries to make both sides even.
The second player picks whichever side looks stronger.
cons: The first player has to guess how it will look to someone else.
An uneven hiding place gets taken at once.

pairs.tendency: A seeker who reaches the far edge of the board turns into a piece that can search more places, such as two rooms in a turn. The race to the far edge matters as much as the hunt.
pros: There is a reason to push forward.
A promoted piece covers more ground.
cons: Seekers may walk past the hiding place on the way.
A promoted piece can end the hunt very fast.

pairs.tendency: Each team runs the hunt in legs. A runner finds a clue at one stop, carries it to the next runner, and the last runner finds the thing.
pros: Each runner depends on the last.
The team shares one hunt.
cons: One slow runner holds up everyone.
A runner waiting for a clue has nothing to do.

pairs.tendency: The hidden thing sits inside a ring of stones. The hider builds a shape that cannot be captured, and seekers try to surround it to look inside.
pros: The hider has a goal to build towards.
Seekers can see where the hiding place is likely to be.
cons: A safe shape can keep seekers out for the whole game.
The shape gives the hiding place away.

pairs.tendency: Some cards are named in advance as worth points, and one of them shows where the thing is hidden. Seekers hunt through the deck for the named cards.
pros: Players know which cards to look for.
One find can score twice.
cons: A seeker can hold the named card without knowing it.
Players hunt for points and forget the hiding place.

pairs.tendency: Clue cards lie face up in the middle, so every seeker works from the same evidence and adds it to their own hand.
pros: Seekers share the same clues.
Players still have private cards to hold back.
cons: Two seekers can reach the same answer together.
The first to read the clues has the advantage.

pairs.tendency: Every seeker puts a counter in the middle before the hunt, and whoever finds the thing takes the pot. If nobody finds it, the pot stays and grows for the next hunt.
pros: The prize grows when the thing stays hidden.
Seekers have a reason to find it quickly.
cons: A big pot makes the next hunt tenser.
A hunt with no winner leaves everyone paying.

pairs.tendency: The hidden thing is under one of a row of pits. A seeker scoops up seeds, drops them one by one round the pits, and checks the pit where the last seed lands.
pros: The seeds decide where to look.
A seeker can plan where the last seed will fall.
cons: A count that is wrong sends the seeker to the wrong pit.
Counting seeds takes a while.

pairs.tendency: An extra hand of clue cards is dealt face down in the middle. One seeker can take it, swap it for their own, or buy it before the hunt starts.
pros: Players can pick up new clues.
The spare hand holds a surprise.
cons: The spare hand may hold nothing useful.
A swap tells the others what the seeker was missing.

pairs.tendency: Some squares on the track are safe spots for the hider, some reveal a clue, and some make a seeker miss a turn. Landing on the wrong one costs a turn.
pros: Squares give the track a character.
Some squares reward searching.
cons: A trap square can lose a turn.
Seekers learn the squares and avoid them.

pairs.tendency: Every search has a price and a wide search costs more. Seekers choose between several cheap looks and one costly one.
pros: Each search has a clear cost.
Players can plan how to spend.
cons: A costly search may find nothing.
A seeker who runs out of money stops looking.

pairs.tendency: A seeker has five searchers to share across several rooms. Many in one room leaves another room empty, and the hider can see where the searchers went.
pros: Players choose where to look.
Seekers weigh a likely room against an unlikely one.
cons: An empty room can be where the thing is.
The hider can move after seeing the split.

pairs.tendency: The seekers move around while music plays, and when it stops they freeze and each checks the spot nearest to them. Where you stand when the sound ends is where you look.
pros: Everyone looks at the same moment.
The signal makes the hunt a surprise.
cons: A seeker may freeze far from the hiding place.
The slowest seeker is caught and out.

pairs.tendency: Seekers can put clue cards back and take new ones from the pile. Each swap tells the others which clue a seeker did not want.
pros: Seekers can change a hand that is missing clues.
A swap shows what someone does not need.
cons: Another player has to agree sometimes.
Swapping can go on without anyone searching.

pairs.tendency: Clue cards that seekers throw away pile up in the middle. A seeker can pick up the whole pile if they can use the top card at once, and so gets every clue the others dropped.
pros: A pile holds old clues.
Taking it can give a seeker a big lead.
cons: A seeker with a big pile holds too many to use.
The others watch the pile and hold back.

pairs.tendency: One suit is named trump, and the hider has to hide the thing in a place that matches it. A low trump can still point seekers there ahead of a high card of another suit.
pros: The trump suit tells seekers where to look.
A low card can still help.
cons: Seekers who lack the suit can only guess.
The hider is limited to a few places.

pairs.tendency: You hide on one board and seek on another at the same time. Your opponent is hunting your hiding place while you hunt theirs.
pros: Every move helps one board and risks the other.
Players have to watch two things.
cons: Turns spent seeking leave your own hiding place unwatched.
It is easy to forget the other board.

pairs.tendency: A wild card can stand for any place, so a seeker can use one card to call a spot nobody expected. The hider can hold one too and use it to bluff.
pros: One card can open any place.
A wild card can finish a search.
cons: A wild card used early is gone.
A hider can use one to move the search elsewhere.

pairs.tendency: The edges of the board join, so a seeker who walks off the right side comes back in on the left. A hiding place near one edge is also near the opposite edge.
pros: No corner is out of reach.
The board has no dead ends.
cons: Seekers can walk in circles.
The hider has no far corner to use.

pairs.tendency: The hider knows the place and the seekers ask questions that can only be answered yes or no. Each answer crosses out some of the places.
pros: Every answer shrinks the list.
Questions give the seekers clues.
cons: A muddled question wastes a turn.
The hider answers the same few words again and again.

pairs.tendency: Everyone hunts at once and the first seeker to find the thing wins. Speed counts, so a seeker who finds a clue early may run straight for the spot.
pros: Every seeker has a reason to hurry.
The game ends the moment someone finds it.
cons: A seeker who is slow may never get a turn.
Clues are not shared, since sharing costs a lead.

pairs.tendency: Seekers score points for each hidden item they find, and whoever has the most at the end wins even if someone else found the last item.
pros: Many finds count, not just the first.
Seekers can build up a score.
cons: The seeker who found the last item may not win.
The hunt goes on after the main item is found.

pairs.tendency: Each hider who is found is out of the game, and the last hider still hidden wins. Hiders watch the seekers closely.
pros: Hiders have a stake in the hunt.
The hunt gets tighter as people drop out.
cons: Players who are found wait out the rest.
Hiders with no safe place are found early.

pairs.tendency: All the players hunt together against a clock or a monster that gets closer each round. They win by finding the thing before it catches them.
pros: Everyone shares the same pressure.
Players plan the search together.
cons: A single mistake can cost the whole table.
A quiet player can be left out of the plan.

pairs.tendency: All the players hunt for the same thing and share what they find. The win is one object found by anyone.
pros: A find helps every player.
Players can split up the places to search.
cons: One loud player can take over the plan.
There is little to separate the players.

pairs.tendency: Each seeker has a secret reason for the hunt, such as wanting one particular item, and keeps it hidden. A seeker may steer the others away from the spot they want.
pros: Players read each other's suggestions.
Every seeker has a private reason to search.
cons: A seeker may lead the others astray on purpose.
The hunt can stall while players doubt each other.

pairs.tendency: The hunt is a chapter of a story, and the game ends when the story does. Finding the thing is the turn of the plot.
pros: Each search adds to the story.
Players are curious about what comes next.
cons: The hunt may stretch to fit the plot.
A story can end before the thing is found.

pairs.tendency: Players hide and find with no winner. When the thing is found, they stop and talk about where it was and why they looked where they did.
pros: Players look at what happened.
Nobody has to hurry.
cons: There is nothing to push the hunt along.
The hunt may end with no clear sign it is over.

pairs.tendency: Each player decides what counts as a successful hunt, such as finding it first or finding it in fewer tries. Two players can finish the same hunt and feel differently about it.
pros: Players choose their own aim.
A slow seeker can still reach a goal.
cons: Players may argue over who succeeded.
Goals are hard to compare.

pairs.tendency: Nobody wins. The first player to be found is the loser and everyone else is safe.
pros: The hunt has a clear end.
Players try hard not to be first.
cons: One player takes all the loss.
The rest of the table is done and has nothing left to play.

pairs.tendency: When the thing is found, the finder hides it again, so the hunt never really ends. The game lasts as long as players keep hiding and looking.
pros: Everyone keeps a role in the game.
Each round starts from the last.
cons: The hunt has no natural end.
A tired table may drift out of the game.

pairs.tendency: The thing is hidden where nobody can ever find it, or it moves whenever a seeker gets close. The hunt never gets there.
pros: Players see what the game refuses to give.
Searching is all there is to do.
cons: Players may feel cheated.
Some players give up early.

pairs.tendency: You search a grid of face-down cards alone, looking for the one card that clears the table. If you flip every card without finding it, you lose.
pros: The layout is a puzzle.
A player can try again at once.
cons: Nobody else is there to share a clue.
A wrong flip early can decide the game.

pairs.tendency: The game is played as three short hunts, and a different player hides each time. Whoever wins two hunts wins the match.
pros: Each player gets a turn to hide.
One lost hunt is not the end.
cons: Players who lose the first two hunts can stop early.
The match takes longer than a single hunt.

pairs.tendency: Every wrong search adds a point against you. When the thing is found, the seeker with the fewest points wins.
pros: Every look counts.
Careful seekers come out ahead.
cons: A seeker who searches many places piles up points.
A seeker who waits can let the others take the points.

pairs.tendency: A seeker has to reach the hiding place with an exact throw. Overshooting the spot means waiting for the next turn.
pros: Seekers can be close and still not win.
The last throw matters.
cons: A seeker near the hiding place can wait many turns.
Others catch up while the leader waits.

pairs.tendency: The seeker who finds the thing first loses, so players try to look close to it without lifting it. The hunt turns into staying near without touching.
pros: Players watch closely where they search.
Looking nearly right is the aim.
cons: A seeker may find it by accident.
The hider's clues do the opposite of their purpose.

pairs.tendency: Each player hides and hunts on their own board at the same time, never touching the others'. Everyone races their own search.
pros: Players work at their own speed.
Nobody waits for another turn.
cons: Players have little to say to each other.
A player may not notice how the others are doing.

pairs.tendency: Seekers attack each other while they hunt, stealing clues or knocking a rival out of a room. The thing hidden is only one of the targets.
pros: Players have to watch each other.
A clue can be taken from a rival.
cons: A seeker can be chased out of the room they wanted.
Players spend more time on each other than on the hunt.

pairs.tendency: Seekers close off rooms with walls or markers, which slows the others without any attack. A closed room is felt by everyone who wanted it.
pros: Blocking is quiet.
The board shows who has been where.
cons: A wall can shut out the player who built it.
Players may not know who closed a room.
