pairs.tendency: All the seekers are on one team, and the hiding is done by the game, which moves the thing by its own rules. They find it together or fail together.
pros: Everyone shares one aim.
Players can split up the search.
cons: One plan dominates when one player talks the most.
A failed hunt belongs to all.

pairs.tendency: Seekers share clues so the thing can be found, but each wants to be the one who finds it. A clever seeker keeps the last clue back.
pros: Seekers need each other for most of the hunt.
A secret reason sits under the teamwork.
cons: Players may hold back clues.
Players doubt each other near the end.

pairs.tendency: One team hides and the other hunts, and the hiding team decides together where to put the thing. The hunters talk through their searches.
pros: Each team plans as a group.
Players learn what their team thinks.
cons: A team can argue over where to hide.
The hunters wait while the hiders decide.

pairs.tendency: A secret traitor sits among the seekers and steers them to the wrong rooms. The group watches each other's suggestions for a place that is too keen.
pros: Every suggestion is read twice.
The traitor can be caught by the way they search.
cons: A seeker may be blamed by mistake.
Players spend time on suspicion instead of searching.

pairs.tendency: The hider writes a clue and posts it, and the seeker replies with a guess. A single hunt can last weeks, and waiting for the next letter is part of it.
pros: Each clue is read slowly.
A long wait gives time to think.
cons: The post can be lost or late.
The hunt may be forgotten between letters.

pairs.tendency: The hider is not at the table. They left clues earlier, or a ghost gives hints and nothing else. Seekers read what has been left behind.
pros: The clues show how the hider thinks.
Seekers have to think about the person who hid it.
cons: The hider cannot answer questions.
A clue that was written in a muddle cannot be fixed.

pairs.tendency: The game master hides the thing and describes each place the players search, deciding what they find there. The hider is also the one who tells the story.
pros: The game master can add details as needed.
Searching feels like walking through a world.
cons: The game master knows the answer and has to keep quiet.
The game master can slip clues in by accident.

pairs.tendency: The hider is a person in the street, and anyone passing can join the hunt, marking places with chalk. People who did not start the game end up in it.
pros: Passers-by can join in.
The hunt uses the real street.
cons: The number of players keeps changing.
Traffic and weather get in the way.

pairs.tendency: One hider takes on all the seekers at once. The seekers work together, and the lone hider is paid more if they stay hidden.
pros: The hider has a big stake.
The seekers can plan together.
cons: The hider has no one to share a plan with.
The seekers can wear the hider down.

pairs.tendency: You hunt alone for something placed by the pack or a shuffled deck. Nobody else acts, so luck and your own choices decide where you look.
pros: You can play at once, any time.
A friend can compare scores later.
cons: Nobody else to share a find with.
A single run can end quickly.

pairs.tendency: Dice or draws decide where the thing is and where each seeker looks. The hunt is a series of throws and nobody can plan.
pros: Anyone can win a hunt.
Players start without any need to know the rules.
cons: Choices make little difference.
A hunt can end in a single throw.

pairs.tendency: Dice pick the spots seekers may look at, but a seeker can throw again once or spend a clue to look a second time. A low throw can be patched.
pros: Dice add surprise to every turn.
A seeker has some control over low throws.
cons: Using a re-throw early leaves none for later.
A patched throw can still miss.

pairs.tendency: Reasoning from clues does most of the finding, and a small throw decides which spot is open on a turn. Careful thinking is worth the most.
pros: Clues reward thinking.
A throw adds a surprise.
cons: An unlucky throw can close the likeliest spot.
A lucky throw can hand over the thing.

pairs.tendency: There are no dice. The hider picks the spot by thought and the seekers reason out where it is. The sharper reader of clues wins.
pros: Careful reasoning pays off.
Players read each other.
cons: A sharp hider is hard to find.
A new player is at a disadvantage.

pairs.tendency: Seekers throw dice or flip a coin and read the result as a hint for where to look, then argue what it means. The same throw can point to two different rooms.
pros: The throw gives a starting thought.
Players explain their reading to each other.
cons: Two readings of one throw can split the table.
A hunt can follow a throw that meant nothing.

pairs.tendency: Seekers try to sense where the hider will be and pick the same spot at once. Friends who know each other's habits find it faster.
pros: Players tune in to each other.
A close group finds it quickly.
cons: Strangers have no way to guess.
A seeker can be right and still not be sure.

pairs.tendency: A roll on a table says what is found in each place, such as an empty room, a note or a creature. The dice write part of the hunt.
pros: Every search has a surprise.
The place gets a story of its own.
cons: The thing may turn up in a place that does not suit the story.
Players spend time looking up each result.

pairs.tendency: If every piece and card is face up, there is nothing left to hide. The hunt turns into walking a route to a place all can see, or a puzzle of reaching it first.
pros: Everyone sees the whole board.
Nobody can claim a trick.
cons: The hiding is gone, so a seeker only races.
The first player to read the board has the lead.

pairs.tendency: Seekers hold cards nobody else can see, and one seeker may hold the clue the others need. The hiding is in the hands and in the room.
pros: Every hand may hold a clue.
Players ask each other what they have.
cons: A seeker may keep the key card in their hand.
A seeker with a thin hand sits out of the hunt.

pairs.tendency: Some players are secretly hiders among the seekers. The seekers hunt for the thing and also guess who is who.
pros: Searching also tests the players.
A hider can look like a seeker.
cons: A seeker may accuse the wrong person.
Players spend time on who instead of where.

pairs.tendency: Seekers get clues and work out the place from a list of rooms. Each clue crosses out some rooms until one is left.
pros: Each clue narrows the search.
Players cross out the rooms in turn.
cons: A single wrong clue sends everyone the wrong way.
The last rooms are guessed more than worked out.

pairs.tendency: The hider points at wrong rooms and says the clues are warm. Seekers decide whether to believe it.
pros: The hider can lead seekers astray.
Players watch faces and voices.
cons: A seeker can trust the wrong clue.
A bluff that works can end a hunt early.

pairs.tendency: The hiding place follows a secret rule, such as always under something red. Seekers learn the rule by searching wrong places and being told no.
pros: Every wrong guess teaches something.
The rule gives a pattern to find.
cons: New players learn by failing.
The hunt waits until someone guesses the rule.

pairs.tendency: The player who knows the place is not allowed to say it and gives hints with pictures. Seekers guess where it is from the pictures.
pros: The hints can be read in many ways.
Seekers argue over what a picture means.
cons: The hider watches seekers go the wrong way.
A muddled hint cannot be taken back.

pairs.tendency: The map is turned over room by room. The hider's spot is among the rooms not yet seen, and each room revealed shrinks the places left.
pros: Each step shows a new room.
Seekers know the hiding place is further on.
cons: A room revealed with nothing in it uses a turn.
Players cannot plan ahead of the map.

pairs.tendency: One hand of clue cards is laid face up so everyone can see it, while the other hands stay secret. A seeker may play the open hand and their own.
pros: The open hand is shared.
Seekers can plan with what they see.
cons: The open hand shows the others a clue.
The secret hands matter less than the open one.

pairs.tendency: Points for finding clues are kept secret, so seekers do not know who is close. A seeker may sit on a find and say nothing.
pros: Players guess who is ahead.
A seeker can bluff about a score.
cons: Nobody can add up the scores.
A hidden lead is hard to catch.

pairs.tendency: One seeker searches at a time and the others watch. Every empty look is seen by the whole table.
pros: Each turn adds to what all know.
Players wait and plan.
cons: Long waits with many seekers.
A watcher may spot what the searcher missed.

pairs.tendency: All seekers pick a spot in secret and reveal together. Two seekers on the same spot share what is found there.
pros: Nobody waits for a turn.
Players guess what the others will pick.
cons: Two picks on one spot waste a look.
The first reveal can end the hunt.

pairs.tendency: Anyone may search at any moment, so the quickest hands get to the spots first. The hunt becomes a scramble across the table.
pros: Fast players get a head start.
The room is lively.
cons: Slower players can be left out.
Two hands may reach the same spot together.

pairs.tendency: Each seeker gets a count of ten to choose a spot to search, and when the count ends the choice is made for them. The hunt keeps moving.
pros: The clock keeps the hunt going.
There is little time to doubt.
cons: A rushed choice can be a wrong one.
A random pick can waste a turn.

pairs.tendency: The thing is hidden and each seeker searches one spot every morning for weeks. The hunt lasts as long as the days it takes.
pros: Waiting is part of the hunt.
Players have time to think between looks.
cons: The hunt can be forgotten midway.
The hider has to keep the secret for weeks.

pairs.tendency: Seekers pause and breathe before each search, so the hunt moves slowly. The pause gives time to notice small things in the room.
pros: Players notice details.
The slow pace is calm.
cons: Players can lose patience.
A short hunt becomes a long one.

pairs.tendency: The timer shrinks each round, so the early rounds are slow and the last ones are a scramble through the rooms. The thing is often found in a rush.
pros: The hunt builds towards the end.
Seekers feel the clock tighten.
cons: A late hunt is mostly guesses.
A seeker with a slow start has no time to catch up.

pairs.tendency: A lucky roll or a found clue gives another search at once. A lucky seeker can look in several spots before anyone else moves.
pros: A find can lead straight to another.
A lucky streak can change the hunt.
cons: Others wait while one player keeps going.
A long streak can end the hunt for the rest.

pairs.tendency: The first stage is hiding and making clues, and the second is the hunt. What the hider sets up in the first stage decides what the seekers meet in the second.
pros: The setup shapes the hunt.
Each stage has its own task.
cons: A thin setup makes a short hunt.
Players wait out a stage that is not theirs.

pairs.tendency: The hidden thing is a leak in a model of a village's water pipes. Each place a seeker searches follows how water moves, so the search works like tracing a real leak.
pros: A search teaches how the system works.
The clues come from the model.
cons: A model that is too simple gives the hiding place away.
Players need to learn the model before searching.

pairs.tendency: Each seeker plays a group such as a farmer, a shopkeeper or a council member, all hunting the same missing thing for their own reasons. They each search different places.
pros: Each group looks in its own places.
Players see the hunt from another side.
cons: Groups may not agree on where to start.
Some roles have more places to look than others.

pairs.tendency: The table shares a limited pool of search tokens. Each look uses some, and if seekers spend too many early, nobody has any left.
pros: The pool makes players think of the others.
Seekers can agree on who searches.
cons: A greedy seeker can empty the pool.
The hunt ends when the tokens run out.

pairs.tendency: A search made now shows its result only after a few rounds. Seekers have to wait to learn whether their spot was the right one.
pros: Each look has a later effect.
Players plan ahead.
cons: A wrong spot is only known late.
Seekers cannot learn from a look at once.

pairs.tendency: Players agree a new rule for the hunt, such as no searching the same room twice, and then play on to see how it changes where people look.
pros: A rule can be tested safely.
The group sees what the rule changes.
cons: A rule may make the hunt slow.
Players have to agree before they begin.

pairs.tendency: When the thing is found, the group talks through where it was, which clues helped and what each person thought. The talk is part of the game.
pros: Players hear each other's thinking.
The hunt can be compared to a real search.
cons: The talk takes longer than the hunt.
A quiet player may have little to say.

pairs.tendency: Each hiding place that has been used is marked or torn, so the next game has to hide the thing somewhere new. The board fills with used places.
pros: Each game leaves a mark.
The next hunt starts from the last.
cons: The hiding places run out.
Nothing can be undone.

pairs.tendency: If the rules let seekers search big houses freely but make them pay to search small huts, the hunt says something about who gets looked for.
pros: The rules make a point.
Players notice what the hunt rewards.
cons: A point made by a rule can be missed.
Players may disagree with the point.

pairs.tendency: The thing hidden is real, such as a friend's phone or a bet on who buys the tea. The hunt carries into real life.
pros: The search matters to everyone.
Players care about the outcome.
cons: A lost hunt can leave a mark outside the game.
Some players do not want to join.

pairs.tendency: Hidden cards stand for something that matters, such as kindness, and each find scores points. Seekers start to chase the cards for the score and step over what they were meant to stand for.
pros: Players see what a number does to a value.
The hunt has a clear score.
cons: The points replace the thing they stand for.
A seeker may skip a find that scores little.

pairs.tendency: Players hunt for a lost thing in a village where everything is shared, to see how a search works there. Nobody owns the rooms, so everyone may look anywhere.
pros: Players try a new way of living.
The hunt shows how sharing feels.
cons: The village is hard to picture.
Habits from outside the game get in the way.

pairs.tendency: Dice say how far you travel along the path, and a piece standing in your way can be hopped over if an empty space lies behind it.
pros: The dice give the distance and the hop gives a way round.
Crowded paths can still be crossed.
cons: A big roll can end beside a gap you cannot use.
Counting spaces and hops together slows young players.

pairs.tendency: Cards go round the table one pick at a time, and the card you keep decides which hop your piece can make next.
pros: A pick sets up a later hop.
Players watch which cards leave the row.
cons: A card taken for hopping leaves the rest of your hand thin.
Waiting for the row to come back is slow.

pairs.tendency: Players offer counters for the right to move first, and the winner spends that turn hopping over a piece.
pros: Paying for a turn makes a hop worth something.
Everyone can see what a move is worth to the others.
cons: A big bid leaves little to spend later.
The winner may find no gap open to hop into.

pairs.tendency: After each hop you may hop again if another gap opens, and a long chain scores more, but one landing in the wrong place leaves your piece open.
pros: Each extra hop adds to what you gain.
Players watch a chain and wait for the slip.
cons: A piece stranded mid-board can be lost in one reply.
Stopping early feels like handing points away.

pairs.tendency: Pieces hop across the map into regions, and a hop into the gap behind an enemy piece takes a spot from its holder.
pros: A hop can reach a region in one move.
Holding a region depends on what stands next to it.
cons: A lone piece in a region can be jumped out.
Players guard the edges instead of the middle.

pairs.tendency: Workers sit on job spaces, and a worker may hop over another to reach a job that looked cut off.
pros: A blocked job can still be reached.
Workers keep moving after they are placed.
cons: Jobs are open from so many sides that few can be guarded.
Players check the gaps before every placement.

pairs.tendency: Pieces hop into gaps to fill out a line or a mosaic, and each hop moves one piece to where the pattern is missing a spot.
pros: Hops fill gaps quickly.
A pattern can change shape in mid-game.
cons: A hop can break the row you were building.
Players look over every pattern before moving.

pairs.tendency: Cards stay in your hand until the right moment, and a held card lets one piece make a hop it could not make before.
pros: A saved card keeps a hop in reserve.
Players guess what the others are holding.
cons: A held card does nothing until it is played.
A full hand makes each turn longer.

pairs.tendency: Each trick goes to the highest card, and the winner moves a piece by hopping over one of the losing side's pieces.
pros: A trick win turns into a move on the board.
Cards and board both give clues to watch.
cons: Losing tricks can leave pieces open to a hop.
Two things to track lengthen each turn.

pairs.tendency: Players talk over who will leave a gap, since an empty space behind a piece is an invitation to hop.
pros: Deals can hold back a hop.
Table talk shows who is allied.
cons: A promise not to hop can be broken in a single move.
Talking stretches out every turn.

pairs.tendency: Every hop lands on or takes a piece, and the pieces you gather build into matching groups.
pros: Each hop collects something.
Players aim at the piece they still lack.
cons: Hunting for one piece pushes other groups aside.
A half-finished group can lose a piece to a hop.

pairs.tendency: A map grows tile by tile while pieces hop over each other across the tiles already laid.
pros: The board changes shape between hops.
New tiles open or close hopping routes.
cons: A hop planned last turn may be gone this turn.
Players recount their routes after every tile.

pairs.tendency: One player makes a move and the next answers with a hop that echoes it, so the game runs like a chain of replies.
pros: Each hop answers the one before.
The game finds a rhythm.
cons: The last hop forces the reply, so choices shrink.
A chain can go on for a long time.

pairs.tendency: Nobody speaks, so a hop over a piece is the only message anyone sends.
pros: A hop shows what a player is after.
Players read each other from the moves alone.
cons: A misread hop cannot be cleared up out loud.
Watching goes quiet and slow.

pairs.tendency: A player may change a rule on their turn, such as whether a hopped piece is taken or stays, so what a hop does shifts mid-game.
pros: Rule changes stop old plans from settling in.
Players learn what a hop does by trying it.
cons: A hop planned under one rule may fail under the next.
Arguments start over which rule applies now.

pairs.tendency: Each player speaks as a character, and a hop is something the character does, like leaping a wall or a stream.
pros: Hops become part of a story.
Players describe the leap before they take it.
cons: The story can stall while spaces are counted.
Quieter players may say little.

pairs.tendency: A piece is flicked to land over another, so a hop comes from the hand and not from a count of spaces.
pros: Hops depend on a steady hand.
Everyone sees how hard a flick was.
cons: A shaky hand turns a plan into a miss.
Pieces knocked off the board need setting back.

pairs.tendency: The board is drawn as play goes on, and pieces hop across lines and spaces that someone drew only a turn ago.
pros: The map is made by the players.
Hops follow the paths people drew.
cons: Drawn spaces can sit too far apart for a hop.
Arguments start over what counts as an empty space.

pairs.tendency: Dice are rolled and some are set aside, and the number of hops you may make comes from the dice you keep.
pros: Kept dice shape your hops.
The roll is shaped by your own choice.
cons: A low roll leaves one short hop.
Rolling again and again adds waiting between turns.

pairs.tendency: A piece hops onto a space held by another piece, and the piece that stood there goes back to the start.
pros: A hop can undo many turns of travel.
Players keep a close eye on their pieces.
cons: Pieces near the end are the most worried.
A long lead can vanish in one landing.

pairs.tendency: Hops move your pieces into a line of three, and a finished row lets you take one of the other player's pieces on top of any hop.
pros: A hop can finish a row.
One turn can take two pieces.
cons: Players watch every row, their own and the others.
A broken row sends a player back to building.

pairs.tendency: The pieces are letters, and a letter can hop over another into an empty square to spell a word along a row.
pros: Hops put letters where words are missing one.
A dictionary settles any dispute.
cons: A letter hopped away can break a word that was nearly done.
Spelling and hopping together take thinking time.

pairs.tendency: A line of tiles grows from its two ends, and a piece may hop over a tile only to land where the number on the end matches.
pros: Hops and matches work together.
Players read the open ends before moving.
cons: A missing number can freeze a hop that looked ready.
Players pass a turn when nothing matches.

pairs.tendency: Sets of cards are laid face up on the table, and a piece may hop over a laid set to reach a gap on the far side.
pros: Laid sets are open for all to see.
Adding to a set can open a hop.
cons: Showing a set tells others what you are holding.
A big laid set can wall off the board.

pairs.tendency: Each piece holds a power that works once, such as a hop that takes two pieces at the same time.
pros: A saved power waits for the right hop.
Players wonder which power the others still hold.
cons: A power spent early is gone for the rest of the game.
A piece with no power left is an easy target.

pairs.tendency: You offer a hop, and the other player may turn it down or choose between two hops you put forward.
pros: Each hop is checked by a second player.
Offers show what a player is willing to give up.
cons: A turned-down hop wastes your turn.
Two players decide one move, which takes longer.

pairs.tendency: A whispered message goes round the table and says where a hop will be made, but it may change on the way.
pros: The message can hide or show a hop.
Players listen for what changed.
cons: A garbled message sends a hop to the wrong place.
Nobody can check the message until it arrives.

pairs.tendency: Before play, each player hands some cards to a neighbour, and the cards you receive decide which hops are open to you.
pros: Players choose cards for others and for themselves.
Hands arrive with surprises in them.
cons: A hand full of passed-on cards may not match your pieces.
The start of the game is slower.

pairs.tendency: One player sets out the first pieces and the other picks a side, so the setup tries to leave the first hops open to both.
pros: The setter tries to keep the start level.
The chooser has a say in who goes first.
cons: A setup with one obvious first hop makes the choice easy.
Setting up takes thinking time before the game starts.

pairs.tendency: A piece that hops its way to the far edge can turn into a more powerful piece, so each hop towards that edge matters.
pros: Hops towards the edge have a prize at the end.
Players race to open a path.
cons: Pieces held back at home feel stuck.
Defenders cluster at the far edge.

pairs.tendency: A team runs in legs, and a piece hops its way along its leg before the next teammate starts.
pros: Hops make each leg different.
Teammates watch each other's legs.
cons: A blocked leg holds up the whole team.
One slow hopper slows the whole team.

pairs.tendency: Pieces make a shape that cannot be taken, and a piece inside the shape cannot be hopped over.
pros: A shape gives a place to build towards.
Opponents hunt for gaps in the shape.
cons: Pieces locked in a shape stop moving.
A shape with a gap is lost to a single hop.

pairs.tendency: Winning a hop is only a step to the named prizes, such as a certain card, and one hop may reach more than one prize.
pros: A hop can bring in two prizes.
Everyone knows what is worth taking.
cons: A hop that takes nothing named is wasted.
Players chase the named cards and ignore the rest.

pairs.tendency: Cards face up in the middle can be used by anyone, and a shared card can give a piece the hop it needs.
pros: Everyone can see the same chances.
A shared card helps whoever reaches it first.
cons: Taking a card gives it away to no one else, yet it opens the same hop to others.
Players wait to see which card the other player uses.

pairs.tendency: Every player puts a counter in the middle, and a hop that takes the last enemy piece wins the lot, which grows if nobody wins.
pros: The prize grows over rounds.
Every hop is aimed at the pot.
cons: A pot that has been growing for rounds makes one hop very large.
Players who fall behind may give up early.

pairs.tendency: Seeds drop one by one into pits, and a last seed landing over a full pit can take its seeds, like a hop over a piece.
pros: A counted sowing sets up a taking.
Players plan the count in advance.
cons: A taking can empty a pit you were saving.
Counting seeds slows each turn.

pairs.tendency: An extra hand lies face down in the middle, and the player who takes it may find cards for the hops they were missing.
pros: The spare hand can fill gaps in a plan.
Players wonder what it holds.
cons: The spare hand may help the wrong player.
Swapping delays the start.

pairs.tendency: Some spaces on the board have rules of their own, and a piece can hop onto or over one of them.
pros: A square can protect or punish a hop.
Players learn which squares to use.
cons: Hopping over a trap square still counts as passing it, if the rule says so.
Rules for squares need checking before each hop.

pairs.tendency: Every piece has a price, and each hop can cost something in coins or cards.
pros: A cheap piece makes small hops.
Spending can be planned in advance.
cons: A costly hop leaves you short of coins.
Players spend a long time counting.

pairs.tendency: You have a fixed number of pieces to spread over several places, and a thin line is easy to hop over.
pros: A spread of pieces protects many places.
The other player has to guess where you are thin.
cons: A thin place is lost to one hop.
A thick place leaves another empty.

pairs.tendency: Everyone moves until the music stops, and then pieces freeze, with any hop half done left where it stands.
pros: A signal ends the moving.
Players keep an eye on the signal and the board.
cons: A hop that was meant to follow is lost.
Some players hop too fast to be safe.

pairs.tendency: Players put cards back and take new ones, and the swap can give a piece a hop that was out of reach.
pros: A swap gives a second go at a hand.
Players see what others discard.
cons: Swapped cards may bring no hop at all.
Swapping takes a turn that might have been a move.

pairs.tendency: All discarded cards pile up in the middle, and one player picks up the whole pile when the top card lets a piece make a hop.
pros: A pile can hold the hop you need.
Players remember what went in.
cons: Taking the pile fills a hand with cards that are no use.
A big pile slows the player who picks it up.

pairs.tendency: One suit is named for the hand, and a trump card played with a hop lets a piece take an enemy piece that stands behind a gap.
pros: A trump gives a hop extra reach.
Players count how many trumps are left.
cons: A low trump can still beat a high card, which surprises people.
The trump suit can decide who is hopped.

pairs.tendency: You play both sides on two boards, and a hop on one board changes what you can do on the other.
pros: A hop attacks on one board and defends on another.
Players plan across both boards.
cons: A hop that wins one board may lose the other.
Two boards are a lot to watch.

pairs.tendency: A wild card can stand for any other card, so it can supply the hop a piece was missing.
pros: A wild card finishes a hop.
Players keep one in reserve.
cons: A wild card used early is gone for the rest of the hand.
A wild card makes it hard to guess what a player is holding.

pairs.tendency: The edges of the board are joined, so a piece that hops off one side lands on the other.
pros: The board has no safe corner.
Hops can go the long way round.
cons: A piece on the edge can be hopped from behind.
Players have to think about every edge as a middle.

pairs.tendency: One player knows a secret, and the others ask yes-or-no questions to find which piece or space to hop.
pros: Each answer closes off some hops.
Players share one list of what the answer could be.
cons: A wrong guess uses up a turn.
Questions can eat the time hopping needs.

pairs.tendency: The first player to reach the far end wins, and a hop lets a piece skip ahead past others.
pros: A hop jumps a queue.
The leader is not always safe.
cons: A hop can take the lead from a rival.
A blocked path ends in a pile of waiting pieces.

pairs.tendency: Each hop earns points for the pieces it takes or the spaces it reaches, and the player with the most at the end wins.
pros: Points tell who is ahead.
Players choose which hops are worth the most.
cons: A big hop can swing the whole count.
Players may chase hops while ignoring the position.

pairs.tendency: Pieces are taken by hops until only one player has any left.
pros: Each hop brings the end nearer.
Players with few pieces play carefully.
cons: A player can be out after one hop that opens a gap.
Out players wait and watch.

pairs.tendency: Players work together and a hop over a piece moves a teammate past a danger, until they all survive or all fall.
pros: Hops help the whole team.
Players plan the crossing together.
cons: One misplaced piece may block a teammate's hop.
A loss is shared by everyone.

pairs.tendency: All the players aim at one goal, such as getting every piece across, and a hop moves a piece past a blocking one.
pros: Hops get pieces where the team wants them.
Each player's move helps the others.
cons: A hop that helps one piece may block another.
Players disagree over who hops first.

pairs.tendency: Each player has a secret aim, and a hop over a piece may look like an attack while it serves that secret goal.
pros: A hop hides its reason.
Players guess at one another's aims.
cons: Players mistake a hop for a threat.
A secret aim can be given away by a single hop.

pairs.tendency: The game ends when the story does, and hops move pieces across places in the tale.
pros: A hop can mark a turning point.
The story gives each hop a meaning.
cons: The story can stop for a count of spaces.
The ending may come before all the hops are used.

pairs.tendency: Nobody wins, and pieces hop over each other just to see what patterns the hops leave behind.
pros: Hops are made for their own sake.
The group looks at what the hops made.
cons: Players may wonder when to stop.
With no prize, some players lose interest early.

pairs.tendency: Each player names their own aim, such as keeping every piece or hopping the most, and hops are judged against it.
pros: Two players can enjoy the same hop for different reasons.
Players say what they were after.
cons: Different aims can make plans collide.
There is no single way to say who came out ahead.

pairs.tendency: Hops take pieces until one player is left without any, and that player is the only one who loses.
pros: Everyone else is safe once they escape.
The pressure falls on the last player.
cons: The last player is picked on by everyone's hops.
Players who are safe may stop paying attention.

pairs.tendency: Players hop pieces over each other with the aim of never ending the game, so a hop that would take the last piece is held back.
pros: Hops are used to keep play alive.
Players share a goal of continuing.
cons: A hop that wins is left unplayed.
The game never settles into an ending.

pairs.tendency: Pieces hop and hop, but the rules are made so that no hop ever wins.
pros: The hops show something about the game.
Players find out what the game refuses.
cons: Players hunt for a winning hop and never find it.
Some players give up on the game.

pairs.tendency: You play alone against a laid-out board, and hopping a piece over another clears it away until the board is empty.
pros: Each hop clears a piece.
Planning ahead can solve the board.
cons: A hop in the wrong order can leave pieces stuck.
Mistakes can mean starting again.

pairs.tendency: Players play several short games of hopping in a row, and the winner is whoever takes the most games.
pros: A lost game can be won back.
The match can stop when nobody can catch up.
cons: One lost opening game can set the whole match going wrong.
A lead of two games can make the rest feel empty.

pairs.tendency: Each hop that takes a piece adds points against the one who hops, so the aim is to hop as little as possible.
pros: Players avoid hops that cost points.
The usual wish to hop is turned upside down.
cons: A forced hop can cost points.
Players may try to push hops onto others.

pairs.tendency: A piece has to land exactly on the end space, and a hop that carries it past the target does not count.
pros: Hops are chosen to land just right.
Players count carefully.
cons: A hop that goes too far costs the win.
A piece can sit near the end for many turns.

pairs.tendency: The aim is to be the player who loses all their pieces, so players hop over their own pieces' enemies in the hope of being taken.
pros: Hops are played backwards.
Players see familiar moves in a new way.
cons: A hop that takes can ruin your own aim.
Players forget which way round the game goes.

pairs.tendency: Everyone hops pieces on their own board at the same time, and nobody's hop touches anybody else's.
pros: Everyone plays at their own speed.
Players can compare boards at the end.
cons: Nobody can block another's hop.
The game can feel like several solo games in the same room.

pairs.tendency: Players hop over and take each other's pieces on purpose, so every hop is an attack on someone.
pros: Every hop has a victim.
The table watches the attacks.
cons: Anyone can be picked on.
Players hold grudges about who was hopped.

pairs.tendency: Players do not attack each other, but a hop changes the board and shuts or opens the next player's route.
pros: A hop is felt through the board.
Players read the board for chances.
cons: Blame is hard to pin on a single player.
A hop that blocks someone may be an accident.

pairs.tendency: All players are on one side against the game, and a hop moves a friendly piece past a blocker.
pros: Every hop serves the one shared side.
Players share the plan.
cons: A hop that helps one player can hurt another.
A loud player may take over the planning.

pairs.tendency: Players work together to cross the board, but each has a small private reason to be first, so some hops help and some hold others back.
pros: A hop can help the group and the hopper at once.
Players watch for the one who hops ahead.
cons: Teammates may wonder about a hop that helps only one person.
Trust gets tested on every turn.

pairs.tendency: Two teams face each other, and teammates set up hops for each other over the opposing pieces.
pros: Teammates help each other's hops.
Players talk plans within a team.
cons: A thin spot on one side is found by the other team.
A quiet teammate can be left out of the planning.

pairs.tendency: One player is secretly on the other side, and a hop that leaves a gap may be a mistake or a trap.
pros: Every odd hop raises a question.
Players watch moves for hints.
cons: A fair hop can be taken for a betrayal.
Players grow wary of anyone who hops near them.

pairs.tendency: Players far apart send each hop by letter, and a game of hopping may last weeks.
pros: Each hop is thought over carefully.
Waiting is part of the game.
cons: A hop sent by letter cannot be taken back.
Letters can cross in the post.

pairs.tendency: One player is not at the table, and their pieces are hopped over, or hop, by someone else's hand.
pros: The missing player still shapes play.
Players think about what the absent side would do.
cons: An absent player cannot answer a hop.
Someone has to move the absent pieces.

pairs.tendency: One player runs the world, and a hop over an obstacle is described by the game master, who decides what lies behind it.
pros: The world answers every hop.
The story grows with the hops.
cons: The game master can slow things down with description.
The other players depend on one person's decisions.

pairs.tendency: The game is drawn in chalk in a street, and a passer-by can join in and hop a stone over another.
pros: Anyone can join.
Games can start and stop quickly.
cons: Players come and go in the middle of a hop.
Rain or feet can rub out the board.

pairs.tendency: One player faces all the others, and the others plan hops together against the single player's pieces.
pros: The group can plan together.
The lone player is paid more for winning.
cons: The lone player faces many hops in one round.
The group may get in each other's way.

pairs.tendency: You hop pieces alone against a pack of cards, and the cards decide which gaps open.
pros: A hop is chosen against the cards.
A friend can compare results later.
cons: Luck in the pack can leave no hop at all.
Nobody else is there to notice a clever hop.

pairs.tendency: Dice or cards decide which hops are possible, so a player hops only when the draw allows it.
pros: Anyone can win.
Games finish quickly.
cons: Choosing a hop matters little.
Players with careful plans see them undone.

pairs.tendency: Dice decide how far pieces move, but a re-roll or a spare card can be used to reach a hop.
pros: A run of low luck can be softened.
Players still have choices.
cons: Using the aid costs the card or the turn.
Players argue over when to use the re-roll.

pairs.tendency: The hops follow the position, with a small draw of luck now and then to change what is open.
pros: Planning pays off.
A little chance keeps games from repeating.
cons: A lucky draw can undo a plan.
A new player can lose to a clever one just the same.

pairs.tendency: There are no dice, so each hop comes from the position alone and the more careful player usually wins.
pros: Every hop is chosen.
Players can see how a game was won.
cons: A beginner meets a clever opponent without a cushion.
One missed hop can decide the game.

pairs.tendency: Dice are thrown and read as a message, and the player decides which hop the message points to.
pros: A throw gives something to think about.
Players talk about what a throw meant.
cons: A hop based on a reading can look odd to others.
Two players may read the same throw differently.

pairs.tendency: Players sense when others are about to act, and hop over a piece at the moment they feel the others are ready.
pros: Players learn to read one another.
Moves can feel in step.
cons: A hop is mistimed when someone reads the group wrongly.
Players who do not know each other find it hard.

pairs.tendency: A roll is looked up on a table, and the table says what lies behind the piece you want to hop.
pros: The dice write part of the story.
A hop can lead somewhere unexpected.
cons: The table may block a hop.
Looking things up slows play.

pairs.tendency: Every piece and every gap is in view, so every player can see which hops are coming.
pros: Players can plan far ahead.
Nothing is hidden.
cons: A flawed plan is seen at once.
Each turn can run long while players study the board.

pairs.tendency: Cards are held in secret, and a hop may depend on a card nobody else has seen.
pros: A hop can be a surprise.
Players guess from what is hopped.
cons: A held card can be wasted.
Players cannot tell whether a hop is a bluff.

pairs.tendency: Some players have secret roles, and a hop over a piece may be a friend's help or an enemy's attack.
pros: Hops give clues about roles.
Players watch who hops where.
cons: A hop can be read the wrong way.
Players grow wary of every hop.

pairs.tendency: Clues point to hidden facts, and a hop over a piece tests a guess about what lies behind it.
pros: A hop can test an idea.
Players narrow down possibilities.
cons: A hop on a wrong guess is a lost turn.
Notes build up as play goes on.

pairs.tendency: A player pretends to have a plan, and a hop over a piece may be made only to look like a threat.
pros: A hop can mislead.
Players have to guess the real aim.
cons: A bluff hop can leave a piece open.
Players may stop trusting any hop.

pairs.tendency: One player knows a secret rule, and the others find it by hopping and being told no.
pros: Hops are tests of the rule.
Newcomers learn by trying.
cons: A forbidden hop wastes a turn.
A newcomer can feel left out until the rule is known.

pairs.tendency: One player sees the right hop but may only give hints, such as pictures, to the others.
pros: Hints turn into hops.
Others have to read the hints.
cons: A hint can send a hop to the wrong place.
The hinting player has to watch the others make mistakes.

pairs.tendency: The map starts hidden, and a piece hops into a space only to find what lies behind it.
pros: A hop explores.
Players learn the map as they go.
cons: A hop into the unknown can land beside danger.
Players do not know whether a hop is safe.

pairs.tendency: One hand is laid face up, and its cards show which hops that player can make.
pros: Everyone can see one set of possible hops.
The open hand gives clues about the rest.
cons: The open hand is easy to counter.
The player who owns the hand has little to hide.

pairs.tendency: Points from hops are kept secret, so nobody can say for certain who is ahead.
pros: Players guess at the score.
A hop might be worth more than it looks.
cons: Players do not know when to stop.
A leader can win without anyone noticing.

pairs.tendency: Players hop one at a time round the table, so everyone watches each hop and plans their own reply.
pros: Every hop can be answered.
Players can see the whole move.
cons: Waiting between turns is long with many players.
Players may lose track of their own plans.

pairs.tendency: Everyone chooses a hop in secret and all reveal together, so two players may aim at the same gap.
pros: Nobody waits.
Hops clash in surprising ways.
cons: Two hops into one space need a rule to settle them.
Plans are hard to keep up with.

pairs.tendency: Anyone can hop at any moment, and the quickest hand takes the gap.
pros: Play is fast.
Quick eyes pay off.
cons: Slower players are often left out.
Pieces are knocked about in a rush.

pairs.tendency: Each hop has a clock, such as a count to ten, and the move is lost or made for you when time runs out.
pros: Hops come fast.
The clock stops long thinking.
cons: A rushed hop can open a gap.
Players watch the timer more than the board.

pairs.tendency: One hop is made each morning over days or weeks, so a game of hopping takes a long time.
pros: Each hop is thought over.
Waiting becomes part of the game.
cons: A missed day leaves a piece open.
The game may be forgotten partway through.

pairs.tendency: A pause is built in before each move, so a hop is slow and everyone has time to see the gap.
pros: Players think before they hop.
The pace is calm.
cons: Players with quick plans have to wait.
A long pause can feel like a delay.

pairs.tendency: The clock shrinks as the game goes on, so early hops are slow and later hops come in a rush.
pros: The game builds up speed.
Late hops carry more risk.
cons: Late mistakes cannot be fixed.
The end comes in a blur.

pairs.tendency: A hop that lands on another piece earns another go at once, so a chain of hops can happen in one turn.
pros: One lucky hop can lead to many.
Players aim for chains.
cons: One player can move many times before anyone else.
The others wait and watch a long turn.

pairs.tendency: The game has a first stage of picking and a second of hopping, so the picks set up the hops.
pros: Early choices shape later moves.
Players plan for a later stage.
cons: A pick that did not fit shows up much later.
The first stage can feel far from the hopping.

pairs.tendency: The board works like a real system, and a hop shows how a thing moves from one place to another, like water jumping from a pond to a field.
pros: A hop has an effect like the real one.
Players learn how the system works.
cons: A hop can look odd to someone who knows the system.
The model can become too simple.

pairs.tendency: Each player plays a real group, and a hop is that group's way of crossing a barrier it faces.
pros: Players see the problem from where a group stands.
Hops come with a reason.
cons: A group's hop may block another group.
Players argue over what each group would do.

pairs.tendency: Everyone draws from one limited store, and a hop that takes from it leaves less for the others.
pros: The shared store shows what each hop costs.
Players see the effect on the group.
cons: One greedy hop can empty the store.
Players blame each other when it runs out.

pairs.tendency: A hop made now shows its effect a few rounds later, such as a gap that opens long after the piece moved.
pros: Hops have long consequences.
Players learn to look ahead.
cons: A hop from three rounds ago is easy to forget.
Players blame the wrong hop.

pairs.tendency: The group agrees on a new rule about hopping, then plays on to see what it changes.
pros: Trying the rule risks nothing outside the game.
Players can compare the games before and after.
cons: A new rule can break a game that worked.
Players disagree on whether it changed anything.

pairs.tendency: After the game, players talk about which hops mattered and why.
pros: Hops can be looked at again.
The talk connects the game to real life.
cons: Players recall hops differently.
Some players say little.

pairs.tendency: A hopped-over piece is torn up or marked, so no hop can be undone and the next game starts where this one ended.
pros: Each hop leaves a mark.
The board holds a record.
cons: A hasty hop cannot be taken back.
Later games begin with fewer pieces.

pairs.tendency: The rules reward hopping over others, so the game says something about getting ahead by passing over people.
pros: The rules say something about the world.
Players can talk about the point the game makes.
cons: Players may disagree with its message.
The message can be missed by someone just playing.

pairs.tendency: Real coins or a real promise ride on a hop, so a hop over a piece can cost a friend.
pros: Hops matter beyond the board.
Players take each hop seriously.
cons: A hop can leave a friendship tested.
Some players do not want to hop at all.

pairs.tendency: A hop earns points that stand for something like kindness, and players begin to hop for the points alone.
pros: The points stand for something.
Players see how numbers can take over.
cons: A hop made for points can ignore what they stand for.
The thing the points stood for is forgotten.

pairs.tendency: Players practise a way of living, such as sharing, and a hop moves a piece past an obstacle that shows how it might feel.
pros: Hops try out ways of living.
Players see how a future might feel.
cons: Hops that skip a problem hide it.
A new way of living is hard to judge in one game.

pairs.tendency: Dice are rolled and some are set aside, and the dice you keep decide how many spaces your piece moves.
pros: A kept die can set the pace.
Choice enters a game of throwing.
cons: The final throw can still undo a plan.
Each extra throw makes the turn longer.

pairs.tendency: Cards go round one pick at a time, and each card may call for a particular roll, so you keep the dice that fit the card.
pros: Cards and dice work together.
Players see which cards others need.
cons: A card picked early may ask for a roll that never comes.
Players sit idle until the cards come round again.

pairs.tendency: Players bid to throw first, and the winner rolls, keeps the dice they like and rolls the rest.
pros: Paying for a turn can buy a chance at higher dice.
Players see what a roll is worth.
cons: A big bid may buy only a low throw.
A spent bid cannot be used again.

pairs.tendency: Each reroll risks the dice you set aside, and going on may lose points that stopping would have kept.
pros: Each extra roll can bring more points.
Players watch for the moment to stop.
cons: A bust loses what was gathered.
Stopping early gives up possible points.

pairs.tendency: Players roll dice, keep some and use them to place pieces on a map, so the kept dice set how many pieces go where.
pros: Dice decide how much a player can spread.
Players choose where to place the dice.
cons: A low roll leaves a region open.
Luck can swing control of a region.

pairs.tendency: Players roll dice to get workers, keep the ones they like, and place them on jobs.
pros: Kept dice become workers.
Rolling gives a number of workers each round.
cons: A low roll leaves jobs unfilled.
Players race for the same spaces.

pairs.tendency: Dice are rolled and kept to match a colour or number pattern, and each reroll goes after the missing piece.
pros: Players aim at one pattern.
Rerolls close in on what is needed.
cons: The last die can refuse to come up right.
Players hold dice they never use.

pairs.tendency: Cards stay in hand until needed, and dice are rolled and kept to power the cards you hold.
pros: A card and a die pair up.
Players plan which cards to spend.
cons: A card with no matching die waits in the hand.
Keeping cards and dice in mind makes a turn long.

pairs.tendency: Players roll and keep dice to name a bid, then play a card each, and the winner of the trick uses the dice they kept.
pros: Dice add a number to each trick.
Players guess what the kept dice are for.
cons: A kept die may be wasted when the trick is lost.
A round takes both rolling and card play.

pairs.tendency: Players talk about which dice to keep, and trade a die they do not need for one they do.
pros: Dice can be traded.
Players show their needs by talking.
cons: A die handed over cannot be taken back.
Talk slows each throw.

pairs.tendency: Dice are rolled and kept toward a set, such as three of one number, and each reroll goes after the missing match.
pros: The set gives the roll a goal.
Players choose which dice to hold.
cons: A set can stay one die short for rounds.
Holding for a set gives up other chances.

pairs.tendency: Each turn the kept dice decide which tiles can be laid, and a map grows from the numbers rolled.
pros: Dice shape the map.
Players choose where tiles go.
cons: An unlucky set of dice leaves a tile with no place.
Players wait for the right number.

pairs.tendency: One player rolls and keeps some dice, and the next answers with a roll that matches or tops it.
pros: Each roll replies to the last.
The game moves like a chain.
cons: A high first roll sets a hard answer.
A reply can be forced by what the last player kept.

pairs.tendency: Nobody speaks, so the dice a player keeps are the only message about what they are after.
pros: Kept dice are visible clues.
Players read each other without words.
cons: A kept die can be misread.
There is no way to ask what a player meant.

pairs.tendency: A player may change a rule on their turn, such as how many rerolls are allowed, so the shape of the throwing shifts mid-game.
pros: Rule changes can add rerolls or take them away.
Players learn how much the rerolls matter.
cons: A plan built on three rolls can fall to two.
Players argue over which rule is in force.

pairs.tendency: Each player speaks as a character, and the throw of the dice is how the character tries a hard task.
pros: Dice give the story a risk.
Players describe what the kept dice mean.
cons: A failed roll can stop a story.
Players may pause the story to count dice.

pairs.tendency: Dice are thrown by hand onto a surface, and a throw that lands off the table or topples a stack is lost.
pros: The hand adds to the roll.
The table can see how each throw was made.
cons: A shaky throw counts for nothing.
Dice that roll away need chasing.

pairs.tendency: Players draw the map as they play, and the dice they keep decide how much of it each turn can fill.
pros: Dice set how fast the map grows.
Players choose which part to draw.
cons: A low roll leaves a blank map.
Players may draw over each other's lines.

pairs.tendency: The dice you keep set how far your piece goes, and a landing on another piece sends it back to the start.
pros: Kept dice can aim a landing.
A careful aim hits a piece.
cons: A sent-back piece loses many turns of travel.
A leader can lose the lead to one throw.

pairs.tendency: Dice choose where pieces go, and a kept roll can finish a row of three that lets you take an enemy piece.
pros: A roll can finish a row.
Players hold dice for a row.
cons: If the row is broken, the player has to start it again.
Players watch the other board for rows.

pairs.tendency: Letter dice are rolled, and some are kept while the rest are rolled again to spell a word.
pros: Rerolls hunt for letters.
Arguments over words go to the dictionary.
cons: A word may need a letter that never comes up.
Players grow stuck on one word.

pairs.tendency: Dice are rolled and kept to match the number on the open end of a line, and a tile is laid if a die fits.
pros: A kept die matches an end.
Players read the line before rolling.
cons: No matching die means a missed turn.
Rolling again and again delays a turn.

pairs.tendency: Dice are rolled and kept to form a set, and a finished set is laid face up for all to see and add to.
pros: A finished set scores.
Others can add to a laid set.
cons: A laid set gives away what you were rolling for.
A set laid early gives others a chance to add to it.

pairs.tendency: Each player holds a power that works once, and one use might be to roll a die again after the throws have run out.
pros: A power can save a low roll.
Players choose when to spend it.
cons: Once used, the power cannot help again.
Players hold powers back too long.

pairs.tendency: You roll and offer a keep, and the other player may turn it down or pick between two sets of dice you put forward.
pros: The other player can veto a keep.
An offer shows which dice a player will part with.
cons: If the keep is refused, the roll is lost.
Every throw needs two people to agree, so turns run long.

pairs.tendency: A message about which dice to keep goes round the table in whispers, and may change on the way.
pros: A message can hide a plan.
Players compare what they heard.
cons: A garbled message sends someone to keep the wrong dice.
The change only shows once the message reaches the end.

pairs.tendency: Before play, players hand some cards to another player, and the dice they roll later has to fit the cards they get.
pros: Players pass cards that match their dice.
Nobody knows which cards will come back.
cons: A card passed on can leave a roll with no use.
Passing adds a step before the first roll.

pairs.tendency: One player sets up the starting dice, such as the target numbers, and the other picks which side to play.
pros: The setter has to pick targets that favour neither side.
The chooser decides which side to play.
cons: An easy-to-read setup makes the choice simple.
The game cannot start until the targets are set.

pairs.tendency: A piece that reaches the far end can turn into a more powerful piece, and the dice you keep decide whether it gets there.
pros: Dice and promotion add up to a goal.
Players race for the edge.
cons: A low roll leaves a piece short.
The far end fills with pieces sent to stop it.

pairs.tendency: A team runs in legs, and each runner rolls, keeps and rolls again to see how far they get before passing on.
pros: Each leg is a fresh throw.
Teammates watch each other's rolls.
cons: A short leg leaves the next runner further back.
Players waiting for a turn are idle.

pairs.tendency: Pieces form a shape that cannot be taken, and kept dice are used to place the last stone of the shape.
pros: A shape gives a goal for the dice.
Players hold dice for the shape.
cons: A shape one die short stays open.
Other players aim for the gap.

pairs.tendency: The prizes are named cards, and kept dice help a player win the tricks that carry those cards.
pros: Dice add to the race for prizes.
The named cards are known from the start.
cons: A roll that misses leaves the prize to others.
Cards that are not named get little attention.

pairs.tendency: Cards face up in the middle can be used by anyone, and the dice you keep decide which of them your roll can use.
pros: Dice and cards pair up.
Everyone sees the same cards.
cons: A card the dice cannot use stays idle.
Players hold back to see what the others take.

pairs.tendency: Everyone puts a counter into the middle, and the player with the highest roll after rerolls takes it all.
pros: The pot grows if nobody wins.
Each reroll is a try for the pot.
cons: A pot left to grow puts a lot on one throw.
Players who lose early may drop out.

pairs.tendency: A throw says how many pits to sow, and seeds are dropped one at a time, with the last seed's pit deciding what can be taken.
pros: A kept die sets the count.
Players plan which pit to start from.
cons: A roll can put the last seed in a pit that gives nothing.
Dropping seeds one at a time takes a while.

pairs.tendency: An extra hand lies face down in the middle, and a player may take it after a roll and keep only the cards that suit their dice.
pros: The spare hand is a second chance.
Players guess what the hand holds.
cons: The spare hand may suit an opponent more than you.
Taking and sorting the spare hand holds up play.

pairs.tendency: Some spaces on the track have rules of their own, and the dice you keep decide whether you reach one.
pros: A die can aim at a square.
Players come to know the squares.
cons: A trap square can undo a high roll.
Each landing means looking up what the square does.

pairs.tendency: Every card or unit has a price, and a roll decides how many coins or points you have to spend.
pros: The roll sets the budget.
Players choose what to buy.
cons: A low roll leaves little to buy with.
Adding up coins slows the turn.

pairs.tendency: You have a fixed number of dice to spread over several jobs, and each reroll goes to a place that is short.
pros: Dice can be shared out.
Opponents look for the job you left short.
cons: A die used in one place is missing in another.
Each job gets less than it might.

pairs.tendency: Everyone rolls until a signal such as music stops, then freezes with the dice they are holding.
pros: The signal ends the rolling.
Players listen while they roll.
cons: A roll cut short is wasted.
Some players stop early to stay safe.

pairs.tendency: Players put cards back and take new ones, and a roll tells them how many they may swap.
pros: A roll sets how many swaps.
Everyone sees the cards put back.
cons: A low roll offers few swaps.
A turn spent swapping is a turn without a roll.

pairs.tendency: Discarded cards pile up in the middle, and the dice you keep tell whether you can use the top card and pick up the pile.
pros: A roll can unlock the pile.
Players keep track of what has been thrown away.
cons: A pile full of cards you cannot use fills the hand.
A large pile takes time to sort.

pairs.tendency: One suit beats the rest for the hand, and dice are kept to decide how many trumps a player may play.
pros: Dice add to the power of the trump suit.
Players keep a tally of trumps played.
cons: A roll can leave a hand with no trump at all.
The trump suit can decide the whole round.

pairs.tendency: You play both sides on two boards, and the dice you keep go to one board or the other.
pros: A die helps one board only.
Players weigh which board needs it.
cons: A die kept for one board is gone from the other.
Keeping track of both boards is hard.

pairs.tendency: A wild card can stand for any card, and a kept die can stand for the number it needs.
pros: A wild card fills a hole in a roll.
Players hold one back for later.
cons: Once spent, the wild card cannot help again.
Players cannot tell what a hand holds.

pairs.tendency: The edges of the board are joined, so a piece that runs off one side comes in on the other, and a roll can take it round.
pros: A roll can carry a piece round.
No edge is safe.
cons: A piece near an edge can be hit from either side.
Players have to count both ways.

pairs.tendency: One player has a secret, and the others use rolls to decide how many questions they may ask.
pros: A roll sets the number of questions.
Each answer narrows the list.
cons: A low roll leaves few questions.
Players run out of questions before they have enough clues.

pairs.tendency: The first player to the end wins, and a throw with kept dice decides how far a piece runs.
pros: Kept dice help the lead.
The race is easy to follow.
cons: A low roll slows the leader.
Players who fall back may lose heart.

pairs.tendency: Dice are rolled and kept for the highest score, and the player with the most points at the end wins.
pros: Players aim at one number.
A lead is easy to see.
cons: A low roll can drop a player behind.
Chasing points may overlook other moves.

pairs.tendency: Players are knocked out one by one, and the dice they keep decide who takes a hit each round.
pros: Each round brings an end nearer.
Players with little left take fewer risks.
cons: A low roll can end a player.
Knocked-out players have nothing to do until the game ends.

pairs.tendency: Players roll and keep dice together to hold off the game, and the whole team wins or loses at once.
pros: Every kept die counts for the team.
Players plan the keeps together.
cons: One low roll can hurt everyone.
The loudest voice can end up choosing every keep.

pairs.tendency: All players aim at one goal, such as a target total, and each adds the dice they keep.
pros: Every roll helps the team.
Players share the aim.
cons: One player's keeps can block another's.
Players argue over which dice to keep.

pairs.tendency: Each player has a secret aim, and a kept die may hint at what that aim is.
pros: Kept dice hide a plan.
Players try to work out what the others want.
cons: Players misread a keep.
A keep that is too obvious gives the secret away.

pairs.tendency: The game ends when the story does, and the dice a player keeps decide how each scene turns out.
pros: Dice give scenes a risk.
Each roll decides part of the story.
cons: A failed roll can leave a scene unfinished.
The story can end with dice still unrolled.

pairs.tendency: Nobody wins, and players roll and keep dice just to see what comes up.
pros: Nobody rolls to win.
The group looks at the pattern of dice.
cons: Nothing tells the players when the game is over.
Some players drift off without a prize to aim at.

pairs.tendency: Each player names an aim before rolling, such as a high total or a matching set, and keeps dice to reach it.
pros: Two players keep different dice for different goals.
Each player explains what they were aiming for.
cons: Different aims can clash over the same dice.
Results cannot be ranked against one another.

pairs.tendency: Rolls are kept and rolled again until one player ends with the lowest total, and that player alone loses.
pros: Everyone else is safe once their roll clears the bar.
The player at the bottom feels it most.
cons: The trailing player can become everyone's target.
Safe players may drift.

pairs.tendency: Players roll and keep dice with the aim of never ending the game, so a roll that would end it is passed over.
pros: Each keep is chosen so the game goes on.
Everyone wants another round.
cons: A winning roll is left alone.
Nobody knows when to put the dice away.

pairs.tendency: Dice are kept and rolled again, but the rules are made so that no roll can ever win.
pros: The dice show how the game is built.
Players learn that no throw will be enough.
cons: Players keep rerolling for a win that is not there.
Some players stop rolling.

pairs.tendency: You play alone against a layout of cards, and each roll tells which card you may clear.
pros: A kept die clears a card.
Planning ahead helps.
cons: A roll that fits nothing leaves cards stuck.
A wrong clear can force a restart.

pairs.tendency: Players play several short rounds of rolling, and the winner is whoever takes the most rounds.
pros: One lost round can be made up later.
Play ends once a lead cannot be caught.
cons: A run of low rolls can lose a match.
Once someone is two rounds up, the rounds left matter less.

pairs.tendency: Each die you keep adds to your total, and the player with the fewest points wins.
pros: Players keep only low dice.
Players want low numbers for once.
cons: A forced high die costs points.
Players may keep too few dice.

pairs.tendency: You have to land exactly on the target number with your kept dice, and going past it loses the hand.
pros: Players pick dice that add up exactly.
Every die is added up before it is kept.
cons: A roll that goes too far costs the hand.
A player can stay just short of the target for many throws.

pairs.tendency: The aim is to end with the lowest score or to be the one who finishes last, so players keep dice that help them lose.
pros: Players chase the low score.
Old habits of keeping high dice have to be dropped.
cons: A lucky high roll can ruin the aim.
Players slip back into keeping high dice.

pairs.tendency: Everyone rolls, keeps and rolls again at the same time on their own, and nobody's throw touches anyone else's.
pros: Nobody waits for anyone else.
Players can compare results at the end.
cons: Players cannot get in each other's way.
It can feel like each person is playing alone.

pairs.tendency: Dice you keep decide how hard you hit another player, and the one hit can hit back next turn.
pros: Every roll has a target.
Everyone sees who is hit.
cons: Any player can become a target.
Players hold grudges after a heavy hit.

pairs.tendency: Players do not attack each other, but the dice they keep change the board and shut or open the next player's route.
pros: A roll changes the board, and that is how it reaches others.
Players look for routes the last roll opened.
cons: Nobody can say for sure who caused a block.
A route may close by chance and not by plan.

pairs.tendency: All players are on one side against the game, and the team rolls, keeps and rolls again to beat it.
pros: Each keep goes towards beating the game.
Everyone has a voice on each reroll.
cons: A poor throw sets the whole team back.
One player can end up deciding every reroll.

pairs.tendency: Players share a goal but each has a small private reason to score more, so dice kept for the group may also help one player.
pros: A roll can help the group and the roller.
Players watch for the one who keeps the highest dice.
cons: A roll that helps only one person raises doubts.
Each turn raises the question of whose side a keep is on.

pairs.tendency: Two teams roll against each other, and teammates pass dice or advice before the rerolls.
pros: A teammate's advice can save a roll.
Each team talks over its dice.
cons: The other team can see a low roll and press on it.
A teammate who says little gets little say.

pairs.tendency: One player is secretly on the other side, and a die they keep or reroll may be a mistake or a trap.
pros: A strange keep draws suspicion.
Players study each roll for a hint.
cons: An honest keep can look like sabotage.
Doubt spreads round the table.

pairs.tendency: Players far apart send their kept dice by letter, and a game of rolling can last weeks.
pros: Players have days to decide each keep.
The gaps between letters are part of play.
cons: Once posted, a keep stands.
Two letters may pass each other on the way.

pairs.tendency: One player is not at the table, and their dice are rolled by someone else for them.
pros: The absent player's dice still count.
Players think about what the absent side would keep.
cons: An absent player cannot argue with a roll.
Someone has to roll for the absent player.

pairs.tendency: One player runs the world, and the game master asks for a roll when a task is hard, then decides what the kept dice mean.
pros: Each roll gets an answer from the game master.
Every throw adds to the story.
cons: Long rulings can hold up play.
The other players depend on one person's reading of the dice.

pairs.tendency: The game is played in a street or a market, and a passer-by can join in and throw dice for a turn.
pros: Passers-by can step in.
A game can begin or end at any moment.
cons: The players change from one roll to the next.
Rain or wind can scatter the dice.

pairs.tendency: One player faces all the others, and the others roll and keep dice together against the single player.
pros: The many share their thinking.
Winning alone earns the single player a bigger reward.
cons: One player has to answer several rolls each round.
Too many voices can trip each other up.

pairs.tendency: You roll alone against the pack, and the cards decide which kept dice are worth anything.
pros: Dice are chosen against the cards.
Results can be set beside a friend's afterwards.
cons: Luck in the pack can leave nothing worth keeping.
Nobody sees a clever keep but you.

pairs.tendency: The throw decides most things, and the choice to keep a die or roll it again is one of the few that remain.
pros: Beginners stand a fair chance.
A game is over fast.
cons: Choosing which die to keep matters little.
Plans get undone by the next throw.

pairs.tendency: Dice decide the roll, and keeping and rerolling is itself a way to soften a low throw.
pros: A low throw can be partly saved.
Each roll still involves a decision.
cons: Using the aid costs a roll.
Players argue over when to reroll.

pairs.tendency: The plan comes from the position, and a roll with a few kept dice adds a small stir of luck.
pros: Thinking ahead wins more often than not.
The dice keep each game a little different.
cons: A lucky roll can undo a plan.
A beginner still tends to lose to a careful player.

pairs.tendency: Dice are set aside and rerolled, but the choice of what to keep is where a clever player wins more often than a careless one.
pros: Careful keeping pays off.
A game can be traced back to the keeps that won it.
cons: A new player has little to protect them from a stronger one.
One unlucky reroll can decide the game.

pairs.tendency: Dice are thrown and read as a message, and a player keeps the ones that seem to answer the question being asked.
pros: The dice start a line of thought.
Players argue over what the dice said.
cons: A keep based on a reading can look odd to others.
One throw can mean different things to different players.

pairs.tendency: Players sense when others are about to act, and reroll at the moment they feel the others are ready.
pros: Players learn each other's timing.
Rolls can fall into step.
cons: A reroll comes too early or too late when the group is misjudged.
Strangers struggle to sense each other.

pairs.tendency: A roll is looked up on a table that says what happens next, and the dice you keep choose which line of the table is read.
pros: The story turns on what is kept.
A keep can lead somewhere unexpected.
cons: The table may send the story somewhere flat.
Each roll means a trip to the table.

pairs.tendency: Every die and every kept die is in view, so every player can see what the others are aiming at.
pros: Players can plan ahead.
No die is secret.
cons: Opponents spot a weak plan straight away.
Turns run long as players study every die.

pairs.tendency: Cards are held in secret, and the dice you keep may be chosen to suit a card nobody else has seen.
pros: A keep may surprise the table.
The kept dice hint at the hidden cards.
cons: A card can sit unused all game.
Nobody knows if a keep is honest.

pairs.tendency: Some players have secret roles, and a die they keep may point to a friend's help or an enemy's attack.
pros: What a player keeps hints at their role.
Players watch who keeps what.
cons: Players misjudge a role from one keep.
Suspicion falls on each throw.

pairs.tendency: Clues point to hidden facts, and a die kept or rolled again tests a guess about which one it is.
pros: Each roll checks a guess.
The list of answers shrinks.
cons: A roll spent on a wrong guess is wasted.
The notes get longer every round.

pairs.tendency: A player keeps their dice covered and says what they hold, and the others have to guess whether it is true.
pros: A false claim can win a round.
Players guess at the real hand.
cons: A bluff that is called loses the round.
After a few lies, nobody believes anyone.

pairs.tendency: One player knows a secret rule about which dice may be kept, and the others find it by trying and being told no.
pros: Each keep tests the rule.
Players work the rule out from refusals.
cons: A forbidden keep wastes a roll.
Until they find the rule, new players may feel shut out.

pairs.tendency: One player knows which dice are right to keep but may only give hints, such as pictures, to the others.
pros: The hints guide which dice to hold.
The others try to decode each picture.
cons: A hint can send a keep the wrong way.
The player who knows has to sit through wrong keeps.

pairs.tendency: The map starts hidden, and the dice you keep decide how far you explore before the next turn.
pros: Each roll uncovers more.
The map fills in turn by turn.
cons: A long roll can lead into trouble.
Every move into the dark is a risk.

pairs.tendency: One hand is laid face up, and the dice that player keeps can be read against the cards everyone can see.
pros: One player's choices are on show.
What is visible hints at what is not.
cons: Opponents can plan against the open hand.
That player cannot keep secrets.

pairs.tendency: Points from kept dice are hidden, so nobody can say for certain who is ahead.
pros: Players estimate who leads.
A keep's value may be hidden.
cons: Nobody knows when they have enough.
The winner may only be known at the count.

pairs.tendency: Players roll one at a time round the table, so everyone watches each keep and plans their own throw.
pros: Each player can reply to the last roll.
Every keep happens in full view.
cons: With many players, turns come round slowly.
Watching others can push a player's own plan out of mind.

pairs.tendency: Everyone rolls, keeps and rerolls at once, then all reveal together.
pros: There is no queue for a turn.
The reveal can bring odd matches.
cons: Two players may finish at the same moment.
Players cannot watch each other's rolls.

pairs.tendency: Anyone can grab dice and roll at any moment, and the quickest hand gets the first throw.
pros: Rounds move quickly.
Speed counts for a lot.
cons: Slow hands miss out.
Dice get scattered in the scramble.

pairs.tendency: Each turn has a clock, such as a count to ten, and a hand with dice still unkept is scored as it stands when time runs out.
pros: Turns move along.
There is no time to dither.
cons: A rushed keep can waste a die.
Eyes go to the timer and off the dice.

pairs.tendency: One roll is made each morning over days or weeks, so a game of rolling takes a long time.
pros: There is a whole day to choose each keep.
The days between rolls are part of play.
cons: A missed day loses a roll.
Players can lose interest before the end.

pairs.tendency: A pause is built in before each roll, so every keep is slow and everyone has time to see the dice.
pros: Each choice gets a moment's thought.
Play stays unhurried.
cons: Fast thinkers sit and wait.
The pause can drag.

pairs.tendency: The clock shrinks as the game goes on, so early rerolls are slow and later ones come in a rush.
pros: Play speeds up round by round.
The last keeps are the riskiest.
cons: Errors near the end stay.
The final rounds are hard to follow.

pairs.tendency: On some throws you get another go at once, so a kept set of dice that hits a target can lead to a second set of rolls.
pros: A hit can bring more rolls.
Players go for runs of hits.
cons: One player may take several turns in a row.
A long run leaves the others idle.

pairs.tendency: The game has a first stage of picking and a second of rolling, so the picks set up what the dice are for.
pros: The picks decide what the dice will do.
Players pick with the rolling in mind.
cons: A wrong pick only shows once the dice come out.
Picking can seem unconnected to the rolls.

pairs.tendency: The dice stand for events in a real system, such as rainfall over a village, and keeping and rerolling shows how a plan copes with it.
pros: Each roll stands for something that happens.
Players see how the system copes.
cons: Someone who knows the real system may find a roll unlikely.
The dice can make the system look simpler than it is.

pairs.tendency: Each player plays a real group, and the dice they keep show what that group manages to do in a season.
pros: Players see the problem through one group's eyes.
Each keep has a group's need behind it.
cons: One group's success can hold another back.
People disagree on how a group would act.

pairs.tendency: Everyone draws from one limited store, and each kept die takes something from it.
pros: Each keep visibly drains the store.
The whole table feels each take.
cons: A greedy player can use it all up.
An empty store starts arguments.

pairs.tendency: A roll made now shows its effect a few rounds later, such as a harvest decided by dice kept in spring.
pros: A roll's effect lasts beyond its turn.
Players think a few rounds on.
cons: Old rolls slip from memory.
The cause of a result is easy to misplace.

pairs.tendency: The group agrees on a new rule about rerolls, then plays on to see what it changes.
pros: Trying a rule costs little.
Games with and without the rule can be set side by side.
cons: A change can spoil a game that ran smoothly.
The group may not agree on what the rule did.

pairs.tendency: After the game, players talk about which keeps mattered and why.
pros: Players go back over the key rolls.
The talk links play to life outside.
cons: Memories of the dice differ.
Not everyone speaks up.

pairs.tendency: A roll marks the board for keeps, so no keep can be undone and the next game starts where this one ended.
pros: Every roll is kept on the board.
Past games stay visible.
cons: A rushed keep is permanent.
Options shrink game by game.

pairs.tendency: The rules reward the player who rolls again and again, so the game says something about risking for a bigger prize.
pros: The rules carry a view about risk.
The game opens a conversation about its point.
cons: Not everyone accepts what it says.
A player focused on winning may not notice the point.

pairs.tendency: Real coins or a real promise ride on a throw, so a roll of kept dice can cost a friend.
pros: Real things change hands with the dice.
Every throw is weighed.
cons: Friends can fall out over a roll.
Some people stay out of it.

pairs.tendency: A roll earns points that stand for something like kindness, and players begin to roll for the points alone.
pros: Each score is tied to a value.
Players notice the score pulling them away from the value.
cons: Chasing points can lose sight of kindness.
The value fades behind the number.

pairs.tendency: Players practise a way of living, such as sharing, and the dice show how often it holds up when luck turns.
pros: The dice test how a way of living copes with chance.
Players get a taste of another future.
cons: A roll can hide a problem.
One game says little about a whole way of life.
