pairs.tendency: Dice set the distance, and a piece that ends its move on another player's space sends that piece back to the start.
pros: One throw can undo a whole trip.
Players watch every roll closely.
cons: A long lead can vanish in a single landing.
A short roll can leave a piece sitting in reach of the others.

pairs.tendency: Pieces move by the cards taken from a shared row, so a card that ends on a rival's space is a card worth taking before the next player does.
pros: A pick can be aimed at one piece.
The row tells everyone which hits are on offer.
cons: Late pickers may be left with moves that hit nothing.
A piece sent home makes the cards that moved it feel wasted.

pairs.tendency: Players bid for the right to move first, since moving first lets a piece land on a rival before the rival can step away.
pros: Turn order becomes something to buy.
A big bid tells everyone who wants a hit.
cons: Money spent on a bid is not spent on anything else.
A paid-for move can still miss its target.

pairs.tendency: Each turn a player stops on a space or throws on for more, and a piece that stops can be landed on and sent back.
pros: Stopping keeps the points already earned.
Rivals wait for a piece that has gone too far.
cons: A long run can be lost in one landing.
Careful players creep past rivals and the game slows.

pairs.tendency: Pieces hold parts of the map, and when a rival lands on a held space the holder goes home and the area is open to take.
pros: A held area can change hands in one move.
Players guard the spots that rivals can reach.
cons: A long hold can end in one turn.
Pieces sent home leave gaps on the map.

pairs.tendency: Workers sit on job spaces and keep others out, so a landing that sends a worker home also frees its job.
pros: A job can be reopened by force.
Placed workers can be threatened.
cons: A worker sent home loses a turn of work.
Players spend turns protecting jobs.

pairs.tendency: Every space a piece passes adds a tile to its owner's pattern, so a landing that sends the piece home tears the pattern up with it.
pros: A hit ruins what the piece had built.
Patterns grow along the track.
cons: The longest pattern loses the most to a hit.
Players steer clear of anyone who can reach them.

pairs.tendency: Cards in hand decide the moves, and a card kept back can be the one that lands exactly on a rival.
pros: Holding a card can set up a hit for later.
Players try to work out what the others keep.
cons: A card held too long may never be used.
Once the piece is sent home, the saved card comes too late.

pairs.tendency: Each trick played also moves a piece, and whoever wins the trick may land on a rival and send it back.
pros: Winning a trick can mean a hit.
The cards on the table show who is within reach.
cons: A lucky trick can send home a piece nobody meant to hit.
Players track the cards and the track at once.

pairs.tendency: Before a landing, players trade words such as "leave my piece alone and I will leave yours".
pros: Deals can hold back hits for a while.
Promises show who is safe from whom.
cons: A broken promise ends with a piece at the start.
Talking slows down each turn.

pairs.tendency: Cards for a set are picked up along the track, and a piece sent to the start drops everything it carried.
pros: A hit can undo a long stretch of collecting.
Players keep close watch over what their piece holds.
cons: A set one card from done can be lost in one landing.
Pieces with full hands avoid crowded spaces.

pairs.tendency: Tiles build the track as the game goes, so a player can lay a tile that puts a rival's piece within reach of a landing.
pros: The shape of the path becomes a way to hit.
Players plan their routes as they lay tiles.
cons: A tile placed for one reason can help a rival hit.
A long track makes for a slow crossing.

pairs.tendency: Each player answers the move before with a move of their own, and an answer that ends on a rival's space sends it home.
pros: Every move has a reply waiting for it.
Hits can follow one another in a chain.
cons: Players wait for their turn to reply.
A hit invites a hit back.

pairs.tendency: Nobody speaks, so the owner of a piece cannot call out a warning or ask for a pause before a landing.
pros: Players learn to read hints in how others move.
A hit arrives with no talk first.
cons: Safe passage cannot be agreed.
Misreading a move can send a piece home.

pairs.tendency: On a turn a player may change a rule instead of moving, such as making their own space safe or changing what a landing does.
pros: The size of a hit can be changed by anyone.
Safe spaces can move around the board.
cons: A rule that protects one player can be undone by the next.
By the end the track is a different game.

pairs.tendency: Pieces are characters, so a landing that sends one back plays out as a scene such as an ambush or a chase.
pros: A hit turns into a story.
Players speak as their characters.
cons: A sent-back character loses its place in the story.
Players may argue over what counts as a landing.

pairs.tendency: A flick or a throw moves the piece, and if it stops on a rival's space that rival goes home.
pros: Hands decide where a piece lands.
A near miss gets everyone looking.
cons: A shaky hand wastes a turn.
Pieces can get knocked off the track by accident.

pairs.tendency: The map is drawn as pieces cross it, so a player can draw a space and mark it safe or add a trap.
pros: Players shape where the hits happen.
The track records what has already happened.
cons: A newly drawn space can put a piece in danger without warning.
The paper fills up and the game slows.

pairs.tendency: A row of three takes a piece off the board for ever, while a landing only sends one back to the start, so there are two sizes of loss in one game.
pros: Players have two kinds of threat to watch.
A piece sent home can still come back.
cons: Players have to decide which threat to answer first.
A piece can be sent home and then taken.

pairs.tendency: Letters are picked up along the track, and a piece sent home drops its letters back onto the spaces behind it.
pros: A hit costs the owner a word in progress.
Spelling plans show as letters are seen.
cons: A half-made word is lost in one landing.
Players hunt for words and for rivals together.

pairs.tendency: The line of tiles is also the track, and a landing on a tile where a piece already stands sends that piece back.
pros: The line decides where pieces can go.
Tiles placed in the line can set up a hit.
cons: A player with no matching tile misses a turn and a chance to land.
A short line puts the pieces close together.

pairs.tendency: Players lay finished sets face up on the table while pieces move round the track, and a hit that sends a piece home can also cost the turn that would have added to a meld.
pros: Melds score while the pieces race.
Open melds show what a player holds.
cons: Hits break up the melding.
Two things need watching at once.

pairs.tendency: A piece may carry a power that works once, such as a shield that blocks one landing.
pros: A shield turns away a hit once.
Players choose when to spend the power.
cons: Once spent, the piece is open again.
Players wait to see who spends first.

pairs.tendency: On your turn you offer a move and the other player can turn it down, so a landing that would send their piece home can be refused.
pros: A hit can be dodged by saying no.
Offering two moves tests the other player.
cons: Players tend to offer harmless moves most of the time.
Every refusal adds waiting.

pairs.tendency: A whisper goes from player to player telling where pieces will land, and it may change on the way.
pros: Warnings can travel round the table.
A changed message can lead a piece astray.
cons: Nobody can check a message until the piece lands.
A garbled warning sends a piece into a hit.

pairs.tendency: Before the game, each player hands cards to a neighbour, so the neighbour holds the moves the giver chose.
pros: The cards passed show the giver's plan.
Players guess what their neighbour will hold.
cons: Long-move cards given away give the neighbour a way to hit.
Nobody sees their new cards until they have handed over.

pairs.tendency: One player sets the pieces out on the track and the other chooses a side, so the setup has to leave neither side an easy landing.
pros: The setter works to make both sides even.
The chooser sees where the hits can come from.
cons: A setup too close to one side gets swapped.
Choosing takes a long look at the board.

pairs.tendency: A piece that reaches the far end turns into a more powerful one, and a piece sent back loses all the ground it had made.
pros: Reaching the end earns a prize.
Pieces near the end draw the most attention.
cons: A hit near the end wipes out the longest trip.
Players hold back to stay out of reach.

pairs.tendency: Teams run in legs, and a runner landed on during a leg goes back to the start of that leg, not the whole race.
pros: A hit costs one leg.
Handovers get timed to dodge rivals.
cons: A sent-back runner holds up the whole team.
Teams wait at handover spaces.

pairs.tendency: A shape that cannot be captured works like a safe space, so pieces in it stay put when a rival lands nearby.
pros: Players build towards a shape no hit can break.
Safe spots follow a pattern everyone knows.
cons: A shape takes several turns to build.
Pieces outside the shape stay open to hits.

pairs.tendency: Cards worth points are picked up along the track, and a piece sent to the start puts them down again.
pros: Everyone knows which cards to chase.
A hit can move a prize from one player to another.
cons: A piece holding a prize draws every rival.
Prizes can be dropped on the way.

pairs.tendency: Cards in the middle are open to all, so anyone can see which move would land on a rival.
pros: Everyone sees the same moves.
A move open to all can be taken by anyone.
cons: The hit on offer is visible to every rival.
No plan can be kept hidden.

pairs.tendency: Every hit adds a counter to the pot in the middle, and one player takes the pot at the end.
pros: Sending a piece home pays into the pot.
The pot grows from round to round.
cons: A growing pot tempts players to hit.
A piece back at the start has little left to gain.

pairs.tendency: Seeds go into pits one at a time, and a last seed that falls into a pit holding a rival's seeds can send them back to the start.
pros: A last seed can empty a pit.
Players count seeds before they scoop.
cons: Counting every pit slows each turn.
A full pit can be lost in one sowing.

pairs.tendency: An extra hand lies face down in the middle, and the cards in it might hold the long move that lands on a rival.
pros: Taking the spare hand changes what a player can hit.
The spare hand is a gamble.
cons: Cards put back give hints to the others.
The hand taken may hold nothing that reaches a rival.

pairs.tendency: Some squares are safe, some send pieces back and some skip a turn, so a landing on a rival's piece sits on top of all those rules.
pros: Safe squares give pieces somewhere to rest.
Squares that send a piece back can hit twice.
cons: A rival on a safe square cannot be sent back, which wastes the roll.
The board fills with rules to remember.

pairs.tendency: A move costs money, so a hit on a rival is paid for and the hitter may be left with nothing.
pros: A hit has a price the hitter knows.
Players count the price before landing.
cons: A hit that misses wastes the cost.
A player with no money cannot move.

pairs.tendency: A player's pieces are split across several routes, so a single hit sends back only part of the force.
pros: Spreading out limits the damage of one hit.
Pieces on several routes share the work.
cons: A lone piece is easy to land on.
Attention is divided between the routes.

pairs.tendency: Everyone keeps moving until the music stops, and when it does, two pieces on one space send the older one back.
pros: The stop comes as a surprise.
Players hurry to get ahead of rivals.
cons: The slowest player is caught at the signal.
A sudden stop can pile pieces on one space.

pairs.tendency: Players may swap cards before moving, trading a short move for a long one that reaches a rival.
pros: Swapping changes what can be hit.
Players dig for the card that hits.
cons: A swap can give away the card that was needed.
Waiting for another player to agree stalls the turn.

pairs.tendency: Discards form one pile, and a player who picks it up also picks up cards that show where hits can land.
pros: The pile shows what has been played.
Picking it up changes the next player's moves.
cons: A pile taken early is small.
A player sent home may have taken the pile for nothing.

pairs.tendency: One suit beats the rest, so a move made with a trump card can land a hit that other cards cannot.
pros: A trump card can hit where others cannot.
Players keep trumps back for hits.
cons: A trump spent early is gone.
Players count which trumps are left.

pairs.tendency: A player takes part in two games at the same time, so a hit in one game may be answered by a hit in the other.
pros: Two boards mean two sets of landings.
A hit on one board can pay off on the other.
cons: Watching two boards takes longer.
A loss on one board can arrive with a hit on the other.

pairs.tendency: A wild card can be played as any move, so it can be called as the exact number that lands on a rival.
pros: A wild card can aim a hit exactly.
Players save wild cards for hits.
cons: Rivals hold back when a wild card is out.
A spent wild card leaves the piece open.

pairs.tendency: A piece that runs off one edge comes back on the other, so a piece can land on a rival from behind.
pros: Pieces can be hit from any side.
The track has no edge to hide behind.
cons: A piece that thinks it is ahead can be hit from behind.
Players watch both ends of the board.

pairs.tendency: One player knows where a piece is hidden and the others ask yes or no questions until they can land on its space.
pros: Each answer shrinks the places a piece can be.
Players share what they learn.
cons: Questions use up turns.
A piece found early goes home early.

pairs.tendency: The first piece to the end wins, and every landing on a rival sends it back to the start of the race.
pros: A hit can end someone's chances.
Players watch the leader.
cons: A leader can drop to last in one move.
The race runs long if hits come often.

pairs.tendency: Landing on a rival scores a point for the hitter and also sends the rival back.
pros: A hit pays twice.
Players score and race together.
cons: The player behind may stay behind.
Scores swing with each hit.

pairs.tendency: A piece sent back too often is out, so the last piece or player on the board wins.
pros: Each hit moves a rival closer to out.
Players pick the closest target.
cons: A player already behind gets no break.
Players who are out early wait for the rest.

pairs.tendency: The team shares one side against a board that sends pieces back, with monsters whose landings send a piece to the start.
pros: Teammates warn one another.
A shared plan is easy to talk through.
cons: One sent-back piece sets the whole team back.
A single doubter can slow the plan.

pairs.tendency: The group works towards one goal, such as getting every piece across, while the board's own landings keep sending pieces back.
pros: The group can see each piece's path.
Players help the pieces left behind.
cons: One sent-back piece holds up the goal.
The group waits for the slowest piece.

pairs.tendency: Each player has a secret goal, so a landing on a rival may look like an ordinary move or part of a plan.
pros: A hit hides its purpose.
Players guess goals from who gets hit.
cons: A friendly player may be the one hitting.
Nobody can tell a hit from an accident.

pairs.tendency: The story ends when the pieces reach the end, and a piece sent back is a setback in the tale.
pros: A hit changes the course of the tale.
The story shapes where pieces go.
cons: A sent-back piece repeats scenes.
The tale can take many rounds.

pairs.tendency: Nobody wins, yet pieces still go back to the start when landed on.
pros: Hits happen with nothing to gain.
Players talk about what happened.
cons: Players decide for themselves what a hit means.
Players may stop hitting each other.

pairs.tendency: Each player says what a successful game means for them, such as staying out of reach or sending back as many pieces as they can.
pros: Hitters and hiders play on the same board.
Goals can change in the middle of the game.
cons: A hider and a hitter can share a table without noticing each other.
A hit counts differently to each player.

pairs.tendency: The game goes on until one player loses, and each time a piece is sent back its owner gets closer to being that player.
pros: Everyone tries to stay out of last place.
Hits go to those in front.
cons: A piece sent home is likely the next loser.
The one left behind is marked early.

pairs.tendency: Pieces sent back go to the start and play again, so the game never runs out of pieces.
pros: Hits keep players near each other.
Nobody is removed.
cons: No one ever finishes.
The game can run on for a whole evening.

pairs.tendency: The track loops with no end, and every landing sends a piece back.
pros: Players discover the loop by playing.
A hit has no result to measure.
cons: Players may wonder why they are playing.
Players may stop after a while.

pairs.tendency: A lone player moves a piece across a laid-out row of cards and tries to stay clear of spaces that send it back.
pros: The layout can be learned.
Every space is known after a few tries.
cons: One landing returns the piece to the start.
Getting stuck ends the game.

pairs.tendency: Several short races are played, and a piece sent back in one race loses only that game.
pros: A hit costs one game.
Players change tactics between games.
cons: A loss early on can decide the match.
Games repeat and may begin to look alike.

pairs.tendency: Being sent back adds points to a player's total, and the lowest total wins.
pros: Players want to keep away from rivals.
Hits add to a score.
cons: Pieces keep their distance.
A hit on the leader can help the others.

pairs.tendency: A piece has to land exactly on the final space, and while it waits for the right roll a rival can land on it.
pros: The final space is a known target.
Players wait near the end for the right number.
cons: A waiting piece can be hit.
Waiting uses up turns.

pairs.tendency: The aim is to be sent back first, so players try to get landed on.
pros: A landing is what everyone wants.
Players invite rivals to hit them.
cons: Hits stop being a threat.
Players may refuse to hit.

pairs.tendency: Everyone has a track of their own, and only the board's rules send a piece back.
pros: Players race side by side.
No rival can land on them.
cons: Hits come from the track alone.
Players only watch each other's progress.

pairs.tendency: Landing on a rival is an attack, and players choose whom to hit.
pros: A hit is aimed at a person.
Players answer a hit with a hit.
cons: A feud can fill the game.
The player ahead becomes the target.

pairs.tendency: Players change the track, and the changed track sends pieces back when they land.
pros: A hit is set up in advance.
Players seldom aim at one person.
cons: Blame is hard to place.
A trap may catch its builder.

pairs.tendency: Everyone is on one team, so a landing by a teammate sends a friend back only by mistake.
pros: Teammates can talk through every landing.
A piece can be covered by a friend.
cons: A hit by a friend hurts the whole team.
Players check each move to avoid hitting a friend.

pairs.tendency: Players mostly help each other, though a player with a private reason can land on a friend and send them home.
pros: Friends can be trusted most of the time.
A hit can pass as a slip.
cons: A betrayal stings more among friends.
Players start to doubt each other's moves.

pairs.tendency: Two teams send each other back, and teammates may share a safe space.
pros: Teammates can guard one another.
A hit is a team event.
cons: Teammates argue over who takes the hit.
A team that falls behind can be hit again and again.

pairs.tendency: One player on the team secretly lands on teammates to send them back.
pros: A hit from a friend raises suspicion.
Players watch who lands near whom.
cons: A traitor's landing looks like a slip.
Teams argue over blame.

pairs.tendency: Moves go by letter, so a piece can be sent back days after the rival made the move.
pros: Each letter holds the next landing.
Players think about a move for days.
cons: Waiting for a reply leaves a piece exposed.
A hit may arrive before the owner has moved.

pairs.tendency: A ghost's piece sits on the track and moves only by hints, and anyone who lands on it sends it back.
pros: The ghost's piece is there for all to see.
Hints set where it goes.
cons: The ghost cannot answer a hit.
Players disagree about the ghost's next move.

pairs.tendency: The game master places monsters on the track, and a player who lands on one is sent back.
pros: The master sets the pace of the hits.
Players tell a story around the board.
cons: The master can rule a hit a near miss.
The master has a lot to run.

pairs.tendency: A game chalked on the street uses stones as pieces, and passers-by can join in and land on other people's stones.
pros: Anyone can join.
Passers-by bring new players.
cons: A newcomer's landing can surprise the table.
Rules differ from street to street.

pairs.tendency: One player's piece is chased by all the others, and any landing on it sends it back.
pros: The lone piece is everyone's target.
The group has to agree on who hits.
cons: The lone player is paid more for a win.
A single hit can end the lone player's trip.

pairs.tendency: A single player moves a piece against the pack, and landing on a pack piece sends the player home.
pros: Luck and choices are the only forces.
The player gets to know the pack.
cons: Nobody else can be blamed for a hit.
A solo player has nobody to share a loss with.

pairs.tendency: Dice decide everything, and a roll that ends on a rival sends it back with no way to avoid it.
pros: Hits come from the dice.
Players cannot plan around them.
cons: The leader can be sent home by any roll.
Skill barely matters.

pairs.tendency: Dice move the pieces, and a re-roll card can turn a landing on a rival into another go.
pros: A re-roll saves a piece from a hit.
Players keep cards for the right moment.
cons: The cards run out.
Re-rolls slow the game.

pairs.tendency: Players choose which piece to move and a small roll decides how far, so a landing on a rival takes both planning and luck.
pros: Choices count for most.
A piece can be placed out of reach.
cons: A hit still depends on a roll.
A careful plan can be undone by a throw.

pairs.tendency: With no dice, every landing is chosen, and a sent-back piece is the result of someone's plan.
pros: A hit can be seen coming.
Players learn from each loss.
cons: A careless step is punished with a hit.
A hit leaves nobody to blame but the owner.

pairs.tendency: The dice are read as signs, so a piece sent back is read as a warning.
pros: A hit is read as a message.
Players talk about what it means.
cons: Meanings differ from player to player.
A hit can start an argument.

pairs.tendency: Players sense when a rival is about to move and try to step out of reach before a landing.
pros: Reading each other gets quicker with practice.
A landing becomes a guess about a friend.
cons: A piece can be hit anyway.
Players need to know each other.

pairs.tendency: A roll looked up on a table says what happens, and a landing on a rival adds a scene of its own.
pros: Each hit adds to the story.
The table decides what comes next.
cons: A sent-back piece repeats scenes.
The table takes time to read.

pairs.tendency: Every piece is in view, so every possible landing can be seen before it happens.
pros: Players can plan a hit.
Nothing is hidden.
cons: Hits can be avoided by looking.
Slow thinking holds up the game.

pairs.tendency: Cards in hand decide the moves and nobody sees them, so no one knows who can land on whom.
pros: A hit can come from nowhere.
Players bluff about their cards.
cons: Players cannot judge the risk.
Suspicion grows round the table.

pairs.tendency: Pieces look alike but belong to secret roles, and a landing on one shows whose it is.
pros: A hit shows a hidden role.
Players guess who is who.
cons: A wrong guess sends a friend home.
Roles come out early.

pairs.tendency: Clues show where a piece sits, and a player works out its place before landing on it.
pros: Players reason from clues.
A hit shows a clue was read right.
cons: A wrong reading wastes a turn.
Long thinking slows play.

pairs.tendency: A player acts as if a piece is out of reach, hoping a rival will not land on it.
pros: A bluff can keep a piece safe.
Players watch each other's faces.
cons: A called bluff ends with a landing.
A bluff may fool nobody.

pairs.tendency: One player knows a secret rule, perhaps that a certain space sends pieces back, and the others find out by being sent home.
pros: Rules are learned by trying them.
A hit is a lesson.
cons: The player who knows has the advantage.
Newcomers are sent home by rules they cannot see.

pairs.tendency: One player knows where the safe spaces are and can only hint, while the others try to avoid being landed on.
pros: Hints help pieces choose.
The hinter watches the others try.
cons: A hint can be read wrongly.
The hinter cannot warn plainly.

pairs.tendency: Spaces are turned over as pieces reach them, so a piece may land on a space that sends it back, or on a rival hidden there.
pros: Exploring finds new spaces.
Every step may hold a surprise.
cons: A step into the unknown can end at the start.
Nobody can plan far ahead.

pairs.tendency: One hand lies face up, so everyone can see the moves it holds, including the ones that land on a rival.
pros: The open hand shows the possible hits.
Players plan around it.
cons: The open hand gives away the plan.
It leaves no room for surprise.

pairs.tendency: Some scores are hidden, so a hit on a rival may help or may not, and nobody can tell.
pros: A hit can change a hidden score.
Players guess who is ahead.
cons: A hit may land on the wrong target.
Guesses about the score can be wrong.

pairs.tendency: One player moves at a time, so everyone can see a landing coming.
pros: Each landing is watched.
Players plan for their own turn.
cons: Waiting for a turn can take a while.
A hit comes at the end of a wait.

pairs.tendency: All players pick a move in secret and then reveal, so a landing on a rival depends on a guess.
pros: A hit is a guess about what the others pick.
Nobody waits.
cons: A guess can miss.
Two pieces can land on the same space.

pairs.tendency: Anyone can move at any moment, so whoever is quickest lands first.
pros: Quick hands win the landing.
Pieces are in danger all the time.
cons: Slow players get hit most.
Players argue over who landed first.

pairs.tendency: Each turn has a clock, so a player may have to land on a rival in a hurry.
pros: A clock forces a choice.
A hit can be hurried.
cons: Moves made in a rush can miss.
A player who runs out of time loses the move.

pairs.tendency: With one move a day, a piece within reach of a rival stays exposed for the whole day.
pros: Each hit comes slowly.
Players think between moves.
cons: A hit can wait overnight.
The game takes weeks.

pairs.tendency: A pause before each move gives time to see a landing coming and step away.
pros: Each landing is watched carefully.
The slowness lets players plan.
cons: Few hits get through.
Games take a long time.

pairs.tendency: The game speeds up, so late landings come in a rush and pieces are sent back more often.
pros: Hits come faster over time.
Late moves arrive quickly.
cons: Players have less time to avoid a hit.
Pieces end up at the start often.

pairs.tendency: Landing on a piece earns another go, so a hit can be followed at once by a second move.
pros: A hit pays with a bonus turn.
Players chain hits together.
cons: A lucky player can hit several times.
The others wait a long time.

pairs.tendency: The first stage places the pieces and the second is a race where landings send pieces back.
pros: The setup shapes the race.
Early choices count later.
cons: A first-stage mistake shows up in the race.
The stages can feel like two games.

pairs.tendency: The track stands for a river, and a piece sent back stands for a loss somewhere along it.
pros: A hit shows what a loss costs.
Players see how a system fails.
cons: Some details are left out.
A model can mislead.

pairs.tendency: Each player is a group such as farmers or a village council, and a landing is one group getting in another's way.
pros: Hits show who blocks whom.
Players take up different views.
cons: Players argue about whether a hit was fair.
Roles pull in different directions.

pairs.tendency: Pieces take from one limited stock as they move, and a piece sent back returns what it took.
pros: A hit puts something back in the stock.
Players keep an eye on the stock.
cons: A sent-back piece may take it again.
The stock can run low before the end.

pairs.tendency: A landing sends a piece back only a few rounds later.
pros: Players plan ahead for a hit.
Hits arrive when they are not expected.
cons: Players forget what they set up.
Cause and effect are hard to follow.

pairs.tendency: Players try a new rule such as making the third space safe, then play on to see whether fewer pieces go home.
pros: Rules can be tried in play.
The group can compare before and after.
cons: One rule may change the whole game.
Testing takes extra rounds.

pairs.tendency: After the game, the group talks about each landing and why it happened.
pros: Hits are talked through.
Players learn why they happened.
cons: Players recall events differently.
Talking takes time after the game.

pairs.tendency: A space torn up after a landing stays gone for the next game.
pros: Hits change the board for ever.
Each game starts where the last one ended.
cons: A spoiled board stays spoiled.
A hit has long after-effects.

pairs.tendency: The rules of the game make a point, and sending pieces back makes a point about who pays for a mistake.
pros: A hit carries a message.
Players argue about it.
cons: The point can be missed.
A player may disagree with the point.

pairs.tendency: A piece sent back can cost something real, such as a promise or a coin.
pros: A hit matters after the game ends.
Players take every landing seriously.
cons: A hit can hurt a friendship.
Players may avoid hitting.

pairs.tendency: Points stand for something like kindness, and a piece that lands on another sends it back and takes the points.
pros: Hits show what the points cost.
Players chase the number.
cons: The number replaces what it stood for.
The loser feels the hit.

pairs.tendency: Players practise a shared future, and a piece sent back shows what could go wrong.
pros: A hit shows a risk before it is real.
The group tests a way of living.
cons: A sent-back piece makes the group stop and talk.
A practice cannot show everything.

pairs.tendency: Dice move the pieces along the path, and when a roll lets a player complete a row of three, one rival piece is taken.
pros: A roll can finish a row.
Players watch for rows forming.
cons: A roll that misses a row wastes a move.
The dice decide who gets to take.

pairs.tendency: Players pick pieces or cards from a shared row, and a pick can finish a row of three.
pros: A pick can stop a rival's row.
Players read the shared row for what a rival needs.
cons: Late picks leave no part for a row.
A pick that blocks costs the picker a piece.

pairs.tendency: Players bid for the right to place the next piece, and the winning bid may complete a row.
pros: A bid is a price paid for a row.
Bids show who is near a row.
cons: Money spent on a bid is gone.
A high bid can still fail to finish the row.

pairs.tendency: A player can take a piece with one row, or hold off and risk it all for a second row at once.
pros: A finished row is a sure prize.
A row can be opened and closed again.
cons: Waiting for a second row risks a break.
Rivals can see the open row.

pairs.tendency: Pieces hold parts of the map, and a row inside a held area takes a rival piece out of it.
pros: A row can clear a region.
Held areas guide where rows form.
cons: Taking a piece can lose the area it stood in.
Rows get built out of the rivals' reach.

pairs.tendency: Workers fill job spaces, and three workers lined up on neighbouring jobs make a row.
pros: A row of jobs removes a rival worker.
Jobs are chosen for the row they make.
cons: A taken worker cannot do its job.
There are fewer jobs than workers.

pairs.tendency: Matching colours or shapes in a line is already pattern building, so a straight line of three tiles can be the row that takes a piece.
pros: Patterns and rows overlap.
A pattern in progress warns rivals.
cons: A row can be broken by a taken piece.
Two players can aim at the same row.

pairs.tendency: Cards in hand give the pieces to place, and holding a card back means a row waits.
pros: Saving a card keeps a row ready.
Players guess what the others hold.
cons: A held card can go unplayed to the end.
A hand full of unusable cards stalls the row.

pairs.tendency: Winning a trick lets a player place a piece, and three pieces in a row take one of a rival's.
pros: A trick won can add a piece to a row.
Tricks and rows are counted in different ways.
cons: Winning a trick can mean breaking up a row.
There are two aims to hold at once.

pairs.tendency: Players talk about rows, with offers such as "don't break my row and I won't break yours".
pros: A deal can save a piece.
Agreed rows stay open.
cons: Deals break once someone sees a row.
Talk takes up turns.

pairs.tendency: Three matching pieces count as a row, so collecting a set also takes a rival's piece.
pros: One goal does the work of two.
Sets and rows overlap.
cons: A set that is one piece short stays unfinished.
Rivals take pieces from a half-made set.

pairs.tendency: Tiles lay out the map, and three tiles in a line make a row.
pros: The map shows where rows can go.
Tiles can block a row.
cons: A tile that helps a rival's row cannot be taken back.
The map fills and fewer rows are possible.

pairs.tendency: A player answers the last move with a move of their own, and the answers may build up to a row.
pros: A chain of answers can build a row.
Replies show what is coming.
cons: An answer can give a row away.
Players wait for their turn.

pairs.tendency: With no talking, a player sets up a row and the others have to guess what it is for.
pros: A row can build without a word.
Players watch the board closely.
cons: Nobody can ask for a pause.
A piece is taken in silence.

pairs.tendency: A player may change a rule instead of moving, such as making four in a row the mill or letting two pieces be taken.
pros: A row can be made harder or easier.
A rule can protect a piece.
cons: A rule changed in mid-game confuses the others.
Players argue about it.

pairs.tendency: Pieces are characters, and a row of three is an ambush that captures a rival character.
pros: A row gets a story.
A taken piece leaves the story.
cons: A character taken out leaves a player with nothing to say.
Players argue over what happened in the story.

pairs.tendency: Pieces are flicked into place, and three that land in a line take a rival piece.
pros: A steady hand makes a row.
A flick can scatter a row.
cons: A knocked piece spoils the line.
Rows sometimes form by chance.

pairs.tendency: The map is drawn by the players, and a drawn line of three spaces makes a row.
pros: Players can draw a row.
The map grows as the game goes on.
cons: A row can be drawn in a place a rival can reach.
Space on the paper runs out.

pairs.tendency: Letters are placed in a line, and a real three-letter word counts as a row.
pros: A row can also be a word.
Players look for spelling and lines together.
cons: A word the dictionary refuses stops the row.
Spelling arguments slow play.

pairs.tendency: Tiles join where their ends match, and a run of three tiles counts as a row.
pros: A run of tiles can take a piece.
Matching ends guide the line.
cons: A tile with no match ends the turn.
Rows depend on the tiles drawn.

pairs.tendency: A meld laid on the table is a row of cards, and a finished meld takes a piece.
pros: Melds count as rows.
The cards are on show.
cons: Rivals can add to a meld.
Open melds give away plans.

pairs.tendency: A piece holds one power that works once, such as stopping a row from taking it.
pros: A power can save a piece.
A used power is gone.
cons: Nobody wants to spend their power first.
A row can still form around a protected piece.

pairs.tendency: The other player may turn down a move that would complete a row.
pros: A row can be refused.
A rival has a say in a row.
cons: Offers can hide a row.
Turns slow down.

pairs.tendency: A message goes along the table saying where a row is forming.
pros: News of a row gets round.
A message can change on the way.
cons: A false message misleads.
By the time a row is built, everyone already knows.

pairs.tendency: Before play, players hand cards to a neighbour, and a card passed on may be the one that completes a row for the neighbour.
pros: A hand can be shaped before the game starts.
Players try to hand over nothing useful.
cons: A card given away cannot be used by the giver.
Cards arrive only after a player has given theirs away.

pairs.tendency: One player sets out the pieces and the other picks a side, so the starting rows are made as even as they can be.
pros: Both sides start level.
The setter has to think about both sides.
cons: A setup with an early row gets swapped.
Choosing takes time.

pairs.tendency: A piece that reaches the far end becomes a more powerful piece, and a row can take it before it gets there.
pros: A promoted piece is a target.
A piece far from home can still be taken.
cons: Players weigh a row against a trip.
Pieces held back stay out of the row.

pairs.tendency: Each leg of the race leaves a marker, and three markers in a line take one from the other team.
pros: Teams plan their markers.
A row can speed a team on.
cons: Markers can be taken from behind.
Rows can delay the handover.

pairs.tendency: A row takes a piece, unless the piece sits in a shape that cannot be captured.
pros: Shapes protect pieces from rows.
Players build safe shapes first.
cons: A safe shape takes time to build.
Pieces outside it can be taken.

pairs.tendency: Winning a card named in advance scores, and a row takes a piece, so there are two ways to score.
pros: Rows and cards both count.
Players keep track of both.
cons: A row may take a piece that carried a card.
Players cannot chase both at once.

pairs.tendency: Cards in the middle can be used by all, so a row of three may be built from them.
pros: All players can see the rows.
A shared card can finish anyone's row.
cons: Nobody can keep a row secret.
A shared card can help a rival.

pairs.tendency: Taking a rival's piece with a row wins the pot in the middle.
pros: A row pays out.
The pot grows when no row forms.
cons: Players race to be first to a row.
Players may hold rows back to let the pot grow.

pairs.tendency: Seeds are dropped along a line of pits, and when the last seed makes a row of three of a player's own pits, that player takes a rival's piece.
pros: A row can be planned by counting.
Seeds show where rows will form.
cons: A count that is out by one misses the row.
All that counting makes each turn long.

pairs.tendency: An extra hand of pieces lies face down, and whoever takes it may build a row sooner.
pros: The spare hand adds pieces.
Taking it shows a plan.
cons: A hand taken may hold nothing for a row.
Putting cards back reveals what was taken.

pairs.tendency: Some squares are safe, so a row cannot take a piece standing on one.
pros: Safe squares protect pieces.
Rows form around the safe squares.
cons: Rows on special squares are hard to make.
Players have many squares to keep track of.

pairs.tendency: Every piece has a price, so each row costs money to place.
pros: Each piece has a known cost.
Players think about price before rows.
cons: A row left unfinished wastes the money.
Players run out of money.

pairs.tendency: A player's pieces are split across the board, so rows are begun in several places.
pros: Rows can begin on several fronts.
Rivals have to watch every front.
cons: Rows take longer when pieces are spread out.
A lone piece can be taken.

pairs.tendency: Players place pieces until a signal stops them, and any row of three at that moment takes a piece.
pros: A row is counted at the signal.
Players hurry.
cons: The slowest player has no row.
Rows made late are lost.

pairs.tendency: Cards can be swapped for new ones, so a player hunting for a third piece may draw it.
pros: Swapping chases a missing piece.
Cards put back tell the others what is not wanted.
cons: A player can swap away the very card they wanted.
Waiting for a swap slows the turn.

pairs.tendency: Taking the discard pile gives a player pieces that may finish a row.
pros: A pile can hold the missing piece.
Players watch what gets thrown.
cons: A pile taken early may hold little.
Throwing a card away can help a rival's row.

pairs.tendency: One suit beats the rest, so a row built in the trump suit takes a piece that no other row can protect.
pros: Trumps give some rows more power.
A trump card can break a row.
cons: Trumps are spent quickly.
Players track which trumps are left.

pairs.tendency: A player has two boards, so a row on one board and a row on the other are built by the same hands.
pros: Rows on two boards can share ideas.
A loss on one board can help on the other.
cons: Watching two boards is slow.
A mistake can be repeated on both boards.

pairs.tendency: A wild card stands for any piece, so it can fill the gap in a row of three.
pros: A wild card finishes a row.
Rivals watch for the wild.
cons: A wild card used for a row cannot be used elsewhere.
The player holding a wild card is watched.

pairs.tendency: The edges are joined, so a row can start on one edge and finish on the other.
pros: Rows can run off the edge.
The board has no corner to hide in.
cons: Rows are easy to miss.
Both edges need watching.

pairs.tendency: Players ask yes or no questions about where a rival's pieces stand, hoping to find a row to break.
pros: Each answer rules out some spaces.
A hidden row can be found.
cons: Questions give away what is being asked.
Every question costs a turn.

pairs.tendency: Pieces race to the end, and a row on the way takes a rival out of the race.
pros: A row can slow a rival.
Players weigh a row against running.
cons: Stopping for a row costs ground.
A taken piece cannot finish.

pairs.tendency: Points come from many places, and a row adds one by taking a piece.
pros: A row scores directly.
Players balance rows against other points.
cons: A row that earns little may cost a bigger chance elsewhere.
Chasing rows can neglect the other scores.

pairs.tendency: Players lose pieces to rows until one side has none, and the last player with pieces wins.
pros: Each row thins a rival's side.
Rows are aimed at the leader.
cons: A player with few pieces cannot form a row.
Knocked-out players sit and watch until the end.

pairs.tendency: The team survives together against the board, and a row of three lets the team take a piece of the enemy.
pros: Teammates plan rows together.
A row clears a threat.
cons: One lost piece can break a row.
A player who disagrees can block the plan.

pairs.tendency: The group builds towards one goal, and a row of three counts as a step on the way.
pros: Rows are steps.
Everyone can see the target.
cons: The group may argue over which row to build.
One slow player holds the group back.

pairs.tendency: Each player has a secret goal, so a row built by one player may serve a private aim.
pros: Nobody can tell what a row is for.
Players read goals into the rows they see.
cons: A row may help a goal nobody guessed.
Rows can mislead.

pairs.tendency: The story reaches its end, and a row of three takes a character out of it.
pros: A row can change the plot.
Rows give the story turning points.
cons: A taken character leaves the tale.
The story may stall while rows are built.

pairs.tendency: No one wins, so a row of three takes a piece for no reward.
pros: Rows happen for their own sake.
Players talk about what they built.
cons: A row has no point beyond itself.
Players may stop building rows.

pairs.tendency: Each player says what a successful game means, such as making many rows or keeping every piece.
pros: Row-makers and keepers share a board.
Goals can change.
cons: Each player judges their own result.
A row-maker may take a keeper's piece.

pairs.tendency: Nobody wins, and the player who loses the most pieces to rows is the loser.
pros: Each player plays to avoid the bottom spot.
Rows decide who is behind.
cons: A taken piece marks a player.
Everyone else is simply safe.

pairs.tendency: The aim is to keep playing, so a row that would take the last piece is held back.
pros: Players hold back from ending the game.
Rows are built but not always used.
cons: A player may refuse to take.
The game has no finish.

pairs.tendency: A row of three takes a piece, but nobody can win, so the rows lead nowhere.
pros: Rows show how the game works.
Players test what happens.
cons: A taken piece changes nothing in the end.
Some players lose interest and stop.

pairs.tendency: A lone player builds rows against a layout of cards.
pros: Rows clear the layout.
Each row removes a card.
cons: If no row can be made, the game is over.
The player has no rival.

pairs.tendency: Several short games are played, and a row decides each one.
pros: A row can win a game.
Players can try a new plan in each game.
cons: A quick early row can settle a game.
The games repeat.

pairs.tendency: Each piece taken by a row counts against its owner, so the fewest points wins.
pros: Players avoid being taken.
Rows are aimed at the leader.
cons: Taking a piece can help a rival.
Players who take less may win.

pairs.tendency: A piece has to land on the last space exactly, and a row can take it while it waits.
pros: Everyone knows which space ends the game.
Waiting pieces are in view.
cons: Waiting costs turns.
A waiting piece can be taken.

pairs.tendency: The aim is to lose all your pieces, so a row becomes something to hand to a rival.
pros: A row gives pieces away.
Players invite rows.
cons: Rows lose their threat.
Players refuse to take.

pairs.tendency: Everyone builds rows on their own board, and a row takes a piece from the pool.
pros: Players build side by side.
Rows are compared at the end.
cons: A row cannot touch a rival.
Players have little effect on one another.

pairs.tendency: A row is an attack, since three in a row takes a rival piece.
pros: A row is aimed at one rival.
Players answer with a row of their own.
cons: A rival may break a row first.
A feud can start.

pairs.tendency: Rows are made on the board, and one player's row blocks the next player's.
pros: Players attack through the board.
A row can block and can take.
cons: Attacks rarely single out one player.
A block may help a rival.

pairs.tendency: Everyone is on one team, so rows are shared and the pieces taken are the board's.
pros: A team can build one row.
Talk can plan the rows.
cons: A taken piece is a loss for all.
Players depend on each other.

pairs.tendency: Players mostly share rows but each has a private reason to take.
pros: Rows help the group.
A private aim can break a row.
cons: A row built for the group may help one player most.
Trust is tested.

pairs.tendency: Teams build rows against each other, and teammates cover each other's pieces.
pros: Teammates guard a piece.
A row is a team effort.
cons: A team argues over a row.
A trailing team keeps losing pieces.

pairs.tendency: A traitor builds a row against their own team.
pros: Players grow wary when a friend builds a row.
Players watch who builds rows.
cons: A traitor's row looks like a mistake.
The team quarrels over who did it.

pairs.tendency: Moves go by letter, so a row takes weeks to build.
pros: Each letter holds a move.
Players think for days.
cons: Waiting leaves a row open.
A letter may arrive late.

pairs.tendency: A ghost plays through hints, and its pieces may form a row.
pros: The ghost has a say.
Hints guide the row.
cons: The ghost cannot answer back.
Players disagree about what the ghost means.

pairs.tendency: The game master places the opposing pieces, and a row of three takes one.
pros: The master sets rows.
Players build a story around the rows.
cons: The master can decide what counts.
The master has many pieces to manage.

pairs.tendency: A game drawn in chalk on a street uses stones as pieces, and anyone passing can join in and make a row.
pros: Passers-by can join.
Rules spread by word of mouth.
cons: Newcomers may not know the row rule.
No two streets play quite the same way.

pairs.tendency: One player's pieces face many, and a row by the lone player takes a piece from the pack.
pros: The pack works together.
A win for the lone player scores extra.
cons: A single row can end the pack's plan.
One against many can be lonely.

pairs.tendency: A lone player builds rows against the pack, and each row takes a piece.
pros: Only luck and the player's own choices decide the result.
The player comes to know how the pack plays.
cons: There is no rival to blame.
Nobody shares a loss.

pairs.tendency: Dice or draws place the pieces, and a row forms by luck.
pros: Rows come from luck.
Planning has little use.
cons: A row takes a piece without anyone choosing it.
Clever play changes little.

pairs.tendency: Dice place the pieces, and a re-roll can help finish a row.
pros: A re-roll can save a row.
Players keep re-rolls for later.
cons: Re-rolls run out.
Each re-roll adds time to the turn.

pairs.tendency: Players choose where to place, and a small draw decides which piece they get.
pros: Choice shapes the row.
A draw adds a surprise.
cons: A draw can spoil a row.
Planning can go to waste.

pairs.tendency: With no dice, every row is planned, and a row takes a piece by design.
pros: A row can be seen coming.
Players learn from the pieces they lose.
cons: Mistakes are punished.
There are few surprises.

pairs.tendency: Dice are read as signs, and a row of three is read as one too.
pros: Each row is given a meaning.
Players discuss the reading.
cons: Players read the same row differently.
Readings can lead to quarrels.

pairs.tendency: Players sense where a rival will place, and try to block a row before it forms.
pros: Players pick up each other's habits.
Placing becomes a guess about a friend's next move.
cons: A row can still form.
It works only among players who know each other.

pairs.tendency: A roll looked up on a table says what is placed, and a row adds a scene.
pros: Rows add to the tale.
The lookup table sets what is placed next.
cons: A taken piece is a scene lost.
Looking up each roll slows play.

pairs.tendency: Every piece is in view, so every row can be seen forming.
pros: A row can be planned.
Every threat is out in the open.
cons: Rows are blocked early.
Players who think long hold up the table.

pairs.tendency: Pieces or cards in hand are hidden, so nobody knows whether a row is coming.
pros: A row can arrive without warning.
Players bluff about what they hold.
cons: Players cannot judge the risk of leaving a gap.
Suspicion builds.

pairs.tendency: Some players hold secret roles, and a row that takes a piece can show whose piece it was.
pros: A row can show a role.
Players try to work out each other's roles.
cons: A wrong guess takes a friend's piece.
Roles are revealed quickly.

pairs.tendency: Clues point to where a rival's pieces stand, and a player works out where a row can be broken.
pros: Players work from the clues.
A broken row shows the clue was read right.
cons: A misread clue costs a turn.
Working out the clues takes time.

pairs.tendency: A player acts as if a row is about to close, to make the others block the wrong place.
pros: A bluff can pull a block away.
Players watch each other's hands.
cons: A bluff that is called leaves the player exposed.
The others may see through it.

pairs.tendency: One player knows a secret rule about rows, and the others find it out by being told no.
pros: Players find the rule by testing it.
A taken piece teaches a lesson.
cons: The player with the secret is ahead.
New players lose pieces to a rule they cannot see.

pairs.tendency: One player knows which row will win and can only hint, while the others try to guess.
pros: Hints guide the others.
The hinter watches them try.
cons: A hint can be misread.
The hinter cannot say it outright.

pairs.tendency: The map is turned over as pieces explore, so a row may form on a space nobody had seen.
pros: Exploring opens new rows.
Each turn can uncover something new.
cons: A row can form where a piece cannot reach.
Long plans are hard to make.

pairs.tendency: One hand lies face up, so everyone can see which pieces would finish a row.
pros: The open hand shows possible rows.
Players plan round it.
cons: Everyone can read that hand's plan.
It cannot surprise anyone.

pairs.tendency: Some scores are hidden, so a row may help a player more than anyone knows.
pros: A row can change a hidden score.
Nobody knows the leader for sure.
cons: A row may go to the wrong target.
Players can misjudge the scores.

pairs.tendency: One player moves at a time, so everyone can see a row forming.
pros: Each row is watched.
Players plan while others move.
cons: Turns can be slow to come round.
A row is closed at the end of a wait.

pairs.tendency: All players place in secret and then reveal, so a row depends on a guess about what the others place.
pros: A row is a guess about what the others do.
Everyone moves together.
cons: A wrong guess wastes the placement.
Two players can reach the same space.

pairs.tendency: Anyone can place a piece at any moment, so whoever is quickest closes the row.
pros: Quick hands close rows.
No piece is ever safe.
cons: Slow players lose most.
Disputes break out over who placed first.

pairs.tendency: Each turn has a clock, so a player may have to close a row in a hurry.
pros: The timer makes players decide.
A row can be hurried.
cons: A move made in a rush can miss.
When time runs out, the turn is lost.

pairs.tendency: With one move a day, an open row stays open for the whole day.
pros: Each row comes slowly.
Players have a day to think.
cons: A row can wait overnight.
A game lasts weeks.

pairs.tendency: A pause before each move gives time to see a row forming and break it.
pros: Each row is watched carefully.
The slow pace gives room to plan.
cons: Few rows get through.
Each game runs long.

pairs.tendency: The game speeds up, so late rows come in a rush and pieces are taken more often.
pros: Rows come faster over time.
End-game moves come in a rush.
cons: Players have less time to break a row.
The board empties fast.

pairs.tendency: Taking a piece with a row earns another go, so one row can be followed by a second move.
pros: A row pays with a bonus turn.
Rows can be linked one after another.
cons: A lucky player can take several pieces.
Other players sit idle meanwhile.

pairs.tendency: The first stage places the pieces and the second moves them, and rows made in the first stage set up the second.
pros: The first stage shapes the second.
Early rows count later.
cons: An early slip carries into the second stage.
Placing and moving can feel like separate games.

pairs.tendency: The board stands for a real system, and a row stands for something that closes a gap in it.
pros: A row shows how a gap closes.
Players see how a system can be broken.
cons: Simplifying leaves parts out.
The model can give the wrong idea.

pairs.tendency: Each player is a group such as farmers or a village council, and a row is one group closing in on another.
pros: Rows show who is in whose way.
Each player sees the board from one group's side.
cons: Players argue over whether a row was fair.
The groups want different things.

pairs.tendency: Pieces draw on one limited stock, and each row taken puts a piece back into it.
pros: A taken piece returns to the stock.
Everyone watches what is left.
cons: Supplies may run out early.
A taken piece may be taken again.

pairs.tendency: A row takes a piece only a few rounds after it is made.
pros: Players plan ahead for a row.
Rows arrive when they are not expected.
cons: Early rows can be forgotten.
It is hard to tell which row caused what.

pairs.tendency: Players try a new rule such as making the row four long, then play on to see how many pieces are taken.
pros: A rule change is tested at the table.
Results before and after can be compared.
cons: A single change can reshape play.
Trials add rounds.

pairs.tendency: After the game, the group talks about each row and how it was built.
pros: Rows are talked through.
Players learn why each one formed.
cons: Memories of the game differ.
The discussion adds time.

pairs.tendency: A piece taken by a row is torn up and stays gone for the next game.
pros: Rows change the game for ever.
Later games carry the losses forward.
cons: Lost pieces never come back.
One row can shape every later game.

pairs.tendency: The rules of the game make a point, and rewarding a row makes a point about who deserves a piece.
pros: Each row restates the game's point.
The point is open to debate.
cons: Some players miss it.
Not everyone agrees with it.

pairs.tendency: A piece taken by a row can cost something real, such as a promise or a coin.
pros: A row matters after the game ends.
Players weigh every row with care.
cons: A row can strain a friendship.
Players may avoid making rows.

pairs.tendency: Points stand for something like kindness, and a row that takes a piece takes the points with it.
pros: Each row moves points from one player to another.
The score becomes the goal.
cons: Players lose sight of what the points meant.
Losing a piece stings.

pairs.tendency: Players practise a shared future, and a row shows how fast a careful plan can be broken.
pros: A row shows a danger while it is still pretend.
The group tries out how it might live.
cons: A lost piece prompts the group to pause and talk.
Rehearsal leaves some things out.

pairs.tendency: Each throw of the dice moves your piece along the path, and the square you land on hands you a few letters to turn into a word.
pros: The dice set how far you go.
Every stop gives a small word puzzle.
cons: A low throw leaves you few letters.
Everyone waits while one person hunts for a word.

pairs.tendency: Letter tiles lie in a shared row and players take one at a time, so each pick tells the others which word you are after.
pros: A pick can show a rival what you need.
Taking a tile can block someone's word.
cons: The last picker gets the odd letters left over.
Long pauses while players study the row.

pairs.tendency: Letters go up for sale one at a time, and a Q is worth far more to a player who holds a U. Players name a price in coins.
pros: Players put a coin value on the letters they want.
Bids show what others plan to spell.
cons: A big bid leaves too few coins for later letters.
Bidding takes longer than spelling.

pairs.tendency: You keep pulling letters from a bag to stretch a word, and one pull too many leaves a heap that spells nothing.
pros: Longer words score more.
Players watch every pull.
cons: A greedy pull can lose the whole word.
Anyone who stops early scores little.

pairs.tendency: Each region of the map holds a pile of letters, and whoever spells the most words from a region takes it.
pros: Words become a way to claim ground.
Players block each other by using the letters nearby.
cons: Short words claim very little.
Turns get spent on moving around the map.

pairs.tendency: Each job spot on the board gives out letters, and once your worker sits there nobody else can use it that turn. Your words come from what your spots gave you.
pros: The choice of spot decides your letters.
Taking a spot can starve a rival of a letter.
cons: Early placers get first pick.
Late placers may end up with letters that fit no word.

pairs.tendency: Every tile carries a letter and also a colour, and your words have to line up with a colour pattern on your board.
pros: Each tile has two jobs.
A finished pattern shows your plan.
cons: Finding a word that fits the pattern takes a long search.
The letter you need may never turn up.

pairs.tendency: A hand of letter cards means choosing between spelling a short word now and saving cards for a longer one later.
pros: Saved letters can make one long word.
Holding cards back hides your plan.
cons: Held letters score nothing meanwhile.
A hand full of one letter stalls you.

pairs.tendency: Everyone lays down one letter card and the one latest in the alphabet takes the trick. Cards you win are the ones you spell with afterwards.
pros: Alphabet order gives every card a rank.
Won cards become word material.
cons: A high letter like Z is hard to use in a word.
Chasing tricks can fill your hand with letters that fit nothing.

pairs.tendency: Players trade letters across the table: "my E for your T", so that each can finish a word.
pros: One trade can finish two words at once.
Talking shows what each person is spelling.
cons: Offers give your word away.
Haggling slows the game.

pairs.tendency: You gather letters into groups, such as every vowel or every letter of a chosen word, and score for each full group.
pros: A word can be planned from the first turn.
Each group is a clear aim.
cons: One missing letter holds up the whole group.
Players sit on letters they will never use.

pairs.tendency: Letter tiles join into a shared grid, and each new tile has to make real words with the tiles beside it.
pros: The grid grows out of everyone's words.
Old letters can be used again in new words.
cons: Space runs out and later turns have little room.
A tile that suits you can break a neighbour's word.

pairs.tendency: One player says a word and the next answers with a word that starts on its last letter. The chain goes round the table.
pros: Words link up into a long chain.
Play moves quickly.
cons: Hard end letters leave players stuck.
Words get repeated or run out.

pairs.tendency: Nobody speaks, so a word is built only by laying down tiles, and the others have to work out what you are spelling from the tiles alone.
pros: Players read each other's tiles closely.
Quiet keeps everyone looking at the board.
cons: A half-spelled word is easy to misread.
A wrong guess cannot be put right without speaking.

pairs.tendency: On your turn you may change a rule, such as making four letters the shortest allowed word, and it holds for everyone after.
pros: A rule change can favour the word you hold.
Players test what counts as a word.
cons: Players argue over whether a new rule covers words already played.
The list of rules grows hard to remember.

pairs.tendency: Each player speaks as a character, and the words they spell have to be ones that character would say.
pros: Word choice shows who the character is.
Players invent reasons for odd words.
cons: A character limits the words you can use.
Players wait while others explain their choice.

pairs.tendency: Letter blocks are flicked or stacked into a word, and a knocked tower sends the letters flying.
pros: Players build words with their hands.
Steady hands count as much as spelling.
cons: A nudge can ruin a finished word.
Balancing blocks slows the spelling.

pairs.tendency: Places on the map get names, and each name has to be a real word spelled out on the page. The map ends up as a sheet of spelled places.
pros: Words fill the map.
Names show who drew what.
cons: Players run out of real words for places.
Spelling disputes hold up the drawing.

pairs.tendency: Tiles carry letters instead of numbers, and a tile joins the line only where its letter matches the open end.
pros: Every tile ties to the one before it.
The open ends show what a player can play next.
cons: A line can reach a letter nobody holds.
A player with no match misses a turn.

pairs.tendency: You lay a finished word face up on the table, and other players can add a letter to it, such as an S for a plural.
pros: Laid words give everyone more to build on.
Showing a word tells others which letters you hold.
cons: Another player can add one letter to your word and score from it.
Players keep words hidden to avoid helping others.

pairs.tendency: Each player has a power that works once, such as swapping a tile or asking for a letter, and it is used up after a single go.
pros: A power can finish a word you were stuck on.
Players pick their own moment.
cons: A spent power is gone for the rest of the game.
Players hold powers too long and never use them.

pairs.tendency: You offer a word on your turn, and the other player can turn it down or pick between two words you put forward.
pros: Each word needs an opponent's yes.
Offers show what each player thinks counts.
cons: A refused word wastes your turn.
Arguments about what a word is.

pairs.tendency: A word is whispered from player to player, and each one writes down what they heard and spells it out. The word changes on its way.
pros: Mishearing shows up in the spelling.
The last spelling can look nothing like the first.
cons: Nobody can check the word until it arrives.
Noise makes words hard to hear.

pairs.tendency: Before play you hand some letter cards to another player, so you build words from letters you did not choose for yourself.
pros: You give away letters you cannot use.
Cards you receive can suggest new words.
cons: You cannot see your new letters until you have chosen.
A letter you pass can finish another player's word.

pairs.tendency: One player lays out the first words on the board, and the other picks which side to take.
pros: The first player works to make both sides even.
Both players study the opening closely.
cons: A lopsided opening gets taken apart by the chooser.
Comparing two sides takes time at the start.

pairs.tendency: A letter tile that reaches the far end of the board can be swapped for a rarer letter that scores higher.
pros: A tile has a reason to travel.
Players plan word paths to the far end.
cons: A tile stuck mid-board sits idle.
Rushing a word to the end can cut its length.

pairs.tendency: Teams race in legs, and each runner spells a word, then hands the pencil or tile to the next runner.
pros: A whole team builds one word.
Each leg is short.
cons: A slow speller holds up the team.
A spelling slip is passed down the line.

pairs.tendency: Letters placed in certain shapes cannot be captured, so a word set in the right shape stays on the board.
pros: Players aim for a shape and a word at once.
A safe word gives a base to build from.
cons: Fitting a word into a shape limits which words you can use.
Rivals sit around the shape to block it.

pairs.tendency: Spelling words is only the road to prize cards named in advance, such as the longest word or the word with a Q.
pros: Players aim at named words.
One word can win more than one prize.
cons: Everyone knows the targets, so rivals block them.
Plain words win no prize.

pairs.tendency: Letter cards lie face up in the middle, and everyone mixes them with their own letters to spell the longest word they can.
pros: Everyone works from the same pool.
Players can see what others can reach.
cons: Two players can make the same word.
The middle cards run low after a few words.

pairs.tendency: Everyone puts a counter in the middle and the first to spell a word of a set length takes the lot. If nobody does, the pot grows.
pros: Prizes grow while nobody spells.
Players race to the target length.
cons: A big pot makes rivals block you.
One word can take everything.

pairs.tendency: Every pit carries a letter, and the pit where your last seed lands gives you the next letter of your word.
pros: Sowing makes a path through the letters.
The last seed decides the next letter.
cons: You cannot pick any letter you like.
Counting seeds slows play.

pairs.tendency: An extra hand of letters lies face down, and one player may swap it for their own before words are made.
pros: The spare hand can rescue a stuck set.
Taking it is a gamble because nobody has seen it.
cons: Others notice the swap and guess its value.
The spare letters may suit you less than your own.

pairs.tendency: Some squares double a letter, skip your turn or send a word back, so where you spell counts as much as what you spell.
pros: Placement changes the score.
Players plan routes to the doubling squares.
cons: A trap square can ruin a long word.
Turns go on studying the board.

pairs.tendency: Every letter has a price in coins and rare letters cost more, so a long word costs a lot to put together.
pros: Players set price against score.
A cheap word is easy to afford.
cons: Rare letters can drain the coins in one turn.
Players stay with short words to save coins.

pairs.tendency: You have a fixed number of letters to share between several words at once, and each letter put in one word is gone from another.
pros: Letters spread across several words.
Rivals spread theirs too, so words race side by side.
cons: A half-finished word scores nothing.
Moving a letter from one word to another is not allowed.

pairs.tendency: Everyone writes words until a signal comes, such as the music stopping, and then pencils go down with whatever you have.
pros: Time pressure drives quick spelling.
All players stop together.
cons: A half-written word at the signal is lost.
Hasty spelling brings mistakes.

pairs.tendency: You put letters back and take new ones from a pile to make the word you want, and sometimes another player has to agree.
pros: A stuck hand can be reset.
Players dig for the letter they need.
cons: Others see what you throw back.
Swapping uses up turns.

pairs.tendency: Every letter anyone discards goes into one pile, and you may take the whole pile if the top letter lets you spell a word at once.
pros: The pile holds letters others did not want.
Taking it gives you a large hand.
cons: Players discard with the pile in mind.
You pick up many useless letters along with the useful one.

pairs.tendency: One suit is named for the hand, and a word spelled from cards of that suit beats words from other suits, even longer ones.
pros: A short word in the named suit can win.
The named suit changes what each letter is worth.
cons: Long words from other suits lose.
Players hunt for cards of one suit.

pairs.tendency: You play two word boards at the same time, building on one and blocking on the other.
pros: Each letter can help one board or the other.
Your words and your opponent's cross between the boards.
cons: Attention splits in two.
Each turn takes longer.

pairs.tendency: A wild card stands for any letter, so it can finish a word that would otherwise be one letter short.
pros: One card can complete a long word.
Players keep a wild card for a big moment.
cons: Wild cards are few, so one player may get several.
Once spent, the card is gone.

pairs.tendency: Words can run off one edge of the board and come back in on the other, so a word can start at the right edge and end at the left.
pros: The grid has no dead ends.
There are more places to fit a word.
cons: Players lose track of where a word ends.
Words across the edges are hard to spot.

pairs.tendency: One player holds a secret word, and the others ask yes-or-no questions about its letters, such as "Does it have an E?"
pros: Each answer narrows the word.
Players learn from the pattern of letters.
cons: Questions about common letters tell little.
The player with the secret answers the same question again and again.

pairs.tendency: The first player to spell a set number of words, or to fill a word grid, wins.
pros: Speed counts.
A short word finishes sooner.
cons: Players hurry past long words.
A slow speller has little way back.

pairs.tendency: Each word scores by its letters, and after the last word the highest total wins.
pros: Long words and rare letters score more.
Players can compare totals during play.
cons: Short words add up slowly.
Counting points slows every turn.

pairs.tendency: A player who cannot make a word is out, so the table thins until one speller is left.
pros: Words get harder as the letters shrink.
Players keep an eye on each other's tiles.
cons: Knocked-out players wait a long time.
An awkward draw early can end your game.

pairs.tendency: The group spells together against the game, and each word spelled keeps everyone going while the letters run out.
pros: Players share ideas for words.
The group can pool its letters.
cons: One loud speller can steer the table.
An unlucky run of the draw ends everyone's game at once.

pairs.tendency: Players work together to spell a set list of words or to fill one grid, and everyone wins when it is done.
pros: Players hand over letters freely.
Everyone can see the aim.
cons: Players argue over which word to do next.
One hard word holds up the whole group.

pairs.tendency: Each player holds a secret word, or a secret kind of word such as one starting with S, and spells towards it without saying.
pros: Others can guess your goal from your words.
Players hide their plan in plain words.
cons: You may help someone else's secret word by accident.
A goal may need letters nobody will give up.

pairs.tendency: The words players spell tell a story, and the game ends when the story does.
pros: Words become the sentences of the story.
Players choose words to fit the plot.
cons: A story can stall if nobody can spell the next word.
A story can end early or run long.

pairs.tendency: Players spell words with no score and no winner, and at the end they look at the words that were made.
pros: Words are made for their own sake.
Players talk over the words.
cons: Without a score some players lose interest.
The game stops when players stop.

pairs.tendency: Each player picks an aim, such as the longest word or the most words with a Z, and plays towards it.
pros: Players need not compete on one score.
Aims can differ widely.
cons: Players can disagree on who reached their aim.
An aim set too low or too high changes the game.

pairs.tendency: The game runs until one player cannot spell a word, and that player loses while everyone else is safe.
pros: Words get harder as letters shrink.
The loser is decided late.
cons: One player takes the loss in front of others.
Safe players stop paying attention.

pairs.tendency: Players keep adding words so the game never ends, and each new word builds on the words before it.
pros: The words form a long chain.
Everyone helps.
cons: The grid can fill up.
Without an end there is no point to stop at.

pairs.tendency: Players spell words, but the rules give no way to win, and play ends when players stop.
pros: Players notice the lack of a goal.
Words are spelled without pressure.
cons: Players keep expecting a winner.
Players give up when nothing changes.

pairs.tendency: You play alone against a layout of letters and win if you clear every letter by spelling words with them.
pros: One player studies the whole layout.
A replay shows which words you missed.
cons: A stuck layout ends the game.
A hard layout can take many tries.

pairs.tendency: Players spell words over a series of short rounds, and whoever takes the most rounds takes the series.
pros: A lost round can be won back in the next.
Each round starts fresh.
cons: A series can end early once one player has enough wins.
Many rounds take a long time.

pairs.tendency: Each letter left in your hand at the end counts against you, so you try to spell your letters away.
pros: Long words get rid of many letters.
Letters like Q cost the most.
cons: Rare letters left in hand hurt.
Players keep words secret until they can use up many letters.

pairs.tendency: You have to reach an exact score with your words, and going over costs you the win.
pros: Players choose word lengths to hit the number.
Short words give fine control.
cons: A long word can push you past the number.
Players sit near the target and wait for the right word.

pairs.tendency: The aim is turned round, and the player who spells the last word loses, so players try to avoid closing the grid.
pros: Players avoid ending words.
Short words leave space open.
cons: Rivals can force you to fill the last gap.
Players slow down each word.

pairs.tendency: Everyone spells on their own board at the same time, and no word touches anyone else's.
pros: Players see only each other's totals.
Everyone plays at their own speed.
cons: Players have little to do with each other.
The slowest speller keeps the rest waiting at the end.

pairs.tendency: You target another player by taking letters from their word or blocking their space.
pros: Words become weapons.
Players guard their words.
cons: Players hold grudges.
Attacks can leave a word half built.

pairs.tendency: Nobody attacks, but a word you place can block the spaces a rival needs.
pros: Rivals feel it through the board.
A placed word has two jobs.
cons: A blocked rival may not know who did it.
Everyone studies the board before each word.

pairs.tendency: The whole table is one team, and the group spells words together and wins or loses as one.
pros: Players share letters and ideas.
A hard letter gets easier with help.
cons: One player can take over.
The group argues over a single word.

pairs.tendency: Players spell towards a shared word list, but each also has a private word that earns bonus points.
pros: Players help with the shared words.
Private words stay secret.
cons: Helping others can hold back your private word.
Players guess who is playing for themselves.

pairs.tendency: Two teams spell against each other, and teammates pool their letters.
pros: Teammates share ideas.
Team words race each other.
cons: A team can lose over one hard letter.
Teams argue among themselves.

pairs.tendency: One player secretly spells words that spoil the group's list, and the others try to spot them by the words they choose.
pros: Odd words can give the traitor away.
Players inspect every word.
cons: An honest player can be blamed for a rare word.
Doubts slow the group.

pairs.tendency: Players are far apart and post a word or send a message each turn, and a game goes on for weeks.
pros: Players have time to look up words.
Each word arrives as a small surprise.
cons: Waiting for the reply is long.
A lost letter can stop the game.

pairs.tendency: One player is not there, and their words are copied from an earlier game or arrive as hints.
pros: The absent player's words are fixed.
Others can study them.
cons: Nobody can ask the absent player anything.
Their old words may not fit the new board.

pairs.tendency: One player runs the word world, reads out clues and says which words count.
pros: One player decides what counts as a word.
The master sets the pace.
cons: The master cannot play for themselves.
Disputes land on the master.

pairs.tendency: The game is played in a street or a market, letters are chalked on the ground and passers-by add words.
pros: Strangers can join.
Words come from local speech.
cons: The crowd can interrupt.
Chalk gets scuffed and letters vanish.

pairs.tendency: One player spells alone against everyone else, while the group spells together to block them.
pros: The lone player is paid more for a win.
The group pools its letters.
cons: The lone player has few letters to work with.
The group argues over which word to block.

pairs.tendency: You spell words from a pack of letters on your own, and compare your total with a friend afterwards.
pros: You choose your own pace.
Luck of the draw shows in your total.
cons: Nobody checks your words as you go.
Scores are compared only afterwards.
