pairs.tendency: Letters are drawn at random, and the draw decides most of what you can spell.
pros: Anyone can draw a lucky hand.
Games are quick.
cons: Spelling skill counts for little.
A player with awkward letters can do very little.

pairs.tendency: Letters are drawn at random, but you can swap some or hold one back, so a hard draw can be repaired.
pros: A hard draw can be fixed.
Choices still matter.
cons: Swaps use up turns.
Luck still shows in the result.

pairs.tendency: Players spell from a few random letters, but most of the score comes from the words they choose.
pros: Choices decide most outcomes.
A little luck changes each game.
cons: Letters sometimes spoil a plan.
A lucky draw can beat a careful plan.

pairs.tendency: There are no dice or random draws, every letter is shown, and the player who knows more words has the edge.
pros: Every move can be planned.
Players can learn from each game.
cons: A new player has little hope against a word-lover.
Games change little from play to play.

pairs.tendency: Letters are drawn and read as a message, not added up as a score, and the words they form are read like a sign.
pros: Players read meaning into letters.
Words start conversation.
cons: Nobody can say which reading is right.
Players may find messages that are not there.

pairs.tendency: Players try to say the same word at the same moment without talking, guided only by a starting letter or a theme.
pros: Players learn each other's habits.
A match brings a shout.
cons: Misses are common at first.
One player out of step can spoil a round.

pairs.tendency: A dice roll is looked up on a table of letters, and you spell the word it points to, which tells you what happens next.
pros: The story follows the dice.
Words become outcomes.
cons: The table limits which words can appear.
The same roll always gives the same word.

pairs.tendency: All letters are face up, so everyone can see what everyone can spell.
pros: Players plan moves ahead.
Players can see a rival's next word coming.
cons: Rivals can block it.
Long thinking slows turns.

pairs.tendency: Each player keeps letters hidden, and the others guess your words from what you play.
pros: Hidden letters allow surprise.
Players can hint without saying.
cons: Nobody knows who is close to finishing.
Guessing eats into spelling time.

pairs.tendency: Players have secret roles, such as helpers and spoilers, and the words they spell give hints about who they are.
pros: Words become clues.
Players study each other's spellings.
cons: A wrong guess can accuse the wrong person.
One slip can reveal a role.

pairs.tendency: Letter clues point towards a hidden word, and players work out which word fits all the clues.
pros: Each clue removes some words.
Players write notes.
cons: A misread clue sends a player the wrong way.
Slow reasoning holds up the table.

pairs.tendency: You claim you can spell a word you cannot, and the others may challenge you to show it.
pros: A claim can win without a word.
Challenging is a bet.
cons: A caught bluff costs points.
Players doubt every claim.

pairs.tendency: One player knows a secret rule about words, such as no words with an E, and the others learn it by being told no.
pros: Each refusal teaches something.
Players test words to find the line.
cons: New players feel lost.
The player with the secret says no many times over.

pairs.tendency: One player knows the word and gives hints with pictures only, while the others spell their guesses.
pros: Guesses are written as letters.
Pictures speed up the guessing.
cons: Hints can mislead.
The hint giver cannot correct a spelling.

pairs.tendency: Tiles lie face down, and letters appear as areas are turned over, so your words come from what you uncover.
pros: Exploring gives letters.
Nobody knows what is coming.
cons: A turned tile may be no use.
Much of each turn goes on uncovering tiles.

pairs.tendency: One hand of letters lies face up, and any player may use it besides their own.
pros: Everyone can see this hand.
Open letters spark shared ideas.
cons: Players take its letters first.
The open hand is picked clean quickly.

pairs.tendency: Your word scores are kept hidden, so nobody can tell who is ahead.
pros: Players guess standings from word lengths.
Hidden scores keep the end open.
cons: Players cannot tell when to stop.
Long words give away high scores.

pairs.tendency: Players spell one at a time while the others watch and plan their own word.
pros: Players can study the board during others' turns.
Turns are simple to follow.
cons: Waiting is long with many players.
The next player's word can change your plan.

pairs.tendency: All players write a word in secret, then reveal together.
pros: Nobody waits.
Players see how others think.
cons: Two players may reveal the same word.
Checking all the words takes time.

pairs.tendency: There are no turns, and the quickest speller grabs letters first.
pros: Speed gets rewarded.
Players watch the whole table.
cons: Fast players take most of the letters.
Arguments over who was first.

pairs.tendency: Each turn has a sand timer, and a word that is not ready when it runs out is lost.
pros: Time pressure favours short words.
Players practise quick spelling.
cons: Panic brings misspellings.
Arguments about when the sand ran out.

pairs.tendency: Each player adds a word each morning, and the game runs for weeks.
pros: Players have time to look up words.
Words arrive in daily pieces.
cons: Waiting for the next word is long.
Players forget what is on the board.

pairs.tendency: Players pause and breathe before each word, and the slow pace is part of the game.
pros: There is time to look for long words.
The table stays quiet.
cons: Games take a long time.
Short games drag.

pairs.tendency: Timers shrink each round, so words have to be spelled faster and faster.
pros: Early rounds allow long words.
Late rounds bring quick small words.
cons: Players are rushed near the end.
Misspellings pile up.

pairs.tendency: A long word earns another go straight away, so a player who finds one can spell several words in a row.
pros: Streaks of words are possible.
A long word has a clear reward.
cons: Others sit out for a long time.
The leader gains more.

pairs.tendency: In the first stage you collect letters and in the second you spell with them.
pros: First-stage picks decide the second.
Two kinds of play in one game.
cons: A wrong pick early stays with you.
Stage one can take as long as stage two.

pairs.tendency: Letter pieces stand for parts of a system, such as a village's wells, and the words you spell name what you do to them.
pros: Words name actions.
Players learn the system's vocabulary.
cons: Spelling can get in the way of seeing the system.
Spelling takes up the time meant for the system.

pairs.tendency: Each player is a group, such as farmers or shopkeepers, and spells words from that group's point of view.
pros: Players use different vocabularies.
Words show what each group cares about.
cons: Players struggle with another group's words.
The same word can mean different things to different groups.

pairs.tendency: Everyone draws letters from one pile, and as the pile runs down words get shorter.
pros: A greedy draw hurts everyone.
Players watch the pile.
cons: Late players get few letters.
Taking letters now leaves the pile bare for others.

pairs.tendency: A word you spell now changes the board only a few rounds later.
pros: Players plan ahead.
Old words matter later.
cons: It is hard to see which word caused a change.
Players forget their early words.

pairs.tendency: Players agree a new spelling rule, such as no four-letter words, and play on to see what the words become.
pros: The rule's effect shows quickly.
Players talk about rule changes.
cons: A rule can end the game early.
A changed rule can cancel words already played.

pairs.tendency: After the game, players talk about the words they spelled and why they chose them.
pros: Words bring the game back to mind.
Players explain their choices.
cons: Talk takes time.
The talk can drift away from the words.

pairs.tendency: Every word you spell is inked onto the board and can never be rubbed out.
pros: Words add up to a record.
Mistakes stay.
cons: Players think before they write.
The board fills up.

pairs.tendency: The scoring rewards only certain words, such as short plain ones, so the game ends up saying something about language.
pros: The rules show what the game thinks of words.
Players notice what scores.
cons: Players argue with the rules.
Not everyone notices the point.

pairs.tendency: Players put real stakes, such as a snack or a promise, on the words they spell.
pros: Players care about each spelling.
Spelling disputes become real.
cons: A dispute can sour a friendship.
The loser has to pay up.

pairs.tendency: Words score points as stand-ins for something that matters, such as kindness, and players start chasing the points.
pros: Points drive word choice.
A number takes the place of what it means.
cons: Players forget the original aim.
Kind words get picked only for their score.

pairs.tendency: Players spell the words of a way of living that does not exist yet, such as a village that shares everything.
pros: Words give the future a name.
Players invent new words.
cons: Made-up words cannot be checked in a dictionary.
Players disagree on what a word means.

pairs.tendency: Your piece moves along the path by the dice, and tiles with matching numbers sit in squares along the way. A tile only joins the line where its number fits.
pros: The dice choose where you land.
Landing on a tile lets you add to the line.
cons: A throw can leave you with no tile that fits.
Players wait on a throw before they can play a tile.

pairs.tendency: A row of tiles lies in the middle and players take one at a time, looking for a number that fits an open end.
pros: Each pick can close an end for someone else.
Players can read what a rival needs.
cons: Late pickers take what is left.
Players freeze while they check the open ends.

pairs.tendency: Tiles go up for sale, and the number on the tile decides which open end you can fill.
pros: Coins show how much an end is worth.
Bids reveal which numbers a player lacks.
cons: A high bid can leave you with no coins for later tiles.
Bidding for a tile that then fits nowhere wastes coins.

pairs.tendency: You keep drawing tiles hoping for one that fits, and every draw adds to your pile. If you draw too many you lose what you scored.
pros: A fitting tile pays off at once.
Every draw is watched.
cons: A long run of misfits piles up.
Stopping early means a small score.

pairs.tendency: Each region of the map has its own line of tiles, and the player who adds the most tiles to a line holds that region.
pros: A fitting tile counts as ground.
Players weigh which line to feed.
cons: A region with a stuck end cannot be added to.
Players spread across lines and fall behind in each.

pairs.tendency: Workers sit on spots that give tiles, and a spot you take is closed to others that turn. You still need a number that fits an open end.
pros: Spots decide which numbers you get.
Grabbing a spot can leave a rival short of a number.
cons: A spot can give a tile that fits nowhere.
The first to place choose first.

pairs.tendency: Tiles also carry colours, and each one has to match the open end in number and also fit a colour pattern.
pros: Two checks narrow the choice.
A finished pattern shows a plan.
cons: Both checks together leave few legal tiles.
A turn can pass with nothing that fits.

pairs.tendency: You hold a hand of tiles and choose which to place now and which to save, since each number fits only certain ends.
pros: Players keep tiles for a late turn.
The hand hides what you can play.
cons: A kept tile can be blocked when the end closes.
Players hold on to doubles too long.

pairs.tendency: Each player lays down a tile, and the highest number takes the trick. The tiles won can later be placed on the line wherever their number fits.
pros: Winning gives tiles to place.
The high numbers have two uses.
cons: A tile won may fit nowhere on the line.
Players track both the tricks and the line.

pairs.tendency: Players swap tiles so each can fill an open end: "I'll give you a 4 for a 6."
pros: A trade can unstick two players at once.
Players learn which numbers the others are missing.
cons: Every offer reveals part of your hand.
Bargaining holds up play.

pairs.tendency: You gather tiles of one number, or of a run of numbers, for points, but you also need tiles to fit the line.
pros: Each tile has a use on the line and in a set.
A set gives a plan.
cons: Keeping a set means not playing those tiles.
A needed tile may end up in the wrong place.

pairs.tendency: Tiles join into a growing shape, and a tile can only be set where its edge matches the one it touches.
pros: The shape grows from every player's tiles.
Open edges show where to play.
cons: Closed edges leave no place for some tiles.
The shape can turn into a dead end.

pairs.tendency: One player lays a tile and calls out its number, and the next answers with a tile that matches it.
pros: The line grows like a chain.
The calls make the open ends plain to everyone.
cons: Players with no matching tile break the chain.
Calls repeat the same few numbers.

pairs.tendency: Nobody talks, so a player who has no matching tile can only pass, and the others see it.
pros: The pass shows what a player lacks.
The table stays quiet and watchful.
cons: Players read a pass wrongly.
Nobody can warn a friend about a blocked end.

pairs.tendency: On your turn you may change a rule instead of placing a tile, such as letting numbers one apart match.
pros: A rule change can free a stuck player.
Players try out matching rules.
cons: Disputes arise over whether a new rule reaches back to tiles already down.
The line can end up following many rules.

pairs.tendency: Each player speaks as a character, and a tile is placed with a short line from that character about why it fits.
pros: Placing a tile comes with a bit of story.
Players picture the line as a road or a river.
cons: Matching does not need a story, so the story can slow it.
Players wait while others speak.

pairs.tendency: You flick or slide a tile to land against an open end, and it only counts if the numbers match.
pros: The hand takes a part in matching.
A miss leaves a tile loose on the table.
cons: A tile can land against the wrong end.
A shaky hand wastes a turn.

pairs.tendency: Players draw the map as they go, and the line of tiles marks a road, so each placed tile adds a stretch to the map.
pros: The line becomes a visible path.
The map shows how play went.
cons: A stuck end leaves the road unfinished.
Drawing delays placing.

pairs.tendency: You lay a finished set of tiles face up, and others can add a matching tile to it besides the open ends.
pros: Players have more places to put a tile.
Laid sets tell others which numbers you hold.
cons: A set may attract tiles that help a rival.
Players hold sets back to avoid helping.

pairs.tendency: Each player has a power that works once, such as playing a tile that does not match, and it is used up after that.
pros: A power frees a stuck player.
Each player decides when to use it.
cons: Once used, it does not come back.
Some powers are kept until the game ends and never used.

pairs.tendency: You choose a tile and the other player can refuse it or pick between two tiles you offer.
pros: The opponent shapes your line.
You think about what they will accept.
cons: A refused tile wastes your turn.
Offers show which numbers you hold.

pairs.tendency: A number is whispered along the table, and each player places a tile matching what they heard. The number changes on the way.
pros: Mishearing leads to odd matches.
The message tells players what to play.
cons: A mistake goes unnoticed until the end.
Noise makes the number hard to hear.

pairs.tendency: Before play you hand some tiles to another player, so you try to fit the line with tiles you did not choose for yourself.
pros: Tiles you cannot place can be passed on.
The tiles that come in may open new plays.
cons: Choices are made before you see what arrives.
A passed tile may fill a rival's open end.

pairs.tendency: One player sets out the first tiles of the line, and the other picks which side to play.
pros: The setter tries to leave neither side ahead.
Both players look hard at the first tiles.
cons: If one side is ahead, the chooser takes it.
Weighing the two sides slows the start.

pairs.tendency: A tile that reaches the far end of the line is swapped for a double, which fits more ends.
pros: Tiles are worth moving towards the end.
A promoted tile gives more ways to play.
cons: A tile that never gets there stays plain.
Players hurry tiles to the end.

pairs.tendency: Teams race in legs, and each runner places one matching tile and hands over to the next.
pros: Every team member adds to one line.
No runner plays for long.
cons: A runner with no matching tile stalls everyone.
One runner's error carries on to the next.

pairs.tendency: Tiles set in certain shapes cannot be taken, so a number placed in the right shape stays on the line.
pros: Players need a shape and a match together.
Tiles in a safe shape anchor the line.
cons: The shape narrows which numbers fit.
Rivals crowd the shape to block it.

pairs.tendency: Players place tiles to win prize cards named in advance, such as the line that reaches ten tiles.
pros: Players work towards the named results.
A single line can take several prizes.
cons: The targets are public, so rivals get in the way.
A line that meets no target scores no prize.

pairs.tendency: Some tiles lie face up in the middle, and everyone may use them to fill an open end.
pros: All players draw on the same tiles.
Everyone can see what the others might play.
cons: Two players want the same tile.
The middle tiles are used up quickly.

pairs.tendency: Everyone puts a counter in the middle, and the first to empty their hand of tiles takes it all. Until someone does, the pot keeps growing.
pros: The prize gets bigger each round nobody finishes.
Players hurry to get rid of their tiles.
cons: As the pot grows, rivals try harder to block.
The winner takes the whole pot.

pairs.tendency: You scoop seeds from a pit and sow them round the board, and the pit where your last seed lands gives you a number to match on the line.
pros: Each sowing points to a number.
The last seed decides the match.
cons: The seeds choose the number for you.
Seed counting slows each turn.

pairs.tendency: An extra hand of tiles lies face down, and one player may swap it for their own before the line begins.
pros: A weak hand can be traded for the unseen one.
Nobody has seen the spare tiles, so taking them is a risk.
cons: The others see the swap and try to judge it.
The spare tiles may fit the line less closely than your own.

pairs.tendency: Some spaces on the track have a rule of their own, and a tile placed there can break the usual matching.
pros: Special squares add surprises.
Players aim for the squares that help.
cons: A trap square can send a tile back.
Players spend turns working out the board.

pairs.tendency: Every tile has a price in coins, and a tile that fits the open end costs more than one that does not.
pros: Each tile's cost is set against how closely it fits.
A cheap tile is easy to afford.
cons: A needed tile may be too dear.
Holding coins back means missing turns.

pairs.tendency: You have a set number of tiles to share between several lines at once, and each tile put on one line is gone from another.
pros: Tiles are shared out among the lines.
The other players split theirs too.
cons: An unfinished line scores nothing.
Once placed, a tile stays on its line.

pairs.tendency: Everyone places tiles until a signal comes, such as the music stopping, and then hands come off the table.
pros: The time limit makes play quick.
Everyone stops at the same moment.
cons: A tile half placed at the signal is lost.
Rushing leads to ends that do not match.

pairs.tendency: You put tiles back and take new ones from a pile, hoping for a number that fits an open end.
pros: A hand with no plays can be refreshed.
Players search the pile for a fitting number.
cons: Others see which tiles you return.
Each swap uses a turn.

pairs.tendency: Every tile a player cannot place goes into one pile, and you may take the whole pile if you can play its top tile at once.
pros: The pile holds tiles others could not play.
Taking it gives you a large hand.
cons: You pick up many tiles that fit nowhere.
Players avoid putting down useful tiles.

pairs.tendency: One colour is named for the hand, and a tile of that colour can be placed even when its number does not match.
pros: A named colour opens up stuck ends.
The named colour changes what each tile is worth.
cons: Other colours still need a match.
Players hunt for tiles of one colour.

pairs.tendency: You play two lines at the same time, adding to one and blocking on the other.
pros: Each tile can go to either line.
Your tiles and your opponent's cross between the lines.
cons: Players have to watch two lines.
Turns run longer.

pairs.tendency: A wild tile fits any open end, so it can pass a blocked line.
pros: One tile can free a stuck turn.
Players hold a wild tile back for a tight spot.
cons: There are few wild tiles, and one player may collect several.
A placed wild tile is spent.

pairs.tendency: The ends of the line are joined, so the last tile can touch the first, and the line closes into a loop.
pros: The line has no dead end.
There is more room to place a tile.
cons: Players lose track of where the line starts.
The loop can shut while tiles are still in hand.

pairs.tendency: One player holds a secret number, and the others ask yes-or-no questions about the open ends, such as "Is it above five?"
pros: Each answer cuts the choices down.
Players work out which tiles remain.
cons: Asking about common numbers gives little away.
The holder of the number answers the same thing over and over.

pairs.tendency: The first player to place every tile wins, so each turn is a step towards an empty hand.
pros: Speed counts.
A tile that fits is a step forward.
cons: A missed turn is a step back.
A player who falls behind rarely catches up.

pairs.tendency: Each tile scores by its number when placed, and the highest total at the end wins.
pros: High numbers score more.
Running totals can be checked as play goes on.
cons: A high tile can fit nowhere.
Adding up points slows each turn.

pairs.tendency: A player who cannot match a tile is out, so the table thins until one player is left.
pros: Missed turns now have a heavy cost.
Everyone watches what the others hold.
cons: Players who are out sit through the rest.
A poor early draw can knock you out.

pairs.tendency: The group builds one line together against the game, and each tile placed keeps everyone going while the tiles run out.
pros: Players suggest plays to one another.
Tiles can be pooled across the group.
cons: A forceful player may decide for everyone.
If the draws go against the group, everyone loses together.

pairs.tendency: Players work together to build one line of a set length, and everyone wins when it is done.
pros: Players pass tiles to one another.
The target is plain to all.
cons: Disputes arise over which end to fill.
A blocked end stops everyone.

pairs.tendency: Each player holds a secret aim, such as ending the line on a six, and places tiles towards it without saying.
pros: The others try to read your aim from your plays.
Players hide their plan among the matching tiles.
cons: A careless tile can serve a rival's secret aim.
The tiles an aim needs may stay in other hands.

pairs.tendency: The line of tiles is told as a story, each tile adding a part, and the game ends when the story does.
pros: Tiles become parts of the tale.
Players choose a tile to fit the plot.
cons: The story stalls when nobody has a fitting tile.
The game's length depends on the story.

pairs.tendency: Players build a line with no score and no winner, and at the end they look at what was made.
pros: Tiles are placed for their own sake.
Players discuss the finished line.
cons: Some players drift off with nothing to score.
Play lasts as long as players want.

pairs.tendency: Each player picks an aim, such as the longest line or the most doubles, and plays towards it.
pros: There is no single score to beat.
Each player's aim can be quite different.
cons: Whether an aim was met can be disputed.
An aim that is too easy or too hard alters play.

pairs.tendency: The game runs until one player is stuck with no matching tile, and that player loses while the others are safe.
pros: Missed turns carry a real cost.
Who loses is not known until near the end.
cons: The loser is singled out at the table.
Players who are safe lose interest.

pairs.tendency: Players try to extend the line for as long as they can, and the aim is a line that never closes.
pros: The line grows long.
All players add to it.
cons: The table can fill up.
There is no natural place to stop.

pairs.tendency: Players match tiles into a line, but the rules give no way to win, and play ends when players stop.
pros: Players come to see there is nothing to win.
Tiles go down with no pressure.
cons: Some keep waiting for a winner.
When nothing changes, players lose heart.

pairs.tendency: You play alone against a layout of tiles and win if you can place every one by matching ends.
pros: A single player reads the whole layout.
A replay shows which tile blocked you.
cons: If no tile fits, the game is over.
A tricky layout may need many attempts.

pairs.tendency: Players build lines over a series of short rounds, and whoever takes the most rounds takes the series.
pros: Losing one round is not final.
Every round begins clean.
cons: Once someone has enough rounds, the series stops.
A long series takes a lot of time.

pairs.tendency: Each tile left in your hand at the end counts its number against you, so you try to empty your hand.
pros: High tiles cost the most.
Players play the big tiles first.
cons: Tiles left in hand add up.
Players hold the small tiles until it is too late.

pairs.tendency: You have to end the line on an exact total, and going over costs you the win.
pros: Players choose tiles to hit the number.
Low tiles let players adjust by small steps.
cons: A big tile can push you past the total.
Players wait close to the total for a tile that fits.

pairs.tendency: The aim is turned round, and the player who places the last tile loses, so players try to be stuck with tiles.
pros: Players avoid closing the line.
Missed turns now help.
cons: Rivals can leave you holding the last tile.
Each play gets slower.

pairs.tendency: Everyone builds a line on their own board at the same time, and no tile touches anyone else's line.
pros: Only totals are shared.
Nobody has to keep up with anyone.
cons: There is little contact between players.
Everyone waits for the slowest line to finish.

pairs.tendency: You target another player by closing an open end they need or by forcing them to pick up tiles.
pros: Tiles are used to attack.
Players protect the ends they need.
cons: Attacks breed grudges.
A line can be left unfinished after an attack.

pairs.tendency: Nobody attacks, but a tile you place can close the end a rival needs.
pros: The line carries the effect to rivals.
One tile can build and block.
cons: The blocked player may not know who blocked them.
Players check every open end before playing.

pairs.tendency: The whole table is one team that builds one line, and the group wins or loses as one.
pros: Players share tiles and ideas.
A stuck end gets easier with help.
cons: A strong voice can run the table.
One play can start a long argument.

pairs.tendency: Players build one shared line, but each also holds a private number that earns bonus points when it ends the line.
pros: Players help with the shared line.
Private numbers stay secret.
cons: Helping the line can hold back your private number.
Players wonder who is chasing a private number.

pairs.tendency: Two teams build lines against each other, and teammates pool their tiles.
pros: Teammates plan plays together.
The lines race each other.
cons: A team can lose over one stuck end.
Teammates can fall out.

pairs.tendency: One player secretly places tiles to jam the group's line, and the others try to spot them by the plays they make.
pros: Strange plays can expose the traitor.
Every tile gets checked.
cons: An honest player can be blamed for a stuck end.
Suspicion slows the group down.

pairs.tendency: Players are far apart and send each tile by post or message, and a game goes on for weeks.
pros: Players have time to think about each tile.
Each tile comes as news.
cons: Replies take a long time.
If a post goes missing, the game stalls.

pairs.tendency: One player is not there, and their tiles are played from an earlier game or arrive as hints.
pros: The absent player's tiles do not change.
The others can look at them in advance.
cons: The absent player cannot be asked.
Their old tiles may not fit the new line.

pairs.tendency: One player runs the game, reads out the open ends and says which tiles fit.
pros: The master rules on what fits.
The master controls the speed of play.
cons: The master does not play a line of their own.
Every dispute goes to the master.

pairs.tendency: The game is played in a street or a market, tiles are chalked on the ground and passers-by add to the line.
pros: People passing can take part.
The line grows along the street.
cons: Onlookers can break into play.
Feet rub out the chalk, and numbers disappear.

pairs.tendency: One player builds a line alone against everyone else, while the group works together to block the open ends.
pros: A lone win earns extra.
The group shares its tiles.
cons: The lone player has only a few tiles.
The group may disagree about which end to close.

pairs.tendency: You build a line from a pack of tiles on your own, and compare your result with a friend afterwards.
pros: You set your own speed.
Your result shows how the draws went.
cons: No one checks the matches during play.
Comparison happens only at the end.

pairs.tendency: Tiles are drawn at random, and the draw decides whether you have a tile that fits.
pros: A beginner can win with a lucky draw.
A game is over fast.
cons: Skill counts for little.
Without a fitting tile, a player can do almost nothing.

pairs.tendency: Tiles are drawn at random, but you can swap some or hold one back, so a hard draw can be repaired.
pros: A poor draw can be put right.
Decisions still count.
cons: Swapping takes time from the turn.
Chance still shapes the outcome.

pairs.tendency: Players draw a few random tiles, but most of the result comes from which ends they choose to fill.
pros: Most results come from choices.
Some chance keeps each game different.
cons: A draw can spoil a plan.
Luck can still beat careful planning.

pairs.tendency: There are no random draws, every tile is shown, and the player who plans the line further ahead has the edge.
pros: Players can plan every move.
Each game teaches something.
cons: A beginner rarely beats a planner.
Each game plays much like the last.

pairs.tendency: Tiles are drawn and read as a message, not added to a score, and the line they form is read like a sign.
pros: Numbers are read for meaning.
The line gets people talking.
cons: No reading can be proved right.
Players may see messages that were never there.

pairs.tendency: Players try to place matching tiles at the same moment without talking, guided only by the open ends.
pros: Players come to know each other's habits.
A shared match gets a cheer.
cons: Early rounds bring many misses.
A single player out of step can spoil it.

pairs.tendency: A dice roll is looked up on a table that says what happens next, and the roll also decides which tile you may try to place.
pros: The dice drive the story.
Each tile links to an event.
cons: The table caps what can happen.
A roll always brings the same event.

pairs.tendency: All tiles are face up, so everyone can see who can fill which open end.
pros: Players can plan ahead.
Players can see a block coming.
cons: Rivals can close the end first.
Long thought slows each turn.

pairs.tendency: Each player keeps tiles hidden, and a pass tells the others you lack the number at the open ends.
pros: Hidden tiles leave room for surprise.
A pass gives away a little.
cons: No one can tell who is near the end.
Players spend time guessing at hands.

pairs.tendency: Players have secret roles, such as helpers and spoilers, and the tiles they place give hints about who they are.
pros: Each tile placed is a clue.
Players watch each other's tiles closely.
cons: Players can blame the wrong person.
A single slip can give a role away.

pairs.tendency: Each tile played and each pass gives a clue about the tiles in other hands, and players work out who holds what.
pros: Each play removes some doubt.
Players keep notes.
cons: A misread pass sends a player the wrong way.
Slow working-out holds everyone up.

pairs.tendency: You pass even though you hold a matching tile, so the others think the end is safe, or you claim a tile you do not hold.
pros: A pass can hide a hand.
The others may misjudge what you hold.
cons: A caught bluff costs a penalty.
Players doubt every pass.

pairs.tendency: One player knows a secret matching rule, such as numbers two apart also match, and the others learn it by being told no.
pros: Every refusal is a lesson.
Players try tiles to find out what the rule allows.
cons: Newcomers can feel lost.
The rule-holder keeps saying no.

pairs.tendency: One player sees which tile completes the line but may only point with hints, while the others place tiles.
pros: The hint giver steers the table.
Hints can come as numbers on cards.
cons: A hint can mislead.
The hint giver cannot correct a placed tile.

pairs.tendency: Tiles lie face down, and a tile is turned over only when someone tries to place it, so nobody knows if it fits.
pros: Exploring is part of placing.
What comes next is unknown.
cons: A turned tile may fit nowhere.
Many turns are spent turning tiles that fit nowhere.

pairs.tendency: One hand of tiles lies face up, and any player may play from it besides their own.
pros: The face-up hand is open to all.
Seeing its tiles gives everyone ideas.
cons: Players grab its tiles first.
It is soon emptied.

pairs.tendency: Your scores are kept hidden, so nobody can tell who is ahead by looking at the line.
pros: Players guess standings from the tiles placed.
With scores hidden, the finish stays open.
cons: Players do not know when to stop.
High tiles give away high scores.

pairs.tendency: Players place one tile at a time while the others watch the open ends and plan their own play.
pros: Players can study the line during others' turns.
Turn order is easy to follow.
cons: With many players, the wait is long.
A tile from the player before you can upset your plan.

pairs.tendency: All players choose a tile in secret and place it together, and clashes happen when two tiles want one end.
pros: No one is left waiting.
The reveal shows how others think.
cons: Two tiles can want the same end.
Sorting out clashes takes time.

pairs.tendency: There are no turns, and the quickest player to place a matching tile takes the end.
pros: Quick players come out ahead.
Players watch the whole line.
cons: Fast players take most of the ends.
Players dispute who placed first.

pairs.tendency: Each turn has a sand timer, and a tile that is not placed when it runs out is lost.
pros: Time pressure favours quick matches.
Players practise scanning the ends.
cons: Panic brings mismatched tiles.
Players dispute whether the sand had run out.

pairs.tendency: Each player places one tile each morning, and the game runs for weeks.
pros: Players have time to think about each tile.
Tiles arrive one a day.
cons: The wait between tiles is long.
Players forget what the line looks like.

pairs.tendency: Players pause and breathe before each tile, and the slow pace is part of the game.
pros: There is time to look at every end.
The table is quiet.
cons: A game runs long.
Even a short game feels slow.

pairs.tendency: Timers shrink each round, so tiles have to be placed faster and faster.
pros: Early rounds allow slow thought.
Late rounds bring quick plays.
cons: The end of the game is rushed.
Mismatched tiles pile up.

pairs.tendency: A tile that fits two ends at once earns another go straight away, so a lucky player can place several tiles in a row.
pros: Players can place several tiles in a row.
A double fit is plainly rewarded.
cons: The others are left out for long stretches.
The player ahead pulls further ahead.

pairs.tendency: In the first stage you collect tiles and in the second you match them onto a line.
pros: What you collect decides what you can match.
The game has two kinds of play.
cons: An early mistake follows you.
Collecting can take as long as matching.

pairs.tendency: The line is a pipe or a canal, and each tile joins a section only when the flow matches, as it would in real life.
pros: A match has a real-life reason.
Players learn how parts connect.
cons: A mismatch ends the flow.
Players spend time checking the model.

pairs.tendency: Each player is a group, such as farmers or shopkeepers, and each group's tiles fit only certain ends.
pros: Groups have different options.
Players see what each group needs.
cons: A group can be stuck for lack of one tile.
Players argue over which group goes next.

pairs.tendency: Everyone draws tiles from one pile, and as the pile runs down the line gets harder to extend.
pros: A greedy draw leaves less for all.
Everyone keeps an eye on the pile.
cons: Those who draw late get few tiles.
Taking many now empties the pile for others.

pairs.tendency: A tile you place now changes the line only a few rounds later.
pros: Players think several rounds ahead.
Early tiles still count later.
cons: It is hard to trace which tile caused a change.
Players lose track of the tiles they placed early.

pairs.tendency: Players agree a new matching rule, such as numbers one apart also match, and play on to see what the line becomes.
pros: The new rule shows its effect fast.
Players discuss the change.
cons: A rule can bring the game to an early end.
A new rule can undo tiles already down.

pairs.tendency: After the game, players talk about the line they made and why they placed each tile.
pros: Looking at the line recalls the game.
Each player says why they placed what they did.
cons: The discussion takes time.
Talk may wander from the tiles.

pairs.tendency: Every tile you place is glued down and can never be lifted.
pros: The line becomes a lasting record.
Errors stay in place.
cons: Each placement needs thought.
Table space runs out.

pairs.tendency: The matching rule favours certain numbers, such as big ones, so the game ends up saying something about those numbers.
pros: The rules reveal a view of numbers.
Players see which numbers fit easily.
cons: Players push back against the rules.
Some players miss the point.

pairs.tendency: Players put real stakes, such as a snack or a promise, on the line of tiles.
pros: Each match matters to the players.
Arguments over a match have real weight.
cons: A quarrel can damage a friendship.
Whoever loses pays.

pairs.tendency: Matching tiles earn points as stand-ins for something that matters, such as honesty, and players start chasing points.
pros: Tiles are chosen for points.
The score stands in for what it means.
cons: The first purpose gets lost.
Fair plays are made only for the points.

pairs.tendency: Players lay tiles for a way of living that does not exist yet, such as a village that shares everything, and each match shows how parts connect.
pros: The line gives the future a shape.
Players make up how the parts fit.
cons: Invented links cannot be checked.
Players read a match in different ways.

pairs.tendency: Each throw of the dice moves your piece, and a landing space lets you lay down a finished set of cards. Others can add to it on later turns.
pros: The track gives the cards a reason to be played.
Sets on the table show who is close.
cons: A run of low throws leaves sets in the hand.
Long gaps between laying down sets.

pairs.tendency: Players pick cards from a passed hand, then lay finished sets face up. Every pick is a step towards a set that can be shown.
pros: Picks have a clear aim.
Open sets tell the others what to pass on.
cons: Picking for a set can starve a neighbour.
Cards you need may be gone before they reach you.

pairs.tendency: Players bid for cards at an auction, and the winner can lay them in a set on the table at once.
pros: Bids go towards a set.
Sets on the table show what a card is worth.
cons: A big bid can leave a player with no money.
A set that is almost whole gets bid up fast.

pairs.tendency: You keep drawing to finish a set, and one draw too many wipes out the cards you hold. Laying the set down early keeps it safe.
pros: Laying down is a way to stop.
Each draw gets a bit more tense.
cons: A player can lose a whole hand at once.
Sets laid early leave points unclaimed.

pairs.tendency: Sets laid beside regions of the map give a claim on them, and other players can add cards to push the claim their way.
pros: A set can mark ground.
Cards added to sets become small fights.
cons: Sets on the table pull attention from the map.
A late addition can flip a region.

pairs.tendency: Workers take jobs that produce cards, and finished sets are laid out on the table. Others add to them after you.
pros: Jobs feed the sets.
A set laid down is easy to read.
cons: A blocked job holds up a set.
Waiting for a job can stall a hand.

pairs.tendency: A set on the table is a pattern made of cards, and other players add to it. The pattern grows as hands are played.
pros: Patterns grow in public.
Added cards show who is helping.
cons: A pattern that grows can be taken over by another player.
Early patterns are easy to copy.

pairs.tendency: You choose which cards to keep and which to lay down as a finished set. Cards in hand are a secret and cards in sets are open.
pros: Each card has a choice.
Players read the sets to guess the hands.
cons: Holding cards too long locks points in the hand.
Laying down early gives away a plan.

pairs.tendency: Players win tricks, and some cards from the tricks go into sets on the table. The sets show what each player has been winning.
pros: Tricks feed sets.
Sets tell the others what is gone.
cons: Trick play and set play pull a hand two ways.
A hand can end with tricks won and no sets.

pairs.tendency: Players talk about which cards to add to whose set. A player may give a card to a rival in return for a favour.
pros: Talk decides who adds to what.
Players learn each other's hands from the deals.
cons: Promises about a card are hard to check.
A group can spend a long time bargaining over one set.

pairs.tendency: You collect groups of matching cards and lay each full group on the table. Other players add matching cards to it.
pros: Finished sets stay in play.
Added cards show which sets are growing.
cons: A full set can be added to by a rival.
Collecting alone feels slow while rivals add on.

pairs.tendency: Tiles join up on a shared map, and a finished group of tiles can be laid out for all to see. Other players can add matching tiles to it.
pros: The map and the sets grow together.
Open sets show where a tile will fit.
cons: A set can block a space on the map.
Players may wait for the one tile that fits.

pairs.tendency: One player lays down a set, and the next player answers by adding to it or laying a set of their own.
pros: Each set is an answer to the last.
The table reads like a chain.
cons: A player with no answer waits for a turn.
Sets can pile up on one side of the table.

pairs.tendency: Nobody speaks, so a set laid down is the only message. Others add to it to show they agree.
pros: A set works as a signal.
Adding a card says something without words.
cons: A wrong guess about a set is hard to fix.
Players cannot warn a partner who is about to waste cards.

pairs.tendency: A rule can be changed on a turn, so what counts as a legal set may change. Sets already on the table keep the old rule or lose it.
pros: The rules can shift to suit the sets.
Players argue about what a set is.
cons: A rule change can wipe out someone's set.
Sets laid under an old rule cause arguments.

pairs.tendency: Characters lay down sets as acts in a story, such as a trade or a meeting. Others join in by adding cards.
pros: A set can stand for an event.
Players can act out the cards they add.
cons: Talking in character slows down the laying of sets.
Players who do not act may feel left out.

pairs.tendency: A set is laid down only after a flick, a stack or a throw. A shaky hand can lose the chance to add a card.
pros: The hand matters as well as the cards.
Players watch each throw.
cons: A clumsy turn can waste a worthwhile set.
Tired hands make late turns messy.

pairs.tendency: Players draw the map as they go, and a set laid beside a place marks something that happened there.
pros: Sets leave marks on the paper.
The map shows the history of the game.
cons: Drawing slows down each set.
A crowded map is hard to read.

pairs.tendency: A set on the table is open to everyone, and each player has a power they can use once to change it, such as to add a card out of turn.
pros: A power can be saved for a big set.
Sets show where a power would help.
cons: A power used too soon cannot come back.
Players may hold powers and wait.

pairs.tendency: You offer to lay a set or add to one, and the other player can turn it down or pick between two offers.
pros: The other player shapes your sets.
Offers show what you hold.
cons: A refusal can waste a turn.
Waiting for an answer slows down the game.

pairs.tendency: A set laid on the table is passed on as news, and the next player may add to it or change it by whisper.
pros: Sets become messages.
The message may be changed on its way.
cons: A set may reach the end of the line wrong.
Nobody can check the first version.

pairs.tendency: Before play each player hands cards to another, then tries to lay sets from the hand they get back.
pros: Passing sets up the first sets.
Players guess what a neighbour is building.
cons: A hand that was passed away may leave a gap.
Cards sent to a rival can help that rival.

pairs.tendency: One player lays out the first sets and the other picks which side to take. The first player tries to make both sides even.
pros: Both sides start with a similar number of sets.
The first player has to think about the other's view.
cons: A careful split makes a slow start.
A split that looks even may not be.

pairs.tendency: A set reaching the end of a row, or a piece reaching the far edge, becomes bigger or worth more. Players aim sets that way.
pros: A set can grow into something larger.
There is a goal to push towards.
cons: Pushing forward leaves a gap behind.
A set that is almost there is easy to attack.

pairs.tendency: Teams take turns in legs of a race, and a set laid down in one leg is handed to the next runner to add to.
pros: Teams build a set together.
Handing over is a clear moment.
cons: One slow player holds up the team.
A mistake in an early leg follows the team.

pairs.tendency: A set laid down in the right shape cannot be taken. Players build towards that shape while rivals try to break in.
pros: A safe shape is a clear goal.
The rival's sets show what is coming.
cons: Safe sets leave less to fight over.
Players may only build and never attack.

pairs.tendency: Named cards give points, and laying them in a set puts them on show. A rival can see which scoring cards are already placed.
pros: Sets make named cards easy to track.
Players know which prizes are left.
cons: A set with a prize card draws attacks.
Laying a prize card early makes it a target.

pairs.tendency: Cards in the middle belong to everyone, and a set laid down can use them, so others can add to the same cards.
pros: Open cards invite many sets.
Players watch the middle for gaps.
cons: Two players may race to use the same card.
A shared card can be taken just before you.

pairs.tendency: Every player puts a counter in the pot, and the first to lay a full set takes it all. If nobody does, the pot grows.
pros: A pot gives sets a prize.
A growing pot draws attention to who is close.
cons: A pot that grows draws wild plays.
Players may hold back until the pot is big.

pairs.tendency: Seeds are sown pit by pit, and a full row of seeds in a pit can be laid out as a set to be added to.
pros: Sowing sets up the groups.
The pits show who is near a set.
cons: A sowing turn can break a set up.
Counting seeds slows down a quick turn.

pairs.tendency: An extra hand sits face down in the middle, and the player who takes it may lay its sets on the table at once.
pros: A spare hand can give a head start.
Players guess what it holds.
cons: The player who takes it gets cards they never chose.
The others may feel the choice was a gamble.

pairs.tendency: Landing on a special square lets you lay down a set, or sends you back and breaks one. Squares are the places where sets are made.
pros: Squares make sets an event.
Players know where to aim.
cons: A risky square can wipe out a plan.
Aiming at squares can leave sets unfinished.

pairs.tendency: Cards cost something to play, and laying down a set costs the most. Others may add cards to it for less.
pros: A costly set can be built on cheaply.
Players see the price of each set.
cons: Paying for a big set leaves a player short.
Others can profit from a set they did not pay for.

pairs.tendency: Cards or counters are shared across several sets, so putting more in one set leaves another short.
pros: Each set is a choice.
Rivals can see which set got the most.
cons: A set left short is easy to attack.
Too many sets spread a hand thin.

pairs.tendency: Players lay sets while the music plays, and when it stops they freeze and the sets on the table count.
pros: The signal sets the pace.
Players act fast.
cons: A set can be left half done.
The stop can come halfway through a move.

pairs.tendency: You swap cards for new ones to build a set, then lay it down. Others may add to it afterwards.
pros: Swaps help finish sets.
Sets show what was swapped for.
cons: Swapping takes a turn that could add to a set.
A swap can hand a rival the missing card.

pairs.tendency: You take the whole discard pile to finish a set and lay it down at once. Rivals can add to it.
pros: A big pile can finish a set in one go.
Discards tell the others what is wanted.
cons: A full pile is a heavy hand to carry.
Taking the pile gives away your plan.

pairs.tendency: A set in the trump suit beats the others on the table, so rivals add trump cards to take it over.
pros: Trump sets are worth building.
The named suit tells everyone which sets matter.
cons: A set of low cards in other suits is easy to beat.
Trump cards are held back until the end.

pairs.tendency: You play two boards, and a set laid in one game can be added to in the other.
pros: One set can help on both boards.
Players plan two things at once.
cons: Attention is split between the boards.
A mistake on one board can spoil the other.

pairs.tendency: A wild card finishes a set that is a card short, and the set is laid down with the wild card in it.
pros: A wild card fills a gap.
Players hold wild cards back.
cons: A set with a wild card can be added to in odd ways.
Arguments start over what a wild card stands for.

pairs.tendency: A line of cards laid out runs off one edge and comes back in on the other. Others can add to either end.
pros: Sets have no dead end.
Players have to look at both sides of the board.
cons: A set can be attacked from places that look far away.
New players miss the join at the edge.

pairs.tendency: One player holds a secret set, and the others ask yes or no questions to learn it before it is laid down.
pros: Each answer shrinks the guesses.
The set is revealed at the end.
cons: A careless answer gives the set away.
Questions pile up while one hand waits.

pairs.tendency: The first player to lay down every set wins. Others add to open sets to slow or speed the finish.
pros: Sets are steps in a race.
Everyone can see how far along the others are.
cons: A set left behind can cost the lead.
The leader is easy to spot and block.

pairs.tendency: Each set laid on the table scores points, and the player with the most points at the end wins.
pros: Every set adds to the score.
Players can add up the table.
cons: Players aim for big sets and ignore small ones.
A late addition can swing a score.

pairs.tendency: Players who run out of cards or sets drop out, and open sets show who is nearly gone.
pros: Sets show who is low on cards.
The table shrinks as players go.
cons: Dropped players wait for the rest.
A big set may be taken apart just to knock someone out.

pairs.tendency: The team lays sets to survive, and everyone adds cards to keep the sets alive against the game.
pros: The group builds together.
Open sets show what the team has left.
cons: A single missing card can doom a set.
One player can end up carrying the table.

pairs.tendency: All the players add cards to one set on the table until it reaches the goal.
pros: Everyone adds to the same set.
The progress is easy to see.
cons: Players with no cards to add wait.
A loud player can take over the set.

pairs.tendency: Sets are open but each player's goal is secret, so a player may add to a set for their own reasons.
pros: Adding a card hides a motive.
Players try to guess goals from the sets.
cons: A card added can give away the goal.
Others may never work out why a card was added.

pairs.tendency: Each set laid down is a scene of a story, and others add to it as the plot goes on.
pros: The sets read like a story.
Players can see the plot growing.
cons: A scene can be pushed off course by a late card.
The story ends when the sets run out.

pairs.tendency: Sets are laid down and added to, but nobody wins. Players look at the table at the end and talk about it.
pros: Sets are made for their own sake.
The finished table is something to look at.
cons: Nothing marks when to stop.
Some players may drift without a goal.

pairs.tendency: Each player picks what a worthwhile set means to them, then lays sets and adds to others with that aim.
pros: Every table looks different.
Players compare what each of them aimed for.
cons: Two players may never agree on what a set is.
Goals that differ make scores hard to compare.

pairs.tendency: Everyone lays sets to stay safe, and the player left holding cards when the sets run out loses.
pros: Laying sets is a way to escape.
The last hand left is easy to spot.
cons: One player is left with a pile of cards.
Everyone else finishes early and waits.

pairs.tendency: Sets are laid and added to with no end, and play carries on as more cards come in.
pros: A table can grow for many sessions.
Old sets become part of the history.
cons: The table gets crowded.
There is no clear moment to stop.

pairs.tendency: Players lay and add to sets that never add up to a win. The game is about what the sets show instead.
pros: The sets are the point.
Players notice that no score appears.
cons: Players keep waiting for a prize.
Some give up when nothing ends.

pairs.tendency: You play alone and try to lay every card out in finished sets. The game says you lost if you get stuck.
pros: A neat table is the goal.
Each set is a step you can check.
cons: One wrong set can lock the rest.
Nobody else is there to share the stuck moment.

pairs.tendency: Sets are laid in each short game, and the player with the most game wins takes the match.
pros: A match is made of small tables.
A lead can be locked in early.
cons: A lost first game weighs on the rest.
Trailing players may give up before the end.

pairs.tendency: Cards left in the hand count against you, so laying down sets quickly lowers the score.
pros: Laying down sets cuts the count.
Players can see who is holding too much.
cons: A big hand left at the end costs a lot.
A rival can add to your set and leave you with the cards.

pairs.tendency: A set has to add up to an exact number to be laid down. A card that goes over spoils it.
pros: Sets are checked by sum.
Players count out loud.
cons: An extra card can waste a whole set.
A near miss is easy to make.

pairs.tendency: Players try to get rid of sets and cards first, and the one who ends up holding the most loses.
pros: Laying down sets is a way to win.
Players dump sets on others.
cons: A rival may refuse to add to a set you want gone.
Players hold back cards on purpose.

pairs.tendency: Everyone lays sets on their own part of the table and never adds to another's.
pros: Each table is its own.
Players can see the others' progress.
cons: There is little to do while others lay down sets.
Players may stop paying attention.

pairs.tendency: Players add cards to each other's sets to ruin them, or take cards from a rival's set.
pros: Sets become targets.
Players know who is attacking whom.
cons: A set can be wrecked in one turn.
Some players give up on building.

pairs.tendency: Sets laid on the board change what is open to rivals, who feel it through the layout and not through a direct attack.
pros: A set can block a route.
Players read the board to plan.
cons: Sets can be walled off by accident.
Cause and effect are hard to see.

pairs.tendency: The whole table adds to the same sets against the game. If a set falls, everyone loses.
pros: All hands help each set.
Everyone sees what is needed.
cons: A slip by one player costs all.
The group may argue about who adds what.

pairs.tendency: Players add to a shared set to move the team on, but each hopes to score a bit more than the rest.
pros: Players help and also compete.
A card added shows who gains.
cons: Adding to a set may help a rival more.
Players may hold cards for their own sets.

pairs.tendency: Each team has its own sets, and teammates add to them. The other team can try to add to them too.
pros: Teammates share the work on each set.
Open sets show the match.
cons: A weaker teammate can drag a set down.
Teams may argue about who adds what.

pairs.tendency: A secret traitor adds the wrong cards to the group's sets, and the rest try to spot who is doing it.
pros: A set can hide a lie.
Players watch each other's additions.
cons: One wrong card is hard to blame on anyone.
Suspicion can stop honest players from adding anything.

pairs.tendency: Players are far apart and send a set by post, and the next player adds to it and sends it on.
pros: A set travels.
Each reply shows a new card.
cons: A set can sit in the post for days.
A lost letter can end the game.

pairs.tendency: A player who is not there leaves sets on the table, and the others add to them as if they were still playing.
pros: A missing player still shapes the game.
The sets show what the absent one would have done.
cons: Nobody can change the absent player's sets.
The empty seat is easy to forget.

pairs.tendency: The game master lays sets for the world, and players add to them with their own cards.
pros: The master sets the scene with sets.
Players see what the world holds.
cons: The master has to keep the sets fair to all.
A busy master slows down the table.

pairs.tendency: Sets are laid on a table in a market or park, and passers-by add a card.
pros: Anyone can join a set.
Strangers can read the table at a glance.
cons: New players do not know the rules.
A set can be broken up by a passing crowd.

pairs.tendency: One player lays sets alone, and the others add to them to hurt it or to share.
pros: The lone player is outnumbered.
The sets show who is winning.
cons: The lone player may be swamped.
The group may add cards that help the lone player by mistake.

pairs.tendency: You lay sets alone from the pack, and nobody adds to them.
pros: You can think through the sets.
Results can be compared later.
cons: The pack decides a lot.
Nobody else shares the table.

pairs.tendency: The cards you draw decide which sets you can lay. Skill is in when to lay them.
pros: Luck fills the hand.
A single lucky draw can finish a set.
cons: A hand without matches has nothing to lay.
Players feel the result was out of their hands.

pairs.tendency: An unlucky draw can be softened by swapping or by adding to a set already on the table.
pros: Sets are a second chance.
Players can recover after an unlucky draw.
cons: Fixes slow the turn.
A fix takes a turn that could have built a set.

pairs.tendency: Most of the play is choosing which sets to lay and add to, with a small draw of luck.
pros: Choices count most.
A lucky draw changes a plan a little.
cons: A small error is easy to punish.
Experienced players find it easy to win.

pairs.tendency: No luck is involved, so every set is laid on purpose and every addition is a plan.
pros: Each set is a decision.
Players can work out what the others hold.
cons: A mistake is hard to fix.
A new player has little chance against an old hand.

pairs.tendency: Sets are laid by what the dice or cards seem to say, as an omen, and others add to them by the same reading.
pros: A set reads as a sign.
Players talk about what the table means.
cons: Two players may read the same set differently.
Nothing can settle an argument.

pairs.tendency: Players lay and add to sets by feeling when the others are ready, with no signal.
pros: The table moves together.
Cards go down at almost the same moment.
cons: One mistimed card breaks the mood.
Players who are not in step get left behind.

pairs.tendency: A roll on a table decides what a set stands for, and others add to the set as the story goes on.
pros: Dice name each set.
The sets form a story told by luck.
cons: A roll may name a set that fits nothing.
Players wait for a roll before they act.

pairs.tendency: All sets and all hands are open. Players see exactly what can be added where.
pros: Everything can be worked out.
The sets show every plan.
cons: Nothing is hidden to surprise anyone.
A slow thinker holds up the table.

pairs.tendency: Sets are open, but the cards still held are secret, so each set hints at what remains in the hand.
pros: Sets give away a little.
Players guess what is left.
cons: Laying a set shows the hand.
A hand can be read from what was kept.

pairs.tendency: A secret role decides which sets a player wants to grow, and open sets let others guess the role.
pros: Sets reveal a role.
Players watch who adds to what.
cons: A careless addition gives away a role.
Players may avoid adding anything.

pairs.tendency: Open sets give clues about the cards that are still hidden, and players work out who holds what.
pros: Each set is a clue.
The table narrows the guesses.
cons: A wrong guess costs a turn.
Players may spend a long time thinking.

pairs.tendency: A player lays a set that looks bigger than the hand behind it, hoping others will not add or challenge.
pros: A set can be a bluff.
Players study each other's faces.
cons: A caught bluff costs the set.
Players may stop trusting any set.

pairs.tendency: One player knows a secret rule about sets, and the others learn it by laying a set and being told no.
pros: Each set is a test.
Players learn the rule by failing.
cons: New players are caught out for a while.
Failed sets give the rule away slowly.

pairs.tendency: One player sees the right set but can only hint, and the others try to lay it.
pros: Hints guide the table.
The others try the set that fits.
cons: The hint may mean something different to each person.
The player who knows has to stay silent.

pairs.tendency: Sets are laid beside the places that are turned over, so the map and the sets grow together.
pros: Each new place can hold a set.
Players see the map open up.
cons: A hidden place hides a set too.
Early guesses about the map can turn out wrong.

pairs.tendency: One hand is face up, and its sets are open for all to add to.
pros: Everyone can see one hand.
The open hand tells the others what is possible.
cons: The open hand's owner has little to hide.
Players plan around the open cards.

pairs.tendency: Sets are open but points are secret, so nobody knows how much a set is worth to its owner.
pros: Sets hide their value.
Players guess who is ahead.
cons: A set may be worth less than it looks.
Nobody can be sure who is winning.

pairs.tendency: Players lay and add to sets one at a time, and everyone watches the table change.
pros: Each turn changes the sets.
Players can plan between turns.
cons: Waiting can be long with many players.
A set can be changed several times before your turn.

pairs.tendency: Everyone lays sets at the same moment, and then adds to the sets together in a rush.
pros: Everyone is busy.
Sets appear fast.
cons: Two players may add to the same set.
The table gets messy.

pairs.tendency: Anyone may lay a set or add a card at any moment, and the quickest hand gets there first.
pros: Speed counts.
The table never stops.
cons: A slow player is shut out.
Disputes about who was first are common.

pairs.tendency: Each turn has a clock, so a set has to be laid or added to before time runs out.
pros: Time puts a stop on a long think.
Players act without waiting.
cons: A set can be left unfinished.
Players hurry and make slips.

pairs.tendency: One set is laid or added to each day, and the table changes over weeks.
pros: A set takes days to grow.
Players come back to see what changed.
cons: A missed day can be felt.
Players may forget the plan.

pairs.tendency: Players pause before every set, and the slow pace is part of the game.
pros: Each set is considered.
The table is calm.
cons: Players with little patience drift.
A short game turns into a long one.

pairs.tendency: Turns speed up, so sets have to be laid and added to faster and faster.
pros: Pressure rises with the turns.
Sets pile up late.
cons: Early turns feel slow.
Late turns end in a scramble.

pairs.tendency: A throw or a hit gives another go, so a player may lay and add several sets in a row.
pros: Luck can give a big turn.
A lead can grow quickly.
cons: Others wait while one player lays sets.
An extra turn can end a set before anyone replies.

pairs.tendency: In the first stage players gather cards, and in the second they lay sets and add to them.
pros: Gathering feeds the laying.
Players can plan from the start.
cons: An early mistake carries on.
The second stage can feel decided already.

pairs.tendency: Sets stand for parts of a real system, such as wells and fields, and adding a card changes how the whole system works.
pros: Sets act like parts.
Players see the effect of a change.
cons: A wrong set can break the model.
Players need to know the real thing first.

pairs.tendency: Each player plays a group, such as farmers, and lays sets that show what that group wants.
pros: Sets show a group's needs.
Other groups can add to help or block.
cons: One group may be outvoted.
Players in a small role may have little to lay.

pairs.tendency: Sets draw on one shared pool, such as water, so each set laid leaves less for the rest.
pros: Sets show who is taking.
The pool is easy to watch.
cons: A large set can use up the pool.
Players may rush to lay sets first.

pairs.tendency: A set laid now shows its effect only a few rounds later, and other players add to it in the meantime.
pros: Sets act slowly.
Players plan ahead.
cons: A set's result may surprise its owner.
It is hard to link an effect to the set that caused it.

pairs.tendency: Players agree a new rule about sets, lay sets under it and see what changes.
pros: A rule can be tested safely.
The table shows the effect.
cons: A rule may change the game by accident.
Players may argue about the outcome.

pairs.tendency: After the sets are laid, players talk about why each was laid and who added what.
pros: The table helps people recall.
Players learn from going back over the sets.
cons: Some players say little.
A long talk can follow a short game.

pairs.tendency: Sets once laid cannot be taken back, and the table keeps them for the next game.
pros: Each set leaves a mark.
The table carries history.
cons: A mistake stays.
New games start from old sets.

pairs.tendency: The rules for what counts as a set make a point about the world, such as which kinds of cards can join.
pros: The set rules say something.
Players may notice what is left out.
cons: The point may go unnoticed.
Players who disagree may find the rules lopsided.

pairs.tendency: Players lay and add to sets with real money or promises at stake.
pros: A set carries a real cost.
Players take care over each card.
cons: A friendship can feel a set going wrong.
Real stakes can make a loss sting.

pairs.tendency: A set stands for something that matters, such as kindness, and players chase the points more than the thing.
pros: Sets turn values into counts.
Players see what a number leaves out.
cons: The number may take over the meaning.
Players start laying sets for the score alone.

pairs.tendency: Players lay sets that show a way of living that does not exist yet, and try adding to each other's sets.
pros: A future takes shape on the table.
Players feel how it might work.
cons: Some parts are hard to picture.
The game can end before anything is settled.

pairs.tendency: Each piece holds a power that can be used once, so a player may keep it until a throw lands them in trouble or near the finish.
pros: A power can fix a missed throw.
Players pick the moment.
cons: A power used early is gone for the rest of the game.
A player may keep it too long and never use it.

pairs.tendency: When cards are passed round, a power marker is picked up with a card, and each player can use it once to take a second pick.
pros: A power can change a pick.
Players see who has used theirs.
cons: Used powers leave empty hands.
Late pickers have fewer choices.

pairs.tendency: A power can be spent in one auction to raise a bid or to cancel another, and the marker goes with it.
pros: One power can win one auction.
Players watch for the big bid.
cons: Spending it early leaves later auctions bare.
Others bid low to draw it out.

pairs.tendency: A power saves you from one bust and no more. You decide how far to push before using it.
pros: A power gives one safe step.
Players watch how far others push.
cons: After it is used, every bust counts.
Players may keep pushing to save the power.

pairs.tendency: Once in the game, a power can move a unit across the map or flip a region. The marker then leaves play.
pros: One region can change hands.
Players guess where it will be used.
cons: The moment to use it is easy to miss.
A region can be lost before the power is used.

pairs.tendency: For one turn, a power lets a worker go to a job that is already taken. The marker is then removed.
pros: A power breaks one block.
Players plan around the one move.
cons: Using it takes a job from another player.
A spent power makes later turns harder.

pairs.tendency: A power swaps a tile or changes a colour a single time, and then the marker is gone.
pros: A power can finish a pattern.
Players keep it for the last piece.
cons: A pattern may have no gap where it fits.
Patterns after it get no help.

pairs.tendency: A power sits beside the hand as one more card that can be played once. Holding it counts as a choice.
pros: The power is a card in disguise.
Players decide when to play it.
cons: A power held too long takes up room in the plan.
Others guess the power from what is kept.

pairs.tendency: One time only, a power can change a trick, such as turning a low card into a winner, and its marker is then discarded.
pros: A power can win a single trick.
Players guess when it will arrive.
cons: Spending it on a small trick throws it away.
Others play around a player with a power left.

pairs.tendency: A player may trade a power for a favour, and the buyer can use it once.
pros: Powers become things to trade.
Players learn who needs what.
cons: A trade cannot be undone.
A power can be sold for less than it is worth.

pairs.tendency: A power can stand in for the missing piece of one set, and then its marker goes.
pros: A power can close one set.
It can wait for a set that comes late.
cons: Using it early on a small set wastes it.
A set may stay open waiting for a power.

pairs.tendency: A tile that would not fit can go in anyway by using the power a single time. The marker is then removed.
pros: A power can fix an awkward tile.
Players choose the space with care.
cons: The odd tile may block later moves.
Others can see the power coming and plan for it.

pairs.tendency: A power can give an answer that nobody expected, once, and it ends the chain.
pros: A power can break a pattern.
The chain has a surprise in it.
cons: An answer used early loses its force.
The response can look odd to those who forget the power.

pairs.tendency: A power is used with no words, so others have to guess what it means from the move.
pros: Silence hides the power.
Players read each other's moves.
cons: A power can be mistaken for an ordinary move.
Players may waste time trying to guess.

pairs.tendency: A power changes one rule, one time. The new rule stays for the rest of the game, and the marker leaves.
pros: A power can alter the game.
Which rule to change takes thought.
cons: A change cannot be undone.
A rule change may help a rival more.

pairs.tendency: A character has a power from their story that works once, such as a secret ally.
pros: A power can be the big moment in a character's story.
Players decide when to reveal it.
cons: A power used at a dull moment is wasted.
The group may argue about whether it fits the character.

pairs.tendency: A power can let a player redo a throw or a flick once. After that the hand has to do the work.
pros: A power gives a second try.
Players pick the most risky moment.
cons: A redo may also miss.
A shaky hand will use it quickly.

pairs.tendency: A power lets a player redraw or erase a piece of the map a single time, and then the marker is spent.
pros: A power can undo a mark.
Players choose what to change.
cons: A map is hard to redraw cleanly.
The mark that was erased may still show.

pairs.tendency: With a power you can ignore the other player's say one time, after which the marker leaves.
pros: A power overrides a refusal.
Players watch for the moment.
cons: Using it may upset the other player.
A spent power leaves you open to refusals.

pairs.tendency: Once, a power lets a player read a message before it passes on. The marker goes after that.
pros: A power can check a message.
Players pick which one to read.
cons: A message may still change after the check.
Messages after that go unchecked.

pairs.tendency: A power lets a player take back one passed card or pass a card face up, and then its marker is removed.
pros: A power can undo a pass.
Players guess what a pass hides.
cons: A taken card may sour a deal.
After it, every pass is final.

pairs.tendency: The first player sets up the game, and the other chooses a side. Both sides get a power that works once.
pros: Sides carry a one-time edge.
The player who sets up has to weigh the powers.
cons: Powers are hard to even out.
A side with a fitting moment for its power may win.

pairs.tendency: A piece can be promoted before it reaches the far end by a power that works once and is then taken away.
pros: A power can skip a long walk.
Players choose which piece to boost.
cons: The boosted piece becomes a target.
Others can plan around a power that is still held.

pairs.tendency: A power lets a runner skip a handover or run a leg twice, once per team.
pros: A power can save a leg.
Teams pick which leg to use it on.
cons: A slow leg may have been the one to save.
A power used on the first leg is gone for the last.

pairs.tendency: A power makes a shape safe, or breaks a safe one, a single time before its marker is taken away.
pros: A power can break a defence.
The target of the power is easy to guess.
cons: A broken shape gives the rival a chance.
A power spent early may not matter.

pairs.tendency: Even when you did not win the trick, a power can claim a scoring card for you. It works once, and then the marker goes.
pros: A power can take a prize.
Players track the named cards.
cons: A small prize can use it up.
Others guard the main prize.

pairs.tendency: A power lets you change one card in the middle for your own use, and its marker is removed after.
pros: A power changes the common cards.
Players see who touched the middle.
cons: A changed card helps others too.
Others can use the new card first.

pairs.tendency: One power lets a player take part of the pot or double a share. It is used once and the marker goes.
pros: A power can swell a prize.
Players wait for a full pot.
cons: Using it early takes a small pot.
Others may block the power before it is used.

pairs.tendency: A player with a power can skip a pit or sow in two directions on one turn, and the marker leaves after.
pros: A power changes where the last seed lands.
Players count the pits with care.
cons: A power wasted on a short sow does little.
Counting takes time.

pairs.tendency: Using a power, a player can look at the spare hand or take it. That uses up the marker.
pros: A power opens a hidden hand.
Players use it before others do.
cons: A look at the hand shows it to only one.
The power may be spent on a thin hand.

pairs.tendency: A power turns a risky square into a safe one, or skips a square, and is then gone.
pros: A power can avoid a trap.
Players hold on to it until a risky stretch.
cons: On a safe stretch it does nothing.
Players who see a trap early may spend it too soon.

pairs.tendency: A power costs a price to start, and then works once. Players have to choose whether it is worth paying for.
pros: A power has a clear price.
Players weigh it against other buys.
cons: A power bought early may never be used.
Paying for a power leaves less for other things.

pairs.tendency: A power moves a share of forces from one place to another, one time only, and the marker is taken away.
pros: A power fixes a split.
Players see how forces were shared.
cons: The shift may arrive after the fight.
Once it is spent, later splits stay as they are.

pairs.tendency: Once in the game, a power lets a player ignore the signal or move on after it. The marker is removed after.
pros: A power beats the clock.
Players watch for the signal.
cons: Before the signal, it does nothing.
Others may copy the power by chance.

pairs.tendency: A power lets a player swap with someone else's hand, or keep a swapped card. It can be used once.
pros: A power can reach into another hand.
Players wait for the card they want most.
cons: Spent on a thin hand, it brings little.
Others guard their hands.

pairs.tendency: With a power, a player can take the pile even when the top card is no use. The marker goes after that one time.
pros: A power opens the pile.
Players choose a big pile.
cons: Taking a big pile leaves a heavy hand.
Later piles stay out of reach without it.

pairs.tendency: A power can change the trump suit or make one card trump, and the marker leaves once it has been used.
pros: A power can turn a hand around.
Players guess what the new suit will be.
cons: A changed suit may help a rival.
A power used on a small hand does little.

pairs.tendency: A power can be used on either board, once, but not on both.
pros: A power helps one board.
Players choose which board needs it.
cons: The other board gets nothing.
A power on the wrong board is wasted.

pairs.tendency: A power makes one card wild, and then its marker goes.
pros: A power creates a wild card.
A hard set is the usual place for it.
cons: A wild card from a power is spent in one go.
Others hold real wild cards back.

pairs.tendency: One time, a power can close the edge of the board or open it. The marker is then taken away.
