pairs.tendency: A message carries a score for something that matters, such as kindness, and players pass it on. By the end, the points are heard instead of the value.
pros: The game shows a score standing in for a value.
The message shows what players care about.
cons: The value can be lost in the telling.
Players may chase points they heard about.

pairs.tendency: A plan for a future village is whispered round, and each person adds a part. The plan that arrives shows what everyone made of it.
pros: A plan comes from many people.
Players try out how news would travel.
cons: The plan can drift.
Players may not believe in the future they are building.

pairs.tendency: Before the first throw, each player hands a few cards to a neighbour, and the cards give small bonuses on the path, such as an extra step or a skipped space. The dice still move everyone, but the cards you received change what a roll is worth.
pros: Each throw has a card plan to be set against.
Players watch what a neighbour does with their gift.
cons: The dice still decide most of the race.
A card handed over can help the player already in front.

pairs.tendency: The hand goes round twice here: once in the blind handoff before play, and again when players pick from a shared row. A card you gave away can turn up in the row later and be taken by someone else.
pros: Players see more of the cards than in either mechanic alone.
The first pass changes what the rows hold.
cons: Two rounds of handling slow the start.
It is hard to keep track of where each card went.

pairs.tendency: Cards are passed first, then players bid for the right to play them. A card that arrived unseen may be worth more to its new owner than to the giver, and the bids show it.
pros: Bids show what players think a card is worth.
The pass sets up what there is to bid on.
cons: A blind pass makes the early bids a guess.
The setup takes a while before anyone bids.

pairs.tendency: Each player gives away some cards, then draws and risks for points. A thin batch of arrivals tempts you to keep pushing, while a full one lets you stop early.
pros: The cards you got set how far you dare go.
Others read your pushes as hints about your batch.
cons: A thin batch can send a player into one risk too many.
Players who stop early never learn what their gift did.

pairs.tendency: The cards passed say where and how many pieces you may put on the map. A giver may send cards that only help in a corner they never plan to visit, and the receiver finds out as the map fills.
pros: Gifts push players into parts of the map they did not plan for.
Each pass hints at which areas matter.
cons: A hand can arrive with cards for places already taken.
The giver has no say over which spots come up.

pairs.tendency: Cards passed before play become one-use bonuses for the workers, such as a free job or a second go at a spot. Each player then fits the gift into a plan built around who takes which spot.
pros: A gift gives one worker a move others cannot copy.
Each pass shows what a neighbour needs.
cons: A gift can arrive for a job someone else already holds.
Planning around gifts slows each turn.

pairs.tendency: Everyone sends a few cards across before building starts, and the cards that arrive are the colours and shapes you now work with. The giver cannot know which piece a neighbour was missing.
pros: The pass brings new pieces to every builder.
Players bend a pattern to fit what arrived.
cons: A gift can break a half-built row.
Givers cannot see what their gift costs a neighbour's plan.

pairs.tendency: Passing is the first move of hand management: you choose which cards to give before you know what comes back. The rest of the game goes on deciding when to play whatever you ended up with.
pros: The first choice already costs a card.
The new hand has to be learned while playing.
cons: What you gave cannot be taken back.
A plan made before the pass can fall apart when the cards arrive.

pairs.tendency: Before the first trick, each player slips cards across the table. Giving away a high card, or your only card of a suit, changes who can win the tricks that follow.
pros: The pass changes who is likely to win each trick.
Players guess a neighbour's hand from what was sent.
cons: Giving up a high card can lose a trick.
A hand heavy in one suit can come out lopsided.

pairs.tendency: Talk comes before the pass. Players promise what they will send and ask for what they want, but nobody sees the incoming cards until they have chosen what to give.
pros: Deals give the pass a reason.
Promises can be checked against what arrived.
cons: A broken promise shows only after the cards are in hand.
Long talk can hold up the start.

pairs.tendency: Cards from sets a player will never finish go across the table, and the cards that come back may start new sets. A gift can hand a rival the very card their set was missing.
pros: The pass lets a player clear out dead sets.
Arrivals can start sets nobody planned.
cons: A gift can finish a rival's set.
Players cannot ask for the card they need.

pairs.tendency: Passed cards act as permissions to lay tiles, so a card from a neighbour decides what part of the shared map you can add to. The map grows where the gifts point.
pros: Gifts steer where the map grows.
Players work with cards they did not pick.
cons: A card can arrive that fits nowhere on the map.
A neighbour's gift can close off a road in progress.

pairs.tendency: Before a chain starts, players trade cards, and each card is a line or a move that can be used to answer. A call can only be answered from the cards you were given, so the chain depends on what neighbours passed.
pros: Answers come from cards someone else chose.
The chain can go in ways no player planned.
cons: A call may have no answer in the hand.
The chain can stall when gifts do not fit.

pairs.tendency: The pass happens without a word, so each card handed over is a message the receiver cannot question. Players pick in silence, then try to read what the gift was meant to say.
pros: Every gift is a message.
Players learn to read each other's choices.
cons: A gift can be read the wrong way with no chance to ask.
Silent choosing can be slow.

pairs.tendency: Some of the cards passed are rule cards, and a rule card you hand over may be played on you later. Players weigh giving a rule away against keeping it to use themselves.
pros: The pass spreads rule changes round the table.
Players think about what a rule does in a neighbour's hand.
cons: A rule can come back to hit its giver.
The game can drift far from the one that began.

pairs.tendency: Each card handed over is a gift to someone's character, such as an object, a rumour or a favour. The receiver says in character how they came by it.
pros: Gifts give characters things to talk about.
Players invent a story for each pass.
cons: Some gifts do not fit the character.
Explaining every gift slows the scene.

pairs.tendency: Cards passed before a stacking or flicking game give each player a helper or a limit, such as a second flick or one shaky hand. The cards set the starting terms and the hands decide the rest.
pros: The pass sets uneven terms before the hands begin.
A giver picks who gets the lighter turn.
cons: A gift can leave a player with a hard task they did not ask for.
A quiet card step sits before a loud physical game.

pairs.tendency: Each card gives a player something to draw: a river, a village, a hill named on the card. The map grows from what neighbours handed over, so it shows traces of who gave what.
pros: The world has parts nobody planned.
Gifts mix different drawing hands.
cons: A river can arrive with nowhere to flow.
Clashing cards can crowd one corner.

pairs.tendency: In a two-player game, one player splits the cards into two piles and the other picks which pile to keep and which to hand over. The splitter tries to make the piles even, because the choice is not theirs.
pros: The splitter has a reason to be careful.
The chooser gets a say in the hand.
cons: A split that looks even can hide a difference.
Splitting takes time before play starts.

pairs.tendency: A card passed at the start may be one saved for the moment a piece reaches the far end of the board. A player who received such a card plans a route to the edge.
pros: A gift gives a reason to push a piece forward.
Receiving a promotion card shapes the plan.
cons: A piece can walk to the edge and find no card to turn it.
A player can give away the very card a neighbour needed.

pairs.tendency: At each handover the runner passes a card along with the baton, so a team's cards travel with the race. Whatever the last runner holds is what the final leg can use.
pros: Cards go along with the team.
A team can build a hand that pays off at the end.
cons: A dropped card costs a leg.
A card sent early may not be needed later.

pairs.tendency: Some cards given at the start are pieces of a safe shape. A player who gets the right one can build towards a position that cannot be captured, while a neighbour may pass the wrong ones.
pros: Gifts can point a player towards a shape.
Hidden pieces hide the plan.
cons: The shape may never come if the pieces go the other way.
A gift can land with a player who cannot use it.

pairs.tendency: When the prizes are named cards, passing one gives the receiver a chance at it. A player who is dealt a prize card they cannot win has to choose whether to pass it on.
pros: Passing decides who holds the prizes.
A prize card gives its holder a goal.
cons: A prize given away may be won by someone else.
Holding a prize makes a player a target.

pairs.tendency: Cards in the middle are open to all, and the cards passed in secret mix with them. A gift can hand a neighbour the card that finishes a set with the middle cards.
pros: The open cards give the secret gifts a use.
Players can guess a neighbour's hand from the middle.
cons: Your gift can close a neighbour's set with the middle cards.
Everyone is guessing what the middle will bring.

pairs.tendency: Everyone puts a counter into the pot, then passes cards. The hand that arrives decides whether you chase the pot or step out, and if nobody wins, the pot grows into the next round.
pros: A gift can raise or lower what a player dares to chase.
The pot makes each pass count.
cons: A thin hand makes the pot feel far away.
A growing pot can tempt players to stay in with little.

pairs.tendency: Cards handed over name a pit or a number of seeds, and the holder uses one to choose where to scoop from. A move on the pits is then limited by what a neighbour passed.
pros: Gifts change which pit can be played.
Players plan where the last seed will land.
cons: A card can name a pit that is empty.
Card rules and pit rules together are a lot to remember.

pairs.tendency: Players pass cards and also have a spare hand face down in the middle to take, swap or buy. A card you gave away can come back to you through the spare hand.
pros: The spare hand can repair a pass.
Players have two ways to change a hand.
cons: Nobody knows what the spare hand holds.
Two ways to swap slow the setup.

pairs.tendency: A card passed to a neighbour can be a way past a special square, such as a card that cancels a missed turn. Givers pass or keep these knowing the track is full of squares that send a piece back.
pros: Gifts can protect a piece.
The track gets a plan.
cons: A protective card can arrive too late.
A giver can pass a card that helps a rival.

pairs.tendency: Every card has a price, and you pass some before you know what you will be given. After the pass you work out what you can afford from the hand that arrived.
pros: The pass sets what each player can pay for.
Players learn to put a price on cards.
cons: A hand can arrive full of cards that cost too much.
A cheap gift can leave a neighbour short of choices.

pairs.tendency: The cards passed set how many units each player has to share between places. A big batch means more spots to cover, and a thin batch means fewer.
pros: Gifts change how much there is to share out.
Players rethink a plan after the pass.
cons: A large batch can be spread too wide.
A small batch leaves little to cover a gap.

pairs.tendency: Cards are passed round in time with the music, and when it stops, the player holding a marked card is caught. Everyone tries to get rid of it.
pros: Passing fits the pace of a noisy game.
The signal gives the pass an ending.
cons: A card can land in a hand just as the music stops.
Fast passing makes it hard to see what moves.

pairs.tendency: There are two kinds of exchange here: a blind gift before play and a chosen swap from the table later. A gift that fits nothing can be put right by a swap.
pros: Swaps can repair a blind gift.
Players try both kinds of trade.
cons: Two exchanges slow the start.
Swapping back can undo what the pass was for.

pairs.tendency: A gift that matches the top card of the discard pile lets the receiver take the whole pile on their first turn. A neighbour may have handed over that match without knowing.
pros: A lucky gift can start a big turn.
Players keep an eye on the top card.
cons: A giver may hand over the key card by chance.
A big pile makes for a heavy hand.

pairs.tendency: If the trump suit is named after the pass, you may have given away your longest run of it by accident. Players weigh what to keep before they know which suit will rule.
pros: The pass is made without knowing the trump.
Naming the trump afterwards shakes up every hand.
cons: A player can give away the cards that would have counted.
The trump draw can undo a careful pass.

pairs.tendency: A passed card can be played on either board, and the receiver chooses which. A gift can go to the board where you are attacking or the one where you are defending.
pros: One gift can serve two games.
Players decide where each card counts.
cons: A card can help a loss on one board and a win on the other.
Watching two boards slows each turn.

pairs.tendency: A wild card is the one a player most wants to keep, so choosing whether to pass it away is a hard choice. One may arrive from a neighbour who decided it was safer to be rid of it.
pros: A wild card gives the pass weight.
Players think hard before giving one.
cons: A gift of a wild card can change a hand.
The giver may regret it.

pairs.tendency: Passed cards carry moves across the edges, so a card lets a piece leave the right side and come back on the left. A neighbour who passes you an edge card has sent you a short cut to the other side.
pros: Gifts open short cuts across the edge.
Players keep an eye on the joined sides.
cons: A piece can slip away from a chase.
Edge cards can give a rival a way round.

pairs.tendency: Cards passed to the guessers can be clue cards, and the ones they hold shape what they ask. The player with the secret answers yes or no to questions built from those clues.
pros: Gifts give guessers a starting point.
Each question is shaped by a card.
cons: A clue card can lead to a question with a useless answer.
The secret keeper sees what clues were sent.

pairs.tendency: A pass at the start puts cards that speed up or slow down the race into neighbours' hands. A racer often finishes first because of cards a rival gave away.
pros: Gifts add a surprise to a plain race.
The race is not decided by dice alone.
cons: A giver may speed up a rival.
The pass can settle a race before it begins.

pairs.tendency: Cards carry points, so a gift is points given away, and a received card is points gained. At the end the score includes the cards that crossed the table.
pros: The pass adds to the final count.
Players weigh what to give.
cons: A neighbour can get ahead from your gift.
Scores change before play begins.

pairs.tendency: Players pass cards before the knock-outs begin, and gifts can be attack cards or shields. Handing an attacker to a neighbour makes them dangerous to you, so players think about whom they arm.
pros: A pass can build a threat.
Players choose carefully who is armed.
cons: An attack card can come back on its giver.
A player can be out before using their gifts.

pairs.tendency: Teammates pass cards to each other to keep everyone alive, and the pass is a gift to the group. A player who gives a key card away may be left short.
pros: The pass spreads help across the team.
Players say what they need.
cons: A card given up can leave its giver short.
Team talk about passing can slow play.

pairs.tendency: The team passes cards towards a goal they all want, and each gift goes to the player who can use it most.
pros: The pass moves cards to where they are used.
Players read each other's needs.
cons: One player can end up with all the useful cards.
The group can argue about who gets what.

pairs.tendency: Each player passes with a secret goal in mind, and a gift that looks careless may help the sender's own aim. Neighbours try to guess goals from what was sent.
pros: Gifts give away hints.
A decoy gift can hide a goal.
cons: A careless gift can show a secret.
Watching every pass takes attention.

pairs.tendency: Passed cards turn into story pieces: each gives the receiver a character, a place or an event that has to appear before the story ends.
pros: Neighbours add to each other's stories.
The story has parts nobody planned.
cons: A card can be hard to fit in.
The ending can get crowded with gifts.

pairs.tendency: Cards are passed and nobody wins. At the end, players lay out what they hold and look at how the gifts moved.
pros: The pass is its own point.
Players look back over the trail of cards.
cons: With no score, gifts may feel pointless.
The game can finish without a clear moment.

pairs.tendency: Players pass cards, then say what they hope to get from the game. A hand that arrives can change the goal they had in mind.
pros: Goals shift with the gifts.
Players say aloud what they want.
cons: A goal can turn out to be out of reach.
Players may disagree on when a goal is met.

pairs.tendency: The last card of the losing kind travels from hand to hand, and the pass is how it gets sent. Each player tries to give it away, and the loser is whoever holds it at the end.
pros: The pass has a clear purpose.
A losing card can be hidden inside a gift.
cons: A player may be stuck with it for many rounds.
Everyone watches the same card.

pairs.tendency: Each handoff gives the next player something to play, so the game does not run dry. Players pass cards to keep the supply moving.
pros: Passing keeps play alive.
Players think about what a neighbour needs.
cons: A hand can run out if cards stop moving.
With no ending, the pass has no last round.

pairs.tendency: Cards go round and round and nobody can win. The pass has no end point, and the game answers one pass with another.
pros: The pass becomes the whole game.
Players notice their habit of giving.
cons: Players look for a goal that is not there.
The game can feel like it goes nowhere.

pairs.tendency: A player passes cards to a partner, or between two hands of their own, and both try to clear the layout. One side's gift is the other side's way through.
pros: The pass lets two hands work together.
Players plan what to send.
cons: A gift can block the layout.
A solo game with a pass needs a partner or two hands.

pairs.tendency: Each short game starts with a fresh pass, so a player can change what they give after seeing what came back last time.
pros: A fresh pass each game lets players adjust.
Players learn from each round.
cons: Early luck can carry into later games.
The repeated pass can start to feel the same.

pairs.tendency: Cards carry points against you, so everyone tries to give away their heaviest cards in the pass. The receiver gets stuck with them.
pros: The pass is the first chance to dump points.
Players guess what a neighbour sent.
cons: A gift can start a neighbour with a heavy hand.
A player cannot refuse what arrives.

pairs.tendency: Cards passed include high numbers that can overshoot the target. A player who gives away a card that would push them over has to hope the replacement fits.
pros: The pass can clear out cards that overshoot.
Players aim for the exact number.
cons: A gift can arrive that overshoots at once.
Exact numbers leave little room for a wrong card.

pairs.tendency: Players pass away the cards they least want to hold, since the aim is to give everything away. The pass becomes the moves of the game.
pros: Passing is the aim.
Players work out what to hold back.
cons: The last card can end up in a hand nobody wants.
Every player is trying to do the same thing.

pairs.tendency: Everyone builds their own thing, and the pass is the one moment when cards cross between them. A gift is the only way to touch a neighbour's game.
pros: The pass links separate games.
Players see one other thing happening.
cons: A gift can disturb a neighbour's plan.
Little else joins the games.

pairs.tendency: Before a fight, a player hands cards to the person they plan to hit. A pass of junk to a target, or an attack card by mistake, can change who wins.
pros: Passing sets up the attacks.
Players pick whom to arm.
cons: A target can get a card to hit back.
A cruel gift can leave hurt feelings at the table.

pairs.tendency: Cards passed shape what each player can do to the board. A neighbour feels the pass through where pieces can go, and not through an attack.
pros: The pass reaches the board.
Players read the board for clues.
cons: A gift can block a neighbour's route.
The effect of a gift shows up late.

pairs.tendency: The pass gives teammates the cards the group needs, with no rival to gain from it. Everyone picks cards to give based on who can use them.
pros: Gifts go where they are needed.
Players agree on a plan.
cons: A gift can arrive too late.
One player may hold the cards nobody else needs.

pairs.tendency: Passing helps the team, but each player keeps a card or two for their private aim. Players can tell from a pass who is holding back.
pros: Gifts help the whole team.
A held-back card hints at a private aim.
cons: A thin gift can look like greed.
Players may doubt each other's gifts.

pairs.tendency: Teammates pass cards to each other and not to the other side. A player has to guess what a partner wants and send it.
pros: Partners learn each other's habits.
The pass stays private to a team.
cons: A wrong guess leaves a partner short.
The other team sees how often a side passes.

pairs.tendency: A card from the traitor can look helpful and not be. Players hunt for the one whose gifts never seem to help.
pros: Gifts become clues.
Players watch each other's passes.
cons: A real helper can be blamed.
The traitor can hide inside a gift.

pairs.tendency: Cards are passed by post, or described in letters, so a pass takes days. Players wait weeks for the cards to arrive.
pros: The wait is part of the game.
Letters can say more than the cards.
cons: A card may be lost in the post.
The game can last a whole year.

pairs.tendency: The absent player cannot pass, so their gifts wait in a pile or come from an earlier game. Others take from the pile as if the absent player had sent them.
pros: Absent players still give.
The pile carries a memory of earlier play.
cons: A pile can run out.
Players cannot answer a gift from someone who is not there.

pairs.tendency: The game master hands out the cards, deciding who gets which, and can pass cards as story items. Players learn what the world gives them.
pros: The master shapes the pass.
Gifts can carry story.
cons: A master's choice can seem to favour someone.
The master has more to do.

pairs.tendency: In a street game, a stranger can be handed a card and asked to hand one back, so the pass pulls new people in.
pros: Passers-by join in.
The pass makes a crowd.
cons: Cards can go missing in the crowd.
A crowd is hard to keep track of.

pairs.tendency: The group passes cards among themselves while the lone player gets fewer. The many can pool what they have.
pros: The many can share cards.
The lone player faces a united side.
cons: The lone player has no one to pass to.
The lone player sees the group planning.

pairs.tendency: With nobody to pass to, a player passes between two piles of their own, choosing a set to put aside before seeing what comes back.
pros: The pass becomes a choice against yourself.
Players learn their own habits.
cons: The pass can feel pointless alone.
Luck decides what comes back.

pairs.tendency: The pass is blind and the deal is random, so every card that arrives is luck. There is little to choose.
pros: The pass adds one more turn of luck.
Players share the surprise.
cons: Choices matter little.
The outcome is out of players' hands.

pairs.tendency: Cards that arrive are luck, but choosing which to give away softens it. A player who sees a thin hand coming can give away cards that might be wasted.
pros: Giving is a way to steer luck.
Players have a plan for the pass.
cons: A thin hand can still arrive.
A plan can be wasted by the draw.

pairs.tendency: Choosing what to give is skill, and what arrives is luck. The pass sits where the two meet.
pros: Skill chooses the gift.
Luck chooses the arrival.
cons: Skill can be wasted on a blind pass.
Luck can undo a plan.

pairs.tendency: With no dice, the pass is the one unknown, and a player who counts the deck can work out which cards went where.
pros: The pass is the one hidden step.
Counting pays off.
cons: A hand reveals its giver's plan.
A keen counter knows more than the others.

pairs.tendency: The cards that arrive are read as a sign, and each received card is taken as a message and talked over.
pros: Gifts become signs.
Players talk about what a card might mean.
cons: A sign can be read two ways.
The giver does not know how the gift will be read.

pairs.tendency: Players sense what a neighbour needs and pass without talking, hoping their guesses match.
pros: Passing becomes a quiet guess.
Close friends match often.
cons: Strangers may miss.
A miss shows only later.

pairs.tendency: Passed cards are bonus items used to change a roll, and the dice say what happens in the story. A neighbour's gift can bend a roll.
pros: Gifts add to the dice.
The story gets help from neighbours.
cons: A gift can be used at the wrong moment.
Bending rolls can change where the story goes.

pairs.tendency: Players choose cards to give before seeing the incoming ones, and then all cards are laid face up. Everyone sees the pass.
pros: Nothing is hidden after the pass.
Players can see every gift.
cons: The first choice is blind.
There is no bluff in the pass.

pairs.tendency: The pass makes each hand secret and slightly changed. Others know you gave something away but not what.
pros: The hand stays a secret.
Others make guesses.
cons: A guess can be wrong.
The pass is a puzzle for all.

pairs.tendency: The cards a player sends suggest their role, and neighbours try to read it. A spy may send cards that point at someone else.
pros: Gifts are clues.
Players watch what is sent.
cons: A spy's gift can point at the wrong player.
Neighbours can read a role that is not there.

pairs.tendency: The cards a neighbour gives are clues about what they hold. Players write down what they gave and what arrived to narrow the options.
pros: Gifts narrow down hands.
Notes pay off.
cons: Notes take time.
A planted card can send the notes the wrong way.

pairs.tendency: A player passes cards chosen to make the receiver believe something false about what is left. A bluff in the pass is hard to check.
pros: The pass can start a bluff.
Players weigh the risk.
cons: A bluff can be caught later.
Distrust can spread round the table.

pairs.tendency: The player who knows can refuse a pass that breaks the secret rule, and the others learn the rule from being told no.
pros: The pass tests the rule.
Players learn from refusals.
cons: Refusals slow the pass.
Learning the rule can take long.

pairs.tendency: The one who knows picks cards to pass as hints in place of words. The others read them.
pros: Hints come without words.
Players read cards for meaning.
cons: A hint can be misread.
Few cards make few hints.

pairs.tendency: Cards passed before exploring tell the receiver what may lie ahead, even though the map stays hidden.
pros: Gifts hint at the map.
Explorers pick where to go.
cons: A hint can be wrong.
Hints spoil some of the discovery.

pairs.tendency: A face-up hand sits open to all, and the pass moves cards into or out of it. Everyone sees what a gift changes in the open hand.
pros: The open hand shows each pass.
Players can plan around it.
cons: A card given to the open hand is lost to its giver.
Open cards show a lot.

pairs.tendency: Cards passed can carry hidden points, so a gift changes someone's secret score and nobody can tell by how much.
pros: Gifts change scores in secret.
Players guess who is ahead.
cons: Totals stay uncertain.
A giver can help a rival without knowing it.

pairs.tendency: The pass goes round the table in order, and each player waits their turn to choose.
pros: Each choice is seen.
Players have time to think.
cons: Waiting is long.
The last to pass sees everything.

pairs.tendency: Everyone chooses and passes at the same moment, so nobody waits and nobody can react to another's pass.
pros: Nobody waits.
Choices are made blind.
cons: Mistakes show only afterwards.
The table gets noisy.

pairs.tendency: Anyone passes whenever they choose, and cards fly round the table. The quickest player gets first pick of what is on offer.
pros: Passing is fast.
Players watch hands.
cons: Slower players fall behind.
It is hard to follow.

pairs.tendency: The pass has a clock, so a player who dithers has a card chosen for them.
pros: The clock forces a choice.
Players act on a first instinct.
cons: A rushed choice can lose a key card.
Players feel hurried.

pairs.tendency: Cards go out in the post or by message over days, and each pass takes a day.
pros: Waiting is part of play.
Players think between passes.
cons: Games take long.
Players forget what was sent.

pairs.tendency: Players take a breath before each card they pass. The slow pace makes each gift feel chosen.
pros: Each gift is weighed.
Players notice each other.
cons: The pass takes long.
The slowness can wear on some.

pairs.tendency: Passes get faster each round, with less time to choose. By the end the cards fly.
pros: Early passes are careful.
Later passes are quick.
cons: Late passes are a blur.
Mistakes pile up.

pairs.tendency: A card that gives an extra turn is worth keeping, so players think about giving one away. A neighbour who gets it can move twice.
pros: The pass can hand out a double move.
Players weigh keeping against giving.
cons: A gift can let a rival race ahead.
A double move given away cannot be called back.

pairs.tendency: The pass is the first stage and play is the second. What a player gives and gets in the first stage sets up the second.
pros: The first stage sets up the second.
Players plan across stages.
cons: The first stage is blind.
A mistake in the pass lasts.

pairs.tendency: Cards passed stand for grain, water or help moving between people in a system. What one player gives, another has.
pros: The pass shows how things move.
Players see the flow.
cons: Real flows are messier.
A simple pass hides detail.

pairs.tendency: Each role passes different cards, such as a farmer sending grain and a council sending permits. The receiver sees what the other group can give.
pros: Roles shape the pass.
Players see each other's needs.
cons: Some roles have little to give.
A role may lack the card it needs.

pairs.tendency: Cards stand for a limited shared resource such as water, and the pass moves it from hand to hand. If players keep too much, others run dry.
pros: The pass shows who holds the resource.
Players see the shared limit.
cons: A hoarder leaves others dry.
The pass can end early if the resource runs out.

pairs.tendency: A card given now shows its effect a few rounds later, when the receiver finally plays it.
pros: A gift's effect arrives late.
Players plan ahead.
cons: A giver cannot see the result at once.
Cause and effect are hard to link.

pairs.tendency: The pass itself is the rule to test: everyone passes two cards to the left, and the table sees what it changes.
pros: The pass is simple to test.
Players compare before and after.
cons: A rule can look the same as luck.
One test may not settle anything.

pairs.tendency: After the game, players talk about what they gave and why. The talk brings out choices that stayed hidden during play.
pros: Players explain their gifts.
The talk links the game to real life.
cons: Memory fades.
Some may not want to explain.

pairs.tendency: Passed cards are torn or marked, so a gift can never be taken back. The next game starts with the marked cards.
pros: Gifts leave marks.
The history stays in the deck.
cons: A wrong gift stays wrong in every later game.
Players may hesitate to give.

pairs.tendency: A rule that makes you give away your highest card says that sharing costs something. Players feel the point in their hands.
pros: The pass makes a point.
Players feel it by doing.
cons: The point can be missed.
A rule can say more than players want to hear.

pairs.tendency: Cards passed stand for real things, such as sweets or a promise to help. A gift in the game is a gift outside it.
pros: Gifts carry real weight.
Players take care.
cons: A friendship can be strained by a gift.
Some players may not want to join.

pairs.tendency: Each card is worth a point for kindness, and the pass earns points for giving. Players start passing to score and not to help.
pros: The pass turns kindness into points.
Players see what a number replaces.
cons: Players chase the number.
The original value can be lost.

pairs.tendency: The pass practises a way of sharing, such as a village where all cards are common. Players feel what it is like to give with no return.
pros: Players try sharing.
The pass is simple to repeat.
cons: Giving with no return can feel odd.
A game village is smaller than a real one.

pairs.tendency: One player lays out the board, deciding where the snakes, ladders or traps sit, and the other picks which counter to play. A setter who leaves a long ladder at one end knows the chooser will take that end.
pros: Setting the board has a stake for the setter.
The chooser has a say before the dice are thrown.
cons: The dice still decide most moves.
A lucky run of dice can undo careful setup.

pairs.tendency: The first row of cards is laid out by one player, and the other picks whether to draft first or second. The setter tries to put out a row where neither place has a clear lead.
pros: The setter weighs every card in the row.
The chooser picks who drafts first.
cons: A row is hard to judge at a glance.
Setting the row takes time.

pairs.tendency: Opening prices are set by one player, and the other picks to be buyer or seller. A price set too high or too low will be used against the setter.
pros: A careless price comes back on the setter.
Both sides see what the setter thinks things are worth.
cons: Few price lists come out even.
The chooser may take the side with the obvious deal.

pairs.tendency: One player sets the limit of the risk, such as how many pushes before a bust, and the other picks whether to push first or second. The setter has a reason to choose a limit that suits neither side more.
pros: The setter thinks hard about where the bust falls.
The chooser decides who risks first.
cons: A limit is hard to judge before play.
A bust on the first push ends the argument at once.

pairs.tendency: One player places the starting pieces on the map and the other picks a colour. The setter spreads them so that neither colour clearly holds more ground.
pros: The map starts close to even.
The chooser sees all the pieces before choosing.
cons: An even map is hard to draw.
One corner can still look more open to the chooser.

pairs.tendency: One player lays out the starting jobs and spots, then the other picks which seat to take. First pick of a spot can matter, so the setter spreads the useful spots out.
pros: The setter thinks about every spot.
The chooser can take the first or last seat.
cons: A spot can look equal and turn out not to be.
Setup takes a while before the first worker is placed.

pairs.tendency: One player makes the starting board of coloured tiles, then the other picks whose patterns to build. A setter who leaves a half-finished line near one colour knows the chooser will take it.
pros: The starting board has a stake for the setter.
The chooser sees where the lines are.
cons: A half-built line is hard to price.
A lucky draw can undo the setup.

pairs.tendency: One player deals two hands, and the other picks which to keep. The setter divides the cards so that neither hand clearly leads.
pros: The setter thinks about every card in both hands.
The chooser keeps the hand they prefer.
cons: Two hands are hard to match.
Looking over two hands takes time.

pairs.tendency: One player names the trump suit and arranges the first lead, then the other picks whether to lead or follow. The setter knows the chooser will take the side the trump helps.
pros: The trump is picked with the chooser in mind.
The chooser decides who leads.
cons: Whether lead or follow wins depends on the cards dealt.
A trump that suits neither side is hard to find.

pairs.tendency: One player offers a split of the things on the table, and the other picks which share to take. It is the old rule of one cutting and the other choosing, and the talk that follows is about the cut.
pros: The cutter has every reason to cut fairly.
The chooser can say no to a cut.
cons: Neither player can be sure a cut is even.
A long argument about the cut can stall play.

pairs.tendency: One player splits the cards into two piles, and the other picks the pile to collect from. The setter tries to put the same sets in each pile.
pros: The setter checks each set in both piles.
The chooser takes the pile they want.
cons: Sets hide in the piles.
A pile can look even and still favour a set.

pairs.tendency: One player lays the first tiles on the map, and the other picks a colour to play. The setter shapes the start so both colours have roads to build.
pros: The setter lays each first tile with both colours in mind.
The chooser sees the whole start.
cons: A start is hard to balance.
The tiles that come next can undo the setup.

pairs.tendency: One player makes the opening call, and the other picks whether to answer it or to swap sides and call it back. A call that is too simple or too odd will be handed back to the setter.
pros: A lazy call comes straight back to the setter.
The chooser can turn it around.
cons: Calls are hard to compare.
A swap can leave the chain stuck.

pairs.tendency: One player sets the opening cards without a word, and the other points to a side. Even the choice is mute.
pros: The start is made with no talk.
The chooser acts by pointing.
cons: A pointing choice can be read wrongly.
Neither can explain the setup.

pairs.tendency: One player writes the starting rules, and the other picks which side to play. A rule written to help the setter might end up helping the chooser instead.
pros: The setter writes each rule knowing it may help the other side.
The chooser reads the rules before taking a side.
cons: Rules that change later can undo the balance.
A rule is hard to judge before play.

pairs.tendency: One player makes the characters for both sides, and the other picks which to play. A setter who gives one character a long story risks losing it to the chooser.
pros: The setter gives both characters the same attention.
The chooser can take the one they like.
cons: Two characters are hard to match.
A story can tilt a choice.

pairs.tendency: One player builds the starting tower or sets out the pieces, and the other picks who goes first. The setter builds a tower that is easy neither to start nor to finish.
pros: The setter thinks about every block in the tower.
The chooser reads the tower.
cons: A shaky tower is hard to judge by eye.
A wobble can end the game early.

pairs.tendency: One player draws the first part of the map, and the other picks which side of it to start from. The setter puts rivers and hills where both sides meet them.
pros: The setter draws knowing either side may be taken.
The chooser sees the whole sketch.
cons: A map is hard to draw evenly.
A line drawn too early can limit the rest.

pairs.tendency: One player places the starting pieces, and the other picks the side. The setter has to think about which side reaches the far end first, because that side promotes first.
pros: The setter thinks about the far end.
The chooser can pick the side nearer it.
cons: A lead in distance is hard to see.
A first promotion can swing the game.

pairs.tendency: One player divides the runners into two teams, and the other picks which team to run for. The setter puts the quick and slow runners on each side.
pros: The setter thinks about who runs fast and who runs slow.
The chooser can read the line-up.
cons: Runners are hard to match.
One slow leg can lose the race.

pairs.tendency: One player places the first stones, and the other picks a colour. Early stones count for a lot here, because a safe shape can start from the first few.
pros: The setter thinks about each early stone.
The chooser can take the side with the shape.
cons: A shape is hard to judge so early.
One early move can set a shape.

pairs.tendency: One player decides which cards are the prizes, and the other picks a side. A prize is named knowing the other side may be taken.
pros: The setter names prizes with both sides in mind.
The chooser can pick the side with more prizes in reach.
cons: A prize is hard to value before play.
A prize can swing a game on one trick.

pairs.tendency: One player turns up the middle cards, and the other picks which hand to hold. The middle cards are open to both, so the setter looks at what each hand can build with them.
pros: The setter checks what each hand can make from the middle.
The chooser sees what all can use.
cons: Open cards rarely suit both hands equally.
The next cards turned can change who leads.

pairs.tendency: One player sets the size of the starting pot, and the other picks whether to go first. A big pot makes the first go count, and a small one does not.
pros: The setter thinks about what the pot size does to the first go.
The chooser decides the order.
cons: A pot size is hard to judge.
A pot that grows can undo the choice.

pairs.tendency: One player sets how many seeds go in each pit, and the other picks which row to play. The setter knows the chooser will take the row with seeds near the store.
pros: The setter counts the seeds in every pit.
The chooser sees all the seeds.
cons: A seed count is hard to even out.
Early moves can change the count a lot.

pairs.tendency: One player decides which hand is the spare and which are dealt, and the other picks a side. The setter has to guess how the spare hand might be used.
pros: The setter weighs the spare hand.
The chooser sees both sides first.
cons: A spare hand is hard to price.
The swap can undo the setup.

pairs.tendency: One player puts the special squares on the track, and the other picks a colour. A square that sends a piece back is placed knowing the chooser may start behind it.
pros: The setter places each square with the chooser's start in mind.
The chooser sees every square.
cons: Squares are hard to weigh.
A single square can decide the race.

pairs.tendency: One player sets the prices of the cards, and the other picks which side buys first. Prices that look fair to the setter might be cheap for the chooser.
pros: The setter thinks about what each price does to the first buyer.
The chooser picks who buys first.
cons: Prices are hard to match.
A price list can favour one side by accident.

pairs.tendency: One player divides the forces between the places, and the other picks an army. The setter puts equal weight in each place or makes a trap for the chooser.
pros: The setter weighs each place before sharing out forces.
The chooser sees each place.
cons: A split is hard to judge.
One place can swing the game.

pairs.tendency: One player sets where the chairs go, and the other picks where to stand. The setter knows the chooser will pick the spot closest to a seat.
pros: The setter thinks about where the chooser will stand.
The chooser takes a place first.
cons: Equal distances to every seat are hard to arrange.
The signal can come when least expected.

pairs.tendency: One player lays out the cards on the table for swapping, and the other picks whether to swap first. The setter puts out cards that make a swap worth less.
pros: The setter thinks about what each card is worth to a swapper.
The chooser decides who swaps first.
cons: A spread of cards is hard to even out.
A swap can undo the setup.

pairs.tendency: One player starts the discard pile with a card, and the other picks who takes the first turn. A pile that starts with a useful card makes the first turn count.
pros: The setter thinks about what the first card offers.
The chooser can take the first turn.
cons: A first card is hard to judge.
A big pile can build fast.

pairs.tendency: One player names the trump, and the other picks whether to lead or follow. Since the chooser will take whichever side the trump helps, the setter looks for a suit that favours neither.
pros: The setter avoids a suit that leans one way.
The chooser picks the lead.
cons: Trumps are hard to balance.
A suit can look neutral until the cards are dealt.

pairs.tendency: One player sets up both boards, and the other picks which side to hold on the first board, getting the opposite on the second. The setter spreads the advantage across the two so that neither choice wins both.
pros: The setter weighs the two boards against each other.
One choice settles both boards.
cons: Two boards are hard to match.
A lead on one board can cancel a loss on the other.

pairs.tendency: One player decides which cards are wild, and the other picks a side. The setter knows a wild card in the chooser's hand finishes sets.
pros: The setter thinks about where each wild card helps.
The chooser sees the wilds.
cons: Wilds are hard to price.
A wild card can swing a hand.

pairs.tendency: One player places the starting pieces, and the other picks a colour. With the edges joined, no side has a back wall, so the setter has to watch every direction.
pros: The setter checks every side.
The chooser sees all the pieces.
cons: A start on a joined board is hard to judge.
A line that wraps can come from an odd side.

pairs.tendency: One player picks the list of possible secrets, and the other picks whether to ask or to answer. A list that is too short or too odd will be handed to the setter.
pros: The setter avoids a list that is too short or too odd.
The chooser decides the role.
cons: A list fair to both asker and answerer is hard to write.
Asking or answering can change the whole mood.

pairs.tendency: One player marks the start lines, and the other picks a lane. Lanes of different lengths show up quickly once the race begins.
pros: The setter checks the length of each lane.
The chooser sees every lane before picking.
cons: Lanes are hard to match.
A short lane can win the race.

pairs.tendency: One player sets the points on offer, and the other picks whether to go first. The setter spreads the points so that neither place has an edge.
pros: The setter thinks about where each point lands.
The chooser picks who goes first.
cons: Points are hard to even out.
A big score on the first turn can settle it.

pairs.tendency: One player sets the starting positions, and the other picks a colour. The setter puts both sides at equal risk of being knocked out first.
pros: The setter checks how exposed each side is.
The chooser sees every position.
cons: Equal risk is hard to measure.
A first knock-out can end it fast.

pairs.tendency: One player builds the challenge the pair will face, and the other picks which part to play. The setter knows the chooser will take the part that looks easier to survive in, so both parts get the same share of danger.
pros: The danger is shared out with care.
The chooser has a say in the team's part.
cons: Two parts are hard to match.
A part that looks safe can turn out to be the one under attack.

pairs.tendency: One player proposes the goal the two will work towards, and the other picks which role to take in reaching it.
pros: The goal is stated with care.
The chooser takes the role they prefer.
cons: A goal can suit one role more.
Both players share a result, so a choice can feel pointless.

pairs.tendency: One player writes two secret goals, and the other picks one to play. The setter tries to write goals that take about the same effort.
pros: Both goals get equal care.
The chooser picks without knowing what the other goal is worth.
cons: Goals are hard to compare in advance.
The goal left over stays unknown to the chooser.

pairs.tendency: One player starts the story, and the other picks whether to carry on the hero's side or the rival's. The setter writes an opening that gives both sides something to do.
pros: The opening gives both sides a path.
The chooser picks a voice.
cons: An opening is hard to balance.
A sad opening may pull both players one way.

pairs.tendency: One player sets up a start, and the other picks a side, but nobody wins. The choice then follows taste, since nothing is at stake.
pros: The pick is made for its own sake.
The setter has no reason to tilt the start.
cons: Without a result, the rule has nothing to guard.
The choice may feel small.

pairs.tendency: One player names the start, and the other picks a side. Each then says what a result means for them, so the setter cannot know what makes a side attractive.
pros: Each player sets their own aim after the pick.
The chooser's reason stays private.
cons: Even is hard to define when aims differ.
The setter has nothing to measure by.

pairs.tendency: One player sets the first hand, and the other picks a side. The setter aims for a start where neither side is more likely to end up the loser.
pros: The setter looks at how either side could end up the loser.
The chooser sees the whole hand.
cons: Losing is hard to predict this early.
A single mistake can decide who loses.

pairs.tendency: One player sets the opening, and the other picks a side. Since the game has no end, the choice only decides how it begins.
pros: The setter still thinks about the first moves.
The chooser decides how play starts.
cons: The pick matters less as the game runs on.
A long game forgets its first choice.

pairs.tendency: One player sets up a game nobody can win, and the other picks a side. Each side is as pointless as the other, so the choice shows nothing.
pros: The rule is carried out for its own sake.
The chooser sees how empty the pick is.
cons: There is nothing to even out.
Players may find the rule silly.

pairs.tendency: One player lays out the cards, and the other picks whether to play the layout or hand it back. A setter who makes a layout too hard knows it will come back to them.
pros: The setter avoids a layout too hard to clear.
The chooser can hand it back.
cons: A layout is hard to judge by eye.
A hidden block shows up only in play.

pairs.tendency: The pie rule is used in every game of the match, with the players swapping who sets and who picks. Each setter learns from the last pick.
pros: Each game gets a new setup.
Both players get to set and to choose.
cons: Setting wears on after several games.
A loss in one game changes how the next is set.

pairs.tendency: One player deals out the points that count against a player, and the other picks a hand. The setter tries to share the heavy cards evenly.
pros: The setter tracks where the heavy cards go.
The chooser can pick the lighter-looking hand.
cons: Hidden points are hard to see.
A hand that looks light can fill with points later.

pairs.tendency: One player sets the target number and the starting totals, and the other picks a side. A target that suits only one side will be left to the setter.
pros: The setter checks the target against both totals.
The chooser picks a total.
cons: Exact numbers are hard to even out.
One total can sit closer to the target by a lucky margin.

pairs.tendency: One player arranges the start, and the other picks which side to lose from. The setter wants both sides to be equally hard to lose.
pros: The setter plays both sides through in their head.
The chooser picks the side to play.
cons: Losing on purpose is hard to measure.
A side that loses too quickly can look like a win.

pairs.tendency: One player prepares two separate boards, and the other picks one. After that the players never touch each other's game.
pros: The setter knows either board may be taken.
The choice is the only contact.
cons: Boards are hard to match.
The choice is over before play begins.

pairs.tendency: One player sets the starting forces, and the other picks a side to attack from. The setter tries to leave both sides with a way to hit first.
pros: The setter checks who can strike first.
The chooser can read each side's reach.
cons: Forces are hard to weigh.
The first strike can settle things.

pairs.tendency: One player lays the first walls and spots on the board, and the other picks a colour. The setter knows the walls will be felt by whoever sits behind them.
pros: The setter places each wall knowing either side may sit behind it.
The chooser can read the board.
cons: Walls are hard to judge for both sides.
One wall can close off a whole side.

pairs.tendency: One player sets up the problem for the pair, and the other picks which job to do. The setter splits the jobs so that neither is left idle.
pros: The setter makes sure each job has work in it.
The chooser takes the job they like.
cons: A job is hard to price.
A team can fail over one idle job.

pairs.tendency: One player writes the private aims of both sides, and the other picks one. The setter knows the aim picked will pull the chooser away from the team a little.
pros: The setter weighs how far each aim pulls from the team.
The chooser picks a pull.
cons: Aims are hard to match.
One aim may tempt a player to let the team down.

pairs.tendency: One player divides the players into two teams, and the other picks which to join. The setter pairs the quick with the slow so the teams come out even.
pros: The setter weighs every player before splitting them.
The chooser can read each team.
cons: Teams are hard to match.
One team may click with one another and the other may not.

pairs.tendency: One player divides the table into two groups, and the other picks which group to join. The setter does not say where the traitor sits.
pros: The setter splits the table without a word about the traitor.
The chooser picks without knowing the traitor.
cons: A traitor's group is hard to tell.
A pick may land next to the traitor by luck.

pairs.tendency: The opening setup is sent by letter, and the reply names the side the other player has picked. A setter waits days to learn which side they will play.
pros: Writing the setup down makes the setter think it through.
The reply is the choice.
cons: The wait comes before play begins.
A reply that never arrives stalls the game.

pairs.tendency: One player sets the side of the absent player, and the other picks whether to take that side or the present one. The absent side has nobody to defend it.
pros: The setter thinks about a side nobody will speak for.
The chooser can take the side with no voice.
cons: An absent side is hard to judge.
Nobody can complain about a setup.

pairs.tendency: The game master sets up the start, and a player picks a side. The master has no side of their own, so the setup has no reason to lean either way.
pros: The master sets the start.
The chooser takes a side.
cons: A master can still lean without meaning to.
A master has more to prepare.

pairs.tendency: One player chalks out the court, and the next person who walks up picks a side. The setter has to draw a court that works for a stranger.
pros: The court is drawn with care.
Any passer-by can choose.
cons: A stranger may not know the rules.
A court drawn in a hurry can be uneven.

pairs.tendency: One player sets the game, and another picks whether to be the lone player or one of the many. The setter pays the lone player more so that the choice is open.
pros: The setter weighs how much extra the lone player needs.
The chooser picks one role.
cons: Pay is hard to even out.
Picking the lone role can be a mistake.

pairs.tendency: A player sets the board alone and then picks which side to play against themselves. They have to live with what they set.
pros: The setter and the chooser are one person.
The player sees both sides.
cons: A player knows what they set.
The rule has nobody to guard against.

pairs.tendency: The dice decide most of the game, so the start matters little and the side picked matters little too. The rule does little here.
pros: The pick is made quickly.
The setter has less to worry about.
cons: The rule guards against little.
The choice can feel empty.

pairs.tendency: One player sets the start, and the other picks a side. Luck still enters, but each side has ways to soften it, so the start counts for less than the way luck is handled.
pros: The setter keeps the start simple.
The chooser sees the ways to soften luck.
cons: A start is hard to measure with luck in it.
One run of low throws can still sink a side.

pairs.tendency: One player sets the start, and the other picks a side. A small amount of luck means the choice counts for most, but not all, of the result.
pros: The pick counts for most of the game.
The setter thinks about skill more than luck.
cons: A little luck can still swing a game.
An even start is hard to judge.

pairs.tendency: The game has no dice, so the start decides a lot. This is where the pie rule matters most: the setter has only the board to work with.
pros: The rule keeps the start close.
Both players use skill to read the board.
cons: The setter needs real knowledge of the game.
A beginner may set a start that looks even and is not.

pairs.tendency: One player throws to set the start, and the other picks a side after reading the sign. The throw is not added up, so the choice follows a feeling for what the sign says.
pros: The sign is read before the pick.
The chooser has something to talk about.
cons: A sign is hard to compare.
The choice rests on one reading.

pairs.tendency: One player starts, and the other picks a side without any words. The two try to sense what the other wants, and the pick shows it.
pros: The choice is made by feel.
The pair learn each other's signs.
cons: A feel is hard to check.
The pick may be a miss.

pairs.tendency: One player rolls to set the opening of the story, and the other picks which side to tell. The roll writes part of the opening, so the setter has less say.
pros: The dice set the start.
The chooser takes a side of the story.
cons: A roll is hard to balance.
The roll may favour one side.

pairs.tendency: Everything on the board is visible, so the chooser can judge the setup fully before picking. The setter has nowhere to hide an edge.
pros: The chooser sees the whole setup.
The setter has to make it even.
cons: Even is hard to judge, even when seen.
An edge may be too small to see.

pairs.tendency: One player deals the hands and the other picks a side without seeing the cards. The setter knows more about the deal than the chooser does.
pros: The setter deals knowing the chooser cannot look.
The pick is made blind.
cons: The chooser cannot judge the setup.
The setter may know which side is lucky.

pairs.tendency: One player deals out the secret roles, and the other picks a seat. Neither knows which role sits where, so the pick is made blind.
pros: No one can steer a role to a chosen seat.
The chooser picks a seat.
cons: Roles are hard to match.
A seat next to a spy can matter.

pairs.tendency: One player sets the hidden facts, and the other picks whether to hunt for them or to hide them. The setter hides things in a way that makes both jobs equal.
pros: The setter weighs how hard each fact is to find.
The chooser picks a job.
cons: Hiding and hunting are hard to match.
A fact hidden too deep can ruin the hunt.

pairs.tendency: One player sets the start and may act proud of a lopsided one to push the chooser. The chooser has to decide whether the pride is a bluff.
pros: The setter has a reason to bluff.
The chooser reads the setter.
cons: A bluff is hard to read.
A bluffed start can mislead.

pairs.tendency: One player knows the secret rule and sets the start, and the other picks a side. The chooser does not know the rule, so the pick is made in the dark.
pros: The setter shapes the start knowing the rule.
The chooser learns by being told no.
cons: The pick has less to go on.
The rule remains the setter's advantage.

pairs.tendency: One player holds the answer and sets the clue cards, and the other picks whether to guess or to give the hints. A setter who gives hard hints may be handed the guessing role.
pros: The setter avoids hints that are too hard.
The chooser takes a role.
cons: Hints are hard to rate.
A role swap can leave a puzzle half-done.

pairs.tendency: One player hides the map tiles, and the other picks a side to start from. Neither can see the map ahead, so the setter cannot tell which side will be favoured.
pros: The map is laid face down.
The chooser picks blind.
cons: A hidden map is hard to even out.
The first tiles turned can favour a side.

pairs.tendency: One player sets the open hand and the other picks which side plays it. Since the hand is face up, the chooser sees exactly what is on offer.
pros: The setter knows every card in it will be seen.
The chooser sees the open hand.
cons: An open hand is hard to balance.
The secret hands stay unknown.

pairs.tendency: One player sets the start with some points hidden, and the other picks a side. The chooser cannot add up the scores, so the pick rests on a guess.
pros: The setter decides which points stay hidden.
The chooser picks on a guess.
cons: Hidden points are hard to weigh.
A guess can be far off.

pairs.tendency: The pie rule handles the edge that going first gives. One player sets up, the other chooses first or second, and the turns then go round in order.
pros: The first-move edge is dealt with.
Turns stay simple.
cons: The setter has to judge the value of going first.
The second player waits longer.

pairs.tendency: One player sets up, and the other picks a side, then both choose in secret at the same moment. Since nobody goes first, the rule has less to guard.
pros: Both choices come at once.
Nobody waits.
cons: There is no first-move edge to protect.
The rule may feel unneeded.

pairs.tendency: One player sets the start, and the other picks a side, but then anyone can act at any moment. The quickest player gets the first move.
pros: The pick is made before the rush.
The setter has little time to adjust.
cons: Speed can overrule the setup.
A fast hand can win before the pick matters.

pairs.tendency: One player sets up with a clock running, and the other picks a side in the same time. Each has seconds to judge the start.
pros: Both players have to choose fast.
The setup shows in a glance.
cons: Judging an even start is hard in seconds.
A rushed pick can be wrong.

pairs.tendency: One player sets the game on day one and the other picks a side the next morning. Play then goes on over days.
pros: The pick has time.
The setter waits for the answer.
cons: A long wait before the first move.
A forgotten pick can stall the game.

pairs.tendency: One player sets up slowly, with a breath at each step, and the other takes time before picking a side. The slowness gives the choice more care.
pros: The pick is made slowly.
The chooser has time to look.
cons: The start takes long.
The calm can feel too slow.

pairs.tendency: One player sets up a game that speeds up as it goes, and the other picks a side. A side that starts slowly may have more time to catch up.
pros: The setter thinks about the rush.
The chooser picks with speed in mind.
cons: Speed is hard to weigh in advance.
The final rush can undo the pick.

pairs.tendency: One player sets the start, including where extra turns sit, and the other picks a side. The setter knows a side near an extra-turn space can move twice.
pros: The setter thinks about who sits near each extra turn.
The chooser can pick the side near one.
cons: An extra turn is hard to price.
A double move can undo a careful setup.

pairs.tendency: One player sets up the first stage, and the other picks a side for it. What the setter does in stage one shapes the second, so they have two things to even out.
pros: The setter plans both stages at once.
The chooser looks ahead to stage two.
cons: Two stages are hard to balance.
Stage one choices last into stage two.

pairs.tendency: One player sets the starting state of the system, such as how much water each field has, and the other picks which group to play. The setter shapes the start so that no group is plainly ahead.
pros: The setter checks how much each group starts with.
The chooser picks a group.
cons: A system is hard to even out.
A small difference can grow over the rounds.

pairs.tendency: One player writes the needs of each group, and the other picks which group to play. A setter who makes the farmers' needs very heavy knows the chooser may take the council.
pros: The setter weighs one group's needs against another's.
The chooser takes a viewpoint.
cons: Groups are hard to match.
A group with few needs can look idle.

pairs.tendency: One player sets how much of the shared resource there is and who holds what, and the other picks a side. A setter who gives one side a bigger share knows the other will be chosen.
pros: The setter checks who holds what.
The chooser picks a share.
cons: Shares are hard to even out.
A shared resource can run out before the pick shows its effect.

pairs.tendency: One player sets the start, and the other picks a side. Since choices show their effects only a few rounds later, neither can tell early which side is ahead.
pros: The setter cannot rig an effect nobody can see yet.
The pick is made without knowing the effect.
cons: Effects are hard to see in advance.
The result may not show until late.

pairs.tendency: The pie rule is itself a rule the group can try. Players use it for one game and see what it changes about how the setter behaves.
pros: The group can try it on the next game.
Players can play once with it and once without.
cons: One game may not show much.
The effect on the setter can be hard to see.

pairs.tendency: After the game, players talk about the setup and the pick. The setter says what they were aiming for and the chooser says what they saw.
pros: The talk shows both viewpoints.
The setter learns how a start is read.
cons: Details of the setup are easy to forget.
Some players may not want to say.

pairs.tendency: One player sets up a game where moves cannot be undone, and the other picks a side. The pick stays with the player for ever.
pros: The pick is lasting.
The setter knows the setup will last.
cons: There is no second try.
A wrong pick shows up in every later game.

pairs.tendency: The pie rule says that whoever sets a start can expect it to be judged by the other. A game built on it makes the point that you cannot keep the whole advantage.
pros: The rule makes a point about sharing.
Players learn it by setting and choosing.
cons: Players may never notice the point.
The rule may tell players what they do not want to hear.

pairs.tendency: One player sets the terms of a bet over real money or a promise, and the other picks a side. The setter knows a lopsided deal will be used against them in real life.
pros: The setter has a real reason to be fair.
The chooser protects their own side.
cons: Real stakes make a mistake cost more.
A friendship can be tested by the pick.

pairs.tendency: One player decides how many points each value is worth, and the other picks which side to score for. Setting the number is setting what counts.
pros: The setter has to put a number on each value.
The chooser sees what the setter thinks matters.
cons: A number is hard to even out.
Players may chase points more than the thing they stand for.

pairs.tendency: One player sketches how the shared future will start, and the other picks a role in it. The setter has to imagine a way of living from every seat.
pros: The setter has to picture each seat.
The chooser tries a seat.
cons: A future is hard to even out.
A sketch can leave some seats thin.

pairs.tendency: Dice carry each piece along the path, and the throw that takes a piece to the far end also decides when it changes into a bigger piece.
pros: Every throw can bring the change closer.
The whole table watches the last few spaces.
cons: A run of low throws holds a piece back for turns.
The change can arrive by luck alone.

pairs.tendency: Cards are taken one at a time from a shared row, and one of them lets a piece at the far end change. A player may grab that card early just to keep it from the others.
pros: A pick can prepare a change for later.
Players read each other's picks for clues.
cons: A piece at the far end can wait for the right card.
Picking for the future can leave today's hand thin.

pairs.tendency: When a piece reaches the far end, the right to change it goes to the highest bidder. The winner pays whether or not the bigger piece turns out to help.
pros: The change has a clear price.
Players learn how much the others want it.
cons: Coins spent here are gone for other buys.
A player with many coins can buy every change.

pairs.tendency: A player keeps sending one piece forward, risking a loss at each step, because the far end turns it into a bigger piece. Stopping early keeps what is safe, and going on can lose the lot.
pros: The prize at the end pulls players forward.
Players watch each other's nerve.
cons: A piece can be lost one step from the change.
Turns run long while a player decides.

pairs.tendency: Pieces spread over the regions of a map, and one that reaches the far edge turns into a bigger piece able to hold a region alone.
pros: A change can turn a region around.
Players guard the road to the far edge.
cons: Each piece sent forward leaves its home region open.
A promoted piece draws attacks from everyone.

pairs.tendency: A worker takes a job space, and one that has walked to the far side of the board becomes a skilled worker. Job spaces near that side fill up first.
pros: Workers have a path to follow.
The plan for the long run shows early.
cons: A worker on the walk leaves its first job empty.
Blocked spaces can stall the walk.

pairs.tendency: Colours are matched to build a pattern, and a piece that reaches the far end turns into one that can sit on any colour. It can fill the one gap in a pattern.
pros: A promoted piece can finish a pattern.
Players plan the walk and the pattern together.
cons: The walk takes pieces away from the pattern.
One gap left open can wait a long time.

pairs.tendency: A player holds back the card that turns a piece into a bigger one until a piece stands at the far end. Playing it too early wastes it, so the hand waits.
pros: A held card gives a plan to follow.
A hand shows who is close to a change.
cons: A held card helps nothing in the meantime.
A stuck piece leaves the waiting card idle.

pairs.tendency: Each trick won moves a piece one step along a path, and the winner of the last step changes it into a bigger piece. Players count tricks to see who gets there.
pros: Each trick has a use beyond its cards.
Players can plan which tricks to chase.
cons: Losing a few tricks leaves a piece stuck.
The last trick carries the whole change.

pairs.tendency: Two players have pieces near the far end and talk over who lets whom through. A deal may trade a free path for a promise, and the change then alters the deal.
pros: Players can trade passage for favours.
A promotion can be agreed before it happens.
cons: Promises made near the far end can be broken.
Talks can hold up the whole table.

pairs.tendency: A set of matching cards is handed in to change a piece at the far end, so a player collects cards while the piece walks. Both jobs finish at about the same time.
pros: Two jobs run side by side.
A player always has something to work on.
cons: A missing card can stop a piece at the line.
Players can neglect the walk while collecting.

pairs.tendency: A piece walks across a map that players build tile by tile. Tiles laid in front of it can lengthen the road to the far end or shorten it.
pros: Players shape the path of the walker.
Each tile can help one piece and block another.
cons: The far end can move out of reach.
Players may lay tiles only to slow others.

pairs.tendency: One player calls a move and the next answers with a move of their own, like a chain. A reply that brings a piece to the far end ends with a call naming the bigger piece.
pros: The chain has a clear goal.
Replies can lead a piece toward the far end.
cons: A call can be answered by blocking the walker.
A long chain makes the change hard to follow.

pairs.tendency: Nobody talks, so when a piece reaches the far end its owner shows the change by placing the bigger piece. The others learn what it became only by looking.
pros: The change is seen, not announced.
Players pay close attention to each move.
cons: Others may miss a change at the edge of the board.
A teammate cannot be warned of a blocked path.

pairs.tendency: A player can change a rule on their turn, so the rule changed may be what a piece becomes at the far end, or where the far end is.
pros: The change itself can be changed.
A rule can open a path for a walker.
cons: A rule can close the far end to a whole table.
Arguments may run longer than the walk.

pairs.tendency: A character walks to a far place and comes back with a new rank or title. After the change the player speaks as that character in a new way.
pros: A promotion gives the story a turning point.
The player has a new voice to try.
cons: Players who prefer to stay as they were may feel pushed.
The walk can feel long without a scene on the way.

pairs.tendency: A piece is flicked or stacked towards the far end, and a steady hand decides when the change comes. A shaky hand can knock it back or off the table.
pros: Each shot is watched by everyone.
A steady player can promote without luck.
cons: One slip undoes a long walk.
Tired hands play differently late in the game.

pairs.tendency: The map is drawn while the piece walks. The far end is wherever the drawn edge stops, so players may draw it nearer or further.
pros: The map shapes the walk.
Players decide how far the far end is.
cons: A piece may walk a long way to an edge that keeps moving.
Drawing takes time from the moves.

pairs.tendency: Each runner on a team carries a flag one leg, and the runner who finishes the last leg turns into a lead runner for the next race. The change belongs to the whole team.
pros: The team gets one shared change.
Each leg matters to the next.
cons: One slow runner holds up everyone.
Only the last runner is noticed at the line.

pairs.tendency: Pieces form a shape nobody can capture, then one of them walks to the far end and changes. The shape keeps the rest safe while that one goes.
pros: The walker has cover at home.
Players can plan a safe base first.
cons: Building the shape slows the walk.
The other player can use the time to surround it.

pairs.tendency: The prizes are named cards, and a promoted piece may carry one across the line. The bigger piece can take prizes that a plain piece cannot.
pros: A promotion can change who wins a prize.
Players know in advance what is worth a walk.
cons: A named card may be held back until the change.
A promotion near the end can swing all the prizes.

pairs.tendency: Cards face up in the middle show what a promotion needs. Anyone can read them, so everyone sees which player is a step away.
pros: The needs of a change are open to all.
Players can plan against a visible target.
cons: A needed card can be taken by someone else.
The middle cards tell rivals what to block.

pairs.tendency: The pot sits in the middle, and the first piece to reach the far end and change takes it. If no piece gets there, the pot grows.
pros: A promotion can win a prize.
The pot grows if the walk fails.
cons: All players rush the same finish.
A growing pot makes the first change worth a lot.

pairs.tendency: A pit on the far side is the promotion pit. A last seed dropped there turns a small pit into a bigger one that holds more.
pros: The last seed has a clear aim.
A single sowing can change a pit.
cons: Players count seeds before every move.
A promoted pit can be emptied in one go.

pairs.tendency: An extra hand lies face down in the middle. A player who takes it may find the card that promotes a piece, and puts a card back to hide that fact.
pros: A taken hand can help a walker.
Others have to guess what was kept.
cons: The spare hand may hold nothing useful.
Taking it can slow the player's own plan.

pairs.tendency: A special square near the far end may be the promotion square itself, or a trap in front of it. Safe squares on the path let a piece rest before the change.
pros: Squares make a route worth planning.
A resting square gives hope to a slow piece.
cons: A trap close to the edge can send a piece back.
Players learn the squares and plan around them.

pairs.tendency: A promotion costs coins. A piece at the far end waits until its owner can pay, and the bigger piece then has a price of its own to use.
pros: The change has a cost to plan for.
Players save up for the right moment.
cons: A piece can wait at the line for a long time.
The bigger piece may cost more than it gives back.

pairs.tendency: Forces are shared out among several places, and a piece sent to the far end is one fewer at home. If it gets there, it changes into a bigger piece that counts for more.
pros: A walk can be a bet on a single piece.
The other player sees where forces went.
cons: Places left bare can be taken.
A piece caught on the way loses the whole bet.

pairs.tendency: Everyone moves until the signal, then freezes. Pieces that stand on the far end when it sounds are changed, and the rest stay as they are.
pros: The signal makes the end of the walk sudden.
Players rush to be at the line in time.
cons: A piece one step short misses the change.
The rush can leave pieces in the way of each other.

pairs.tendency: A player swaps cards to find the one that promotes a piece, putting back those that do not help. Each swap tells the others what was not wanted.
pros: A swap can fix a missing card.
Others can read the swaps for clues.
cons: Swapping can take many turns.
A swapped card might be exactly what another player needed.

pairs.tendency: Whoever picks up the discard pile gets the card on top, which may be the one that promotes a piece. Everyone watches what is thrown down near the far end.
pros: Discards give away what a player needs.
A pile can give a promotion card at once.
cons: A big pile is a heavy load to carry.
Throwing the wrong card can hand the change to a rival.

pairs.tendency: A piece that reaches the far end changes into a trump piece that beats the others in any clash. Before that it can be taken by any plain piece.
pros: The change turns a loser into a winner.
Players watch the walker closely.
cons: A trump piece draws every attack.
A plain piece may hold back until the others are promoted.

pairs.tendency: A player has a piece near the far end on one board while defending on the other. A promotion on one board changes what is possible on the other.
pros: One board can help the other.
A change can come as a surprise.
cons: Attention is split between boards.
Slow moves on one board hold up the other.
