pairs.tendency: A wild card stands in for the missing step of a promotion, so a piece changes even when its owner has no matching card. Holding one is a quiet advantage.
pros: A wild card can finish a change.
Players keep track of who might hold one.
cons: The wild card has to be saved for the right moment.
Others may stop walking until the wild cards are gone.

pairs.tendency: The edges are joined, so a piece that runs off one side comes back at the other. Players agree on one edge as the promotion edge, or the far end loses its meaning.
pros: A walker can come from behind.
The far end can be reached from two sides.
cons: The edge needs a clear rule.
A piece can run past the promotion edge without noticing.

pairs.tendency: One player knows which piece is about to be promoted. The others ask questions that can be answered yes or no, and each answer narrows the choice.
pros: Each answer rules out some pieces.
The secret can be found by asking.
cons: The player with the secret can be stuck with a long list.
Guessing wrong lets the piece reach the far end.

pairs.tendency: The far end is the finish line, so the change happens at the same place the game ends. It may come at the moment of winning or just before it.
pros: One line has two meanings.
A promoted piece can end the game with a single step.
cons: A promotion may mean nothing if the game is over.
Players race for the line with no other aim.

pairs.tendency: Points are counted at the end, and a promoted piece earns more. Players weigh a long walk to the far end against points close at hand.
pros: A promotion can be turned into a score.
Players choose between a long walk and quick points.
cons: A late change may come too late to score.
Players who stay home can still win.

pairs.tendency: Pieces are knocked out until one side stands. A piece that reaches the far end turns into a bigger piece that is harder to remove.
pros: A change can keep a side alive.
Players guard their walker.
cons: A walker sent forward leaves the others thin.
A promoted piece is chased by the whole table.

pairs.tendency: Everyone shares the same fate, so a piece that reaches the far end is promoted for the whole team. Players guard the walker as it goes.
pros: The team celebrates one change.
Players work out a route together.
cons: The walker is a single point of risk.
One lost piece can end the walk for all.

pairs.tendency: All players work towards one goal, and a promotion is a step on the way. One player walks a piece to the far end while the others clear the road.
pros: Players divide the jobs.
A change moves everyone closer.
cons: One slow walker holds up the goal.
Players may not agree on whose piece goes first.

pairs.tendency: A player with a secret goal may need a promoted piece, or may hide the fact by letting others walk theirs to the far end. The walk itself can give the secret away.
pros: A walk may hide a secret aim.
Players watch who goes towards the edge.
cons: Walking early can give away a goal.
A promoted piece may be useless to a secret aim.

pairs.tendency: The story reaches a point where a character is given a new role, and that is the promotion. The far end is a chapter, and the change is what the chapter gives.
pros: A change marks the end of a chapter.
The story gets a clear turning point.
cons: A story with no far end has no promotion.
Players may rush to the edge to get the next chapter.

pairs.tendency: Nobody wins, but pieces still walk to the far end and change. Afterwards the group looks at who changed and who did not.
pros: A promotion is something to look at.
Players walk for their own reasons.
cons: No reward waits at the end.
Some players may not walk at all.

pairs.tendency: One player aims to promote a single piece, and another aims to keep every piece back. Both play on the same board and see the same far end.
pros: Players can aim at different things.
A promotion can mean something different to each.
cons: Two aims may block each other.
The table may not agree on who did well.

pairs.tendency: The game goes on until one player loses, and a promoted piece helps its owner stay out of trouble a little longer. Others see the bigger piece and decide where to attack.
pros: A promotion buys time.
Players can pick on the side with the fewest pieces.
cons: A walk to the far end leaves home open.
A player in the lead can still be the last one caught.

pairs.tendency: A piece that reaches the far end changes, then walks back, and the game goes on. Each change opens another walk.
pros: The edge is a turning point and not an end.
Players always have a next walk.
cons: Nobody can say when it is over.
The game can wander without a high point.

pairs.tendency: Pieces walk to the far end and change, and the change brings no win. Players find that the reward they chased does nothing.
pros: The change shows what a reward is worth.
Players discuss why they walked.
cons: The walk can feel empty.
The game may annoy players who want a result.

pairs.tendency: A player alone walks a piece across a laid-out table. The change at the far end decides whether the layout clears.
pros: The change is the key move.
The player has one clear aim.
cons: A single stuck piece ends the game.
Nobody else is there to help.

pairs.tendency: Each short game is decided by who promotes first, and the winner of three out of five takes the set. The walk is the same each time but the result can change.
pros: Each game is short and clear.
A lost game can be tried again.
cons: A first promotion can feel like the whole set.
The last games can be played with nothing at stake.

pairs.tendency: A promoted piece carries a higher point value, and every point counts against its owner. A walk to the far end adds to the score.
pros: The change has a price in points.
Players hold their pieces back.
cons: A piece at the line has to choose to stop.
A rival can push a piece to the edge on purpose.

pairs.tendency: A piece needs the exact number of steps to reach the far end. If a throw is too big, it stays where it is and no change comes.
pros: Players count the steps to the edge.
A near-miss is easy to see.
cons: A piece can wait at the edge for many turns.
A change depends on one number.

pairs.tendency: The aim is to lose pieces, so players keep away from the far end. A piece pushed into promotion by someone else becomes a gift nobody wanted.
pros: A promotion is something to dodge.
Players push pieces on each other.
cons: A piece can be stuck with its change.
The walk is slow because nobody wants to reach the edge.

pairs.tendency: Each player walks a piece on their own board, and the changes happen side by side. Nobody can stop another player's change.
pros: Players keep their own pace.
A change on another board is easy to follow.
cons: There is little to do about a rival's walk.
The game can feel like a quiet race.

pairs.tendency: A piece near the far end is a target. Others attack it before it can change, and its owner guards it with other pieces.
pros: The edge is where the fight is.
Defenders and attackers both have a job.
cons: A piece can be lost just as it arrives.
A player under attack may hold back the whole walk.

pairs.tendency: Players place pieces on the path to the far end. Nobody attacks the walker, but it cannot get past.
pros: The board does the blocking.
Players think about the shape of the road.
cons: A walker can be stuck by a wall made for another reason.
The blocker often cannot be named.

pairs.tendency: Everyone is on one team against the game, and each player walks a piece to the far end. Each promotion gives the team a bigger piece to face the game's pieces.
pros: Each change helps the whole team.
Players share the job of guarding walkers.
cons: One walker caught early costs the team a piece.
Players can argue over whose piece goes first.

pairs.tendency: Players help each other get pieces to the far end, but each wants their own piece promoted first. Help given to a rival is also help given to the team.
pros: Players have a reason to help.
A promotion can be shared in part.
cons: Helping a rival can cost a place.
Trust can drop when one player jumps ahead.

pairs.tendency: Two teams race to promote a piece. Teammates clear the road for their walker and try to block the walker of the other team.
pros: Teammates have clear jobs.
A change is cheered by the whole team.
cons: The walker is a single target.
A team can lose all its effort to one block.

pairs.tendency: A traitor lets the walker reach the far end, and then the promoted piece works for the wrong side. The others see a bigger piece and wonder who gains.
pros: A change can be a trap.
Players watch each other's help closely.
cons: Players may stop helping anyone.
A true helper can be accused when a change goes wrong.

pairs.tendency: Each move arrives by letter, so a piece takes weeks to walk to the far end. The letter announcing the promotion is the one players wait for.
pros: A change is a news item.
Players have time to think.
cons: A move can be lost in the post.
The game can run out of patience before the edge.

pairs.tendency: A player who is not at the table has a piece that walks to the far end on set rules. Its promotion happens without them.
pros: The missing player still has a walker.
Their change can surprise the others.
cons: Nobody can answer the missing player's questions.
Players may argue over what the rules say.

pairs.tendency: The game master decides what a promotion gives. A character reaching a far place may get a new rank, a title, or a power that the game master names.
pros: The reward of a change can fit the story.
Players ask for something specific.
cons: The game master has to invent the change on the spot.
Players may disagree with a change that has been named.

pairs.tendency: Passers-by can join in. A piece that crosses the street or park to the far end becomes a bigger piece, and a crowd sees it.
pros: A change is seen by many.
New players can join and walk.
cons: A crowd can crowd the board.
Players may be pushed by onlookers.

pairs.tendency: The lone player tries to stop everyone else from reaching the far end, while the team shares the walk. A promotion helps the team most.
pros: The team has a clear aim.
The lone player can concentrate on a single walker.
cons: The lone player is outnumbered at the edge.
A team may stop working together once one piece is through.

pairs.tendency: A single player walks a piece across the table, and the promotion is the reward. The luck of the pack decides how soon it comes.
pros: The aim is clear.
A change can be replayed.
cons: A player has no one to share the change with.
The result depends on the shuffle.

pairs.tendency: Dice or cards decide when a piece reaches the far end, so promotion is a matter of luck. Players cannot plan it.
pros: Everyone has the same chance.
Games are short.
cons: A change cannot be earned.
Players only wait.

pairs.tendency: A low throw can be softened by a re-roll, and the re-roll is often saved for the last steps before the promotion. The change is then a matter of timing.
pros: Players keep a re-roll for the line.
A slow start does not end the walk.
cons: Using the re-roll early can leave the end open to luck.
Players hold back re-rolls for many turns.

pairs.tendency: Players plan routes to the far end, and a small amount of luck decides which routes open. A careful plan can still be spoiled by one throw.
pros: Plans matter most of the time.
A little luck keeps rivals within reach.
cons: One throw can undo a plan.
A skilled player may feel cheated by a late result.

pairs.tendency: There are no dice. The path to the far end is a puzzle, and the promotion is the result of many careful moves.
pros: The change is earned.
Each move can be studied.
cons: A mistake early is hard to repair.
New players can feel behind.

pairs.tendency: The throw is read as a sign, and a piece reaching the far end is taken as the sign coming true. The change can mean something to the player beyond the game.
pros: A promotion gives the throw a meaning.
Players read each throw with care.
cons: The meaning is for each player to decide.
A throw that is read wrongly may spoil the walk.

pairs.tendency: Players sense when the walker is about to cross and move together to the same step. The change comes when the table is in step.
pros: The change is shared.
Players learn to read each other.
cons: Without a shared sense, nothing happens.
The walk cannot be rushed.

pairs.tendency: A table says what a promotion means. Dice give the new title, and the story gets a new role.
pros: Each change adds to the tale.
Players are curious about the result.
cons: A throw can give a title that does not fit.
A story can lose its path.

pairs.tendency: Everything is open, so everyone can see which piece is a step from the far end. Others plan around it.
pros: Nothing about a change is hidden.
Players can line up a block.
cons: A walk that is seen is easy to stop.
A plan has no surprise.

pairs.tendency: Hands are secret, so a promotion card may be waiting in someone's hand. A piece at the far end tells the others something about that hand.
pros: A walk can hint at a hand.
A bluff can hide a card.
cons: Players guess wrongly about a card.
A piece can wait at the line for a card that never comes.

pairs.tendency: A piece's role is hidden until it reaches the far end, where it is shown as it changes. Before then, no one knows what it will be.
pros: The change is also a reveal.
Players watch which piece is walking.
cons: A role can be guessed from where a piece goes.
A revealed piece is at once a target.

pairs.tendency: Clues point to which piece will be promoted. Players work it out from who moves towards the far end and who holds back.
pros: A move gives a clue.
Players can predict a change.
cons: A false clue can lead the table astray.
A late guess comes after the change.

pairs.tendency: A player pretends a piece near the far end has a promotion card in hand. The others guess whether to block it.
pros: A bluff can stop attacks.
A real change can look like a bluff.
cons: A called bluff costs the walk.
Players may stop believing anyone.

pairs.tendency: A hidden rule says what happens at the far end. A piece that gets there learns it, and the others learn it by watching.
pros: The first walker learns for the rest.
A discovered rule is remembered.
cons: The first change may go wrong.
Newcomers walk blind.

pairs.tendency: One player knows which piece will change at the far end and gives only hints. The others guess from pictures or gestures.
pros: The hints can be clever.
The others can work together.
cons: A hint can be missed.
The knowing player can only watch a wrong guess.

pairs.tendency: The far end is hidden until a piece gets there. A promotion square might be found by luck, and the walk is also a search.
pros: A walk can find the edge.
A discovered square is a surprise.
cons: A piece may walk the wrong way for a long time.
Where the edge is can change from game to game.

pairs.tendency: One hand is open, so everyone can see the promotion card sitting in it. The player who plays the open hand can promote a piece on its behalf.
pros: An open card gives a clear target.
A player can plan around the open hand.
cons: The open hand's owner has no say.
Others block the card before it is used.

pairs.tendency: Points are secret, so promoting a piece lifts a score that others cannot see. Players guess who gained.
pros: A change lifts a score quietly.
Players watch the walks.
cons: Nobody can tell what a change was worth.
A bigger piece may mislead the guessing.

pairs.tendency: One player moves at a time, so a piece at the far end waits while others take their turns. The change comes on its owner's turn.
pros: Each change gets a turn to itself.
Players can see it coming.
cons: A piece may wait at the edge for a long time.
Others have time to attack it.

pairs.tendency: All players choose at once, so several pieces may reach the far end on the same turn and change together.
pros: Changes can land side by side.
No one waits for a turn.
cons: Two players can arrive at the same spot.
Plans may collide.

pairs.tendency: Anyone may move at any time, so a piece reaching the far end can be promoted by the quickest hand.
pros: The quick player gets the change.
Play is lively.
cons: A slow player may never reach the edge.
Players can grab pieces mid-walk.

pairs.tendency: A clock runs on each turn. A player with a piece near the far end has a few seconds to decide on the change.
pros: The change feels urgent.
Players do not dwell.
cons: A rushed move can lose the piece.
A slow thinker may lose the chance.

pairs.tendency: One move a day means a piece takes weeks to reach the far end. The promotion is the day that players remember.
pros: A change is an event.
Waiting builds hope.
cons: A walk can lose its thread.
Some players drop out before the edge.

pairs.tendency: Each move comes after a pause, so the last steps to the far end are slow. The change feels heavy when it arrives.
pros: A walk is noticed step by step.
A change is given weight.
cons: Waiting can make players restless.
Play can lose its pull.

pairs.tendency: The game speeds up, and pieces reach the far end faster each round. Promotions come in a rush near the end.
pros: The first walks are slow and the last are quick.
Changes pile up late.
cons: Early walks can seem pointless.
The last rounds can pass too quickly to follow.

pairs.tendency: A throw or a hit can give another go, so a piece can run to the far end in one turn. The promotion comes in the same turn.
pros: A chain of moves can end in a change.
Luck can feel like skill.
cons: One player can take many turns at once.
The others watch and wait.

pairs.tendency: In the first stage players walk pieces to the far end, and in the second stage they play with the promoted pieces. The first stage sets up the second.
pros: Each stage has its own aim.
A change sets the next rules.
cons: Players who fall behind in stage one stay behind.
The second stage can feel decided before it starts.

pairs.tendency: The far end stands for something real, such as a farmer moving from field to market, and the change shows what the move does to them.
pros: A change shows a real effect.
Players can talk about what it means.
cons: A simple change may leave things out.
Players may take the model too literally.

pairs.tendency: Each role has its own idea of what the far end is. A shopkeeper's promotion looks different from a farmer's.
pros: The same edge means different things.
Players learn each other's views.
cons: Roles may not agree on the rules.
A change that helps one role can hurt another.

pairs.tendency: A promoted piece can draw more from the shared stock. When several pieces change at once, the stock drains faster.
pros: A change has a cost to all.
Players watch the stock.
cons: Everyone suffers when changes bunch up.
A promoted piece makes others wait.

pairs.tendency: A promotion shows its effect only a few rounds later. Players see what the bigger piece did after the fact.
pros: A change is judged after it happens.
Players learn to wait.
cons: The link between change and effect is hard to see.
A careless walk may not be noticed until late.

pairs.tendency: Players agree a new rule about promotion, such as where the far end is, and play on to see what it changes.
pros: A rule can be tested.
Players see the effect straight away.
cons: A rule that fails costs a whole game.
The group may not agree on what changed.

pairs.tendency: After the game, players talk about promotions. Why did some pieces walk to the far end while others stayed back?
pros: A change gives something to talk about.
Players explain their choices.
cons: Quiet players may say little.
The talk can wander from the game.

pairs.tendency: A promotion cannot be undone. The bigger piece stays bigger in later games too.
pros: A change leaves a mark.
Players think before they walk.
cons: A piece cannot go back to what it was.
A hasty change can spoil many games.

pairs.tendency: A game that rewards only the walk to the far end makes a point about reaching the top. The promotion is the argument.
pros: A promotion says what the game values.
Players can disagree with it.
cons: The point may be missed.
The game may feel like a lecture.

pairs.tendency: A promotion carries real meaning, such as a real rank or a promise. The walk is no longer only a game.
pros: A change matters beyond the table.
Players think over each step.
cons: A friend can be hurt by a loss.
Players may refuse to walk.

pairs.tendency: A promotion turns into points. Players chase the change and forget what it was meant to stand for.
pros: A change is easy to count.
The chase shows what players value.
cons: The meaning can be lost.
Players may chase the number alone.

pairs.tendency: Players practise a village where workers rise to new jobs. The far end shows how a promotion would feel, before anyone tries it for real.
pros: A change can be tried safely.
Players see how it might feel.
cons: A pretend promotion may not match the real one.
Players may play it too lightly.

pairs.tendency: Each runner on a team throws a dice and moves along the path, then hands the flag to the next runner. The throw sets how far each leg goes.
pros: Every leg has a throw of its own.
Teams swap runners often.
cons: A low throw can slow a whole team.
Teams wait for each other's throws.

pairs.tendency: Team members take cards from a shared row, and each leg of the race uses the card its runner picked. A runner may take a card that helps the next runner.
pros: A pick can help a teammate.
Players read what the other team takes.
cons: The last picker gets what is left.
Taking cards slows the race.

pairs.tendency: Teams bid coins for the right to run the next leg, and the highest bid picks the runner. The bid is lost whether or not the leg is won.
pros: Teams choose which leg to buy.
Coins turn into running time.
cons: A team that bids too early may have nothing left for the last leg.
A team with many coins can buy every leg.

pairs.tendency: A runner can keep going past the handover point to gain a few more steps. Going too far loses the lead, and the next runner starts late.
pros: A runner can gain steps for the team.
Teammates watch the risk.
cons: A greedy leg can cost the whole race.
A team may argue over when to stop.

pairs.tendency: Teams race to hand a flag across a map and to hold regions on the way. A runner who stops to claim a region slows the handover.
pros: Runners can claim ground as they pass.
A team can control the route.
cons: A claimed region can cost running time.
A handover can be cut off.

pairs.tendency: Each runner is also a worker who takes a job space before running. A job can speed up the next leg, and the first team to take it keeps it.
pros: A job can help the leg.
Teams plan their order.
cons: A taken job is gone for others.
A team can lose a leg to a missing job.

pairs.tendency: Each runner brings back a coloured tile and the team builds a pattern from them. The race is won when the pattern is done.
pros: Tiles show each runner's work.
Teams plan their colours together.
cons: A wrong colour can undo a leg.
Runners wait while others fit the pieces.

pairs.tendency: Each runner plays one card from a shared team hand for the leg, and the cards left have to last for the other legs. The team decides the order.
pros: The team shares the hand.
Order is a team decision.
cons: A card used early is gone.
Players can disagree on which card to play.

pairs.tendency: Each leg is a trick, and the team that wins the trick runs the next stretch of the track. Winning many tricks takes a team far ahead.
pros: Tricks set the pace.
A team can plan which runner leads.
cons: A lost trick can leave a team behind.
The team needs many cards to run the race.

pairs.tendency: Teams make deals on the track, such as a swap of runners or a shared stretch, so the flag can pass. Deals can speed up one team and slow another.
pros: Teams can trade help.
A deal can change the race.
cons: A broken deal costs a team.
Talks hold up the race.

pairs.tendency: Each runner brings back one item and the team collects a set. The first team with a full set crosses the line.
pros: Each leg adds a piece.
Teams plan who fetches what.
cons: A duplicate item is wasted.
One missing item holds up the team.

pairs.tendency: Each runner lays a tile before handing over, so the track is built as the race goes on. A tile can make the next leg shorter or longer.
pros: The track grows leg by leg.
A runner can help the next one.
cons: A carelessly placed tile slows a team.
Teams may lay tiles only to hinder.

pairs.tendency: A runner calls out a line and the next runner answers before taking the flag. The relay is a chain of calls and answers from start to end.
pros: The handover is also a reply.
Teams get a shared rhythm.
cons: A missed reply holds the flag.
A long chain tires the voices.

pairs.tendency: Nobody talks, so runners hand over by a look or a nod. The team that reads its runners closely passes the flag in one smooth move.
pros: Teammates learn each other's signs.
The handover is quick when it works.
cons: A missed sign drops the flag.
A new runner has no way to ask.

pairs.tendency: A runner may change a rule at the handover, such as the length of the next leg. The next runner then races under a new rule.
pros: A rule can help the next runner.
Teams watch the handover closely.
cons: A rule can slow the other team.
Arguments hold up the race.

pairs.tendency: Each runner plays a character carrying a message through a story, and hands it on in character. The flag becomes a letter, a torch or a secret.
pros: Each leg has its own scene.
Players try different characters.
cons: A scene can take longer than the run.
A shy player may find the handover hard.

pairs.tendency: The flag is a ball or a stack that has to be carried without dropping. Each runner balances it for one leg and hands it over steadily.
pros: A steady hand wins a leg.
Everyone watches each handover.
cons: A drop sends the team back.
A tired runner shakes the whole team.

pairs.tendency: Each runner draws a stretch of the track before running it, and the next runner continues from where the line stops. The map is made by the team.
pros: The map belongs to the team.
Each runner leaves a mark.
cons: A drawn route can be too long.
A runner can draw a path for the other team to follow.

pairs.tendency: Runners carry stones across the board and make a shape nobody can capture. Each leg adds a stone, so the shape grows leg by leg.
pros: A shape is built by the team.
Each runner has a task.
cons: A missed leg leaves a gap.
The other player may cut in before the shape is closed.

pairs.tendency: Each leg is run to win a card from the named prizes. The team that holds the most valued cards at the end wins the race.
pros: Legs have a clear prize.
Teams aim at particular cards.
cons: A prize can be won by a single leg.
The last runner may carry the whole result.

pairs.tendency: Cards face up in the middle can be used by any runner on any team. A runner takes one on the way, and it is gone for the next team.
pros: Cards give runners a choice.
A runner can help the next one by leaving a card.
cons: A taken card is gone for the other team.
Runners may pause to read the middle cards.

pairs.tendency: A pot sits at the finish and goes to the first team across the line. If no team finishes, it grows for the next race.
pros: A prize waits for the winner.
Teams push hard in the last leg.
cons: A lost race grows the stakes.
All teams race for one thing.

pairs.tendency: Each runner sows seeds for one leg, dropping them one by one into pits, and hands the pit to the next runner. The last seed of each leg decides who carries on.
pros: A leg is a single sowing.
Teams count seeds together.
cons: A wrong count hands the pit to the other team.
A leg can end early.

pairs.tendency: An extra hand lies in the middle, and a runner who takes it can swap cards before the leg starts. The team that takes it first runs with the cards it likes.
pros: A runner can fix a thin hand.
The spare hand is a prize.
cons: Taking it uses up time.
Others can read what was kept.

pairs.tendency: Special squares on the track give a runner a skip or a delay. A team plans each leg to land on the skips and away from the delays.
pros: Squares give legs a route to plan.
A team can use a skip to make up time.
cons: A delay square can cost a leg.
Runners may take the long way to avoid a square.

pairs.tendency: Each runner pays to use a card or an item on the leg. The team shares a purse, so one leg's spending leaves less for the next.
pros: The team has a shared budget.
Runners think before they buy.
cons: An early spend leaves the last leg bare.
Teammates may disagree about the purse.

pairs.tendency: A team has a fixed number of runners to place across several tracks. Putting more on one track leaves another short.
pros: Teams decide where to put their runners.
Each track has a different cost.
cons: A track left short is easy to lose.
The other team sees where the team put its strength.

pairs.tendency: Runners move until the signal, then freeze where they are. The team whose runner is closest to the handover when the signal comes passes the flag first.
pros: The signal gives a clear end to a leg.
Runners watch for it.
cons: A runner can freeze too early.
A signal heard late can lose the race.

pairs.tendency: A runner may swap cards with the team before a leg, and each swap changes what the next runner can do. The swap pile is shared by the whole team.
pros: Teams plan their swaps.
A swap can hand a teammate a useful card.
cons: A card swapped away may be wanted later.
Swapping takes time off the clock.

pairs.tendency: Runners throw cards onto one pile, and a runner who reaches the handover may pick the whole pile up. The team then carries every card in it to the next leg.
pros: A pile can hand a team many cards at once.
Teams watch what the other side throws.
cons: A big pile is slow to carry.
The pile can slow a leg that was running fast.

pairs.tendency: One suit is named for the race, and a runner who plays a card of that suit beats every other card on the leg. A low card of that suit still outruns a high card of another.
pros: A named suit gives teams a plan.
Runners save those cards for the legs that matter.
cons: Runners without the suit have little to play.
Teams can end up with all their cards in one suit.

pairs.tendency: Each team plays the relay on one board while running a second game on another. A runner is one side on the first board and the other side on the second.
pros: A handover on one board can help the other.
Teams have two things to watch.
cons: Attention is split between boards.
A slow leg on one board holds up both.

pairs.tendency: A wild card lets a runner stand in for any teammate for one leg. A team that holds one can cover for a runner who is not ready.
pros: A wild card fills a gap in the team.
Teams keep it for the hardest leg.
cons: Other teams guess who holds it.
A wild card used early leaves nothing for the last leg.

pairs.tendency: The track is a ring, so a runner who passes the edge comes back at the start. A long relay can circle the board more than once before the flag crosses the line.
pros: A runner can cut across the join.
A runner can come at the line from behind.
cons: Players have to agree where a lap ends.
A runner can lose count of laps.

pairs.tendency: The last runner knows a secret and the team asks yes or no questions to find it before the other team. Each question is asked by a different runner, one per leg.
pros: Each leg adds one answer.
The list of possible answers shrinks.
cons: A wasted question cannot be taken back.
A team may reach the end of the track with questions left.

pairs.tendency: The first team to hand the flag over the last line wins. Every leg is part of one race to the same line.
pros: The aim is clear from the start.
Every runner is watched.
cons: A single slow leg can decide the result.
Teams behind may have no way back.

pairs.tendency: Each leg scores points for its team, and the team with the highest total at the end wins, whoever crosses first. A team may run fast or run carefully.
pros: Teams choose between speed and score.
A slow team can still win.
cons: A team can lose points for hurrying.
Counting points slows the handover.

pairs.tendency: Runners who are caught drop out, and the last team with a runner still standing wins. The flag has to be carried by whoever is left.
pros: A team can run on with fewer runners.
Players guard the runner who holds the flag.
cons: A lost runner means a longer leg for someone else.
Teams with few runners left have nothing to spare.

pairs.tendency: All teams run the same track against the game, and the flag has to get through every leg. The game sends obstacles and the runners clear them together.
pros: Runners help each other along the track.
Every handover matters to the whole group.
cons: One stumble can end the run for all.
Runners may argue over who goes where.

pairs.tendency: All teams carry one flag to one place, each taking a few legs. The goal belongs to everyone and nobody races another team.
pros: Teams share the load.
Everyone cheers the last leg.
cons: A slow team holds up the others.
There is no clear winner to point to.

pairs.tendency: Each runner has a secret goal, and the leg they run may help the team or help the goal. Other runners guess from how a leg is run.
pros: A leg can serve two aims.
Teammates read each other closely.
cons: A secret aim can pull a leg off course.
Suspicion can slow a handover.

pairs.tendency: Each runner takes a part of the story, and the flag is passed with the next line. The race ends when the story reaches its last scene.
pros: The story grows leg by leg.
Teams share a plot.
cons: A runner can run the story off course.
The ending depends on the last runner.

pairs.tendency: Nobody wins. The team runs the legs, hands over the flag, and stops, and the group looks at how the run went.
pros: Players run for the run's sake.
The handovers can be watched closely.
cons: There is no line to run towards.
Some players may stop caring about speed.

pairs.tendency: One runner aims to be the fastest and another aims to hand over without a drop. Both run the same leg for different reasons.
pros: Runners choose their own aims.
A team can value different things.
cons: Two aims can clash on one leg.
The team may not agree on how it did.

pairs.tendency: The race goes on until one team is last, and every other team is safe. The team that falls behind is the one that carries the loss.
pros: Only the last team loses.
Teams in front can ease off.
cons: A team behind may stop trying.
A slow runner is easy to point at.

pairs.tendency: The flag is never finally handed in. Teams pass it round the track again and again, and the aim is to keep the relay running.
pros: Runners keep a rhythm.
New runners can join at any handover.
cons: There is no last lap.
The game can lose its pull as the laps add up.

pairs.tendency: Teams run legs and hand over the flag, and no line ends the race. Players see that the running counts for nothing in the end.
pros: The run shows what a race is for.
Players ask each other why they ran.
cons: Running with no line can feel hollow.
Players who want a result may stop.

pairs.tendency: One player runs every leg alone against a laid-out table, passing the flag from one hand to the other. The player wins by clearing the table.
pros: One player holds every leg.
The aim is clear.
cons: One leg that cannot be run ends the game.
The player cannot hand the work to anyone.

pairs.tendency: A team that wins the relay takes one point, and the first team to win three out of five games takes the set. Teams can change their running order between games.
pros: Teams can learn from each game.
A lost relay can be answered.
cons: A team that wins the first two can ease off.
Once the set is won, the remaining relays mean nothing.

pairs.tendency: Each leg a runner is caught on adds a point, and the team with the fewest points wins, even if it crosses last. A slow, careful team can win.
pros: Teams can take their time.
Last across the line can still come first.
cons: Rushing a leg costs points.
Keeping the tally holds up each leg.

pairs.tendency: The last runner has to land on the exact number to end the race. A throw that goes past it means waiting for the next turn.
pros: The end of the race needs care.
Teams count steps together.
cons: A team ahead can be held at the line.
A team behind can catch up while it waits.

pairs.tendency: The team that finishes last wins. Runners aim to hand the flag over as slowly as the rules allow without stopping.
pros: Each leg is a careful crawl.
Teams watch each other's pace.
cons: Runners cannot tell who is slowing on purpose.
Races can last a very long time.

pairs.tendency: Each team runs its own track at the same time, and no team can touch another. Players watch the other tracks without getting in the way.
pros: Teams run at their own pace.
A rival's handover is easy to see.
cons: No team can slow a rival down.
The game can feel like separate races.

pairs.tendency: Runners can block, tag or knock the flag from the other team. A handover is the moment when a team is open to attack.
pros: Teams guard their handovers.
Attacks give the race a turn.
cons: A lost flag costs a whole leg.
The race can turn into a fight.

pairs.tendency: Teams do not touch each other, but a runner can place a barrier on the track that the other team has to go round. Each handover leaves something behind on the board.
pros: The board carries the effects.
Teams think about the route ahead.
cons: A barrier may slow the team that placed it.
The source of a block is hard to see.

pairs.tendency: All runners are on one team against the game, and each handover is a step towards beating it. The game takes its own legs after every one of theirs.
pros: Runners share the load.
Every handover helps all.
cons: A single mistake costs everyone.
The game's legs can come too fast to follow.

pairs.tendency: Runners pass the flag along for the team but each has a private reason to cross the line first. Help is given and held back in turn.
pros: Players have a reason to hand over.
A team can choose to share the lead.
cons: A runner may drag a leg for private gain.
Handovers can become suspect.

pairs.tendency: Two teams run the same track and swap the flag leg by leg. Teammates help their own runner and get in the way of the other team.
pros: Every teammate knows their part.
A win belongs to the whole team.
cons: A slow leg is easy to see.
One block in the right spot can cost a team the race.

pairs.tendency: One runner on the team secretly runs for the other side. The flag passes through their hands each time, and the others watch for a slip.
pros: A handover is a moment to watch.
Runners can compare their legs.
cons: An honest runner with a slow leg draws suspicion.
Teams may stop trusting any handover.

pairs.tendency: Each runner is in a different place, and the flag travels by letter from one to the next. A single relay can last weeks, and a late letter holds up the whole team.
pros: Each handover is awaited.
Runners can plan between letters.
cons: A letter can be lost.
The race can stop for a long wait.

pairs.tendency: One runner is not at the table. Their leg is run for them by a rule, or by a ghost that can only give hints.
pros: The team has a runner who is not there.
The missing leg can surprise the others.
cons: Nobody can ask the missing runner a question.
The team may argue over the rule for that leg.

pairs.tendency: The game master runs the track, describes each place a runner reaches, and decides who meets whom on the way. The team passes the flag from one character to the next.
pros: The track has a voice.
Each leg can have its own event.
cons: The game master's pace sets the pace of the race.
Players wait for the next description.

pairs.tendency: The relay is run in a street or park, and anyone passing can take a leg. The flag may be handed to a stranger who joins in.
pros: New runners can join at any handover.
The route can be any street.
cons: Runners may not know the rules.
A crowd can get in the way.

pairs.tendency: One runner takes every leg alone while a team of others shares the track against them. The lone runner is paid more if they win.
pros: The team shares the load.
The lone runner has one clear aim.
cons: The lone runner runs every leg.
The team can lose a leg if one member slips.

pairs.tendency: A single player runs each leg in turn with the pack of cards, passing a flag from one hand to the other. Luck and choices decide how it goes.
pros: The player sets the pace.
The run can be repeated.
cons: There is no one to hand the flag to.
The result can be compared only afterwards.

pairs.tendency: Dice or cards decide how far each leg goes, and teams do little but hand over the flag. The race is a wait for the throws.
pros: No team starts ahead.
The race is over fast.
cons: Teams can do little to change it.
Runners stand about until the throw.

pairs.tendency: A low throw on one leg can be softened by a re-roll, and a team may share the re-rolls among its runners. The team decides which leg gets one.
pros: Teams plan their re-rolls.
A low throw does not end the race.
cons: A re-roll spent on the first leg is missing on the last.
Runners may argue over who gets the re-roll.

pairs.tendency: Teams plan who runs which leg, and a small amount of luck changes how far each one goes. A careful plan can still be upset by one throw.
pros: The running order is in the team's hands.
Luck keeps a weaker team in the race.
cons: One low throw can spoil the order.
A careful team may feel robbed by the dice.

pairs.tendency: There are no dice. The team that plans its running order and its handovers with the most care wins.
pros: Every handover is earned.
Teams can study the track.
cons: A slip on an early leg stays with the team.
A team new to the track starts at a loss.

pairs.tendency: The throw for each leg is read as a message, and the team passes the flag on with that meaning in mind. A run is a reading of many signs.
pros: A throw gives a leg a meaning.
Each runner looks for a message in the throw.
cons: Each team may read a sign in its own way.
The meaning can drift from the race.

pairs.tendency: Runners hand over when they sense the next runner is ready, with no signal. A team in step passes the flag smoothly, and a team out of step drops it.
pros: Runners get to know each other's timing.
The handover is smooth when it works.
cons: The sense can fail on a tired day.
A new runner has no way to learn the rhythm fast.

pairs.tendency: Each leg is looked up on a table that says what meets the runner on the road. The dice write a part of the story as the flag moves from hand to hand.
pros: Each leg has its own event.
Teams tell a shared tale.
cons: A throw can send a leg off the plot.
A team may lose track of the story.

pairs.tendency: Every card, runner and handover is in plain view. Teams plan their legs knowing what the other side holds.
pros: The whole race is on the table.
Teams plan with all the facts.
cons: A plan is easy to read.
Nothing can catch a team off guard.

pairs.tendency: Each runner holds cards the other team cannot see, and plays one on a leg. A handover may carry a hint about what is left in the hand.
pros: A card can be a surprise.
Teams bluff about what they hold.
cons: A hidden card can be forgotten.
Teammates cannot share a hand openly.

pairs.tendency: Some runners have a secret role, and the flag passes through their hands without anyone knowing who is who. Roles come out as the legs are run.
pros: A role may be shown on a leg.
Players read each other's runs.
cons: A secret role can be guessed from a leg.
Once shown, a runner draws the other team's attention.

pairs.tendency: Each leg gives a clue, and the team works out a hidden fact from the legs run so far. The first team to name it hands over the winning flag.
pros: Each leg adds a clue.
Teams share what they know.
cons: One wrong clue can send a team after the wrong answer.
A team can run the track without finding the answer.

pairs.tendency: A runner says the next leg is easy or hard, true or not, and the other team guesses. A handover can be a lie about what comes next.
pros: A claim can steer a team.
Runners read each other's faces.
cons: A runner caught lying loses the leg.
Once caught out, claims stop being believed.

pairs.tendency: One runner knows a secret rule about the handover. The other runners learn it only by breaking it and being told no.
pros: Each failed handover teaches something.
A team learns the rule together.
cons: The first legs may be lost.
New teams are always behind.

pairs.tendency: The last runner knows where the flag has to go but cannot say. Each runner before hands over a picture, and the next has to guess.
pros: Each handover carries a hint.
Teams learn to read pictures.
cons: A picture can be read the wrong way.
The runner who knows has to stay silent through a wrong guess.

pairs.tendency: The track is hidden until a runner reaches each leg. The team does not know what the next leg looks like until the flag arrives.
pros: Each leg is a discovery.
Teams have to learn the track together.
cons: A runner may meet a leg that is longer than expected.
A team cannot plan ahead.

pairs.tendency: One hand lies open on the table for the whole team to see, and a runner may play from it as well as from their own. The open cards are known to both teams.
pros: An open hand is a shared tool.
Teams can plan around the open cards.
cons: The other team can plan against them too.
A card from the open hand cannot be kept secret.

pairs.tendency: Teams do not know each other's scores, so a handover does not show who is ahead. Every leg could be gaining or losing.
pros: A runner cannot tell who leads.
Teams guess from the pace.
cons: A team may run too fast or too slowly.
Nobody knows when to stop.

pairs.tendency: One team runs at a time while the other watches. Each team takes its turn leg by leg until the flag crosses the line.
pros: Each handover gets full attention.
Teams know which leg comes next.
cons: Waiting turns can be long.
The watching team has time to plan.

pairs.tendency: All teams choose their runner at once and reveal together, and all the legs are run side by side. The handovers happen at the same time.
pros: No team waits.
Choices stay secret until the reveal.
cons: Two teams can pick the same route.
A plan can be spoiled by a reveal.

pairs.tendency: There are no turns, so any runner may take the flag at any moment. The quickest hand gets there first.
pros: Teams stay alert.
The race moves quickly.
cons: A slow runner can be left out.
Players can grab the flag at the wrong time.

pairs.tendency: Each leg has a clock, such as a sand timer or a count to twenty, and the flag has to be handed over before it runs out. A late handover costs the team a leg.
pros: The clock gives each leg a clear end.
Runners learn to hurry.
cons: A rushed handover can drop the flag.
A runner who stops to think loses the leg.

pairs.tendency: The relay runs over days or weeks, with one leg each morning. The flag moves slowly and the waiting is part of the game.
pros: The race lasts a long time.
Runners can think between legs.
cons: A leg may be forgotten.
Teams can lose players over the weeks.

pairs.tendency: Each runner pauses and breathes before taking the flag, and the pause is part of the leg. The race moves slowly by rule.
pros: Each handover is noticed.
The race has a calm pace.
cons: Teams who like speed may be restless.
A race can seem to stand still.

pairs.tendency: The legs get shorter and the clock gets faster as the race goes on. The last runners hand over in a rush.
pros: The race builds towards its end.
The final legs are close.
cons: Early legs can seem slow.
The last handovers blur together.

pairs.tendency: A high throw or a hit gives a runner another go straight away. A lucky runner may take two or three legs in a row.
pros: A chain of moves can swing a race.
A runner can catch up in one go.
cons: The other team stands idle meanwhile.
Luck can feel bigger than the plan.

pairs.tendency: The first stage is a draft of the cards, and the second stage is the relay run with those cards. What the team picked in the first stage sets up the legs.
pros: The draft and the run ask for different things.
Picks in stage one change stage two.
cons: A slow start is hard to fix.
A weak draft can settle the relay before the first leg.

pairs.tendency: The relay stands for a real system, such as water carried from a well to a field, hand to hand. Each leg shows what is lost or gained along the way.
pros: A handover shows a real step.
Players can talk about where the system leaks.
cons: A line of hands leaves out much of a real water system.
Players may treat the relay as the real thing.

pairs.tendency: Each runner plays a group in the chain, such as a farmer, a trader and a shopkeeper, and passes the flag along as that group. Each leg is seen from a different place.
pros: Runners see different views.
A chain shows who depends on whom.
cons: Roles may not agree on the pace.
One role can hold up all the others.

pairs.tendency: All teams draw their running energy from one stock, so a team that runs hard leaves less for the others. The stock is used up if every team hurries.
pros: Everyone sees the stock go down.
Teams can choose to run gently.
cons: A rush by one team costs all.
Teams may argue over who took too much.

pairs.tendency: A leg run now shows its effect a few legs later, such as a rest that pays off or a push that tires the next runner. Teams see the result after the fact.
pros: Teams learn what each leg costs.
A plan has to look ahead.
cons: Teams struggle to tell which leg caused what.
A rushed leg shows its cost after the race has moved on.

pairs.tendency: Teams agree a new rule for the handover, such as a longer leg or a double flag, and run the race to see what it changes.
pros: A new handover rule takes one race to try.
The difference shows in the next race.
cons: A rule that does not work wastes a race.
Teams may argue over what the rule did.

pairs.tendency: After the race, the teams sit down and talk about the legs. What happened at each handover, and what would they change?
pros: The handovers give something to talk about.
Runners say why they handed over when they did.
cons: Some runners may keep quiet.
The talk can drift off the race.

pairs.tendency: Each handover leaves a mark on the board that cannot be removed, such as a sticker on the track. The next race starts from the marks of the last.
pros: The track keeps a record.
Each handover gets more thought.
cons: A hasty handover marks every later race.
A mistake cannot be cleaned up.

pairs.tendency: A relay that only rewards the team that never drops the flag makes a point about carrying a job together. The rules say what the game thinks matters.
pros: The race makes a point.
Players can argue with the point.
cons: Players may not notice it.
The race may feel like being taught.

pairs.tendency: The relay carries real stakes, such as who cleans up or a promise kept. A team that loses pays the price after the game.
pros: The race matters beyond the table.
Teams think about every leg.
cons: A loss can sour a friendship.
Some players may sit the race out.

pairs.tendency: Each leg earns points for something that matters, such as care or kindness, and teams start running for the points alone. The number takes the place of what it measured.
pros: The score is easy to read.
Running for points shows what the team values.
cons: Teams run for the number only.
What the points stood for can fade.

pairs.tendency: Players practise a village where work is passed hand to hand, one leg at a time. They feel how it would be to share a load before anyone tries it for real.
pros: Nothing real is at risk.
Players feel the load being shared.
cons: A village on a table is not a real village.
Some players may treat it as a joke.

pairs.tendency: A throw of the dice moves a piece along the path, and a few pieces can sit together in a shape that nothing can capture. A throw that pulls one piece out of the shape leaves the rest open for a turn.
pros: The shape gives players a goal between throws.
Pieces inside the shape can wait for the count they need.
cons: A throw can break up a shape you spent turns on.
Much of the game is waiting for the right number.

pairs.tendency: Each player picks from a shared row of cards, and some cards add a stone to a shape that cannot be captured. Taking the card a rival needs for their shape slows that rival down.
pros: Every pick can block a rival's shape.
Players read plans from what gets taken.
cons: Slow with many players.
The card you need may be gone before your turn.

pairs.tendency: Players bid for the right to place the next stone, and the spot that completes a shape is the one everyone bids for. Rivals see which spot you want and can raise the price.
pros: Bids show which spots matter.
Money turns into a place on the board.
cons: A big bid leaves little money for later turns.
Rivals can raise a bid just to cost you.

pairs.tendency: Players keep adding stones to a shape for more points, and an unfinished shape can still be lost. Stopping early leaves a small shape that cannot be captured.
pros: There is a clear moment to choose to stop.
A finished shape marks a place to stop.
cons: One greedy turn can lose a lot.
Players who stop early score little.

pairs.tendency: Groups of stones spread across the map, and a group that makes the shape holds its ground against any attack. Rivals go for the groups that are still open.
pros: A held area stays held.
Attackers know which groups to aim at.
cons: Making a shape uses turns that could grab more ground.
A held corner can leave the rest of the map open.

pairs.tendency: Workers take jobs on the board, and a few jobs add stones to a shape. If a rival takes the job spot you wanted, the shape stays unfinished that turn.
pros: Job spots become worth racing for.
The shape is a long goal for the workers.
cons: One blocked spot can stall a plan.
The first player gets the first pick of spots.

pairs.tendency: A pattern that closes up becomes a shape with no gap for a rival to cut into. Until it closes, one stone in the gap can ruin it.
pros: A finished pattern stays finished.
Players can see who is close to closing.
cons: An open gap draws attack.
Waiting for one missing tile can take many turns.

pairs.tendency: Cards in hand decide when and where stones go down. Holding back the card that completes a shape keeps rivals guessing, but waiting gives them time to attack the open shape.
pros: Timing choices on every card.
The finishing card can be saved for later.
cons: Holding cards means doing less now.
A hand of the wrong cards stalls the shape.

pairs.tendency: Each trick won adds a stone to a shape, and a shape that cannot be captured keeps what the trick gave. A lost trick can leave a gap open.
pros: Every win leaves something that lasts.
Players count tricks to see who builds fastest.
cons: A lost trick can leave a shape open.
The deal decides who has the cards to begin.

pairs.tendency: Players talk over who attacks whom, and the talk often turns on a shape one player is close to finishing. A deal to leave a shape alone lasts only until somebody breaks it.
pros: Promises about which shapes to leave alone.
Players can team up against the builder.
cons: A broken promise ends the talking.
Long talks slow the turns.

pairs.tendency: Sets of matching things can be locked into a shape that cannot be taken, while sets still being gathered stay open to rivals.
pros: Finished sets are safe.
Players see which sets a rival still needs.
cons: Half-built sets can be taken.
Chasing one set leaves the others empty.

pairs.tendency: Tiles go down to build a shared map, and a few of them close into a shape. A tile placed across a rival's shape changes what it can become.
pros: The map shows everyone's shapes.
One tile can block a closing move.
cons: The tile you need may be used by someone else.
The map grows slowly with many players.

pairs.tendency: One player puts down a stone and the next answers with one of their own, so a shape grows out of the back and forth. A reply that closes the shape ends the exchange.
pros: Each move invites an answer.
Shapes grow out of pairs of moves.
cons: A reply has to fit the call.
Slow if players think for long.

pairs.tendency: Nobody talks, so a shape is built with no warning of where the next stone will land. Players read a rival's plan only from what is placed.
pros: Plans are read from the board.
The table stays quiet.
cons: No way to ask a partner for help.
A move is easy to misread.

pairs.tendency: On a turn a player can change a rule instead of moving, so what counts as a safe shape can change in mid-game. A shape that could not be captured may become open on a rival's turn.
pros: A rule change can protect or expose a shape.
Players watch the rules as closely as the board.
cons: A safe shape may stop being safe.
Planning is hard while the rules move.

pairs.tendency: Each player speaks as a character, and a shape of stones becomes a fort or a walled village that the character defends. The story gives the reason attackers cannot get in.
pros: A shape gets a reason in the story.
Characters give players choices about where to build.
cons: Players can talk longer than they play.
Story and rules can pull in different directions.

pairs.tendency: Stones are flicked or stacked into place by hand, so a shape depends on steady fingers. A shape that cannot be captured can still be knocked over by a shaky hand.
pros: Building is done by hand.
Players watch every flick.
cons: A shaky hand can wreck a finished shape.
Very young or older hands may find the placing hard.

pairs.tendency: Players draw the map as the game runs, and a safe shape can be drawn as a walled corner of it. Each new line changes where a rival can attack.
pros: The map shows what has been built.
A drawn wall is clear to everyone.
cons: Drawing takes time between turns.
Messy lines lead to arguments.

pairs.tendency: Some prizes are named in advance, and a shape that cannot be captured keeps the stones behind a prize out of reach. Everyone knows from the first turn what to build towards.
pros: A goal that is clear from the start.
Players can plan around the named prizes.
cons: Rivals can see your goal too.
One prize can decide the whole game.

pairs.tendency: Face-up cards in the middle are open to all, and one of them can be the card that finishes a shape. Whoever reaches it first gets the shape and the others see what they lost.
pros: Everyone sees what could finish a shape.
The middle gives players a shared race.
cons: Anyone can take the card you wanted.
The first player gets the first look.

pairs.tendency: Counters go into a pot that grows when nobody wins, and a player with a shape that cannot be captured can wait for the pot without fear of losing the shape. Rivals have a reason to attack before it closes.
pros: The pot keeps growing.
There is a reason to finish the shape early.
cons: A big pot makes every attack worth trying.
Players who miss out lose their counters.

pairs.tendency: Seeds are dropped round the pits, and some pits can be arranged so that a rival's last seed never lands where it could take them. Players count seeds ahead to see where each turn ends.
pros: Counting ahead shows which pits are safe.
A safe group keeps its seeds for later.
cons: One extra seed changes where a turn ends.
Counting every pit slows the turns.

pairs.tendency: An extra hand lies face down in the middle, and the player who takes it may find the cards that finish a shape. Swapping it in changes which shapes that player can still build.
pros: A hidden chance to finish a shape.
Taking it is a gamble.
cons: The spare hand may hold nothing useful.
Others see who took it and guess why.

pairs.tendency: Some squares keep a piece safe and others send it back, so a shape standing on the safe squares has two kinds of protection. A rival may try to push you off those squares.
pros: Safe squares give a place to build.
Players learn which squares to aim for.
cons: Squares that send pieces back can pull stones out of the shape.
Everyone races for the same safe squares.

pairs.tendency: Every stone has a price, and a shape that cannot be captured costs several of them to build. Players save up and spend in one turn so a rival cannot attack a half-built shape.
pros: Saving up to finish a shape in one go.
Prices show what matters most.
cons: Saving leaves the board open for a while.
A shape that is cut off wastes the money spent.

pairs.tendency: A fixed number of stones is shared between several places. Putting enough into one place makes a shape there, but the other places have too few and can be taken.
pros: A choice about where to be safe.
Rivals watch where the stones go.
cons: Every safe place leaves another one open.
A wrong guess about the rival's attack costs a place.

pairs.tendency: Everyone keeps moving until the signal, then freezes, and stones left outside a shape are caught. Players hurry to join the shape before the music stops.
pros: A clear rush to safety.
The signal ends each round at once.
cons: The slowest are caught.
Players crowd into the shape.

pairs.tendency: Cards can be put back for new ones, so a hand can be changed to fit a shape. A swap tells rivals which cards you did not want.
pros: A second go at a hand that does not fit.
Swaps hint at a plan.
cons: A swap uses up a turn.
The new cards may be no use.

pairs.tendency: The discard pile holds everything thrown away, and picking it up can hand a player the cards for a shape. It also lets rivals see what you now hold.
pros: A chance to collect many cards at once.
The pile shows what players threw away.
cons: A big pile is slow to sort.
A pile with nothing useful ends your lead.

pairs.tendency: A shape built from trump cards wins against any card of another suit. Players hold trumps back until the shape needs them.
pros: Trumps give a way to finish a shape.
The named suit tells everyone what matters.
cons: Trumps can be spent too early.
Players with few trumps cannot keep up.

pairs.tendency: One player attacks on one board and defends on the other. A shape on the board where you defend frees your attention for the board where you attack.
pros: Safety on one board frees attention.
Moves on one board affect the other.
cons: Two boards are hard to watch.
A rushed shape on one board loses ground on the other.

pairs.tendency: A wild card stands for any card, so it can finish a shape that is one card short. Players keep wild cards back and use them when a shape is nearly closed.
pros: A wild card can close a shape.
Holding one is a secret.
cons: Players with no wild card have to wait.
Using one early wastes it.

pairs.tendency: The edges join, so a line of stones can run off one side and come back on the other. A shape with no edge has no side to attack from.
pros: Shapes can ring the board.
No corners to hide in.
cons: Players lose track of where lines meet.
Tricks that rely on the edge stop working.

pairs.tendency: One player knows where a shape is hidden and the others ask yes or no questions to find it. Each answer narrows the places to look.
pros: Each answer narrows the search.
Questions show what players suspect.
cons: A wide question teaches little.
The answerer has to stay honest.

pairs.tendency: The first player to the end wins, and a shape gives a base to run from. Players choose between building the shape and running ahead of it.
pros: A choice between speed and safety.
A shape guards the runner's back.
cons: Building takes turns from the race.
A rival who skips the shape can arrive first.

pairs.tendency: Points are counted at the end, and a shape keeps the points it holds from being taken. A player who builds one early can spend later turns going after other points.
pros: Points that stay held.
Free turns for scoring elsewhere.
cons: Early building scores little at first.
Rivals may score fast while you build.

pairs.tendency: Players are knocked out one by one, and a shape that cannot be captured keeps its owner in the game. Rivals leave that player until last and go for the others.
pros: A shape keeps its owner alive.
Attacks fall on players without shapes.
cons: A player with a shape can sit back and watch.
Players knocked out early wait a long time.

pairs.tendency: All win or lose together, so a shape guards the whole group and players decide together who builds it. The game's own attacks go for the gaps.
pros: One shape protects everyone.
Players plan it together.
cons: One careless move opens a gap for all.
A loud player can take over the plan.

pairs.tendency: The table aims for one goal, and a shape can be the goal or the base to reach it from. Every stone placed helps everyone.
pros: Everyone's stone counts.
Building is shared.
cons: Players disagree over where to build.
Some players do less of the work.

pairs.tendency: Each player has a secret goal, so a shape may help one player and block another. Others try to guess who is building what.
pros: Shapes mean different things to different players.
Guessing about goals.
cons: A shape can give a goal away.
Players may block each other by accident.

pairs.tendency: The game runs until the story ends, and a shape can be the village or the fort that lasts to the last page.
pros: A shape that lasts through the story.
A set piece for the ending.
cons: Building can slow the story down.
Players may guard the shape and ignore the plot.

pairs.tendency: Nobody wins, so a shape is built for its own sake. Players look at the shapes at the end and talk about them.
pros: Shapes made to be looked at.
Talk afterwards about what each one shows.
cons: No pressure to finish.
Players may not know when to stop.

pairs.tendency: Each player decides what doing well means. One builds a single shape that cannot be captured, another spreads stones and takes risks. Each judges their own result afterwards.
pros: Players choose how safe to be.
Different styles at one table.
cons: Results are hard to compare.
A player may change the goal mid-game.

pairs.tendency: Nobody wins, and play goes on until one player loses. A shape keeps its owner out of danger, so attacks fall on the others.
pros: A shape is a place of safety.
Attention moves to players without one.
cons: The last player without a shape is the target.
Players in shapes just watch the rest.

pairs.tendency: The aim is to keep playing, and shapes give players a base that survives each round. Play stops only when a shape is lost.
pros: Shapes last across many sessions.
A base to come back to.
cons: Nothing forces an end.
A shape nobody can take can stall the game.

pairs.tendency: The game cannot be won, so a shape that cannot be captured makes a point about how long things last. Safety changes nothing about the result.
pros: A shape shows what lasts.
Players notice the result stays the same.
cons: Effort has no prize.
Players may ask why they bother.

pairs.tendency: A lone player works against a layout of cards, and the shape forms once the right cards are cleared. The game says you lost if the layout sticks first.
pros: Quiet puzzle play.
A shape is easy to check.
cons: One wrong move can stick the layout.
No rival to learn from.

pairs.tendency: Several short games are played in a row, and a player who learns to build a shape fast can win the early ones. Rivals learn the pattern and attack sooner in the next game.
pros: Players learn between games.
Early wins change how the rest is played.
cons: A player who falls behind may give up.
A shape that worked once gets countered.

pairs.tendency: Points count against you, and being captured costs points. A player inside a shape that cannot be captured stays clear of them.
pros: Shapes shield players from points.
Attackers have to pick targets.
cons: Players outside shapes carry the points.
Staying safe can leave a player with little to do.

pairs.tendency: A player needs the exact number to finish, and a shape holds a piece close to the goal while it waits for the right count.
pros: A safe place to wait.
Counting ahead for the exact number.
cons: Waiting for the number is slow.
Going past the number wastes a turn.

pairs.tendency: The aim is turned round, so a shape that cannot be captured is the last thing a player wants. Players build shapes with gaps on purpose.
pros: A puzzle in making a shape that fails.
Habits are turned upside down.
cons: Hard to explain to new players.
A player can win by mistake.

pairs.tendency: Everyone builds on their own board at the same time, so a shape is never attacked and the race is to finish it first.
pros: Quiet play.
Easy to compare results.
cons: The shape is never tested.
Little to say to each other.

pairs.tendency: Players attack each other on purpose, and a shape is where you stand when a rival comes for you. Rivals aim at stones still outside it.
pros: A safe place under attack.
Targets are clear.
cons: Players building shapes give up attacks.
Rivals rush at an unfinished shape.

pairs.tendency: Rivals feel each other through the board, so stones placed to cut off a route work as an attack from far away. A shape cannot be cut.
pros: Attack with no contact.
Shapes change the board for all.
cons: The cause of a loss is hard to see.
New players take time to follow it.

pairs.tendency: The whole table works against the game itself, and a shape that cannot be captured protects the team's key stones. Each player adds a stone to it in turn.
pros: Every player's stone adds to it.
Players talk it over.
cons: The game's attack finds the last gap.
One loud voice can steer the plan.

pairs.tendency: Players share a shape that helps everyone, though each also wants their own stones inside it. The jostling for a place in the shape is quiet.
pros: Shared safety.
A private reason to join.
cons: Trust can wear thin.
Help and self-interest are hard to tell apart.

pairs.tendency: A shape belongs to a team, and teammates guard each other's stones inside it. The shape becomes a shared home.
pros: Teammates guard each other.
Plans are shared inside the team.
cons: Teammates may disagree about where to build.
One careless teammate can open a gap for the other side.

pairs.tendency: Most players share a team and one is secretly against them. The team builds a shape and the traitor can leave a gap in it.
pros: Suspicion about every stone.
Players watch each placement.
cons: Trust breaks down.
Honest players may be accused.

pairs.tendency: Moves go out by letter, so a shape grows over days or weeks. Because the shape cannot be captured, one reply cannot undo weeks of work.
pros: Time to think about each stone.
A shape grows steadily.
cons: Long waits between moves.
One lost letter stops the game.

pairs.tendency: One player is away from the table, maybe a ghost, and their stones form a shape nobody can capture. The others have to play around it.
pros: A fixed shape to play around.
A voice from outside the table.
cons: The absent player cannot reply.
Hard to know what the shape means.

pairs.tendency: One player runs the world and decides whether a shape holds. The others build inside the world the master describes.
pros: The master settles arguments about the shape.
The story fits the shape.
cons: The master's call can be argued.
The master has no shape of their own.

pairs.tendency: The game is played on the street or in a park, and a shape drawn in chalk is seen by every passer-by who may join in to attack it.
pros: Shapes are seen by all.
Newcomers can join.
cons: Shapes get scuffed by feet.
The players keep changing.

pairs.tendency: One player builds a shape to hold off the whole group, and the group works together to break through.
pros: The lone player has a refuge.
The group has to plan together.
cons: The group can be slow to agree.
A lone player inside the shape can be left alone and the game stalls.

pairs.tendency: When you play alone against the pack, a shape is the point where you are out of danger. Nobody else acts, so it comes down to the pack and your choices.
pros: A quiet puzzle.
Results can be compared afterwards.
cons: There is nobody to watch.
The order of the pack decides when a shape forms.

pairs.tendency: Dice and draws decide most things, so a shape arrives by luck more than by plan.
pros: Anyone can end up with a shape.
Quick turns.
cons: Planning counts for little.
A long wait for the right throw.

pairs.tendency: Re-rolls and choices soften the dice, so a player can use them to finish a shape that an unlucky throw would have broken.
pros: Re-rolls protect the shape.
Choices keep players in the game.
cons: Saving re-rolls for the shape leaves none for later.
Extra rules to learn.

pairs.tendency: A planned shape can be knocked off course by a lucky draw for a rival. Choices matter most, with a little luck on top.
pros: Planning pays off.
A touch of surprise.
cons: One lucky draw can undo a plan.
Newer players may blame the luck for a loss.

pairs.tendency: There are no dice and no surprises, so a shape comes from planning many moves ahead, and the rival sees all of it.
pros: Every loss traces back to a choice.
Shapes are built by thinking.
cons: Experienced players win often.
Long thinking slows the game.

pairs.tendency: A throw is read as a sign about where to build, and the shape becomes the answer to what the throw said.
pros: Throws give a reason to build in a place.
Talk about what a throw means.
cons: Readings can be argued.
The throw gives no count of points.

pairs.tendency: Partners sense when the others are about to act, so a shape builds without a call. Several stones go down at the same moment.
pros: Partners move in step.
No one has to speak.
cons: Attempts to match often miss.
New players take a while to fall in step.

pairs.tendency: Dice are looked up on a table, so a roll can bring a siege to the gate of a shape. The table says what turns up on the road.
pros: Dice add events around the shape.
Stories grow around it.
cons: A roll can undo plans.
Looking up tables slows the turns.

pairs.tendency: Everything is in view, so a shape that cannot be captured is seen by all, and rivals can see which stones to take first and which gaps are left.
pros: No surprises.
Rivals plan against the shape.
cons: Nothing is hidden.
A gap is seen at once.

pairs.tendency: The shape is on the board for all to see, but the cards that could break it sit hidden in rival hands.
pros: Guessing about rivals' cards.
Bluffs about finishing.
cons: A player cannot be sure the shape is safe.
Players may play safe all game.

pairs.tendency: A player building a shape may be protecting a hidden role, and the others watch who builds and why.
pros: Every shape raises a question.
Suspicion at the table.
cons: Honest builders get accused.
A safe shape can look like a trap.

pairs.tendency: A shape that cannot be captured is the one fixed fact in a game of hidden facts. Clues show where it is.
pros: A fixed point among the unknowns.
Clues point at shapes.
cons: A shape tells rivals what you know.
Players spend long on small clues.

pairs.tendency: A player can say a half-built shape is finished, or pretend a finished one is still open. Rivals have to guess which.
pros: The state of a shape can be hidden.
Rivals guess.
cons: A bluff can be caught.
A real shape needs no bluff, so it gives itself away.

pairs.tendency: One player knows a secret rule and the others learn it by breaking it. Newcomers learn why stones in a certain shape stay put by trying to take them.
pros: Learning by testing.
Failed captures teach the rule.
cons: Newcomers lose stones along the way.
Being told no again and again wears on people.

pairs.tendency: One player knows where the shape is and can only give hints. The others guess from the hints.
pros: Hints keep everyone thinking.
Guessing together.
cons: Hints can be misread.
Slow when hints are vague.

pairs.tendency: The map starts hidden, so a shape found in unexplored ground is a surprise.
pros: Discovery.
A shape in unknown ground.
cons: It may sit in the wrong place.
Players may avoid exploring.

pairs.tendency: One hand lies face up, so everybody sees which cards could finish a shape and what the shape still needs.
pros: Open cards to plan around.
Shared reading of the shape.
cons: Rivals know what the shape needs.
The owner of the open hand has no secrets.

pairs.tendency: Some points are kept secret, and a shape that holds points hides how many. Nobody can add up the totals.
pros: Guessing who is ahead.
Shapes hide totals.
cons: A late reveal can change everything.
Hard to know when to attack.

pairs.tendency: One player acts at a time, so a rival sees every stone and can reply before the shape closes.
pros: Time to reply.
A clear order.
cons: Waiting for your turn.
The first player has a head start.

pairs.tendency: All choose in secret and reveal together, so two players may place stones in the same gap at the same moment.
pros: No waiting.
Surprises.
cons: Two players may build the same shape.
Hard to answer a move you did not see.

pairs.tendency: Anyone acts at any moment, and the quickest hand closes the shape.
pros: Fast play.
Shapes close in a rush.
cons: Quick hands win.
Arguments about who was first.

pairs.tendency: Each turn has a clock, and a shape has to be placed before the sand runs out. Hurried stones leave gaps.
pros: Turns move quickly.
A little pressure on each move.
cons: Rushed stones leave gaps.
Slow thinkers lose moves.

pairs.tendency: One move a day, so a shape is built over weeks and a rival has a day to answer each stone.
pros: A slow, steady build.
Time to think.
cons: A very long game.
Players forget their plan.

pairs.tendency: A pause comes before each move, so a shape grows calmly and every stone is thought over. The slowness is part of the play.
pros: A calm table.
Each stone is considered.
cons: A long game.
Attention drifts.

pairs.tendency: The game speeds up, so early turns have time to build a shape and later attacks come quickly.
pros: Early building matters.
A rush at the end.
cons: Late shapes are left unfinished.
Players who fall behind panic.

pairs.tendency: Some throws give another go, so a player with an extra turn can close a shape before a rival can react.
pros: A chance to close a shape at once.
Surprise moves.
cons: Luck of the extra turns decides a lot.
A rival cannot reply in time.

pairs.tendency: The first stage is set-up and the second is play, so a shape built in the first stage protects stones in the second.
pros: Early work pays off later.
Plans reach across stages.
cons: First stage choices cannot be undone.
A shape may fit one stage and not the next.

pairs.tendency: The board works like a real system, and a shape stands for the part that survives shocks, such as a dam that holds.
pros: Safe parts show how a system holds up.
Players talk about real cases.
cons: Real life is less tidy than a shape.
Players may trust the model too far.

pairs.tendency: Each player is a group, and a shape is that group's protected ground, such as a farmer's fields with a boundary. Another group may want the same ground.
pros: Groups see what they need to protect.
Disputes over ground.
cons: One group may end up with no shape.
The roles can start unequal.

pairs.tendency: Everyone draws from one limited thing, and a shape guards one player's share of it while the rest draw from what is left.
pros: One share is secure.
Others see the gap.
cons: The unguarded part runs out first.
Arguments over who gets a share.
