pairs.tendency: Effects show up later, so a shape built now may only prove safe a few rounds on.
pros: Planning ahead.
Surprises later.
cons: Hard to tell if the shape works.
Mistakes show late.

pairs.tendency: Players agree a new rule and play on to see what it changes. A rule that changes what makes a shape safe shows quickly.
pros: A safe way to test a rule.
Effects show on the board.
cons: Changing a rule mid-game confuses.
Shapes built under the old rule may break.

pairs.tendency: After the game, players talk about which shapes held and why.
pros: Shapes become examples.
Players learn from them.
cons: Talk can run long.
Players recall things differently.

pairs.tendency: What is built stays for the next game, so a shape lasts beyond one night.
pros: A history on the board.
The next game starts from it.
cons: Mistakes last.
New players inherit old shapes.

pairs.tendency: If only shapes that cannot be captured score, the rules say that safety counts for more than risk.
pros: A rule that says something.
Talk about the point it makes.
cons: Players may disagree with it.
Safe play dominates.

pairs.tendency: A shape protects a real stake, so players take it seriously.
pros: Shapes carry weight.
Players take care.
cons: Friendships can strain.
Players avoid risks.

pairs.tendency: Points stand for something like kindness, and a shape holds the points, so players chase the shape instead of the value it stood for.
pros: The game shows what counting does.
Talk about it afterwards.
cons: The value gets lost.
Players find ways to game the points.

pairs.tendency: Players practise a way of living, and the shape is the part of that future that holds up.
pros: A feel for the future.
A view of what lasts.
cons: Hard to know how real it is.
Players may follow rules nobody has tried.

pairs.tendency: Pieces run along a path, and some spaces let a player go after a named prize card. The dice decide how often anyone gets there.
pros: The dice decide who reaches prizes.
Everyone knows the prizes before the throw.
cons: A low roll can keep a player away from a prize.
One player holding the prizes can end the race early.

pairs.tendency: Cards are picked from a shared row, and the named prize cards are the ones everyone eyes. Taking a prize card can matter more than a card that helps your own hand.
pros: Every pick can take a prize from a rival.
Players read each other's aims.
cons: The prize cards go first.
The last to pick gets leftovers.

pairs.tendency: Each named prize goes to the highest bidder. Bids climb fast on a card everyone knows is a prize.
pros: Bids show what prizes are worth.
Money buys points.
cons: Bids can climb too high.
Players with little money are shut out.

pairs.tendency: A player keeps going for the named card and loses what they had if it does not come. Stopping early keeps a small score.
pros: A clear prize to risk for.
A player decides each turn whether to go on.
cons: Going on once too often costs the lot.
Players who stop early see the prize go to others.

pairs.tendency: Groups fight for parts of the map, and holding a place can give a player a named prize card.
pros: Prizes tied to places.
Rivals know where to attack.
cons: Fighting for a prize place can leave other ground free.
One area can be worth too much.

pairs.tendency: A job spot lets a worker take a named card. Once a worker sits there, nobody else can take that prize that turn.
pros: Players hurry for the prize spots.
Workers have a clear aim.
cons: One taken spot blocks the others.
Whoever places first has the widest choice.

pairs.tendency: A finished pattern earns a named card, so players know which patterns count. A single pattern can win more than one prize if it fits.
pros: A clear goal for each pattern.
One pattern can win two prizes.
cons: Rivals can see what you are building.
A pattern that misses the prize scores little.

pairs.tendency: Cards in hand are kept for the tricks that win prizes. Players hold back high cards until a prize card is in play.
pros: Each card can be played now or kept for a prize.
A hand can be planned around the prizes.
cons: Cards kept back do nothing this turn.
A hand of low cards cannot reach the prizes.

pairs.tendency: Tricks are the way to reach the prizes. A trick that holds the highest trump or the Jack of trumps is worth more than its count, and one trick can win several prizes at once.
pros: Each trick can carry a prize.
Players count the prizes still to come.
cons: Winning many tricks can still miss the prizes.
One trick can swing the whole game.

pairs.tendency: Players trade and talk about who gets the named cards. Deals about prizes are made before the cards are played.
pros: Deals about which prize goes where.
Promises that shape the play.
cons: Once a deal is broken, nobody wants to bargain.
Bargaining takes up time.

pairs.tendency: Sets of matching things score, and the named cards are prizes on top. A player can complete a set and take a prize card with the same pick.
pros: One pick can do two jobs.
Sets and prizes pull together.
cons: Players chase prizes and leave sets half done.
Rivals see which sets you are close to.

pairs.tendency: A tile placed in the right spot takes a named prize. The shared map shows which prizes are still open.
pros: The map shows open prizes.
A single tile can claim a prize.
cons: A rival can lay the tile first.
Blocking a spot costs a tile.

pairs.tendency: One player plays a card and the next answers, so a reply can take a named card out of the first player's reach.
pros: Replies can win prizes.
Every card played asks for a reply.
cons: An answer is limited by what was played before it.
A slow answer holds up the chain.

pairs.tendency: Nobody talks, so partners show which prize card they hold only by when they play it.
pros: Timing shows what a player holds.
Play goes on without a word.
cons: Partners can misread each other.
There is no way to ask for a prize card.

pairs.tendency: A player can change which cards count as prizes, so the named cards stop being fixed.
pros: A rule change can make a card worth more.
The prize list needs watching too.
cons: A plan for a prize can fall apart.
Players argue over which list is right.

pairs.tendency: Each player acts as a character who wants something named, such as a crown or a key. The prize cards become objects in the story.
pros: Each prize has a part in the story.
Characters choose which prize to chase.
cons: In-character talk can run on past the play.
What the story wants and what scores may differ.

pairs.tendency: Hands flick or stack to take a card, and the named prize cards sit where they are hardest to reach.
pros: Prizes need steady hands.
Players watch every attempt.
cons: A shaky hand loses the prize.
Some players find the reach harder than others.

pairs.tendency: Players draw the map and mark which places hold the prizes.
pros: The map shows where the prizes sit.
Drawn marks are clear to everyone.
cons: Turns wait while someone draws.
A smudged mark starts a dispute.

pairs.tendency: Face-up cards in the middle can be the named prizes, so everyone can see which ones are up for grabs.
pros: Everyone sees the open prizes.
Players race for the same cards.
cons: A rival can take your prize first.
The player who goes first sees the prizes first.

pairs.tendency: The pot goes with the prize cards, so whoever takes a named card takes the pot too. If nobody takes it the pot grows.
pros: The pot gets bigger each round nobody claims it.
Prizes carry extra weight.
cons: A big pot makes every prize a target.
Those who take no prize lose what they put in.

pairs.tendency: Some pits carry the named prizes, and where the last seed lands decides who can take one. Players count seeds ahead to aim for those pits.
pros: Counting ahead leads to prizes.
A clear target for each sowing.
cons: Being one seed out misses the prize pit.
Turns drag while players count.

pairs.tendency: A spare hand, face down in the middle, may hold prize cards. Whoever takes it gambles on what is inside.
pros: A hidden chance at a prize.
Taking it changes the plan.
cons: The spare hand may hold no prize.
The table notices who took it.

pairs.tendency: Certain squares carry prize cards, and a piece that lands on one collects. Other squares send pieces back before they reach it.
pros: Squares give prizes a place.
The prize squares become the ones to reach.
cons: A square that sends a piece back loses the prize.
Pieces bunch up near the prize squares.

pairs.tendency: Prize cards have prices, so spending on a prize leaves less for everything else.
pros: Prices show what a prize is worth.
Saving up for a prize.
cons: A prize bought leaves little to spend.
Rivals see what you are saving for.

pairs.tendency: Prizes lie in several places, so a player shares forces to win some prizes and give up others.
pros: A choice about which prizes to fight for.
Rivals can see how forces are shared.
cons: Every prize won leaves another open.
Misreading a rival loses a prize.

pairs.tendency: At the signal, the player holding a named card scores. Everyone hurries to grab one before the music stops.
pros: A clear rush for the prizes.
Rounds end the moment the signal comes.
cons: The slowest hold nothing.
Players crowd around the prize cards.

pairs.tendency: Players trade cards from their hand for new ones, looking for the cards that win prizes. Whatever you put back shows rivals what you do not need.
pros: A second go at a hand that misses the prizes.
A swap points at what you want.
cons: Swapping costs a turn.
The new cards may still miss the prize.

pairs.tendency: The discard pile may hold named prize cards, and picking it up takes them. It also shows rivals what you now hold.
pros: A chance to take many prizes at once.
The pile shows what was thrown away.
cons: Sorting a large pile takes time.
Taking a pile with no prizes in it can cost your lead.

pairs.tendency: The trump suit is named, and the highest trump and the Jack of trumps are prizes. One trick holding both wins both.
pros: Trumps carry prizes.
Everyone knows which cards count.
cons: A trump played too soon cannot come back.
A short trump hand falls behind.

pairs.tendency: Prizes lie on both boards, and a card won on one board can help on the other.
pros: Prizes on both boards tie them together.
Each board feeds into the other.
cons: Keeping an eye on both boards is hard.
Chasing a prize on one board loses ground on the other.

pairs.tendency: A wild card can stand in for a named prize card to complete a set. Players keep one back for the prize.
pros: A wild card can complete a prize.
Nobody knows who holds one.
cons: Without a wild card, a player waits for the real card.
Played too soon, it does nothing for the prize.

pairs.tendency: The edges join, so a named prize card at the edge can be reached from either side.
pros: Prizes at the edge are reachable from both sides.
Corners give no cover.
cons: It is easy to forget which edges join.
A prize at the edge draws a crowd.

pairs.tendency: The others ask yes or no questions to find the prize card, which only one player knows. Each answer narrows the list.
pros: Players close in on it step by step.
What players ask shows their guesses.
cons: A broad question gives away little.
Everything rests on honest answers.

pairs.tendency: Whoever reaches the end first wins, and prizes along the way can slow a runner or speed one up. A prize card may be worth stopping for, or worth running past.
pros: A choice between speed and prizes.
Prizes make the route matter.
cons: Stopping for a prize costs time.
A rival who skips the prizes can arrive first.

pairs.tendency: The prize cards are where the points come from, so players count prizes. Because the names are known in advance, everyone knows what is on offer.
pros: A clear count of points.
Prizes name what matters.
cons: Rivals see how far ahead you are.
One prize can decide the end.

pairs.tendency: As players drop out one at a time, a named prize card can keep its holder in. Rivals go after whoever holds it.
pros: A prize card keeps its owner alive.
Attacks fall on prize holders.
cons: A prize holder is the target.
Early losers sit out the rest.

pairs.tendency: The group wins or loses together, so prize cards are won for everyone. The game itself attacks the prizes.
pros: One prize helps everyone.
Players plan who takes it.
cons: One careless move loses a prize for all.
The most vocal player may decide for all.

pairs.tendency: The table aims at one goal, and the named cards are steps on the way to it.
pros: Each prize moves the group on.
Everyone's win counts for all.
cons: Players disagree over which prize comes first.
The work may fall on a few.

pairs.tendency: Secret goals sit beside prize cards that everyone can name. A secret goal may need a named card, and chasing it gives the goal away.
pros: Prizes mean different things to different players.
Players guess at each other's aims.
cons: Chasing a prize can reveal a goal.
A player can spoil another's goal without meaning to.

pairs.tendency: Prize cards mark turning points in the story, such as a crown found or a door opened.
pros: Prizes give the story steps.
Players know what comes next.
cons: Chasing prizes can rush the story.
Players may skip the story for the cards.

pairs.tendency: Nobody wins, so the named cards score nothing. Players may collect them anyway and talk about who held which.
pros: Cards to look at and talk about.
No pressure to win them.
cons: Nothing pushes players to finish.
It is unclear when the game is over.

pairs.tendency: Each player decides which named card matters most to them. One goes for the Jack, another ignores it.
pros: Players choose their own prize.
Players chase different things side by side.
cons: Comparing results is hard.
A goal can shift during play.

pairs.tendency: The named cards can be the ones nobody wants, and whoever holds one at the end loses.
pros: Prizes turn into things to avoid.
Players pass them along.
cons: The last holder is the loser.
Players gang up on whoever has the card.

pairs.tendency: Prize cards go back into play after they are won, so the game does not end and the named cards pass round as rewards.
pros: Prizes keep circulating.
Players keep a reason to play.
cons: The game has no set finish.
The same cards can feel repeated.

pairs.tendency: The prizes are named, but the game cannot be won, so the cards point at something that never pays out.
pros: Prizes make a point about chasing.
Players notice the missing result.
cons: Effort has no payoff.
Players may wonder what the point is.

pairs.tendency: Playing alone against the layout, a player has to clear the named prize cards. If the layout sticks first, the game is lost.
pros: A clear aim for a quiet puzzle.
Prizes tell a player where to start.
cons: A single slip can leave the layout stuck.
Nobody plays against you.

pairs.tendency: Several short games are played with the same named prizes, so players learn which prize cards decide a game.
pros: Each game teaches the next.
Early wins change the rest.
cons: A trailing player may lose heart.
A plan for the prizes gets countered.

pairs.tendency: Prize cards count against you, so the named cards become the ones to avoid. Players try to hand them on.
pros: The named cards become a burden.
Players watch who holds what.
cons: The last holder collects the points.
Everyone works against the holder.

pairs.tendency: The named card with the exact value ends the hand, so the prize is the card that makes the number. Going past it costs the win.
pros: A clear card to wait for.
Players count towards the target.
cons: Waiting for the card is slow.
Overshooting loses the turn.

pairs.tendency: With the aim reversed, the named cards are the ones to give away.
pros: A puzzle in losing the prizes.
Players unlearn the usual aim.
cons: Newcomers need it spelt out.
Someone may win without meaning to.

pairs.tendency: Everyone plays their own game and the named prizes are the same for all, so players compare results at the end.
pros: Results line up side by side.
Everyone works in silence.
cons: No attacks between players.
Players have little reason to talk.

pairs.tendency: Players take cards from each other on purpose, and the named cards are the targets.
pros: Everyone knows what to go after.
Prizes draw attacks.
cons: A prize holder is a target.
Players chasing one prize leave others open.

pairs.tendency: Players affect each other only through the board, and a prize card lying on it draws them towards it.
pros: Prizes shape where players go.
Players hurt each other without touching.
cons: It is hard to tell why you lost.
Beginners take a while to see what is happening.

pairs.tendency: The table wins together, so prize cards are collected for the team.
pros: Every prize helps all.
Choices are made out loud together.
cons: The game strikes where the team is thin.
A dominant player can run the team.

pairs.tendency: Players work together, but each wants the named card for themselves. The jostling for the prize is quiet.
pros: Shared prizes.
A private reason to chase one.
cons: Players start to doubt each other.
It is hard to tell who is helping the team and who is helping themselves.

pairs.tendency: Two teams chase the same named cards, and partners pass each other the prizes. The team that holds more of them leads.
pros: Teammates pass prizes along.
Partners plan together.
cons: Teammates may disagree over who takes a prize.
One careless teammate hands the other side a prize.

pairs.tendency: The traitor wants a named card to go to the wrong team and can steer it there.
pros: Suspicion about every prize.
Players watch each pick.
cons: Players stop believing each other.
The innocent can be blamed.

pairs.tendency: Each move is sent by letter, so a prize card can wait days for a reply.
pros: Time to think about each prize.
The chase grows steadily.
cons: Replies are slow to come.
A letter lost in the post halts play.

pairs.tendency: An absent player, perhaps a ghost, holds a named card that nobody at the table can reach.
pros: A prize nobody can take.
Someone not present still has a part.
cons: The missing player gives no answer.
Hard to know what the card means.

pairs.tendency: One player holds the prizes, names them and decides who earns them. The others play for what the master puts up.
pros: The master settles arguments over prizes.
The story fits the prizes.
cons: Players may dispute the master's decisions.
The master has no prize of their own.

pairs.tendency: The game is played where anyone passing can see, and the prize cards are shown in public so a passer-by can see what is at stake.
pros: Prizes are seen by all.
Passers-by can join in.
cons: Cards get scuffed or lost.
Who is playing changes all the time.

pairs.tendency: One player takes on the whole group, and prize cards give the lone player a way to win that the group cannot block.
pros: The lone player has a way through.
The group needs a joint plan.
cons: Agreement within the group takes time.
A prize in the lone player's hand can end the game early.

pairs.tendency: When you play alone against the pack, the named cards are the ones you need to find. With nobody else acting, luck and your own choices decide it.
pros: A quiet puzzle with a clear aim.
Players can compare scores later.
cons: Nobody across the table to read.
The order of the pack decides when a prize shows.

pairs.tendency: Prize cards come mostly by luck, since dice and draws settle most things.
pros: Anyone can land a prize.
Turns pass fast.
cons: Thinking ahead does little.
A long wait for the right draw.

pairs.tendency: A player can re-roll or choose again to reach a named card that an unlucky throw would have missed.
pros: Re-rolls help reach prizes.
Choices give players a way back.
cons: Saving re-rolls for a prize leaves none for later.
More rules to remember.

pairs.tendency: A player plans a route to the prize cards, and a lucky draw can still hand one to a rival. Choice decides most of it and luck a little.
pros: Careful play is rewarded.
Some luck keeps the game open.
cons: A rival's lucky draw can wreck a route.
Beginners may put a loss down to luck.

pairs.tendency: There are no dice, so prize cards go to the player who counts the deck most carefully.
pros: A lost prize comes from a choice someone made.
Prizes reward planning.
cons: The practised player usually wins.
Turns stretch while players think.

pairs.tendency: Each throw is taken as a sign and points to a named card, which gives it a meaning. Players then talk about what it says.
pros: Throws give prizes a meaning.
Talk about what a throw says.
cons: People may read a throw differently.
No points come from the throw itself.

pairs.tendency: Partners sense each other, so prize cards pass between them without a word.
pros: Partners learn each other's timing.
Nothing is said aloud.
cons: Partners often get the timing wrong.
Beginners find the timing hard to catch.

pairs.tendency: A roll is looked up on a table that names a prize card as what the road gives.
pros: Dice hand out prizes as events.
Stories grow around each prize.
cons: One roll can upset a plan.
Checking the table takes time.

pairs.tendency: Everything is in view, so everyone knows where every prize is and who could take it.
pros: Nothing comes as a surprise.
Rivals plan against each prize.
cons: A player cannot keep a plan secret.
The player behind sees the lead clearly.

pairs.tendency: The named cards are known, but nobody knows who holds them. A player may be sitting on a prize card in secret.
pros: Players guess at what others hold.
Bluffs about prizes.
cons: A player cannot be sure where the prizes are.
Caution can last the whole game.

pairs.tendency: Prize cards are public, so a player who chases one may give away a secret role.
pros: Every chase raises a question.
Players grow wary of each other.
cons: Honest chasers get accused.
A player who avoids prizes stands out too.

pairs.tendency: Clues point to who holds the named cards, and finding the holder is part of the chase.
pros: A clear target for each clue.
Clues point at prize holders.
cons: A clue tells rivals what you know.
Small clues can eat up time.

pairs.tendency: A player can pretend to hold a prize card, or pretend not to. Nobody else can be sure which is true.
pros: The prize holder can be hidden.
Rivals are left guessing.
cons: A bluff may be called.
A real prize holder has to act calm.

pairs.tendency: One player knows a secret rule, and newcomers learn which cards count as prizes only by taking the wrong ones.
pros: Players find out by trying.
Wrong picks teach the rule.
cons: Newcomers lose points along the way.
Repeated refusals can be tiring.

pairs.tendency: Only one player knows the prize card, and they may hint at it but not name it. The rest work from those hints.
pros: Every hint keeps the guessers working.
The guessers work it out as a group.
cons: A hint can point the wrong way.
Vague hints drag the game out.

pairs.tendency: Prize cards lie face down on the map until a player explores the place.
pros: Prizes turn up as the map opens.
A prize in unknown ground.
cons: A prize can turn up in an awkward spot.
Some players hold back from exploring.

pairs.tendency: A face-up hand shows everybody which prize cards it holds, and they plan around them.
pros: Everyone can plan around the face-up prizes.
Shared reading of the prizes.
cons: Rivals know what the open hand holds.
The open hand's owner cannot hide anything.

pairs.tendency: Prize card points are kept secret, so only the holder knows the total. Nobody can add up who is ahead.
pros: Nobody is sure who leads.
Prizes hide totals.
cons: The final count can upset the order.
Hard to know when to chase.

pairs.tendency: Turns go round the table, so each player sees which prize cards have gone before their turn comes.
pros: Each player can answer the last pick.
Everyone knows whose go it is.
cons: Players sit out while others pick.
Going first gives the first prize pick.

pairs.tendency: Picks are made in secret and shown together, so two players may go after the same prize card at once.
pros: Nobody sits idle.
Reveals bring surprises.
cons: Two players may claim the same prize.
You cannot react to a pick you have not seen.

pairs.tendency: With no turns, the quickest hand grabs the prize card.
pros: Nobody waits for a turn.
Prizes go in a rush.
cons: The fastest grab takes the prize.
Disputes over who touched it first.

pairs.tendency: A timer runs on every turn, and prize cards have to be claimed before the sand runs out.
pros: Short turns.
A little pressure on each pick.
cons: Rushed picks miss prizes.
Players who think slowly miss their chance.

pairs.tendency: Players make one move a day, and a prize card can sit unclaimed for days while they think.
pros: A slow, steady chase.
Each choice can be slept on.
cons: The game runs a long time.
Plans slip out of mind.

pairs.tendency: Every move starts with a pause, and the prize cards wait while players think. The game is meant to be slow.
pros: Nobody is hurried.
Each pick is considered.
cons: The game takes its time.
Minds wander.

pairs.tendency: As the end comes near, play speeds up and prize cards are claimed faster and faster.
pros: Early prizes can be planned.
The last turns are a scramble.
cons: Late prizes are grabbed in a hurry.
Trailing players may panic.

pairs.tendency: A player whose throw earns another go can take two prize cards in a row.
pros: A chance to take two prizes at once.
Moves nobody saw coming.
cons: Who gets the extra turns is largely luck.
Rivals get no chance to answer in between.

pairs.tendency: The first stage picks the cards and the second plays them, so the prize cards are named in one stage and fought over in the next.
pros: Early choices point at prizes.
A plan made early carries into play.
cons: Picks made in stage one are fixed.
A prize picked for stage one may not suit stage two.

pairs.tendency: The board copies a real system, and a prize card stands for something a real group wins in it, such as a share of the village water.
pros: Prizes show who gains from a system.
Talk turns to how it works in real life.
cons: Real life is less tidy than a card.
Players may take the model as the whole truth.

pairs.tendency: Each player is a group with a prize card of its own, such as a farmer with a field. Groups see what each one is chasing.
pros: Groups see their own prize.
Disputes over prizes.
cons: One group may have a smaller prize.
Some groups begin with more.

pairs.tendency: All players take from one limited supply, and a named prize card goes to whoever takes the biggest share. The rest take from what is left.
pros: A prize for the biggest share.
The others see how little is left.
cons: What nobody guards is used up first.
Arguments over who earned the card.

pairs.tendency: A prize card won now pays out a few rounds later, so a win today shows only later.
pros: Players think several rounds on.
Payouts arrive unexpectedly.
cons: Hard to tell if a prize works.
An error only shows after the fact.

pairs.tendency: A rule that adds or removes a prize card is agreed, and play goes on to see what follows.
pros: A safe way to test a prize.
Effects show on the table.
cons: A mid-game change can muddle players.
Plans for the old prize list may break.

pairs.tendency: Once the game is over, players go back over which prize cards decided it and why.
pros: Prizes become examples.
Lessons carry to the next game.
cons: The talk may go on a while.
Memories of the game differ.

pairs.tendency: A prize card won is torn or marked and stays changed for the next game.
pros: A history on the cards.
Each game begins with the marks of the last.
cons: An error stays on the card.
New players inherit marked cards.

pairs.tendency: What the game names as prizes makes a point. If only the highest card is a prize, the game says high counts for most.
pros: The prize list carries a view.
Players can discuss what the game claims.
cons: Not everyone will accept the point.
One kind of play dominates.

pairs.tendency: Prize cards carry real stakes, such as money or a promise, so players take each one seriously.
pros: Prizes carry weight.
Each choice is made carefully.
cons: Real stakes can test friendships.
Players play cautiously.

pairs.tendency: The named cards stand for a value like kindness, and players end up chasing the card and forgetting the value.
pros: Players see the number take over from the value.
There is plenty to discuss after.
cons: The value drops out of sight.
Players learn to work the cards for points.

pairs.tendency: The game rehearses a way of living, with the named cards as the things that future cares about. Players watch how people act around those cards.
pros: A feel for what the future values.
A view of what players chase.
cons: Nobody can say how close it is to life.
The rules are untested in the world.

pairs.tendency: Where your piece stops on the path decides which of the open cards you can reach for. The same row sits in front of everyone, so a throw that helps you may help the player behind you.
pros: The dice choose when you get to use the open cards.
Everyone can plan around the same row.
cons: A short throw can leave you far from the card you wanted.
A rival may land first and take it.

pairs.tendency: Each pick from the hand you are passed is made with the middle cards in view. A card that matches an open one is easy to spot, and so is one that matches nothing.
pros: Picks are made with the open cards in mind.
Passed hands show what others are missing.
cons: The open cards limit what you can keep secret.
Two players may keep chasing the same card.

pairs.tendency: Money is offered for a card while the cards in the middle show every bidder what it could join up with. Bids climb on a card that finishes a set everyone can see.
pros: All bidders can see what a card could do.
The price follows what is open on the table.
cons: One card in the middle can start a bidding war.
Money runs out before the later cards come up.

pairs.tendency: Another card is turned up in the middle after each choice to go on, and the risk is in plain view. A player who stops early leaves the open cards for the others to use.
pros: Everyone watches how close the risk is.
Stopping early still gives something to the others.
cons: A long run of risk can hand the next player a full row.
Some players press on only because others did.

pairs.tendency: A few cards in the middle are up for grabs, and each one is used to add pieces to a region of the map. Whoever uses a card first holds that region for the round.
pros: Open cards turn into pieces on the map.
Rivals see the next move coming.
cons: A card taken early blocks a rival's plan.
Late players get what is left over.

pairs.tendency: Some job spaces on the board each hold a face-up card, and placing a worker there lets you take it. Once a space is taken, its card is gone for everyone else that turn.
pros: Each open card has a place on the board to go to.
Blocking a space blocks a card.
cons: The first to place gets the pick of the row.
A late worker may find only empty spaces.

pairs.tendency: Colours and shapes show on the middle row, and each player tries to match them to a pattern at home. Two players may need the same colour from the same row.
pros: Everyone can see which shapes are on offer.
Planning a pattern is easier with the row in view.
cons: A card you need may vanish before your turn.
Two similar patterns lead to a quiet race for cards.

pairs.tendency: Cards in your hand are kept back to finish what the open cards in the middle start. The cards you hold are the only ones nobody else can see.
pros: Hidden cards and open cards work together.
A held card can wait for the right open one.
cons: Holding on too long leaves a full hand.
A rival can take the open card you were saving a space for.

pairs.tendency: One card from the middle is added to each trick, so everyone can see part of what is being played for. The winner of the trick takes that open card along with the rest.
pros: Everyone knows what a trick is worth.
A low card can still win a useful prize.
cons: Some tricks are played only for the open card.
A player with a low hand finds that out early.

pairs.tendency: Players talk over who takes which open card and what they will give in return. Because everyone sees the same row, a promise is easy to check.
pros: Deals are about cards everyone can see.
A broken promise shows at once.
cons: Talk about the row can run long.
The player holding the most wanted card gets asked the most.

pairs.tendency: Sets are built from your own cards plus whatever is open in the middle. One open card can finish a set for three players at the same moment.
pros: Every set has a chance of being finished from the row.
Players can see how near others are to a set.
cons: The row empties fast when many need one colour.
A rival taking the last card can spoil a set.

pairs.tendency: Open cards in the middle say which kind of tile may go down next on the shared map. Whoever takes a card also takes the choice of where the map grows.
pros: The row decides how the map can grow.
Everyone sees what is coming.
cons: A card taken early changes the map for the next player.
A tile you wanted may stop fitting by your turn.

pairs.tendency: A card turned up in the middle is the call, and each player answers it with a card from their own hand. The row gives every answer something in common.
pros: Each answer is tied to a card all can see.
The chain of replies is easy to follow.
cons: Replies start to sound alike.
A new player has little to add once the row is full.

pairs.tendency: Without talking, players treat the open cards as a signal for what they plan to play. A card left lying in the middle can mean "I need this" to the whole table.
pros: The middle row carries messages for everyone.
Teams can read each other's plans from the cards.
cons: A player can read the wrong message into a card.
A silent table cannot ask what a card meant.

pairs.tendency: A rule can be changed so that the middle cards work differently, such as who may take them or how many lie there. Every change shows at once on the open row.
pros: Rule changes are easy to see on the table.
The row is a clear place to try a new rule.
cons: One change can make the open cards useless to some players.
Arguments start when two changes touch the same cards.

pairs.tendency: Cards in the middle stand for things that happen in the story, and each player decides what their character does about them. The open row works as a scene everyone shares.
pros: Everyone reacts to the same events.
Characters get pulled into each other's scenes.
cons: The same card is read in different ways.
Talk about what a card means can run long.

pairs.tendency: Cards in the middle are reached by flicking, stacking or balancing, and a clumsy hand can knock the open row over. Whatever you can reach and keep standing is yours to use.
pros: Hands decide who gets which open card.
The row changes shape as it is handled.
cons: A shaky hand can scatter the row for everyone.
Quick hands collect most of the open cards.

pairs.tendency: Each open card in the middle names a place or a feature, and players draw it onto the map as they go. The map grows from what the row says.
pros: Everyone adds to one picture.
The cards give the drawing a starting point.
cons: The map follows the order of the cards.
Slow drawers fall behind the row.

pairs.tendency: The pot sits in the middle beside the open cards, and a hand that uses those cards can win it. Everyone can count what the pot holds and what the row offers.
pros: The prize and the cards are both in view.
Players can work out who has a chance.
cons: The pot can grow while the row stays the same.
A close hand is hard to hide.

pairs.tendency: Cards in the middle say which pit to scoop from, and the seeds are dropped round the board one at a time. Players can plan a few moves ahead from the open row.
pros: The row narrows the choice of pit.
Where the last seed lands can be worked out ahead.
cons: Every player sees the same options.
A card taken early removes a pit from play.

pairs.tendency: An extra hand lies face down in the middle beside the open cards. A player who takes it looks in secret, then lays cards back among the open ones.
pros: Players may gamble on a hand nobody has seen.
Cards put back change what the others can use.
cons: The spare hand changes the row.
The player who looks first knows more than the rest.

pairs.tendency: Landing on a marked square lets you take or swap an open card, or makes you give one up. Each special square has a rule that works on the middle row.
pros: Squares and cards affect each other.
Everyone sees what a square will give.
cons: A square can empty the row for the next player.
Some squares are crossed over and never used.

pairs.tendency: Every open card in the middle has a price, and you pay from what you hold to take it. Cheap cards go first while dear ones sit waiting.
pros: Prices are printed where everyone can read them.
Saving up for a dear card is a visible plan.
cons: A dear card may sit untouched for many turns.
Spending early leaves little for later.

pairs.tendency: Open cards in the middle each offer a prize, and you share out your pieces or points between them. Putting many on one card leaves another with few.
pros: Every card has a visible price in effort.
You can guess where others will go.
cons: A card left alone may be taken cheaply.
Rivals can aim at the place you left thin.

pairs.tendency: When the signal comes, everyone grabs for an open card in the middle. The slowest hand goes without, and the row is thinner for the next round.
pros: Open cards turn the signal into a scramble.
Everyone is paying attention together.
cons: Quick players take more than their share.
Fewer cards are left each round.

pairs.tendency: Cards from your hand can be put back and swapped for open ones in the middle. The row changes with every swap, so what you saw last turn may be gone.
pros: Swaps are made in the open.
The row keeps changing.
cons: A swap tells others what you did not need.
Players may wait to see what others put down.

pairs.tendency: The discard pile and the open row both hold cards anyone may reach for. Taking the whole pile can bring in cards that suit the ones lying in the middle.
pros: The pile and the row are two places to look.
A big pile can be worth the wait.
cons: Taking the pile makes your hand heavy.
Others can see what you now hold.

pairs.tendency: With a trump suit named, a low trump lying in the middle row can beat a high card of another suit. Players look at the row first to see which suit is winning.
pros: The trump suit gives the row a clear order.
Players can count trumps in the middle.
cons: Trumps on the row can decide a round on their own.
Hands without trumps have little to add.

pairs.tendency: Two boards share one open row, so a card taken for one game is gone from the other. You are attacking in one place while defending in the other.
pros: One row feeds two games.
A single card can help on both boards.
cons: A choice for one board hurts the other.
It is easy to lose track of which board a card was meant for.

pairs.tendency: A wild card turned up in the middle can stand in for any card, and everyone sees it. The player who takes it can finish a set that was one piece short.
pros: Anyone can see when a gap could be filled.
The wild card changes the plans of the whole table.
cons: It is taken the moment it appears.
Without it, some sets may never close.

pairs.tendency: Each face-up card in the middle shows a move, and a piece that runs off one edge comes back on the opposite side. A card can send you far in one step.
pros: The row shows where pieces can end up.
A line can run all the way round.
cons: Pieces on opposite edges are close neighbours.
It is harder to see who is in range of whom.

pairs.tendency: The others ask yes or no questions about the cards in the middle, which are the clues. Each answer rules out some of the open cards.
pros: The open cards give questions something to aim at.
The answers narrow the row.
cons: A vague question wastes an answer.
The one answering can be asked too many times.

pairs.tendency: The first to reach the end wins, and open cards in the middle give the moves that get you there. Taking the card that fits you leaves a less useful one for the player behind.
pros: Players watch which cards speed up the others.
The race is easy to follow.
cons: The leader can empty the row.
A late player may find only cards that do not help.

pairs.tendency: Points come from using the open cards in the middle together with your own. Everyone can see what each card is worth, so the score is open to guess at.
pros: Scores can be worked out from the table.
The row gives every player the same chances.
cons: One high-scoring card can swing the score.
Players may take cards only to keep them from others.

pairs.tendency: Players are knocked out one by one, and the open cards in the middle go on being used by those still in. The row gets shorter as fewer players are left.
pros: Open cards give knocked-out players something to watch.
Those left can use more cards.
cons: Early losers wait a long time.
The last few players see the same few cards every turn.

pairs.tendency: The face-up row warns the team what the game is about to throw at it. Together the players decide who takes which card and who gets protected.
pros: Everyone sees the same danger.
Planning is shared.
cons: The loudest voice can take over the choices.
One wrong pick can sink the whole team.

pairs.tendency: A goal is shared by everyone, and each open card in the middle is a step towards it. Players work out together which cards to take and in what order.
pros: The team can see what is needed.
Each card has an agreed purpose.
cons: One player may do most of the planning.
A card taken out of order can hold everyone up.

pairs.tendency: The middle row is the same for everyone, but each player reads it against a secret goal. Two players may take the same card for very different reasons.
pros: The same cards mean different things to each player.
A pick gives little away.
cons: It is hard to guess what another player is doing.
Someone who takes a card nobody expected is noticed.

pairs.tendency: The next parts of the story lie face up in the middle, and players choose which to use and how it ends. The story is over when the cards that finish it have been played.
pros: The story is built from visible pieces.
Players can steer it together.
cons: The ending can be settled early by one card.
Several players may want to end it differently.

pairs.tendency: Cards sit in the middle for everyone, but no one is trying to win. Players take cards, arrange them and look at what the row has become.
pros: The row becomes the thing to look at.
Talk comes easily.
cons: Without a goal, players may not know when to take a card.
The game can end without anyone noticing.

pairs.tendency: Each player picks what doing well means before the game and then reads the middle row against it. One player wants a full set, another wants only a single card.
pros: Each player can reach a goal from the same row.
The row makes it easy to say what is being aimed at.
cons: Players may take cards others need for their own goals.
The table cannot compare scores.

pairs.tendency: Nobody wins, and the game goes on until one player is stuck with the unwanted card. The middle row shows what the others are able to pass on.
pros: Players can see who is close to being stuck.
Everyone but one is safe.
cons: The last card passed can be seen coming.
The one who loses may be the one who took longest to decide.

pairs.tendency: The middle row is topped up so that there are always open cards for the next player. The aim is to keep play moving, so players choose cards that leave useful ones for others.
pros: The row keeps the game supplied.
Players think about each other's next turn.
cons: A row that empties stops the game.
Nobody can win, so nothing marks the end.

pairs.tendency: Cards are laid out in the middle and nobody can win with them. Players pick them up and find that the game does not reward them.
pros: The row is the whole game.
Players notice their own habits.
cons: Some players keep looking for a way to score.
The game can feel pointless to those who expect a result.

pairs.tendency: The cards laid out in the middle are the puzzle, and one player works to clear them or build them into place. Every card in the row is in view from the start.
pros: The whole puzzle is visible.
The solver can plan many moves ahead.
cons: One wrong move can leave the table stuck.
Nobody else shares the puzzle.

pairs.tendency: The same open cards can be set out again for each short game, so a row seen in game one comes back in game two. Players remember which cards helped them.
pros: Players learn the cards across games.
A loser can try a new plan on the same row.
cons: A lead from one game may carry into the next.
The later games can feel the same as the first.

pairs.tendency: Cards in the middle carry points that count against whoever takes them. Players avoid taking a heavy card and wait for someone else to give in.
pros: Players can read each card's price on sight.
Waiting is a choice that shows.
cons: Taking a card can hurt more than it helps.
The row can freeze while everyone waits.

pairs.tendency: A target number is set, and open cards in the middle give the amounts that can reach it. Going past the target ruins the hand, so the row is read closely.
pros: The row shows which amounts are left.
Players can count how close others are.
cons: Going over costs the win.
The last few points are hard to land.

pairs.tendency: The aim is to give everything away, and the open cards in the middle are the ones you can drop into the row. A card that helps another player empty their hand helps them win.
pros: The row is a place to send cards.
Players watch each other's hands shrink.
cons: A player who is close to done is easy to spot.
Dumping on the row can help a rival.

pairs.tendency: Each player works on their own plan, and the open cards in the middle are the only thing they share. A card taken by one player takes a choice from the rest.
pros: Players get on with their own work.
The row is the one place where they meet.
cons: Little talk happens apart from the row.
A card taken by a quiet player can surprise the table.

pairs.tendency: Players attack each other and the open cards in the middle supply the weapons. A card taken is a card denied, so each pick is aimed.
pros: Attacks are made with visible tools.
Players can see what an attack will cost.
cons: Cards go to the player with the most reach.
A player under attack can lose most of their choices.

pairs.tendency: Players never hit each other directly, and the open cards in the middle are used to change the board. Others feel the effect through where the pieces now stand.
pros: The row shows how the board may change.
Rivals meet only through the board.
cons: A move can hurt someone with no warning.
It is hard to say who caused a change.

pairs.tendency: The whole team shares the open cards in the middle, deciding together which to use. All win or lose on how the row is spent.
pros: The row is a shared stock.
Everyone can see the problem.
cons: Spending one card leaves less for others.
Players may argue over the same card.

pairs.tendency: The team uses the open cards in the middle to meet a shared aim while each player has a small reason to want more than the rest. A card taken for the team may also help one player.
pros: Everyone is helped by the row.
Players can see who takes extra.
cons: A card can serve two purposes.
Trust wears down when one player always benefits.

pairs.tendency: Each team uses the open cards in the middle against the other, and teammates talk over which to take. A card one team takes is lost to the other.
pros: Teammates plan together on a shared row.
Teams can see each other's choices.
cons: Quiet players may go unheard.
A pick for one teammate can leave another without a card.

pairs.tendency: Everyone takes from the middle row, and one player secretly uses those cards against the team. A card used oddly is the first clue.
pros: The row gives the others something to check.
A strange pick stands out.
cons: Players start to doubt each other's picks.
A careful traitor can hide among normal picks.

pairs.tendency: Each letter describes the face-up cards, so players far apart see the same row. Several days can pass before a card is taken.
pros: Everyone reads the same row at their own pace.
Plans can be thought through between letters.
cons: The row may change while a letter is on its way.
A player can lose a card they named a week ago.

pairs.tendency: One player is not at the table, but their pick from the open cards in the middle is made for them. The ghost or earlier player leaves their mark on the row.
pros: The missing player still shapes the row.
Present players have a rival they cannot argue with.
cons: Their cards are gone from play.
Nobody can ask them what they meant.

pairs.tendency: The game master sets out the open cards in the middle and tells what they mean. Players choose what their characters do with the row.
pros: The master controls what the row shows.
Players share a scene.
cons: The master has to decide quickly which cards to open.
Players depend on the master's reading of each card.

pairs.tendency: The face-up cards are laid out where anyone passing can see them and join in. A newcomer can pick up a card and be part of the game.
pros: Strangers can take part at once.
The game is easy to read from a distance.
cons: Passers-by can take cards away.
The row may be disturbed by people who do not know the rules.

pairs.tendency: One player uses the open cards in the middle against all the others, who share them as a team. A card taken by the team is not available to the lone player.
pros: The lone player faces the whole row alone.
The team can talk about the row.
cons: The lone player has fewer cards to use.
The team may argue over which card to take.

pairs.tendency: A row of open cards in the middle is dealt out and you work through it alone. Nobody else takes a card, so the row only changes when you change it.
pros: The whole row is yours to plan.
You can try a different plan on the same cards.
cons: There is no rival to react to.
The game ends when you run out of moves.

pairs.tendency: Cards turned up at random in the middle decide almost everything. Players take what appears and wait for the next card.
pros: Open cards make the luck visible.
The game moves fast.
cons: Choices matter very little.
Players can feel the result was decided before they played.

pairs.tendency: Cards in the middle come up at random, but players have ways to swap or set them aside. An unlucky draw can be softened by taking a different open card.
pros: The row gives you a way out of an unlucky draw.
Luck is shared out in the open.
cons: Using the way out costs a turn.
The luck of the draw still shows in the end.

pairs.tendency: Mostly your own choices decide the game, with a little chance in which cards turn up in the middle. A skilled player makes use of whatever the row shows.
pros: Planning counts for most.
The row adds a surprise to each round.
cons: A lucky row can help a weaker plan.
A skilled player can be held back by a row that does not suit them.

pairs.tendency: Every card in the middle is in view and nothing is left to chance. Players work out the row and pick the move that suits them.
pros: Nothing is hidden.
Careful play is rewarded.
cons: Thinking can take a long time.
Players who spot the pattern first have a head start.

pairs.tendency: Nobody counts the cards in the middle; they are read as a message. Players talk about what the row seems to say and what it means for them.
pros: The row gives something to talk about.
Different people read different things.
cons: Readings cannot be checked.
Players may disagree about what a card says.

pairs.tendency: Players take from the middle row when they sense the others are about to act. A card taken at the right moment shows that the table has the same idea.
pros: Players learn each other's habits.
The row marks a shared moment.
cons: Misjudged timing leaves two hands on one card.
Newcomers find it hard to join in.

pairs.tendency: A dice roll is looked up on a table, and the result tells which open cards in the middle come into play in the story. The dice choose which part of the row matters.
pros: The dice pick from a visible row.
Story and cards fit together.
cons: Luck can leave a card unused.
The roll can send the story somewhere nobody planned.

pairs.tendency: Everything is in view, and the open cards in the middle are no secret. Players know what is on the row and what the others are likely to take.
pros: Plans can be worked out.
There are no surprises in the row.
cons: Planning takes a long time.
A hand that is already behind is easy to see.

pairs.tendency: Each player holds cards that no one else can see, and the open cards in the middle are the one part everyone shares. Reading the row against your hand is where the guessing starts.
pros: The row and hand work together.
Bluffing has a base to stand on.
cons: What you take from the row gives your hand away.
Players cannot be sure what the others hold.

pairs.tendency: Players have secret roles and the open cards in the middle are the only common ground. Which card a player takes tells the table something about who they are.
pros: The row gives clues to roles.
A pick is a small piece of evidence.
cons: A clever player picks cards that mislead.
Players may accuse others on thin evidence.

pairs.tendency: Each face-up card is a clue, and players work out hidden facts by what is on the row and what is missing. Each card taken or left tells you something.
pros: The row offers clear clues.
Each card taken leaves a mark.
cons: Players may take a clue to keep it from others.
A wrong reading takes a long time to correct.

pairs.tendency: You may take an open card in the middle only to make others think you need it. Your hand and the row together are what you pretend about.
pros: The row gives bluffs something to point at.
Others can check what you say against the table.
cons: A bluff that is caught costs a turn.
A true pick can be doubted.

pairs.tendency: One player knows a secret rule about the open cards in the middle, and the rest find it out by taking cards and being told no. The row is the test ground.
pros: Each wrong pick teaches something.
The row stays in view while players learn.
cons: The rule is found only by trial.
Players who have not found it yet may feel lost.

pairs.tendency: One player knows which face-up card is right but can only hint at it. The others pick from the row and learn from the hint whether they are close.
pros: The hints point at cards everyone can see.
The row narrows as guesses are made.
cons: A hint can be read the wrong way.
The one who knows can only watch.

pairs.tendency: Open cards in the middle are turned over as areas of the map are explored. Each reveal adds a card to the row and a place to the map.
pros: The row grows with the map.
Players learn the board together.
cons: A reveal can change the row for everyone.
An early explorer shows the others where to go.

pairs.tendency: One hand is spread face up beside the open cards in the middle. Everyone can see two sets of cards at once, and one player plays the open hand as well as their own.
pros: The table sees more than usual.
One player has two hands to plan.
cons: The player with two hands has more to think about.
The others can predict the open hand's plays.

pairs.tendency: The cards in the middle are open, but some points are kept secret. Everyone sees what is taken and nobody is sure what it adds up to.
pros: Cards are public and scores are not.
Players guess who is ahead.
cons: A pick can be misread as a plan.
Surprises come at the final count.

pairs.tendency: One player at a time takes from the open cards in the middle. Everyone else watches the row change and plans their own turn.
pros: The row changes in clear steps.
Waiting players can plan.
cons: The row may change a lot before your turn.
Long waits with many players.

pairs.tendency: All players pick from the open cards in the middle together and in secret. When the picks are shown, two people may have chosen the same card.
pros: Nobody waits.
The row is shared fairly.
cons: Two players taking one card causes a tie.
The picks are hard to take back.

pairs.tendency: Anyone may reach for an open card at any moment, and the quickest hand takes it. The row is a scramble from the start.
pros: Everything happens at speed.
Everyone is watching the row at once.
cons: Quick players take most of the cards.
It is hard to keep track of who took what.

pairs.tendency: Each turn has a clock, and the open cards in the middle have to be chosen before it runs out. A player who hesitates loses the pick or has one made for them.
pros: The clock keeps turns short.
The row is read quickly.
cons: A rushed pick can be a mismatch with the hand.
Players who read slowly feel pressed.

pairs.tendency: Open cards in the middle stay out for days or weeks, and each player takes one when their turn comes round. The row changes slowly.
pros: Players have time to think.
A card can be watched for days.
cons: A slow player holds the game up.
Waiting is part of the game.

pairs.tendency: The game slows down on purpose, and the open cards in the middle are looked at for a long while before anyone reaches out. A pause is built in before each pick.
pros: The row can be studied in full.
Each pick is made slowly.
cons: Players may lose the thread.
The pace tests patience.

pairs.tendency: Rounds get shorter, and open cards in the middle are taken faster each time. The row has less time to fill before it is emptied again.
pros: The pace builds up.
Players learn the row quickly.
cons: Late rounds are rushed.
Slow players get left behind.

pairs.tendency: A player who earns an extra turn can reach into the open cards in the middle twice in a row. The row can change a lot before anyone else moves.
pros: One player can take two cards.
The extra turn is easy to see.
cons: The row may be emptied by a lucky player.
The others cannot respond in between.

pairs.tendency: The game has stages, and the open cards in the middle are chosen in the first stage and used in the second. What you took from the row sets up what you can do next.
pros: The first stage prepares the second.
The row can change between stages.
cons: A pick made too early may be a mistake later.
The rules change halfway.

pairs.tendency: Open cards in the middle stand for parts of a real system, such as water, grain or workers. Taking a card from the row changes what is left for the rest of the system.
pros: The row shows real pressures.
Players see cause and effect.
cons: One card taken can change the whole row.
The model leaves many things out.

pairs.tendency: Each player speaks for a group, and the open cards in the middle are the things all groups want. A farmer, a council and a shopkeeper may each reach for the same card.
pros: Players see the problem from different sides.
The row makes the conflict visible.
cons: One group may take most of the cards.
Roles can pull players away from the aim.

pairs.tendency: All players take from the middle row, and its supply is limited. If too many are taken, none are left for the next round.
pros: The row shows what is left.
Players can see who takes most.
cons: The row can run out for everyone.
One heavy taker affects the whole table.

pairs.tendency: Take a card from the row and its effect shows only some rounds later. The row changes now, but the result comes after.
pros: Choices are linked across rounds.
Players see patterns develop.
cons: Cause and effect are hard to link.
A pick can have a late effect nobody expected.

pairs.tendency: Players agree a new rule for the open cards in the middle, then play on to see what changes. The row shows the effect at once.
pros: Rules are tried in the open.
Players can compare before and after.
cons: A new rule may confuse the table.
One round may not show the whole effect.

pairs.tendency: After the game the open cards in the middle are talked through one by one. Players say why they took or left each card.
pros: The row helps people remember.
Players hear each other's reasons.
cons: Memory fades for early picks.
Talk can drift away from the cards.

pairs.tendency: A card taken from the open row may be torn or marked, and the next game starts from that changed row. Nothing can be put back.
pros: Each pick leaves a trace.
The row records the game.
cons: A mistake stays on the card.
Later games begin from what is left.

pairs.tendency: The rules for the open cards in the middle make a point about the world. If only some cards can be taken, the game says something about who gets what.
pros: The row carries the argument.
Players feel the rule through play.
cons: The point can be missed.
Players may argue with the rules.

pairs.tendency: Each card taken from the row costs real money or a real promise. Each pick has weight beyond the table.
pros: Picks feel more serious.
Players pay close attention.
cons: Some players may avoid taking anything.
A friendship can be tested over one card.

pairs.tendency: Open cards in the middle carry points that stand for something like health or kindness. Players chase the points and may forget what they stood for.
pros: The row shows how a number replaces a value.
Players can talk about the swap afterwards.
cons: Chasing points can push other aims aside.
The values on the cards are simplified.

pairs.tendency: The face-up cards describe a way of living that does not yet exist. Players take cards and act as if that world were real.
pros: The row sets out the new world.
Players feel how it might be.
cons: Cards cannot show every detail.
A rehearsal may differ from real life.

pairs.tendency: Everyone puts a counter in the middle before the first throw, and the one who reaches the end collects it all. Each throw is watched with the pot in mind.
pros: The prize is clear from the start.
Every throw matters to the pot.
cons: A long game keeps the pot out of reach.
Players behind may give up hope of it.

pairs.tendency: Players add to the pot, then pick cards one at a time from the shared row. The prize goes to whoever's picks make the highest hand.
pros: The pot makes each pick count.
Players watch the others' choices.
cons: A pick that blocks a rival may cost your own hand.
The player who picks last gets what is left.

pairs.tendency: The pot is the prize in an auction, and bids are offered for it. Bidders know they are paying for something that grew from their own counters.
pros: The prize is known to all.
Bids can climb toward the pot's value.
cons: Bids may exceed what the pot holds.
A winner can end up paying for their own money.

pairs.tendency: Each player risks what they have for a bigger share of the pot. A bust leaves the pot for the others.
pros: The pot grows with the risk.
Players watch each other's choices.
cons: A bust can enrich a rival.
The pot tempts players into one more try.

pairs.tendency: When the round ends, whoever holds the most areas collects the pot. Pieces spread across the map with the pot in mind.
pros: The pot gives the map a purpose.
Areas are clear targets.
cons: A late move can take the pot.
Players who hold nothing have no share.

pairs.tendency: The pot is on the board as a job space, and the worker who takes it wins what is inside. Others can only block it by placing first.
pros: The pot is a place to go.
Placing first is a real choice.
cons: A blocked pot waits and grows.
Workers placed for the pot do not do other jobs.

pairs.tendency: The pot goes to the first player to complete a pattern. Everyone's counters sit in the middle while patterns grow.
pros: The pattern has a clear prize.
Players can see rivals' progress.
cons: A pattern started late may never finish.
Players might copy each other's pattern.

pairs.tendency: Whoever holds the winning hand takes the pot. Cards are held or played with the prize in the middle in mind.
pros: A held card can win the pot.
The pot raises the cost of mistakes.
cons: Playing too early gives your plan away.
A hand held too long never wins anything.

pairs.tendency: The pot goes to whoever takes the final trick, or the most tricks. Each trick is played with that prize in view.
pros: Every trick leads towards the pot.
Players watch the count of tricks.
cons: An early lead can be lost late.
The pot may be won by a single card.

pairs.tendency: Players bargain over how to share the pot. A promise to split it can win help now.
pros: Deals can be made about a prize all can see.
Players can agree to share.
cons: A deal may be broken at the last move.
Talk about shares can take a long time.

pairs.tendency: The first full set takes the pot. Players keep their sets hidden or open while the prize waits in the middle.
pros: A full set has a clear reward.
Players hurry to finish.
cons: A rival can finish first by one card.
The pot passes over everyone who is one card short.

pairs.tendency: Completing a road, city or field on the shared map wins the pot. Each tile is laid with the pot in mind.
pros: The map has a prize to build towards.
Tiles are chosen with care.
cons: A tile placed to help can help a rival.
The pot may be won by whoever lays the last tile.

pairs.tendency: Whoever keeps the chain going longest wins the pot. Each answer in the chain is made with the prize in view.
pros: The chain has a clear reward.
Answers get more careful.
cons: One missed answer ends the chain.
A pot of counters can make a light game tense.

pairs.tendency: Everyone puts a counter in, then plays without a word. The pot goes to the table if the silent plan works.
pros: The team needs one plan to win it.
Signals are watched closely.
cons: A misunderstanding costs everyone.
No one can explain a mistake.

pairs.tendency: A rule can change how the pot is paid, who adds to it or who wins it. Players change the rules with the prize in mind.
pros: Rule changes have a visible target.
Players debate the pot's rules.
cons: A change made for one player may hurt the rest.
Arguments about the pot can stop play.

pairs.tendency: Players add to the pot as their characters, and the pot is paid out when the story reaches a turning point. A character may win it by what they do.
pros: Characters have something to gain.
The story gets a prize.
cons: Characters may be driven by the pot alone.
The prize can pull attention from the story.

pairs.tendency: The steadiest hand at flicking, stacking or balancing wins the pot. Everyone watches the fingers.
pros: A skill test has a clear prize.
The table goes quiet at the deciding throw.
cons: A shaky hand loses the pot.
The same player may win again and again.

pairs.tendency: The pot is shared out as places on the map are drawn in. A player who draws a feature first may claim a share.
pros: The map gives out the prize.
Players draw with a purpose.
cons: Early drawing wins the pot.
Late players are left with the edges.

pairs.tendency: The pot is a pit of its own and the seeds collect in it as players sow. Whoever ends a sowing there takes all that has gathered.
pros: Seeds make the pot grow.
The last seed matters most.
cons: A player can miss the pot by one pit.
Players may avoid the pit to keep others from it.

pairs.tendency: A spare hand sits face down beside the pot. A player may pay to take it and hope it beats the cards in play.
pros: The spare hand and the pot sit side by side.
Taking a spare hand is a gamble.
cons: Paying for a hand that fails costs counters.
Whoever looks first learns the most.

pairs.tendency: A special square sends counters into the pot or lets a player take from it. Landing on the right square becomes worth a lot.
pros: Squares change the pot.
Everyone sees where the prize can be had.
cons: A square can empty the pot for the next player.
Some players walk into a square by chance.

pairs.tendency: Spending something to use a card or item also feeds the pot. Dear things add more to the prize.
pros: Spending has a second effect.
Players see the pot grow with each buy.
cons: Paying for a big card can feed a rival's prize.
Saving can mean giving up a chance at the pot.

pairs.tendency: Pieces or points are shared between several places, and the pot is awarded to the one who wins the most places. The pot is only for the player who shares out their pieces most cleverly.
pros: The pot rewards careful sharing.
Rivals guess where you will go.
cons: Thin cover loses places.
Everything on one place leaves others bare.

pairs.tendency: When the signal comes, the slowest player pays into the pot or goes out. The pot grows from each round of grabbing.
pros: Each stop feeds the pot.
The signal keeps everyone alert.
cons: A slow player pays most often.
The pot can grow quickly.

pairs.tendency: Players swap cards to improve their hands, with the pot waiting for the highest one. A swap shows what you are after.
pros: Swapping is a way to chase the pot.
Players watch what others give up.
cons: A swap can help a rival.
The last swap before a show decides much.

pairs.tendency: The discard pile is taken by a player who can use the top card, and the pot sits beside it as a second prize. A big pile and a big pot together raise the stakes.
pros: The pile and pot are both prizes.
Taking the pile has a clear use.
cons: A heavy pile holds you back.
Others can read the pile you took.

pairs.tendency: A player who wins with trumps takes the pot, and a low trump can beat a high card. Players count trumps while the pot waits.
pros: The trump suit gives a clear order.
Players look at the pot while counting.
cons: One trump card can take the whole pot.
Hands without trumps have little hope.

pairs.tendency: The pot is shared between two boards, and a player can win it on one of them. Attacking on one board and defending on the other both matter.
pros: One pot sits over two boards.
A win on either board can take it.
cons: Time spent on one board costs time on the other.
The pot is easy to forget in the middle of a move.

pairs.tendency: A wild card can complete the hand that takes the pot. A player holding one has a stand-in for any missing piece.
pros: One wild card can win the pot.
Players guess who holds one.
cons: A wild card in the wrong hand costs others the pot.
Without it, some hands cannot close.

pairs.tendency: The pot goes to the first line that runs off one edge and back on the other. Edges that join make lines longer than they look.
pros: A joined edge gives more ways to win.
Lines are harder to block.
cons: A line can come back from an unexpected side.
Players need time to learn the edges.

pairs.tendency: Finding the secret wins the pot, and every yes or no takes the others a step closer. A wrong guess may add a counter.
pros: Each question narrows the search.
The pot rewards the final guess.
cons: A guess too early costs a counter.
The one answering has a hard job.

pairs.tendency: The first player to the end takes the whole pot. Each player's counter is the price of entry to the race.
pros: The prize is clear and the race is short.
Players follow each other closely.
cons: The leader is chased by everyone.
Last place has little reason to go on.

pairs.tendency: The pot is added to the final score of the player with the most points. Players count the pot as part of what they play for.
pros: The pot adds to the final count.
Players can see who is ahead.
cons: A pot can decide a close game.
A player far behind may stop trying.

pairs.tendency: Players drop out one by one, and the last one takes the pot. Every counter is paid in before the first player is knocked out.
pros: The prize goes to the survivor.
The game gets tense near the end.
cons: Early losers have nothing to hope for.
The pot is out of reach for those who leave first.

pairs.tendency: The team builds the pot together and shares it if everyone survives. The pot is the team's reward for getting through.
pros: The prize is shared.
Everyone has a reason to help.
cons: One lost player can cost the pot.
A team that fails loses its counters.

pairs.tendency: The pot is paid out to the whole team when the shared goal is reached. Players add to it as they go.
pros: The goal has a prize.
The team follows the pot's growth.
cons: Reaching the goal late costs nothing but time.
A team that fails shares the loss.

pairs.tendency: Each player has a secret goal, and only one of them wins the pot. Counters are in the middle while goals stay hidden.
pros: The prize hides who is close.
Players guess at each other's goals.
cons: A show of interest in the pot gives your goal away.
A player can win by seeming not to try.

pairs.tendency: The pot is paid out when the story ends, to the player who shaped its ending. Players add to it while the story grows.
pros: The ending has a prize.
Players push the story towards their own end.
cons: Several endings may each claim the pot.
The story may bend to fit the prize.

pairs.tendency: Counters go into the middle and nobody wins them. At the end the pot is looked at, shared or given away.
pros: The pot is a thing to look at.
Players decide together what it is for.
cons: Nobody knows what to do with it.
The game can stop without a clear end.

pairs.tendency: Each player says what doing well means, and the pot may be shared out according to those goals. One player may only want to save a single counter.
pros: Goals come first and the pot follows.
Players can ask each other what they want.
cons: No score settles who gets the pot.
Players with large goals can claim most of it.

pairs.tendency: Everyone puts in a counter and the one who loses pays more. The pot grows each round the loser stays unsettled.
pros: Only one player carries the cost.
Everyone else is safe.
cons: A loser may be stuck for many rounds.
The loser may have put in the most.

pairs.tendency: The pot is passed on and added to each round so there is always a prize for the next. Winning one round only feeds the next.
pros: The pot never ends.
Players look ahead.
cons: Prizes are small compared to the game's length.
There is no moment where the game is done.

pairs.tendency: Counters go into the middle but nobody can take them out. The pot piles up and the game shows what players do when there is nothing to win.
pros: The pot is only there to be looked at.
Players notice what they expected.
cons: Some try to take it anyway.
The game can feel strange to those who expect a prize.

pairs.tendency: You put counters into a pot that is only yours if you clear the layout. A stuck table can lose the lot.
pros: The prize is a clear reward for solving the puzzle.
You decide how much to put in.
cons: A stuck game costs your counters.
Nobody else shares the prize.

pairs.tendency: Each short game has its own pot, and the winner of most games wins the biggest prize. Counters from earlier games can be carried forward.
pros: Every game has something at stake.
The leader can be caught late.
cons: Pots from early games pile up.
A losing player can stop trying early.

pairs.tendency: At the end, the lowest score takes the pot. Each point you pick up is a step away from it.
pros: The prize rewards avoiding points.
Players watch each other's totals.
cons: A heavy score drops you out of the running.
Giving points to others can win the pot.

pairs.tendency: The pot goes to the first player who lands exactly on the target. A throw past the number puts a counter in the pot instead.
pros: Overshooting feeds the prize.
Players count closely.
cons: An exact finish is hard to land.
The pot grows while players miss.

pairs.tendency: The player who gives everything away wins the pot. Each card dropped is a step towards it.
pros: The prize goes to the emptiest hand.
Players watch each other's hands.
cons: Helping another player empty their hand helps them win.
The pot is out of reach for the last to finish.

pairs.tendency: Players work alone, and the pot goes to whoever finishes first or scores most. The only way players affect each other is through the prize.
pros: The pot is the one shared thing.
Players focus on their own work.
cons: Little happens between players.
The winner is clear only at the end.

pairs.tendency: Players attack each other for control of the pot. Whoever takes a rival's counters adds them to their own claim.
pros: The pot gives a reason to attack.
Targets are easy to pick.
cons: A leader is attacked by everyone.
Early hits can end a player's chances.

pairs.tendency: Players change the board and the pot is paid to the one whose changes pay off. Nobody attacks, yet the pot moves with the board.
pros: The pot follows the board.
Players meet only through their effects.
cons: A board change can cost someone the pot.
It is hard to see who helped whom.

pairs.tendency: The whole team builds the pot together and shares it, or loses it together. The pot measures how the team did.
pros: Everyone has the same stake.
Players help each other.
cons: One mistake can lose the pot for all.
Disagreements affect everyone's share.

pairs.tendency: The team works for a shared pot while each player hopes for a bigger share. A player may help the team and help themselves with the same move.
pros: Cooperation has a prize.
Players can see who takes more.
cons: Trust wears down if one player takes the most.
The team may fall apart at the last moment.

pairs.tendency: Each team pays into the pot and the winning team shares it. Teammates plan together to bring it home.
pros: Teams pool their effort.
The prize is split among teammates.
cons: One slow player holds the team back.
Splitting the pot can lead to arguments.

pairs.tendency: The team plays for the pot while one player secretly works against it. If the traitor wins, the traitor takes the pot.
pros: The pot raises the cost of a traitor's success.
The team watches for odd moves.
cons: A false accusation harms the team.
A careful traitor can go unseen.

pairs.tendency: Each player sends a counter by post to the pot, and the pot grows over weeks. The winner is told by letter.
pros: The pot grows slowly.
Players have time to plan.
cons: Waiting for the prize takes long.
Counters can get lost on the way.

pairs.tendency: An absent player may have a share in the pot, kept for them or given up. Their counter is in the middle although they are not there.
pros: The missing player still has a stake.
Present players think about the absent one.
cons: The absent player's share has to be dealt with.
Nobody can ask what the absent player wants.

pairs.tendency: The game master holds the pot and decides who gets it. Players act in the story to earn it.
pros: The master controls the prize.
Players try to win the master's favour.
cons: A choice by the master can seem to favour some players.
The master cannot win the pot.

pairs.tendency: Passers-by add counters to the pot as they join in. A street crowd can grow the pot quickly.
pros: Anyone can add to the prize.
The pot can grow large.
cons: Strangers may join and leave with the counters.
It is hard to say who has paid in.

pairs.tendency: The lone player and the team each pay in, and the lone player gets more if they win. The pot is paid out by who wins the contest.
pros: The lone player has a bigger prize.
The team faces a clear target.
cons: The team has to share the pot between them.
The lone player may have little chance.

pairs.tendency: You play against the pack for a pot you set aside yourself. The pot is only a mark of how well you did.
pros: The pot is a personal measure.
You can try again and compare.
