cons: There is nobody to win it from.
Without rivals the pot means little.

pairs.tendency: The pot goes to whoever the dice or cards favour. Nobody can do much to change who wins it.
pros: The prize is open to all.
Play is quick.
cons: Choices make little difference.
A player may lose counters with no say.

pairs.tendency: Chance decides who wins the pot, but players have ways to soften a low throw. Re-rolls and cards give some control.
pros: The pot is not decided by luck alone.
Players can protect their counters.
cons: Using a re-roll costs something.
The luck of the draw still shows.

pairs.tendency: The pot mostly goes to the player who plays with most skill, with a small chance element. A skilled player is more likely to take it but not sure to.
pros: Skill earns the pot most of the time.
Luck keeps others in the race.
cons: A skilled player can still lose.
A lucky player can take the pot with little effort.

pairs.tendency: Nothing is left to chance, so the most careful player takes the pot. Players work through each move with the prize in mind.
pros: Planning decides the prize.
Nothing comes as a surprise.
cons: One player can keep winning.
Players behind can see they have little hope.

pairs.tendency: Players throw dice or cards and read the result as a message, and the pot is shared by what the reading says. The meaning of a throw is argued over.
pros: The throw gives people something to discuss.
Players explain their readings.
cons: Nobody can prove a reading right.
The pot may be shared out by agreement, with no rule to settle it.

pairs.tendency: The pot goes to the players who act in step with one another. Nobody wins alone if the table is out of tune.
pros: The pot rewards a shared sense of timing.
Players watch each other.
cons: One player out of step costs the pot.
New players find it hard to join in.

pairs.tendency: The dice are looked up on a table that says what happens, and the pot is paid out when a certain result comes up. Luck writes part of the story and also decides the prize.
pros: The pot ties a result to a story.
Players wait for a key roll.
cons: The story can end on one roll.
A prize won by chance may feel odd in a story.

pairs.tendency: Everything is in view, including the pot and what each player has added. Players can work out how to take it.
pros: All the facts are on the table.
Players can plan with care.
cons: Nothing unexpected happens.
The pot may go to the player who thinks longest.

pairs.tendency: Each player holds hidden cards while the pot sits in the middle for all to see. The pot is won by the player whose hidden hand turns out highest.
pros: The pot adds a reason to bluff.
Players guess from the bets.
cons: A big bet gives your hand away.
Players cannot be sure what they are paying for.

pairs.tendency: Secret roles divide the table, and the pot goes to the winning side. A player who watches the pot closely may give away which side they are on.
pros: The pot is a target for each side.
Players guess roles from what they do.
cons: A hidden player may be found by their interest in the pot.
Accusations can be mistaken.

pairs.tendency: Working out the hidden fact first wins the pot. A wrong guess may cost a counter.
pros: The prize rewards clear thinking.
Clues are worth a lot.
cons: A wrong guess is paid for.
Players may wait for others to guess first.

pairs.tendency: Players bet counters into the pot while pretending to have a higher hand. A bluff that works takes the pot with nothing behind it.
pros: The pot makes a bluff worth trying.
Players watch faces and bets.
cons: A bluff that fails costs counters.
A true hand can be doubted.

pairs.tendency: Players try things to find a secret rule, and the pot goes to the first who works it out. Each wrong try may add a counter to the pot.
pros: Wrong tries feed the pot.
The prize rewards learning.
cons: New players pay more at the start.
Only trial and error reveals it.

pairs.tendency: The player who knows the answer cannot say it, and the pot goes to the guesser who gets it right. Hints are the only help.
pros: The prize rewards reading the hint.
The one who knows has a hard task.
cons: A hint can mislead.
Players might guess wildly for the pot.

pairs.tendency: The pot is hidden on the map and goes to the player who finds it first. Each area turned over brings players closer.
pros: The map holds the prize.
Exploring has a purpose.
cons: An early reveal helps all players.
The pot may be found by chance.

pairs.tendency: One hand is shown face up and every player can see what it can do. The pot goes to whoever plays the open hand, or their own hand, to the highest result.
pros: The open hand shows what is possible.
One player has two hands to play.
cons: Running two hands is hard work.
The others can see what is coming.

pairs.tendency: Scores are partly secret, so nobody knows who will take the pot. Players guess who is ahead from what they see.
pros: The pot hides who is close.
Guessing becomes part of the game.
cons: Surprises come at the end.
A player may give up when still ahead.

pairs.tendency: Turns pass round the table, each player adding to or taking from the pot while the rest watch it change.
pros: Each change to the pot is easy to follow.
Others think while they wait.
cons: By your turn the pot may look very different.
With a big table, the wait is long.

pairs.tendency: All players choose in secret and reveal together, and the pot goes to the winning choice. Nobody waits for anybody.
pros: The pot is settled in one go.
Everyone acts at once.
cons: Two players may pick the same thing.
Choices are hard to take back.

pairs.tendency: There are no turns, and the first hand to reach the pot wins it.
pros: Rounds are over quickly.
Everyone watches the pot.
cons: The fastest hands collect the most.
Nobody is sure who grabbed what.

pairs.tendency: A player who runs out of time on the turn clock puts a counter in the pot. The pot grows from slow decisions.
pros: Time costs counters.
Turns stay short.
cons: Slow thinkers pay most.
Rushed choices can be careless.

pairs.tendency: The pot grows over days or weeks as players take their turns. Each morning someone adds to it or takes from it.
pros: The pot builds up slowly.
Players think between turns.
cons: The prize is slow to come.
A player who forgets a day loses a turn.

pairs.tendency: Play is kept slow on purpose, and the pot sits waiting while players pause before each move. Each counter is added with care.
pros: The prize is in view for a long time.
Each move is slow and clear.
cons: Players may lose interest.
The pot can seem far away.

pairs.tendency: Each round is shorter than the last, and the pot grows faster as play speeds up. The end comes in a rush.
pros: The pot swells in later rounds.
Play gets quicker.
cons: The last rounds leave little time to think.
Slower players cannot keep up.

pairs.tendency: An extra turn lets one player take from the pot twice before anyone else moves. A lucky streak can empty it.
pros: One player can take a lot.
Everyone sees the double move.
cons: Nobody can answer until both moves are done.
A lucky player may take the whole pot.

pairs.tendency: The pot is built in the first stage and paid out in the second. What you did in the first stage decides your claim.
pros: The first stage feeds the pot.
The second stage uses it.
cons: A stake put in too early may be lost.
Play shifts to new rules midway.

pairs.tendency: The pot stands for a real shared supply, such as a village fund, and players add to it or take from it the way the system would.
pros: The pot shows how a supply behaves.
Players watch one action lead to another.
cons: A pot emptied early stays empty.
Much of real life is missing from it.

pairs.tendency: Every player represents a group, and the pot is what all of them want a share of. Farmers, a council and a shopkeeper each argue their claim.
pros: The pot shows the conflict between groups.
Each group's view of the problem comes out.
cons: One group may end up with most of it.
Speaking for a group can distract from the goal.

pairs.tendency: The pot is the limited supply everyone takes from. If players take too much, nothing is left.
pros: Everyone can see how much is left.
The biggest taker is plain to see.
cons: Once empty, it is empty for all.
One player who takes a lot leaves less for all.

pairs.tendency: A counter put in the pot shows its effect rounds later, as a payment or a loss. The pot changes at once; the result arrives later.
pros: What you do now matters rounds later.
Players notice trends over time.
cons: It is hard to say which move caused what.
A late effect can surprise the table.

pairs.tendency: A new rule for paying out the pot is agreed and tried in the next rounds. Any change shows in the pot straight away.
pros: Changes are tested where everyone can see.
Players see the difference the rule makes.
cons: The table may be confused by the change.
A single round may hide some effects.

pairs.tendency: Once play ends, players go over the pot: who put in what and who took it. Each explains why they acted as they did.
pros: The pot is a record to talk from.
Reasons come out in the open.
cons: Early rounds are hard to recall.
The talk may wander off the pot.

pairs.tendency: Counters put into the pot cannot be taken back, and the pot is carried into the next game. Nothing is undone.
pros: Every counter paid in stays.
The pot holds a history of play.
cons: A counter paid by mistake is lost.
The next game inherits the pot.

pairs.tendency: How the pot is paid out carries a view of the world. A pot only the wealthiest player can claim says something about who gets what.
pros: The payout rule makes the case.
The rule is felt by playing it.
cons: Some may not notice the point.
Players may push back against it.

pairs.tendency: The pot holds real money or a real promise. What happens at the table carries into life outside it.
pros: Every move feels heavier.
Nobody plays carelessly.
cons: Some players may avoid joining in.
Real stakes can strain friendships.

pairs.tendency: The pot's points stand for something like health or kindness, and in chasing the pot players can lose sight of what it meant.
pros: Players see a number stand in for a value.
The swap is worth discussing after the game.
cons: The pot can crowd out other aims.
A value becomes a plain number.

pairs.tendency: The pot stands for what a village that shares everything might hold in common. Players add and take the way people in that world would.
pros: The pot gives the new world a shape.
Players get a taste of that life.
cons: The pot leaves details out.
Real life may not go the same way.

pairs.tendency: The dice name the pit you scoop from, and then the seeds travel round one at a time. Where the last of them lands decides what you take.
pros: The dice choose the pit, so nobody plans far ahead.
One throw gives every turn a clear start.
cons: A throw can point at an empty pit.
You cannot pick the pit you wanted.

pairs.tendency: Each player picks a card from a shared row, and the card says which pit to scoop. Taking a card also takes that pit away from the next player.
pros: Every pick closes a choice for someone else.
Players can guess which pit the next person wants.
cons: Picking a card adds a step before each sowing.
The last to pick gets what is left.

pairs.tendency: Before sowing, players bid seeds for the right to scoop a full pit. Seeds spent on a bid leave the pits, so the bid changes what is left to sow.
pros: Bids show how much each pit is wanted.
Seeds count as money as well as moves.
cons: Winning a bid leaves fewer seeds to sow.
Bidding stops the sowing for a while.

pairs.tendency: After a sowing you may scoop again from the pit where your last seed landed, and keep going for a bigger haul. A seed that lands in an empty pit ends the turn at once.
pros: Each extra scoop can add a big haul.
Players watch each other's chains.
cons: One last seed can end a turn with nothing.
Stopping early leaves seeds on the board.

pairs.tendency: Rows of pits belong to players, and seeds sown into a rival's row add to their store. Each sowing shifts who holds more seeds on which side.
pros: Sowing into the rival's row changes who holds it.
A side with many seeds is easy to see.
cons: Seeds you sow into a rival's row are theirs.
Counting both rows takes time.

pairs.tendency: Your workers sit on pits as markers, and no one else can scoop a pit that has a worker on it. You sow around your own workers and over the rival's.
pros: A marked pit is safe from the other player.
Workers give pits different jobs.
cons: Seeds can drop into blocked pits and sit there.
A few workers mean few safe pits.

pairs.tendency: The seeds are coloured, and each sowing tries to leave colours lined up in the pits. Every seed dropped is a piece of the pattern and cannot be taken back.
pros: Every seed adds to a pattern.
A run of colours can be planned ahead.
cons: One seed in the wrong pit breaks a line.
A rival can scoop your line away.

pairs.tendency: Cards in hand change how you sow, such as dropping an extra seed or skipping a pit. You keep some cards back for a later, bigger sowing.
pros: Saved cards turn a plain sowing into a special one.
You choose when to spend each card.
cons: Holding cards back leaves their effect unused.
Cards in hand make the pits harder to count ahead.

pairs.tendency: Each player plays a card, and the winner of the trick scoops the pit of their choice. The seeds go to whoever takes the trick.
pros: A won trick gives a clear prize of seeds.
The leader of the next trick picks the pit.
cons: Losing tricks leaves your pits to others.
Players follow the cards and the pits at once.

pairs.tendency: Players agree who sows from which pit and trade promises to leave each other's seeds alone. A deal lasts until a last seed lands where it was not meant to.
pros: Players can make pacts about pits.
Talk can stop a rival's big capture.
cons: A broken promise ends a pact quickly.
Long talks slow the sowing down.

pairs.tendency: Captured seeds are kept as groups, such as three seeds of one colour from a single pit. Where the last seed lands decides which group you can add to.
pros: Each capture adds to a set.
Players aim the last seed at a colour they need.
cons: Seeds of the wrong colour come along with the capture.
Sets are slow to finish when seeds run low.

pairs.tendency: Tiles are laid to build the row of pits as the game goes, and seeds are sown into them. A new tile adds a pit and changes where a last seed can land.
pros: The board grows between sowings.
Players shape where seeds will travel.
cons: Counting seeds round a changing board takes care.
A tile can cut off a pit someone planned to use.

pairs.tendency: One player sows from a pit, and the next answers by sowing from the pit where that last seed landed. Each turn starts where the one before it ended.
pros: Each sowing tells the next player where to start.
The play moves back and forth at a steady pace.
cons: A player has little say over their starting pit.
A long chain can leave a player with no pit to answer from.

pairs.tendency: Nobody speaks while sowing. Your plan shows only in the pit you pick and the order you drop seeds, and the others read it from where the seeds go.
pros: Pit choices become the only message.
Players watch each other's hands closely.
cons: Plans cannot be explained.
A wrong guess about a move goes uncorrected.

pairs.tendency: On your turn you can change how sowing works, such as dropping two seeds at a time or sowing the other way, and then sow. The same pits give a different result from round to round.
pros: A new sowing rule changes what a pit holds.
Old plans can stop working.
cons: Turns go on rule talk.
Counting is harder when the direction can flip.

pairs.tendency: Each player speaks as a character, such as a farmer sowing a field, and describes each pit as a plot of land. A seed dropped in a pit is a seed planted on that plot.
pros: Pits get names and owners.
Captures turn into events in the story.
cons: Players stop to describe each move.
Counting slips when the talk runs long.

pairs.tendency: Instead of counting seeds in, you flick or toss them at the pits, and only the ones that stay in a pit count. A shaky hand drops seeds in the wrong place.
pros: Hands decide where seeds go.
Fast players need no counting.
cons: Seeds roll out of the pits.
A steady hand counts for more than the plan.

pairs.tendency: Players draw the pits as they go, adding a new pit each turn before sowing into it. The row of pits looks different in every game.
pros: Each game has its own board.
Drawing a pit is a move in itself.
cons: A roughly drawn pit is hard to count.
Drawing takes time between sowings.

pairs.tendency: A spare hand of cards sits face down in the middle, and the player who takes it can use those cards to change how they sow. The other player sows by the plain rules.
pros: The spare cards give one player extra options.
Taking them is a choice everyone can see.
cons: One player sows without the extra cards.
Swapping the spare hand delays the first sowing.

pairs.tendency: Some pits have a rule of their own, such as a pit that keeps its seeds safe or one that sends a seed back. A sowing that crosses these pits changes along the way.
pros: A safe pit gives a place to keep seeds.
Players learn which pits to avoid.
cons: Sowing across special pits needs care.
A seed can be lost to a pit you passed.

pairs.tendency: Each sowing costs seeds from your store, and bigger moves cost more. You choose how many seeds to spend on a sowing and how many to keep.
pros: Spending shows how much a move is worth.
Players pick between small moves and big ones.
cons: Spent seeds are not there for captures.
A low store limits the next sowing.

pairs.tendency: A fixed pile of seeds is shared out among several pits at the start, and each sowing moves seeds on. Putting many in one pit leaves another thin, and the other player is doing the same.
pros: Players choose where to place their seeds.
A full pit can sow a long way.
cons: A thin pit is easy to capture.
The first spread is hard to change later.

pairs.tendency: Everyone sows at once until the signal comes, and then all hands freeze with a seed in the air or in a pit. Whoever sowed least is caught short.
pros: Everyone sows at the same time.
A signal ends each round without warning.
cons: Seeds are dropped in the wrong pit in a rush.
Slow players fall behind on the count.

pairs.tendency: Before sowing you may put cards back and take new ones, hunting for the card that names the pit you want. The hand you end up with decides the sowing.
pros: A swap gives a second chance at the card you need.
Players can look for one particular card.
cons: Swapping uses up part of the turn.
A swap shows others what you are missing.

pairs.tendency: Captured seeds go onto a shared pile, and on your turn you may take the whole pile if you can sow the top seed at once. A big pile waits for whoever can use it.
pros: Piles grow until someone can use them.
Players keep an eye on the pile all game.
cons: Taking a pile uses up the whole turn.
A pile can sit untouched for many rounds.

pairs.tendency: One colour of seed is named, and a pit holding that colour wins a capture over the others. A single seed of that colour can decide a whole pit.
pros: A named colour makes some seeds count for more.
Players aim to sow that colour.
cons: Plain seeds lose to it every time.
Many rounds are settled by one colour.

pairs.tendency: You sow on two boards at once, attacking on one and defending on the other. A sowing on the first board changes what a sowing on the second can reach.
pros: Two boards give two sets of pits to watch.
A move can help on one board and cost on the other.
cons: Counting both takes long.
Players lose track of which board is next.

pairs.tendency: A wild seed can stand for any colour, so one wild seed finishes a run that was a seed short. Where it lands decides what it turns into.
pros: A wild seed fills a gap in a run.
Players hunt for the wild seed in the pits.
cons: Wild seeds are fought over.
A captured wild seed swings a result.

pairs.tendency: The ring of pits joins at the ends, so a long sowing goes round and drops seeds back into the pit it started from. A big pit can lap the whole board.
pros: Sowing never runs off the edge.
Seeds can land back near where they began.
cons: A big sowing can end in your own row.
It is hard to count where the last seed lands.

pairs.tendency: One player hides a seed in a pit, and the others ask yes or no questions to find which one. Each answer rules out pits, and the sowing starts once it is found.
pros: Each answer shrinks the pits left to check.
Questions can be planned along the row.
cons: A lucky first guess ends the hunt.
Questions run on while the sowing waits.

pairs.tendency: The first to sow a seed into their last home pit wins. Each sowing is a step towards that pit, and a capture sends a rival back to refill.
pros: Every sowing moves you nearer to the end.
Captures reshuffle the race.
cons: The leader can be caught in one scoop.
A run of short sowings leaves a player behind.

pairs.tendency: Captured seeds are counted at the end, and the player with the biggest store wins. Every last seed that lands in the right pit adds to the total.
pros: Each capture adds to a running score.
Players can see the count at any moment.
cons: Late captures can change the result.
A small early lead is easy to lose.

pairs.tendency: A player with no seeds left in their pits is out. Sowing into a rival's row feeds them, and capturing from it empties their side.
pros: Captures push players towards the exit.
Players watch rivals' stores run down.
cons: Players who are out wait for the rest.
Sowing a rival's row too often keeps them alive.

pairs.tendency: The pits stand for a village store, and the game removes seeds each round. All players sow together to keep every pit filled until the last round.
pros: Players share a single store of seeds.
Each sowing helps the others too.
cons: One empty pit can end the game for all.
Players have to agree where seeds go, which takes time.

pairs.tendency: All players sow towards one target, such as filling a set of marked pits with a set number of seeds. A seed dropped by one player helps the others.
pros: Everyone sows towards the same pits.
Players plan each sowing with the team in mind.
cons: One careless sowing undoes the work of others.
A player with a big pit may sow for everyone.

pairs.tendency: Each player holds a secret card saying which pits they want filled. Your sowing hides its aim in the long chain of seeds, and others try to guess it.
pros: Each player has a private aim.
Sowing hides its purpose in many drops.
cons: Rivals sow into your pit by accident.
A secret aim is hard to follow with so many seeds moving.

pairs.tendency: The pits are places in a story, and sowing a seed into one moves the tale on. The game ends when the last pit is filled and the story is told.
pros: The story grows with each seed.
Sowing gives a reason to describe a place.
cons: Counting seeds can interrupt the telling.
The ending depends on where seeds finish.

pairs.tendency: Players sow for as long as they like, with no store to beat. When they stop, they look at where the seeds ended up.
pros: Seeds make patterns people can look at.
Players sow with no count to keep.
cons: Nothing marks when to stop.
A long sowing can run on without a point.

pairs.tendency: Before the first scoop each player says what doing well in a sowing means to them, such as filling one pit or capturing as many seeds as they can. Two players can sow side by side with different aims.
pros: Players pick their own reason to sow.
Sowing can look the same while the aims differ.
cons: Players cannot tell who is ahead.
Aims can clash when seeds land in someone's pit.

pairs.tendency: Sowing carries on until one player runs out of seeds, and that player loses. Everyone else counts as safe the moment their own store is full.
pros: Captures aim at the smallest store.
Players who are safe can watch the rest.
cons: The last two players bear all the risk.
Games can drag on while one store drains slowly.

pairs.tendency: The aim is to keep seeds moving round the pits, so each player sows to give the next player a move. Taking seeds out of play ends the game sooner.
pros: Each sowing leaves a move for the next player.
The game can run for a long time.
cons: Captures cut the game short.
Nothing marks a finish.

pairs.tendency: The seeds go round and round the pits and no capture ever ends the game. Playing it shows a round that goes on with nobody winning.
pros: Players watch seeds circle the ring.
Players sow for the sake of sowing.
cons: Nobody can aim at a finish.
Players may stop only because they tire.

pairs.tendency: You play alone against a row of pits laid out by the game. You win if you sow every seed into its place, and you lose if no sowing is left.
pros: A single player can sow at their own pace.
Each puzzle has a clear end.
cons: A wrong first scoop can block the rest.
A stuck layout means starting again.

pairs.tendency: Players sow several short rounds, and each round is a game of its own. Whoever wins the most rounds wins the match.
pros: A lost round is not the end.
Players can try a new plan in the next round.
cons: A match takes longer than one game.
A player who is far behind stops hoping early.

pairs.tendency: Seeds in your own pits count against you, and the player with the fewest at the end wins. Sowing into a rival's row passes the seeds on to them.
pros: Players sow to get rid of seeds.
Sowing into the rival's row has a point.
cons: A big pit is a worry for its owner.
The usual urge to hold on to seeds works against you.

pairs.tendency: You win by ending a sowing with exactly the target count in your store. Too many seeds pass the mark and cost you the win.
pros: Players count their store each turn.
A small last capture can be the one that wins.
cons: Going over the target undoes earlier work.
A player near the target may wait for the right pit.

pairs.tendency: The player who ends up with no seeds in their row wins. Each sowing is a way to hand seeds on, and a capture is something to avoid.
pros: Seeds travel towards the rival's row.
Players search for sowings that give seeds away.
cons: Captures bring unwanted seeds.
Some players forget the aim and take seeds by habit.

pairs.tendency: Each player sows on a board of their own, at the same time as the others. Nobody's seeds can be captured, and the result is read off the pits at the end.
pros: Players sow without waiting for each other.
Each person can set their own speed.
cons: Players cannot change what others do.
The game feels like several games in a row.

pairs.tendency: Sowing is used as an attack: you drop seeds into a rival's pit to set up a capture on the next turn. They sow back at you in return.
pros: Each turn changes the other side's pits.
Players target particular pits.
cons: A rival can empty your pit in one scoop.
Turns can pass in a cycle of revenge.

pairs.tendency: Players never touch each other's seeds. They shape the pits by how they sow, and the other player feels the change when their turn comes.
pros: Every sowing changes the board for the next player.
Players read the pits for what happened.
cons: You cannot reach a rival's seeds directly.
Plans can be undone by a sowing you did not see coming.

pairs.tendency: All players are on one side against the game. They sow together to keep pits filled while the game takes seeds away.
pros: Players share every seed.
Plans are made together.
cons: One player can lead the rest.
A single wrong sowing hurts everyone.

pairs.tendency: Players sow together to keep a shared store alive, and each has a small private store of seeds to protect. Sowing for the group can leave your own pit short.
pros: Players have a reason to help each other.
Each sowing can serve two aims.
cons: A private pit can be left to empty.
Players doubt each other's sowing.

pairs.tendency: Two teams share a row of pits each. Teammates take turns sowing from their side, and a capture takes seeds from the other team's row.
pros: Teammates can plan a sowing in two steps.
A team can protect its pits together.
cons: A player may wait for a teammate's move.
Teams with different numbers of players sow at different speeds.

pairs.tendency: One player secretly sows to empty the shared pits while the others try to fill them. A sowing that looks like a mistake could be a trick.
pros: Every odd sowing makes players look hard.
The group learns to read each other's habits.
cons: A mistake can look like a plot.
The traitor can stay hidden for many rounds.

pairs.tendency: Each player sends their sowing by letter, naming the pit and the direction. The other player sows the seeds on their own board and writes back.
pros: Each move has time to be thought through.
Both players keep a record of every sowing.
cons: One slip in counting spreads to later letters.
A game can take weeks.

pairs.tendency: A third row of pits belongs to a player who is not there, and it is sown by a fixed rule, such as one pit after another. The two players at the table sow around it.
pros: The absent row acts the same every time.
Seeds enter and leave the missing row.
cons: No one can bargain with it.
The empty seat can change who wins.

pairs.tendency: One player runs the pits and describes where each seed lands, while the others tell them which pit they scoop. The master can also add seeds or take them away.
pros: One person keeps the count.
The master can react to what players try.
cons: The master has no pit of their own to win.
A mistake by the master carries into every move.

pairs.tendency: The pits are scratched in the dirt of a street or a market and anyone passing can sit down and sow. Players come and go while the seeds stay in the holes.
pros: A new player can join at any time.
The board is cheap and easy to rebuild.
cons: A game can end when someone leaves.
Passers-by may knock the seeds.

pairs.tendency: One player owns the long row of pits, and the rest share a short row. The lone player takes bigger prizes for each capture.
pros: The lone player can take a lot at once.
The group sows with a shared plan.
cons: The group has to agree on every scoop.
One mistake in the lone row can cost many seeds.

pairs.tendency: You scoop and sow both rows yourself, trying to top your highest count from the last game. Nothing a rival does can change the pits.
pros: Players can set the pace.
The count can be compared across games.
cons: There is nobody to capture from.
A run of luck is the only surprise.

pairs.tendency: Seeds are drawn at random into the pits at the start, and a coin picks the direction of each sowing. The seeds do the work and players watch them land.
pros: Games are quick to set up.
Anyone can win a round.
cons: Plans make little difference.
Players have little to decide.

pairs.tendency: A throw of the dice picks the pit, and a player can spend a seed to throw again. A low throw can be softened, but it costs part of the store.
pros: Players can answer a low throw.
Dice make each turn different.
cons: Every re-throw costs a seed.
Some players re-throw too often and run low.

pairs.tendency: The pits start in a fixed layout, and a few seeds are added from a shuffled pile each round. Players plan each sowing and now and then meet a surprise.
pros: Plans mostly pay off.
A shuffled seed keeps the layout changing.
cons: A random seed can wreck a long plan.
Counting is easy until the new seeds arrive.

pairs.tendency: The layout is fixed and every seed can be counted ahead. A sowing is chosen by working out where the last seed lands.
pros: Each sowing can be worked out ahead.
Players who count well do well.
cons: Beginners find the counting hard.
A new player can lose without knowing why.

pairs.tendency: Seeds are scooped by hand and sown round the pits, and where the last one lands is read as an answer to a question. The player decides what the answer means.
pros: Each sowing can answer a question.
A reading can be talked over together.
cons: The result gives no score.
The reading depends on who is telling.

pairs.tendency: Players sow at the same moment, and each tries to drop a last seed into the same pit as the other. They sense the timing from each other's hands.
pros: Players watch each other closely.
A match brings both players the same result.
cons: Nobody can plan the match.
Hands that drift out of time miss each other.

pairs.tendency: A roll is looked up on a table that says what happens to the seeds, such as a storm that washes a pit empty or a harvest that doubles it. The dice write part of the tale.
pros: The table gives events a name.
Seeds change in surprising ways.
cons: Rolling can stall a sowing.
The table may overturn a plan.

pairs.tendency: All seeds sit in open pits, so every player can count every pit at any time. Any capture can be seen coming.
pros: Players can plan far ahead.
Nothing is hidden.
cons: The leader's moves are easy to answer.
Slow thinkers hold up the game.

pairs.tendency: Cards in hand name the pits or tell how to sow, and the others cannot see them. The pits are open but the next sowing is not.
pros: Players have to guess a rival's next move.
A card can surprise the table.
cons: Plans need guessing about the hidden cards.
A rival's hand can undo a count.

pairs.tendency: Each player has a secret role, such as farmer or thief, and sows by what that role wants. Seeds in a pit show less about the owner than they seem to.
pros: Sowing can mislead.
Others read every move for clues.
cons: A pit looks the same whoever owns it.
Roles may be guessed from the first moves.

pairs.tendency: Seeds are hidden under cups and players work out the number in each pit from the sowing. Each sowing gives a clue about what is in the pits.
pros: Every sowing gives information.
Players check counts against each other.
cons: Wrong counts spread.
Puzzling slows the sowing.

pairs.tendency: A player sows with a closed fist and says how many seeds are in it. Others decide whether to believe the number.
pros: A bold claim can stop a rival's capture.
Players read each other's faces.
cons: A caught lie costs the player a seed.
Doubting every claim slows the game.

pairs.tendency: One player knows a secret rule about how seeds may be sown, and the others find it out by being told no. Sowing is allowed or refused until the rule shows.
pros: Beginners learn the rule by playing.
Each refusal gives a clue.
cons: The first sowings are mostly guesses.
Players who know the rule have to keep quiet.

pairs.tendency: One player knows which pit holds the prize seed. They cannot say so and can only sow in ways that hint at it.
pros: Hints use the whole row.
The others read the sowing for meaning.
cons: A hint can be missed.
The hinter cannot correct a wrong guess.

pairs.tendency: The pits are covered at the start, and a pit is only turned over when someone sows into it. Each seed may open up new ground.
pros: Every sowing uncovers something.
Players take risks with the first drops.
cons: Nobody can plan far ahead.
A sowing can end in a pit nobody has seen.

pairs.tendency: One hand of cards lies face up on the table and can be used by a player to decide a sowing. Everyone sees what that hand can do.
pros: One hand is open to all.
Players can plan around known cards.
cons: The open hand cannot be hidden.
The owner of the open hand can get help from the table.

pairs.tendency: Captured seeds go into a cup that others cannot see into. Nobody can say for sure who is ahead until the end.
pros: Sowing hides who is leading.
Players guess each other's stores.
cons: The final count can surprise everyone.
A player may sow carelessly if they think they lead.

pairs.tendency: Players sow in turn round the table, one scoop each. Everyone else watches the seeds travel and plans their own scoop.
pros: Each sowing can be followed closely.
Players think while others sow.
cons: Waiting is long with many players.
A plan made while waiting can be spoilt.

pairs.tendency: All players scoop and sow their own rows at the same moment, then compare. Seeds that cross into a rival's row are counted after.
pros: There are no waits.
Turns run fast.
cons: Mixed-up counts are common.
Players cannot react to each other mid-sowing.

pairs.tendency: Anyone may scoop and sow at any time, and the quickest hands get the pits they want. Seeds fly round while players grab.
pros: The quick take the pits.
Rounds end soon.
cons: Slow players are shut out.
Disputes about who scooped first are likely.

pairs.tendency: Each sowing has a sand timer. If the timer runs out before the last seed drops, the rest of the seeds go back to the pit.
pros: A clock keeps the game moving.
Players learn to count at speed.
cons: A rushed count drops seeds in the wrong pit.
Time runs out in the middle of a long sowing.

pairs.tendency: Each player sows once a day and sends the result to the other. A game of sowing can last through a month of mornings.
pros: Players have time to think.
A sowing can be a daily habit.
cons: Waiting for the reply takes days.
A forgotten day holds up the game.

pairs.tendency: Players take a breath before each seed drops, and the sowing moves at the pace of a slow count. The seed in hand is held for a moment over each pit.
pros: Each seed gets full attention.
Players notice every pit.
cons: A short game can take long.
Patience wears thin with many seeds in a scoop.

pairs.tendency: The sowing speeds up each round: the timer gets shorter and the seeds per scoop grow. Late rounds are fast and cramped.
pros: Rounds get more tense.
Players learn the pits by heart.
cons: Mistakes grow near the end.
Slow beginners drop out early.

pairs.tendency: If your last seed lands in your own store or a set pit, you sow again. A lucky chain of scoops can last across the board.
pros: A lucky landing gives another move.
Players plan to end on a certain pit.
cons: One player can sow many times in a row.
The other player waits.

pairs.tendency: The game begins with a stage where seeds are placed by turns, and a second stage where they are sown and captured. The first placing sets what the second can do.
pros: Early choices matter later.
The game changes shape half-way.
cons: A careless first stage is hard to repair.
Players have to learn two sets of rules.

pairs.tendency: Pits stand for fields and wells in a village, and seeds are rain or crops. A sowing carries water from one place to the next the way it would in real life.
pros: Seeds follow a real path.
Players see where a shortage starts.
cons: The model is simpler than the real thing.
Players follow the seeds and miss the reasons.

pairs.tendency: Each player acts as a group, such as farmers or a village council, and sows for what that group needs. A capture is one group taking from another.
pros: Each role has its own view of the pits.
Players argue from where they stand.
cons: Groups with few pits struggle.
Hard feelings can come from role conflicts.

pairs.tendency: All the pits belong to a common store, such as the water under a village. Every sowing draws from it, and when the seeds run out they are gone for everyone.
pros: Each scoop affects every player.
Players watch the common pits shrink.
cons: One greedy scoop can empty the store.
Players may wait for others to use it first.

pairs.tendency: Seeds dropped now only count three rounds later, once they have rested in the pits. A scoop today decides a result far down the game.
pros: Early sowing pays off late.
Players learn to plan ahead.
cons: The reward is slow to show.
Players forget which seeds are waiting.

pairs.tendency: Players agree to a new sowing rule for everyone, such as skipping the pit just left, and play on to see what it does. The seeds show the effect after a few rounds.
pros: A rule can be tested in play.
The seeds show what changed.
cons: A rule can break the game.
Rounds are spent on testing.

pairs.tendency: After the last scoop, players talk over where the seeds went and why. They ask how the pits stood for the village or the farm.
pros: Players explain their sowing.
The game links to real life.
cons: The talk can run longer than the game.
Quiet players may say little.

pairs.tendency: A pit that is emptied is covered over permanently, and a captured seed is taken from the game. The board gets smaller with each round.
pros: Every scoop leaves a mark.
The board shows the game's history.
cons: Nothing can be undone.
Late games have few pits left.

pairs.tendency: The sowing rules reward hoarding in one pit, so a village game says something about who keeps the grain. Players see what the rules favour as they sow.
pros: The rules carry a point of view.
Players can argue with the design.
cons: The rules push the players one way.
Players may disagree on what the game says.

pairs.tendency: Players put real coins or promises behind the seeds. A capture moves the coins and a lost game costs something outside the table.
pros: Every scoop counts.
Players take care over each pit.
cons: A lost game can sour a friendship.
Some players avoid the game.

pairs.tendency: Seeds stand for something that matters, such as a family's health, and the player with the most seeds wins. Players start sowing for the count and forget what the seeds mean.
pros: Seeds give a number to things that are hard to count.
Players see what happens when numbers replace things.
cons: The count hides what it stands for.
Players may chase the seeds alone.

pairs.tendency: Players sow a village store that is shared by all, and see how it feels to hold nothing of their own. Pits are shared fields, and every scoop is agreed.
pros: A new way of living can be tried in play.
Players feel how sharing works in practice.
cons: Agreement slows down each sowing.
A real village has more to settle than the game shows.

pairs.tendency: An extra hand of cards lies face down in the middle, and the first player to land on a certain space can take it. The dice choose who gets there.
pros: Dice decide who reaches the spare hand.
A hidden hand waits along the path.
cons: A late roll can miss it.
Who gets the hand comes down to luck.

pairs.tendency: Drafters pick from the shared row, and the spare hand is added to it as one more choice. Taking the spare hand means giving up a card from the row.
pros: A pick can be a whole hand.
Players weigh one big pick against many small ones.
cons: A wrong pick shuts out the hand.
The row is bigger and slower to pick from.

pairs.tendency: Players bid for the right to take the spare hand before play begins. The winner pays, then swaps cards and puts some back.
pros: The price shows how much the hand is wanted.
Bids tell others what a player lacks.
cons: The winner starts with less to spend.
Bidding adds a step before play.

pairs.tendency: A player can keep swapping cards with the spare hand one at a time, hoping for a set that fits. Each swap is a risk, and a swap that misses ends the chance.
pros: Each swap can improve a hand.
The spare hand stays in view.
cons: A missed swap ends the turn.
Players stop too soon or too late.

pairs.tendency: The player who takes the spare hand starts with extra pieces on the map. Others know the hand is gone and guess which areas it favours.
pros: The extra cards give a head start in an area.
Rivals can see who took the hand.
cons: The owner becomes the target.
Areas are won early, before others can answer.

pairs.tendency: One job on the board lets a worker take the spare hand. Only one worker can sit on it, so that spot is fought over.
pros: The spare hand gets a spot of its own.
Players choose when to send a worker there.
cons: Other jobs lose a worker.
Players who miss the spot start with less.

pairs.tendency: Pieces for patterns that nobody else holds sit in the spare hand. A player who takes it may have the missing colour.
pros: A spare hand can fill a gap in a pattern.
The cards in it can be read before taking.
cons: The hand may not fit any pattern.
A player may take it and find nothing useful.

pairs.tendency: A player may swap their own hand with the spare one, then put some cards back before play begins. Which cards to keep is the first choice of the game.
pros: The first choice shapes the whole hand.
Cards put back give the next player a clue.
cons: Players spend time on a hand before playing.
A swap can lose a card you needed.

pairs.tendency: The spare hand gives one player a chance to swap in a high card, or a card of the trump suit, before the first trick. Putting cards back sets the hand for the whole round.
pros: A swap can bring a winning card.
Putting back cards gives away a plan.
cons: The player who skips the swap leads with less.
The hand taken is hard to follow.

pairs.tendency: Players talk about who will take the spare hand and what they will give for it. A promise of a trade in the game can buy the right.
pros: A deal can settle who takes the hand.
Players can trade cards later.
cons: A broken promise ends the trust.
Talking delays the start.

pairs.tendency: Players eye the spare hand for the cards that finish a set. Taking it may give one set at once, while the player puts back cards that do not belong.
pros: A spare hand can complete a set.
Put-back cards show what a player is not gathering.
cons: The set in the spare hand might not match.
A player can start with a set and lose the chase.

pairs.tendency: Extra tiles make up the spare hand. The player who takes it places them first, which sets part of the shared map.
pros: The map begins with one player's choices.
Extra tiles give more ways to build.
cons: Others start with a map they did not shape.
Putting tiles back takes time.

pairs.tendency: Whoever takes the spare hand holds the first line and begins the chain. The next player answers from their own hand.
pros: The first answer is set by the spare hand.
A new hand starts a new chain.
cons: The opener has little to draw on.
The chain may end where the spare hand ends.

pairs.tendency: Nobody talks about the spare hand. A player takes it, swaps cards and puts some back, and the others read what happened from the cards on the table.
pros: Cards put back are a silent message.
The hand is taken with no talk.
cons: Others may read the swap wrongly.
A swap cannot be explained.

pairs.tendency: A rule change can let a player take the spare hand twice, or let a second hand be dealt. Changing the rules changes who gets the extra cards.
pros: Rule changes can move the extra cards around.
Players use new rules to claim a hand.
cons: The spare hand may lose its purpose.
The first swap is open to dispute.

pairs.tendency: A character's hidden past, such as a bag of tools or a stack of letters, sits in the spare hand. The player who takes it speaks as someone who now holds that past.
pros: A hand can give a character a history.
Players invent why they took it.
cons: The story depends on the cards.
A player may take a hand that does not fit.

pairs.tendency: Cards in the spare hand are scattered, and players flick or catch them to take them. A card that lands face up is out of the hand.
pros: Hands decide who gets the cards.
A quick grab can win a hand.
cons: Dropped cards go to the wrong player.
Cards can slide off the table.

pairs.tendency: Spare map pieces make up the spare hand, and whoever takes it may draw them in first. That player gets to place the first roads.
pros: One player shapes the start of the map.
Drawing a piece is a way to claim land.
cons: Others draw round what is already there.
Putting pieces back leaves gaps.

pairs.tendency: One special space on the track lets a player take the spare hand. Landing there swaps cards in the middle of the race.
pros: A square becomes a chance to swap.
The hand waits along the path.
cons: Squares can be missed.
A player can land there with no use for the cards.

pairs.tendency: Taking the spare hand costs something, such as coins or a unit. The cost makes players check whether the cards are worth the price.
pros: A price makes the hand something to weigh.
Spending shows a player's need.
cons: Paying leaves less for play.
The hand may be worth less than the price.

pairs.tendency: Taking the spare hand brings extra units to share out between places. A player who takes it has more to spread but also more to guard.
pros: Extra units give more choices.
A big hand can cover several places.
cons: Spreading too thin leaves gaps.
Others match the hand with their own sharing.

pairs.tendency: When the signal sounds, players grab for the spare hand and the first hand on it takes it. The rest freeze and wait.
pros: The spare hand goes to the quickest.
Each signal starts a scramble.
cons: Slow players miss it.
Cards get torn or dropped in the grab.

pairs.tendency: Players swap cards with the spare hand and with a pile as well. One swap can follow another until they stop.
pros: There are many chances to swap.
A hand can change a lot before play.
cons: Swapping can go on a long time.
A player who swaps too much loses the cards they started with.

pairs.tendency: At the bottom of the discard pile lies the spare hand. A player who takes the pile gets the spare hand under it.
pros: A pile can hide a surprise.
Taking the pile gives more cards than it seems.
cons: The pile is bigger to carry.
A pile of unknown cards is risky.

pairs.tendency: Cards of the named trump suit may be in the spare hand. A player who takes it can gain a high trump before play begins.
pros: The hand can change the fight over trumps.
Trump cards in it are worth the swap.
cons: Others know which suit the hand changed.
The owner of trumps can be guessed.

pairs.tendency: There is one spare hand for both boards. A player who takes it can use it on either board, but not on both.
pros: The hand serves two games.
Choosing a board is part of the plan.
cons: The other board loses out.
A player may take it for the wrong board.

pairs.tendency: A wild card may be in the spare hand, so taking it can give a player a card that fits any set. Others know the chance and bid on it.
pros: A wild card in the hand raises its worth.
Putting back cards can hide a wild card.
cons: A hand with no wild card is a letdown.
Players fight for the hand.

pairs.tendency: The spare hand's cards let a player place a line across an edge, so the line reappears on the opposite side. The hand taken opens that extra route.
pros: An edge becomes a way through.
The board feels bigger.
cons: A line can join up where nobody expected.
Players forget to check the far side.

pairs.tendency: The spare hand holds the secret, and the questioner asks yes or no to learn what is in it. Each answer shrinks the list of cards it could hold.
pros: Answers show what is in the hand.
Players can work out the cards.
cons: Questions use up turns.
A taker may not wait for the answers.

pairs.tendency: The spare hand gives one player a head start in the race. Others see who has taken it and rush to catch up.
pros: A hand can give a lead.
The race begins with an unequal start.
cons: Late starters cannot catch up.
The winner may be decided at the start.

pairs.tendency: Scoring cards in the spare hand count at the end. Taking it adds to a player's total before play begins.
pros: Points can be taken early.
The hand shows who might lead.
cons: An early lead is hard to catch.
Players who skip it start behind.

pairs.tendency: The spare hand is a reserve that a player can bring out when they are close to being knocked out. Holding it can keep them in the game.
pros: A reserve hand extends a player's life.
Others hunt for the player who holds it.
cons: The reserve can be used up in one turn.
Players wait to see who needs it.

pairs.tendency: The spare hand is a store for the whole team. One player takes it, swaps in what the group needs and puts the rest back for later.
pros: The team starts with a plan.
One player speaks for the group.
cons: If the swap misses, the whole team pays.
The group spends time deciding who takes it.

pairs.tendency: Cards that help reach the shared goal sit in the spare hand. The player who takes it passes cards to the team after the swap.
pros: Everyone gains from one pick.
Players share a first plan.
cons: One choice shapes the whole team.
A player may hold back the cards.

pairs.tendency: A player who takes the spare hand may find cards that match their secret goal. The swap tells others little about what that goal is.
pros: A hand can bring a goal closer.
Swaps keep the goal secret.
cons: A taker gives away a hint by what they put back.
A spare hand can pull the player away from the goal.

pairs.tendency: The spare hand holds story cards, and the player who takes it decides which part of the tale opens the game. The cards put back stay as unused turns.
pros: A first scene is set by one player.
The story begins with a choice.
cons: Put-back cards leave gaps.
The ending depends on the first pick.

pairs.tendency: Anyone may look through the spare hand. Players take or leave its cards, with no score to win.
pros: A spare hand can start a session.
Players make something from what they find.
cons: Nothing tells players when to stop.
The hand may sit unused.

pairs.tendency: The spare hand lets each player pick the cards that match the goal they have named. A player who aims small can take a few cards and leave the rest.
pros: Each player picks cards to match an aim.
Aims shape what is taken.
cons: Others cannot tell who is ahead.
The same cards mean different things to each player.

pairs.tendency: Cards from the spare hand join the pile that decides who loses. A player who takes it may drop the cards that would sink them.
pros: A hand can shift who loses.
Players dread the last cards.
cons: The player who takes it is seen as safe.
The player left with it can be caught.

pairs.tendency: Whenever play stalls, the spare hand refills the table. The player who takes it may change cards so play goes on.
pros: The game can restart from the spare hand.
Players share a store of fresh cards.
cons: The hand runs out.
Nobody knows when it will be needed.

pairs.tendency: The spare hand holds cards that cannot be played to win. Players take it and find that the swap changes nothing.
pros: The hand shows what the game withholds.
Players look for a way to use it.
cons: The swap has no reward.
Players may stop trying.

pairs.tendency: The spare hand gives a single player a second chance. They take it, swap in a card that clears the layout, and put back the one that blocked it.
pros: A solo player gets a fresh start.
The hand can open a stuck layout.
cons: The swap is used once.
A wrong swap blocks the rest.

pairs.tendency: The spare hand is dealt again in each game and goes to whoever lost the last one. The loser of a round starts the next with an extra choice.
pros: A lost round gives a small lift.
Each game starts with a new hand.
cons: A winner starts without the extra.
The match can swing back and forth.

pairs.tendency: Low penalty cards fill the spare hand. A player who takes it can swap their heaviest cards away before play begins.
pros: The hand is a way to dump high cards.
Others see who has swapped.
cons: A taker may get cards with heavy points.
Putting back high cards passes them on.

pairs.tendency: Numbers in the spare hand can help a player land exactly on the target. A swap can bring the card that fits the count.
pros: One swap can supply a missing number.
Players think about the target before play.
cons: A hand with the wrong numbers leaves the count off.
Taking it can overshoot the aim.

pairs.tendency: The spare hand is a place to get rid of cards. A player who wants to lose takes it and swaps in cards that are easy to give away.
pros: A swap can empty a hand quickly.
Players study which cards to drop.
cons: The hand may hold cards no one wants.
A player who swaps may end up winning by mistake.

pairs.tendency: Each player has a spare hand of their own and swaps it with their cards. They never see the other players' swaps.
pros: Each player gets a fresh start.
Nobody waits for the others.
cons: Players cannot compare swaps.
The game feels like separate games.

pairs.tendency: Players fight over who takes the spare hand, and the one who loses may take cards from the winner's hand later. A taker is a target from the start.
pros: Taking the hand starts the fight.
Players see their enemies early.
cons: The taker is hit first.
A hand can cause an early grudge.

pairs.tendency: The spare hand's cards go onto the board, and the other players feel them through the changed spaces. Nobody touches the taker's hand.
pros: A swap changes the board for everyone.
Players read the board for the new cards.
cons: A taker's choice is open to see.
Rivals cannot stop the swap.

pairs.tendency: The spare hand is for the team, and the group agrees who takes it and what to put back. The swap is made for all.
pros: The team shares one big choice.
Everyone helps decide.
cons: Agreeing takes time.
A poor swap sets back every player.

pairs.tendency: The spare hand helps the team, but the taker can slip a card meant for their own aim. Others watch what comes back from the swap.
pros: The hand can serve the group.
A small private gain stays possible.
cons: Players suspect the taker.
Trust can drop on the first swap.

pairs.tendency: Each team may send one player to take the spare hand, and the team that gets it shares the cards among its players. The other team starts without it.
pros: A team shares the extra cards.
Teams plan who goes to take it.
cons: The losing team starts behind.
A hand shared out is slow to split.

pairs.tendency: The traitor takes the spare hand and swaps in cards that hurt the group, putting back the cards the team needed. The others see the swap but not the reason.
pros: A hand can hide a traitor's plan.
Players hunt for clues in the swap.
cons: A harmless swap looks suspicious.
Unmasking the traitor can take a long time.

pairs.tendency: Each player receives the spare hand by post, makes a swap and mails it on. Each reply shows what was put back.
pros: Each swap is written down.
There is time to think about the cards.
cons: Waiting for the mail holds up play.
A lost letter breaks the chain.

pairs.tendency: The spare hand belongs to a player who is not there. The others can take it in turns but have to put the cards back as the absent player would.
pros: The hand stands in for the missing player.
The table agrees on what the absent player would do.
cons: The missing player gets no say.
Arguments can come up over what they would choose.

pairs.tendency: The game master deals the spare hand and decides who takes it. They can also describe what the cards hold before the swap.
pros: One person controls the extra cards.
The master can set the pace of play.
cons: Players depend on the master's choice.
A master's slip can alter the start.

pairs.tendency: The spare hand is left face down on a street table, and any passer-by can swap a card with it. The hand changes all day.
pros: New players can join by taking a card.
The hand is always changing.
cons: Nobody can plan around it.
Cards go missing.

pairs.tendency: The lone player takes the spare hand, and the others share what is left. The lone player puts back cards to make up for facing a team.
pros: A lone player gets an extra edge.
The team starts with less.
cons: The team has no spare.
The lone player may keep the hand too long.

pairs.tendency: You deal yourself a spare hand and swap it with your own cards before play. Nobody else sees what you put back.
pros: You can pick your own start.
A swap can fix a thin deal.
cons: There is nobody to learn from.
A wrong swap spoils the whole game.

pairs.tendency: Chance deals the spare hand, and the swap is made without looking. The deal decides most of what follows.
pros: Setup is quick.
A new player can beat an old hand.
cons: The deal does most of the deciding.
A swap is a guess.

pairs.tendency: A thin deal can be fixed by taking the spare hand and swapping in a set that fits. The swap is a way to soften luck.
pros: A thin deal can be repaired.
Players have a choice after the deal.
cons: Only one player gets the spare hand.
The spare hand may be as thin as the deal.

pairs.tendency: The deal is mostly fair, and the spare hand adds a small chance for a player to improve their cards. The swap takes skill and a little luck.
pros: The spare hand gives a small lift.
A clever swap can win the round.
cons: A random card can undo a plan.
Players cannot know what is in the hand.

pairs.tendency: Anyone can inspect the spare hand, and players choose by reading it. The right swap goes to the player who reads it fastest.
pros: Players can work out the hand.
Careful reading is rewarded.
cons: Beginners may pick wrongly.
Experts have an edge from the start.

pairs.tendency: The spare hand is turned face up as a message, and the cards in it are read as an answer. A player may take the hand as advice.
pros: The cards give a thing to think about.
The hand can start a talk.
cons: Readings may differ.
The player does not score.

pairs.tendency: Two players reach for the spare hand together and try to take the same card at the same moment. Neither says a word.
pros: A shared reach can match two minds.
Players watch each other's hands.
cons: Timing cannot be planned.
A mismatch ends in a tug.

pairs.tendency: A roll on a table decides what is in the spare hand, and the dice tell a short tale about where the cards came from. The taker uses that tale.
pros: The hand has a story.
The dice shape the swap.
cons: Rolling slows the start.
The tale may not fit the hand.

pairs.tendency: The spare hand is dealt face up, so all can see what the taker gets. The swap is made in the open.
pros: Everyone can count what the taker holds.
There are no secrets about the swap.
cons: A taker is easy to read.
The likeliest swap is often clear to all.

pairs.tendency: The taker puts back cards from a face-down spare hand in secret. The others only know that a swap took place.
pros: The swap adds a mystery.
A hand can change without anyone seeing.
cons: The others guess what was put back.
A taker's hand is harder to read.

pairs.tendency: A role card may sit in the spare hand, so whoever takes it might change who they are. Nobody knows who took the new role.
pros: A swap can change a secret role.
Players watch who takes the hand.
cons: A role can be lost in a swap.
A taker may look guilty.

pairs.tendency: Clues sit in the spare hand, and players use the swap to learn about the hidden facts. A card put back shows what a player already knows.
pros: The hand gives clues.
Players can reason about what was put back.
cons: A swap can mislead.
A player may take the hand only for the clues.

pairs.tendency: A player takes the spare hand and says they swapped in a set of high cards, whether they did or not. Others have to guess.
pros: A claim about the swap can scare others.
Players watch for a twitch when the claim is made.
cons: A false claim can be caught.
If everyone questions every swap, play drags.

pairs.tendency: A secret rule decides which cards can go back from the spare hand. A taker finds the rule by being told no.
pros: A swap teaches a rule.
Every no narrows the rule down.
cons: Nobody knows the rule on the first swap.
A taker may lose a card to a rule they did not know.

pairs.tendency: One player knows what the spare hand holds and cannot say. They hint at it so that the taker chooses well.
pros: The hinter helps the taker without speaking.
The hint can be a picture or a sign.
cons: The taker may not notice the hint.
If the taker picks wrong, the hinter has to stay quiet.

pairs.tendency: The spare hand holds map cards that are still face down. The player who takes it reveals the first area and places it.
pros: The map starts with a surprise.
The taker sees the land first.
cons: Others plan around a map they cannot see.
A reveal can ruin a plan.

pairs.tendency: There is a spare hand and an open hand on the table. A taker may swap with either, and the open hand shows what is on offer.
pros: Players can compare two hands.
The open hand is a guide for the swap.
cons: A choice between two hands takes time.
A swap with the open hand tells everyone.

pairs.tendency: The spare hand holds hidden points, so a taker adds to their score in secret. Nobody knows who took how many.
pros: A swap can add points in secret.
Players guess who took the hand.
cons: The reveal at the end can upset every guess.
A player may ignore the hand and fall behind.

pairs.tendency: Players take turns at the spare hand, one swap each. Each player sees what the last one put back.
pros: Each swap can be read by the next player.
Players can plan their own swap.
cons: At a big table the hand takes a long time to come round.
The last swap gets what is left.

pairs.tendency: All players choose in secret whether to reach for the spare hand, and everyone reveals at the same time. If two reach, they share or lose it.
pros: Nobody waits for a turn.
A secret choice adds a guess.
cons: Two players may clash.
The hand can go unclaimed.

pairs.tendency: Anyone may grab the spare hand at any time, and the quickest takes it. The rest play on without it.
pros: Whoever is fastest gets the hand.
No time goes on waiting.
cons: Slow players miss out.
Two hands on the cards at once start an argument.

pairs.tendency: The taker has a short time to swap cards with the spare hand. When the timer runs out, the hand goes back to the middle as it stands.
pros: A clock keeps the swap short.
Players choose fast.
cons: A rushed swap can miss the card you wanted.
A hand may be left half changed.

pairs.tendency: The spare hand sits in the middle for a week, and each player may take it once during the days of the game. The swap is made on the day you choose.
pros: The hand stays open for days.
Players choose their day.
cons: Waiting holds up the first move.
A player may forget to take it.

pairs.tendency: The taker looks at the spare hand slowly, and then makes the swap one card at a time. The table waits in silence.
pros: The swap gets time.
Each card is looked at.
cons: A start takes long.
Players grow restless.

pairs.tendency: The spare hand is taken at the start, and each round afterwards it shrinks by one card. The swap has to be made sooner each time.
pros: The hand loses cards as time goes.
Players learn to decide fast.
cons: Later takers get little.
The first round matters most.

pairs.tendency: A player who takes the spare hand gets another turn at once. The swap and the extra go together.
pros: The taker moves again.
The hand brings two gains.
cons: Everyone else sits through both moves.
Others fall further behind.

pairs.tendency: The spare hand is used in the first stage, where players pick and swap cards. The second stage is played with the hand each player ends up with.
pros: The first stage sets up the second.
A swap has a lasting effect.
cons: The first stage is a guess about the second.
Players have to keep two sets of rules in mind.

pairs.tendency: In the model the spare hand stands for a reserve, such as grain stored in a village. A player who takes it draws on that reserve.
pros: The hand acts as a stock.
Players see why a reserve matters.
cons: The model leaves out much.
Players may take the reserve too early.

pairs.tendency: Each role has its own claim on the spare hand, such as the council or the shopkeeper. The group argues over who takes it.
pros: Each role makes a case.
Players see the needs of others.
cons: One role may get nothing.
Arguments take time.

pairs.tendency: The spare hand is part of the common store, so a taker uses up what belongs to all. The cards put back are returned to the common store.
pros: The hand is a shared supply.
Putting cards back helps the rest.
cons: Take too much and the others go short.
Some hold off, hoping someone else will take first.

pairs.tendency: The cards taken from the spare hand work only after a few rounds. The swap pays off late, while the taker waits.
pros: A swap has a result later.
Players plan for the long run.
cons: The wait is hard to watch.
Others may take the hand first.

pairs.tendency: The group tries a new rule about who takes the spare hand, and plays on to see what happens. The next round shows the effect.
pros: The new rule gets a trial on one hand.
Players compare the rounds.
cons: One change can tip the whole game.
Testing takes a round.

pairs.tendency: After the game, players talk about who took the spare hand and why. They ask what a different swap would have done.
pros: The swap can be talked over.
Players learn what each saw.
cons: The talk can run on.
Players may defend their swap.

pairs.tendency: The cards put back from the spare hand are torn or marked, and the next game starts with the changed hand. A swap leaves a permanent mark.
pros: Each swap shapes later games.
Marks on the cards record past games.
cons: There is no taking a swap back.
A hand can wear out.

pairs.tendency: The rules give the spare hand to whoever has the least, and the game says something about who gets help. Players see what the rule favours when they take it.
pros: Who gets help is built into the rule.
Players can push back on the rule in talk.
cons: Play leans the way the rule points.
Readings of the rule can split the table.

pairs.tendency: Players put real coins on who gets the spare hand. Taking it means taking a risk with something outside the game.
pros: Real coins ride on the hand.
Nobody reaches for it lightly.
cons: A lost bet carries over.
Some players stay away from it.

pairs.tendency: Cards in the spare hand stand for things that matter, such as health or time. Players take them for the points and forget what they stand for.
pros: Health or time becomes a card you can hold.
Players catch themselves trading a value for points.
cons: The cards lose their meaning.
The score becomes the whole game.

pairs.tendency: The group practises deciding who takes from the spare hand, a store held in common. The swap shows how sharing might work.
pros: Sharing gets tried at the table.
Players feel how it is to decide together.
cons: Every agreement costs time.
Outside the game, a group faces far more than one hand of cards.

pairs.tendency: The dice carry a piece along the track, and the squares it lands on may keep it safe, send it back or skip its next turn. Nobody picks where to stop, so the squares catch players by chance.
pros: Every throw ends on a square that might matter.
Players watch the dice and the track together.
cons: A leader can be sent back by one landing.
Nothing a player chooses changes where the piece stops.

pairs.tendency: Cards in the shared row are worth different amounts depending on the square you are heading for, so a pick starts with a look down the track. A card that helps on a safe square does little on a skip square.
pros: Cards get a reason to be picked.
Players plan a few squares ahead.
cons: Picking takes longer when the track is checked first.
A card taken for one square can arrive too late.

pairs.tendency: Bids go on the right to stand on a particular square, such as a safe one that only one piece may use. Players offer more for squares close to their own pieces.
pros: Squares get a price.
Bids show which square a player is aiming for.
cons: Money can run out before the track does.
A player with more money can hold a safe square for many turns.

pairs.tendency: Each extra step is a peek at the next square and a guess about what it holds. A square that sends you home with nothing makes players stop and count what they would lose.
pros: The danger ahead is visible.
Stopping early keeps what you have.
cons: One square can wipe out a long run.
Players hang back at the edge of a danger square.

pairs.tendency: Regions of the map hold squares that shelter visiting pieces or send them away, so those regions matter more than their size. Pieces crowd around the safe squares.
pros: Safe squares become places worth holding.
Players can read which regions matter.
cons: Fights pile up in a few squares.
A send-back square can empty a region in one move.

pairs.tendency: A job that sits on a special square comes with the square's rule, so a worker placed there may be kept safe or lose a turn. A square taken by one worker is closed to the rest.
pros: Special jobs are worth racing to.
Taking a square also blocks the others.
cons: A worker stuck on a skip square wastes a round.
Early players take the useful squares first.

pairs.tendency: A tile laid on a doubling square counts twice, and a tile laid on a clearing square is wiped off. A pattern planned in one corner can be spoiled by the square under it.
pros: Players plan around the squares.
The same tile means different things in different places.
cons: A pattern can be undone by a clearing square.
New players take time to learn what each square does.

pairs.tendency: Holding a card is a bet on where the piece will land, since a card kept for later may meet a square that makes it useless.
pros: Cards gain a timing.
Players think about the squares ahead.
cons: Cards held too long can lose their use.
Hands get checked again after every move.

pairs.tendency: The winner of a trick moves along a track whose squares reward or punish them, so taking a trick can land you somewhere you did not want to be.
pros: A won trick can help or hurt.
Players think about whether to win at all.
cons: A trick won on purpose can send a piece back.
The track and the card rules are two things to learn.

pairs.tendency: Squares become things to bargain over: one player offers to share a safe square, another asks to be spared a send-back square. Deals get made across the board.
pros: Squares give deals something to trade.
Alliances form around shared safe spaces.
cons: Promises about squares can be broken.
Talk can run long before a move.

pairs.tendency: Some squares hand out an item, take one away or skip a turn, so a player short of one piece steers towards the square that holds it.
pros: Squares become places to visit.
Players plan routes for the missing piece.
cons: A missed turn can lose a set to a rival.
Players may circle the same few squares.

pairs.tendency: Some tiles carry special squares, so laying a tile grows the map and its rules at the same time. A tile put next to your piece can make a square safe for you or set a trap for others.
pros: Laying tiles adds rules to the map.
Each new tile moves the traps.
cons: A trap can catch the player who laid it.
The map is hard to read once many tiles are down.

pairs.tendency: A square can twist the call, such as one where the answer has to rhyme or be a single word. The chain of calls keeps going, with the squares setting its shape.
pros: Squares give the chain new turns.
The chain stays easy to follow.
cons: A tricky square can stop the chain.
Others wait while one player thinks of an answer.

pairs.tendency: With nobody talking, a warning about a trap square has to come through when and how a card is played. Teammates learn the squares by watching what each other does.
pros: Players read each other's moves closely.
The squares are learned by watching.
cons: A missed signal can send a teammate onto a trap.
A muddle cannot be cleared up by talking.

pairs.tendency: A rule change can reach a square, so a safe square turns into a trap in the middle of the game. The board stops being fixed.
pros: The board shifts as people play.
Players watch for changes to the squares.
cons: A square a player counted on can switch sides.
Everyone checks the current rules again and again.

pairs.tendency: Each special square becomes a place in the story, such as a gate that keeps you out or a market where you rest. The rule on the square is something the character goes through.
pros: Squares turn into scenes.
Characters have places to be.
cons: A square's rule can stop the story.
Players may argue whether their character would stop at a square.

pairs.tendency: A flick or a throw decides where a piece ends up, so some spots are worth aiming at and others worth missing. A steady hand can reach a safe square.
pros: Skill with the hands changes the result.
A target square is easy to see.
cons: A shaky hand can land on a trap.
A knocked piece can slide onto the wrong square.

pairs.tendency: Players mark the squares themselves, so a pit or a shelter is there because someone drew it. The finished map is full of traps and shelters put there by the people playing.
pros: Players decide where the traps lie.
The board shows what players were thinking.
cons: A player can mark a trap for a rival.
Drawn squares can start arguments about what they mean.

pairs.tendency: Using a special square costs something: a coin to step onto the safe square, a card to leave the send-back square. The squares turn into things to buy.
pros: Each square has a cost.
Players decide what a square is worth.
cons: Coins run out.
Players pay for squares they did not need.

pairs.tendency: A trap square may need many pieces to keep rivals out, while a safe square needs few to guard it. The squares guide where players spread out.
pros: The board shows where pieces are needed.
Players guess how the others will share theirs.
cons: Too thin a spread leaves squares open.
Pieces on safe squares add nothing elsewhere.

pairs.tendency: When the signal comes, the square under each player decides what happens next. Players on safe squares stay in and players on skip squares lose out.
pros: The signal makes the squares matter at once.
Players aim for safe squares before it comes.
cons: Not everyone can reach a safe square in time.
The slowest player is caught by the signal and the square both.

pairs.tendency: A card in hand can be tied to a square, so players swap to reach squares they want. The hand is chosen with the board in mind.
pros: Swaps steer players towards squares.
Swapping becomes part of planning.
cons: A swap can leave a hand with no matching square.
Players pause to compare the board and the hand.

pairs.tendency: Some squares let you take the discard pile and others make you leave it, so the square you stand on decides whether a big pile is yours.
pros: The pile follows the squares.
A big pile is worth a trip to the right square.
cons: A player can miss a pile by one square.
The pile keeps growing while players wait.

pairs.tendency: Squares coloured like the suits give trump cards a place to be used. A low trump played on the matching square can beat a high card of another suit.
pros: Colour gives a reason to hold trumps.
Players track the suit and the square together.
cons: A trump can be spent on the wrong square.
Two sets of suit rules are harder to remember.

pairs.tendency: A skip square on one board can cost you a move while you are attacking on the other. You watch both boards for squares that might catch you.
pros: A safe square on one board buys time on the other.
Players keep two plans going.
cons: Attention is split between two boards.
One trap square can cost a move on both.

pairs.tendency: A wild card played at the right square can open a safe path or escape a send-back square. One card changes what a square does to you.
pros: A wild card gives a way out.
A wild makes the squares less certain.
cons: The player holding one may wait too long to play it.
Once wilds are around the square rules count for less.

pairs.tendency: A square on the right edge sits beside the square on the left edge, so a safe square may have a trap right next to it across the join.
pros: Pieces never run out of track.
Squares on opposite edges become neighbours.
cons: Players lose track of which edge is near which square.
A piece can wrap round into a trap it passed.
