pairs.tendency: Until the signal, a wild card can be played as any card, and it keeps whatever value it has been given when the signal sounds. A player who has not decided on a value loses it.
pros: A wild card can be a quick fix.
Players decide at speed.
cons: A late choice may leave it with no value.
Others may not know what a wild card stands for.

pairs.tendency: Pieces run round a board with joined edges and freeze where they are at the stop. A piece close to the edge may find itself next to a piece on the other side.
pros: Pieces can meet in odd places.
There is no corner to hide in.
cons: A freeze can leave pieces side by side by chance.
It is easy to lose sight of a piece that has wrapped round.

pairs.tendency: Questions go round the table until the music stops, and then the answer is due. A player who asked too few questions has to guess.
pros: Questions come thick and fast.
Players have to choose what to ask quickly.
cons: A guess at the stop may be wild.
Players may skip careful questions.

pairs.tendency: Runners race for the finish, and the one furthest ahead when the music stops wins. A runner close to the line can be passed by a late burst.
pros: The race has a sudden end.
A lead can be held or lost.
cons: A race may stop before anyone crosses the line.
The signal may favour one runner.

pairs.tendency: Points pile up fast, and the totals are read out at the stop. A player who was slow to bank their points has fewer to show.
pros: Scores climb fast.
The signal gives a clear moment to total up.
cons: A slow player falls behind.
Late points may be missed.

pairs.tendency: Everyone keeps moving, and each time the music stops the slowest player is out. The last one left wins.
pros: Each stop removes one player.
The game gets harder as the number drops.
cons: The first to go sits out for a long time.
One slow moment ends a player's game.

pairs.tendency: The team works against the dangers until the stop, and at that moment everyone has to be in place. A single player who is not in place loses it for all.
pros: The team learns to watch the signal together.
Everyone depends on the slowest member.
cons: A slow member puts the whole team at risk.
Players may hurry each other.

pairs.tendency: The team builds towards its goal and, at the stop, checks how far it has come. The signal sets how long the team has to work.
pros: Everyone works to the same clock.
The team can see how much is missing.
cons: The goal may be left short.
A rush can lead to mistakes.

pairs.tendency: Each player works towards a private aim and shows their position when the music stops. Others look at how everyone is placed and guess who wanted what.
pros: A frozen scene gives clues.
Players act without thinking about hiding.
cons: Haste gives a goal away.
A player caught mid-move may reveal too much.

pairs.tendency: The story is told fast, and when the music stops the tale has to end. A story left in the middle is told to the end in one line.
pros: The story is told in a rush.
The tale cannot run on for ever.
cons: A tale may be cut short.
The ending may feel sudden.

pairs.tendency: Players move to music and freeze when it stops, with no winner to find. The group looks at the shapes it made and talks about them.
pros: The frozen shapes can be looked at.
Nobody is caught out or sent away.
cons: Without a goal the freeze has little purpose.
Players may not know why they stopped.

pairs.tendency: Each player picks what doing well means, such as grabbing a seat or staying in the middle, before the music starts. When the signal sounds, each one checks their own aim.
pros: Players pick what suits them.
The stop gives a point to check.
cons: Aims are hard to compare.
A player can decide afterwards that the aim was met.

pairs.tendency: Everyone moves, and at each stop the slowest player loses that round. The game ends when one player has lost enough rounds.
pros: Only one player is caught each time.
Others are safe for the moment.
cons: The same player can lose again and again.
Safe players may stop trying.

pairs.tendency: The group moves to music that starts again after each stop, so nobody ever wins and the game carries on. Each freeze begins a new round.
pros: The game can run for a long time.
Players pick up the pace together.
cons: There is no end to look forward to.
Players may drift off after many rounds.

pairs.tendency: When the music stops nobody wins, whatever they grabbed or held. Players stand still with nothing to claim.
pros: The freeze invites thought.
Players see what they expected from the game.
cons: The signal gives no result.
Some players leave in confusion.

pairs.tendency: You play alone against the cards, and a timer or sound ends your try. If the layout is not cleared when the signal sounds, the game counts as lost.
pros: The player works against a clock.
A clear end is set from the start.
cons: A layout left half-cleared is lost.
A rush can lead to cards put in the wrong place.

pairs.tendency: Each short game ends at a signal, and the winner of the most games wins the match. A close game can be decided by the exact moment the signal sounds.
pros: Short rounds follow one another quickly.
A match can be won in few games.
cons: A single sound can decide a round.
A close match can feel like a lottery.

pairs.tendency: Players try to take as few points as they can, and the count happens at the stop. A player who is stuck with a high card at the stop loses out.
pros: Players try to dump points quickly.
The stop settles the count.
cons: A late high card is costly.
Dumping in a rush can pass points to others.

pairs.tendency: You count towards an exact number and need to be on it when the signal comes. A step too many or too few means you miss.
pros: Players count steps with care.
The stop shows who landed on the number.
cons: Overshooting wastes the effort.
A short wait for the signal can leave you one step short.

pairs.tendency: Players try to give everything away, and whoever holds least at the stop wins. A player who is slow to give away is left holding cards.
pros: The usual aim is turned round.
Players hand things over at speed.
cons: It is easy to confuse who is winning.
A gift in a rush may go to the wrong player.

pairs.tendency: Everyone works on their own board until the signal sounds. Players compare how far they got, but nobody can touch another board.
pros: Everyone shares a clock.
Each board is a separate puzzle.
cons: Players see no effect from others.
Slow workers have nothing to react to.

pairs.tendency: Players grab, tag or block each other until the signal ends the fight on the spot. A player caught in a hold when it sounds stays caught.
pros: Nobody has to decide when the scrap is over.
Players choose targets in a hurry.
cons: A pursuit can be cut short.
Quick players keep going after a slow player.

pairs.tendency: Players rush to change the board and stop when the signal sounds. The state of the board at that moment is what counts.
pros: The board shows who moved fastest.
Players never aim at each other.
cons: A change made late can be missed.
Players find it hard to see who caused what.

pairs.tendency: The whole team moves together towards a goal, and all of them have to be in place at the stop. A player who lags puts the others at risk.
pros: The team learns to move at one pace.
Players help the slowest.
cons: One late player fails the team.
Players may hurry a friend and get in the way.

pairs.tendency: The team works on a shared task, and each player tries to slip in a private move before the stop. A private move made at the wrong moment can be seen by all.
pros: The team works towards a goal.
Private aims add a twist.
cons: A grab for yourself can cost the team.
Trust drops when players are seen grabbing.

pairs.tendency: Two teams race to place their members, and the team further along when the music stops is ahead. A team with a slow member may be caught.
pros: Teammates help each other.
The stop gives both teams an equal moment to be judged.
cons: One slow runner can sink the side.
A team may blame one player.

pairs.tendency: As the team moves together, the traitor tries to slow them so that someone is caught at the stop. A sudden delay can be an accident or a trick.
pros: Players watch each other closely.
The traitor hides in the rush.
cons: A slow player is suspected.
An honest player may be accused for a stumble.

pairs.tendency: Each letter sets a time limit for the reply, and when the signal passes, the move is made for the sender. A late letter means the game moves on without you.
pros: Players write with care and on time.
The game keeps going even if someone is away.
cons: A missed deadline loses a turn.
A letter lost in the post can cost the game.

pairs.tendency: The absent player's piece moves by a rule and freezes with all the others at the stop. The group sees where the absent player would have been caught.
pros: The absent player is still caught.
Players have a reason to think about them.
cons: The absent player cannot dodge.
Their rule may favour or hurt them by chance.

pairs.tendency: The game master controls the signal and decides when it sounds. Players watch the game master as well as the board.
pros: The game master can time the stop for the story.
Players learn to read the game master.
cons: The stop may feel arbitrary.
A game master who is distracted can stop the game at the wrong moment.

pairs.tendency: Players in a street or park run until a whistle or shout, then freeze, and passers-by may be caught up too. A person who walks past at the wrong time can be made to freeze.
pros: Anyone nearby can join.
The signal can be a shared sound.
cons: Onlookers may not know the rule.
A noisy street can hide the signal.

pairs.tendency: The lone player controls the signal, or is the one who has to freeze, while the others try to get past. When it sounds, the group has to stop where they stand.
pros: The lone player sets the pace.
The group has to keep an eye on one person.
cons: The group is caught if the signal comes suddenly.
The lone player has to keep watch over many.

pairs.tendency: You race a timer by yourself, and when the signal sounds your work is judged where it stands. Nobody else is caught, so the only rival is the clock.
pros: You can try again straight away.
The clock sets a clear aim.
cons: There is nobody to learn from at the stop.
A solo run can feel short and lonely.

pairs.tendency: Dice or cards decide the moves, and the signal ends the game at a random moment. Who is ahead when it stops depends on luck.
pros: The game is easy to learn.
Players cheer on the dice.
cons: A stop can happen when the luckiest player is ahead.
Skill has no place in the result.

pairs.tendency: The dice decide moves, and before the stop a player can use a re-roll or a card. A saved re-roll is worth keeping for the last seconds.
pros: Players have some control over luck.
The signal gives a reason to use the saved help.
cons: A re-roll saved too long goes unused.
A low throw at the stop is hard to fix.

pairs.tendency: The player in front usually leads, though a lucky roll can shift things before the stop. The signal draws a line under the result.
pros: Skilful play tends to show.
A small surprise stays possible.
cons: Luck can undo a lead at the very end.
Players who took the lead early may relax.

pairs.tendency: Moves are chosen with care, and the plan is judged when the signal sounds. A player who is slow to think loses ground.
pros: Clear thinking pays off.
The signal sets a firm limit.
cons: A long think leaves you caught mid-plan.
Nobody can blame luck for a loss.

pairs.tendency: The throw is read as a sign, and each player acts on their reading before the stop. Then the group compares what they did.
pros: The readings give players much to say.
The stop fixes everyone's choice.
cons: A reading in a hurry can be shallow.
Players may disagree on what a sign meant.

pairs.tendency: The group tries to move or speak at the same moment, and to stop together when the signal sounds. Friends who know each other stop at the same time.
pros: A group can feel as one body.
Players listen to each other.
cons: One person out of step breaks the moment.
A group that is not used to each other struggles.

pairs.tendency: The dice pick events from a table, and the story stops where it is when the signal sounds. The tale is left at an odd moment.
pros: Dice give a quick run of events.
The stop leaves a clear scene.
cons: A story may end in the middle of something.
Events pile up faster than players can tell them.

pairs.tendency: Everything is in view the whole time, so each player knows who is closest to being caught. The stop only confirms what was already clear.
pros: Players plan against what they see.
The slowest player is easy to name.
cons: Nothing is hidden before the stop.
A player in the lead can be targeted.

pairs.tendency: Cards stay secret until the stop and are shown then. A player holding a low hand has no time to fix it.
pros: A hidden hand adds a surprise at the stop.
Players bluff about what they hold.
cons: A hand cannot be improved in a hurry.
A secret can be given away by a nervous face.

pairs.tendency: Players move with their roles kept secret, and the roles are shown at the stop. A role that acted odd in the rush may be spotted.
pros: The stop is a reveal.
Players act on instinct and give clues.
cons: A rushed action can give a role away.
A player may be blamed for a stumble.

pairs.tendency: Players follow clues and have to name the answer when the music stops. A clue found late may not be used.
pros: Clues are chased at speed.
The stop forces a guess.
cons: A guess may be made with half the facts.
A clue can slip past unseen.

pairs.tendency: You act sure of yourself, and at the stop you are called on your claim. A player who bluffed late has less time to be questioned.
pros: Claims are made fast.
The stop gives a clear moment to call a bluff.
cons: A call on a true claim costs the caller.
Nervous players give themselves away.

pairs.tendency: The group plays under a secret rule, and the first player caught breaking it at the stop is the one who learns it. A broken rule is told only at the end.
pros: Players learn by trying.
The stop is a time to say what was found.
cons: A player who guessed wrong is caught.
New players can feel lost.

pairs.tendency: The clue-giver hints until the music stops, and then the guessers have to name the answer. A hint given late may not be understood in time.
pros: Hints are given in a rush.
The stop forces a guess.
cons: A late hint is wasted.
Guessers may blurt out wrong answers.

pairs.tendency: Players explore and turn over parts of the map, and stop where they stand when the music ends. A player far from home at the stop may be caught out.
pros: The map opens fast.
The stop shows who went furthest.
cons: A player who explored far is exposed.
Unseen parts of the map stay hidden.

pairs.tendency: One hand lies open, and everyone can see how it would be played when the signal sounds. Players guess what the open hand will do at the stop.
pros: Open cards give all a chance to plan.
The signal brings an end to the play.
cons: The open hand gives nothing away.
The player of the open hand may be rushed.

pairs.tendency: Points are gathered in secret and shown at the stop. Nobody knows who is ahead until the reveal.
pros: The reveal is a surprise.
Players act without checking each other.
cons: A player may mistake who is leading.
Late points are hard to count.

pairs.tendency: Turns pass round the table, and the player whose turn it is when the signal sounds is caught. A turn spent thinking is a turn at risk.
pros: Turns are short.
Each player feels the signal in turn.
cons: A slow turn is penalised.
Players waiting for a turn may get restless.

pairs.tendency: Everyone acts at the same moment and freezes together at the stop. The slowest to freeze is easy to see.
pros: There is no waiting.
The stop catches everyone in the same instant.
cons: Many players move at once and may collide.
It is hard to see who moved first.

pairs.tendency: Players act whenever they like, and the signal catches whoever is still moving. Quick hands take the front spots before the freeze.
pros: The game flows freely.
The freeze cuts everything off at once.
cons: Slow players have little chance to act.
Two players can reach for the same spot.

pairs.tendency: Each turn has its own clock, and a signal ends the whole game at a moment nobody knows. A player midway through a turn when the signal sounds loses that move.
pros: Two clocks run at once.
Players act quickly in each turn.
cons: A move may be lost at the stop.
Players may not know which clock to watch.

pairs.tendency: The signal comes at the end of each day and the day's move is locked in. A move not made by then is lost.
pros: Each day has a clear deadline.
Players make a plan for the next day.
cons: Being away for a day costs a turn.
The game goes on for a long time.

pairs.tendency: The game moves slowly until a signal cuts in, and the sudden change catches players off guard. A player who has grown calm is slower to freeze.
pros: A quiet game has a sharp moment.
Players pay close attention to the signal.
cons: The slow pace can make players drift.
The sudden stop can startle people.

pairs.tendency: The music speeds up as the game goes, and the signal comes after the quickest stretch. Players are moving at their fastest when they have to freeze.
pros: The pace builds to a peak.
The stop brings relief.
cons: The fast end leaves little time to think.
Players trip over each other near the end.

pairs.tendency: A lucky player gets an extra move and uses it before the signal sounds. Extra moves are worth most just before the stop.
pros: A lucky player can leap ahead.
The signal makes the extra move urgent.
cons: An unused extra turn is lost at the stop.
Others may feel they were left behind.

pairs.tendency: The first stage ends at a signal, and the second stage begins with whatever you held at that moment. What you did in the rush sets up the next stage.
pros: The signal marks a clear change.
Players can plan the first stage with the second in mind.
cons: A rough end to the first stage carries on.
Players may not know when the signal will come.

pairs.tendency: The model runs until the signal and is read at the moment it sounds. The numbers show what the system looked like at that instant.
pros: A snapshot of the system is easy to see.
Players can compare snapshots.
cons: A single moment can mislead.
Real systems do not stop on a signal.

pairs.tendency: Each group acts for its own needs, and the signal shows who has what at that moment. A group that was slow to act is left behind.
pros: Each role feels the pressure differently.
Players see how timing affects each group.
cons: A group with less power reacts slowly.
Roles may be played in a hurry.

pairs.tendency: Everyone takes from the common stock until the music stops, and what is left then is shared. A player who took early got more than a late one.
pros: The stock shrinks in view of all.
Players see the cost of grabbing.
cons: A fast taker leaves little for others.
The stock may be gone before the stop.

pairs.tendency: Actions are taken before the stop, and their results show only after it. Players do not know the full effect of a move until the signal has passed.
pros: Players learn to think ahead.
The stop marks the start of the reckoning.
cons: Results come when it is too late to change.
It is hard to link an effect to its cause.

pairs.tendency: The group tries a new rule for the length of the music, and talks about what happened when it stops. The signal ends the test.
pros: A rule can be tested for a short time.
The stop is a natural moment to talk.
cons: A short test may miss the long-term effects.
A rule judged at speed may be judged unfairly.

pairs.tendency: The signal ends play and starts the talk. Players say what they were doing when it sounded and why.
pros: The stop has a clear use.
The frozen position can be studied.
cons: Reasons from the rush are hard to recall.
Some players do not want to talk after the rush.

pairs.tendency: Anything done while the music plays stays for ever, and the signal ends the time for making marks. A tear or sticker made in a rush cannot be undone.
pros: Each move adds to what the next game inherits.
The stop saves what has been done.
cons: A hasty mark is permanent.
The next game starts from a rushed state.

pairs.tendency: The rules reward speed and punish whoever is slowest at the stop, which says something about the world. Players ask what a game that always catches the slowest is claiming.
pros: A freeze turns the rule into a talking point.
The signal makes the argument plain.
cons: Not everyone takes the same claim from it.
Players may be too busy moving to notice the point.

pairs.tendency: Real favours or money ride on who is caught when the music stops. A player who loses the freeze pays up outside the game.
pros: Each stop costs someone something real.
Nobody treats the freeze as a joke.
cons: A friendship can be tested by a freeze.
Some people sit this one out.

pairs.tendency: Points for kindness or health are gathered fast, and the stop counts them. A player chasing points may skip the thing they stand for.
pros: The count at the stop shows what players valued.
Players see how a rush changes their choices.
cons: The values are reduced to numbers.
A hasty chase can leave out what matters.

pairs.tendency: Players act out a new way of living while the music plays and freeze when it stops. The group looks at the frozen scene and asks what it shows.
pros: A frozen scene can be studied.
Trying it costs nothing outside the game.
cons: A stop cuts the scene short.
Problems that take years do not show in one round.

pairs.tendency: A throw of the dice moves your piece, and a few spaces let you hand cards back for new ones. Between those spaces the hand stays as it is.
pros: The board tells you when a swap is coming.
Each throw shows how near the next swap is.
cons: A hand can stay unchanged for many turns.
Cards kept for later may never get used.

pairs.tendency: Cards are picked from a passing hand first, and afterwards a player may put some back and take new ones. The early picks shape the hand and the swaps patch the gaps.
pros: A wrong pick can be mended later.
Players choose twice before play starts.
cons: Turns run long with two kinds of choosing.
A card picked with care can end up put back.

pairs.tendency: Money buys the cards, then a player may give some back for others from the table. The price paid is gone even when the card goes.
pros: Players learn what each card is worth to the others.
A lost bid can be made up with a swap.
cons: Money spent on a swapped card is lost.
Players may hold off bidding until the swaps are done.

pairs.tendency: Cards are drawn one at a time for points, and a swap lets you throw back the cards that would end the run. Every swap buys a few more risks.
pros: A swap resets a risky hand.
The run can last a little longer.
cons: New cards carry new risks.
Others watch for the swap that goes wrong.

pairs.tendency: Cards decide how many pieces reach the map, and a swap trades away the cards that suit no region you want. Next turn you can reach for a different area.
pros: The hand can follow the plan on the map.
A lost area can be answered with new cards.
cons: A turn spent swapping adds nothing to the map.
The card you want may not turn up.

pairs.tendency: Cards pay for jobs on the board, and a swap lets you drop cards for jobs already taken. A rival who fills a spot first can make your old hand useless at once.
pros: Cards can follow the spots still open.
A blocked plan can change in one turn.
cons: Swapping uses time while spots fill.
A rival may take the spot before the new card comes.

pairs.tendency: The cards supply the colours and shapes, and a swap hands back those that break your line. The pattern grows by trial, one replaced card at a time.
pros: A gap in the pattern can be filled with a fresh draw.
The plan can change halfway.
cons: The one card you need may never show.
A card you put back may be the one another player needs.

pairs.tendency: Keeping and playing cards is already your choice, and a swap adds a way to turn the cards you will never play into new ones. You keep changing the hand all game.
pros: Dead cards can be turned into live ones.
Holding a card has a price you can see.
cons: There are many choices on every turn.
You may fear putting back the one card that mattered.

pairs.tendency: Before the first trick, each player puts back cards that cannot win and takes new ones, hoping for a high card or a short suit. The swaps settle who leads with confidence.
pros: Hands can be built towards winning tricks.
Others can guess your suits from what you give up.
cons: New cards may hold nothing high.
A swap shows which suit is short.

pairs.tendency: Some swaps need another player to agree, so talk fills the table. A promise of a card can count for more than the card.
pros: Talk has a clear purpose.
Players can trade favours across turns.
cons: Deals can be broken after the swap.
Long talks hold up the table.

pairs.tendency: Everyone gathers matching groups, and each swap sends off a stray card for one that might match. Sets grow in jumps instead of one card at a time.
pros: Odd cards turn into a chance at a set.
A set can be aimed for from the first turn.
cons: A swap can send away a card another set needs.
The new card may be another stray.

pairs.tendency: Tiles go onto a shared map, and a swap lets you change the tiles you hold when none fit an open edge. The map decides what each swap is worth.
pros: A stuck turn can be mended.
Tiles can be kept for a chosen spot.
cons: A swap takes a turn that could have placed a tile.
New tiles may fit no more easily.

pairs.tendency: One player calls and the next answers, and a swap lets you trade a card that has no answer for one that does. The chain keeps going for longer.
pros: There is nearly always a reply.
The chain can run on.
cons: Replies grow easy to guess.
Swapping breaks the flow of the call.

pairs.tendency: Nobody talks, so the swap turns into a message. What you put back and what you take shows what you need, and partners learn to read it.
pros: A swap says something without words.
Partners can guess what you hold.
cons: A swap can be misread.
A swap made by mistake sends a false message.

pairs.tendency: A rule can change on your turn, including the rule about swapping. Swaps may become free, banned or costly.
pros: The swap rule itself can be changed.
Players can adjust how often swapping happens.
cons: A rule change may give one player free swaps.
Players keep rechecking the rule.

pairs.tendency: Cards are your character's traits and tools, and a swap is something the character does, such as trading a rope card for a lantern card at a market.
pros: A swap can be told as part of the story.
The character can change during play.
cons: Play stops to explain each swap.
A new card may clash with what the character did before.

pairs.tendency: Cards name a physical task, such as a tower to stack or a coin to flick, and a swap lets you hand back a task your hands cannot manage.
pros: Players pick tasks that suit their hands.
Shaky hands can avoid a hard task.
cons: Swapping skips the skill the game is testing.
Others wait while one player swaps.

pairs.tendency: Cards say what to draw on the shared map, and a swap lets you put back a card that would spoil the picture for one that adds to it.
pros: Players steer the map through their swaps.
The map follows what players choose.
cons: A card put back may be drawn by someone else.
The map can drift away from one player's plan.

pairs.tendency: Swapped cards go to the pile, so the pile fills with what players gave up. Taking the whole pile later brings all those cards back into one hand.
pros: Swapped cards stay in play.
Players can follow what is in the pile.
cons: A big pile shows everyone's old swaps.
Taking the pile can undo a careful swap.

pairs.tendency: Once the trump suit is named, you put back low cards of other suits and hope to draw trumps. Every swap becomes a search for the same suit.
pros: Swaps have a clear aim.
A low trump can still win a trick.
cons: Everyone swaps for the same suit.
Trump cards run short.

pairs.tendency: One hand serves both boards, so a swap made for one board changes what you can do on the other. Each swap leaves one side with fewer choices.
pros: A swap can help both boards.
Cards can shift between the two games.
cons: A swap for one board costs the other.
Two boards need checking before every swap.

pairs.tendency: A wild card can stand for anything, so a swap that brings one fixes any gap in the hand. Soon every player is swapping to find the wild.
pros: Any missing piece can be filled.
A wild card is worth hunting for.
cons: Wild cards go to whoever swaps first.
Swapping away a wild card is a loss.

pairs.tendency: Cards move pieces on a board whose edges join, and a swap for a card that sends a piece over the edge brings a line back in on the other side.
pros: A swap can set up a surprise return.
No corner exists to be pinned in.
cons: Threats can arrive from behind.
Players watch both sides at once.

pairs.tendency: One player holds a secret and the others ask yes or no questions. If the secret is a card, a swap can change it halfway, so answers given earlier stop being true.
pros: Questions can be asked again after a swap.
The hidden thing can shift under the guessers.
cons: Earlier answers lose their use.
Players may doubt every reply.

pairs.tendency: The first to the end wins, and every swap costs a turn. A player weighs the chance of a bigger move against the ground lost.
pros: A swap can find a long step.
Players choose between ground and cards.
cons: A swap costs a turn in a race.
The leader can skip swaps and run.

pairs.tendency: Points sit in the cards you hold, so you swap low cards for new ones and count what you kept at the end.
pros: A low hand can be rebuilt.
Final scores stay open until the last swap.
cons: New cards can score less than the old.
Players count and recount their hands.

pairs.tendency: Players drop out one by one, and someone near the end swaps for cards that keep them in. Each swap is a bet on staying alive.
pros: A threatened player has a way out.
Others read each swap as a sign of trouble.
cons: Players already out stop swapping.
A failed swap leaves you with nothing to play.

pairs.tendency: The group wins or loses together, so a swap becomes a gift. One player hands cards back so another can find what the group lacks.
pros: Swaps serve the whole group.
Players talk about which cards to give up.
cons: One careless swap can doom everyone.
A careful group swaps slowly.

pairs.tendency: Everyone aims at one goal, and each player swaps out the cards that do not help it and takes cards that do.
pros: Hands move towards the same goal.
A card useless to one player can serve another.
cons: Players may all wait for the same card.
One player can take most of the swaps.

pairs.tendency: Each player holds a secret aim, and the cards you swap away and take hint at it. Others watch what you keep.
pros: Swaps can be used to hide your aim.
Others pick up clues from what you swap.
cons: A careless swap tells your goal.
Holding back from swaps looks odd.

pairs.tendency: The game ends when the story does, and a swap lets a player trade in cards that point to a scene the story has already left behind.
pros: Players can steer the story.
The next scene can be prepared.
cons: The story pauses for swaps.
Cards about a past scene go to waste.

pairs.tendency: Nobody wins, so swapping is done to see what the new hand will do. At the end players look over what they hold and talk about it.
pros: Swaps can be tried freely.
Players talk about what they received.
cons: Nothing marks when to stop swapping.
Swaps lead to no score.

pairs.tendency: Each player decides what doing well means, so one swaps for matching pairs while another keeps a mixed hand on purpose.
pros: Players swap for different reasons.
Different plans share the same table.
cons: A swap is hard to read.
Players can argue about who did well.

pairs.tendency: The game runs until one player loses, so swaps are used to dodge the losing card. Everyone dreads the card that cannot be passed on.
pros: A swap can save you.
Everyone watches the losing card.
cons: A swapped-away card lands with someone else.
The last player to swap is left holding it.

pairs.tendency: The aim is to carry on, so swaps keep cards moving and no hand runs dry.
pros: Hands refill all the time.
The game can last long.
cons: There is no clear moment to end.
Swaps can go round in circles.

pairs.tendency: Nobody can win, so swapping is one more thing to do that leads nowhere. The cards come and go and the hand never settles.
pros: Players see what a game does without a goal.
Swapping becomes the play itself.
cons: Players may stop swapping.
Nothing marks progress.

pairs.tendency: You play alone against cards laid out on the table, and a swap lets you change cards when the layout is stuck. If you are still stuck, the game says you lost.
pros: A stuck layout can be eased.
A swap gives a second try.
cons: Swapping can use up cards you need.
The game can end when swaps run out.

pairs.tendency: Several short games are played in a row, and every game begins with its own round of swaps. The player who is behind has more reason to swap.
pros: Each new game brings a new round of swaps.
A lost game can be answered.
cons: Swapping repeats every game.
Players learn each other's swap habits.

pairs.tendency: Cards count against you, so swaps are used to send away high cards and take ones that cost less.
pros: High cards can be sent away.
Players can aim for a low total.
cons: Cards you send off reach someone else.
The new card may be high too.

pairs.tendency: An exact total is needed, so a swap lets you hand back a card that would carry you past it. A near miss can turn into a hit.
pros: A total can be fixed.
Swaps are useful when you are close.
cons: The wanted number may never come.
Players sit one short and wait.

pairs.tendency: The aim is turned round, so swaps are used to take the cards that make you lose. Everyone swaps in the same direction, away from winning.
pros: Players give away their winning cards.
The game looks odd and new.
cons: It is easy to forget which way the aim runs.
A swap may win the game by chance.

pairs.tendency: Everyone plays at once with their own hand, so swaps go on at each end of the table without touching anyone else.
pros: Each player swaps at their own pace.
Nobody waits for a turn.
cons: There is little reason to watch others.
Swaps do not change what others do.

pairs.tendency: Players attack each other, and a swap lets you trade in cards for an attack or a defence you lack.
pros: Attacks can be prepared.
Defence can be restocked.
cons: A swap tells an opponent you lack attacks.
An attack can land while you swap.

pairs.tendency: Players act on the board and feel each other through it. A swap gets you the card for the move the board now needs.
pros: Hands follow the state of the board.
A change on the board shows what to swap for.
cons: A swap may come too late for the board.
Board changes can leave held cards useless.

pairs.tendency: The team plays against the game, and a swap lets the team pass useful cards round the table.
pros: Cards go to the player who uses them.
The team plans swaps together.
cons: One player can take over the swaps.
The team may talk too long.

pairs.tendency: Players mostly work together, and a swap can help the group or help a private aim. Nobody can tell which one it is.
pros: A swap can carry two reasons.
Swaps show who trusts whom.
cons: Others wonder why you swapped.
A swap for yourself can look like betrayal.

pairs.tendency: Two teams play, and teammates swap cards among themselves while the other side watches the traffic.
pros: Teammates build hands that fit together.
Teams can plan swaps ahead.
cons: Opponents see which cards move.
A teammate's wrong swap hurts both.

pairs.tendency: One player secretly works against the others, and routine swaps give them cover for taking useful cards out of play.
pros: A traitor can hide in plain swaps.
Others watch each swap closely.
cons: Honest swaps look suspicious.
Players hesitate to swap.

pairs.tendency: Players are far apart, so a swap takes days. You post cards back and wait for new ones to come.
pros: A swap has a long wait built in.
Players plan far ahead.
cons: Post can be lost or late.
A swap can arrive after the need has passed.

pairs.tendency: One player is not at the table, so someone swaps for them or their hand stays as it was.
pros: The absent hand can still change.
Players choose for another.
cons: Swaps for the absent player are guesses.
Others may argue about what the absent player would have done.

pairs.tendency: The game master runs the world and says when swaps are allowed, such as at a rest stop or a market.
pros: Swaps become part of the story.
The game master can offer special swaps.
cons: The game master has more to track.
Players ask for swaps at odd moments.

pairs.tendency: The game is played in a street or park and passers-by can join, so a swap lets a newcomer pick up a usable hand quickly.
pros: Newcomers get a hand fast.
Hands refresh as people come and go.
cons: Cards get lost in the crowd.
The swap rule needs saying again and again.

pairs.tendency: One player faces all the others, and the lone player may swap more cards than any single teammate.
pros: The lone player can adapt fast.
The team shares its swaps.
cons: The team swaps one at a time.
The lone player's swaps are hard to read.

pairs.tendency: Playing alone against the pack, a swap is your main way to change your luck. Afterwards you can compare results with a friend.
pros: You choose when to swap.
Results can be compared later.
cons: Nobody competes with you over swaps.
Too many swaps lead nowhere.

pairs.tendency: Dice and draws decide most things, and a swap is a draw on top of a draw.
pros: A second go at luck.
Turns stay quick.
cons: The new card is as random as the old.
Choices matter little.

pairs.tendency: Luck is softened by choices, and the swap is one of them. An unlucky draw can be put back for another.
pros: Luck can be eased.
Players plan around swaps.
cons: Swapping can be overused.
Luck returns with the new card.

pairs.tendency: Your choices matter most, with a little luck, and a swap hands a small amount of control back. You choose what to put back, and chance chooses what you get.
pros: Skill picks which cards go back.
Luck still decides the new card.
cons: A practised player swaps with ease.
Beginners may put back the wrong cards.

pairs.tendency: With no dice, a swap from a known pile is a plain decision. The player who remembers the pile swaps with the most information.
pros: Each swap is a decision.
Memory counts.
cons: Newcomers lack knowledge of the pile.
Working out each swap slows turns.

pairs.tendency: Cards are read as signs, and a swap is asking again. You put a card back and draw another, hoping the message changes.
pros: A new card gives a new reading.
Players talk over what it means.
cons: Asking again can look like refusing an answer.
Meanings get muddled.

pairs.tendency: Players try to act at the same moment by feel, so a swap works with a partner. Both hand over a card together with no count.
pros: Swaps need shared timing.
Partners learn each other's pace.
cons: A swap out of step breaks the moment.
Strangers find it hard.

pairs.tendency: A roll gives an event from a table, and a swap lets you trade the card that says how you respond.
pros: Players have a say in events.
The story takes shape from two sources.
cons: Dice and cards can disagree.
The story can stall while hands change.

pairs.tendency: Everything is visible, so every swap is seen. Others know what you give up and what you take.
pros: Swaps can be planned around.
Nothing is hidden.
cons: Every swap hands over information.
Opponents can answer each swap.

pairs.tendency: Hands are secret, so a swap hides what you put back unless you show it. Others read your face for hints.
pros: A swap can cover a bluff.
Guesses come from behaviour.
cons: Secret swaps invite suspicion.
Cheating is hard to check.

pairs.tendency: Some players hold a secret role, and their swaps follow it, so the cards they put back hint at who they are.
pros: A role can leak through swaps.
Players study each swap for clues.
cons: A swap can give away a spy.
Honest players can look guilty.

pairs.tendency: Clues come from cards, and a swap lets you gather a clue again or hide one by trading it away.
pros: A clue can be traded for another.
Players can hide what they know.
cons: A traded clue is lost to you.
The picture of who did it shifts.

pairs.tendency: You pretend to hold more or less than you do, and a swap gives you something to pretend with. A card put back loudly can be a lie.
pros: Swaps become part of a bluff.
Cards can be used as props.
cons: A bluff can fall apart on the next draw.
Others learn to ignore swaps.

pairs.tendency: One player knows a secret rule and the others find it by breaking it. A swap that gets refused is a clue.
pros: A refused swap teaches something.
Players test the rule through swaps.
cons: Newcomers waste swaps.
The knowing player says no often.

pairs.tendency: The one who knows gives hints with cards, and a swap lets them change which hint cards they hold.
pros: The hint giver can try other hints.
Guessers get a new clue.
cons: A swap can confuse the guessers.
Time passes while hints are swapped.

pairs.tendency: The map is hidden until explored, so a swap made before it is revealed is a guess about what lies ahead.
pros: Cards can be traded for what the map shows.
Exploring gives swaps a reason.
cons: A swap can be wasted on a guess.
Cards swapped early may not fit the map.

pairs.tendency: One hand lies face up, so swaps can be planned around cards everyone can see.
pros: Players can see what is on offer.
A swap with the open hand is easy to follow.
cons: Opponents read your plan.
Taking from the open hand can feel risky.

pairs.tendency: Part of each score is hidden, so swaps hint at it. A player who drops many cards may be covering a lead.
pros: Swaps can bluff.
Guessing who is ahead stays open.
cons: Nobody can add up the scores.
Players read too much into swaps.

pairs.tendency: One player swaps while the rest watch and wait. The wait lets others work out what that swap means for them.
pros: Others see the swap before their own turn.
Players have time to plan.
cons: Turns come round slowly at a full table.
Each swap slows the round.

pairs.tendency: Everyone chooses in secret together, so a swap stays hidden until all reveal. You never know whether the card you want has just gone.
pros: Swaps stay secret until the reveal.
Nobody waits.
cons: Two players can want the same card.
The reveal can bring surprises.

pairs.tendency: Anyone can swap at any moment, so cards on the table go to the quickest hand.
pros: Quick players have an edge.
Swaps happen all the time.
cons: Slower players miss the cards.
Hands are grabbed in a scramble.

pairs.tendency: Each turn has a clock, so a swap has to be decided in seconds. Players put back cards in a hurry and may take the first thing offered.
pros: Swaps come fast.
The clock forces decisions.
cons: Hurried swaps go wrong.
Time runs out before a swap is done.

pairs.tendency: The game runs over days, so a swap is a request sent in the morning and cards that arrive by evening.
pros: Swaps have time to be thought over.
Cards change as days pass.
cons: A hand may be out of date.
Some players forget to swap.

pairs.tendency: The game is slowed on purpose, so each swap comes with a pause and a breath before the new card is turned over.
pros: A swap feels weighty.
Players look at each card.
cons: Swaps stretch out the game.
Waiting wears on some players.

pairs.tendency: The game speeds up, so swaps get shorter as timers shrink, until players are putting back cards almost without thinking.
pros: Swaps get quicker as play speeds up.
The end comes in a rush.
cons: Late swaps are done without thought.
Early swaps feel slow beside later ones.

pairs.tendency: A lucky throw gives an extra go, and a swap can set up the cards for it before the throw.
pros: An extra turn can start with a new hand.
Swaps can set up a chain.
cons: A lucky player gets far ahead.
Others wait through long runs.

pairs.tendency: The first stage is for picking cards and the second for playing them, so swaps belong to the first and set up the second.
pros: Swaps shape what comes later.
Each stage has its own job.
cons: A wrong swap shows only later.
The second stage depends on the first.

pairs.tendency: The board works like a real system and cards stand for actions in it, so a swap is a change of plan inside that system.
pros: Swaps can show how plans change.
Players see the effect of a new plan.
cons: The model gets complicated.
A swap can hide how the system works.

pairs.tendency: Each player is a group with its own needs, so each swaps for the cards that serve that group.
pros: Roles shape what is swapped.
Players see the problem from where they stand.
cons: Groups can swap against each other.
A swap for one group hurts another.

pairs.tendency: Everyone draws from one limited stock, and a swap puts cards back into it or takes more out.
pros: Swaps show how the stock changes.
Putting back helps everyone.
cons: A taker can empty the stock.
Players watch each other's swaps.

pairs.tendency: What you do shows up a few rounds later, so a swap pays off only after a while.
pros: Swaps are long bets.
Players think ahead.
cons: A swap's result is hard to link back.
A wrong swap is found late.

pairs.tendency: Players agree a new rule and play on, and the rule can be about swapping, such as one swap a turn or none.
pros: A swap rule can be tested.
Players see what a change does.
cons: A rule may be dropped after one round.
Changed rules confuse swaps.

pairs.tendency: After the game, players talk it through, and swaps give them something to look back on. Why was that card put back?
pros: Swaps give things to talk about.
Players explain their choices.
cons: Memories of swaps differ.
Talk can wander from the game.

pairs.tendency: Nothing can be undone, so a swap is final. The card put back may be torn or marked and cannot return.
pros: Swaps carry weight.
Players think before a swap.
cons: A wrong swap stays wrong.
Cautious players may never swap.

pairs.tendency: The rules make a point about the world, and the swap rule says what happens to unwanted things: they can be traded away, or they cannot.
pros: The swap rule carries a view of unwanted things.
Players notice what is allowed.
cons: Players may disagree with that view.
Some players never notice it.

pairs.tendency: Real money or a promise rides on the game, so a swap can cost something real.
pros: Swaps feel serious.
Players think twice.
cons: Friends can fall out over a swap.
Some players avoid swaps.

pairs.tendency: Points stand for something that matters, so each swap shows what a player will give up for points.
pros: Swaps reveal choices.
Players see what the points hide.
cons: Players chase points.
Players forget what the points stand for.

pairs.tendency: Players practise a future that does not exist yet, and swaps rehearse how things might be shared or traded in it.
pros: Swaps try out new ways to share.
Players feel how it might go.
cons: The rehearsal may not match real life.
People may swap for show.

pairs.tendency: Dice decide where your piece lands, and the pile of thrown-away cards sits by the board. Reaching a certain space lets you scoop it up, if the top card helps.
pros: The pile is a prize on the track.
The dice decide when you can reach it.
cons: A low roll leaves the pile to rivals.
Cards in the pile may fit no space ahead.

pairs.tendency: Cards are picked from a passing hand, and the ones nobody wants end up in the pile. A later player can take that whole heap of leftovers.
pros: Passed-over cards get a second chance.
Players learn what others ignored.
cons: Leftovers fill the pile.
Taking it means a big hand to sort.

pairs.tendency: Players offer money for cards, and unsold cards are thrown on the pile. A player can later take the pile for the price of using its top card.
pros: Cheap cards come to a patient player.
Bids show what the pile is worth.
cons: Money paid and cards thrown can be wasted.
A full pile draws many bids.

pairs.tendency: The pile is a gamble. It may hold many cards, and each one is a new risk to carry. Taking it keeps your run going.
pros: A full pile feeds a run.
Others watch your risk grow.
cons: Too many cards raise the risk of ending your run.
A loss costs you the whole pile.

pairs.tendency: Cards place pieces on the map, and the discard pile is a second source when your own cards run out.
pros: The pile gives cards to contest an area.
A late player can catch up.
cons: Taking the pile gives away the plan.
Piles of useless cards crowd the hand.

pairs.tendency: Jobs on the board are filled by cards, and the pile gives you cards for a job you want when the spots are going fast.
pros: The pile can unlock a job.
Players watch which job cards are thrown.
cons: Pile cards might fit no free spot.
Picking up costs a turn while spots fill.

pairs.tendency: Everyone searches the pile for the colour or shape the pattern needs, and the top card shows whether a grab is worth it.
pros: The pile may hold the missing piece.
Everyone can see the top.
cons: Taking the pile also brings in cards that break the pattern.
Players wait for the top card to turn.

pairs.tendency: Taking the pile gives you many new choices at once, and the hand grows fast. Then you decide which to keep and which to throw back.
pros: Many options come in one turn.
A big hand lets you plan.
cons: Large hands take long to sort.
Cards you throw feed the pile for others.

pairs.tendency: Won tricks are heaped into one pile, and taking it brings all those cards in at once. Whoever collects the heap sees what everyone played.
pros: Winning has a visible reward.
Players know what will come.
cons: A won pile can swell the hand.
Some players dodge hands they cannot use.

pairs.tendency: Players bargain over who takes the pile, and a promise of a card from it can buy a favour.
pros: The pile is something to trade.
Talk has a clear target.
cons: Promises about the pile can be broken.
Haggling slows the turn.

pairs.tendency: A pile often hides cards for your set, and taking it pulls in many at once. The top card has to match something you hold.
pros: A set can jump forward.
The pile gives clues about who needs what.
cons: A big grab brings many stray cards.
Players hold on to the pile to stop rivals.

pairs.tendency: Used tiles are heaped up, and taking the heap lets you choose a tile that fits an open edge on the map.
pros: Tiles unfit for one player may fit another.
The heap gives choice.
cons: The heap grows heavy with stray tiles.
Others see what you need.

pairs.tendency: Each call and answer is thrown on the pile, so the pile records the chain. Taking it means picking the whole chain up.
pros: The chain is kept in view.
A broken chain can be restarted.
cons: Taking the pile ends the chain.
Players lose track of whose turn it is.

pairs.tendency: Nobody talks, so a player who picks up the pile says something loud without a word: I need that top card. The others read the move.
pros: Taking says a lot without words.
Partners understand each other.
cons: A grab can be misread.
A wrong grab goes unexplained.

pairs.tendency: A rule can say who may take the pile, how many cards, or when. Changing it on your turn changes who gets the heap.
pros: The pile rule can be changed.
Players tune how big a grab is.
cons: A rule change can strand the pile.
Players argue over the new rule.

pairs.tendency: The pile is the heap of things characters left behind, and taking it is like picking over a camp after a fight.
pros: Left-over things become props.
Characters can take on a story.
cons: Play stops to say what the pile holds.
A character's find may break a scene.

pairs.tendency: Discards are stacked in a tower, and taking the pile means lifting the tower without it falling.
pros: A tall pile is a challenge.
Hands show their skill.
cons: A shaky grab spills cards.
Players wait while one slowly lifts.

pairs.tendency: Cards add to the shared map, and the pile of used cards records what has been drawn. Taking it lets you add again.
pros: The pile keeps a record of the map.
A late draw can fill gaps.
cons: Taking the pile lets you draw too much.
The map gets crowded with extra marks.

pairs.tendency: Trump cards thrown on the pile turn it into a prize, since taking it means taking the cards that beat all others. Everyone watches the trumps going in.
pros: A heap with trumps is worth taking.
Players track which trumps are gone.
cons: Throwing a trump hands a rival the prize.
Taking a pile of low cards helps nobody.

pairs.tendency: A single pile feeds both boards. Taking it helps one game and leaves the other waiting.
pros: One grab can help both boards.
Players think across two boards.
cons: A pile suited to one game fails the other.
There is much to track before taking.

pairs.tendency: A wild card thrown away lands in the pile, and the next player can scoop it up. Everyone thinks twice before throwing one when the pile can be taken.
pros: A wild card is worth watching for.
A pile holding a wild draws all eyes.
cons: Throwing a wild by mistake hands it over.
The pile is hard to leave alone.

pairs.tendency: Pile cards move pieces over the joined edges, so taking the pile gives a hand of moves that can bring a piece round the board.
pros: A big hand covers many routes.
A piece can return from the other side.
cons: Rivals see you coming.
Moves from the pile might carry a piece past its target.

pairs.tendency: Each question asked gets a card laid on the pile, so the pile is the list of questions so far. A player may pick it up to read it again.
pros: The questions stay in view.
Players avoid asking twice.
cons: Picking up the pile hides the list.
Reading takes time.

pairs.tendency: The leader's thrown cards pile up, and a trailing player can scoop them for a quick move forward.
pros: Players behind get a lift.
A race can tighten.
cons: A leader's throws help a chaser.
Taking the pile costs a turn.

pairs.tendency: A pile of cards is a pile of points to anyone who can take it. Each grab lifts a score at once.
pros: Points move in lumps.
The pile pulls the lead back and forth.
cons: Players hold back throws that score.
Big grabs make the final count unclear.

pairs.tendency: Cards dropped by a knocked-out player pile up, and those still in can take them as fuel.
pros: Survivors gain cards.
A threatened player can take a pile to stay in.
cons: Piles from knocked-out players come late.
The last players hold huge hands.

pairs.tendency: The team shares the pile, and whoever can use the top card takes the lot and shares it out.
pros: The pile is a shared store.
The team can plan who takes it.
cons: The pile may go to the wrong player.
A grab may leave others bare.

pairs.tendency: The pile holds cards for the common goal, and the player who can use the top card takes all of them.
pros: Cards for the goal gather in one place.
Players decide who uses what.
cons: Cards for the goal get buried.
One player may hold all the useful cards.

pairs.tendency: Taking the pile shows what you need, since only certain top cards make a grab worth it. Others read your aim from your grabs.
pros: A grab can be a bluff.
Players hide goals behind big grabs.
cons: A grab gives your aim away.
Others stay away from the pile to avoid giving hints.

pairs.tendency: The pile holds scenes already played, and taking it lets a player bring one of them back into the story.
pros: Old scenes return.
The story can circle round.
cons: The story may lose its end.
Players disagree about what to bring back.

pairs.tendency: Nobody wins, so the pile is just a heap that grows and shrinks. Players take it to see what is in it.
pros: The pile is there to explore.
Players talk about what they find.
cons: There is no reason to take it.
The heap just goes up and down.

pairs.tendency: Each player takes the pile for their own reasons. One wants the top card and another wants the whole heap.
pros: Players use the pile in their own way.
Different aims share one heap.
cons: It is hard to see why someone grabbed.
Players disagree about who used it well.

pairs.tendency: The pile can be a trap, because the losing card may sit at the bottom. Taking the pile risks taking it.
pros: Taking the pile can make you the loser.
Players watch for the losing card.
cons: A pile full of dud cards is risky.
Players avoid the pile.

pairs.tendency: Taking the pile feeds the hand, so the game does not run dry. Thrown cards keep coming back.
pros: Cards keep moving.
The game can run long.
cons: There is no end in sight.
The same cards go round again.

pairs.tendency: The pile fills and empties with no result. Players pick it up, throw cards back, and nothing is won.
pros: The pile becomes the thing to watch.
Players see a game without an end.
cons: Players lose interest.
There is no progress to see.

pairs.tendency: You play alone against the layout, and the pile is your own discards. Taking it gives a second go at cards you threw away.
pros: A throw can be undone.
Solo play gets a chance to recover.
cons: The layout may need cards you buried.
The pile grows with your mistakes.

pairs.tendency: In a run of short games, each game leaves its own pile. A player who has lost two games may risk a big grab to catch up.
pros: A big grab can win back a game.
Each game starts with a fresh pile.
cons: A grab can fail and lose the series.
Players learn rivals' habits.

pairs.tendency: Every card in the pile counts against whoever takes it, so a player who grabs the pile pays heavily.
pros: Players avoid the pile.
Taking the pile is a visible risk.
cons: A big grab ruins a score.
Players push cards onto others.

pairs.tendency: A heap holds many numbers, and taking it can supply the one you need to reach your total.
pros: The pile may have the exact card.
Players can watch for it.
cons: A grab can push you past the number.
You may sit and wait.

pairs.tendency: With the aim turned upside down, the pile can become the thing everyone hands to someone else, or the thing grabbed to lose faster.
pros: Players throw cards onto the pile with care.
The pile's meaning flips.
cons: It is easy to forget the aim.
A wrong grab can end the game early.

pairs.tendency: Everyone plays beside each other with their own hand, and the pile is the only shared thing. Taking it reaches into someone else's throws.
pros: A shared pile is a link.
Players otherwise act alone.
cons: Taking can feel like stealing.
Any quarrel is over the pile.

pairs.tendency: Taking the pile is an attack, since the cards your rival threw are used against them.
pros: Players use pile cards to strike.
Rivals feel each grab.
cons: A grab starts an argument.
Players stop throwing useful cards.

pairs.tendency: The pile is part of the board that players change. Taking it changes what the others find.
pros: The pile affects others without a hit.
Players read the pile.
cons: A grab leaves nothing for others.
Players may not see the cause.

pairs.tendency: The team shares the pile and decides who takes it, and the top card shows which player can use it.
pros: The team plans the grab.
Cards flow to the one who needs them.
cons: One player may rule the pile.
Planning slows play.

pairs.tendency: Players share the pile and sometimes take it for a private aim.
pros: The pile is common ground.
A grab can serve the group or one player.
cons: Others doubt why you took it.
Trust wears thin.

pairs.tendency: Two teams share one pile, and a team that takes it hands the cards to the player who can use them.
pros: Teams plan grabs.
Teammates can build on a grab.
cons: Opponents see the pile move.
Taking the pile can leave your team open.

pairs.tendency: A traitor can take the pile to remove cards the team needs, and nobody can say why.
pros: A traitor hides behind a grab.
Players watch who takes it.
cons: Honest grabs look odd.
Players distrust the pile.

pairs.tendency: Players post their throws, so the pile is a list of letters, and taking it means asking for them all by return post.
pros: The pile is a record.
Players plan ahead.
cons: Post may delay the grab.
Rivals may take it first.

pairs.tendency: The absent player's throws sit in the pile, like a message from someone who is not there. Taking them means using their cards.
pros: The absent player is still felt.
Their cards stay in play.
cons: Players guess at what they meant.
Disputes arise over using their cards.

pairs.tendency: The game master decides what is in the pile and when it can be taken.
pros: A scene can be set with what the pile holds.
The game master can add surprises.
cons: There is one more thing for the game master to track.
Players ask for the pile at awkward moments.

pairs.tendency: A pile in the street or park grows as people come and go, and anyone can try to take it.
pros: Newcomers join in by taking.
The pile shows who has been there.
cons: Passers-by may take cards away.
Each newcomer has to be told the rules.

pairs.tendency: The lone player and the team throw onto the same pile, and whoever takes it gets cards from both sides.
pros: The lone player can catch up in one grab.
The team can share its find.
cons: Team cards feed the lone player.
The lone player's big grab is hard to read.

pairs.tendency: You throw onto and take from your own pile, so the pile is a record of your past choices.
pros: You see your history.
You can plan ahead.
cons: Taking back the same cards makes a loop.
There is nobody else to learn from.

pairs.tendency: Cards come from the draw and go to the pile, and the pile gives a second source with no skill needed. Whether you can take it depends on the top card.
pros: Another chance in the game.
Play moves fast.
cons: Luck decides the top card.
What a player decides counts for little.

pairs.tendency: The pile is one way to soften luck. An unlucky draw can be fixed by taking the pile if the top card helps.
pros: An unlucky draw can be repaired.
Players plan around the top card.
cons: The top card may not help.
The new cards bring their own luck.

pairs.tendency: Skill lies in judging when the pile is worth taking, while luck decides what the top card is.
pros: You choose when to grab.
Reading the pile pays.
cons: A lucky top card helps.
Beginners misjudge piles.

pairs.tendency: With no dice, the pile is known, since every card in it was thrown by someone you saw. Taking it is a plain calculation.
pros: Players can count the pile.
A grab is a planned move.
cons: Newcomers cannot recall the pile.
Counting slows turns.

pairs.tendency: The top card of the pile is read as a sign, and taking the pile means taking the message together with its history.
pros: Signs build up.
Players talk over the heap.
cons: Meanings pile up and clash.
A grab carries too many readings.

pairs.tendency: Players sense when to take the pile, and two may reach for it at once.
pros: Sensing a move without words.
Matching without a count.
cons: A clash when two reach.
Strangers mistime it.

pairs.tendency: Dice give events and the pile holds cards from earlier events. Taking it brings an old event back.
pros: Past events return.
The story loops back.
cons: Dice and old cards may clash.
The story gets crowded.

pairs.tendency: The pile is face up for all, so everyone knows what a grab will bring.
pros: Grabs can be planned.
Nothing is hidden.
cons: Opponents see your plan.
The pile gets guarded.

pairs.tendency: Hands are secret but the pile is public, so a grab shows part of what you need.
pros: The pile gives clues.
A grab can bluff.
cons: A grab gives away a hand.
Players avoid the pile.

pairs.tendency: A player with a secret role takes or leaves the pile according to that role, and others watch.
pros: Taking hints at a role.
Players study grabs.
cons: Honest players look false.
Players grab to mislead.

pairs.tendency: The pile records what players threw, and each grab is a clue to what they hold.
pros: The record of play is open.
Grabs give clues.
cons: Records get long.
Players forget what was thrown.

pairs.tendency: You can grab a pile you do not need, to make others think you do.
pros: A grab can be a lie.
Others doubt your hand.
cons: A big grab costs cards.
After a few bluffs, nobody reads much into a grab.

pairs.tendency: One player knows a secret rule about the pile, and the others learn it by trying to take and being refused.
pros: Each refusal tells players something.
Players test the pile.
cons: Turns are wasted.
The one who knows has to refuse again and again.

pairs.tendency: The hint giver's laid cards pile up, and taking the pile brings back old hints.
pros: Old hints return.
Guessers recover clues.
cons: Hints get mixed.
Guessers confuse old with new.

pairs.tendency: The pile holds cards already used to explore, and taking it lets you replay a path across the map.
pros: Old paths can be reused.
Players recall what was found.
cons: Taking repeats old moves.
The map may no longer fit.

pairs.tendency: One face-up hand sits near the pile, and players compare the two.
pros: There are two public stocks.
A grab can be matched against the open hand.
cons: Opponents can tell what you are after.
Too much is on show.

pairs.tendency: A heap can hold points, so taking it moves your score by an amount nobody can see.
pros: The swing stays hidden.
Guessing goes on.
cons: Scores stay unclear.
Players distrust grabs.

pairs.tendency: One player takes the pile while the others wait, and the pile changes between turns.
pros: Others see the grab coming.
There is time to plan.
cons: A big group means a long wait.
Every grab alters the round.

pairs.tendency: Everyone chooses in secret whether to take the pile and then reveals together. If two players choose it, they have to settle the clash.
pros: Taking is secret until the reveal.
Everyone decides at the same moment.
cons: Two players may want the same pile.
Ties need a rule.

pairs.tendency: Anyone can take the pile at any moment, and the quickest hand gets the heap.
pros: Quick players win the pile.
Something is always happening.
cons: Slow players miss out.
Hands collide over the heap.

pairs.tendency: A clock runs on each turn, so judging the top card and taking the pile happens in seconds.
pros: Decisions come fast.
Nobody can stall.
cons: A rushed grab is often a mistake.
Time may run out before a grab.

pairs.tendency: Over days a pile builds up, and each day one player may take it.
pros: The pile grows slowly.
There is time to think.
cons: The pile may be taken while you are away.
Players forget to check it.

pairs.tendency: A pause comes before taking the pile, so each grab is slow and watched by everyone.
pros: A grab becomes a ritual.
Players study every card that comes up.
cons: The game runs long.
Some players tire of the pauses.

pairs.tendency: The game speeds up, so the pile grows faster and grabs come sooner.
pros: Piles grow quickly.
The last rounds are frantic.
cons: Late grabs are hurried.
Early piles seem slow.

pairs.tendency: A lucky throw gives an extra turn, which can be spent taking the pile at once.
pros: An extra turn plus a grab.
Moves can chain together.
cons: A lucky player can run away.
The rest of the table sits out the run.

pairs.tendency: In the first stage the pile builds up, and in the second stage players take from it.
pros: The first stage fills the pile.
The second stage uses it.
cons: Early throws matter later.
Players pile up cards without knowing how they will be used.

pairs.tendency: The pile stands for stock in a system, such as waste, and taking it is like recycling.
pros: Waste gets reused.
Players see cycles.
cons: The model is simple.
The real world is messier.

pairs.tendency: Each group sees the pile differently. One group wants it and another wants it cleared.
pros: Roles give different views of the pile.
Groups bargain.
cons: A grab upsets others.
Roles clash.

pairs.tendency: The pile is one stock that all share, and taking it all leaves nothing for the others.
pros: The pile shows how stock is used.
Players watch each other.
cons: A greedy grab empties the pile.
Others go without.

pairs.tendency: Cards thrown now come back later when someone takes the pile, so the effect of a throw shows rounds on.
pros: Throws have a later cost.
Players plan ahead.
cons: The link is hard to see.
A throw can return to you.

pairs.tendency: Players agree a new rule on who may take the pile and test it for a few rounds.
pros: The rule gets a test.
Players see the effect.
cons: A rule may break the game.
Players argue about it.

pairs.tendency: After the game, players look at who took the pile and why.
pros: Each grab has a reason to explain.
Players say why they took it.
cons: Two players can recall the same grab differently.
Talk turns to other things.

pairs.tendency: Cards taken from the pile may be marked or torn, so the pile cannot be put back as it was.
pros: Every grab is final.
Players pause before reaching for the pile.
cons: A mistake cannot be taken back.
Players avoid the pile.

pairs.tendency: Taking the pile says something about the world: what is thrown away can be picked up again, or it cannot.
pros: The pile rule carries a view of the world.
Players see what can be picked up again.
cons: Players may push back against that view.
It can pass unnoticed.

pairs.tendency: Real money rides on the heap, so a grab carries weight.
pros: Every grab costs or wins something real.
Players hesitate before taking.
cons: Quarrels can start over a grab.
Some players leave the pile alone.

pairs.tendency: The heap stands for what players throw away, so taking it shows what a player will pay for points.
pros: A grab shows a choice.
The points show what players will trade away.
cons: Players chase the heap for its points.
The value behind the points is lost.

pairs.tendency: Players practise a future where thrown-away things are shared, and the pile is the shared store.
pros: Players practise sharing.
Players get a feel for a shared store.
cons: Real life may work differently.
Some players take for show.

pairs.tendency: The dice take you along the path, and some spaces make you play a card against another player. The named suit wins those card contests, so a lucky square is only useful if you hold a trump.
pros: Dice and cards both matter on a turn.
A low roll can be made up with a trump card.
cons: Two kinds of luck land in one turn.
Newcomers forget which suit is named.

pairs.tendency: A row of cards sits in the middle and players pick one at a time. Cards from the named suit go first, so the last pickers see mostly plain suits.
pros: Trump cards are the first to be taken.
Each pick shows what a player is planning.
cons: Early pickers collect the trumps.
Late pickers get the leftovers.

pairs.tendency: Before the cards are played, players bid for the right to name the trump suit. The winner names the suit they hold most of, and everyone hears what is in their hand.
pros: The bid gives away part of the winner's hand.
The suit choice has a price.
cons: A high bid is a promise that has to be kept.
Low bidders play in a suit they did not choose.

pairs.tendency: One more trick can always be taken with one more trump, so players keep going. Every trump spent is gone for later tricks, and a long run ends when the trumps run out.
pros: Another win is always on offer.
A low trump can beat a high card.
cons: Spent trumps do not come back.
A long run can end with an empty hand.

pairs.tendency: Each part of the map goes to whoever wins the trick played for it. A player with a few trump cards can take a big area from a player with high cards of other suits.
pros: A small army can take a large area.
The suit gives everyone one thing to plan around.
cons: Trump cards get saved for the areas that matter.
A player with no trumps loses most contests.

pairs.tendency: Some job spots on the board hand out cards, and the named suit decides which of those cards are worth fetching. Workers head for the spots that give trumps.
pros: Spots with trump cards are taken first.
Cards and spots link up.
cons: The first player grabs the trump spot every round.
Later players find those spots empty.

pairs.tendency: One colour of tile is named, and it counts for more or can stand in for the others in a pattern. Tiles of that colour get kept back for the last step.
pros: One colour matters more than the rest.
Patterns have an obvious centre.
cons: Players hoard tiles of one colour.
Other colours stay on the table.

pairs.tendency: A hand holds a few trump cards, and each one is worth saving for a hard trick. A trump spent early is gone when a late trick needs it.
pros: Each card played says something about the rest of the hand.
Saving a trump gives a plan for later.
cons: An early trump leaves a gap.
A hand with no trumps feels stuck.

pairs.tendency: The named suit sits on top of all the others, so a low trump takes a trick from the highest card elsewhere. Players count the trumps they hold and the ones still out.
pros: Counting cards pays off every trick.
A small card can win a big trick.
cons: Players who lose count lose tricks.
The player with the most trumps usually leads.

pairs.tendency: Players trade cards before play, and everyone wants the trump suit. Asking for trump cards pushes up the price of every deal.
pros: Trump cards become what everyone asks for.
Trades show what each player holds.
cons: Deals gather around one suit.
The other suits are hard to trade away.

pairs.tendency: Matching cards are gathered into sets, and a set in the named suit also wins tricks. Collecting and winning pull on the same cards.
pros: One set does two jobs.
Choosing which set to chase gets simpler.
cons: Players keep trumps instead of playing them.
Sets in other suits get little attention.

pairs.tendency: Tiles build a shared map, and tiles in the trump colour win any argument over who owns a region. Players lay trump tiles next to their own pieces.
pros: The trump colour settles disputes.
The map shows who holds the key colour.
cons: Players hold trump tiles back.
Regions in other colours attract little fighting.

pairs.tendency: One player lays a card and the next answers with the same suit if they can. A player who has none can answer with a trump, and a trump cuts the chain short.
pros: Every answer is easy to read.
A trump ends a chain at once.
cons: Chains rarely go all the way round.
Players with no trumps keep following.

pairs.tendency: Nobody talks, so players watch the cards to guess who is holding the trumps. A trump played late says "I had one all along" without a word.
pros: Plays send messages.
A quiet table reads closely.
cons: Partners can misread a play.
One missed signal loses a trick.

pairs.tendency: On your turn you may name a different trump suit. A hand built around hearts turns into a plain hand when someone names spades.
pros: The ranking of cards changes mid-game.
Players keep rethinking their hands.
cons: A long-planned hand can lose its value in one turn.
Few players plan far ahead.

pairs.tendency: Each player speaks as a character who belongs to a suit, and the trump suit is the group in charge that round. Players argue why their own group ought to lead.
pros: Characters get a reason to compete.
Speeches have a goal.
cons: The ruling group shapes the story.
Characters from other suits can feel left out.

pairs.tendency: A flicked or stacked piece wins the round, and the trump colour counts for more. Everyone aims at the trump pieces first.
pros: The target is clear before each throw.
Steady hands win more rounds.
cons: Players crowd around the trump pieces.
A wobbling stack can bring down the trump piece.

pairs.tendency: Players draw the map and mark each region with a suit. The trump region wins every dispute, so everyone wants to draw it near their own land.
pros: The map has one place everyone wants.
Drawing the trump region is a big choice.
cons: Players draw regions to match the suits they hold.
Arguments start at the drawing stage.

pairs.tendency: Two card games run on two boards and each board names its own trump suit. A suit that is trump on one board is plain on the other, so the same card changes value as you turn.
pros: Two hands need two plans.
A suit swaps its value between boards.
cons: A card for one board is useless on the other.
Players lose track of which suit rules which board.

pairs.tendency: A wild card can stand for a trump of any rank, so one wild card can beat a high card. Players hold wilds for the trick that settles the round.
pros: A wild can become a trump.
Hands have another way to win.
cons: A wild can decide a round alone.
Players wait on their wilds and slow the game.

pairs.tendency: A piece that runs off one edge comes back in on the other, and a trump card decides who wins when two pieces land on one space. Attackers can come from behind.
pros: Pieces can attack from any side.
Edges stop being safe.
cons: Players watch all four sides.
Trump cards get used in odd places.

pairs.tendency: The knower holds a hand with one named trump suit, and the others ask yes or no questions to find which suit it is. With only four suits the list is short.
pros: Four suits keep the list short.
Questions about one suit get quick answers.
cons: Clues run out within a few questions.
Guessers repeat each other's questions.

pairs.tendency: Each trick won moves your piece forward, and the first piece home wins. A player with few cards can still jump ahead with a trump.
pros: Trump cards give sudden jumps.
A trailing player can catch up.
cons: A leader can lose the lead in one trick.
Players save trumps for the last stretch.

pairs.tendency: Tricks carry points and the highest total wins. Trump cards take the high-scoring tricks, so players hunt for them from the first deal.
pros: Trump cards turn into points.
Adding up is easy at the end.
cons: The player with the most trumps often leads.
One high-scoring trick can swing the whole score.

pairs.tendency: Losing a trick takes a player out, and trump cards are what keep you in. A player with no trumps left drops out first.
pros: Trump cards keep players in.
Dropping out is easy to see.
cons: Players with no trumps wait for the end.
A hand without trumps leaves early.

pairs.tendency: The team survives if it wins enough tricks against the game, and the trump suit is its shared reserve. Players agree who spends each trump and when.
pros: The team shares one resource.
Talk centres on spending the trumps.
cons: One careless trump loses a round for all.
Players watch each other's plays closely.

pairs.tendency: The whole table aims at one trick total, so players holding trumps support those who have none. A player with several trumps carries the team through the hard tricks.
pros: The trump holder knows the job.
Everyone reaches the target together.
cons: Players without trumps can feel small.
One player ends up carrying the table.

pairs.tendency: Each player holds a secret aim, such as winning a trick with a low card, and the trump suit can help or block it. Others study trump plays for clues.
pros: Trump plays hint at secret aims.
Hidden aims make plays hard to read.
cons: A trump meant for one aim spoils another.
Players guess wrong about each other.
