pairs.tendency: The story moves on each time a trick is won, and a trump is the card that turns a scene. Playing a trump changes what happens next.
pros: Cards drive the plot.
A trump marks a big event.
cons: The story waits for the cards.
Trumps can run out before the story does.

pairs.tendency: Nobody wins, yet the trump suit still beats the others, so tricks have a shape. Afterwards players look at who held the trumps and how they were played.
pros: Hands can be compared afterwards.
The suit gives play a shape.
cons: A trump has no prize to win.
Players may stop caring about winning tricks.

pairs.tendency: Each player says what success means to them, such as taking one trick with a trump. The named suit makes some goals easy and others hard to reach.
pros: Goals can be matched to the hand.
Players with few trumps pick goals they can meet.
cons: Different goals clash at the table.
Unlike results are hard to compare.

pairs.tendency: The game goes on until one player has lost, and a trump is the safest card to hold. Players keep their trumps for the last tricks.
pros: Trump cards keep a player safe.
The loser is clear at the end.
cons: Players pile up trumps and hold them back.
The rest of the table relaxes near the end.

pairs.tendency: The aim is to keep play going, so the trump suit is named again at the start of each round. A card that was useless last round may rule the next.
pros: Each round starts fresh.
Old hands do not settle.
cons: New suits keep cards useful.
No round feels like the last.

pairs.tendency: One suit beats all the others, yet nobody can win, so the beating changes nothing. Players see a ranking that leads nowhere.
pros: Players look at the ranking for itself.
Players notice what a win would look like.
cons: Tricks are won with nothing to gain.
Some players stop after a few hands.

pairs.tendency: A lone player faces a laid-out table, and a trump card clears a pile that other cards cannot. The trumps are saved for the stuck moments.
pros: A trump unblocks a stuck pile.
Solo play gets a clear tool.
cons: The game is lost if the trumps go early.
The same layout can be replayed.

pairs.tendency: Several short card games make up a match, and a new suit is trump each time. Taking the match means winning in different suits.
pros: Each game starts with a new plan.
An early loss does not end the match.
cons: Players keep a running match score.
A match can stop once one side cannot be caught.

pairs.tendency: Tricks carry penalty points, and trumps win tricks, so a hand full of trumps collects points. Players dodge tricks by playing low cards in suits where trump is rare.
pros: Winning a trick is a risk.
Low plays can be a plan.
cons: A trump can turn into a heavy load.
Players avoid the very cards that win.

pairs.tendency: Tricks add to a running total and you need to land exactly on the target. A trump win adds a big jump, so players think hard before playing one.
pros: Trump wins give big jumps.
Players watch their own totals.
cons: Going past the target loses.
A trump play can overshoot.

pairs.tendency: Players try to lose tricks, but a trump wins even when played low. A player holding trumps cannot always give a trick away.
pros: Holding trumps makes losing hard.
Players choose which cards to hold.
cons: Unwanted wins arrive by accident.
A hand full of trumps is a burden.

pairs.tendency: Each player plays their own hand from the same deal, and the trump suit is the same for all. Afterwards they compare how each of them used their trumps.
pros: Everyone faces the same cards.
Results are easy to compare.
cons: Players cannot affect each other.
Little happens between players during play.

pairs.tendency: A trump played onto your high card takes it, and everyone sees who did it. Players aim their trumps at each other's high cards.
pros: Trump plays feel like attacks.
Players notice who targets them.
cons: Revenge gets planned.
Players with no trumps feel helpless.

pairs.tendency: Players change the board, and the trump colour wins whenever pieces meet. Players build near trump tiles to protect what they hold.
pros: The board shows who holds the trump tiles.
Attacks come through the map.
cons: Trump tiles become landmarks.
A hit can come without a clear culprit.

pairs.tendency: The whole table plays tricks against the game, and the trump suit is one shared reserve. Players talk about who leads the trumps.
pros: The team plans around the trumps.
Everyone shares a single resource.
cons: Loud players can run the plan.
One mistaken trump costs the whole team.

pairs.tendency: Players mostly work together, but each has a private reason to win more tricks. A trump helps the team, and the player who plays it takes the credit.
pros: A trump helps the team and one player.
Credit gets shared out.
cons: Players hold trumps back for themselves.
The team can lose when trumps are hoarded.

pairs.tendency: Partners sit opposite each other, and trump cards win tricks for the whole team. A player can trump a partner's winning trick by mistake.
pros: Partners plan around the trumps.
A trump win counts for the team.
cons: Partners can cut each other's tricks.
Secret signals get banned or invented.

pairs.tendency: Most players work together while one plays against them in secret. A trump played at an odd moment may be an honest slip or a traitor's move.
pros: Trump plays raise suspicion.
Players study each other's choices.
cons: Honest players get blamed.
Suspicion slows the game.

pairs.tendency: Each letter carries a card, and the trump suit is agreed in the very first one. The game runs for weeks, so everyone remembers the suit between letters.
pros: The trump suit is fixed for the whole game.
Waiting leaves time to plan.
cons: A lost letter stalls the game.
A single game takes weeks.

pairs.tendency: One hand is dealt for a player who is not there, and the trump suit tells the table what that hand will do. The ghost plays by a set rule.
pros: The absent hand follows a known rule.
The ghost is easy to predict.
cons: Players count on the ghost's trumps.
The ghost can win by rule alone.

pairs.tendency: One player runs the world and names the trump suit for each scene. Characters quickly learn which suit rules the day.
pros: The game master sets each scene's top suit.
Players read the story from the suit.
cons: The game master makes all the rulings.
Players wait on the game master's call.

pairs.tendency: Passers-by can join a street game of tricks, and the trump suit is chalked on the ground where everyone can see it. Newcomers pick up the rule from the drawing.
pros: Anyone can see the trump suit.
New players join in one round.
cons: A crowd changes the hands.
A hand ends when its player walks away.

pairs.tendency: One player faces all the others, and the lone player's trumps are the main help. The rest pool their cards to wear those trumps down.
pros: The lone player has trumps to lean on.
The others have to talk.
cons: The lone player's trumps get targeted.
The pack can wear the lone player down.

pairs.tendency: You deal a hand and name a trump suit, then play the tricks against the pack. A second go with a different trump suit shows what changes.
pros: A solo hand shows how trump works.
The same deal can be tried twice.
cons: There is nobody to bluff.
A deal can end very fast.

pairs.tendency: The deal decides who holds the trump cards, and the cards you get decide most tricks. A hand with five trumps wins most tricks and a hand with none loses them.
pros: Each hand is a surprise.
Games are short.
cons: Skill matters little.
A hand with no trumps has nothing to do.

pairs.tendency: After the deal you may swap two cards, and a trump is the card most worth keeping. A swap can turn a hand with no trumps into one with a chance.
pros: A swap can fix an empty-looking hand.
The first deal does not decide everything.
cons: Swaps take extra time.
Players with luck have less need to swap.

pairs.tendency: The deal brings luck, but when to lead a trump is up to you. Two players with the same hand can finish far apart.
pros: Luck sets the hand.
Choices decide the tricks.
cons: A lucky deal can be wasted by early trumps.
Skilled players lead trumps at set moments.

pairs.tendency: Players track which trumps have been played and plan their leads. The player who remembers every card has the edge.
pros: Memory wins tricks.
Plans show over several tricks.
cons: Memory is tiring.
Newcomers cannot keep up.

pairs.tendency: The suit turned up for trump is read as a sign for the round. A round of hearts might raise a question about care.
pros: The suit gives a topic.
A round becomes a conversation.
cons: Readings differ from player to player.
Winning tricks may matter less.

pairs.tendency: Partners feel when the other is about to play a trump and play to match. After a while two partners trump together without a word.
pros: Partners start to read each other.
Trump plays line up.
cons: A new partner is hard to read.
A distracted player breaks the rhythm.

pairs.tendency: A roll picks the scene from a table, and the trump suit says which group holds the upper hand in it. A roll of hearts means the heart characters lead.
pros: Dice and cards set each scene.
The story has a rule for who leads.
cons: A roll can clash with the cards.
Scenes can seem random.

pairs.tendency: All the cards are face up, so everyone can see every trump. Players plan several tricks ahead and know what each opponent can do.
pros: Plans can be checked.
No trump comes as a surprise.
cons: Players spend long minutes thinking.
The slowest thinker holds up the table.

pairs.tendency: Nobody sees another player's hand, so trump cards stay secret until played. A sudden trump on a high card is a surprise.
pros: A played trump reveals something.
Surprise cuts happen often.
cons: Players guess who holds trumps.
Holders hide their cards easily.

pairs.tendency: Some players have secret roles, and a trump play hints at which side someone is on. Players read every trump as a clue.
pros: Trump plays leak roles.
Players watch for slips.
cons: An innocent trump looks suspicious.
Suspicion spreads fast.

pairs.tendency: Players work out who holds the trumps from what has been played. A player who fails to follow suit is out of that suit and may hold a trump.
pros: Failing to follow gives information away.
Clues add up trick by trick.
cons: Missing one clue spoils the count.
Careful note-taking is needed.

pairs.tendency: A player leads a low card as if holding a trump, or hides a trump to look short of them. Others guess what is held from how it is led.
pros: Bluffs hide the trumps.
Leads say things.
cons: A bluff can be answered by a real trump.
Players stop trusting leads.

pairs.tendency: Newcomers do not know which suit is trump and find out when a low card wins. They test the rule by playing and being told no.
pros: Newcomers learn by losing a trick.
The trump rule is found through play.
cons: The first tricks are confusing.
The teacher has to keep the rule secret.

pairs.tendency: One player knows the trump suit and cannot say it. They can only play and hint with cards, and their partner works it out.
pros: Hints use the cards themselves.
Partners learn each other's signs.
cons: A wrong guess loses tricks.
The knower may get frustrated.

pairs.tendency: The map is hidden and turned over tile by tile, and the trump suit shows on tiles as they come up. A region found late can hold the trump.
pros: Exploring reveals the trump areas.
Hidden tiles keep players curious.
cons: Players rush to unseen areas.
A trump region found late changes the plans.

pairs.tendency: One hand is laid face up, so everyone sees its trumps. The player who runs it plans with an open view, and opponents plan against it.
pros: Open trumps change what opponents do.
The open hand is easy to read.
cons: One player plays two hands at once.
The open hand gets used up fast.

pairs.tendency: Points from tricks are kept secret, and trump wins add points nobody can count. Players guess the leader from who holds trumps.
pros: Nobody knows the leader.
Trump plays hint at points.
cons: Guessing replaces counting.
The final reveal can surprise the table.

pairs.tendency: Turns go round the table in order, and the trump suit changes what a turn is worth. A player late in the order sees how many trumps have gone.
pros: Later players see more.
The order shows how much to risk.
cons: Early players guess blindly.
A turn can pass with nothing to play.

pairs.tendency: Everyone lays a card face down at once and all reveal together, and any trump wins the round. Players guess what others will lay before choosing.
pros: A reveal decides the round.
Nobody waits for a turn.
cons: Two trumps in one round tie.
Players hold trumps back for later.

pairs.tendency: Anyone can play a card at any moment, and a trump slapped down first takes the pile. The quickest hand wins the trump.
pros: Speed counts.
Trumps go down fast.
cons: Slow readers lose out.
Cards get thrown down in a scramble.

pairs.tendency: Each player has a short clock to pick a card, and a trump is the play that rarely goes wrong. When time runs out, a random card is played.
pros: A trump is a quick safe play.
The clock pushes quick choices.
cons: Time can run out with a trump unplayed.
A random card can waste a trump.

pairs.tendency: One trick is played each morning for weeks, and the trump suit stays fixed across the whole span. Players keep their trumps through many days.
pros: Players plan across weeks.
Trumps are kept a long time.
cons: A hand can be forgotten.
Days pass with no play.

pairs.tendency: Players take a breath before each card, and a trump played after a long pause lands heavily. The slow pace gives everyone time to follow.
pros: Each trump is noticed.
Slow play lets everyone follow.
cons: Games drag.
Impatient players leave.

pairs.tendency: Rounds get shorter as the game goes on, and trumps are played faster each time. Late tricks go to whoever kept a trump.
pros: Hands empty fast.
Trumps decide the late tricks.
cons: Players cannot plan far.
The ending comes in a rush.

pairs.tendency: A trick won with a trump gives you another go at once. A player with several trumps can chain wins one after another.
pros: Trumps earn more turns.
One player can move ahead alone.
cons: Others wait while one player plays.
A lucky hand dominates the table.

pairs.tendency: In the first stage players pick their cards, and in the second they play tricks with them. The trump suit is named between the stages, after the picks are made.
pros: Picks are made before the trump is known.
The second stage shows who guessed right.
cons: A picked set can lose its value.
The naming can feel sudden.

pairs.tendency: The board works like a village's water through the year, and the trump suit stands for the monsoon. In that season rain cards beat the others.
pros: The season changes what wins.
Players see why timing matters.
cons: The season can seem arbitrary.
A real year has more than one season.

pairs.tendency: Each player is a group in a village, and the trump suit is the group with the most say that year. The ruling group changes each round.
pros: The ruling group changes each round.
Players see each other's needs.
cons: Small groups lose most disputes.
The same group can feel ignored round after round.

pairs.tendency: Everyone draws from one limited pool, and trump cards let the holder take more from it. Players with trumps drain the pool quicker.
pros: Trump cards grant a bigger share.
The pool is easy to watch.
cons: The pool can empty quickly.
When it runs dry, everyone is hit.

pairs.tendency: A trump played now changes what the table can do several rounds later. The result shows up only after players have forgotten the cause.
pros: Trumps have long effects.
Players plan ahead.
cons: Cause and effect drift apart.
Results surprise players.

pairs.tendency: Players agree on a new rule for trump, such as the lowest trump winning, and play on to see. One hand is enough to see what the rule changes.
pros: A rule can be tested in one hand.
Groups learn by changing it.
cons: A new rule can break old plans.
Agreeing takes time.

pairs.tendency: After the game players talk about when each trump was played and why. Each person remembers a different trick.
pros: Choices can be revisited.
Trump decisions get discussed.
cons: Players remember differently.
Talk can run longer than the game.

pairs.tendency: Each trump played is torn or marked, so it can never be used again. The trump suit thins out over rounds and later hands begin with fewer.
pros: Trump cards wear out.
Each play matters.
cons: The game changes for later hands.
A trump torn too soon is gone.

pairs.tendency: One suit always beats the rest, which says something about power. Players feel this each time they lose a trick to it.
pros: The rule carries an argument.
Players feel it in their hands.
cons: The rule is easy to resent.
Not everyone agrees with it.

pairs.tendency: Players bet real things on tricks, and the trump suit changes who gets paid. A trump in one friend's hand moves real money.
pros: Trumps have a real price.
Players take each play seriously.
cons: Friends can fall out.
Winning can sting afterwards.

pairs.tendency: Each suit stands for something like health or kindness, and the trump suit is the one that wins. Players start to collect that suit.
pros: The game shows which value wins.
Players chase one suit.
cons: Other values are ignored.
Players may not see what the suits stand for.

pairs.tendency: Players practise a village that shares everything, and the trump suit stands for the shared goal. Players see one goal win out over the others.
pros: The winning goal is plain to see.
The practice is a safe try.
cons: The future may feel odd.
Players may disagree on the goal.

pairs.tendency: One roll moves a piece on both boards, so a single throw helps on one path and may hurt on the other. Players choose which board gets the bigger move.
pros: One throw does two jobs.
Players pick where the move goes.
cons: A lucky roll helps one board only.
Two paths are hard to keep track of.

pairs.tendency: Cards picked from the shared row can go to either board, so every pick has two homes. Players pick for one board and give up the other.
pros: Every card has two uses.
Picks show which board matters to you.
cons: Choosing takes longer.
A card for one board leaves the other short.

pairs.tendency: Players bid coins for the right to move first on one board, and the same coin cannot be spent twice. Winning one auction leaves less for the other.
pros: Money is shared across both boards.
A bid shows which board you value.
cons: Winning one board costs coins for the other.
Players run out of coins early.

pairs.tendency: Another risk on board one leaves board two undefended. A run of luck on one can cost you the other.
pros: Risks on one board show on the other.
Gains arrive fast.
cons: Players overreach and lose both.
Attention gets split.

pairs.tendency: Pieces hold areas on two maps, attacking on one and defending on the other. A gain on one map can be a loss on the other.
pros: Territory is fought over twice.
Both maps give a view of the opponent.
cons: A defence on one map thins out the attack on the other.
Both maps need watching.

pairs.tendency: Workers go to jobs on two boards, and each worker sent to one board is missing from the other. Spots on both boards fill quickly.
pros: Each worker has two possible places.
Spots fill on both boards.
cons: Players run short of workers.
A spot lost on one board stays lost.

pairs.tendency: A tile placed on one board builds your pattern, while the same colour on the other board builds your opponent's. Every tile helps one side and hurts the other.
pros: A single tile can shift both patterns.
Patterns grow on both boards at once.
cons: Players stop to check which board a tile is for.
Tiles get set down on the wrong board.

pairs.tendency: One hand of cards serves two boards, so each card played to one is gone from the other. Players keep cards back for whichever board needs them.
pros: Each hand is used twice.
Choices stay open longer.
cons: Hands empty fast.
A card saved for one board waits too long.

pairs.tendency: Two tricks are played at once on two tables, and the same cards cannot be on both. Players split their high cards between the tables.
pros: Winning one trick can lose the other.
High cards have to be shared out.
cons: Counting cards is twice the work.
The order of play gets tangled.

pairs.tendency: Players talk about trades while moving on two boards, and a deal on one board shifts the other. A promise made on board one is tested on board two.
pros: Deals reach across both boards.
Trades pair with moves.
cons: Promises tangle.
Players forget what they promised.

pairs.tendency: A set started from pieces on board one can be finished with pieces from board two. Players watch both boards for the missing piece.
pros: Collecting runs on two fronts.
A set can fill from either board.
cons: Both boards need attention.
A set can sit half-built on a board nobody checks.

pairs.tendency: A tile goes on one map or the other, and a road built on one may be cut on the other. Players place carefully because there are two places to be wrong.
pros: Each tile has two homes.
Both maps grow at once.
cons: Tiles end up in the wrong place.
The two maps can drift apart.

pairs.tendency: A move on one board is answered by a move on the other, so the two boards trade replies like a conversation. Each answer asks a new question.
pros: The boards answer each other.
Each move prompts the next.
cons: Chains grow long.
Players forget which board is next.

pairs.tendency: Nobody speaks, so a player can only show the next move on each board by what they play. Partners learn to read plays from both boards.
pros: Players read both boards carefully.
Partners learn to signal in plays.
cons: A signal for one board is mistaken for the other.
Silence makes errors last longer.

pairs.tendency: A rule changed on one board can be changed back on the other, so players argue over which version is in play. Each board ends up with its own set of rules.
pros: Rules can differ between boards.
Players try each version.
cons: Rules clash.
The list of changes grows long.

pairs.tendency: One character is in two places at once, so players swap between two scenes. Words said in one scene are remembered in the other.
pros: One character has two stories.
Players switch voices often.
cons: Scenes interrupt each other.
Memory of what was said is split.

pairs.tendency: Players flick pieces on two boards, one hand for each. Skill splits across the hands, and a throw on one board can knock the other.
pros: Each hand has its own job.
Skill is shared between hands.
cons: A throw on one board can bump the other.
Tired hands drop pieces.

pairs.tendency: Two maps are drawn side by side, and each region drawn on one is mirrored or flipped on the other. Players decide whether the maps match.
pros: Two maps grow together.
Features can echo across maps.
cons: Drawing takes twice as long.
Maps can contradict each other.

pairs.tendency: A wild card can be named one thing on one board and another on the other, so the same card does two jobs. Players think about where the wild is needed most.
pros: One card serves two boards.
Wilds can finish sets on either.
cons: Wilds run out.
A wild used on one board leaves the other short.

pairs.tendency: Both boards wrap round at the edges, so a line that runs off one side comes back on the other. A piece can come at you from behind on either board.
pros: Attacks can arrive from any direction.
No edge offers cover.
cons: Players watch eight sides, four on each board.
Plans for one board fail on the other.

pairs.tendency: The secret holder keeps two secrets, one for each board, and the guessers split their questions between them. Each answer narrows one of the lists.
pros: Every answer rules out options for one secret.
A question can be spent on either board.
cons: The question count is short.
Players mix up which board a question was for.

pairs.tendency: Two races run at once and the first across the line on either board wins. Players choose where to push, and a lead on one can be dropped for the other.
pros: Players decide where to push.
A late jump can win the other race.
cons: A lead on one board can slip away.
Effort is spread thin.

pairs.tendency: Points are added from both boards, so a low score on one can be made up on the other. Players trade effort between the two.
pros: Totals come from two sources.
Players shift effort between boards.
cons: Adding up takes longer.
A mistake on one board shows in the final total.

pairs.tendency: Players can be knocked out of one board and stay in the other. The last one alive on both wins.
pros: A knockout is not always final.
Players guard both boards.
cons: Knocked-out players keep watching.
Games go long.

pairs.tendency: The team faces two attacks at once, and each worker sent to one front leaves the other open. One board can fall while the other holds.
pros: The team splits its workers.
Talk is about who covers which board.
cons: A board left thin can be lost.
Both losses are shared.

pairs.tendency: The table works towards one goal that needs progress on both boards. Some players take one board each and report back.
pros: Both boards feed one goal.
Players split the jobs.
cons: One board can lag behind.
The team waits on the slower side.

pairs.tendency: Each player holds a secret aim tied to one board, and moves on the other board can cover for it. Opponents have trouble guessing which aim goes with which board.
pros: Moves on one board cover for the other.
Hidden aims stay hidden longer.
cons: Players guess the wrong board.
Aims get tangled together.

pairs.tendency: Two stories run side by side and the game ends when both reach an ending. Events in one story echo in the other.
pros: Two stories move along together.
Events echo across them.
cons: The endings can clash.
One story can finish while the other has barely started.

pairs.tendency: Nobody wins, and players move on two boards and then stop to look at both. The two results can be set side by side and talked about.
pros: Two results can be compared.
Players see how their choices differ.
cons: Neither board has a prize.
Looking at both boards takes time.

pairs.tendency: Each player sets a target for each board, such as winning one and merely surviving the other. Players pick one board to care about most.
pros: Goals differ for each board.
Players choose where to care.
cons: Goals can clash at the table.
Results are hard to compare.

pairs.tendency: The game ends when one player loses on either board, and everyone else is safe. Players watch both boards for danger.
pros: There are two ways to lose.
Players keep watch on both boards.
cons: The collapse of one board ends both.
The loser can be decided by a small slip.

pairs.tendency: When one board ends, players start it again while the other goes on. There is always a board in play.
pros: Nobody waits for a new game to start.
Play never stops.
cons: Boards drift out of step.
The table never gets a clear ending.

pairs.tendency: Both boards refuse to be won, and moves on one cannot help on the other. Players compare two failures.
pros: Each board resists play.
The two dead ends can be set side by side.
cons: Effort goes nowhere.
Players stop when they see the pattern.

pairs.tendency: You clear one layout while a second layout piles up beside it, all alone. Progress on one can unstick the other.
pros: There are two puzzles at once.
Clearing part of one layout can free the other.
cons: Both layouts can jam.
A stuck board loses both.

pairs.tendency: Each game in the match is played on two boards, and the match goes to whoever wins more boards. Early mistakes carry over to later games.
pros: The match counts both boards.
Early losses can be made up.
cons: A single game takes longer.
Matches run long.

pairs.tendency: Points pile up on both boards and the lowest total wins. Safe plays on one board leave room to take risks on the other.
pros: Players dodge points on two fronts.
Safe plays on one board give room on the other.
cons: A big penalty on one board ruins the total.
Counting is split across boards.

pairs.tendency: An exact count is needed on each board, and a roll that suits one board may overshoot the other. Players wait for the right number on both.
pros: Rolls have to fit two targets.
Players choose which board to finish first.
cons: Exact finishes are hard twice over.
Players wait for the right number.

pairs.tendency: Players try to lose on both boards, and a clever loss on one can win the other by accident. Giving things away needs care in two places.
pros: Losing needs care twice.
Players set up losses.
cons: Accidental wins happen.
Two boards mean two ways to slip.

pairs.tendency: Everyone runs their own two boards and compares notes at the end. Nobody touches anybody else's pieces.
pros: Each player has two boards.
Comparing is simple.
cons: Little contact.
Each player has a lot to track alone.

pairs.tendency: You attack on one board while the same opponent attacks you on the other. Every hit has a reply waiting on the other side.
pros: Attack and defence go together.
Opponents know each other's habits.
cons: Revenge crosses boards.
Players overreact.

pairs.tendency: Changes on one board show up on the other as side effects. Players feel each other through two maps.
pros: Rivals affect each other without a direct attack.
A wall on one board changes moves on the other.
cons: Cause is hard to trace.
Blame is unclear.

pairs.tendency: The team plays one side on each board against the game, so the same people win or lose both. Players split jobs between the boards.
pros: The team splits tasks.
Both boards share one result.
cons: A slow board holds back the team.
Talk is needed all the time.

pairs.tendency: Players help each other on one board and compete on the other. A friend on one board is a rival on the other.
pros: Friends and rivals at once.
Alliances get tested.
cons: Trust is hard to read.
A helper on one board can turn on the other.

pairs.tendency: Each team has one player per board, so partners sit at different tables. Messages between partners are slow.
pros: Partners cover one board each.
Teams share one result.
cons: Partners cannot see each other's board.
Partners wait a long time to hear from each other.

pairs.tendency: The traitor works against the team on one board while seeming to help on the other. The two boards give the traitor cover.
pros: The traitor can act one way on each board.
Boards give cover.
cons: Loyal players can be accused.
Spotting a traitor takes time.

pairs.tendency: Moves for both boards go out in the same letter, and a reply may carry two moves. A game can run for months.
pros: One letter handles both boards.
The waiting is shared.
cons: Games take months.
A lost letter loses two moves.

pairs.tendency: The absent player's pieces on one board move by a set rule while the others play the second board.
pros: The absent side acts by rule.
Players learn its habits.
cons: The ghost can surprise the table.
Extra rules pile up.

pairs.tendency: The game master runs two worlds and players travel between them.
pros: One voice runs two worlds.
Players hear about both.
cons: The game master's work doubles.
Scenes wait on the game master.

pairs.tendency: Passers-by can join either board of a chalk game, and the boards fill up with players. Sides change as people come and go.
pros: Onlookers pick a board.
Players come and go.
cons: Sides change mid-game.
A crowd mixes up the boards.

pairs.tendency: The lone player runs both boards against the pack, while the pack splits itself to cover both.
pros: One mind covers two fronts.
The pack has to coordinate.
cons: The lone player tires.
The pack can overlook one board.

pairs.tendency: You play both sides of both boards, so you attack yourself and have nothing to hide. Different plans can be tried one after the other.
pros: You see everything.
You can try different plans.
cons: There is no opponent.
Play is slow.

pairs.tendency: Both boards run on dice, and a lucky run on one can be cancelled by an unlucky one on the other. Players watch two sets of throws.
pros: Luck evens out across boards.
Games are quick.
cons: Players have little to choose.
Two sets of throws give twice as much waiting.

pairs.tendency: A re-roll can be spent on either board, so players choose where to soften a low throw. Some saved re-rolls wait for the second board.
pros: Re-rolls can go to either board.
Players choose where luck is softened.
cons: Re-rolls run out.
Saving a re-roll can cost a board.

pairs.tendency: A little luck turns up on each board, but where you spend your attention is your own choice. Two players with the same luck can finish far apart.
pros: Luck is small on each board.
Choices decide where effort goes.
cons: Neglecting one board shows quickly.
Lucky throws can be wasted on the wrong board.

pairs.tendency: Both boards are open puzzles with no dice, and the player who thinks ahead on both gains the most. Time to think is split between boards.
pros: Planning pays on both boards.
Thinking time is split.
cons: Slow thinkers fall behind.
Newcomers can't hold both boards in mind.

pairs.tendency: A throw is read as a sign on two boards, and the two readings may disagree. Players talk through which sign to follow.
pros: Two readings sit side by side.
Players talk over what they mean.
cons: The signs may clash.
Players may follow the wrong sign.

pairs.tendency: Partners sense when the other is about to move and play on opposite boards to match. After a while a move on one board is answered on the other without a word.
pros: Partners sync across boards.
Moves answer each other quietly.
cons: Someone new takes time to learn.
One lapse of attention breaks the timing.

pairs.tendency: A roll picks a scene from a table for each board, and the two scenes happen at once. Players decide how the two stories touch.
pros: Dice write two stories.
Scenes can meet in odd ways.
cons: Rolls can clash.
Players lose track of two plots.

pairs.tendency: Both boards are fully open, so every piece on both can be seen. Players plan against what the opponent can do on each board.
pros: Plans can be checked on both boards.
Every piece is in view.
cons: Thinking takes a long time.
Everyone waits for the player who takes longest.

pairs.tendency: Nobody sees another's cards, and the same hand serves both boards. A card held for one board hints at what is wanted on the other.
pros: One hand hides two plans.
Cards played on one board hint at the other.
cons: Players guess wrongly.
Hidden cards make play slower.

pairs.tendency: Some players have secret roles, and a move on one board shows a side on the other. Players watch both boards for slips.
pros: Moves on one board hint at roles on the other.
Slips show on two boards.
cons: A harmless move can look like a giveaway.
Doubt soon reaches every player.

pairs.tendency: Clues from one board help to work out hidden facts on the other. Players keep notes on two boards.
pros: Clues cross between boards.
Notes grow quickly.
cons: One missed clue spoils two puzzles.
Notes get mixed up.

pairs.tendency: A bluff on one board is backed up by a move on the other. Players watch for lies on both.
pros: Lies get support from the other board.
Bluffs are harder to read.
cons: A failed bluff on one board shows on the other.
Players stop trusting any move.

pairs.tendency: One secret rule applies to both boards, and newcomers find it only by breaking it on either board. Each told-off move teaches twice.
pros: One rule is learned twice.
A single mistake shows the rule on both boards.
cons: Players break the rule on both boards.
The teacher has to watch two boards.

pairs.tendency: The knower hints at an answer by playing on two boards, and guessers read both. Hints can be hidden in the second board.
pros: Hints use both boards.
Guessers read more clues.
cons: A clue on the wrong board is missed.
The knower may find it hard to stay silent.

pairs.tendency: Two maps are hidden and turned over tile by tile, and what turns up on one board hints at the other. Exploring means choosing which map to open.
pros: Exploring has two choices.
Tiles on one map hint at the other.
cons: Players open the wrong map first.
Plans keep changing.

pairs.tendency: One hand is laid face up for both boards, so everyone can see what might be played on either. Whoever runs it can plan with every card in sight.
pros: An open hand helps on both boards.
Opponents can plan against it.
cons: The player running it handles two hands.
Its cards run out quickly.

pairs.tendency: Scores from the two boards are kept secret, so nobody can add them up for sure. Players guess who is ahead on each board.
pros: The lead stays uncertain to the end.
Players have to estimate.
cons: A big surprise comes at the end.
Players doubt every total.

pairs.tendency: Players take turns, and each turn is spent on one board or the other. Whoever waits sees both boards change.
pros: A turn is spent on one board.
The waiting player watches both boards.
cons: Neglected boards fall behind.
Long waits with many players.

pairs.tendency: Everyone picks a move for each board at once and reveals together. Each player makes two choices in secret.
pros: Two picks come at once.
Reveals decide both boards.
cons: Players can't wait for each other.
Mistakes are doubled.

pairs.tendency: Anyone can move on either board at any moment, and speed decides who gets the move. Quick hands win on both boards.
pros: Speed counts on both boards.
Moves arrive in a rush.
cons: A slow player gets fewer moves.
Pieces get knocked over in the rush.

pairs.tendency: Each turn has a short clock, and the player picks which board gets the time. When the clock runs out the move is lost.
pros: Time is shared out.
Players choose where to spend time.
cons: Choices are quick.
Moves get lost on the clock.

pairs.tendency: Each morning you make one move on one board, and the other board waits for tomorrow. Games run for weeks.
pros: Moves are spread over days.
Players plan across weeks.
cons: One board waits.
A board can sit untouched for days.

pairs.tendency: Players pause and breathe before each move, and the second board makes the pause longer. A slow pace helps keep track of two boards.
pros: Both boards are easier to follow.
Each move is noticed.
cons: The game takes much longer.
Restless players drift off.

pairs.tendency: Both boards speed up as the game goes on, so the second board arrives faster than players can plan for. Play is fastest at the very end.
pros: Moves arrive faster.
Late play is hectic.
cons: Players cannot plan.
Boards slip out of hand.

pairs.tendency: An extra turn can be spent on either board, so a lucky player makes many moves on one. Players choose where the bonus goes.
pros: A bonus move has two possible homes.
A player on a streak can pull away.
cons: The rest of the table sits idle.
A lucky run decides a board.

pairs.tendency: The first stage sets up the boards and the second plays them. What was picked for one board in stage one shapes the other in stage two.
pros: Stage one shapes both boards.
Players see choices pay off.
cons: A set-up for one board can leave the other short.
The second stage starts from the first.

pairs.tendency: One board models a village's wells and the other its fields, and water moved on one shows up on the other. Players watch both to see the effect.
pros: Cause and effect cross boards.
Players see how one change reaches another.
cons: The models can be too simple.
Players struggle to follow both.

pairs.tendency: Each player is a group in a village and plays on both boards for that group. A farmer's win on the field board can be a shopkeeper's loss on the market board.
pros: Each group has two stages.
Needs conflict across boards.
cons: Groups work against each other.
Small groups lose.

pairs.tendency: Both boards draw from one pool, so each move on one board shrinks what is left for the other. Players watch the pool alongside their own board.
pros: One pool serves both boards.
Everyone can see how much is left.
cons: It drains fast.
When it runs dry both boards stall.

pairs.tendency: A move on one board shows up several rounds later on the other. Players link cause and effect across the two boards only after the fact.
pros: Effects cross between boards.
Players look several rounds ahead.
cons: The cause is hard to trace back.
Players are caught off guard.

pairs.tendency: Players agree on a new rule and try it on one board while the other keeps the old rule. The two boards can then be compared.
pros: Two rules can be compared.
A test and a control run together.
cons: Rules clash.
Players mix up the two rule sets.

pairs.tendency: After the game players talk about both boards, what happened on each and how the two linked up. Each person remembers different moves.
pros: Both boards can be talked over.
Links between boards show up.
cons: Players recall different moves.
The talk can outlast the play.

pairs.tendency: Changes on one board are permanent, and they carry over to the second board. Cards torn up for one board are gone for the other.
pros: Changes carry across boards.
Each move counts for both.
cons: Later games start altered.
A mistake stays all game.

pairs.tendency: Two boards with different rules put two arguments side by side. Players feel the difference as they cross between boards.
pros: Two arguments sit side by side.
Players feel the contrast.
cons: Players may argue over which is fair.
Switching boards can blur what each one argues.

pairs.tendency: Real bets can ride on either board, and a loss on one hurts a different friend than a loss on the other. Players take care about which board matters to whom.
pros: Real stakes are spread over two boards.
Players weigh each move.
cons: A loss can strain a friendship.
A win can leave a sour feeling.

pairs.tendency: One board scores health and the other scores kindness, and players start to chase whichever has the points. A win on one board costs the other.
pros: Each board scores something different.
Players see trade-offs between values.
cons: Players chase one board.
A value without points is ignored.

pairs.tendency: Players practise a shared village on two boards, one for how it works and one for how it feels. They compare how the two practices match up.
pros: The practice has two views.
Players can compare how it works and feels.
cons: The imagined village may feel strange.
Players may disagree on what they saw.

pairs.tendency: Dice move the pieces, and a wild card can stand in for any throw the holder names. A piece one square short of the finish can use the card instead of waiting for a six.
pros: An unlucky throw can be undone.
The holder gets one sure move.
cons: Players with the card wait for the right moment.
The race can end on a card instead of a roll.

pairs.tendency: A wild card sits in the row, and every player eyes it as the hand is passed round. Whoever takes it keeps the use open, so the pick tells nobody what comes next.
pros: One pick keeps options open.
Rivals cannot guess what the card is for.
cons: The wild card is usually gone in the first picks.
Later players see fewer useful cards.

pairs.tendency: A wild card goes up for sale, and bidders guess what it is worth to others, since its use is named only after the sale. Bids climb past the price of a plain card.
pros: Prices show how much players want it.
The winner gets a flexible card.
cons: The winner may spend most of their money.
Bids are hard to compare.

pairs.tendency: Cards are drawn one after another, and a wild card turns up just as a run was about to fail. After that, players draw for longer because the next card might be wild too.
pros: A rescue softens a lost run.
Runs get longer.
cons: Players keep drawing for one hoped-for card.
A run that ends without it loses everything.

pairs.tendency: Each area asks for a card of its own kind before a piece can enter, and a wild card works for any of them. The holder can step into an area nobody expected.
pros: A sudden move into any area.
A held card hides the next target.
cons: Rivals guard every area against one card.
One card can undo a long build-up.

pairs.tendency: Some job spaces ask for a matching card before a worker can use them, and a wild card satisfies any of those jobs. A worker can take a space that looked closed.
pros: The holder can reach any job.
Plans stay open until the last moment.
cons: Other players cannot tell which spaces are safe.
The card is worth most on the busiest turns.

pairs.tendency: A wild card fills the gap in a row of colours or shapes. A pattern one tile short is finished at once.
pros: Gaps in a pattern get filled.
Players can plan a pattern before they have all the pieces.
cons: Patterns finish sooner than expected.
A pattern made with wild cards can look the same as a pattern without.

pairs.tendency: The wild card is the one card in a hand that never has to match anything. Players choose between playing it early for a small gain or holding it for a late emergency.
pros: The hand has one flexible card.
Holding it is a plan.
cons: A long-held card is a card not used.
The card can be stuck in the hand when the game ends.

pairs.tendency: The holder names the suit and rank of the wild card when it is played, so it can follow suit even with an empty hand of that suit. Other players cannot count it when working out who holds what.
pros: A hand with no matching suit can still follow.
Card counting gets harder.
cons: Players cannot be sure what a card stands for.
A trick can be won by a card that did not exist before.

pairs.tendency: A wild card comes up in every deal, because its value depends on who needs it. One player offers it for a promise, another asks for two cards in return.
pros: The card gives deals something to centre on.
Deals have a clear object.
cons: Everyone argues about its price.
Holders can be pressed to give it up.

pairs.tendency: A wild card completes a set that would have stayed one card short. A player with three of a kind and one odd card adds the wild one and scores.
pros: Near-finished sets get finished.
Fewer cards are wasted.
cons: Sets can come together too quickly.
Players hold on to the card instead of using it.

pairs.tendency: A wild tile matches any edge, so it fits in a spot where no other tile would. Roads and fields on both sides join up neatly.
pros: A blocked spot can be filled.
Awkward corners get closed.
cons: A map can lose its odd gaps.
One tile can spoil a rival's plan to leave a spot open.

pairs.tendency: Whoever holds the wild card can answer any call in the chain, and then says what it stood for. The next caller carries on from that choice.
pros: A hard call can be answered.
The chain bends in a new direction.
cons: The next player has to take up whatever was named.
The chain can wander away from where it began.

pairs.tendency: A wild card is played without a word, so nobody can ask what it stands for. The others work out its meaning from when it was put down and what came before.
pros: Timing carries the meaning.
Players read each other closely.
cons: Two players may read the same card differently.
A wrong guess is only found out later.

pairs.tendency: One rule says what a wild card can stand for, and another turn can change that rule. A player might make wild cards cost a turn, or make more of them.
pros: The card's meaning can be reset.
Rules about it become part of the play.
cons: Players argue over what the card does now.
A rule change can make a held card useless.

pairs.tendency: A wild card marks a moment when the character may do something outside their usual skills. A quiet cook suddenly knows how to pick a lock.
pros: Characters can surprise the table.
A stuck scene gets a way forward.
cons: Such moments are limited in number.
The surprise needs the table to agree it fits.

pairs.tendency: A wild card lets a player skip one shaky move, such as a risky pull from a tower of blocks. The tower stays up for the next player.
pros: One hard move can be skipped.
Steady hands get a short rest.
cons: The skipped move is passed on to the next player.
The card can be wasted on an easy turn.

pairs.tendency: A wild card lets a player draw whatever place they like, such as a river or a market, instead of the place the prompt names. The map gets a feature nobody asked for.
pros: The map can take an odd turn.
A player can draw what they imagine.
cons: Prompts get ignored.
The map can stop hanging together.

pairs.tendency: With joined edges, a wild card that names the direction of a move lets a piece leave the board on one side and arrive on the other. The holder can pick the side it comes back in.
pros: A piece can leave and return anywhere.
Moves have more routes.
cons: Players watch all four edges at once.
A threat can appear from any side.

pairs.tendency: A wild card lets the asker put one question that is answered with a name instead of yes or no. A player who has cut the list down to three things can ask which one it is.
pros: The list can shrink quickly.
A stuck guesser gets a lead.
cons: The answerer gives away more than usual.
The long run of questions gets shorter.

pairs.tendency: Because a wild card counts as any step, a player near the end plays it to close the gap. Rivals keep an eye on who is holding one.
pros: A gap near the end can be closed.
A lead can be made in one turn.
cons: Everyone watches the holder.
A race can be decided by a single card.

pairs.tendency: A wild card scores as the highest card the holder needs. At the end, the tally depends on who kept theirs and who spent them early.
pros: Points can be made late.
Hand size counts at the end.
cons: Players count how many wild cards are still out.
The player who drew more wild cards scores more.

pairs.tendency: A wild card saves a player from knock-out by standing for the card that would have kept them in. The attacker sees the player survive against the odds.
pros: One knock-out can be avoided.
Players who look beaten stay in.
cons: The attacker cannot tell who holds one.
A game can run on longer than expected.

pairs.tendency: The team keeps a wild card for the one need nobody covers. Players argue about whether to spend it early or save it for the final crisis.
pros: The team has one safety net.
Players talk about timing together.
cons: Spending it early leaves nothing for the end.
One player may hold it too long.

pairs.tendency: A wild card fills the one missing piece of the shared goal. The team talks over who plays it, and each of them has a reason to keep it.
pros: A stuck goal can be finished.
The team shares the choice.
cons: Players disagree on who plays it.
The team may wait too long for the right moment.

pairs.tendency: A wild card helps any secret goal, so playing it gives little away. Others only learn that the player needed a piece.
pros: A secret goal stays secret.
The card helps whichever goal the player holds.
cons: Others see it taken.
A player known to hold one is watched closely.

pairs.tendency: A wild card is a twist the storyteller can slot in anywhere. A stranger arrives, a river floods, a letter turns up.
pros: The story can turn.
Players can steer the plot.
cons: Twists come at odd times.
The ending can go somewhere nobody planned.

pairs.tendency: Wild cards stand for anything as players lay things out, and there is nothing to win. Each player picks what the card becomes by what they want to see made.
pros: Players choose what they build.
The card has no price.
cons: Nothing says when to stop.
Some players leave the card unused.

pairs.tendency: Each player decides what the wild card is worth to them. One player treats it as the key to a goal, and another leaves it alone because their goal is small.
pros: The card means different things to different players.
Goals can be reached in more than one way.
cons: Scores are hard to compare.
A player with a low goal may never use it.

pairs.tendency: In a game where the last holder of an unmatched card loses, a wild card matches anything. Whoever holds it is safe, so everyone else tries to take it.
pros: The holder is safe for a turn.
Cards are passed with care.
cons: Others try to grab it.
The loser is often whoever missed the wild card.

pairs.tendency: A wild card can stand in for whatever is missing, so a game that stalled starts again. Players spend it to keep a round alive.
pros: A stalled round can carry on.
Gaps in the cards do not stop play.
cons: Wild cards run out.
The game can end for lack of them.

pairs.tendency: A wild card is meant to stand for anything, but the rules refuse to let it stand for a win. Players reach for it and find it does nothing.
pros: The card can stand for anything but a win.
Players learn what the game will not allow.
cons: The card feels like a trick played on the holder.
Players may stop using it.

pairs.tendency: A player alone against the cards uses a wild card to clear a stuck pile. Spending it too early leaves no help when the layout jams.
pros: A stuck layout can be freed.
The player chooses when to use help.
cons: There is only one such rescue.
Using it early can end the game later.

pairs.tendency: A wild card kept from the first short game may be carried into the next one, or it may reset. A player who saved one is ahead after game one.
pros: A saved card helps in the next game.
A series can turn on one choice.
cons: The player who lost game one may hold no card.
Players hold back in early games.

pairs.tendency: A wild card can take the place of a high-point card in a set, so the holder drops points they would otherwise carry. At the end, the cards still in hand are added up.
pros: Points can be shed.
A heavy hand can be lightened.
cons: A held card still counts at the end.
Players race to get rid of it.

pairs.tendency: A wild card stands for the exact number needed. A player who is two short or three over can still land on the target.
pros: The exact number is easier to reach.
A player over the target can be saved.
cons: The card is used on the last move.
Others wait for the holder to finish.

pairs.tendency: A wild card can be played onto any pile, so it helps whoever wants to lose cards fastest. The player empties a hand in fewer turns.
pros: Cards leave the hand quicker.
A stuck hand can be emptied.
cons: Rivals can pass cards to the holder.
The card ends the game early for the player who plays it.

pairs.tendency: Everyone builds alone, and wild cards fill gaps without touching rival tables. Players see each other using theirs but cannot take them.
pros: Each player's gaps get filled.
Nothing is lost to a rival.
cons: Players only compare what they see.
Wild cards cannot change another player's game.

pairs.tendency: A wild card lets the holder answer any attack with a matching defence, or play as an attack of any kind. A target who held one turns a sure loss into a draw.
pros: An attack can always be answered.
The holder is hard to read.
cons: An attacker may hold back.
Fights are decided by who has the card.

pairs.tendency: A wild card placed on the board takes on whatever shape is needed. Other players feel it as a blocked space or an open road.
pros: The board gets a flexible piece.
Rivals work around it.
cons: Players cannot plan on how it will be used.
A blocked square can appear late.

pairs.tendency: The team shares its wild cards and talks about who needs them. A player with a full hand hands one to a teammate whose turn is stuck.
pros: Cards go where they are needed.
The whole team plans the use.
cons: Talk can slow the turn.
A card spent early cannot help later.

pairs.tendency: One wild card is wanted by everyone for private reasons. The team has to agree who gets it, and each player can argue for their own claim.
pros: The card makes players talk.
The team's choice reveals private aims.
cons: The team may argue over who gets it.
A player may take it without asking.

pairs.tendency: A wild card passes between teammates, and the other team tries to guess which gap it covers. The team holding it plans round it in whispers.
pros: Teammates share the use.
The card can be passed at the right time.
cons: The other team watches the hand-over.
A team may wait to play it.

pairs.tendency: The traitor can use a wild card to fake any card, so others cannot tell whether a stand-in is honest. A team may suspect anyone who plays one.
pros: The traitor can hide.
Any card might be honest or not.
cons: Suspicion falls on whoever plays one.
Honest players avoid using it.

pairs.tendency: A wild card sent in a letter takes days to arrive, and the receiver names what it is in the next letter. A reply can change what the card meant.
pros: Meaning is settled in the reply.
Players plan during the wait.
cons: Letters cross in the post.
A card can be forgotten in a long gap.

pairs.tendency: The absent player's hint says what a wild card stands for, while the players at the table cannot ask. A ghost may point to a card and say it can be anything.
pros: The hint holds the meaning.
Players read it carefully.
cons: Nobody can check the answer.
Players may read the hint wrongly.

pairs.tendency: The game master decides what a wild card turns into when it is played, or rules on whether the player's choice is allowed. A player asks for a bridge and the game master says yes or no.
pros: One person settles each case.
The game master can shape the scene.
cons: Players wait for a ruling.
Rulings can change from one scene to the next.

pairs.tendency: In a street game with passers-by, a wild card can be handed to a newcomer to get them started. A stranger who joins mid-game uses it to catch up.
pros: A newcomer can join at once.
The card can be shared round.
cons: Regular players watch where it goes.
The card can be lost in a crowd.

pairs.tendency: The lone player holds more wild cards, or the many share a single one. The many agree together before they spend it.
pros: The odds can be balanced.
Sides get different tools.
cons: The group has to agree on use.
The lone player's card can be missed.

pairs.tendency: Playing alone, the wild card is the only helper. The player keeps it for a stuck moment and decides when the moment has come.
pros: A stuck game gets a way out.
The player chooses their own help.
cons: No one else can share the choice.
A single wild card may be used too soon.

pairs.tendency: Cards are drawn at random, and a wild card is one more lucky draw. A player who finds it does nothing to earn it.
pros: The draw has a happy surprise.
A run of dull draws can end.
cons: Skill hardly changes who gets one.
A game can be settled by who draws it.

pairs.tendency: A wild card is a way to soften a low draw. A player with a hand of low cards plays it to turn the draw into something useful.
pros: A low draw can be eased.
Players are not helpless.
cons: The card runs out.
A player may wait for a wild card and play too slowly.

pairs.tendency: The wild card is the small touch of luck in a game of planning. Skilled players plan round when it will turn up and when to play it.
pros: A little luck adds variety.
Planning still counts.
cons: The luck can upset a careful plan.
A rare wild card can decide a close game.

pairs.tendency: A wild card adds one flexible piece to a game of pure planning, and players can count how many are left in the deck. A careful player knows how likely it is to turn up.
pros: Planning has one flexible piece.
Counting wild cards is possible.
cons: The card can break a long plan.
Skill is spent working out when it comes.

pairs.tendency: A wild card is read as an open sign that points wherever the reader chooses. The reader decides what it means.
pros: The sign fits the question.
Readers bring their own meaning.
cons: Two readers can read it differently.
The meaning can drift.

pairs.tendency: Players try to act at the same moment, and a wild card played by one is read by the others as a signal. A glance and a card come down together.
pros: A signal can pass without words.
Groups get used to each other.
cons: A signal can be misread.
The card can lead the others at the wrong time.

pairs.tendency: A wild card lets a player pick the result from the table instead of rolling. Where the dice would say a bandit appears, the player chooses a friendly traveller.
pros: The player picks a result.
The story turns the way the player wants.
cons: The dice are set aside.
Other players see the choice and may object.

pairs.tendency: Everyone sees every wild card, so each player knows what the others hold. The only open question is what each card will turn into.
pros: No wild card is a surprise.
Plans can be made round the open cards.
cons: Little is hidden.
Players can block the card's most useful play.

pairs.tendency: A wild card in a hidden hand lets the holder claim to have almost anything. Others guess from the way it is played.
pros: The holder can bluff.
A hand can look larger than it is.
cons: Others cannot read the hand.
Players doubt every play.

pairs.tendency: A wild card played could pass as the card a secret role would use. Players wonder whether it was a trick or a real part of the role.
pros: A role can be disguised.
The card hides an identity.
cons: Players blame each other.
A wrong accusation can fall on an honest player.

pairs.tendency: A wild card muddies the clues, since a clue card might really be wild. Investigators have to test each clue before trusting it.
pros: A clue can be tested.
Investigators check more than once.
cons: A false clue can mislead.
Careful players spend extra turns.

pairs.tendency: A wild card makes any claim partly true. A player who claims three kings and holds two and a wild card is half telling the truth.
pros: A bluff is easier to make.
A claim is hard to call.
cons: Players call more often.
A caught bluff is harder to prove.

pairs.tendency: Newcomers learn that the wild card follows the secret rule too. They find out by playing it somewhere the rule forbids and being told no.
pros: The secret rule is found by trying.
A wild card shows the edge of the rules.
cons: Newcomers waste the card on a wrong try.
Players quit after a wrong guess.

pairs.tendency: The player who knows the answer holds a hint card that fits many answers. They place it down without a word and the others work out what it could be.
pros: One hint covers many answers.
The guessers talk it over.
cons: Guessers may read the hint in different ways.
The hint can lead everyone the wrong way.

pairs.tendency: A wild card lets a player turn over any hidden area, or stand in for the key to open it. A player can see what lies ahead before going there.
pros: A hidden area is opened early.
The map comes out faster.
cons: The surprise of exploring is lost.
Rivals see the area too.

pairs.tendency: A wild card in the open hand is seen by everyone, and the player who plays it for the open hand names its use. Others can see it coming.
pros: Its use is easy to follow.
Both hands are used well together.
cons: Its power is no secret.
The open hand's player has to say what it is.

pairs.tendency: Wild cards complete sets and give points that are kept secret. Others cannot tell how much a wild card was worth.
pros: Points are kept private.
The card hides its value.
cons: Players guess at the scores.
A late wild card can upset the guesses.

pairs.tendency: A wild card is played on one turn, and the next player sees what it became and plans round it. The table waits while the holder decides.
pros: The next player sees the choice.
Each play is easy to follow.
cons: Others wait for the holder.
A held card makes turns longer.

pairs.tendency: All players reveal at once, so the wild card is named at the reveal. Nobody can change a plan after seeing it.
pros: The reveal has a surprise.
Nobody waits.
cons: Choices cannot be changed after the reveal.
The card gives one player a sudden edge.

pairs.tendency: A wild card goes to whoever grabs it first, and the grabber names its use afterwards. The quickest hand at the table gets it.
pros: The fastest player gets help.
The card changes hands in a flash.
cons: Slower players rarely hold one.
Arguments arise over who grabbed first.

pairs.tendency: With the clock running, a wild card saves time because there is no need to hunt for the right card. A player with ten seconds left plays it.
pros: A tight turn gets a quick move.
Searching stops.
cons: The card is spent in a hurry.
A name picked in a rush can be the wrong one.

pairs.tendency: A wild card may be kept for days before it is played. Players wait for the day it fits and watch the others do the same.
pros: A card can wait for its day.
The wait is part of the plan.
cons: The card can be forgotten.
The gap between plays is long.

pairs.tendency: A wild card is played slowly, with a pause before the holder says what it stands for. The group waits for the answer.
pros: The choice is made with care.
Players take time to notice it.
cons: Everyone waits for the answer.
The pause can run long.

pairs.tendency: As the game speeds up, more wild cards turn up or players play them faster. The last rounds fill with names called in a rush.
pros: Late rounds are busier.
Plays come in quick bursts.
cons: Players have less time to think.
Mistakes are likelier at the end.

pairs.tendency: A wild card can finish a chain of matching cards that earns an extra turn. One player plays it and goes again.
pros: A chain can be finished.
One player gets two turns in a row.
cons: The next player waits longer.
Whoever holds it can pull ahead.

pairs.tendency: A wild card kept from the first stage into the second takes whatever the second stage's rules allow. A card picked early comes into use later.
pros: An early pick pays off later.
The two stages are linked.
cons: Stage two is hard to plan for.
Players hold back in stage one.

pairs.tendency: A wild card stands for an event nobody modelled, such as a sudden flood or a broken pump. The system takes a shock it was not built for.
pros: The model meets a surprise.
Players see how a shock knocks a system off course.
cons: The model's results can be hard to read.
A random shock can hide the cause of a failure.

pairs.tendency: A wild card lets one group act outside its usual need. A farmer group can play it to behave like a shopkeeper for one turn.
pros: A group can try another role.
Players see the problem from another side.
cons: The role loses its usual limits.
The card can blur who needs what.

pairs.tendency: A wild card counts as one unit of the shared resource, so a player can take from a pool that has run dry. Others see the pool stay empty while the holder still has some.
pros: A shortage can be covered.
Players have a backup.
cons: The holder keeps using what others have run out of.
The pool can be drained faster.

pairs.tendency: The wild card is named now, but its effect arrives a few rounds later. A player who calls it a harvest sees the grain only after the wait.
pros: A choice has a lasting effect.
Players plan ahead.
cons: The result comes late.
A wrong name is found out too late.

pairs.tendency: A new rule can say what wild cards do, and the group plays on to see the result. One round with wild cards worth two and the next with them worth none.
pros: A rule can be tested with them.
Players compare two rounds.
cons: The card changes how rounds feel.
Players argue over which round was clearer.

pairs.tendency: Afterwards the group asks what each wild card stood for and why it was played there. A card played to save a village prompts a talk about who gets saved.
pros: The talk has real examples.
Players explain their choices.
cons: Some choices are hard to recall.
The talk may last as long as the game.

pairs.tendency: Once a wild card is named and played, it stays that card for the rest of the game. The next game starts with the card still marked.
pros: The card leaves a mark.
Choices carry over.
cons: A hasty name cannot be undone.
Players hesitate before they play it.

pairs.tendency: If the rules hand wild cards to whoever is behind, the game says that help goes to those who need it. If they go to whoever is ahead, it says the opposite.
pros: The rules make a point about help.
Players can discuss who gets it.
cons: The point may annoy some players.
The point can overshadow the play.

pairs.tendency: A wild card is traded for a promise or real money, so the card's flexibility becomes worth something outside the game. A friend promises a chore for it.
pros: The card has real value.
Players barter honestly.
cons: A promise made for it has to be kept.
Friends may fall out over it.

pairs.tendency: Since a wild card can stand for any value, a player can use it to claim points in a value they have neglected. A player with no kindness points says the card is kindness.
pros: A neglected value can be topped up.
Players see which values they have missed.
cons: Points can be claimed without effort.
The number loses its link to what it stands for.

pairs.tendency: A wild card is the surprise in an imagined future, such as a flood in a village that shares everything. Players practise answering it together.
pros: Players meet an unplanned event.
They try their own answers.
cons: The surprise can overturn the plan.
The answer may not hold in real life.

pairs.tendency: A piece that passes the last square comes back to the first, so the track becomes a loop. Throws never run out of road, and a piece can lap another one.
pros: The track has no end.
A player can catch up from behind.
cons: A finish needs a clear rule.
The game can run on for a long time.

pairs.tendency: Cards picked from a shared row give moves, and a move off the right edge comes back in on the left. Players pick cards with the joined edges in mind.
pros: Moves can use the join.
A pick can aim across the board.
cons: Players think about two edges at once.
A card that looks useless can open a route.

pairs.tendency: Players bid for a spot on the board, and with joined edges every spot has neighbours on all sides. There is no safe corner, so bids for every spot are close.
pros: Every spot has a price.
Bids reflect the neighbours.
cons: Prices are hard to compare.
A high bid can buy a spot next to a rival.

pairs.tendency: A runner can keep going round the loop for more points, until a hazard on the loop catches up. Each lap earns more, and each lap meets the same trap.
pros: Each lap earns more.
The runner chooses when to stop.
cons: The same trap comes round again.
A player can lose everything on the last lap.

pairs.tendency: Areas along one edge touch the areas on the opposite edge, so a player can attack from behind. A held area is open on every side.
pros: No area is safe at the back.
Attacks come from unexpected sides.
cons: Players guard every border.
A held area is hard to keep.

pairs.tendency: The job spaces run round a ring, with the first and last side by side. A worker on the last space is next to the first job.
pros: Jobs sit in a loop.
A worker can reach distant jobs.
cons: Spaces next to each other are hard to tell.
A job at the far end blocks the first.

pairs.tendency: A line can run off one edge and carry on from the other. A pattern is finished across the join.
pros: A pattern is longer than the board looks.
A line has no end.
cons: Players can lose track of a line.
A pattern can be blocked from the other side.

pairs.tendency: Cards give moves, and a player keeps one for a jump across the join. Holding it means other cards are played first.
pros: A jump is planned.
Cards have a long-term use.
cons: Cards wait in the hand.
A planned jump can be blocked.

pairs.tendency: Each trick won moves a marker along a ring of scoring spaces, and the marker passing the last space comes back to the first. A player who wins many tricks laps the others.
pros: Winning tricks moves round a ring.
A lead can be lapped.
cons: A high score can be matched.
Tricks and track both need tracking.

pairs.tendency: Players on opposite edges are now neighbours, so deals between them cross a shared border. Two people who sit far apart on the board trade like next-door farmers.
pros: Distant players can trade.
Borders run in a ring.
cons: Deals reach across the board.
A player may be asked by both neighbours at once.

pairs.tendency: A set of matching spots can be collected across the join, so a set of three can sit at both edges. Players aim for sets that straddle the seam.
pros: A set can cross the join.
Collecting is spread over the board.
cons: Sets are harder to guard.
A set may be broken from either side.

pairs.tendency: Tiles at one edge connect to tiles on the opposite edge, so roads loop back on themselves. A road laid east comes round to its own beginning.
pros: A road can close into a ring.
The map has no edge.
cons: Players track a loop of tiles.
A loop gives few places to add new tiles.

pairs.tendency: A call and its answer are moves on the board, and a move that leaves one side is answered from the other. The chain keeps going round.
pros: The chain has no end.
An answer can cross the join.
cons: Calls reach far.
A reply may be missed on the far side.

pairs.tendency: Nobody can say that a piece is about to cross the join. The others see it coming only from where the pieces stand.
pros: A piece can cross the join without a word.
Players watch pieces closely.
cons: A crossing can surprise the table.
Players may miss a sign.

pairs.tendency: A rule change can join the edges or cut them again, turning a flat board into a loop and back. Players vote on when the world is round.
pros: The shape of the board can change.
Rules about the join become a move.
cons: Pieces may be stranded after a cut.
Players argue about the shape.

pairs.tendency: On a map where walking far enough west brings a character back in the east, the world becomes round. Characters notice they have come home from the wrong side.
pros: The world has a shape to explore.
A trip can end where it began.
cons: Characters can feel lost.
The game master has more to track.

pairs.tendency: A flicked disc that leaves one edge comes back in from the opposite edge, so shots can be aimed off the board. A player can hit a piece by flicking away from it.
pros: Shots can be aimed off the board.
Rebounds are replaced by joins.
cons: Players find a new way to aim.
A shot can hit a rival's piece by mistake.

pairs.tendency: Players draw a map where the edges meet, so a place drawn at the right edge carries on at the left. A river runs off the paper and comes back.
pros: A river or road has no end.
The sheet has no edge.
cons: Drawings have to line up at the join.
Players at the edge have little room.

pairs.tendency: The secret is a square on the board, and questions such as is it on the left half treat the edges as joined, so left and right are neighbours. Players learn to ask in rings.
pros: The list shrinks in new ways.
Halves of the board work differently.
cons: Familiar questions give odd answers.
Players take time to learn the ring.

pairs.tendency: With joined edges the track has no end, so a finish line or a count of laps has to be set. Pieces race round and meet themselves.
pros: Racing can go on for laps.
A finish line is a choice.
cons: The race can feel endless.
A fast piece meets slow ones from behind.

pairs.tendency: Points come from squares held, and with no edge squares every square has the same number of neighbours. Scoring across the join counts as much as scoring in the middle.
pros: Every square is treated alike.
Scoring is even.
cons: A held square can be attacked from all sides.
Counting near the join takes care.

pairs.tendency: Pieces cannot flee to an edge because there are none, so chasers meet runners from behind. A player running east runs into the one who was behind them.
pros: There is no safe edge.
Knock-outs come from all sides.
cons: Players are cornered more often.
A runner is easily caught.

pairs.tendency: Threats arrive from all sides, and there is no safe edge to fall back to. The team has to watch the whole ring.
pros: Every player guards a stretch.
The team covers all sides.
cons: No side is safe.
The ring is hard to hold with few players.

pairs.tendency: The team aims to cover the board, and the join helps them connect the far sides. Two players at opposite edges meet in the middle of the seam.
pros: Far places link up.
Teammates meet at the join.
cons: Planning needs both edges.
The team may overlook the seam.

pairs.tendency: A player secretly heading for the far edge is really next door, so the goal is hidden in plain sight. Others think the piece is going away when it is coming round.
pros: A goal is hard to read.
A near goal looks far.
cons: Players misread each other.
A rival may find it by chance.

pairs.tendency: In a story where the traveller returns to the start place, the board ends where it began. The story ends at the place where it opened.
pros: The story closes in a ring.
The ending can echo the start.
cons: The route has no far end.
A story can circle without ending.

pairs.tendency: Pieces wander and loop, and nobody wins. Players stop and look at the paths that criss-cross the board.
pros: Paths form patterns.
The board has no corners.
cons: There is no pull to finish.
Some players ask what they are meant to do.

pairs.tendency: One player aims to reach the far edge, which is only a step away, and another aims to stay far from everyone, which can never be done. Goals sit oddly on a ring.
pros: Goals feel different on a ring.
Players test what far means.
cons: Some goals cannot be reached.
A goal may be met too soon.

pairs.tendency: In a chase round a loop, the last piece caught loses. Nobody can hide in a corner, so the chase never has a back wall.
pros: The chase goes round.
Players cannot hide.
cons: The last piece is hunted from both sides.
A chase can last a long time.

pairs.tendency: With no edge there is no natural end, so play can roll on from lap to lap. Players stop only when they agree to.
pros: Play can run on.
The board never limits the game.
cons: Nothing marks the end.
Players tire before the game stops.

pairs.tendency: A board with no end and no goal, where every move lands on a square already visited. Players walk and come back to where they started.
pros: Every path returns.
The game never ends.
cons: Players may feel stuck.
Moves lose their point.

pairs.tendency: A player alone lays out cards in a grid, and cards at the left edge can be built on from the right. A row can be finished across the seam.
pros: Cards link across the grid.
A stuck row can be freed.
cons: The layout is harder to read.
A mistake at the seam spoils both rows.

pairs.tendency: The board is reset after each short game, and the joined edges mean both sides start with the same view. Two wins out of three decides the series.
pros: The opening is even.
Each game starts fresh.
cons: Players repeat the same start.
A series can be won on one opening.

pairs.tendency: Pieces loop forever, so a player who wants to avoid points cannot run off an edge to escape. They keep moving round to stay clear.
pros: No piece can hide in a corner.
Escape means running.
cons: A runner tires out.
Points arrive from behind.

pairs.tendency: A piece that goes past the target comes round again and tries once more. The exact landing is still needed, but a miss costs a lap, not the game.
pros: A miss costs a lap.
A second try is built in.
cons: Laps take time.
A player can pass the target many times.

pairs.tendency: A piece that wants to be last cannot hide in a corner, so the player keeps moving round to stay behind. The slowest piece keeps changing places.
pros: No corner to hide in.
Staying behind takes effort.
cons: Moves go round in circles.
