Greedy players show themselves quickly.
cons: One bold choice can ruin a round.
Careful players can stall the game.

pairs.tendency: Holding a region adds points to your total, so players hold back and try to leave the regions to others. Standing off the map becomes a plan of its own.
pros: Players hold back instead of rushing in.
Neighbours get pushed into the costly regions.
cons: Someone is forced to take the last spots.
Nothing happens if everyone waits.

pairs.tendency: Some job spots add to your total and others do not. Workers go to the spots that give what they need without penalty, and players block the safe spots to leave rivals with the costly ones.
pros: Blocking a safe spot hurts a rival.
Each spot has a clear price.
cons: Late players take whatever is left.
Turn order carries a lot of weight.

pairs.tendency: Players build patterns that use every tile they take, because tiles left on your board at the end count against you.
pros: Tidy patterns matter.
Players plan which tiles to take.
cons: One awkward tile can add a heap of points.
Players may skip tiles they would like.

pairs.tendency: Cards still in hand at the end count as points, so every card played shrinks your total. Holding a high card for later is a risk that grows with each turn.
pros: Players empty their hands early.
Each play shrinks the pile of penalties.
cons: A player can be stuck with high cards at the end.
Waiting for a later moment can backfire.

pairs.tendency: Tricks carry points against you, so players play low cards and try to slip under the winning card. A player who is forced to win a trick takes the penalty.
pros: Playing low becomes a plan.
Leaders try to dump tricks on others.
cons: A hand of high cards is hard to get rid of.
One player can end up with most of the tricks.

pairs.tendency: Players bargain to hand penalty cards to someone else. Deals sound like "I take this one if you take that one", and a promise can be broken the next round.
pros: Talk becomes useful at once.
Players find out who dislikes which card.
cons: Trading can gang up on one person.
Deals slow the game down.

pairs.tendency: Matching sets wipe points off your total and loose cards add to it. Players hunt for sets so nothing is left over.
pros: Sets lower your score.
Players watch what others collect.
cons: Single odd cards stay costly.
Hoarding for a set can leave extra cards in hand.

pairs.tendency: Owning a road or a field adds points to your total, so players place tiles to stay out of scoring features. The map grows round the spaces nobody wants to claim.
pros: Placing a tile is a way to dodge.
Tiles become gifts for others.
cons: The map can grow into odd shapes.
Players run out of safe places to put a tile.

pairs.tendency: Each answer in the chain can carry a point against you, such as a repeated word or a stumble. The chain grows, and players try to keep their replies clean.
pros: Keeping the chain going takes care.
A slip is noted by everyone.
cons: A stumble marks you for the whole game.
Players slow down to avoid slips.

pairs.tendency: Cards laid in the wrong order give a point, and nobody may speak to warn the others. Mistakes are counted plainly at the end.
pros: Players watch each other's faces and hands.
Every slip shows in the count.
cons: Confusion spreads when two players play at once.
There is no way to explain a slip.

pairs.tendency: Players change rules to send points to someone else. A new rule such as "the player who plays last takes a point" changes who is losing at once.
pros: Rules turn into tools for dodging.
Players watch every rule change.
cons: Arguments start over which rule applies.
The scoring can become hard to follow.

pairs.tendency: Each scene can leave marks on your character, such as wounds or debts, and the player with the fewest marks at the end wins. Characters talk their way out of trouble and steer it towards others.
pros: Talking keeps a character's marks down.
Scenes carry a visible cost.
cons: Players may avoid any risky scene.
The story can stall.

pairs.tendency: Every knocked tower or dropped piece adds a point against you. Steady hands keep your total low.
pros: Slips are counted.
Players watch hands closely.
cons: Shaky hands add points quickly.
A tired player falls behind.

pairs.tendency: Every road, river or town you draw can cost a point, so players draw as little as they can. The map ends up sparse.
pros: Each mark becomes a decision.
Players draw few things.
cons: A sparse map gives little to explore.
Players may leave the drawing to others.

pairs.tendency: Everyone plays their own board and counts their own penalties. Nobody can touch another player's total, and the sheets are compared at the end.
pros: Players work quietly.
Results are easy to count.
cons: There is little to do with other players.
An early mistake cannot be repaired by anyone.

pairs.tendency: Cards push penalty points onto rivals, so a "take that" card hands someone three points. The player with the lowest total becomes the target.
pros: Leaders get attacked.
Players pick sides fast.
cons: It is hard to stay in front for long.
A gang-up can finish one player's game.

pairs.tendency: Players leave penalty squares and blocked paths for others to walk into. Nobody is hit directly, but a rival steps onto a costly square because the board leaves no other way.
pros: The board seems to do the pushing.
Players read the board closely.
cons: It is hard to see who caused a penalty.
The last player to place sees the whole layout.

pairs.tendency: The team shares one pile of penalty points and tries to keep it under a limit. Each player's mistake lands on everyone.
pros: Players share the penalty.
The group warns each other.
cons: One careless move costs the whole team.
A loud player can run the team.

pairs.tendency: The table shares a limit on penalty points, and each player also keeps a personal count. If the team stays under the limit, the player with the fewest wins.
pros: Helping and dodging mix together.
Players weigh their own score against the team's.
cons: A player can let the team take the blame.
Trust wears down over the game.

pairs.tendency: Each team adds up its members' penalty points and the lowest total wins. Teammates swap tips and cover each other's slow turns, though only one score counts.
pros: Teammates guard each other.
Teams count their points together.
cons: One careless player drags the team down.
Teams argue over who takes a penalty.

pairs.tendency: A hidden traitor feeds penalty points to chosen players, and the loyal players watch for whoever always seems to dodge them.
pros: Odd luck draws suspicion.
Players study who avoids points.
cons: Players blame whoever is unlucky.
Accusations can stop the game.

pairs.tendency: Moves go by post, and each letter carries a count of penalty points. By the time a reply arrives, the totals have moved on.
pros: Slow play gives time to count.
Letters leave a record of the points.
cons: A wrong count may travel for weeks.
Long waits make dropping out likely.

pairs.tendency: The empty seat collects the points nobody wants, and players aim their penalties at it. The absent player never gets a chance to answer.
pros: There is a place to dump points.
Players race to feed the seat.
cons: The absent player cannot answer back.
A seat that takes everything lowers the stakes.

pairs.tendency: The game master hands out penalties as events unfold, and the player with the fewest at the end wins. The master decides how costly each choice turns out.
pros: Events give penalties a story.
The master can make rulings fast.
cons: Players court favour with the game master.
A harsh ruling can sink one player.

pairs.tendency: In a street game, passers-by who join late start with no points while old players carry plenty. In a count where fewer is the aim, arriving late is an advantage.
pros: Newcomers begin clean.
Scores can be tallied on a chalk wall.
cons: Late arrivals get an easy start.
Counting is hard with people coming and going.

pairs.tendency: The lone player hands out penalty points to the group, and the group tries to keep theirs low while passing points back. The lone player wins if the group's points pile up.
pros: The lone player has one clear job.
The group shares warnings.
cons: The lone player faces many people at once.
The group can pile points on one member.

pairs.tendency: You turn over the pack alone and count the penalty cards that come up. Your total is then compared with your earlier tries or a friend's.
pros: The game is easy to repeat and compare.
Each try ends with a plain number.
cons: There is nobody else to argue with.
The draw sets the total.

pairs.tendency: Dice and draws hand out the penalties, so the lowest total goes to the luckiest player. The game is a short stretch of waiting and counting.
pros: Anyone can win.
Games are short.
cons: There is nothing to plan.
The winner could not have done much about it.

pairs.tendency: Dice add penalties, but a re-roll or a swap lets you shave them down. Players choose when to spend these soft landings.
pros: Players have some control over the dice.
Spending a re-roll is a decision.
cons: Re-rolls run out.
A string of high throws can still pile up points.

pairs.tendency: Skill decides most penalties, but a random draw now and then throws in an extra point. A careful player usually ends lowest, though not always.
pros: Careful play shows in the totals.
Luck keeps results open.
cons: A random card can undo a plan.
A lucky newcomer can beat an old hand.

pairs.tendency: No dice and no hidden cards, so every penalty comes from a choice. The players who see furthest ahead take the fewest points.
pros: Each penalty has a clear cause.
Learning pays off.
cons: Beginners hand over points all game.
Players think long before each move.

pairs.tendency: A throw is read as a sign, and a gloomy reading adds a point to your count. Players talk over what the sign means before the points go down.
pros: Throws spark talk.
Readings differ from person to person.
cons: Players argue about what a throw means.
Totals depend on who reads the sign.

pairs.tendency: Players try to act at the same moment, and every out-of-step move adds a point. After a few rounds the totals show who is in step.
pros: Players watch each other for signs.
Matching timing is rewarded.
cons: One restless player throws everyone off.
It is hard to say why a round went smoothly.

pairs.tendency: Each event on the table has a cost in points, and players tell the story of how their character got through it. The total grows as the road gets rougher.
pros: Rolls become story.
Totals follow events.
cons: A rough table entry can land on one player.
Players can lose track between story and counting.

pairs.tendency: Every penalty and every card is face up, so each player can work out who will end up with the points.
pros: Everyone sees the totals.
Players plan with all the facts.
cons: Moves can be predicted.
Players spend a long time working out every path.

pairs.tendency: Each hand holds some penalty cards and nobody knows whose hand is heavy. Players guess from what others play and what they avoid.
pros: Guessing who holds penalties is part of every turn.
A played card tells a little.
cons: A player can be stuck with penalties unknown to the rest.
Fear of the unknown can make the table stall.

pairs.tendency: A secret role may let a player quietly pass penalties along. Others watch for whoever keeps a low total in odd ways.
pros: Odd totals draw attention.
Roles change how players dodge.
cons: Suspicion lands on lucky players.
Players hold back to avoid looking odd.

pairs.tendency: Every dodge is a clue. Players work out who holds the high penalty cards from what other players avoid playing.
pros: Avoiding a card tells others something.
Players track the hidden cards.
cons: Careful dodging gives away a hand.
Players slow down to work things out.

pairs.tendency: Players claim they hold no penalty cards, or pretend they hold plenty. A call of "I'm clean" may be a lie, and a wrong call costs the caller a point.
pros: Claims need checking.
A calm face carries weight.
cons: A wrong call costs points.
Honest players get doubted.

pairs.tendency: One player knows a secret rule that adds points to anyone who breaks it. The others learn it by picking up points and being told no.
pros: Early penalties teach the rule.
The knowing player stays low.
cons: Newcomers start well behind.
Frustration builds for new players.

pairs.tendency: The one who knows the answer can only give hints, and a hint that misleads costs the guesser a point. Guessers try to read the hints and keep wrong guesses few.
pros: Hints get studied closely.
Wrong guesses are counted.
cons: A vague hint costs the guessers.
Guessers hold back from guessing.

pairs.tendency: Because tiles you turn over may hide penalty squares, exploring risks points. Players send others into the unknown squares first.
pros: Exploring carries a visible risk.
Players watch who steps first.
cons: Early steps are blind.
If nobody wants to explore, the game stalls.

pairs.tendency: The open hand shows which cards carry penalties, so everyone can plan around them. The player who also controls the open hand can steer the penalties.
pros: Everyone can read one hand.
Players plan around visible penalty cards.
cons: Whoever plays the open hand gets more control.
The others have little to guess.

pairs.tendency: Penalty points are kept private, so nobody knows who is lowest. Players guess from behaviour, and the final reveal can surprise the table.
pros: The ending reveals every total.
Players watch behaviour for hints.
cons: Players may play on blind.
A hidden lead is easy to lose track of.

pairs.tendency: Players take turns picking up or dodging penalties and wait while others take theirs. Each player can see the total of the person before them and change their move.
pros: Each turn can answer the last.
The game is easy to follow.
cons: There is waiting time between turns.
Players near the end know all the totals.

pairs.tendency: All players choose at once and then reveal. Players who chose the same item share the penalty, so each tries to pick something nobody else will.
pros: Players guess what others will pick.
Rounds are quick.
cons: Two players who match both take the points.
There is no time to correct a pick.

pairs.tendency: Anyone may act at any moment. The quickest player grabs the safe cards and leaves the penalties lying, so slow players find only penalties left.
pros: Quick hands get the safe cards.
The pace builds fast.
cons: Speed decides who takes the points.
Grabbing leads to disputes.

pairs.tendency: When the timer runs out, a penalty point is added. Players speed up to save points, and a rushed move can add more penalties.
pros: The clock adds its own penalty.
Decisions come quickly.
cons: Haste causes slips.
Slow thinkers fall behind.

pairs.tendency: One move each morning for weeks, with penalty points creeping up a little each day. Players can check totals daily and plan a long way ahead.
pros: There is time to think each day.
Small changes are easy to see.
cons: A missed day can add a penalty.
The wait for a result is long.

pairs.tendency: A forced pause before each move gives time to weigh every penalty. Players count carefully before they touch a piece.
pros: Pauses help counting.
Few moves are rushed.
cons: Games take a long time.
Impatient players drift off.

pairs.tendency: Penalty points rise with every round, so late ones weigh more than early ones. A lead built in the early rounds can be undone in the last.
pros: The last rounds decide the most.
The pace picks up.
cons: A late rush can wipe out early care.
Careful players can run out of time.

pairs.tendency: A lucky throw gives another go, and another go is another chance to pick up a point. Players try to land extra turns only when the next move is safe.
pros: Extra turns can be risky.
Players watch for chains of moves.
cons: A free turn can cost points.
A player cannot refuse one.

pairs.tendency: The first stage picks the cards and the second stage plays them, with penalties counted in the second. What you picked decides how many points you can avoid.
pros: Early picks matter later.
Players plan ahead.
cons: A wrong pick in stage one cannot be undone.
The first stage feels far from the scoring.

pairs.tendency: The board models something like traffic or rubbish, and each harm to the system adds points to the player who caused it. The player with the fewest has harmed it least.
pros: Harm to the system can be traced to a player.
Players see cause and effect.
cons: Slow harm is hard to score.
Players may try to hide their harm.

pairs.tendency: Each group has its own list of penalties, such as a farmer losing a crop. Players keep their own group's points low, even if another group suffers.
pros: Each group's losses look different.
Players see whose losses get counted.
cons: Groups push their losses onto others.
Totals are hard to compare across roles.

pairs.tendency: Taking from the common supply adds a point to your count, so players take as little as they can. If everyone holds back the supply is safe, and if one player takes plenty the others follow.
pros: Holding back protects the supply.
Players watch each other's takings.
cons: One heavy taker starts a rush.
Players may take too little for their own needs.

pairs.tendency: Penalties from an early move arrive several rounds later. A player with a low total in round three may watch it climb in round six.
pros: Totals change after a delay.
Players think about later rounds.
cons: Early leaders can mislead.
The cause of a penalty gets forgotten.

pairs.tendency: Players test a rule that hands out penalty points, then play on to see who picks up more. The totals show whether the rule hits one player harder.
pros: Totals show what a rule does.
A test round is short.
cons: A rule can hit one seat harder.
Players may disagree about changes.

pairs.tendency: After the game, the table looks at where each point came from. The player with the fewest explains how they dodged and the others ask about it.
pros: Each penalty gets a name.
Players share their dodges.
cons: Talk can single out the loser.
A long talk can follow a short game.

pairs.tendency: Penalty cards that are torn or marked stay that way, so the next game starts with the points still on the table. A mark on the board stays for later games.
pros: Penalties leave a mark.
The next game opens with those points in place.
cons: A player who lost early may stay behind in later games.
Nothing can be erased.

pairs.tendency: The rules charge for what the game wants players to avoid, such as waste. Players notice the point through what costs them.
pros: Players learn what the game counts against.
The score tells the message.
cons: Not everyone agrees with what it says.
Players who never look at the scores miss it.

pairs.tendency: The player with the most points pays a real forfeit, such as buying tea for the table. Players guard their totals closely because the cost is real.
pros: Players care about every point.
Even small totals matter.
cons: Friends can fall out over a forfeit.
Some players may refuse to play.

pairs.tendency: Each penalty point stands for something that matters, such as time wasted or harm done. Players learn to dodge the number and may forget what it stood for.
pros: A number stands for a value.
Players see what dodging looks like.
cons: Players treat the number as the goal.
What the number stood for drops out of sight.

pairs.tendency: Players practise a way of living in which harm to others adds points, such as a village that shares water. The winner is whoever harmed the least.
pros: Players feel what sharing costs.
The score keeps track of harm.
cons: Real life has no fixed score.
The rehearsal may not match what comes later.

pairs.tendency: The last stretch of the track needs an exact throw, so a piece one space from home keeps waiting until the right number shows. A roll that is too big wastes the turn or sends the piece back.
pros: Final turns hold everyone's attention.
A trailing player can catch up while a leader waits.
cons: A player can wait many turns for one number.
The last few spaces take longer than the rest.

pairs.tendency: Players pick cards with numbers until the total reaches the target exactly. A pick that goes past it ruins the hand, so people draft small numbers near the end.
pros: Each pick is a sum check.
Players watch rivals' totals to take the card they need.
cons: The card someone needs may never appear.
Late picks leave few options.

pairs.tendency: A player has to spend exactly the price of a lot, so a rival who bids one coin more takes it away. Bidders count their coins as carefully as their bids.
pros: Small bids matter.
Odd coins gain value.
cons: A player holding the wrong coins cannot bid properly.
Counting slows each auction.

pairs.tendency: Players keep adding to a running total. Landing exactly on the target banks it and going over loses it, so stopping at 19 when the target is 21 is a common worry.
pros: Each draw raises the question of stopping.
Players learn the chance of each number.
cons: Going over throws away the whole round.
Close players keep drawing together.

pairs.tendency: A region counts only if you hold exactly the number of pieces it asks for. Players trim their armies, since extra pieces are wasted.
pros: Players count pieces closely.
Extra units can go elsewhere.
cons: A surplus piece sits idle.
A player one piece over can be locked out.

pairs.tendency: A job spot takes exactly three workers, no more and no fewer. Players pool workers with each other or hold some back until the numbers fit.
pros: Workers get grouped to fit each spot.
Players time their moves to fill a spot.
cons: A spare worker has nothing to do.
A spot left short stays empty.

pairs.tendency: A pattern is complete only when it uses exactly the number of tiles it asks for. One tile too many spoils it, so the last piece gets chosen with care.
pros: Players count before each tile.
Players plan the size of each pattern.
cons: One extra tile can undo a nearly finished pattern.
Players keep spare tiles they cannot place.

pairs.tendency: Hitting the target needs the right cards in hand on the last turn, so players save exact change and refuse to spend it early.
pros: Exact change is held back.
Counting the hand becomes a habit.
cons: Hoarded cards slow early play.
One wrongly spent card breaks the plan.

pairs.tendency: A player wins exactly the number of tricks called, no more and no fewer. A spare trick counts against you, so players lose tricks on purpose once their number is reached.
pros: Players dodge tricks as well as win them.
Calls are checked at the end.
cons: A high card in hand can force an extra win.
Late tricks go to whoever has high cards left.

pairs.tendency: Players trade to reach the exact amount, such as swapping a three for a four. A rival who needs your spare will ask a high price.
pros: Spare pieces gain value.
Players find each other's needs.
cons: A player who needs one number gets squeezed.
Deals take up much of the time.

pairs.tendency: A set scores only at its exact size, so a fourth card in a set of three gets you nothing. Players avoid taking cards they cannot use.
pros: Players stop collecting at the right size.
Extra cards go to others.
cons: A surplus card sits in hand.
A set cannot be finished if the needed card is gone.

pairs.tendency: Roads and fields close up only when tile edges match exactly, and a gap of one tile leaves a feature open. Players hunt for the single tile that finishes a shape.
pros: Each draw is checked against the gap.
Waiting for a tile keeps eyes on the pile.
cons: The tile needed may never arrive.
Open shapes block the map.

pairs.tendency: Players count their words so the last reply lands on ten. One word too many breaks the chain and ends the exchange.
pros: Players count while they answer.
Short replies buy time.
cons: A counting slip ends the chain early.
Counting takes attention from the rhyme.

pairs.tendency: Cards add up to the target while nobody speaks. Each card changes the total, and a silent player can only show what they mean by when they play.
pros: Timing signals the number.
Players read each other's pauses.
cons: A card that overshoots cannot be explained.
Players disagree on what a pause meant.

pairs.tendency: A player changes the target number to one they can reach next turn, and others change it again. The finish line keeps moving.
pros: The target is up for argument.
Players keep checking totals.
cons: Nobody can plan far ahead.
Rule changes can trap a leader.

pairs.tendency: Your character needs to pay off a debt of exactly forty coins, so the player hunts for jobs that bring in just that. The game master tells you how close you are.
pros: A number gives the story a goal.
Players hunt for odd jobs.
cons: A windfall can ruin the plan.
The count may pull attention from the story.

pairs.tendency: A flick or throw has to land in a scoring spot of exactly the needed value. Hitting a high spot first forces a later aim at a smaller one.
pros: Players aim with a number in mind.
Soft throws gain value.
cons: A hard flick can overshoot the target.
Players waste turns fiddling for a tiny target.

pairs.tendency: Players draw exactly the number of regions, rivers or roads the sheet asks for. An extra line spoils the count, so drawing slows near the end.
pros: Players pace their drawing.
The count is easy to check.
cons: A stray mark spoils the count.
Players hold back from drawing a shape they want.

pairs.tendency: Everyone aims for the same target on their own sheet. Players glance at each other's counts, and the first to land exactly says so.
pros: All players share one goal number.
Progress is easy to see.
cons: A player who overshoots has no one to blame.
Nothing a rival does changes your count.

pairs.tendency: A player close to the target is hit by a card that adds or removes a point, which throws off the count. Rivals aim at whoever is nearly there.
pros: Leaders draw attacks.
A small hit can undo a lot.
cons: Players stuck at the threshold stay stuck.
Targets change often.

pairs.tendency: Blocks and walls leave only certain squares open, so landing on the final square gets harder. A player can crowd the last spaces and make others miss them.
pros: Board shape decides who can finish.
Players block without a fight.
cons: It is hard to tell who caused a miss.
Crowded final squares slow the game.

pairs.tendency: The team needs its combined total to hit the target exactly. Each player adds a number and everyone checks the sum before the next player goes.
pros: Players agree on every addition.
The sum is checked as a group.
cons: One wrong addition upsets the team.
Fast players take over the sums.

pairs.tendency: The table works towards an exact team total, but each player also has a personal number to land on. A move that helps the team can move you off your own number.
pros: Team and personal sums pull apart.
Players explain their sums.
cons: Players hide a personal number.
Helping the team can cost your target.

pairs.tendency: Two teams count towards the same exact target. A teammate can add or hold back to land the total, while the other side tries to push the number past it.
pros: Teammates share the counting.
One side can spoil the other's total.
cons: A teammate's wrong number costs the side.
Teams wait while the other side works out a move.

pairs.tendency: The traitor slips in a number a little too large to make the team overshoot. The loyal players re-add each total to catch the lie.
pros: Team members double-check each sum.
A small wrong number draws suspicion.
cons: Honest slips look like sabotage.
Re-adding slows the game.

pairs.tendency: Everyone checks their arithmetic before posting, because a number that overshoots cannot be taken back once it is in the letter. The total sits on paper for all to see.
pros: Letters leave a written total.
Players check sums slowly and carefully.
cons: A wrong sum takes weeks to repair.
Players lose track of whose total is whose.

pairs.tendency: The absent player's number sits on a card in the middle, and the table works to land on it exactly. Nobody can ask the absent player to change it.
pros: A fixed number sits on the table.
Players plan around it together.
cons: The absent player cannot adjust it.
The table can get stuck on a number nobody can make.

pairs.tendency: The game master sets the exact number a challenge needs, such as a roll of exactly twelve, and players pool their bonuses to hit the figure.
pros: The game master sets a clear mark.
Players team up to reach it.
cons: Missing by one happens often.
The game master may set numbers at odd values.

pairs.tendency: A street game with a target count of hops. Passers-by who join in count aloud and shout when somebody goes past the exact number.
pros: Onlookers count along.
Anyone can see a miss.
cons: Shouted advice can put off the player.
Crowds make counting mistakes.

pairs.tendency: The lone player needs an exact total to win, and the group tries to push it past that number. The group wins by making the single player overshoot.
pros: The group has a clear target to defeat.
The lone player counts carefully.
cons: The lone player faces many hands at once.
The group may overshoot by accident.

pairs.tendency: Alone with the pack, you draw cards and try to land on the exact number before the cards run out. Nobody else is counting, so a miscount is yours alone.
pros: A single number gives a clear aim.
You can start again fast.
cons: Nobody catches a slip.
The luck of the draw can block the number.

pairs.tendency: Dice decide the total, so landing on the exact number is mostly luck. Players wait their turn and hope the right number comes.
pros: Anyone can land on it.
Each throw has a chance of finishing.
cons: Waiting can last many turns.
There is nothing to plan around the number.

pairs.tendency: Dice give a number and a re-roll or a choice lets you adjust it. A player one short of the target spends a re-roll to try for the number they need.
pros: Re-rolls help at the finish.
Players save re-rolls for the end.
cons: Players can run out before they need one.
Re-rolls slow the ending.

pairs.tendency: Planning gets a piece close, so the last move needs only a small number, and a small dose of luck decides whether it comes. Careful steps get you near and luck takes you over the line.
pros: Planning does most of the work.
Luck leaves the ending open.
cons: A planned route can fail on one throw.
Players near the end wait on luck.

pairs.tendency: Every move is a chosen number, so a player can work out a sequence that arrives exactly on the target. Players count ahead and plan the final few moves with care.
pros: Planning ahead pays.
Counting is clear.
cons: Beginners overshoot.
Players spend long on small sums.

pairs.tendency: Players ask a question with a number in it, throw, and look for a total that fits. A throw that lands on it is read as an answer.
pros: A throw is taken seriously.
A match carries weight.
cons: Most throws match nothing.
Readers argue about near misses.

pairs.tendency: Players try to count up together to a number with no signals, each saying one number at the right moment. The group hits the exact total when each person senses the others.
pros: Players listen to each other.
A group total feels shared.
cons: Two people speaking at once breaks the count.
Quiet players may never join in.

pairs.tendency: A table says what happens, and one entry on it needs an exact roll, such as a seven. Players tell what happens when they land it, or when they miss.
pros: One number opens a part of the story.
Players tell stories about missing.
cons: A key scene waits on one number.
Players may skip scenes that need a rare roll.

pairs.tendency: All numbers sit face up, so each player can work out which moves reach the target. Rivals can see when you are one step away and block you.
pros: Everyone sees who is near.
Blocking is easy.
cons: A player who is near gets stopped every time.
Players spend a long time working out paths.

pairs.tendency: Each hand holds numbers nobody else sees. A player close to the target hides the card they need, and rivals guess the total from the cards played.
pros: Players guess at hidden totals.
A played card gives a hint.
cons: Players cannot tell who is near the target.
A needed number can sit stuck in a hand.

pairs.tendency: A secret role has its own target number. A player who lands on a number at an odd moment gives away their role.
pros: Reaching a target hints at a role.
Players watch each other's totals.
cons: Hitting your number exposes you.
Players may hold back to stay hidden.

pairs.tendency: Clues name numbers, and players work out which total is the target. Each guess that overshoots narrows the list.
pros: Overshoots teach as much as hits.
Players keep a note of guesses.
cons: Guessing can run on long.
One wrong clue sends everyone off.

pairs.tendency: A player claims to be on the target total without showing it. Others choose to believe or challenge, and the claim is checked against the real count.
pros: Claims get tested.
A steady voice helps a claim.
cons: A wrong challenge loses the round.
A true claim can be challenged.

pairs.tendency: One player knows the exact number that ends the game. The others learn it by overshooting and being told no, until they find the figure.
pros: Overshooting is a clue.
The knowing player watches rivals miss.
cons: Newcomers keep missing.
Finding the number takes many turns.

pairs.tendency: The knower can only hint at the target number with pictures or gestures. Guessers offer totals until one matches exactly.
pros: Hints turn into numbers.
Guesses are checked at once.
cons: A vague hint stretches the guessing.
Close guesses do not count.

pairs.tendency: The finish square stays hidden until a player reaches it, so the exact count is learned by walking. Players step carefully since the distance is unknown.
pros: Players explore with a count in mind.
Revealed squares help with counting.
cons: The first moves are guesses.
A player may pass the finish without knowing.

pairs.tendency: One hand of numbers lies face up, so everyone can see which totals it can make. Players use that open hand to plan or block the exact finish.
pros: Open numbers show what is reachable.
Planning gets easier.
cons: The player who also plays the open hand sees more.
Rivals know whom to block.

pairs.tendency: Each player's running total is private, so nobody knows who is near the target. A player announces they are done and the table checks.
pros: Nobody knows who is close.
A reveal ends the game at once.
cons: Players may overshoot without knowing.
Checking a claim takes time.

pairs.tendency: Each turn adds to your total in order, and the others watch you creep up on the target. A player can wait for the number they need while rivals wait for their turn.
pros: Each total is in view.
Each turn is a short sum.
cons: Waiting for a number takes turns.
Players near the end have long waits.

pairs.tendency: Everyone picks a number in secret and reveals together. A pick that matches the target scores, but a pick that matches another player's gets cancelled.
pros: Players guess at each other's picks.
Rounds go by fast.
cons: Many picks cancel.
Nobody can wait to see what others choose.

pairs.tendency: Anyone can add to the shared total at any moment, and whoever lands exactly on the target takes the round. A grab at the wrong time pushes the total over for everyone.
pros: Quick fingers matter.
Everyone watches the running total.
cons: A hasty add ruins the round for all.
Quick players crowd out slow ones.

pairs.tendency: A clock runs while the player works out the exact number. A rushed sum is likely to be wrong, and a sand timer running out forces a guess.
pros: The clock tests quick sums.
Players learn to count in chunks.
cons: Rushed sums miss by one.
Slow counters lose turns.

pairs.tendency: One move a day for weeks, with the total creeping towards the target. A player may sit one short for days, watching for the number.
pros: Players have time to plan the count.
Progress shows daily.
cons: Waiting a day for a number is long.
Missed days break plans.

pairs.tendency: A deliberate pause before each move gives time to count the distance to the target. A player can check the sum twice before committing.
pros: Counting gets a second check.
Fewer slips happen.
cons: A game with an exact finish drags.
Waiting players lose interest.

pairs.tendency: The steps get bigger each round, so the exact finish gets harder to hit as the game speeds up. A player who could land on a small step may be forced to jump over.
pros: Early small steps allow exact planning.
Late rounds are hard to land.
cons: Big steps skip over the target.
Players cannot slow down.

pairs.tendency: A bonus throw can finish a player who needs one number. It can also push them past, so a bonus near the target is not always welcome.
pros: A bonus can finish a game.
Close players watch for bonuses.
cons: A bonus near the target may push you over.
The bonus has to be taken.

pairs.tendency: In the first stage players pick pieces whose numbers add up to the target, and in the second stage they play them. A wrong sum in the first stage shows up later.
pros: Early sums are checked in later play.
Players plan across the stages.
cons: A wrong early pick shows late.
Pieces cannot be swapped after stage one.

pairs.tendency: The system has a limit, such as a well that holds exactly its capacity. Landing on it shows the system in balance, going over spills and going under runs dry.
pros: Balance becomes visible.
Players see over and under.
cons: Hitting it exactly is rare.
A small error shows a big effect.

pairs.tendency: Each group needs a share of an exact amount, such as a village water tank split between farmers and a shopkeeper. Everyone argues for their exact share.
pros: Players speak up for their group.
Players see who gets less.
cons: Splitting leaves remainders nobody wants.
Groups argue over small differences.

pairs.tendency: The common supply has exactly enough for the target, so the last person to take has to count what is left. A take that is too large empties the store.
pros: Every take is counted.
Players track the store.
cons: One big take empties it.
The last person bears the risk.

pairs.tendency: A move adds to the total a few rounds later, so players count forward to land on the target. They count what is already on its way.
pros: Players count moves not yet landed.
Planning looks forward.
cons: A forgotten delayed move overshoots.
Counting takes more notes.

pairs.tendency: Players test a rule such as "exact numbers only" and see how many rounds pass before anyone finishes. They compare the test with the usual rule.
pros: Tests show how long the rule takes.
Players compare both games.
cons: The test can drag on.
What changed is open to argument.

pairs.tendency: After the game, players talk about the throw that ended it and the near misses on the way. Each person tells how close they were.
pros: Near misses get told.
Players compare paths.
cons: Talk can dwell on the one missed throw.
Players may recall counts differently.

pairs.tendency: Once a total passes the target, the sheet carries the mark into later games. A torn card or a crossed-out number cannot be restored.
pros: Overshoots are remembered.
Later games start from marks.
cons: One slip stays on the sheet for every later game.
Players grow cautious.

pairs.tendency: Rules that reward only exact landings say that near enough is not enough. Players learn that lesson by missing by one.
pros: Players feel the message.
Misses make the point.
cons: Players may disagree with it.
A harsh rule can put off new players.

pairs.tendency: A real wager rides on landing exactly on the number, such as a promise to pay for lunch. Players take the last step with care.
pros: The last step is careful.
Each step is watched.
cons: Friends may argue over a miss by one.
A real stake changes who volunteers to play.

pairs.tendency: A point stands for a value such as time given to others, and the game wants an exact amount. Giving too much counts the same as giving too little.
pros: Players weigh giving against taking.
A number carries a meaning.
cons: Players may aim at the figure alone.
An overshoot gets read as a failure of care.

pairs.tendency: Players try a way of life with fixed quotas, such as a village where each family gets exactly its share of grain. They find out how it feels to count to the last handful.
pros: Players feel exact sharing.
Everyone counts together.
cons: Exact counts take effort.
Real life rarely comes out even.

pairs.tendency: The first piece to the end loses, so after each roll a player chooses to move slowly or send a piece backwards. A high roll becomes a problem to dodge.
pros: Every roll makes players think twice.
Leaders feel nervous.
cons: The dice can force a move nobody wants.
Players may stall at the start.

pairs.tendency: Each player picks the card they want to keep least and passes the rest, so the row fills with cards nobody wants.
pros: The picks follow a strange logic.
Players learn each other's dislikes.
cons: It is easy to forget which way to pick.
The last player takes what remains.

pairs.tendency: Bidders try to lose the auction, since the player who gets the lot loses points. Everyone bids low, and when all bid low someone is stuck with the lot.
pros: Bids sink.
Auctions run backwards.
cons: Nobody wants to take the lot.
Stalling is likely.

pairs.tendency: A player keeps going on purpose, since the one who busts first wins. Stopping early gains nothing, so the plan is to press on until the bust.
pros: Busting is the aim.
Rounds end quickly.
cons: Little is left to decide once a player presses on.
Players may fake a mistake.

pairs.tendency: Players give away regions to rivals, and the owner of the smallest territory wins. A map where nobody wants anything is a stand-off.
pros: Givers become suspected.
Players trade land away.
cons: A rival who refuses a gift can stall the game.
The map fills with rival pieces.

pairs.tendency: Players put workers on spots that give nothing, and rivals block those spots to force useful ones on them.
pros: Blocking forces rivals to take useful spots.
Useless spots fill up.
cons: Players run out of useless spots.
Rounds take long.

pairs.tendency: A finished pattern counts against you, so players build and stop short. Players leave every shape open on purpose.
pros: Players build and stop short.
Unfinished work shows.
cons: Tiles can still force a pattern to close.
It is hard to stop a pattern from closing.

pairs.tendency: Players hold cards back and play slowly, since whoever empties their hand first loses. Every card played is a step towards defeat.
pros: Holding cards pays.
Players weigh each play.
cons: Full hands slow the table.
Nobody wants to be first to play.

pairs.tendency: The player who wins the most tricks loses, so everyone plays low cards. A high card in hand is a hazard, and players try to slip under the winner.
pros: High cards are things to lose.
Players study who holds the high cards.
cons: Players with high cards cannot avoid winning tricks.
Tricks pile on the unlucky.

pairs.tendency: Players bargain to lose, offering gifts and pushing wins onto others. A deal such as "take my trick and I'll take your next one" shifts the loss around.
pros: Giving becomes a bargaining chip.
Players find who can take a loss.
cons: Deals can leave one player with all the wins.
Trust runs short.

pairs.tendency: Players pass cards that match and keep the odd ones, so nobody completes a set. The player with the fewest sets wins.
pros: Players pass and split sets.
Odd cards become useful.
cons: Collections can build by accident.
Players track which sets others hold.

pairs.tendency: Each player tries to leave the map broken, with roads that do not link and fields that do not close. Mismatches are the aim.
pros: Maps grow into messy shapes.
Players hunt for tiles that do not fit.
cons: The pile may supply tiles that fit.
Someone else can close a shape.

pairs.tendency: The player who answers correctly loses, so players give replies that break the chain. A reply that rhymes or fits is a mistake.
pros: Wrong answers take skill.
Players invent odd replies.
cons: Arguments start over what counts as wrong.
Chains fall apart quickly.

pairs.tendency: Players try to lay cards in the wrong order without speaking, so the one who keeps the order loses. Silence hides each player's plan.
pros: Nobody can explain a move.
Players study each other's timing.
cons: It is hard to tell a slip from a plan.
Rounds end in confusion.

pairs.tendency: A player changes the rules so that losing becomes easier to reach, and rivals change them again to push the loss onto someone else.
pros: Rule changes aim at the loss.
The loss shifts about.
cons: Nobody can tell who is ahead.
Rules pile up.

pairs.tendency: A character wants to be caught, or to give away a fortune, while other players play characters who try to stop them. The scenes turn on that odd wish.
pros: Strange goals drive scenes.
Characters act in odd ways.
cons: It is hard to say when a character has lost.
Other players may not understand the goal.

pairs.tendency: The player who drops the tower first wins. Skilled players have to fail on purpose, which takes skill too.
pros: Deliberate misses need control.
Watchers laugh.
cons: Players doubt that a miss was an accident.
Skilled players get no reward for skill.

pairs.tendency: Players draw so that their own region is the one that loses, with the smallest town and the shortest road. The map tilts towards the others.
pros: Players shrink their own corner.
Rivals get the bigger regions.
cons: Rivals fill the map with gifts.
A tiny map is hard to read.

pairs.tendency: Each player tries to be last on their own track while the others do the same. Nobody can push another, so the race is to be slowest.
pros: Each player runs a slow race.
Who came last is plain to see.
cons: No move reaches another player's track.
The game can end in a tie.

pairs.tendency: Players attack by forcing wins on rivals, such as handing over the card that scores. A "take that" card now means "take this win".
pros: Attacks look like gifts.
Rivals refuse gifts.
cons: Refusing may not be possible.
Players begin to doubt each gift.

pairs.tendency: Players shape the board so rivals cannot avoid winning, for instance by clearing the path to the finish. Nobody is attacked directly.
pros: Players help by shaping the board.
The board makes the attack.
cons: It is hard to see who cleared the path.
A cleared path can help anyone.

pairs.tendency: The team shares the aim of losing, and the game pushes back by making wins easy. Everyone speaks their plans aloud.
pros: Everyone shares the odd aim.
Plans are made aloud.
cons: Accidental wins spoil it.
Easy wins keep coming.

pairs.tendency: Players work to lose together, but each also wants to be the last to lose, so a private race runs inside the shared aim.
pros: A shared aim has a private twist.
Players watch their teammates.
cons: Teammates cannot be trusted fully.
It is hard to tell which aim a move serves.

pairs.tendency: Each team tries to lose first. Teammates feed wins to the other side, and the other side refuses them.
pros: Teams plan to give things away.
Refusals show.
cons: Teams may refuse in a loop.
It is hard to tell who is ahead.

pairs.tendency: The traitor plays to win while everyone else plays to lose. The loyal players watch for anyone who plays like a winner.
pros: A winning move gives away the traitor.
Players watch closely.
cons: A clumsy player looks like a traitor.
Players hold back from taking moves.

pairs.tendency: Players post moves that push the win onto others. A letter takes days, so a plan to lose is spread over weeks.
pros: There is time to plan each loss.
Letters record every move.
cons: A win can slip in by accident.
There are long gaps between moves.

pairs.tendency: The absent seat is set to win whatever happens, and the others try to lose to it. The empty seat collects every prize.
pros: A ghost takes all the prizes.
Players try to hand things to the seat.
cons: Nobody can reply.
The absent seat gets all the credit.

pairs.tendency: The game master hands out easy wins and the players try to refuse them. Each refusal makes the master offer a bigger one.
pros: Gifts from the master get examined.
The master reacts to refusals.
cons: The master may hand over wins players cannot decline.
The story can drift to nothing.

pairs.tendency: Passers-by join in and try to lose, for example by stepping on the chalk line on purpose. The crowd laughs when a player fails.
pros: Onlookers cheer a slip.
Anyone can join.
cons: It is hard to tell a real slip from a fake.
Younger players may not get the rule.

pairs.tendency: The lone player wants to lose and the group wants the same, so both sides push the win across the table.
pros: Giving becomes the main move.
The lone player gets many offers.
cons: A win may get stuck in the middle.
The group crowds the single player.

pairs.tendency: Alone against the pack, you try to let the deck beat you. With no opponent, a loss takes real effort because you know all the moves.
pros: You learn the game by losing it.
It is quick to repeat.
cons: It is hard to lose on purpose with no opponent.
Nobody sees what you did.

pairs.tendency: A player cannot aim at losing at all when dice decide who loses. The game ends when the dice say so.
pros: Everyone has the same chance to lose.
Players have no way to steer it.
cons: Playing to lose is just waiting.
The aim hardly matters.

pairs.tendency: Re-rolls help a player avoid winning, so the aim is to throw low and use the re-roll when the dice come up high.
pros: Players use re-rolls to dodge wins.
There is a choice about when to spend them.
cons: A re-roll can bring a higher number.
Re-rolls are limited.

pairs.tendency: Skill steers a player towards losing, and a lucky draw may save them from it. A skilled loser can still win by accident.
pros: Skill is needed to lose neatly.
Luck keeps the result open.
cons: An accidental win spoils a plan.
Players cannot be sure of the result.

pairs.tendency: With no dice to blame, a loss is entirely your own doing. Players need to know the game well to lose cleanly, since losing takes planning too.
pros: A loss shows careful thinking.
Spectators see the plan.
cons: Beginners cannot lose cleanly.
Players pretend to blunder.

pairs.tendency: The throw is read as a sign, and a reading of "give way" is what the player wants. Players ask for a sign that tells them to give up.
pros: A throw has a reading.
Players discuss it.
cons: Readings disagree.
A throw can read as the opposite.

pairs.tendency: Players try to act at different moments on purpose, so the group is out of step. The one who matches someone else's timing loses.
pros: Players try to be odd.
Being out of step is easy to see.
cons: It is hard to avoid matching by chance.
Players overthink their timing.

pairs.tendency: A table says what happens, and the player who wants to lose hopes for results like "you lose your horse". An unlucky entry becomes the one everyone wants.
pros: Unlucky entries become wanted.
Players tell the loss as a story.
cons: A lucky roll may turn up at the wrong time.
The story can feel stuck.

pairs.tendency: With all cards face up, every player sees how to lose and how to stop others from losing. Players block a rival's slow path to defeat.
pros: Everyone sees the way to lose.
Blocks are seen at once.
cons: It is hard to hide a plan to lose.
A leader in losing is easy to stop.

pairs.tendency: Players hide cards that would make them win and try to play the card that makes them lose. A rival has to guess whether a play is on purpose.
pros: A play may be a trick.
Hands hide intent.
cons: Guessing intent is hard.
Players cannot tell who is winning.

pairs.tendency: A secret role may want to win while everyone else wants to lose. A player who plays like a winner gives themselves away.
pros: Winning moves give away a role.
Players watch everyone.
cons: A real slip looks like a disguise.
Everyone holds back.

pairs.tendency: Players work out which cards would make the others win, then give those cards away. The clues point to a hidden answer that nobody wants to reach.
pros: Clues lead away from the answer.
Players track the hidden fact.
cons: Reaching the answer by accident ends the game.
Players avoid guessing.

pairs.tendency: Players claim to be far ahead so that a rival will take the lead. A calm "I'm winning" may hide the plan to lose.
pros: Claims push the lead onto others.
Keeping a straight face helps.
cons: Believers pick up the win.
Players stop believing true claims.

pairs.tendency: The secret rule sets what loses, and players find it by breaking it, so each early loss is a clue. The player who knows tries to keep from winning.
pros: Early failures are clues.
Rules appear by trial.
cons: The player who knows cannot help openly.
Newcomers lose and do not know why.

pairs.tendency: The one who knows gives hints that lead guessers away from the answer. Guessers try not to be right.
pros: Hints mislead on purpose.
Guessers read hints for traps.
cons: Guessers may stop trusting hints.
A right guess ends the round.

pairs.tendency: Players explore to find the spot where they lose, such as a trap square. The map shows the way to defeat only as it is uncovered.
pros: Exploring seeks the end.
Hidden squares add surprise.
cons: Players cannot aim at an unseen square.
Lost players wander.

pairs.tendency: Players see the open hand and plan who wins with it. The player who plays the open hand tries to lose with both hands.
pros: Open cards show who might win.
One player plays two hands.
cons: Playing two hands to lose is awkward.
Others can read the plan.

pairs.tendency: Scores are secret, so players cannot be sure who is losing. A player may think they are losing when they are really ahead.
pros: Nobody knows who is losing.
The reveal surprises.
cons: Players lose on purpose blind.
A hidden win slips through.

pairs.tendency: Players take turns passing a win along, each trying to hand it on. The game circles round with each player declining.
pros: Each turn answers the last.
Everyone can see where the win is.
cons: A loop of refusals can form.
Players sit out while others decline.

pairs.tendency: Everyone picks in secret and reveals together, and the player with the least-picked answer loses. So each player tries to pick something odd.
pros: Picks try to be odd.
Picking and revealing take little time.
cons: Odd picks may match by chance.
A pick cannot be changed after the reveal.

pairs.tendency: Nobody waits, so players race to fail first. The first to fail ends the round.
pros: Quick failing draws attention.
The pace is fast.
cons: Rounds end at once.
Slow players get stuck.

pairs.tendency: The clock helps those who want to lose, since running out of time costs the move. A player can stall until the timer ends.
pros: Stalling is a plan.
The timer becomes a tool.
cons: Waiting for the timer drags.
Others can lose without trying.

pairs.tendency: One move a day for weeks, with players trying to lose slowly. A player can skip a day to give a win away.
pros: Skipping becomes a move.
Days pass between moves.
cons: Players forget their moves.
The wait is long.

pairs.tendency: The pause before each move gives time to think how to lose without looking like it. Slow play suits a plan to lose quietly.
pros: Slow turns allow subtle losses.
Players watch pauses.
cons: It takes a long time to lose.
Impatient players hurry.

pairs.tendency: As the game speeds up, a player trying to lose finds the end rushing at them. A quick finish arrives before the plans are set.
pros: The ending comes fast.
Players plan early.
cons: There is less time to lose on purpose.
Accidental wins happen.

pairs.tendency: A bonus turn is a chore for a player who wants to lose, since another move may bring a win. Players try to avoid hits that give another go.
pros: A bonus becomes unwelcome.
Players dodge landing on rivals.
cons: A bonus cannot be refused.
Chains of moves hurt the plan.

pairs.tendency: In the first stage players pick what they will use, and the picks are made to lose in the second stage. A pick that looks clumsy may be the plan.
pros: Early picks set up the loss.
Plans span two stages.
cons: It is hard to tell a plan from a slip.
Stage two cannot repair stage one.

pairs.tendency: The system fails when players lose, such as a well running dry. Players trying to lose cause the failure the game warns about.
pros: Players see how a failure builds.
Loss shows cause and effect.
cons: Failure may come sooner than planned.
Players learn by breaking the model.

pairs.tendency: Each group tries to lose in its own way, a farmer by giving up land and a council by giving up a vote. Players see how each role can fail.
pros: Each group loses differently.
Each role's interests show.
cons: Roles clash over losses.
Results are hard to compare.

pairs.tendency: Players try to run the supply dry. Everyone takes as much as they can, and the group ends by losing the common stock.
pros: Taking too much shows the problem.
The supply empties fast.
cons: Nothing is left to play with.
Players copy each other's grabbing.

pairs.tendency: A move to lose takes effect rounds later, so the loss arrives after the player has moved on. A player has to remember what they set up.
pros: The loss arrives later.
Players plan the timing.
cons: A plan can be forgotten.
The ending may come as a surprise.

pairs.tendency: Players test a rule that rewards losing and play on to see what changes. The group acts differently once losing pays.
pros: Testing shows the effects.
A trial is quick.
cons: The rule may be gamed.
Players disagree on the result.

pairs.tendency: After the game, players talk about who tried to lose and how. Each person tells their plan and the others say whether they noticed it.
pros: Plans come out.
Surprises show.
cons: Telling the plans can take a while.
Players recall things differently.

pairs.tendency: A loss changes the game for every later round, with a torn card or a crossed-out space. Players think twice before losing for real.
pros: A loss leaves a mark.
Later rounds begin from the change.
cons: A torn card stays torn.
Players stop wanting to lose.

pairs.tendency: The rules reward giving up. A game that pays you to lose says something about what winning is.
pros: Winning loses its usual value.
Players think about it.
cons: Some players reject the point.
A player who forgets the aim misses the argument.

pairs.tendency: A real forfeit sits on winning, such as paying for tea. Players try to lose in order to keep their money.
pros: Players gain by losing.
Everyone feels the stake.
cons: Money can come between friends.
Losing on purpose can be called cheating.

pairs.tendency: Points stand for something that matters, and the winner is whoever gives the most away. The number rises as the player gives time or help to others.
pros: Giving away becomes a score.
Players see a value turn into a number.
cons: The score can become the point.
The giving itself is forgotten.

pairs.tendency: Players practise a way of life where giving up first counts as the move, such as a village that gives before it takes. They feel what it costs.
pros: Giving first is practised.
Players picture sharing.
cons: Life outside has no such count.
Players may feel it is only play.

pairs.tendency: The lone player's pawn runs the same track as the team's pawns, and everyone throws in turn. The team has several pawns in the race and the lone player has one.
pros: Each throw is easy to follow.
The team can talk over which pawn to move.
cons: A lucky throw can hand the lone player a lead from nowhere.
The team gets more throws in a round.

pairs.tendency: The team members pick cards one at a time and pass the rest on, agreeing between them who takes which. The lone player picks from a row of their own and has nobody to talk to.
pros: The team can plan its picks together.
The lone player never shares a card.
cons: The lone player has no one to pass cards to.
Team talk can slow the picking round.

pairs.tendency: The team pools its money to bid against the lone player for each prize. One purse faces several, so the team wins most bids unless its members argue over who pays.
pros: The team can combine its money.
The lone player bids without having to ask anyone.
cons: One big bid from the team can empty every purse.
The lone player is outbid on most prizes.

pairs.tendency: The lone player keeps drawing for more points while the team watches and calls out. If the draw turns, the whole pile of points goes and the team takes the round.
pros: The team sees every risk as it is taken.
A long run pays the lone player a lot.
cons: One unlucky draw wipes out a whole turn.
The calling out can rattle the lone player.

pairs.tendency: The lone player holds one or two spots on the map and the team spreads out over the rest. The team can close in along the borders, while the lone player picks one place to push through.
pros: The team covers many areas at once.
The lone player strikes one place at a time.
cons: Team members can get in each other's way.
The lone player can be pinned into a corner.

pairs.tendency: Workers go on to the job spots. The team has many workers and the lone player has few, so the team can fill the spots the lone player needs before their turn comes.
pros: The team can block a key spot.
The lone player has few choices to think about.
cons: The lone player may find every useful job taken.
The team has to agree who takes which spot.

pairs.tendency: The team builds one pattern between them and the lone player builds another alone. The team can pass tiles around, while the lone player works from a smaller pile.
pros: The team can split the work.
The lone player knows the whole plan.
cons: Team members can lay tiles that clash.
The lone player needs luck with the colours.

pairs.tendency: The lone player holds one big hand and each team member holds a small one. The team can trade hints about what to play, and the lone player decides alone what to keep back.
pros: The lone player has more cards to choose from.
The team can cover for each other.
cons: The team cannot say much without giving its plan away.
The lone player has nobody to ask.

pairs.tendency: The team plays several hands against one, and its members can save high cards for the trick where they will count. The lone player has to win tricks against all of them.
pros: The team can pass the lead along.
The lone player's hand stays private.
cons: The lone player faces several hands in every trick.
Team members can clash over who plays high.

pairs.tendency: The team agrees a joint offer before it speaks to the lone player, who has nobody to plan with. The lone player can try a private deal with one team member to split the others.
pros: The team can agree its offers in advance.
The lone player can split the team with side deals.
cons: Talking takes up a lot of the game.
The lone player is left out of the planning.

pairs.tendency: The team collects sets between them while the lone player collects alone. Team members can hand each other missing cards, but the lone player has to finish every set from their own pile.
pros: The team finishes sets sooner.
The lone player keeps every set they make.
cons: Two team members can chase the same set.
The lone player needs the right cards without any help.

pairs.tendency: All tiles go on one shared map. The team lays tiles to shut the lone player's roads in, and the lone player lays tiles to break out.
pros: The map shows who is boxed in.
The team can build a wall together.
cons: The lone player can be walled in early.
A team tile can open a road for the lone player by accident.

pairs.tendency: The lone player calls and the whole team answers, or the team calls and the lone player has to answer every voice. The lone player's voice is set against the whole team's.
pros: A chorus of answers is easy to hear.
The caller sets the rhythm.
cons: The lone player tires of answering many calls.
Team answers can drift apart.

pairs.tendency: The team plays without a word and reads each other from the cards they put down. The lone player plays too, and the team cannot warn each other about them.
pros: The team learns each other's habits.
The lone player cannot talk their way around anyone.
cons: The team cannot say what it is planning.
A silent team can misread one card and lose the round.

pairs.tendency: A rule changed on the lone player's turn lands on the whole team, and a rule changed by the team lands on one person. Each side writes rules to suit its own numbers.
pros: Rule changes touch everyone.
The team can vote on a change.
cons: The team's votes can overturn the lone player's rule.
The list of rules grows long to remember.

pairs.tendency: The lone player plays the dragon, the guard and the weather, and the team plays the group that meets them. The team meets each of them as a group, and the lone player speaks for everyone else in the world.
pros: Roles are plain from the start.
The team can act out scenes together.
cons: The lone player has to voice many parts.
Team scenes can leave the lone player waiting.

pairs.tendency: The lone player flicks or stacks alone while the team takes turns one by one. The team can hand the job to whoever has the steadiest hand, and the lone player does every attempt.
pros: The team can pick its steadiest hand.
The lone player's skill is used on every go.
cons: The lone player's hand tires.
Cheering from the team can put the lone player off.

pairs.tendency: The team draws the map together on one sheet and the lone player adds a corner of their own. Each side draws roads that the other has to live with.
pros: The map carries both sides' marks.
The team can split the drawing.
cons: The lone player can run out of room on the sheet.
Team drawings can crowd the lone player's corner.

pairs.tendency: The lone player races a whole team, and the first of the team to finish ends the game for all of them. The team has many runners and the lone player has one.
pros: The race is easy to follow.
A win pays the lone player more.
cons: The team has many chances to cross the line.
The lone player has to beat every runner.

pairs.tendency: Scores are counted at the end, the lone player's against the team's total or against its top scorer. Everyone has to agree which of the two counts before play starts.
pros: The final count is a clear line.
The lone player knows the target.
cons: Team members can fight over who scores.
Agreeing how to count can stall the start.

pairs.tendency: The team knocks the lone player out, or the lone player knocks the team out one by one. If the lone player falls the team has won, and if the whole team falls the lone player has won.
pros: Every knock-out is plain to see.
The team can guard members who are low on lives.
cons: The lone player is out in one go if caught.
Knocked-out team members sit and watch.

pairs.tendency: The team has to last against the lone player, who plays whatever is trying to wipe them out. The team wins by lasting, and the lone player wins by breaking through.
pros: The team shares each loss.
The lone player aims each attack at one group.
cons: Team members can drag each other down.
The lone player takes more risk on each move.

pairs.tendency: The whole team works on one goal while the lone player tries to stop it. Every team move pushes one marker forward, and the lone player's moves pull it back.
pros: Team progress sits on a single track.
The lone player has one clear thing to stop.
cons: One blocking move can set the team back a long way.
The team can argue over the order of moves.

pairs.tendency: Each team member holds a secret aim and the lone player holds one too. The team has to work together without showing its aims, while the lone player hides what they want.
pros: Everyone has a reason to keep quiet.
The lone player's goal can surprise the team.
cons: Team members can work against each other without knowing it.
The lone player's secret is easy to guess from their moves.

pairs.tendency: The lone player pushes the story one way and the team pulls it another, and the story ends when it reaches its last scene. The ending comes from who gets the final say.
pros: The story has two voices.
The team can add scenes together.
cons: The lone player's twist can be talked down by the team.
The ending depends on who speaks last.

pairs.tendency: Nobody wins, so the lone player and the team just play and see what happens. With no prize, the lone player's extra pay never comes up and the team has no reason to gang up.
pros: The lone player is not singled out.
The team can try things freely.
cons: The team can drift without a plan.
Play can stop without anyone saying why.

pairs.tendency: The lone player names their own aim and each team member names theirs. Team members on the same side can still aim at different things.
pros: Everyone has a reason of their own.
The lone player can aim higher or lower than the team.
cons: Team members may not agree on what winning means.
It is hard to tell when the game is over.

pairs.tendency: The game runs until one player loses, and the lone player is the obvious target for everyone else. The team can all aim at one person.
pros: The loser is easy to name.
The team can unite on one target.
cons: The lone player is under attack for the whole game.
Team members can turn on each other once the lone player is safe.

pairs.tendency: The lone player and the team pass the story back and forth, and the aim is to keep it alive. The lone player makes trouble so the team always has something to answer.
pros: Play can run over many sessions.
The lone player gives the team something to push against.
cons: With no ending, the lone player's extra pay never falls due.
Someone has to bring a session to a stop.

pairs.tendency: A lone player and a team push against each other in a game that nobody can win. The lone player's extra reward never arrives.
pros: Neither side can get past the limit.
The team can compare how far it gets.
cons: Facing the team alone earns nothing extra.
Players may stop caring whose turn it is.

pairs.tendency: Dice or draws settle the clash between the lone player and the team. The team has more throws, and each throw only brings luck.
pros: Anyone can win a round.
The lone player's win pays a lot.
cons: Teamwork changes little.
Nobody can plan a round.

pairs.tendency: The lone player and the team both throw dice, and both have re-rolls or cards to patch up a low throw. Neither side is stuck with its first throw.
pros: Each side can recover from a low roll.
The team can pool its re-rolls.
cons: The lone player holds all their re-rolls alone.
A re-roll spent early leaves none for later.

pairs.tendency: Choices decide most of the game between the lone player and the team, with a little luck mixed in. The lone player can outplay the team on a turn, and the dice can still change a round.
pros: Careful play pays off.
A little luck keeps rounds open.
cons: The team's decisions can run long.
A lucky roll can undo a plan.

pairs.tendency: With no dice, a lone player and a team of several heads look at the same position. The team can talk its moves over while the lone player thinks alone.
pros: The result follows the thinking.
The team can check each other's moves.
cons: Team talk can slow the turns.
The lone player cannot hope for luck.

pairs.tendency: The lone player and the team each throw and read the signs as messages. The team argues over what a throw means while the lone player decides alone.
pros: Throws start conversation.
The lone player reads at their own speed.
cons: Team readings can clash.
There is no clear way to settle which reading is right.

pairs.tendency: The team tries to act at the same moment with no signal, and the lone player tries to catch the beat. The team slowly falls into step, while the lone player has no partner to fall into step with.
pros: The team gets in step over time.
The lone player can break the team's rhythm.
cons: Nobody steadies the lone player's timing.
The team can lose step after a distraction.

pairs.tendency: A throw is looked up on a table. The lone player's throw says what the team meets, and the team's throws say how they get through it.
pros: The table gives each roll a meaning.
The story is made by both sides.
cons: Looking up results slows the turn.
Odd results may not suit the story.

pairs.tendency: Everything lies open on the table for the lone player and the team. The team can think aloud over what it sees, and the lone player sees all of the team's cards too.
pros: There are no secrets to dig out.
The team can plan out loud.
cons: The lone player cannot surprise the team.
The lone player sees the team's plans as they are made.

pairs.tendency: The lone player holds a hidden hand and so does each team member. The team can pass hints between them, and the lone player has nobody to trade hints with.
pros: Hints can pass among the team.
The lone player's hand stays secret.
cons: Team hints can give away too much.
The lone player guesses alone.

pairs.tendency: Roles are dealt face down, and nobody knows who is playing against the rest until they act. The others read each move to guess who it is.
pros: Everyone watches everyone.
The lone player starts with surprise.
cons: Wrong guesses cost the team.
Quiet players can get the blame.

pairs.tendency: The team follows clues together to work out what the lone player has hidden. The lone player knows the answer and watches the team close in.
pros: The team shares the clue hunt.
The lone player knows where the clues lead.
cons: Two team members can chase the same clue.
The lone player has to keep a straight face.

pairs.tendency: The lone player bluffs a whole team, whose members can compare notes before calling. The team asks if it was true and decides together whether to challenge.
pros: The team can compare what it saw.
The lone player's bluff pays more if it works.
cons: The lone player has to fool only the one who decides.
The team can call a bluff wrongly together.

pairs.tendency: The lone player knows a secret rule and the team finds it by breaking it. The team shares what it learns after each no.
pros: The team collects pieces of the rule.
The lone player holds the answer.
cons: The lone player has to say no again and again.
The team can chase wrong guesses together.

pairs.tendency: The lone player knows the answer and can only hint, while the team works it out. The team can throw guesses at the hints in a heap.
pros: Hints can take many forms.
The team guesses quickly together.
cons: The lone player watches wrong guesses go by.
Many guesses can drown the right one.

pairs.tendency: The map starts face down. The team spreads out to turn over areas, and the lone player turns over areas on their own.
pros: The team covers more ground.
Each reveal surprises everyone.
cons: The lone player explores unknown ground alone.
Two team members may turn over the same place.

pairs.tendency: The lone player plays the open hand along with their own, so they hold two hands against a team that cannot see their private cards. The team sees one of the lone player's hands in full.
pros: The lone player has two hands to use.
The team can read the open hand.
cons: The lone player has twice the cards to decide on.
The team has only the private hand to guess at.

pairs.tendency: Scores are kept secret from everyone. The team cannot tell if the lone player is ahead, and the lone player cannot add up the team's total.
pros: Nobody knows who is ahead.
The lone player can bluff about their score.
cons: The team can guess wrongly together.
Players may ease off or push without knowing why.

pairs.tendency: The lone player takes one turn for each team member's turn, or one long turn before the team's. The rest wait while one player goes.
pros: Everyone knows whose go it is.
The lone player's turn can be big.
cons: The team waits through the lone player's long turn.
The lone player has long gaps between goes.

pairs.tendency: Everyone picks in secret at the same moment, then all reveal. The lone player's single pick is set against a spread of team picks.
pros: Nobody waits.
One pick can surprise the whole team.
cons: Team picks can overlap.
Quick rounds hide who did what.

pairs.tendency: Anyone can act at any moment, and the team has more hands to grab with. The lone player can only be in one place.
pros: Many hands can act at once.
The lone player has to be quick.
cons: The team can overrun the lone player.
The lone player cannot keep up a fast pace for long.

pairs.tendency: Each turn runs on a clock, and the team can share its thinking between members. The lone player has the same clock and nobody to share it with.
pros: The clock keeps play moving.
The team can split the thinking.
cons: The lone player rushes alone.
Team members can run the clock out arguing.

pairs.tendency: The game runs over days, with the lone player making a move in the morning and the team answering by evening. The team can talk in between, and the lone player waits.
pros: There is time to think.
The team can chat between moves.
cons: The lone player waits alone.
Messages pile up between turns.

pairs.tendency: The game slows down on purpose, and the team uses each pause to whisper while the lone player sits through the same pause alone.
pros: Each move gets a slow look.
The team can talk during pauses.
cons: The quiet gives the lone player nobody to turn to.
A long game can end in a small result.

pairs.tendency: The pace picks up round by round. The lone player has to do everything alone as it quickens, while the team divides the jobs.
pros: The game ends in a rush.
The team can split its tasks.
cons: The lone player loses ground as the pace rises.
Late rounds leave no time to talk.

pairs.tendency: A lucky throw gives the lone player another go, while the team can chain extra goes across several members. A team on a run can take many goes in a row.
pros: A lucky streak is possible.
The team can pass extra turns around.
cons: A streak can run away from the others.
Others stand by while someone chains their goes.

pairs.tendency: In the first stage the lone player and the team choose how to set up. In the second they play it out against each other.
pros: The first stage sets up the second.
The team can plan its setup together.
cons: A slip in the first stage shows up much later.
There are two sets of rules to learn.

pairs.tendency: The board stands for a real system, such as a river running past a village. The lone player stands for one big user, like a factory, and the team stands for many small ones.
pros: Big and small users share one board.
The lone player can take a lot at once.
cons: The team shares what is left.
The model can get hard to read.

pairs.tendency: The lone player plays one big group, such as a landlord, and each team member plays a smaller one, such as a tenant. The two sides see the same problem from different places.
pros: Different views come up.
The lone player speaks for one view only.
cons: Team members have to find common ground.
The lone player can feel outnumbered.

pairs.tendency: Everyone draws from one pile, such as a village borehole. The lone player can drain it in a few turns, and the team can only protect it by agreeing to take less.
pros: A shortage becomes easy to see.
The team gets a shared reason to act.
