Players have to keep track of whose go it is.

pairs.tendency: When everyone moves at once, an extra turn means one player gets a second choice in the same round.
pros: A player gets two choices in one round.
The round is longer for them.
cons: The others sit through it.
The shared reveal stops being even.

pairs.tendency: With no turns at all, a rule that gives another go has nothing to attach to, since the quickest hands already get more moves.
pros: Quick hands move often anyway.
Nobody waits for a go.
cons: The rule gives no way to tell who is owed one.
Players may argue over who moved last.

pairs.tendency: A clock runs on each turn, and an extra turn gives a second clock. Two moves come under pressure.
pros: Two moves under a clock.
The extra turn adds a scramble.
cons: Mistakes can pile up.
Others wait for both clocks to finish.

pairs.tendency: In a game played over days, an extra turn means two moves on the same morning.
pros: A player moves again at once.
Waiting is cut short.
cons: Others wake to a changed board.
The slow rhythm of one move a day is broken.

pairs.tendency: The game slows down with a pause before each move, and an extra turn means another pause.
pros: Each go comes with its own breath.
A second turn is a second slow move.
cons: Others wait longer.
The pace stretches.

pairs.tendency: As the game speeds up, extra turns speed it more. A lucky player can finish a round in a rush.
pros: The game ends sooner.
Late rounds are crammed.
cons: Players cannot keep up with the changes.
A leader can race out of reach.

pairs.tendency: An extra turn in the first stage gives a player more to carry into the second, so one lucky go can shape the whole game.
pros: A first-stage run carries forward.
Stage rules can decide what a turn is worth.
cons: An early lucky turn can decide too much.
Players in the later stage feel the effects of early luck.

pairs.tendency: In a model of a real system, an extra turn means one actor changes it twice before the others respond.
pros: Changes can run ahead of the reaction.
It shows how fast one actor can act.
cons: The system may be damaged before others answer.
The balance of the system is hard to read.

pairs.tendency: A group that gets an extra turn can press its case twice. The others see how a second chance changes the table.
pros: One group's case gets a second move.
Unequal turns show unequal power.
cons: Other groups sit and wait.
The group with the extra turn may crowd out the rest.

pairs.tendency: An extra turn lets a player draw twice from the shared store before the others take their share.
pros: A player can take more in one round.
Others see the store drop fast.
cons: The store shrinks sooner.
Players may race to win extra turns.

pairs.tendency: An extra turn adds a move whose effect shows up later, so two actions can land in the same delay.
pros: Two actions can pay off together.
The delay is less of a wait.
cons: Cause and effect can blur.
Which of the two moves did what is unclear.

pairs.tendency: The table tries extra turns as a new rule and sees what changes.
pros: A new rule can be tested in play.
Lucky streaks show up quickly.
cons: The effect depends on the dice.
One test may not show what a rule does.

pairs.tendency: After a game with extra turns, the talk can start from the lucky runs. What did they change, and was it the dice or a choice?
pros: Lucky runs give the talk something to start with.
Players compare notes on what the extra turns changed.
cons: Hard to tell what was luck.
The talk may drift to who was lucky.

pairs.tendency: An extra turn gives a second change that cannot be undone, so a hasty move is doubled.
pros: Two permanent changes in one go.
The next game starts further along.
cons: A mistake is carried twice.
Others inherit the result.

pairs.tendency: Rules that give extra turns for some acts say that those acts matter. The game makes a point by what it rewards.
pros: The reward says something about the world.
Players can ask why the rule is there.
cons: Players may read the rule as a message.
The rule can seem to favour one kind of act.

pairs.tendency: An extra turn with real money or promises at stake makes a lucky run matter beyond the table.
pros: A lucky run counts for something.
The stakes make a repeat go count.
cons: A friend's lucky run can sting.
Others watch their own stake sit idle.

pairs.tendency: Extra turns give more chances to gather points that stand for something like kindness, so the points pile up fast.
pros: The count rises quickly.
A player can chase the number.
cons: The value behind the number may be forgotten.
A lucky run can look like virtue.

pairs.tendency: In a rehearsal, an extra turn lets one person try a way of living twice while the rest watch.
pros: A person can test an idea twice.
The rehearsal shows the idea in action.
cons: Others watch and do not join.
Lucky people get to rehearse more.

pairs.tendency: In the first stage players choose a path or a piece, and in the second they roll and race along it.
pros: Early choices shape the later race.
The dice have something to carry out.
cons: A choice made before the dice can be wasted.
The second stage can feel short after a long first.

pairs.tendency: Stage one is a draft of cards from a shared row, and stage two is played with what you took.
pros: Drafting gives the second stage its tools.
Each pick has a later use.
cons: A pick that looks fine can fail later.
Drafting takes a long time before play starts.

pairs.tendency: An auction opens the game, and what each player wins is used in the second stage.
pros: Bids decide what a player has to work with.
Money spent early shapes later play.
cons: A player who overspends starts the second stage short.
Auctions can take a long time.

pairs.tendency: A first stage builds up a stake and a second stage lets players risk it.
pros: Risks are taken with something earned.
The first stage gives the risk a size.
cons: A bust in the second stage wipes out the first.
Risk-takers and careful players may split.

pairs.tendency: Pieces go onto the map in the first stage, and the second stage is the fight over who holds what.
pros: Early setup decides the later fight.
A map with a plan behind it.
cons: Late arrivals find it already full.
The second stage can feel decided by the first.

pairs.tendency: Workers collect goods in the first stage, and the goods are spent in the second.
pros: The jobs and the spending are separate.
The first stage sets a budget.
cons: A wrong job in the first stage cannot be fixed.
Players wait for the second stage to find out if jobs paid.

pairs.tendency: The first stage collects pieces and the second lays them in patterns.
pros: Patterns grow from a pile gathered earlier.
The second stage is calm.
cons: A thin pile limits the patterns.
Gathering may feel like a chore.

pairs.tendency: Before the real play starts, a first stage fills the hand, and the second plays it out.
pros: Hands have time to be shaped.
Choices in the first stage affect the second.
cons: A mistake in the first stage sits in the hand.
A hand built for the wrong stage cannot be used.

pairs.tendency: Players state their aims in the first stage, and tricks are played to meet them in the second.
pros: Aims are set before playing.
Hands are fixed before the tricks begin.
cons: A wrong plan shows by the third trick.
A hand fixed in the first stage cannot be swapped once tricks begin.

pairs.tendency: The first stage is a round of talk and deals, and the second is play with what was agreed.
pros: Talk sets up what play will be.
Promises are tested when play starts.
cons: A broken deal can sour the second stage.
Long talks can wear on the table.

pairs.tendency: One stage gathers cards and a later stage turns them into sets for points.
pros: Gathering and scoring are separate jobs.
The second stage has a clear aim.
cons: A set missed in the first stage cannot be bought later.
Gathering can feel long.

pairs.tendency: The first stage lays out the map and the second stage uses it.
pros: The ground is laid before anyone moves on it.
Early tiles decide where play happens.
cons: A tile laid in the first stage may block a plan.
Players in the second stage inherit a map they did not choose.

pairs.tendency: The first stage sets the words or moves, and the second stage chains them in answers.
pros: The first call gives the chain a start.
The rules for answering are clear.
cons: A short first stage leaves little to answer.
Players may run out of things to say.

pairs.tendency: Talk and agreed signals fill the first stage, and the second stage goes silent.
pros: Players can agree on a code.
The silence has a reason.
cons: A code forgotten in the second stage cannot be asked about.
Players who talk a lot may find the silence hard.

pairs.tendency: The first stage fixes a rule set, and the second stage lets players change it.
pros: The rules to change are known.
Changes are made with a plan in mind.
cons: Changes in the second stage may break the first.
Players argue about which rules are open.

pairs.tendency: Characters are made in the first stage, and the scene is played in the second.
pros: Characters have time to form.
The scene has a shape.
cons: Making a character takes a long time before play.
A character who does not fit the scene feels awkward.

pairs.tendency: A tower or a set of targets goes up in the first stage, and the second stage knocks or tests it.
pros: Building and testing are two jobs.
Hands get a rest in between.
cons: A shaky first stage ends the second early.
The build may take longer than the test.

pairs.tendency: The land is drawn in the first stage and lived on in the second.
pros: The map exists before anyone walks it.
Players know the ground.
cons: A map drawn in a hurry limits the second stage.
Drawing may take longer than play.

pairs.tendency: The first stage picks a starting place and the second stage is the race.
pros: Early choices set the starting line.
The race is clear.
cons: A late start can be hard to recover from.
A chosen route might be too long.

pairs.tendency: Resources build up in the first stage, and the second stage counts points from them.
pros: Points depend on early gathering.
The score is not settled until the second stage.
cons: A thin first stage leaves little to count.
Points from the second stage can overturn the first.

pairs.tendency: A calm build comes first, then a fight in which players drop out.
pros: Players enter the fight with a plan.
The knock-outs have a start.
cons: A player with a thin start leaves early.
The first stage can seem a long wait before the fight.

pairs.tendency: Supplies are prepared in the first stage, and the danger is faced together in the second.
pros: Preparing makes the danger easier to take in.
The group has a shared plan.
cons: A shortage from the first stage hurts all.
Preparing may take too long.

pairs.tendency: Parts are gathered in the first stage and assembled towards a goal in the second.
pros: Everyone adds a piece.
The goal is built in steps.
cons: A missing piece shows up late.
Players may blame each other.

pairs.tendency: Secret aims are handed out in the first stage and played towards in the second.
pros: Aims are fixed before moves.
The second stage has a reason for each move.
cons: A secret aim cannot be changed once play starts.
A player who forgets the aim loses the thread.

pairs.tendency: The first stage sets the scene and the second plays to the end of the story.
pros: The beginning has time to settle.
The ending has something to answer.
cons: A long setup delays the story.
A story that changes in the second stage may leave the first unused.

pairs.tendency: The first stage builds something and the second stage looks at it. No winner is needed.
pros: The second stage is a time to look.
Building has a purpose.
cons: Nothing marks the end of the first stage.
Players may not know when to switch.

pairs.tendency: Each player picks a goal in the first stage and plays towards it in the second.
pros: Goals are chosen before play.
The second stage holds many aims.
cons: A goal may seem wrong once play starts.
Players cannot compare their results.

pairs.tendency: A build-up comes first, then a run towards one loser.
pros: Players have something to protect.
The second stage cuts it down.
cons: Players may spend the first stage dreading the second.
The loser is known only at the end.

pairs.tendency: A change of stage can keep the game going by giving it new rules when the first set wears out.
pros: A second stage renews play.
The game does not stop at its first end.
cons: A stage may be hard to leave.
Players who liked the first stage lose it.

pairs.tendency: In a game nobody can win, a change of stage tells players the rules have shifted again.
pros: Each stage shows a new side of the game.
The game refuses a winner in both stages.
cons: Stages do not lead to a finish.
Players may tire of changes with no end.

pairs.tendency: Each player goes through both stages alone, side by side with the others.
pros: Players share a pace but not a board.
Each stage is the same for all.
cons: Players cannot affect each other.
A player who falls behind in the first stage has no help.

pairs.tendency: Forces are prepared in the first stage, and in the second players hit each other.
pros: There is time to prepare before the clash.
The second stage has weight.
cons: A hit in the second stage can undo the first.
Players may feel the first stage was wasted.

pairs.tendency: In the first stage players shape the board, and in the second they feel what others built.
pros: The board holds the first stage's work.
Players see each other's effects.
cons: A block built early can stop a plan late.
Nothing can be changed in between.

pairs.tendency: The group plans together in the first stage and faces the game together in the second.
pros: Planning has a real use.
The group works as one.
cons: The plan may fail on contact.
Players may talk too long in the first stage.

pairs.tendency: Shared supplies are built up first, and then players pull for themselves.
pros: Cooperation comes first and rivalry after.
Private reasons are held back until the second stage.
cons: A group that trusted may be let down.
Players may sabotage in the second stage.

pairs.tendency: Teams prepare in the first stage and are set against each other in the second.
pros: Each team shapes its plan.
The clash has a build-up.
cons: A team with a thin first stage starts behind.
The first stage can be a long wait.

pairs.tendency: Everyone works together in the first stage, and in the second the traitor is named or acts.
pros: Trust is built before it is broken.
The second stage has a twist.
cons: The traitor's plans from the first stage are hard to see.
Players may stop trusting in the second.

pairs.tendency: In a game by post, one stage might take a month of setup and the next a month of play.
pros: Each stage has its own pace.
Waiting is part of the shape.
cons: Players may forget the first stage.
A long wait for a stage to start.

pairs.tendency: The absent player might be present in the first stage and gone in the second, or the other way round.
pros: The game has a past and a present.
The absent player's move is remembered.
cons: The rules for the absent player change.
Players may forget who is missing.

pairs.tendency: The game master runs the first stage as a setup and the second stage as an adventure.
pros: The world is prepared.
Players enter a place that already exists.
cons: The game master has more work in the first stage.
Players wait while the world is made.

pairs.tendency: A street game with stages lets passers-by join at the start of the second.
pros: Newcomers join at a clean point.
Stages give a game a start and a middle.
cons: A newcomer has missed the first stage.
Regulars have to explain.

pairs.tendency: A stage of dice rolls can set up a stage where choices count, or the other way round.
pros: Luck can set the board before choosing starts.
A game of luck can end on a stage of choice.
cons: A low roll in the first stage follows a player.
Choice in the second stage may not count for much.

pairs.tendency: The first stage rolls the dice and the second stage lets players soften the results.
pros: Luck is met by a plan.
Players can see what needs fixing.
cons: Softening a result can feel like repair.
Players may wait for the second stage to fix a roll.

pairs.tendency: The luck comes in the first stage, like a deal, and skill shows in the second.
pros: Players start with luck and then use skill.
Skill has a clear stage.
cons: A lucky start can matter more than skill.
A skilful player may be stuck with a thin deal.

pairs.tendency: Both stages are all choices, so a plan from the first is open to study in the second.
pros: Plans can be read.
Careful players get the most from the stages.
cons: Players who see more of the board win more.
A mistake in the first stage cannot be blamed on luck.

pairs.tendency: A throw is read as a sign in the first stage, and the second stage plays out what it says.
pros: The sign gives the play a start.
A player acts on a message.
cons: Players may argue over what the sign means.
A reading made early may fit badly later.

pairs.tendency: The first stage lets players get to know each other's timing, and the second tests it.
pros: There is time to get in tune.
The second stage shows what was learned.
cons: A stranger who joins late misses it.
Rushing the first stage spoils the second.

pairs.tendency: The first stage rolls up the world and the second stage tells what happens in it.
pros: A rolled world gives the story something to meet.
The tale starts from a surprise.
cons: A strange roll can leave the story with no way in.
The story may drift from the roll.

pairs.tendency: Both stages are open, so every player can see how the first stage sets up the second.
pros: Plans can be read from the first stage.
Nobody is surprised by a rule change.
cons: Nothing is hidden about a choice.
Players can be slow to choose because they see everything.

pairs.tendency: Hidden hands are dealt and built in the first stage, and played out in the second.
pros: A hand is known only to its holder.
The second stage is a reveal.
cons: A hand built for the wrong plan cannot be changed.
Players wait for the second stage to find out.

pairs.tendency: Secret roles are handed out in the first stage and played in the second.
pros: Roles are set before moves.
Players can start slowly.
cons: A role revealed early can wreck the second stage.
Players may spend the first stage guessing.

pairs.tendency: Clues are gathered in the first stage, and in the second players put them together.
pros: Clues can be gathered at leisure.
The second stage has an answer to find.
cons: Players may forget a clue from the first stage.
A missed clue cannot be gathered again.

pairs.tendency: A position to bluff from is built in the first stage, and the bluff comes in the second.
pros: The bluff has something behind it.
Rivals can see the position build.
cons: A bluff fails if the first stage showed too much.
A player who was honest in the first stage may be doubted.

pairs.tendency: A few rules are taught in the open in the first stage, and the second stage hides a rule to be found.
pros: Newcomers get a footing before the secret.
Discovery has a start.
cons: A player who missed the first stage is lost.
The hidden rule may clash with the known ones.

pairs.tendency: The one who knows learns the answer in the first stage and hints at it in the second.
pros: The answer is fixed before hints begin.
The hinting stage is clear.
cons: A hard answer is chosen with no chance to change it.
The hinter holds the secret through a long first stage.

pairs.tendency: Players explore in the first stage and use what they found in the second.
pros: Exploring has a use.
The map is known when it counts.
cons: Explorers who find little reach the second stage short.
Players wait to see what they have found.

pairs.tendency: A turn in the first stage might be a different kind of move from a turn in the second.
pros: Turns change meaning when the stage changes.
The order can be learned once.
cons: Players have to recall which stage they are in.
A long first stage can try patience.

pairs.tendency: Everyone chooses at once in the first stage, then takes turns in the second.
pros: A fast stage then a slow one.
Nobody waits at the start.
cons: Moving from one to the other can confuse.
Simultaneous choices may be forgotten by the time turns start.

pairs.tendency: There are no turns in the first stage, so anyone can grab, and the second stage may bring turns in.
pros: A rush then a calm.
Quick players get first pick.
cons: Slow players start behind.
Players may be unsure when the second stage starts.

pairs.tendency: A clock can run in the first stage and be taken off in the second, or the other way round.
pros: Fast thinking in one stage and slow in the other.
The change of pace is clear.
cons: A player who likes one pace is slowed in the other.
The untimed stage may seem to drag.

pairs.tendency: The first stage runs over days to set things up, and the second stage runs in a short sitting.
pros: The slow part leaves a mark.
The sitting has a shape.
cons: Players may lose track in the long stage.
A player who misses days falls behind.

pairs.tendency: A slow first stage with a pause before each move can lead to a quick second stage.
pros: The slow stage gives time to think.
The quick stage puts that thinking to use.
cons: Impatient players find the first stage long.
The second stage can feel rushed.

pairs.tendency: Each stage can run faster than the one before, so the end comes quickly.
pros: Pace rises with the stages.
The last stage is short.
cons: Players may not follow the later stages.
Early choices may count more than late ones.

pairs.tendency: The system is set up in the first stage and players act in it in the second.
pros: The system is known before action.
Moves in the second stage show how it works.
cons: A setup error spreads.
Players wait for the system to be built.

pairs.tendency: Groups and their needs are assigned in the first stage, and their dealings are played in the second.
pros: Each group's needs are clear before play.
The dealings have a reason.
cons: A group with thin needs has little to do.
Roles assigned late can feel arbitrary.

pairs.tendency: A shared store is filled in the first stage and drawn from in the second.
pros: The store is known.
Players plan from a clear amount.
cons: A small first stage leaves a short second.
Players may argue over how much is enough.

pairs.tendency: Choices are planted in the first stage whose effects show in the second.
pros: Early moves show up later.
The change of stage marks the delay.
cons: Cause and effect are separated by the stage.
Players may forget what they did.

pairs.tendency: The first stage plays normally and the second stage plays with a new rule, so a table can compare.
pros: The change is visible.
A rule is tested against a plain stage.
cons: Players are in a different frame the second time.
The first stage may colour how the new rule looks.

pairs.tendency: The talk after the game can be a stage of its own, with rules about who speaks and what is asked.
pros: The talk has a place.
Players leave with questions.
cons: Players may be tired by then.
The talk may be hurried.

pairs.tendency: What happens in the first stage leaves marks that the second stage has to use.
pros: Marks tell the story of the game.
The second stage starts from the first one's end.
cons: A mistake cannot be erased.
A new group cannot start fresh.

pairs.tendency: Stages change the rules, so a game can make one point in the first stage and a different one in the second.
pros: The game can argue two things.
Players see the change.
cons: The two points can pull apart.
The argument may be unclear.

pairs.tendency: A change of stage might make the stakes real in the second stage only.
pros: Players practise before the stakes.
The second stage matters.
cons: Players who join late face stakes without practice.
Friends can feel the shift.

pairs.tendency: Points that stand for something that matters are gathered in the first stage, and the second stage asks what they were for.
pros: Players can look at what they chased.
Points have a life and then a test.
cons: The gap between number and value shows.
Players may feel foolish for chasing points.

pairs.tendency: A new way of living is set up in the first stage and tried in the second.
pros: The new way is described before it is lived.
Players know what they are testing.
cons: A way that looks fine on paper may fail in the second stage.
The first stage can run long.

themes.line: The abstract theme gives the game no story or setting, just shapes, colours and moves, so the rules are the whole experience.
The historical theme sets the game in a real time and place from the past, so the moves can stand for real events.
The fantasy theme brings dragons, magic or quests, so the same moves can feel like an adventure.
The science-fiction theme sets the game in space or the future, so the same moves can feel like exploring or inventing.
The everyday-life theme uses places players already know, like a market or a school, so the rules are easier to picture.
The absurd theme makes the setting silly on purpose, so players can laugh at their own moves.
The educational theme ties the game to something to learn, so playing also teaches a fact or a skill.
The real-world-issue theme connects the game to a problem people face today, so the moves can start a conversation.
The poetic theme makes the game short and a little strange, so the moves ask players to notice something rather than to win it.
The ritual-or-sacred theme turns the board into a path towards something holy, so each move can feel like a step in a practice.
The mortality-and-loss theme ties the game to time running out or someone being lost, so the moves can carry weight beyond the table.
The war-and-conquest theme sets the game among armies and borders, so the moves can stand for taking and holding ground.
